note: The Pattern Decoder's own data, copied verbatim out of content/prose/_raw/playbook.html. Regenerate with design/extract-playbook-data.py --apply. Nothing here is summarised or reworded.

compendium.name: Gaslighting
compendium.what: Repeatedly denying what someone saw, heard or remembers until they stop trusting their own account of events.
compendium.why: When you can't rely on your own memory, you lose the ability to say what happened, notice a pattern, or ask for change. Naming the pattern accurately, without overclaiming, usually helps more than either ignoring it or assuming the worst.
compendium.healthy: "I remember it differently — can we compare notes on what happened?"
sounds: That never happened.
You're imagining things again.
I never said that. You're making it up.
You're remembering it all wrong.
You know how you get. You always twist things.
Everyone else agrees with me. You're the only one who sees it that way.
I'm worried about you. You've been so confused lately.
nots: Two people recalling a long-ago conversation differently, and both willing to check a text or ask someone else.
A single correction of a small detail, such as which night a dinner was or who said what at a party.
Someone saying 'I see it differently' about how an event felt, which is a difference of view and not a denial of the facts.
Plain forgetting. Memory fades and merges events, and an honest 'I don't remember that' is not an attack on yours.
Disagreeing with your explanation of why something happened while accepting that it did happen.

compendium.name: Countering
compendium.what: Flatly contradicting someone's account of an event, again and again, so that no shared version of what happened can ever be settled.
compendium.why: Constant contradiction makes shared reality impossible to establish. If every account you give is overruled on the spot, you lose the ability to settle even small facts, and the problem you meant to raise never gets heard.
compendium.healthy: "My memory of that is different. Let's check the messages."
sounds: "That's not what happened."
"You're remembering it wrong."
"That's not what happened and you know it."
"That's not how it happened at all."
"You're twisting my words."
"You're putting words in my mouth."
"No. I didn't say that. Stop making things up."
nots: A real factual dispute where the person truly believes their version and will look at a text or ask a witness to settle it.
Someone saying 'that's not how I experienced it', which speaks about their own view and does not overrule yours.
A correction of a small detail, such as the day of the week, that is dropped once the calendar is checked.
Honest confusion between two similar events, such as last month's argument and this month's.
Pushback on an exaggeration, like 'you always do this', when the person is objecting to the word 'always' and not to the event.

compendium.name: Selective Memory
compendium.what: Claiming not to remember what was said or agreed, but only when the forgotten item would cost the person something to remember.
compendium.why: Agreements only work if both people carry them. When one side's memory conveniently fails, the other ends up holding every promise alone, re-asking, re-proving and eventually giving up on getting things done.
compendium.healthy: "I honestly don't remember — can you remind me what I said?"
sounds: "I never said that."
"You must be confusing me with someone else."
"I have no memory of saying that."
"Hmm, I don't remember agreeing to that."
"That was a long time ago, how would I know?"
"Did we actually say Friday? I don't think so."
"I told you I'd think about it, I never said yes."
nots: Ordinary forgetting. Busy, stressed, sleep-deprived people lose track of things and are embarrassed when they remember.
Memory problems linked to health, medication, grief or age, which may reach every topic, not just the costly ones.
A truly ambiguous exchange, such as a casual 'maybe we should', that each person heard differently.
A person who forgot the plan and then took responsibility as soon as you reminded them.
Someone who has forgotten because the promise was made in a conversation they were not really present for, such as while distracted.

compendium.name: Moving Goalposts
compendium.what: Changing what counts as success after you have met the standard that was set, so that you can never quite finish.
compendium.why: When success keeps moving, effort stops buying anything. You can work harder for months and still be told it is not enough, which wears down confidence and makes you chase approval you cannot earn.
compendium.healthy: "You did what I asked. I realize I now also need X — that's new, and I own that."
sounds: "That's still not good enough."
"Now do it properly this time."
"That doesn't count."
"You should have done more."
"That was the bare minimum."
"Now do it again."
"I never said that would be enough."
nots: A real change in the requirements, with an explanation of what changed, such as a client who revised the brief.
Feedback that raises the quality bar once, with clear criteria, so that you know when the work will be accepted.
A reasonable ask for more once you have shown you can do the basic version, for instance a manager giving harder tasks as you grow.
Honest disagreement about what 'done' meant, where a written brief would have prevented the confusion.
Your own perfectionism, where nobody else has moved anything but you keep raising the line yourself.

compendium.name: Thought-Stopping Clichés
compendium.what: Stock phrases, said in a closing tone, that end a conversation about a problem before anything in it has been examined.
compendium.why: A concern that is shut down by a slogan does not go away; it goes underground. You may start to feel that wanting an answer is itself the fault, and stop raising things that need attention.
compendium.healthy: "I don't have an answer, but your question is fair."
sounds: "It is what it is, drop it."
"Everything happens for a reason, stop dwelling."
"Don't overthink it."
"Just let it go already."
"You're blowing this out of proportion."
"Just stay positive."
"We don't talk about that."
nots: Comfort offered in grief, where the speaker sits with you and the saying is one small part of the support.
Sensible advice to let go of something that is truly over and cannot be changed, offered kindly and with room to talk.
A friend's clumsy attempt to cheer you up that stops when you say 'I'd rather talk about it'.
A cultural or religious phrase that is a normal part of how a person speaks, with no intent to end your question.
A tired person saying 'let's drop it for tonight' who agrees to return to the topic tomorrow.

compendium.name: Normalization
compendium.what: Presenting harmful or hurtful treatment as ordinary, expected and not worth questioning, so that objecting to it seems like the problem.
compendium.why: If harmful treatment is called normal, you lose the language to describe it. People can put up with something painful for years because they had been taught that it was simply what relationships, work or family life were like.
compendium.healthy: "This is how I've always done it, but that doesn't make it right — let's look at it."
sounds: "Every couple fights like this."
"This is just how families are."
"That's just how it is."
"Everyone does it."
"All men are like this."
"This is just normal, so stop."
"I went through the same thing, and I turned out fine."
nots: A real, accurate comparison, such as a friend who says that many new parents argue about chores, and who still listens to the details.
A genuine cultural or family norm that is shared by everyone involved and comfortable for them, even though it differs from yours.
Reassurance from an older person who has been through something similar and says so to comfort you, not to close the topic.
Realism about a job that is hard in known ways, such as long hours in a busy kitchen, when pay and terms were agreed beforehand.
A person's own habit of treating a hurt as normal because they were raised that way, with no one else pushing it.

compendium.name: Guilt-Tripping
compendium.what: Using guilt about past help, sacrifice or hurt feelings to make saying no feel like a moral failing.
compendium.why: Guilt that is attached to ordinary refusals makes your own limits feel wrong. Over time you may agree to things you do not want to avoid the sting, and stop being able to tell real obligations from pressure.
compendium.healthy: "I'm disappointed, and I also know it's your decision to make."
sounds: After everything I've done for you.
I never ask you for anything.
I sacrificed everything for you kids.
I guess I just don't matter to you any more.
If you really cared about me, you would.
How could you do this to me?
You owe me.
No, it's fine. Don't worry about me. I'll manage on my own.
nots: Honest disappointment said once, with the decision left to you: 'I'm sad you can't come, and I understand.'
Real reciprocity in a long relationship, where each of you has given and received and both feel it.
Telling someone how their choice affected you, once, as information and not a lever.
A person who feels guilty easily on their own, with nobody applying pressure.
Cultural norms of family duty that are mutual, openly discussed and open to negotiation.
A direct request for the favor to be returned that accepts a 'no' without a penalty.

compendium.name: Emotional Blackmail
compendium.what: Making love, closeness or the relationship itself depend on doing what someone wants, so that saying no feels like risking the bond.
compendium.why: When affection is held hostage, a choice made under threat is no longer a free one. You may give in to keep the bond, then lose track of what you wanted, and learn to scan for the other person's mood before you speak.
compendium.healthy: "This matters a lot to me. Can we find something that works for both of us?"
sounds: If you really loved me, you'd stay.
Leave, and everyone will know what you did.
Do it, or don't bother coming back.
I could love you so much more if you'd just lose the attitude.
Be sweet like before and we'll be fine.
Prove you love me by dropping that friend.
When you do it my way, we're great. Why can't it always be like that?
You'll be sorry if you go through with this.
nots: A real boundary: 'I can't stay in a relationship where lying keeps happening' states what the speaker will do, not a price for your compliance.
Honest hurt about a decision, said once and leaving the choice with you: 'I'm sad about this, and it's your call.'
A heated line said in the middle of a fight and taken back soon after, with warmth continuing.
A parent enforcing a rule and still showing the child affection.
A person asking for time apart after being hurt, who says so and comes back whether or not you give in.
A reasonable expectation such as honesty, where stepping back is protection and not a bargain.

compendium.name: Self-Harm Threats as Leverage
compendium.what: Saying one will hurt or kill oneself if the other person leaves or refuses, which ties their decision to the speaker's survival.
compendium.why: Hearing that your decision could cost a life is one of the heaviest things a person can carry. Many people stop making ordinary choices, like ending an evening or taking a trip, because the stakes feel too high, while the underlying distress goes unaddressed.
compendium.healthy: "I'm in a bad place and I need support — I'll reach out to someone who can help."
sounds: If you walk out that door tonight, I don't know what I'll do to myself.
I'll end it. Then you'll be free of me.
You're the only reason I'm still here, so if you go, that's it.
Go ahead and sleep at your sister's. You'll find out in the morning.
I swear I'll do it this time.
I'm not safe right now, and it's because of you.
Answer me in five minutes or you'll have my death on your hands.
nots: A person in real crisis who says they are thinking of suicide, with no link to anything you are doing. That calls for care, not analysis.
Telling a friend or counselor 'I've been having dark thoughts' in order to get help, with no demand attached.
A safety plan made with a therapist, where the person texts you a code word when they are struggling.
Flat exhaustion after a loss, such as 'I can't do this any more', that signals depletion and not a plan.
A statement of hopelessness made on a day when you were not leaving or refusing anything.
Someone overwhelmed at a breakup who blurts out the biggest words they have because they cannot find another way to say how bad it is.

compendium.name: Pity Plays
compendium.what: Answering a concern with displays of helplessness or victimhood, so the person who raised it ends up offering comfort and the concern is dropped.
compendium.why: When every concern ends in reassurance, the problem stays where it was and your need to be heard shrinks. Over time you may stop raising things at all, which makes the relationship quieter but no more honest.
compendium.healthy: "I feel awful about this, and that's mine to sit with. You were right to raise it."
sounds: Fine, I'm just a terrible friend. Everyone's better off without me.
You'd abandon me too, like everyone else.
I can't do anything right, can I.
After the week I've had, this is what you bring up?
I'm always the bad guy, aren't I.
Look at me, I'm shaking. Are you happy now?
Never mind. I'll stop talking about anything.
nots: Depression or low self-worth speaking, which shows up outside conflict too and calls for care.
Someone overwhelmed by shame who cries and goes quiet, then comes back the next day and talks it through.
A grieving or exhausted person who truly cannot have the conversation tonight and says so plainly.
A person who says 'that hurts to hear' and then listens to the rest.
A family style of speaking in strong emotional terms about everything, not only when challenged.
A request for comfort in a moment unrelated to anything you asked of them.

compendium.name: Martyrdom Display
compendium.what: Pointing out one's own unrewarded effort and sacrifice in a way that leaves the other person feeling indebted and unable to say no.
compendium.why: A debt you never agreed to is hard to pay, because the total keeps changing. You may give more time or help than you wanted and then resent it, while the real need for support never gets spoken.
compendium.healthy: "I'm overloaded and I need help — can you take X?"
sounds: Don't mind me, I'll sit here alone.
I guess I'll just do it myself like always.
I gave up my whole twenties for this family, but sure, go.
No, no, go and enjoy yourself. I'll be fine with the dishes.
I haven't sat down since six this morning. Not that anyone noticed.
I'd never ask you for anything.
Twelve hours on my feet, and I'm not complaining.
nots: Honest tiredness said once, such as 'I'm worn out tonight', that asks you to do nothing.
Someone who truly carries an unfair load and is clumsily trying to say so. They may need a better way to ask, not a label.
A direct request: 'I'm overloaded. Could you do the school run on Thursdays?'
A caregiver describing the facts of their week to a friend who asked.
A person who gives generously and does not mention it or expect a return.
A team meeting where everyone lists what they have finished.

compendium.name: Duty Scripts
compendium.what: Using a role such as daughter, son or parent as an unarguable rule for what one must do, so refusing sounds like failing at the role.
compendium.why: When 'what a good daughter does' replaces 'what do you think', your own judgment about your life is outranked by a rule you did not write. People can lose track of what they want, and the relationship starts to feel like a test they can fail.
compendium.healthy: "I'd love your help with this — no pressure if you can't."
sounds: A good daughter would never say that.
Family comes first. You owe us this.
I didn't raise you to talk back to your father.
It's your duty as the eldest.
You're a mother now. Your own plans don't count.
Because I am your mother, that's why.
A real friend would have been there.
Who's going to look after her if not you?
nots: A family or cultural value stated as one consideration, with room to say 'I see it differently' and still be loved.
An honest 'we are counting on you for Sunday', which names a need and accepts a no.
A relative sharing what duty meant to their own generation without requiring the same of you.
Obligations you chose, such as caring for your child or keeping a promise, where the duty is plain and shared.
Religious or community teaching about duty given in a sermon or lesson, not aimed at a particular decision.
A parent setting house rules for a young child.

compendium.name: Demand for Gratitude
compendium.what: Expecting thanks on demand, in the right words or amount, as the price of help given, so that generosity ends up with conditions attached.
compendium.why: When thanks is required, help stops being a gift and starts to feel like a loan with interest. People can start to avoid accepting help, even when they need it, or hide small wins so nobody feels unappreciated.
compendium.healthy: "It stung a little that the effort went unmentioned — a thank-you means a lot to me."
sounds: A thank-you would be nice for once.
After everything I did to get you that job, not even a card?
I'm still waiting to hear thank you.
You said thanks, but you didn't sound like you meant it.
Other people would be on their knees thanking me.
I don't ask for much. Just a little appreciation.
Did you thank her properly? Look how much she's done for you.
nots: Hurt feelings that help went unmentioned, said once and kindly: 'It would mean a lot to hear that it helped.'
Teaching a child to say please and thank you, a normal part of manners.
A charity or club that thanks donors publicly, with the acknowledgement agreed in advance.
Close friends who say thanks for small things as a habit both of them enjoy.
A person who gave a great deal, is worn thin and wants to be seen, which is different from wanting to be repaid.
A workplace that recognizes effort in a review.

compendium.name: Favor Debt
compendium.what: Citing past gifts, money or support as the reason someone must agree to a present request, so past kindness is treated like a signed contract.
compendium.why: A debt you never agreed to has no settlement date, so you can be asked to pay it over and over. People may stay in jobs, relationships or cities they would have left, or hand over money they cannot spare, because refusing feels like taking from someone who helped.
compendium.healthy: "I've supported you a lot and I'm asking for support back — as a request, not a bill."
sounds: Remember who paid for your school.
You owe me after everything.
Everything you have is because of me.
I put a roof over your head when nobody else would.
Who do you think got you that interview?
I covered your rent for a year. The least you can do is cover for me.
After what I spent on your wedding, you can host us.
nots: A friend saying 'I lent you money in March, can we talk about when you might pay it back?', which is an openly agreed loan.
Mutual support in a long relationship mentioned honestly: 'We have always helped each other.'
A request for help after helping, offered as a request that accepts a no.
A written agreement to repay, such as a mortgage or family loan, and a reminder of its terms.
A parent saying once, while sad, what they gave up for a child, with no demand attached.
Proper credit within a team for work that helped you.

compendium.name: Catastrophizing as Control
compendium.what: Predicting that someone will fall into ruin, loneliness or disaster if they act independently, so that leaving or choosing differently begins to feel unsafe.
compendium.why: Fear of the future can keep a person in place more firmly than any rule. When every independent step is described as the start of ruin, you may stop trying, stay where you are, and lose confidence that you could cope.
compendium.healthy: "I worry about how you'd manage — but that's my anxiety, and it's your life."
sounds: If you take that job, this family falls apart.
You'll end up alone and broke without me.
No one else will put up with you the way I do.
You can't survive out there. You've never even paid a bill.
You'll lose the kids, the house, everything, and then who will take you in?
Everyone who tried that ended up on the street.
You won't last a month in that city.
nots: Worry named as one's own: 'I'm anxious about the move, and I know it's your decision.'
An accurate warning about a real risk, such as a lease with penalties, with figures you can check.
A friend or relative asking hard questions about a plan, then helping you test it.
A financial adviser or lawyer laying out the realistic downsides of a risky choice.
A person with an anxiety condition who sees danger in most changes, including their own.
Advice you can verify that still leaves the choice with you.

compendium.name: Love Bombing
compendium.what: Flooding someone with intense affection, praise and attention very early, at a pace that outruns how well the two people actually know each other.
compendium.why: A rush of being adored can feel like finally being seen, so it is easy to let other parts of life shrink around it. If the warmth later cools or gets conditional, you may chase the early version and blame yourself for losing it.
compendium.healthy: Affection that grows at the pace of actual knowledge of the person.
sounds: I knew the first night we talked that you were the one.
I've never felt this way about anyone. Nobody else has ever come close.
Let's get away this weekend, just us. I already booked it.
You don't need to see your friends tonight. Stay with me, I miss you too much.
I think we should move in together. Why wait when we both know?
You're literally perfect. I can't believe you're real.
I'll text you all day, I just can't help myself.
nots: Two people who fall quickly and openly for each other, both comfortable with the pace and both able to say 'a bit slower' without it landing as rejection.
A naturally effusive person who is warm and generous with everyone, and has been for years.
A long-distance or whirlwind romance in which fast contact reflects circumstance, such as time zones or a short trip, rather than pressure.
Genuine enthusiasm that settles into steady, ordinary care once the novelty passes, instead of flipping to coldness.
A cultural or family style in which grand romantic language is simply how love is spoken.

compendium.name: Exclusive Meaning
compendium.what: Claiming that only this one person truly understands you, which gradually makes everyone else in your life seem less worthy of your trust.
compendium.why: If one person becomes the only one who seems to understand you, your other relationships lose weight. That leaves you with fewer people to check reality with, and less ability to leave or disagree safely.
compendium.healthy: "I feel really close to you" — without demoting everyone else.
sounds: Your friends don't actually get you. I do.
Nobody has ever listened to you the way I do. You can tell me things you'd never tell your mother.
Why would you talk to her about this? She'll only judge you.
I'm the only person who's ever seen the real you.
They love the version of you that's easy for them. I love all of you.
What we have is on a different level. Other people just can't reach it.
nots: Telling someone 'I feel so understood by you', which describes a feeling of closeness without ranking anyone else.
A close confidant, like a best friend or counselor, whom you rely on heavily while still keeping other ties alive and welcome.
A new couple's enthusiasm in the first months, expressed once or twice and then left alone.
Honest concern about a particular friend's behavior, specific and open to your own view of that friend.
A therapist or mentor whose role is to hear you, where the limited scope is clear and everyone else is not put down.

compendium.name: Hoovering
compendium.what: Reaching out to draw someone back into a relationship after they have pulled away or ended it, often with promises that things will change.
compendium.why: Each return restarts hope and resets the cycle. You may go back repeatedly, losing time and confidence, and may feel guilty or foolish when it falls apart again.
compendium.healthy: Demonstrated change over time, before asking for another chance.
sounds: I've been in therapy. I'm a different person now. Just let me show you.
I found your old jacket, and the memories came flooding back.
I can't eat or sleep without you. I don't know what I'll do.
Everyone says we belong together. Even my mother asked about you.
I know I messed up. One coffee, that's all I'm asking.
It's your birthday, and I wanted to be the first to say it. Can we talk?
I have something of yours and need to return it. Are you home?
nots: A person who truly changed over many months, did the work, and asks once, respectfully, for a chance, then accepts your answer.
Contact required to sort out kids, shared property, a lease or money after a split.
A kind check-in from an ex who marks a loss or a birthday and leaves the response to you.
Reconciliation that both people choose with open eyes and clear terms.
A single message sent in a lonely hour that the person regrets and does not repeat.

compendium.name: Future Faking
compendium.what: Making vivid promises about a better future together that keep you invested in the present, while the promised things never seem to arrive.
compendium.why: Waiting on a promise can use up years, savings or other options. When the future never comes, you may also doubt your own judgment for having believed it, which makes the next decision harder.
compendium.healthy: Small kept promises now, instead of large deferred ones.
sounds: Once the divorce is final, we'll get married. I promise it won't be long.
We'll buy the house by next spring. I've already picked out the street.
After this project, I'll have time for us. Just hang in there.
I'm going to quit drinking after the holidays. This time I mean it.
Give it a year and you'll see. I'm going to make it all up to you.
I'll introduce you to my family once things calm down.
We'll have the baby when the money situation is sorted.
nots: A sincere plan delayed by a layoff, illness or family emergency, where the person says so honestly and adjusts the plan with you.
A hopeful dream shared in conversation that was never offered as a promise or a reason for you to wait.
A couple jointly deciding to put off a goal until they can afford it, with both agreeing on the timeline.
A person who keeps small promises each week and also speaks about larger hopes for the years ahead.
A promise that does come true, even later than first hoped.

compendium.name: Negging
compendium.what: Slipping in a subtle insult, wrapped as a compliment or a joke, so that you feel a little smaller and a little more eager for approval.
compendium.why: Small digs add up. Over weeks you may begin to trust the other person's opinion of you above your own, and work hard for compliments that always come with a sting.
compendium.healthy: A compliment with no asterisk.
sounds: You're pretty smart for someone who didn't go to college.
That dress is bold. Most people couldn't pull it off, but you do you.
I'm surprised you finished that so fast. Good for you!
You'd be gorgeous if you smiled more. Seriously, it's a shame.
Wow, you actually cooked this? Not bad!
I like that you don't care what people think of how you look.
Not many guys with your job would be this thoughtful.
nots: Mutual, playful teasing between people who both enjoy it and would both stop if one asked.
An awkward compliment from someone who is clumsy with words and winces when you point it out.
Honest, kind feedback about a mistake, aimed at the work and offered to help.
A cultural or family style of ribbing that everyone in the group takes in fun.
A compliment that surprised you because it was higher than you expected from yourself, not because of a dig.

compendium.name: Silent Treatment
compendium.what: Withholding all communication, warmth or answers from someone, with no stated end, until they apologize or give way to what the other person wants.
compendium.why: Being frozen out hurts in a way the body treats as real pain. The open-ended wait can leave you desperate to end it at any cost. Ordinary things like a reply or basic warmth turn into rewards, and the issue itself is never resolved.
compendium.healthy: "I'm too angry to talk right now. I need until tomorrow, then let's resolve this."
sounds: Nothing. No reply for two days after you asked a question.
I'm not talking to you until you admit what you did.
A flat 'fine' and a walk out of the room, then no words for the evening.
Don't speak to me. You know what you did.
Messages read, with no answer, while they chat happily with others.
Talking to the dog and the kids but never to you.
No reply to texts for two days after you said no to something, then a cheerful message once you changed your mind.
A partner who stops sharing the plan for the week, or the state of the shared accounts, after you disagreed.
nots: Saying 'I'm too angry to talk about this right now. Can we pick it up after dinner?', which has a reason and a return time.
A person who goes quiet from shutting down, depression or overwhelm, and who is silent with everyone and not just you.
A break agreed on by both people during a heated argument, with a time to return.
Not sharing information because it is private, such as a friend's confidence or a medical matter that is theirs to keep.
Quiet from someone whose communication style is slow or private, and who has always been that way.
A cultural or family style of cooling off that everyone practices and that is not aimed at one person.

compendium.name: Isolation
compendium.what: Steadily cutting a person off from friends, family and other outside support until one relationship is the only one left.
compendium.why: With fewer people around, nobody is left to say 'that doesn't sound right' or to help when things go badly. A small circle can make a hard situation feel like the only one available, and it makes asking for help much harder.
compendium.healthy: "I feel tense around your friend — but your friendships are yours."
sounds: Your sister only calls when she wants something. I don't know why you bother.
Fine, go. I'll just sit here on my own again.
Do you really need to see them again this weekend?
Nobody understands us the way we understand each other.
Why would you tell Dana about our argument? That stays between us.
Every time you come back from your mom's you're in a mood with me.
I just want you to myself. Is that so terrible?
nots: A single worry about one friend who really is a bad fit, such as someone who pushes you to drink, raised once and then left alone.
A new baby, a long commute, illness or a house move, any of which can shrink a social life with nobody pushing.
A couple choosing a quiet season mostly together, both content, with friends still welcome.
A partner saying 'I miss you when you're out so much' as a feeling, with no attempt to stop you going.
A person who has always had a small circle and likes it that way.
A decision you made yourself to step back from relatives who hurt you.

compendium.name: Monitoring & Surveillance
compendium.what: Demanding constant access to a person's phone, messages and movements, so that every part of their day has to be explained.
compendium.why: Living under audit changes how you behave, even when you have done nothing wrong. You may start editing what you say, deleting harmless messages, or avoiding people, simply to avoid the next round of questions.
compendium.healthy: "I've been feeling insecure — can we talk about it?" (a feeling, not a search warrant).
sounds: Who was that? Let me see the message.
You were online at two in the morning. Who were you talking to?
Send me a picture right now of where you are.
Why did it take you forty minutes to answer?
Hand me your phone. If there's nothing there, it won't be a problem.
Couples don't keep secrets. Give me your passwords.
I only looked because you've been acting strange.
nots: Two adults who have both chosen to share a calendar or a passcode for practical reasons, and either of whom can stop.
A parent checking a young child's devices in a way that suits the child's age.
Workplace security rules that apply to everyone and are written down.
A one-off request for a text when you arrive home safely, after a frightening evening.
Open questions after a real breach of trust, asked for a limited time with an agreed end, as part of deciding together whether to stay.

compendium.name: Location Tracking
compendium.what: Requiring a person to keep their live location visible, and treating any gap in it as a problem to be explained.
compendium.why: When every stop might be questioned, ordinary choices start to feel risky. You may drop errands, visits or detours, not because anyone forbade them, but because explaining them has become tiring or frightening.
compendium.healthy: Optional location-sharing both people genuinely want, revocable without a fight.
sounds: Why does your dot say you're at Kelly's? You told me the gym.
Your location was off for an hour. What were you hiding?
Keep it on. If you've got nothing to hide, it costs you nothing.
I just want to know you're safe.
Turn it back on. Now.
I saw your car wasn't at work when I went past.
Funny how your phone dies right when I want to check.
nots: Mutual location sharing that both people picked, and either can turn off without a row.
A parent using a family-sharing app with a child who knows about it and for whom it suits their age.
A temporary arrangement for something specific, such as a solo hike or a late walk home, that ends afterward.
A workplace fleet tracker that the employer has disclosed and that applies to the job only.
Someone sharing their location with a carer or relative of their own choosing because of a medical condition.

compendium.name: Behavior Control
compendium.what: Setting rules about what another adult may wear, where they may go and who they may see, and enforcing them.
compendium.why: When another adult's rules govern your clothes, your outings and your friendships, you can lose the habit of deciding for yourself. Complying quietly can come to feel safer than the conflict that follows, and your sense of what is yours to choose can narrow.
compendium.healthy: "That outfit makes me feel insecure — that's my thing to work on."
sounds: You're not wearing that.
You're not going unless I say so.
Take that photo down right now.
I forbid you to see him again.
Text me when you get there and when you leave.
Real partners don't go out without each other.
If you cared about me, you wouldn't want to.
nots: A partner saying 'that outfit makes me feel insecure, and that's mine to work on', owning the feeling and leaving the choice with you.
Parents setting rules for a minor, which is part of their role.
A dress code at work or a faith community that you joined freely, or house rules that roommates agreed together.
Restrictions set by a doctor, probation officer or court for a stated reason.
Two partners asking each other to dress up or to be home for dinner on a particular night, and being free to say no.

compendium.name: Infantilization
compendium.what: Treating a capable adult as if they cannot manage their own money, tasks or decisions, and taking those over.
compendium.why: Skills and confidence both fade when they are not used. A person who is told often enough that they cannot cope may stop trying, and may end up unable to manage money, paperwork or decisions they once handled well.
compendium.healthy: "Want help with this, or do you have it?"
sounds: You can't handle money, sweetie. Let me.
You'd be lost without me organizing your life.
Give me that. You'll only mess it up.
You wouldn't understand anyway.
She's very sensitive, so I deal with the paperwork.
Don't worry your head about it.
Look at you, you did it all by yourself!
nots: An offer of help with something you have not done before, which you can accept or decline.
Carers of an adult with a real impairment who still ask them, explain things and include them in decisions.
Parents who have not caught up with the fact that their grown child has changed, and who respond when told.
A partner who is simply better at spreadsheets and takes them on by agreement, and would hand them back if asked.
A temporary need for extra help during illness, grief or a crisis.

compendium.name: "I Know Best" Paternalism
compendium.what: Overriding another adult's choices in the name of what is good for them, and expecting them to be grateful.
compendium.why: Care that cannot accept your no is hard to turn down, because refusing can feel ungrateful. Over time you may stop trusting your own judgment, or stop telling the person what you are deciding.
compendium.healthy: "Here's my concern. You decide — I'll back you either way."
sounds: I know what's best for you.
Trust me, I know better than you do.
You'll thank me later.
I've already moved your appointment. It's for your own good.
After everything I've done for you, the least you can do is listen.
You're making a mistake, and I won't let you.
One day you'll understand why I did this.
nots: Advice offered once, with a plain 'it's your decision', and support afterward whatever you pick.
An elder who really does know better on a specific matter, such as a roofer on roofs, whose view you can weigh.
A mentor, doctor or teacher whose guidance you sought and whose expertise you expect to carry weight.
Fear for your safety, such as a parent worried about a risky plan, voiced openly while leaving the choice with you.
A strongly argued disagreement between equals, where each can concede.

compendium.name: Punishment of Boundaries
compendium.what: Answering a limit someone has set with a penalty, such as coldness, withdrawn help or a taken-away privilege, until saying no starts to feel costly.
compendium.why: People learn from what a no costs. When every limit is followed by a chill, a lost favor or a week of silence, many stop setting limits at all, and the relationship quietly shrinks to whatever the other person will accept.
compendium.healthy: "Your limit stings, and I'll respect it."
sounds: Fine. Have your 'boundary.' See how the weekend goes.
Oh, you need space? Enjoy the silence, then.
Oh, so now you have boundaries.
If you can't do Sunday dinner, don't bother coming at all.
I drove you everywhere for years, and this is what I get.
Don't ask me for anything this week.
Go ahead, take the night off. Don't expect me to cover for you next time.
nots: A quick hurt reaction to a new limit, such as 'that stings', that settles within a day and ends in acceptance.
A natural consequence that comes with the limit itself: if you won't drive on Fridays, you can't also be the Friday driver.
Someone needing a few hours alone to absorb a no, and saying so, without making you pay for it.
Two people renegotiating a shared arrangement, each saying what they can still offer.
A policy that applies to everyone, such as a workplace rule on canceled shifts, applied to you as it is to others.
Sadness about a limit that is spoken as sadness, with no penalty added.

compendium.name: DARVO
compendium.what: A three-part reply to being confronted: deny it happened, attack the person raising it, then claim to be the one who was wronged.
compendium.why: People who raise a hard subject often do it at real cost. When the reply turns them into the accused, they can leave convinced the original problem was never real, or that speaking up is not worth the price.
compendium.healthy: "Let me hear the whole complaint before I respond."
sounds: That never happened, and I can't believe you'd say it.
Oh, so now I'm the villain?
After everything I've put up with from you, you have the nerve to accuse me?
You're the one who's been cruel to me.
I'm the real victim here, and you know it.
I'm getting hurt just listening to this.
You always twist things so you look innocent.
nots: A person who is falsely accused and says, with specifics, which part is wrong. Disputing a claim is different from reversing the roles.
A two-sided conflict in which both people carry real grievances and each gets a turn to be heard.
Visible hurt or tears from someone told they caused harm. Feeling wounded is not the same as flipping the blame.
A first, defensive burst of denial that settles into 'let me think about what you said' after a few minutes or a day.
A counter-complaint that is raised after the first one has been answered, and is treated as a separate matter.

compendium.name: Blame-Shifting
compendium.what: Placing the cause of your own action on the other person, so that your choice is described as something they did to you.
compendium.why: If every hurtful act is explained as a reaction to you, you can end up policing your own behavior to head off theirs. That is a heavy job nobody can do, and it keeps the real problem from ever being talked about.
compendium.healthy: "I did that, and it was wrong — regardless of what led up to it."
sounds: Look what you made me do.
I wouldn't have yelled if you had just answered the phone.
You drove me to it.
If you hadn't brought up money, none of this would have happened.
You know how I get when you do that, so this is on you.
I only lied because you would have overreacted.
You brought this on yourself.
nots: Honestly describing a real trigger, such as 'I was exhausted and your comment landed badly', while still owning the response.
A mutual conflict where both people admit what they added and neither claims to be the only cause.
A true statement of fact about timing, such as 'I was late because the train was canceled'.
A child or very stressed adult who blames the nearest person in the heat of the moment, then settles and takes responsibility.
Explaining your reasons for a decision without claiming the other person left you no option.

compendium.name: Whataboutism
compendium.what: Answering a complaint by raising a different wrong from the other side, so that the original issue goes unanswered.
compendium.why: When each complaint is met with another one, nothing is ever finished. Real issues pile up unresolved, and the person who raised the first one starts to wonder if it was fair to speak at all.
compendium.healthy: "I'll answer for mine, and then I'd like to talk about yours separately."
sounds: What about that time you forgot?
And you've never been late once in your life?
Well, what about when you left me waiting at the airport?
You did the exact same thing last year.
Funny that you bring it up, given how you treated my mother.
If we are keeping score, I could list yours too.
nots: Pointing out a true double standard and then returning to the original issue to answer it.
Asking to talk about a related concern after the first one has been dealt with, as a separate conversation.
A comparison that helps explain the point, such as 'I was late too last week, so I understand how it happens'.
A reasonable request that both people apply the same rule, made while still engaging with the complaint.
Two people with overlapping grievances who agree to take turns and keep to it.

compendium.name: Non-Apology Apology
compendium.what: A statement that sounds like an apology but regrets your reaction or feelings, not the thing that was actually done.
compendium.why: An apology is how people close a wound and rebuild trust. When the form is there and the substance is not, the hurt stays open and you may feel unreasonable for still being upset after being told sorry.
compendium.healthy: "I'm sorry I did X. It was wrong and I'll do Y differently."
sounds: I'm sorry you feel that way.
I'm sorry if you were offended.
I'm sorry, but you started it.
I apologize that you took it the wrong way.
Sorry you're so upset about this.
I'm sorry you chose to be hurt by it.
Mistakes were made, and I'm sorry it came to this.
nots: An imperfect apology that clearly names what was done, such as 'I'm sorry I forgot, that was careless of me'.
A speaker who does not yet understand why something hurt and says honestly, 'I'm sorry it hurt, and I want to understand what I did'.
A sincere expression of sympathy for how someone feels, offered where no wrongdoing is involved, such as at a loss.
A clumsy first attempt from someone who has not learned to apologize, followed by a better one once they are shown how.
An apology in a language or culture where regret is expressed through the situation instead of the person.

compendium.name: Denial
compendium.what: Refusing to accept that any wrongdoing took place, whatever the evidence or how the concern is raised.
compendium.why: If nothing is ever admitted, there is nothing to fix and nothing to forgive. The person raising a concern can be left with the hurt, no acknowledgment, and a sense that the problem was them for noticing it.
compendium.healthy: "Parts of that are fair, parts I see differently — let's go through it."
sounds: I did absolutely nothing wrong.
I have nothing to apologize for.
None of that is true.
I would never do something like that.
There is nothing to talk about.
I don't know what you are talking about, and I never have.
nots: Being wrongly accused and saying so, particularly if the person offers evidence of their own and listens to yours.
Correcting one wrong detail, such as the date or the place, while accepting the rest of the account.
Honest memory failure about something minor that was not memorable at the time.
A brief first reaction of shock that opens into a real conversation once the details are laid out.
A person who disagrees that something was wrong, while willing to discuss why they see it that way.

compendium.name: Minimization
compendium.what: Shrinking how serious something was so that your reaction looks too big for what actually happened.
compendium.why: If the size of the problem is always reduced, you may start to doubt your own sense of what is serious. Real harms can go unaddressed because raising them feels like making a fuss.
compendium.healthy: "I hear that this landed harder than I intended — walk me through it."
sounds: You're overreacting.
It's really not that big a deal.
It was just a joke. You can't take a joke.
You're being dramatic. Stop making a mountain out of a molehill.
Why are you so upset over nothing?
It wasn't even that bad. You'll get over it.
Honestly, other people have it much worse.
You're way too sensitive.
nots: A friend with a calmer view saying so and then asking why it hit you hard.
An accurate remark that something really was a small, one-time slip that has already been fixed.
Reassurance offered to someone who is spiraling, such as 'this is fixable', which supports them instead of dismissing the matter.
Different thresholds: people differ in what they find upsetting, and neither view is a fault.
Honest ignorance about how much something mattered, which is corrected once you explain.

compendium.name: Tone Policing
compendium.what: Responding to how something was said and not what was said, so the complaint is never actually discussed.
compendium.why: People raising real concerns are often upset, and upset is hard to say politely. If tone is always the topic, the people with the most reason to be upset are the ones whose points are never heard.
compendium.healthy: "I want to hear this — can we take ten minutes and restart calmer?" (and then actually restart).
sounds: Watch your tone.
I'm not discussing anything while you're like this.
I won't talk to you when you shout.
Lower your voice with me.
When you can speak calmly, then we'll talk.
You would get further if you were nicer about it.
Take the emotion out of it and I'll listen.
nots: A real request to pause a heated talk, followed by actually coming back to it later.
Self-protection from yelling, name-calling or threats, where stepping away is reasonable even if the topic is important.
A person who cannot take in information while overwhelmed, who asks for ten minutes and then returns.
Honest feedback that a particular word or insult hurt, offered along with willingness to hear the rest.
A workplace rule on conduct that is applied evenly to everyone, not only to one complaint.

compendium.name: Kafka Trapping
compendium.what: Treating a person's denial of an accusation as proof of guilt, so that no answer they give could ever clear them.
compendium.why: When innocence cannot be shown, the person accused stops trying to explain and starts trying to survive the conversation. They may confess to things that never happened, just to end it, or lose faith that they can ever be believed.
compendium.healthy: "Your denial doesn't prove anything either way — let's look at what actually happened."
sounds: Denying it just proves you did it.
Only a guilty person would get this defensive.
If you weren't hiding something, you wouldn't be so upset.
Notice how calm you are. That's exactly what someone with something to hide would do.
Your silence says everything.
The fact that you keep explaining shows you know what you did.
An innocent person wouldn't need to say it three times.
nots: Doubt based on something concrete, such as a message, a receipt or a witness, which you can look at and answer.
A person who says 'I hear you deny it, but I still feel uneasy', which names a feeling instead of declaring you guilty.
A lawyer, investigator or manager who asks pointed questions because that is their job, and who will weigh your answers.
A friend who notes that your story changed between two tellings and asks you to clear that up.
Plain disbelief. Someone can think you are wrong or lying without having built a trap; the trap is the part where nothing could convince them.

compendium.name: Contempt
compendium.what: Treating a person with open disgust or superiority, aimed at who they are rather than at anything they did.
compendium.why: Anger about an action can be answered with an apology or a fix. Scorn for who you are offers nothing to fix, so it can leave you feeling lower, more guarded, and less willing to bring up any problem at all.
compendium.healthy: "What you did made me furious" — the act, not the human.
sounds: You're pathetic.
You disgust me.
I'm embarrassed to be seen with you.
Listen to yourself. Honestly, who could take you seriously?
A sneer, then 'Wow. Of course you did.'
Mimicking your accent or your whine while others watch.
You're a waste of space.
nots: Loud, hot anger at something you did, as long as it stays about the act: 'I'm furious that you forgot the pickup.'
A blunt, unpleasant review of your work that criticizes the draft and not your worth.
One cruel sentence in the worst fight of a year, followed by a real apology.
Eye-rolls between close friends that you both know are a shared joke and that you can answer back in kind.
Disgust at something you did that truly was serious, such as lying about money, when the disgust is about the deed.

compendium.name: Name-Calling Disguised as Humor
compendium.what: Delivering an insult or demeaning label inside a joke, so that objecting to it can be called overreacting.
compendium.why: You are left with two bad choices: swallow the sting or be labeled humorless. Over time, many people stop objecting, and that silence can be mistaken by everyone, including you, for being fine with it.
compendium.healthy: Teasing that the *target* also finds funny — and stops instantly on request.
sounds: Relax, 'idiot' is a pet name.
Can't you take a joke, drama queen?
I'm kidding. God, so sensitive.
Everyone else laughed. What's your problem?
She's slow, bless her. Just teasing!
It's called banter. Look it up.
If you can't laugh at yourself, that's on you.
nots: Mutual teasing where both people give and take, and either can say 'too far' and be heard.
A single joke that misfired, followed by 'sorry, that came out wrong' and no repeat.
A nickname you chose or like, even if it sounds rude to outsiders.
Roast-style humor at an event where everyone agreed to the format and the target is in on it.
Gentle irony about a shared experience, such as a team's terrible road trip, that does not single out one person.

compendium.name: Comparative Devaluation
compendium.what: Holding a person up against someone else, again and again, in a way that always leaves them coming up short.
compendium.why: A comparison with no finish line cannot be won, because there is always another person who seems better. It can wear down confidence and also harm your relationships with the people you are being compared to.
compendium.healthy: "Here's what I need more of" — stated directly, no third party required.
sounds: Why can't you be more like your sister?
My ex never made this kind of scene.
Dana's husband would have planned this weeks ago.
Look at how well the neighbors' kids are doing.
Everyone on my team gets this done in half the time.
She posts her whole routine online. I don't see you doing anything like that.
I wish you had half of his drive.
nots: A person trying to describe what they need, using someone they know as an example: 'Could you handle the school forms the way Sam does for his kids?'
A teacher or manager showing an example of a good result as a model without ranking you against a named person.
Admiration for a friend that is not meant as a rebuke and not tied to your shortcomings.
One careless comment after a rough day, quickly regretted.
A coach pointing to a teammate's technique so you can learn from it, with no verdict on you.

compendium.name: Emotional Invalidation
compendium.what: Telling someone that what they feel is wrong, silly or not allowed, instead of accepting that they feel it.
compendium.why: Feelings are often the first thing people reach for when they need to explain what is wrong. When they are routinely dismissed, people can stop reporting them and then stop recognizing them, which makes everything else, from asking for help to leaving a bad situation, harder.
compendium.healthy: "I don't fully get it, but I believe you that it hurts."
sounds: You have no reason to be upset.
Stop being so dramatic, nothing happened.
You shouldn't feel that way.
Other people have it much worse.
You're making a big deal out of nothing.
Stop crying, it's nothing.
I'm not going to argue with your feelings. They're just wrong.
nots: A friend who disagrees with your reading of events but still says 'that sounds painful'.
Someone who does not understand why a thing upset you, asks, and accepts the answer.
A person offering practical help first when you are in crisis, before talking about feelings.
A caring reminder of context, such as 'this has happened before and you got through it', given after listening.
A busy or overwhelmed person saying 'I can't hear this right now, can we talk tonight?'

compendium.name: Shame Installation
compendium.what: Treating a person's mistake as proof that something is wrong with them as a whole, so shame replaces guilt.
compendium.why: Guilt can lead to an apology and a repair. Shame often leads to hiding, which makes repair less likely. A person who believes they are the problem can find it hard to ask for help or to trust their own judgment.
compendium.healthy: "That behavior was not okay" — specific, bounded, repairable.
sounds: You should be ashamed of yourself.
What is wrong with you?
How can you even live with yourself?
Any normal person would know better.
I don't know who raised you.
After everything, this is who you really are.
Shame on you.
nots: 'What's wrong with you?' as an exasperated idiom, said about a spilled drink and gone a minute later.
Guilt that comes from your own conscience after you really did hurt someone, which can be healthy.
A clear, serious statement that what you did was wrong, with an invitation to make amends.
A community or family naming a harm and expecting accountability for it.
A mentor being blunt about a serious professional error while still saying you can do better.

compendium.name: Intimidation
compendium.what: Using a hint or open warning of unwelcome consequences to push someone toward giving in or staying quiet.
compendium.why: When you comply out of fear, the other person may never learn whether you agree, and you may stop saying what you think at all. The fear can also grow, because the unspoken consequence never needs to be tested to keep working.
compendium.healthy: There is no healthy version of a threat; the alternative is a request.
sounds: You don't want to see me angry.
Keep pushing and find out what happens.
You'll regret this.
You don't know what I might do.
Nice life you've got here. It would be a shame if something happened to it.
A hand slammed on the table, then a quiet 'say that again'.
I know where you work and what time you leave.
nots: A plain statement of a real consequence, said without heat, such as 'if the rent isn't paid, the landlord will start eviction.'
A person saying they are very angry and need to leave the room to calm down.
A prediction of how someone else will react: 'if you tell your boss that way, you'll regret it.'
A firm boundary with an ordinary consequence, such as 'I won't ride with you if you've been drinking.'
Someone venting a frightening-sounding sentence during a rage and then horrified by it afterward, which is still serious but different from a campaign to control you.

compendium.name: Triangulation
compendium.what: Bringing a third person, real or invented, into a two-person disagreement so their supposed opinion carries the argument.
compendium.why: You end up arguing with people who are not in the room and cannot be questioned. It becomes hard to know what anyone actually said, and relationships with the people being quoted can sour without a word being exchanged with them.
compendium.healthy: "Here's *my* problem with it" — owned, first-person, no chorus.
sounds: Even your mother thinks you were out of line.
Dana told me what you said about me at lunch.
I've talked to the whole team and none of them see it your way.
Ask anyone. They'll all tell you the same thing.
Your brother called me last night, and he agrees with me.
I'm not the only one who feels this way, you know.
Marcus says you've been talking behind my back.
nots: A person who says 'I talked this over with my sister and she gave me a useful angle' while owning the view as their own.
A group conversation, such as a family meeting, that everyone knowingly joined to settle something together.
A caring group raising a worry directly and openly with someone, for example friends speaking up about a risky situation.
Venting to a close friend after a hard day, with no plan to bring the friend's opinion back as proof.
A mediator or manager who is brought in by agreement and hears both sides.

compendium.name: Forced Teaming
compendium.what: Declaring a shared 'we' that the other person never agreed to, so a separate choice starts to look like betrayal.
compendium.why: Obligations you never accepted can pile up under a word that sounds warm. Declining then costs you the belonging you were offered, so people often go along to avoid being cast out of the 'we'.
compendium.healthy: "I'd like us to approach this together — are you in?"
sounds: We're in this together whether you like it or not.
People like us have to stick together.
It's us against the world.
We both know what we have to do about this.
After everything we've been through, you can't back out now.
We've decided to handle this ourselves, so don't mention it to anyone.
Come on, we're a team. Teams don't ask questions.
nots: A genuine invitation such as 'Would you like to work on this with me?', where a no is welcome.
Ordinary team language at a shared job, where roles were assigned openly and everyone knows what they signed up for.
A couple or friends who use 'we' because they actually decided something jointly.
An enthusiastic person who says 'we should do this' as a suggestion and drops it when you are not keen.
A coach or organizer who builds team spirit, but allows people to leave or opt out of particular tasks.

compendium.name: "We're Family" Erasure
compendium.what: Invoking family loyalty so that fairness, limits and the right to say no no longer seem to apply between relatives.
compendium.why: The people you love most can be the hardest to refuse. When the family bond is used to cancel every limit, you may give up money, time and peace, and feel guilty for even wanting fairness.
compendium.healthy: "We're family, so let's find something that's fair to both of us."
sounds: We're family, so you can't say no.
Family doesn't need boundaries.
You can't charge your own cousin.
Blood is thicker than water.
I can't believe you'd make your own mother ask twice.
In this family we don't keep score.
After all we've done for you, this is how you repay us?
nots: A relative who says 'we're family, I'd love to help' and genuinely accepts it if you cannot.
A family where help flows in every direction over the years and everyone knows it evens out.
A relative who is truly in a crisis and asks once for help, with openness about what they can do in return.
A cultural or religious tradition of shared duty that everyone in the household values and chooses to honor.
An older relative who feels hurt by distance and says so, without demanding that you drop your limits.

compendium.name: Concern Trolling
compendium.what: Voicing worry for someone's wellbeing as the cover for telling them what to do, so refusing the advice looks like harming themselves.
compendium.why: Care is hard to argue with, so a directive dressed as care leaves you with two bad choices: comply, or be treated as someone who cannot look after themselves. Over time you may stop trusting your own judgment.
compendium.healthy: "I'm worried. Do you want my input, or just support?"
sounds: I'm only saying this because I worry about you.
As your friend, I have to say everyone's noticed.
I'm just worried, which is why you really should quit that job.
As someone who cares about you, I can't watch you do this.
You've seemed so off lately. I think you need to cut her out.
If you cared about your health you'd listen to me.
I'd hate for you to regret this. Please just trust me on it.
nots: A friend who says 'I'm worried about you' once, asks if you want advice, and accepts it if you say no.
A doctor, therapist or other professional giving health guidance as part of their role.
Family members raising a serious worry together, such as a safety concern, and asking what you want from them.
Someone who offers practical help, such as a ride or a meal, without attaching conditions.
A worry that is repeated because the situation is truly getting worse and is still offered as concern, not as an order.

compendium.name: Ultimatums
compendium.what: Demanding that someone pick one of two outcomes immediately, with a loss attached to the option the speaker does not want.
compendium.why: A decision made with a loss hanging over it is rarely a free one. You may agree to things you would have weighed differently, and you may stop raising concerns at all, because every concern risks turning into a showdown.
compendium.healthy: "This is really important to me — can we find a way through it together?"
sounds: It's me or your sister. Pick.
Quit the band by Friday or we're done.
Hand over your password or don't bother coming home.
This is your last chance. Last one.
Either you sign it tonight or I'm telling everyone why.
I'm not asking twice. Yes or no.
Choose: your mother or me.
nots: A boundary about the speaker's own wellbeing, such as 'I can't stay in the room while there is shouting, so I'm going to step out.'
A deadline set by the outside world, such as a lease renewal, a job offer that expires, or a visa date.
A dealbreaker stated calmly after long thought, with room to talk about it, such as 'I do not want children, and I need to know where you stand.'
A parent or manager naming a real consequence that follows from a rule everyone already knew.
A heated 'I can't take this anymore' said once in tears and taken back or explained afterward.

compendium.name: Urgency Manufacturing
compendium.what: Pressing for an immediate decision, often by creating or inflating a deadline or emergency, so there is no time to think or ask anyone.
compendium.why: Without time you cannot compare, check facts or ask anyone you trust. A yes given under that squeeze is hard to take back, and afterwards you may feel foolish for agreeing to something you would have turned down on a calm day.
compendium.healthy: "No rush — take the time you need and tell me tomorrow."
sounds: You have to decide right now.
This offer is gone by tonight.
There's no time to think about it. Just sign.
If you call anyone, it will be too late.
It's an emergency and only you can fix it, so I need you to act this minute.
Everyone else has already agreed. We're only waiting on you.
Answer me now. I can't wait until tomorrow.
A countdown timer on a checkout page that starts over when you reload it.
nots: Real deadlines exist, such as a sale end date or a flight boarding time. Ask what actually happens if you take one more day.
Real emergencies feel exactly like this from the inside, and a burst pipe does need a call now.
Someone anxious who voices urgency because they feel it, with no view about how you decide.
An honest request for an answer by Friday because the venue needs a headcount, with the reason given.
Excitement, such as 'I'd love to do this soon', with nothing lost by waiting.
Time pressure from a process you both face, like an exam or an application window.

compendium.name: False Dilemma
compendium.what: Describing a situation as having only two possible answers when more exist, so that the person feels pushed toward one.
compendium.why: When the list of choices has been trimmed for you, you can feel you chose freely while only picking from what was left. Over time you may stop looking for options at all, and start treating a normal disagreement as a test of loyalty.
compendium.healthy: "Here are the options I see — what am I missing?"
sounds: Either you trust me completely, or you don't trust me at all.
You're with us or you're against us.
If you're not paying for the premium plan, you clearly don't care about your data.
Either we move to his city or you choose your job over our family.
There's no middle ground here. It's all or nothing.
You can be honest, or you can be nice. You can't be both.
We either do it my way or we do nothing.
nots: A situation that really does come down to two options, such as accepting a job offer or turning it down.
A quick way of speaking when someone is tired, such as 'we either go now or we miss the train', that changes once you point out the next train.
A simplified choice offered by someone who invites you to add what they missed, as in 'I see two options. Is there a third?'
A narrow question set openly in a quiz, a poll, or a debate class, where everyone knows the format.
Someone's honest belief that no middle path exists, held without any intent to steer you and dropped when shown otherwise.

compendium.name: Sunk Cost Exploitation
compendium.what: Pointing to the time, money or effort already spent as a reason you cannot stop, change course or leave now.
compendium.why: Past investment cannot be recovered whether you stay or go, yet it can feel like a debt that has to be paid. When the years, money or effort already spent are used to stop you leaving, you may end up putting more in just to avoid admitting the loss.
compendium.healthy: "We've built a lot — I want to fight for it. Do you?" (an invitation, not a debt).
sounds: You'd throw away eleven years over one argument?
After everything I gave up to move here for you, you're going to walk?
We've put forty thousand dollars into this. You can't stop now.
You've come this far. It would be a shame to quit.
Think of all the hours you've given to this group. For nothing?
I stayed for you all those years. Now it's your turn.
Do you know what I sacrificed to get us here?
nots: Honest sadness about losing a shared history, said once and followed by 'but it's your decision.'
A real financial planning point, such as 'if we cancel, we lose the deposit; let's weigh that.'
Someone reminding you of your own stated goals because you asked them to keep you on track.
A caring plea to try counseling before ending something that mattered, offered as an invitation.
Your own mixed feelings about leaving after years, which belong to you rather than to anyone pressing you.

compendium.name: Response-Time Policing
compendium.what: Treating the time taken to answer a message as a failing that must be explained, so you feel permanently on call.
compendium.why: If every delay needs a defense, your attention is no longer fully yours. You may carry your phone like a leash, cut things short with other people, and feel guilty for being away from it, even when you were doing nothing wrong.
compendium.healthy: "I get anxious when I don't hear back — a quick 'busy, later' helps me a lot."
sounds: I can see you read it at 3:41. It's now 4:20. Where were you?
Why did it take two hours to answer me?
You were online and you didn't text back. Who else was on your phone?
If you cared, you'd have answered right away.
Seven missed calls. What could possibly be more important?
Left me on read again. Nice.
Next time, text me the second you arrive. I mean it.
nots: A worried 'just checking you got home safe' sent once, with no reproach if you were asleep.
A shared agreement, such as parents and teens texting arrival times, applied to both sides.
A reasonable expectation at work or in an emergency role, such as on-call nursing, that is written down and shared.
Disappointment said once, such as 'I missed hearing from you today', with no demand attached.
Real anxiety after a loss or a scare, such as an accident, where a person asks for more contact and accepts a limit.

compendium.name: Exaggeration
compendium.what: Stretching a claim with words like always, never, everyone or nothing, so it sounds bigger and harder to answer than the facts support.
compendium.why: A stretched claim is hard to answer. Defending yourself against 'never' can make you look petty for listing the one time, and a fair point buried inside the claim gets lost along with the exaggeration.
compendium.healthy: "The last three times, X happened" — specific and checkable.
sounds: You ALWAYS do this.
You never listen to me.
Nobody on the team agrees with you.
Every single time I ask for one thing, it turns into a fight.
You've ruined the whole trip.
You haven't called me once this month.
nots: Ordinary venting, such as 'ugh, you always leave the cupboards open' said with a sigh and a half-smile.
A claim that is close to literally true because the thing really has happened nearly every time.
Casual rounding, like 'I've told you a hundred times' when the number is five.
Strong feeling put into big words by someone tired or hurt, who steps back when asked for an example.
Enthusiastic overstatement such as 'best day ever', which is mood rather than a charge against anyone.
A real disagreement over how often something happens, where both people are counting honestly.

compendium.name: Vague Allegations
compendium.what: Hinting that unnamed people have unspecified complaints about someone, so the claim cannot be checked, answered or corrected.
compendium.why: You can't correct what you can't see. People hit by a vague claim often spend weeks searching their memory and scanning faces for who knows what, while their standing with others may shift without a word being said to them.
compendium.healthy: "Here is who said what, specifically."
sounds: People are talking about you.
I've heard things, and I'm not going to say from whom.
There have been concerns about your attitude.
Everyone knows what you're really like.
Word is going around.
I'm not the only one who feels this way.
nots: A colleague who says 'a few people struggled with the handover' and then offers specifics when asked.

A manager under a formal confidentiality process who cannot name a complainant but describes the behavior and offers a way to respond. Awkwardly protecting a source while relaying a real concern is not the same as hiding the concern.
A friend who says 'I might be wrong, but I got the impression you upset Sam' and is open to hearing your side.
A summary of feedback from many people, such as a 360 review, that reports themes without names and gives examples of behavior.
A person who honestly has only secondhand talk and says so.

compendium.name: Identity Hooking
compendium.what: Claiming that someone's identity, skills or successes belong to you, so that standing apart from you means giving up the self they have built.
compendium.why: If you are told you were made by someone, walking away may seem to mean disowning your own history. Wins stop feeling like yours, and independence starts to look like ingratitude or self-destruction.
compendium.healthy: "I'm proud of what I contributed to your growth" — contribution, not ownership.
sounds: I made you who you are.
Everything you have, you have because of me.
Without me you would still be waiting tables.
That promotion is really mine. Who do you think taught you to speak up?
Go ahead and leave, but whatever you build, remember whose idea you were.
People only listen to you because of the name I gave you.
You're nothing without me.
nots: A mentor, coach or parent saying they are proud and glad to have helped, while still treating your choices as yours.
Someone accurately noting that a past favor mattered, such as a reference letter or tuition money, without tying it to what you owe now.
A founder, teacher or relative who feels hurt when you move on and says so, without claiming your accomplishments.
An exaggerated boast made once in a heated argument, then taken back when things cool.
A culture or family where credit is shared by tradition, and everyone, including you, claims credit for the group's successes.

compendium.name: Conditional Worth
compendium.what: Treating a person's value as something that rises and falls with their usefulness and their willingness to comply.
compendium.why: A worth meter held by someone else makes rest feel like failure and a no feel dangerous. You can end up working harder for a feeling of acceptance that keeps moving away.
compendium.healthy: "I need X from you" — a need, with the person's worth left out of it.
sounds: You're only worth something when you're useful.
Earn your place in this family.
I'll be nice to you once you've done what I asked.
What do you even bring to this house?
Funny how I only hear from you when you want something, and funnier how I only like you when you're handy.
Good girl. See, that's the version of you I like.
You were great last week. Today you're a disappointment.
nots: A direct request such as 'I need you to pick up your brother today', which asks for a task and says nothing about your worth.
Reasonable performance standards at work, where a bad quarter leads to a coaching talk rather than contempt.
Someone who is stressed and curt for a day but returns to ordinary warmth afterward.
Clear house rules or chores in a family, applied fairly and without suggesting anyone's place is at stake.
A person saying 'I felt let down by that' and still treating you as a full member of the relationship.

compendium.name: Learned Helplessness
compendium.what: Repeatedly telling someone they could not cope alone, until they start to believe it and stop trying.
compendium.why: Abilities shrink when they go unused. If you are told often enough that you cannot manage, you may stop trying, and then the lack of practice looks like proof that they were right.
compendium.healthy: "You've handled hard things before. This one's yours too, and I'm here."
sounds: You can't survive without me.
You'd fall apart in a week on your own.
Let me handle the bank. You'll only get it wrong.
Nobody else would put up with how scattered you are.
You know you can't drive on the motorway. Just stay home.
I'm only doing this because I know you can't.
Remember what happened last time you tried? Exactly.
nots: Honest worry about one specific, real limit, such as a medical condition or a lack of experience with a task, stated once and with offers to help you learn.
A caregiver doing more for someone who really is ill, injured or newly bereaved, and planning with them to get abilities back.
Over-protectiveness from a parent or partner who is anxious and says unhelpful things, but is glad when you succeed.
Someone sharing out chores by who is quicker at what, not by who is deemed hopeless.
A warning given once because a plan really did look risky, followed by respect for your decision.

compendium.name: Loyalty Binds
compendium.what: Defining loyalty as obedience and silence, so that disagreeing, asking questions or telling outsiders counts as betrayal.
compendium.why: When disagreeing means betrayal, problems stay inside the group. You may carry something heavy alone, because getting help would feel like a breach of loyalty, and the guilt can outlast the situation.
compendium.healthy: "Loyalty to me includes telling me when I'm wrong."
sounds: If you tell anyone, you're betraying this family.
What happens in this house stays in this house.
A real friend wouldn't go around questioning me.
I never thought you'd take their side over mine.
Loyalty means never questioning.
After everything this team did for you, you go to HR?
If you really loved us you wouldn't make us look bad.
nots: A request to keep one specific private matter private, such as a medical diagnosis or a surprise, while you stay free to disagree on everything else.
A professional duty of confidentiality, for instance for therapists or lawyers, which has stated limits and a purpose.
Real hurt from a friend who felt you did not stand by them, said once and open to your side of it.
A family or team culture of pulling together under stress that still allows questions and objections.
Your own strong commitment to someone, which you have chosen and can still examine.

compendium.name: Legal/Administrative Threats
compendium.what: Raising the prospect of police, lawyers, HR, courts or other authorities as a lever in a personal or workplace dispute, instead of as a step in a real process.
compendium.why: A threat that borrows an institution's weight can make you agree to things you would otherwise question, because you cannot tell how real it is and the possible loss, such as a job, a lease or time with your kids, is large. You may stop raising fair concerns at all.
compendium.healthy: Using institutions for their actual purpose — safety and rights — not as a club in an argument.
sounds: One more word and I'm calling the cops.
You'll be hearing from my lawyer.
I know people in HR. Keep this up and see what happens to your file.
I can make one phone call and your whole situation changes.
If you tell your side to anyone, I'll report you to your licensing board.
I have everything screenshotted. A judge would love to see this.
Do you really want this going on your record?
nots: Telling someone plainly that you intend to file a police report, see a lawyer or go to HR, and then using the proper channel, with no conditions attached.
A landlord, employer or agency stating a consequence that is written in a contract or policy, such as a notice period or a late-fee rule.
An honest explanation of your own rights, like 'you are allowed to bring someone with you to that meeting'.
Someone afraid for their safety who says they will phone the police if a behavior continues. That is a protective limit, not leverage in an argument.
