A single angry sentence in a fight that is taken back later and does not return.
A lawyer's letter that follows real attempts to settle a debt or dispute.

compendium.name: Weaponized Therapy-Speak
compendium.what: Using therapy words such as boundaries, projecting or triggered to recast someone's limits and complaints as the problem, so the real issue goes unanswered.
compendium.why: A specific, checkable complaint is converted into something untestable about your inner life, and your limit is renamed as a symptom. You may leave with the problem unsolved, a new doubt about your own instincts, and a habit of apologizing for the limit.
compendium.healthy: Therapy language used on oneself: "I notice I'm getting defensive."
sounds: That's not a boundary, that's control.
That's not self-care, that's avoidance.
You're projecting right now.
That's your trauma talking, not me.
I'm setting a boundary: you're not allowed to be upset.
Your attachment style is making this harder for both of us.
I'm only saying this because I care about your healing.
Your email about the missing invoice is answered with 'I think you have some things to unpack.'
nots: 'You're projecting' is sometimes accurate, and in a therapy room that kind of exploration is the agreed purpose of being there. The marker here is a psychological reading offered as the whole reply to a concrete complaint.
A good friend gently noting that a pattern of withdrawal might be hurting you, with curiosity and an open door for you to disagree.
Someone applying the same lens to themselves, such as 'I think I was being defensive there'.
A couple or family in therapy together, where looking at each person's patterns is the shared task.
A real case of avoidance. People do sometimes dodge hard talks, and saying so kindly is not a trap.
A pause to settle ('I'm too upset to talk well, can we come back at six?') that is followed by a return.

compendium.name: Trash-Can Diagnosis
compendium.what: Using a mental-health label about someone as an insult, a verdict, or a way to treat their limits and reactions as symptoms.
compendium.why: Self-protection gets reclassified as a symptom, so your boundaries cost you credibility and any pushback is read as further evidence of the alleged problem. You may stop setting limits at all, since each one can be turned into proof.
compendium.healthy: "I'm finding your behavior really hard" — behavior, not diagnosis.
sounds: You're a textbook narcissist.
This is your BPD talking, not you.
That's just your anxiety talking.
You're being paranoid. Normal people don't ask that.
Maybe you should get that checked, because it's not normal to react like this.
You need serious help, seriously.
A group chat describes your request for quiet as 'one of her moods.'
A message to your family says you have 'been struggling with your mental health' right after you declined a request.
nots: A trusted person can gently name a real escalation out of care, and a diagnosis someone has disclosed themselves can be referred to supportively. What is described here is a boundary answered with a label instead of a response.
A clinician who has assessed you explaining a diagnosis you asked about.
Someone using these words about themselves: 'I'm anxious about this, can we slow down?'
'You need help' said as clumsy, honest worry for someone who is clearly struggling.
A friend saying 'you don't seem like yourself lately,' then asking and listening to the answer.
Calling for help when someone seems truly unsafe, which responds to a crisis and does not rebut a limit.

compendium.name: Stalking-by-Notification
compendium.what: Using a person's last-seen times, read receipts, story views and online status as evidence in a running case about where they were and why they did not answer.
compendium.why: When every green dot can become a question, ordinary use of your own phone turns into something to defend. People start planning when to be online and when to look away, and the hours spent explaining can crowd out the relationship itself.
compendium.healthy: "I felt low when I saw you online and hadn't heard back — irrational maybe, but real."
sounds: I saw you were online at 2am.
You posted a story but couldn't answer me?
It says seen at 11:42. So you read it and just left it.
Why were you active at midnight if you were going to bed?
You liked her photo. Explain that.
Your last seen says 3:10. Who were you talking to?
I'm not checking up on you. It just shows up on my screen.
nots: One honest feeling report, such as 'I felt low when I saw you online and hadn't heard back', which asks for comfort and not for an account.
A location-sharing arrangement you both chose, for a long trip or a late commute, that either of you can switch off.
A parent following open household rules about a young child's phone.
Checking when someone does not reply after a flight or a storm, because you are worried they may be hurt.
A passing 'oh, you're up late too' that is left there and not followed by questions.
A work chat status your team agreed means available, used only to see who can pick up a task.

compendium.name: Baiting
compendium.what: Provoking someone into an angry or upset reaction, then pointing to that reaction as the real problem.
compendium.why: If your reaction is the only part anyone remembers, you can start to distrust your own temper and your own account. It can also cost you at work, in custody talks or with friends, where the reaction is seen and the poke is not.
compendium.healthy: "I can see you're upset — I'd rather hear it than poke at it."
sounds: What, are you going to cry now?
Go on, say it. I dare you.
There she goes again.
Calm down. Wow. Everyone can see how unstable this is.
I was just asking a question. Why are you screaming?
A sly remark about your late father, then a raised eyebrow as your voice rises.
A message timed late at night that gets you to fire back, followed by a screenshot of what you sent.
nots: A mutual argument in which both people throw barbs and both raise their voices.
An honest, pointed question that you found hard to hear but that was a real attempt to understand.
Your own reaction to something that really was unfair, with no one steering it.
A sibling-style wind-up between people who both play the game and enjoy it.
Someone saying 'you seem upset' because they honestly noticed it.

compendium.name: Interrogation
compendium.what: Demanding that someone explain, justify or defend themselves on command, as though an answer were owed whether or not they want to give one.
compendium.why: If you are always the one explaining, you can start behaving as though every choice needs permission. The habit of defending yourself can spread to people who never asked, and a small question from a friend can start to feel like an attack.
compendium.healthy: "Help me understand what happened?" — a question, not a summons.
sounds: You owe me an explanation. Start talking.
Explain yourself. Right now.
Answer me when I'm talking to you.
Where were you? Who with? Why didn't you say?
Why would you even think that? Justify it.
So walk me through it again, from the start.
I'm waiting. I'm going to ask until you tell me.
nots: A caring question asked once, such as 'You seem quiet, what happened?', that you are free to leave unanswered.
A formal process such as a job review or a police report, in which giving an account is a defined part of the procedure.
A parent asking a young child to explain what happened after a broken window, with warmth and an expectation of honesty.
A person who truly needs to understand after a real breach of trust, who asks in a way that leaves room to say 'not now.'
Friends going back and forth in lively debate, each asking and answering with equal ease.

compendium.name: The Exception Script
compendium.what: Telling you that you are uniquely different from everyone around you, so that keeping that special status depends on staying close to the speaker.
compendium.why: Being the exception means having no peers. Your worth becomes conditional on staying above the very people who might offer perspective, which can leave you with fewer places to go when something goes wrong.
compendium.healthy: "I like how you think about this" — praise that doesn't require distancing you from anyone else.
sounds: You're not like the other girls on the team. You actually take this seriously.
You're not like your friends. They could never understand you the way I do.
You're so mature for your age. The kids in your class wouldn't get you.
You're too good for that crowd. They're holding you back.
Your family doesn't appreciate you. I do.
I don't tell this to just anyone. Don't mention it to the rest of them, they'd be jealous.
Why do you waste your time on people who can't see how special you are?
Don't let them bring you down to their level.
nots: Specific praise for something you actually did, such as 'your analysis of the data was the strongest in the group'.
A teacher or mentor who sees promise in you and also encourages you to share it and learn from peers.
Being chosen for a role on merit, which is stated openly and is the same for others in your position.
A friend who says 'you're the one I call when things get hard', a statement of closeness that leaves your other ties alone.
Two people bonding over feeling like outsiders together, without either of them asking the other to drop anyone.
A friend venting about coworkers who were truly unkind to you, without asking you to cut them off.

compendium.name: "You're Too Emotional"
compendium.what: Treating a person's visible feelings as proof that their point can be ignored, so the feeling becomes the topic and the complaint disappears.
compendium.why: People who hear this often learn to read their own feelings as a defect. They may stop raising problems, or rehearse a flat voice, so the actual issue never gets heard and nothing changes.
compendium.healthy: "You seem really upset — help me understand what's going on for you."
sounds: "We can't talk about this while you're like this."
"You're being so emotional that I can't take anything you say seriously."
"Call me when you've calmed down and can be rational."
"This is exactly why nobody can bring things up with you."
"I'd listen if you weren't crying."
"Your feelings are getting in the way of the facts."
nots: A person who is flooded themselves and says they need twenty minutes, then comes back and hears the whole concern.
A friend who asks, "Do you need a minute?" and stays ready to listen either way.
A group rule, such as in an emergency room or a debate club, that asks everyone to keep voices level so that all points can be heard.
Honest worry about someone who seems unwell, offered with no attempt to settle the argument by it.
A real difference in how loudly two people show feeling, where neither one uses that to win.

compendium.name: Gotcha Framing
compendium.what: Taking an honest, tentative remark and presenting it as a confession, so that being open with someone has a price.
compendium.why: People who are punished for candor learn to go quiet, hedge everything, or stop admitting a mistake at all. That makes the relationship less honest for both sides and leaves the person with nowhere safe to work things out.
compendium.healthy: "Thanks for being honest about that — let's figure out what to do next."
sounds: Aha, so you admit it.
So you're saying you were there after all.
You just said you might have been wrong. So you were.
There it is. That's what you really think.
I knew you'd confess eventually.
Write that down, everyone. He finally said it.
Funny how you only say that when you're cornered.
nots: Holding someone to a clear, deliberate statement such as a promise or a direct yes or no. People are rightly expected to stand behind those.
A listener who truly feels relieved and says 'thank you for telling me, that helps', which welcomes the honesty.
Asking a follow-up question about something you just said, with real curiosity and without a victory lap.
A lawyer or investigator noting what a witness said in a formal setting where statements are on the record.
Teasing between close friends who both enjoy it and both know the other has said nothing damaging.

compendium.name: False Authority
compendium.what: Presenting a personal opinion or bias as neutral fact, so that disagreeing with it seems like arguing against reality.
compendium.why: Being told your view is a feeling while theirs is a fact can wear away your confidence in speaking up at all. Over time you may stop offering a view, or you may defer on decisions that are rightly yours.
compendium.healthy: "Here's my take, and I recognize it's one perspective."
sounds: I'm just being objective here.
I'm stating facts, not opinions. You're the one being emotional.
Anyone sensible would see it this way.
That's not my opinion, that's just how it is.
I've looked at this from every angle, and there's only one answer.
You can't argue with logic.
Everyone knows that. I shouldn't have to explain it.
nots: A real expert stating what the evidence shows, who can show you the source and will revise if the evidence changes.
A confident person who says 'I'm sure about this' and then listens to your response.
Someone who sincerely believes they are being fair, and who can say, when asked, 'fair point, that part is my view'.
A rule that exists for good reasons, like a safety standard, being stated as a rule instead of as an opinion.
A blunt communication style, which can sound like false authority but is open to challenge when you give it.

compendium.name: Confidentiality as Weapon
compendium.what: Citing confidentiality rules to withhold from someone the accusation, the evidence or even the source of a complaint against them, leaving them unable to answer it.
compendium.why: Being judged on information you are not allowed to see leaves you unable to correct a mistake, give context or show that something is untrue. A decision can follow that affects your job, grades, standing or care, with no visible reasoning to appeal.
compendium.healthy: "Here's what's been raised, and here's what I legally/ethically can and can't share — let's talk through it."
sounds: I'm afraid the details of the complaint are confidential.
We can tell you there was a concern, but not who raised it or what was said.
The findings of the review are privileged, so we can't share them with you.
You'll receive the decision. The reasoning stays within the committee.
Because of confidentiality, you also can't discuss this meeting with your colleagues.
That information is protected. You'll have to trust the process.
Sharing the file would breach other people's privacy.
nots: Protecting the name of someone who reported harm while still telling you the substance of what is alleged and giving you room to respond.
A legal bar on disclosure that is explained, with the specific rule named and a summary offered in its place.
A process in its early stage, with a stated date when you will be told more.
A doctor or therapist declining to share another person's information, which is their duty.
Documents with names or private details blacked out, where the content of the concern is still readable.

compendium.name: Pressure to Sign
compendium.what: Pressing someone to sign or accept a document, agreement or statement of blame immediately, without the time or access to read it, ask questions or consult anyone first.
compendium.why: A signature can bind you to debts, waive rights, accept blame, or end a job or a lease. Signing before you understand removes your options, and it can be hard to undo afterward, even when you later learn the terms were not what you were told.
compendium.healthy: "Take the weekend to read this over and ask any questions before you sign."
sounds: Just sign here and we'll sort the rest out later.
This offer is off the table when you walk out the door.
It's a formality. Everyone signs it.
If you need a lawyer to read it, that tells me you don't trust me.
Sign the statement now, and we can say it was resolved.
I need it back before end of day or it won't be processed.
There's no point reading all that. Initial each page.
nots: A real, outside deadline, such as a filing date or an offer expiry, with the terms given to you in advance and room to ask questions.
A simple document like a delivery receipt or a permission slip, where a quick signature suits what is being agreed.
Someone who offers a copy to take home, says you can ask a lawyer, and then keeps to the timeline.
Signing only to confirm you received information, with a form that says so plainly.
A busy clerk who hurries everyone along the same way, with no extra push applied to you.

compendium.name: False Equivalence
compendium.what: Presenting very uneven harm as equally shared fault, so that no one is left holding the larger share.
compendium.why: When a large wrong is weighed the same as a small one, the person who was hurt ends up apologizing and the real issue is never fixed. It can also make them doubt their sense of proportion about what happened.
compendium.healthy: "I did X, which was wrong, separate from anything you did."
sounds: We both made mistakes here.
We're both equally to blame, honestly.
You raised your voice too, so let's not pretend you're innocent.
It takes two people to wreck a marriage.
I forgot your birthday, you forgot the trash. We're even.
Neither of us is perfect.
There's wrong on both sides, so let's call it a draw.
nots: A conflict in which both people did contribute in a similar degree, and each can name their part in detail.
Someone adding their own smaller mistake to the account, as in 'I was wrong to snap at you, and I also need to talk about the money'.
A mediator who encourages both parties to look at their own role, as a process step before sorting out size.
A true statement that nobody is perfect, said alongside an honest account of what each person did.
A group project or team failure where responsibility really is spread across many people.

compendium.name: Aftercare Control
compendium.what: Recasting a hurtful act as a kindness after it happened, so the person who was hurt begins to doubt their own memory of the harm.
compendium.why: If a painful event gets renamed as help, you lose the word for what you went through. Without that word it is hard to ask for change, and gratitude ends up expected where an apology was owed.
compendium.healthy: "I'm sorry that hurt you — that wasn't okay, regardless of my intentions."
sounds: I only did that because I care about you.
One day you'll thank me for it.
It wasn't punishment. It was discipline, and you needed it.
You call that hurtful? I was helping you.
If I hadn't pushed you like that, you'd still be stuck.
Be grateful someone was willing to be honest with you.
Nobody else would have taken the trouble.
nots: A parent explaining why a curfew exists while also saying 'I know it felt unfair.' The reason and the hurt are both allowed to stand.
A later, honest realization that a painful choice did protect you, offered without telling you how to feel about it.
Someone describing what they were thinking at the time. Giving a reason is different from ruling out your experience.
Hard feedback from a coach or editor who stays open to hearing that it landed roughly.
An apology that carries context, such as 'I was scared for you, and I handled it badly.'
You, years on, deciding for yourself that something rough was good for you. That reframe belongs to you.

compendium.name: Clinical Tone Policing
compendium.what: Responding to a person's report of pain, fear or distress by judging how they express it, as 'dramatic' or 'catastrophizing', instead of addressing what they reported.
compendium.why: When a person with training and a title calls a worry excessive, you may drop it, even when it was reasonable, and it may then go unexamined. The label can also stay in your records and shape how the next person reads you.
compendium.healthy: "This sounds really distressing — let's go through what we know and what we don't."
sounds: Let's not catastrophize.
I can see you're quite worked up. Let's calm down before we talk about the pain.
You're being a bit dramatic about your symptoms.
That sounds like health anxiety.
Try to take the emotion out of this and stick to the facts.
I think you're reading far too much into this.
You seem to be very emotional today.
nots: A clinician gently pointing out that a worry has grown larger than the evidence supports, while still examining the thing worried about.
A therapist using the word catastrophizing in a session you chose, as part of a method both of you are working with.
A direct, brisk bedside manner that says little about feelings but still takes the symptoms seriously.
A reasonable request to slow down so the professional can take a history without being talked over.
An assessment that you are not at risk, with reasons given and an invitation to return if things change.

compendium.name: False Conclusion from Normal Labs
compendium.what: Treating a normal test result as proof that ongoing symptoms are not real, when the test could not have detected the cause of what the person describes.
compendium.why: When symptoms are dismissed on the strength of one result, diagnosis can be delayed and you can be left in pain or exhaustion with nothing to try next. You may also begin to wonder whether what you feel is real.
compendium.healthy: "Your labs are normal, and I still believe something is wrong — let's look further."
sounds: Your labs came back completely normal.
The scan is clear. There's nothing there.
All your numbers are within range, so I don't see what else we can do.
We've done the tests. It's not physical.
The bloodwork looks perfect for someone your age.
I'd suggest you speak to someone about stress.
If something were really wrong, it would show up by now.
nots: A normal result honestly explained as excluding a specific serious condition, followed by a plan for the symptoms that remain.
A provider saying 'we have not found the cause yet' and booking a follow-up.
Symptoms that settle over time, as the earlier normal results had suggested.
A clear statement of what the test cannot show, with an offer of other tests or monitoring.
A reasoned choice not to test further when a symptom is mild and brief and has no warning signs, explained to you.

compendium.name: Medical Gaslighting
compendium.what: Dismissing, minimizing or reattributing a patient's symptoms or pain in a medical setting until the patient is left doubting what their own body is telling them.
compendium.why: Dismissal delays diagnosis and treatment, and it teaches people, especially those from groups that medicine has often disbelieved, to distrust their own symptoms and to avoid seeking help the next time something is wrong.
compendium.healthy: "I don't have an answer yet, but I believe something is happening and we'll keep looking."
sounds: It's probably just anxiety.
There's nothing medically wrong with you.
Have you thought about losing a little weight?
Lots of women your age feel like this.
Pain isn't something we can measure, so I can't do much.
You're young and healthy. It's stress.
I'm not going to order that. It won't change anything.
Maybe you're just more sensitive to pain than most.
nots: A clinician who thinks anxiety or stress is the most likely cause, says why, and agrees to look further if symptoms continue.
A diagnostic work-up that is still in progress and has not yet produced an answer.
A wrong diagnosis made in good faith and corrected when new information appears.
A decision not to order a test because guidelines do not support it for this symptom, explained to you plainly.
A brisk appointment in an overloaded clinic where the pace, not disbelief, limited what could be done.
An accurate assessment that the symptom is minor, with a plan to review it if it changes.

compendium.name: Sexual Coercion
compendium.what: Using pressure, guilt, obligation or implied consequences to push someone into sexual activity without their free consent.
compendium.why: Saying yes under pressure is not the same as wanting to, and living with the difference can leave real marks: shame, numbness, loss of trust in your own signals. You are not to blame for what pressure made you do. Naming it can help restore your sense of your own limits.
compendium.healthy: A healthy dynamic treats "no" as a complete sentence, every time, with zero relational cost.
sounds: You owe me this after everything I've done for you.
If you really loved me, you would.
Everyone else does it. What is wrong with you?
Fine. I guess I'll find someone who will.
I'll be in a terrible mood all week if you say no again.
Don't be so dramatic. Just give in and get it over with.
You said you wanted to keep this job, didn't you?
nots: Telling a partner honestly that you feel disappointed or want more closeness, and then accepting 'not tonight' without a penalty.
Flirting and asking once, with the other person free to decline and no change in the mood afterwards.
Partners who talk openly about a mismatch in desire and work out together what to do about it.
Changing your mind in the moment and saying so, with the other person stopping straight away.
Your own mixed feelings after saying yes, which can be worth talking over with a counselor but do not by themselves show that pressure occurred.

compendium.name: Financial Control
compendium.what: Restricting someone's access to money, financial information or earning, or using money and assets as leverage, so that they depend on one person.
compendium.why: Money decides whether a person can pay rent, buy food, hire a lawyer or leave a bad situation. When access depends on compliance, every disagreement carries a price, and the practical options narrow without anyone saying so out loud.
compendium.healthy: Shared, transparent finances that both people can see and neither can unilaterally lock the other out of.
sounds: "You don't need your own bank account."
"I'll decide what you get to spend."
"You're not allowed to work."
"My money, my rules."
"You'll get your allowance when you behave."
"Ask me for permission before you spend."
"Everything here is in my name."
"I'll cut off your card."
nots: Agreed household budgeting where one person tracks the books and the other can see everything and change the arrangement.
A temporary arrangement during real hardship, discussed openly and with an end in sight.
A one-earner household with shared rules, where both people have access to the money.
Long-term financial interdependence built through a mutual relationship, which is common and not used as leverage.
A couple who agree to run big purchases past each other, in both directions.
A parent or guardian managing a minor's money, or an adult's money under a formal legal or care arrangement.

compendium.name: Weaponized Incompetence
compendium.what: A pattern in which someone seems unable to do an unwanted task, so that it falls to another person for good.
looks: 'You're just better at it' as a permanent division of labor.
Tasks done deliberately badly once, then never assigned again.
nots: A real gap in skill, such as someone who never learned to cook, who is willing to be taught and does improve.
Disability, ADHD, chronic illness or exhaustion, which can make some tasks truly harder, in ways that are not a choice.
A division of labor you both chose after talking it over, where the other person takes tasks of equal weight elsewhere.
A person new to a task who fumbles at first and gets better with each go.
One bad attempt on a day when someone was sick or distracted.
sounds: You're just better at it than I am.
I'll only do it wrong, and then you'll be annoyed.
I loaded the dishwasher and now nothing fits. You'd better do it.
I can't work out that form. Could you handle it?
You do it so much faster. It makes sense for you to keep doing it.
Don't ask me, I never know where anything goes.
A shirt returned pink from the wash, with the remark 'well, I tried'.
compendium.why: The task lands permanently on one person, along with the work of noticing it, asking about it, and eventually giving up on asking. Raising it also makes them sound as if they are complaining about help they were offered.

compendium.name: Strategic Apathy
compendium.what: Declaring 'I don't care' or 'whatever you want' at decision points, then criticizing whichever choice the other person makes.
looks: Refusal to state any preference, followed by criticism of whatever was chosen.
'I don't care' deployed precisely at decision points.
nots: Honest indifference about a small thing, with no later complaint about the outcome.
Depression, burnout or decision fatigue, where choosing really does feel impossible and the person says so openly.
A couple who agreed that one of them handles certain kinds of decisions, such as holidays or finances, and who trust each other's judgment.
Someone from a family or culture where deferring to the host or the other person is polite, and who means it.
A person who truly has no strong feeling on the matter and is happy with any result.
sounds: I don't care, you decide.
Whatever you want is fine with me.
Do what you want, you always do anyway.
It's your call. Don't blame me if it goes wrong.
(After the choice) Well, I wouldn't have picked that one.
(After the choice) I said I didn't mind, but I didn't think you'd pick that.
I'm not the one who chose it.
compendium.why: One person makes every decision alone and then carries the criticism for whichever way it went. Over time, deciding stops feeling like having a say and starts feeling like exposure.

compendium.name: Reverse Psychology
compendium.what: Arguing against the outcome you actually want, so that the other person's wish to resist or prove you wrong carries them to it.
looks: 'You probably couldn't handle it anyway' before a wanted commitment.
'Fine, don't come' delivered as a dare.
nots: Playful teasing between friends who both know it is a game, such as 'you will never beat me at chess.'
Honest doubt about your readiness, voiced out of concern, that the speaker would accept if you agreed with it.
A parent's mild trick with a toddler about eating vegetables, which is a common and openly understood game.
A coach challenging you to prove yourself, with the goal stated openly and your success wanted either way.
Plain reluctance to push you, in which the speaker truly would be fine with whichever way you choose.
sounds: You probably couldn't handle it anyway.
Fine, don't come. I'm sure you have better things to do.
I wouldn't ask you to take on that project. It might be too much for you.
Oh, you wouldn't want to move in with me. It would cramp your style.
Don't apply for it. They'd never pick you anyway.
You can say no. I'm sure you will.
compendium.why: The target's own resistance is what does the deciding, so a choice that felt like their own defiance may not have been theirs at all. Over time you might lose track of which of your decisions were really yours.

compendium.name: Malicious Compliance
compendium.what: Doing exactly what was asked, to the letter, in a way that predictably defeats the point of the request.
looks: A task completed in a way that satisfies the literal words of a request while clearly defeating its purpose.
"You told me to do X, so I did exactly X" delivered with visible satisfaction at the resulting failure.
nots: Genuine literal-mindedness. Many people, including many autistic people, take words at face value, and the result can look the same with no hostility behind it.
A declared work-to-rule action, where a team announces openly that it will follow every rule strictly as a protest. That is stated, not hidden.
A vague request that was met exactly as phrased. The gap may be in the instruction.
Declining to do unpaid or out-of-scope extras after being refused fair terms, which is a boundary about the job.
Following a safety or legal rule that is inconvenient but real.
Weak results from someone who lacked the context or skill and tried their best.
sounds: You said to send it to everyone on the list, so I did. All four hundred of them.
You told me to wait for your sign-off before ordering anything, so we've been without supplies all week.
You asked me to wash the dishes. You didn't say to dry them or put them away.
You said 'by Friday.' It's Friday, 11:58 at night.
I just did it the way you told me to, said flatly after something goes wrong.
Happy to. Just tell me every single step and I'll do exactly those steps.
A colleague follows a new procedure line by line for a job that used to take ten minutes, and it now takes the whole afternoon.
compendium.why: The person on the receiving end absorbs the failure with no clear grievance to name. The instruction was followed, so pointing at anything risks sounding unreasonable, and they are left wondering whether they asked badly.

compendium.name: Moral Licensing
compendium.what: Pointing to a good character or past good deeds as a reason the present complaint does not need an answer.
looks: "I'm one of the good ones" or a résumé of past virtue offered in place of addressing a specific, current complaint.
nots: Relevant context given alongside an answer: 'I know that stung and I was wrong about the deadline. I hope the last two years count for something.'
Someone hurt that an accusation overlooks years of effort, who says so while still engaging with the complaint.
A character witness in a formal process such as a hearing, where track record is relevant by design.
Genuine surprise: 'That doesn't sound like me. Tell me more about what happened.'
The private tendency, described in research, to relax standards after doing good. That is not a conversational move and cannot be seen in one exchange.
Two people in a long relationship reminding each other of their shared history with honesty and goodwill.
sounds: I have given up so much for this family. You're really going to bring this up now?
I volunteer every weekend. Ask anyone who knows me.
Do you know how many people I've helped? I'm not that kind of person.
In twenty years I've never had a single complaint.
After all the favors I've done for you, I'd expect a little trust.
I've always supported equality. I'd never say something like that.
A manager points to their leadership award when an employee reports how a meeting went.
compendium.why: A specific, current complaint goes unanswered because the conversation turns into a ruling on someone's overall goodness. The person who raised it never asked that question and cannot win it, and the original problem stays exactly where it was.

compendium.name: Strategic Self-Deprecation / Performed Humility
compendium.what: Putting yourself down or sounding modest at the moment criticism is due, so the other person ends up comforting you instead of raising their concern.
looks: Self-deprecating comments that reliably appear right before or during moments the person might otherwise be criticized.
The target frequently finds themselves comforting the person who was about to be held accountable.
nots: Genuine humility and self-aware humor. Plenty of people joke about their flaws with no concern waiting to be raised, and the joke changes nothing about what happens next.
Someone who is truly ashamed and spirals when a mistake is pointed out. Their distress is real, and it can still be a reason to slow the conversation rather than a sign of strategy.
A person who takes responsibility, such as 'I dropped the ball, here's what I'll change.' Naming a fault and then dealing with it is the opposite of deflecting.
Modest talk from someone raised to avoid sounding proud, who plays down real achievements in every setting.
Depression or low self-esteem, where harsh self-talk shows up all day and not only when feedback is due.
sounds: Oh, I know, I'm hopeless. I forget everything. You must be sick of me.
Go ahead, tell me what I did wrong this time. I'm sure it's terrible.
I'm such a bad friend. I don't even know why you put up with me.
Honestly, I'm not good enough for this job. I keep letting the whole team down.
You're so patient with me. I really don't deserve you.
I'm the worst at this, so whatever you were going to say, you're probably right.
Never mind, it's fine, I'm just a mess. Can you tell me it's okay?
compendium.why: You arrive with a concern and leave having given reassurance. The thing you came to say never gets said, and you may feel unkind for having wanted to say it. Over months, small concerns can pile up unspoken.

compendium.name: Priming / Narrative Seeding
compendium.what: Planting an interpretation of a person or event in someone's mind ahead of time, so that what they later see gets read through it.
looks: A pointed comment or story shared right before an event that quietly shapes how the event gets interpreted afterward.
nots: A briefing that gives you facts you can check, such as a colleague telling you the client moved the deadline twice last month.
A sincere warning from someone who had a bad experience and presents it as their experience, not as a fact about the person.
Reading someone through your own history with them, which is memory and not a frame handed to you.
A reputation that formed because many people independently reported the same thing.
A hunch you formed yourself from earlier meetings.
Ordinary scene-setting, such as a host mentioning that Grandpa is hard of hearing so you speak up.
sounds: Not to prejudice you, but you'll see what I mean when you meet him.
Just a heads-up before the meeting: she tends to take things personally.
I'm sure it's nothing, but keep an eye on how he reacts when money comes up.
You'll notice she goes quiet when something is off.
A relative describes your partner to the whole family before the first dinner, in a tone of concern.
A new manager's first week opens with a colleague's three-minute account of who to be careful around.
Everyone says the last team lead was awful, so watch how this one handles it.
compendium.why: You read an event through a lens you never chose and mistake a supplied conclusion for your own judgment. The frame is hardest to question because it arrived before the evidence did, so by the time you look, you already know what you expect to see.

compendium.name: Push-Pull
compendium.what: Swinging between closeness and distance in repeating cycles, so the other person keeps working to get back to the warm stretch.
looks: Affectionate messages followed by sudden distance without explanation, repeatedly.
The temperature of the conversation swings on the manipulator's schedule, not events.
nots: A person who goes quiet under real pressure, such as a death in the family, an illness, or a work crunch, and tells you so.
An introvert who needs regular solitary time and says so plainly, with a predictable rhythm you can plan around.
Two people early in dating who are still working out how much contact suits each of them.
Ambivalence that is stated openly: 'I'm unsure about this' is hard to hear but is an honest message, not a cycle.
A relationship with a real distance difference, such as shift work or time zones, where the gaps follow the schedule.
sounds: Three days of good-morning texts and plans for the weekend, then no reply until Thursday night.
"I've just been really busy," said with no mention of the plans that were dropped.
"I missed you so much," arriving the day after you finally went out with friends.
"I'm not sure what I want right now," followed two weeks later by "Why are you being so distant?"
A warm voice call at midnight after a week of one-word texts, and no mention of the week.
"Don't read into it. I'm just like this sometimes."
compendium.why: You start organizing your attention around a temperature you cannot predict, and you tend to read every cold spell as something you must have caused. That can crowd out your own plans, friendships and sleep.

compendium.name: Intermittent Reinforcement
compendium.what: Handing out affection, praise or kindness unpredictably and rarely, so that the few good moments hold a person more tightly than steady warmth would.
looks: Long stretches of criticism or indifference punctuated by occasional, intense warmth.
The target works harder and harder for rarer and rarer good moments.
nots: A relationship with ordinary variation in mood, where kind days are still the large majority.
A partner or boss who is consistently reserved, and shows appreciation in small, steady ways that do not look like praise.
A season of grief, illness or overwhelm in which the other person has less warmth to give.
A family culture that rarely says 'I love you' aloud but shows it reliably through actions.
A pleasant surprise after a difficult period of real conflict, with an honest conversation attached.
sounds: Weeks of 'fine' and 'whatever you want,' then one evening of "You're the best thing in my life."
A supervisor who ignores your reports for months and then praises you in front of the team.
"See, this is how it could always be, if you tried a bit harder."
A parent who is cold through most of a visit and then hugs you tightly at the door.
Silence when you do well, and a thank-you only when you stay late or give up something you wanted.
"I do love you. You just don't see it."
compendium.why: Effort goes up while the returns go down. The rarity of the good moments is what makes them feel worth waiting for, so the loop can feed itself, and you may end up measuring the whole relationship by its best hour.

compendium.name: Breadcrumbing
compendium.what: Sending just enough sporadic attention to keep someone hopeful and available, while the contact never turns into real plans or commitment.
looks: Occasional low-effort messages ('hey stranger', a like, an emoji) after long silence, never converting to plans.
Warmth spikes whenever the target seems to be moving on.
nots: A person who is busy in a demanding season and is honestly slow, but makes real plans when they are free.
A mutual casual connection in which both of you know what it is and neither expects more.
Someone shy or anxious who sends small signals because bigger ones feel risky, and who speeds up when you reach out.
A friendship that runs on occasional contact and is fine with that on both sides.
A new connection that is honestly still undefined, where both of you are working out what you want.
sounds: "Hey stranger" after six weeks of nothing.
A heart on your photo and no reply to your actual message.
"We need to catch up soon!" and then no day suggested.
"Sorry, work has been insane. Let's talk this week," repeated each month.
A late-night text that says only "thinking of you."
Plans that are agreed in principle and then 'let's see how the week goes' when you propose a date.
Messages that become frequent and warm right after their other plans fall through, then thin out again.
A direct question about where this is going gets a compliment, an emoji, or a new subject.
compendium.why: You may hold a place open for a relationship that never arrives, on the strength of contact that costs almost nothing to send. Time, other opportunities and your sense of what you are worth can quietly drain away.

compendium.name: Trauma Bonding
compendium.what: A strong attachment that forms through cycles of hurt followed by comfort from the same person, so that fear and closeness become tangled together.
looks: Intense reconciliations after intense harm, described as proof of how deep the connection is.
Feeling most attached right after the worst episodes.
nots: Two people bonded by shared hardship from outside, such as caring for a sick child or surviving a disaster, where neither is the source of the pain.
A couple who quarrel loudly, apologize honestly and change something afterwards, so the same fight does not repeat.
Ordinary attachment to someone you love who has hurt you once, and who has since taken full responsibility.
The strong loyalty of family members who have been through difficult years together, with no one inflicting the harm.
A person's long-standing attachment style, which may make partings painful without anyone causing the pain.
sounds: "I've never felt closer to anyone than I do right now," said the night after a screaming match.
"Nobody understands us. We've been through so much."
A tearful apology, a long hug and a promise, a few hours after you were threatened or humiliated.
Your own voice saying, "It's not always like this. You should see how good it is when it's good."
"If I didn't love you this much, I wouldn't get this upset."
A friend asking why you stay, and your sense that they could not understand the part after the fight.
compendium.why: Relief and harm come from the same person, so your strongest feeling of closeness can arrive just after the worst treatment, and then becomes a reason to stay. Knowing this can help you tell the strength of a feeling from the safety of a relationship.

compendium.name: Relief Bait
compendium.what: A burst of kindness placed right after hurtful treatment, so that relief takes the place of an honest reckoning with what happened.
looks: Cruelty followed within hours by uncharacteristic sweetness, gifts, or tenderness — then the cycle repeats.
The 'good moments' cluster suspiciously right after the bad ones.
nots: A sincere apology that names what was done, explains what will change, and comes with a gift or a kind act as an addition.
A couple who often comfort each other after tension and do so with open acknowledgement of what was said.
A person who is warm by nature and offers kindness as a gesture of care at many different times, not only after hurting you.
A move to lighten the mood after a minor disagreement that both of you consider settled.
Reaching out after an argument because they cannot bear the distance, followed by a talk the next day.
sounds: A bunch of flowers and "Let's not fight anymore, okay?" the morning after being called useless.
"Come here. I'm making your favorite dinner." with no mention of what was said at lunchtime.
A sudden "I booked us a weekend away!" the day after a week of silence.
"Why bring it up now? We were having such a nice evening."
A gentle back rub, a joke, and "See? We're fine."
A sweet message at 9 p.m. after a harsh one at noon, with no reference to it.
compendium.why: Each round of kindness resets what you will put up with, so the level of treatment you accept can drop without you noticing it move. You also lose the chance to have the original harm discussed.

compendium.name: Dr. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde
compendium.what: Showing one warm, admired face to the world and another harsh one to a particular person, which leaves nobody else seeing the treatment that person receives.
looks: Message history swings between two unrecognizably different voices.
Witnesses see only the charming version; the target has screenshots of the other.
nots: A shy or tired person who is quiet at home and animated at work, with no harshness toward anyone in either place.
A professional who is polished with clients and grumpy after a long day, but who owns it and repairs it.
Someone with a hard private temper who is open about it, so others also know and can judge.
A relationship where outsiders simply have not seen ordinary arguments, which many couples keep to themselves.
A person who is guarded in public but relaxed and kind at home, which is the reverse of this split.
Someone whose public warmth is genuine and consistent with, if more understated than, their private behavior.
sounds: A friend says, "But he's so lovely whenever I see him. Are you sure?"
In front of guests: "Isn't she wonderful? I'd be lost without her." At home, hours later, a cold silence.
"No one is going to believe you. Look how everyone sees me."
A pleasant, joking voice at the party; a flat, hostile one on the drive home.
"You've got everyone fooled into thinking I'm the bad one."
Warm texts to your family, curt and critical ones to you.
Affectionate posts and public compliments that rise on the days the private mood is worst.
compendium.why: You have no witnesses. The version other people know makes your account of the other version sound implausible, including to yourself, and anyone you might turn to has only seen the public one.

compendium.name: Ambient Abuse
compendium.what: A steady climate of tension, criticism and unpredictability in which no single moment looks serious but the whole leaves a person worn down.
looks: No individual line is extreme, yet reading the whole thread feels like walking on eggshells.
Constant low-grade correction, sighing disapproval, and conditional moods.
nots: A season of money worry, illness or a new baby, when everyone in the house is snappy and the tension eases as things settle.
A family or workplace culture of blunt speech, where criticism is frequent but applied the same to everyone and not held over anyone.
A person's own anxiety making a mostly calm home feel tense, which a counselor might help sort out without blaming anyone.
An argument that was loud but ended, was talked about afterward, and did not leave days of dread.
A housemate with a bad mood they own and apologize for.
sounds: A heavy sigh when you walk into the kitchen, and no reply when you ask what's wrong.
"Oh, you're doing it that way."
A cheerful morning followed by a slammed cupboard at six, with no explanation given.
"Fine. Do whatever you want." said in a tone that makes clear it is not fine.
A dinner where everyone talks lightly and watches one person's mood.
Compliments that arrive only on the days when nothing went wrong.
compendium.why: There is nothing to quote, so the exhaustion has no justification the target can offer to anyone, themselves included. They stay braced without being able to say what for.

compendium.name: Ghosting-Orbiting Cycle
compendium.what: Going silent in direct messages while still viewing, liking or reacting to someone's posts, so they are neither in contact nor free of it.
looks: No replies for weeks, but every story viewed within minutes.
Reappearing with a small reaction whenever the target seems to be moving on.
nots: Passive scrolling by someone who simply drifted away and never got round to unfollowing, with no pattern of returns.
A person who said they needed space, even clumsily, and still glances at public posts.
Slow or absent replies from someone who is ill, grieving or overwhelmed and has no energy to write.
An app that puts familiar names at the top of lists, so a view is the algorithm and not a choice.
Two people staying on each other's feeds after an ending both understood, as many do within shared friend groups.
sounds: Three weeks of unanswered messages, yet their name is first in your story viewer list every day.
A heart on a photo from two years ago, the same day you post about a new job.
Hey stranger, I was just thinking about you, arriving after a month of nothing and followed by silence again.
A single emoji reply to your story, with no answer to the question you sent last week.
Messages marked seen within minutes and never answered.
A fresh follow request soon after you muted or unfollowed them.
compendium.why: You are neither in contact nor free of it. Attention keeps arriving with no reply attached, and each small sign can revive hope at exactly the point it was beginning to fade.

compendium.name: Sealioning
compendium.what: Pressing someone, again and again and in a polite tone, to produce evidence or explanation, in a way that wears them out without moving toward understanding.
looks: Every point is met with 'source?' or 'prove it' rather than engagement with the substance.
The questions never stop, no matter how much evidence is provided.
nots: A real question from someone new to a subject, who thanks you and moves on to the next point.
Peer review, fact-checking or cross-examination, where demanding evidence is the job.
One careful request for a source on a surprising claim.
A skeptic who tells you what would change their mind, and then either changes it or states where they stand.
A heated argument where both sides question each other hard but stay on topic and either can end it.
A forum moderator asking for sources because the community's rules require them.
sounds: Sorry, I'm just trying to understand. Which study?
That source is one outlet. Do you have another?
What exactly do you mean by 'often'? Can you give me a number?
I'm only asking questions. Why are you getting upset?
You still haven't answered my earlier question.
Can you define 'harm' before we go any further?
If you can't provide that, I'll have to assume you're wrong.
A reply lands within minutes of each message, for days, each asking for one more item.
compendium.why: The target's energy goes into finding sources and proving points rather than being heard. The point they set out to make often gets dropped, not because it was answered but because they ran out of stamina.

compendium.name: Idealize-Devalue-Discard Cycle
compendium.what: A three-stage arc in which someone is first placed on a pedestal, then steadily criticized and diminished, and finally dropped.
looks: An opening period of intense, almost scripted-feeling admiration, followed by a slow reversal into criticism and eventual discard.
If there's a 'replacement,' they may describe an eerily similar opening phase.
nots: The normal end of infatuation, where the first intensity settles into something calmer and both people are still kind.
A relationship that ended because of real, specific problems both people could name, such as different wants about children or place.
Disappointment that goes both ways, with each person feeling let down and able to say why.
One painful break-up after a fast start, with no sign of the same arc elsewhere in the person's history.
A person ending a relationship plainly and respectfully, even if the way it ended hurts.
sounds: "I've never met anyone like you. It's like I've known you forever."
Later: "You used to be so interesting. What happened to you?"
"The ambition I loved is just selfishness, honestly."
Mentioning a former partner as 'crazy' who 'never appreciated me', in a story that sounds like the early praise you got.
"I don't know who you are anymore."
A final message or a block, with "I gave you everything" and no way to reply.
compendium.why: You measure the ending against the extraordinary beginning and conclude you must have caused the decline, which is also the conclusion that keeps you trying to earn the beginning back. It can be hard to grieve a relationship that changed shape so completely.

compendium.name: Extinction Bursts
compendium.what: A sudden, sharper surge of a pressure tactic right after it stops working, as the person tries harder to get the old result back.
looks: A sudden spike in intensity or a new, harsher tactic appearing right after the target successfully resisted or set a boundary for the first time.
"This has never happened before" moments that follow a clear act of resistance.
nots: Hurt or panic after a surprising boundary. Most people react badly to a change in a long-standing arrangement and then settle.
A person who is upset, says so once, and then adjusts over the next few weeks.
Honest persistence about something urgent, such as a bill that really is due, which is not tied to your having said no.
Grief or fear in someone who is already struggling, where the intensity comes from their situation and not from the old method failing.
Your own wish to find a pattern in a rough week. A bad few days after a hard talk is not yet a shape.
sounds: "You've never done this to me before. What has gotten into you?"
Eleven missed calls and a stream of texts the evening after you said no to a request.
"Fine. If that's how you feel, I'll just stop trying. Is that what you want?"
A cold week of silence that suddenly flips into flowers, tears and a long apology on day eight.
"I can't believe you'd do this after everything."
A family group chat that fills with messages about you a day after you declined the usual favor.
A coworker who used to ask once and now copies your manager after you said you could not take the extra shift.
compendium.why: The first boundary that actually works is the one that costs the most. It can teach you that holding a limit makes things worse, so giving in starts to feel like the only way to get peace again.

compendium.name: Competitive Victimhood
compendium.what: Meeting someone's hurt with a bigger hurt of your own, so the conversation ends up about whose pain is worse.
looks: Every time you raise something that hurt you, the conversation ends up about how much worse it's been for them.
This happens consistently enough that you've stopped bringing things up.
nots: Someone in a crisis of their own who says so honestly and comes back to your concern later.
A friend or parent sharing a similar experience ('I felt like that too') to show they understand.
Two people taking turns, with both concerns getting airtime in one conversation.
Weighing relative need when help is limited, such as deciding who gets a scarce place on a program.
Someone too overwhelmed to take it in who says 'I can't absorb this right now, can we talk tomorrow?'
sounds: You think that's bad? Try being me this month.
At least you have somewhere to go home to.
I've had it much worse, and you don't see me complaining.
Well, if we're comparing, I'm the one who's actually suffering.
You have no idea what I'm carrying.
That's nothing compared to what I went through at your age.
Funny, I don't hear you asking how I'm doing.
compendium.why: Your own pain never gets a hearing. Rather than enter a contest you cannot win, you may stop raising things at all, and the relationship goes on with nothing said.

compendium.name: Ambient Sexual Threat
compendium.what: A sexually charged or menacing atmosphere around a person, kept alive through repeated small signals, so they stay on guard with nothing definite to report.
looks: A pattern of comments, looks described secondhand, or 'jokes' that consistently leave you uneasy, across many separate incidents.
You find yourself managing your schedule or location around this person without being able to say exactly why.
nots: A single clumsy compliment or off-color joke that the person took back as soon as it was pointed out.
A friendly colleague who greets everyone warmly and has no pattern of focusing on you.
A culture of bawdy humor shared evenly by everyone who takes part, where nobody is uncomfortable and anyone could opt out.
Your own feeling of unease with someone whose behavior has not changed and who has done nothing you can describe, which is worth taking seriously but does not prove a pattern.
A partner or date whose sexual remarks are welcomed and reciprocal.
sounds: "You look good in that. Don't tell anyone I said so."
A running joke about what you would be like in bed, said in front of others.
"Relax, I'm only kidding. You're no fun."
Appearing at the edge of the break room, again, when you are alone.
A look from across the room, held a beat too long, on more days than not.
"I always know where you are." said with a smile.
compendium.why: The target reorganises their movements, schedule and attention around one person while holding nothing concrete enough to report, or even to explain to a friend.

compendium.name: "Polite Hostile" Environments
compendium.what: A workplace or social setting that stays courteous on the surface while quietly penalizing anyone who speaks plainly or disagrees.
looks: Every formal interaction is impeccably polite, yet raising real concerns is consistently followed by subtle exclusion, cooled relationships, or stalled opportunities.
Colleagues describe a 'vibe' they can't quite name in official terms.
nots: A workplace where politeness is a real norm and people who disagree respectfully are still heard and promoted.
A company going through budget cuts, where several people's projects stall for stated business reasons.
A single raised concern that went nowhere because the issue was weighed and judged minor.
A reserved culture where people are formal with everyone, not only with those who spoke up.
Honest feedback about how a concern was delivered, which may be fair even when it stings.
sounds: Every formal exchange is warm, and raising a real concern is followed by weeks of cooler replies.
A manager says 'thanks for flagging this, really valuable' and the next project goes to a colleague.
Staff describe a 'vibe' that no one can name in official terms.
Someone who questioned a decision is described as 'not quite aligned with the team'.
A review lists no problems, yet the person is repeatedly left off planning meetings after speaking up.
Colleagues say privately 'you can think that, just don't say it in the meeting'.
Invitations to informal events stop arriving after a complaint, with no one ever saying why.
compendium.why: Nothing that happens is documentable, so whoever spoke up carries the cost alone, with no evidence to present. Everyone watching learns that silence is the sensible option, and the place slowly loses its honest voices.

compendium.name: Self-Gaslighting Induction
compendium.what: The habit of doubting your own memory and perception on reflex, long after anyone else has needed to challenge it.
looks: Catching yourself saying 'maybe I'm remembering it wrong' about things you documented.
Pre-editing your account of events to match their version.
nots: Everyday epistemic humility: checking a calendar or admitting an error is healthy and shows an open mind.
Honest haziness about something long ago or something you only half noticed.
Updating your view after credible new evidence, which is an ordinary use of reasoning.
A normal memory slip under stress, tiredness or distraction, which happens to everyone.
A medical memory problem, which has its own causes and needs a doctor, not a pattern label.
sounds: Catching yourself saying 'maybe I'm remembering it wrong' about something you wrote down at the time.
Rehearsing an account that matches someone else's version before you have said what you remember.
Feeling a jolt of uncertainty about an event you can picture clearly.
Opening a sentence with 'I'm probably overreacting, but...' about something that plainly upset you.
Rereading your own saved messages to see whether you are allowed to be upset.
Telling a friend the story and then adding 'but I might have it wrong' unprompted.
compendium.why: The doubting continues with nobody present to do it. You discount things you clearly remember and edit your own account before anyone has even challenged it.

compendium.name: Fawning
compendium.what: Responding to a threatening person by pleasing, agreeing and shrinking yourself, as an automatic way of staying safe.
looks: Apologizing for things that were done to you.
Feeling your own opinions dissolve mid-sentence when they frown.
nots: Everyday kindness, tact or good manners in which you choose to be agreeable and could do otherwise.
Cultural norms of respect or deference toward elders, which are about values and not about fear.
Fair compromise between two people who each give something up and neither is afraid.
A preference for peace or a dislike of conflict that shows up in safe relationships too.
Professional courtesy to a customer or boss, which follows the job and not a sense of danger.
sounds: Apologizing for something that was done to you, before anyone asks.
Hearing yourself say 'you're right, I'm sorry' while privately thinking you are not wrong.
Laughing along with a cruel joke because the room feels tense.
Feeling your opinion drain away mid-sentence when someone's face changes.
Noticing you have already rehearsed an apology for something you do not think you did.
Telling someone what they want to hear, then feeling sick afterward.
Offering help before being asked, to read their mood.
compendium.why: Safety is bought with the target's own position: they apologize for things done to them, and lose track of what they actually think while they are still saying it.

compendium.name: Identity Erosion
compendium.what: The slow loss of your own tastes, opinions, limits and friendships inside a relationship, until the person you were earlier is hard to find.
looks: Not remembering what music you liked before them.
Answering 'we think' to questions about what you think.
nots: Growing and changing in a good partnership, where both people try new things and both keep parts of their old selves.
A move, a new job or a new baby that naturally replaces old routines and friends for a while.
Falling out of an old hobby because you lost interest, with nobody encouraging that.
Ordinary compromise, which is mutual and bounded: each person gives something up and both can say what.
Putting a partner's urgent need first during an illness or crisis, then returning to your own baseline afterwards.
The ordinary blur of early adulthood, when many people are still working out who they are.
sounds: "I don't know, whatever you want is fine."
"I used to love painting, but I haven't picked up a brush in years."
"I haven't seen my college friends since we moved in together. It just sort of happened."
"What do I think about it? I'd have to check what we think."
"I can tell you what would keep things calm. I can't tell you what I want."
Finding an old playlist and not recognizing a single song as yours.
"I swore I would not say yes to that again, and I just said yes."
"I can't remember what I wore before I met them."
compendium.why: You can say what would keep the peace far more readily than what you want, and your own limits stop being information you are willing to act on. That makes it harder to judge a situation, to describe what you need, or to reach the people who could help.

compendium.name: Internalized Conditioning
compendium.what: Following rules and reactions that once came from another person, now enforced from inside your own head even when that person is nowhere near.
looks: Hearing their voice narrate your choices when they're not present.
Pre-punishing yourself before they even react.
nots: A conscience or personal values. Values you have examined and would choose again are yours, even if a parent first taught them.
Thinking about how a partner or friend will feel before you act. That is care, and it is one input among several.
Ordinary habits picked up from the family you grew up in, such as how you load a dishwasher or when you say thank you.
A loved person's remembered advice that comforts you and leaves the decision with you.
Anxiety or perfectionism with no single origin in one person, which has its own causes and its own treatments.
Respect for a workplace or faith rule that you understand and accept.
sounds: She would hate this haircut. I'll cancel the appointment.
I haven't told anyone yet and I already feel like I'm in trouble.
I can't eat that in front of people. Nobody has said a word, I just can't.
Why am I rehearsing an apology for something nobody is angry about?
I know he isn't here. I still keep my voice down on the phone.
It's my own apartment and I still scrub the counters the second I get home, because otherwise I hear him.
I turned down the offer before I even asked myself whether I wanted it.
compendium.why: The rules keep running when the other person is gone, so distance, even the end of the relationship, does not bring the relief you expected. You can leave the room and still find yourself obeying.

compendium.name: Silence Installation
compendium.what: A learned inability to speak about specific things, where the thought of naming them brings dread because raising them has repeatedly cost more than staying quiet.
looks: Rehearsing a sentence for weeks and never saying it.
Physical dread at the thought of naming the problem.
nots: Privacy or discretion, which is a choice made with a clear head about who needs to know.
Waiting for a better moment, such as holding a hard topic until after a deadline or a funeral.
Shyness or introversion that shows up across every subject and not around particular ones.
A cultural habit of not discussing certain topics at the table, where leaving them unspoken costs you nothing.
Social anxiety or selective mutism, which are separate conditions with their own clinical assessment.
Not being ready to talk about a loss, where silence is part of coping and was never a response to penalties.
sounds: I have practiced it in the shower for a month. Then they walk in and I ask about dinner.
I opened my mouth and nothing came out.
It's not worth bringing up. It never goes well.
The sentence is ready in my head, and then my chest locks.
Every time I almost mention the money, I end up talking about the weather.
I told my friend everything was fine again. I don't know why I keep doing that.
Please don't ask me about it. I can't.
compendium.why: The problems most in need of raising become the ones you physically cannot raise, so they go unaddressed and quietly grow. Meanwhile other people may read your silence as agreement, or as proof that all is well.

compendium.name: Approval Addiction Cultivation
compendium.what: Coming to depend on one person's approval, often built through warmth that comes and goes unpredictably, until their reaction counts for more than your own judgment.
looks: Checking how they'll react before knowing how you feel.
A good day is defined by their mood toward you.
nots: Ordinary attachment, since wanting a partner or parent to be pleased with you is part of closeness.
Healthy attunement, such as noticing a partner's mood and adjusting while still keeping your own view.
Wanting honest feedback from a teacher, coach or manager so that you can improve.
General people-pleasing that shows up with everyone and has roots in temperament or earlier life.
A short stretch of extra care around someone who is grieving or ill.
Pride in your work that also welcomes other people's praise.
sounds: Did he sound happy when he said good morning? Maybe I did something.
I thought the presentation went well, but she hasn't said anything, so it probably didn't.
I'll decide what I think about the movie once I hear what she thought.
She called me brilliant on Tuesday. Now she's barely answering my texts. What did I do?
My whole weekend depends on whether he's in a good mood.
I changed my answer halfway through the sentence when I saw her face.
I only feel proud of something once they've said it was good.
compendium.why: Your sense of how you are doing gets handed to someone else's mood, and your own view of a thing arrives too late to count for much. A good day depends on a face you do not control.

compendium.name: Parentification
compendium.what: Being placed, as a child or partner, in the permanent role of caring for an adult's emotions, practical needs and crises, at the cost of your own development.
looks: Being the family's therapist, mediator, and crisis line since childhood.
Guilt at having needs of your own.
nots: Age-appropriate chores, such as setting the table or looking after a pet, which teach skill without displacing a child's needs.
A short season of extra help during illness, job loss or a death, which eases when the crisis does.
Caring for a sick or disabled relative as a free adult choice, with support and a way to step back.
Families where older children help raise siblings as a shared, supported arrangement and still receive care themselves.
A parent saying 'I'm sad today' once, without handing the child the job of fixing it.
Adult children helping aging parents, which is a normal turn in the life cycle.
sounds: You're the only one I can talk to. Sit down, I need to tell you about your father.
I don't know what I'd do without you. You're my rock.
Can you call the landlord? You're better at this than I am.
Don't upset your mother, you know how she gets.
You are so mature for your age.
Go and see if he's okay. I can't deal with him tonight.
If I take one evening off, I think everything will fall apart.
compendium.why: You come to treat your own needs as an imposition, and the growing-up that was postponed to keep an adult afloat does not happen later on its own. Resting may seem like neglecting someone.

compendium.name: Process Exhaustion
compendium.what: A process that keeps adding steps, forms, meetings and re-reviews until the person gives up from tiredness, not because their matter was decided.
looks: Every complaint triggers a new process that restarts the clock.
Resolution is always one more form away.
nots: A complex matter that really needs several expert steps and a long time, with each step building on the last.
A slow office short of staff, where every applicant waits the same long time.
Required documents and safeguards meant to prevent fraud or protect others, which feel heavy but apply equally to everyone.
An appeals ladder that is long but stated up front, with stage timelines you can plan around.
A delay caused by a real error, such as a lost file, that is then fixed with credit for the time already waited.
Waiting on a third party, such as a lab or a court date, that nobody in the process controls.
sounds: We received your form, but we need it on the new version. The review period starts again from today.
That office handles part of this. You'll need to file the other part with them.
Your request was closed because we did not hear back within ten days.
We need those documents again. The earlier ones have been archived.
The review committee meets quarterly. Your case will be considered at the next meeting.
To appeal, first request a reconsideration, then the appeal form, then a hearing date.
Your case manager has changed. Please explain the situation to them from the beginning.
compendium.why: You lose through depletion instead of a decision, and the record shows it as your choice: you withdrew, you did not follow up, you stopped replying.

compendium.name: HR Shielding
compendium.what: A workplace complaints process that in practice protects the organization's reputation and the accused person more than the employee who reported harm.
looks: Reports met with concern for 'how this looks' rather than what happened.
The reporter, not the behavior, becomes the problem to manage.
nots: Due process protects the accused too. A fair process lets them respond and limits who learns the details, which can feel one-sided to the person who reported.
HR staff who explain the limits of confidentiality at the start, follow a policy that disappoints you, or reach a conclusion you disagree with are doing the job as designed, not colluding.
A finding of 'not substantiated' means the evidence did not meet the standard. It is not the same as being disbelieved.
An under-trained or overloaded HR team producing a slow, clumsy process through lack of capacity.
HR advising a manager on how to handle a case, done openly and fairly to both sides, which is part of the role.
sounds: We want to make sure this doesn't get blown out of proportion.
Let's think about how this looks for the team.
Before we go further, can you tell me everything, including who else you have spoken to?
I can't share the outcome with you. It's confidential.
Your manager knows the details of your report before you have been told what happens next.
The case is closed as 'no further action' without the witnesses you named being interviewed.
You are offered a move to another team, while the person you reported stays where they are.
A performance review that was fine last year now lists new concerns about you.
compendium.why: Someone brings a complaint believing they are speaking to a protector, and finds that what they said has been used to shape the response against them. They absorb the disruption while the situation continues, and colleagues learn what reporting costs.

compendium.name: Pseudo-Consultation
compendium.what: Asking for opinions, feedback or comment after the decision is already settled, so the input has nothing left to change.
looks: Feedback sessions scheduled after contracts are signed.
'All voices heard' followed by the original plan, unchanged.
nots: A consultation that says up front what is fixed, for example, "The budget is set, but you can shape how it is spent." Honest limits are not staged influence.
Feedback on how to carry out a decision that really is final, when that narrower scope is stated plainly.
A real consultation where the decision went against most of the people who spoke. Losing a fair process is not the same as never having had one.
A legal requirement to hold a comment period that the body treats seriously, even if the final text changes only a little.
A leader who listened, weighed everything and kept the original plan, and can say why.
sounds: "We value your input. The new schedule starts Monday, and we'd love to hear how you feel about it."
A town hall where the slides already show the final floor plan, and the sign-in sheet is collected at the door.
"Thank you all for your feedback, which has been carefully noted." Nothing in the next announcement differs from the draft you saw before the meeting.
A survey with a comment box, closing the day after the vendor contract was announced.
"The consultation showed broad support" cited in a report, when most people at the session objected out loud.
A staff meeting where the manager says, "Nothing is set in stone," and the new policy is in the handbook by the end of the week.
compendium.why: You spend real effort and real candor on input that could never have changed anything, and the decision is afterwards described as shared with you. Next time you may speak up less, or feel you gave up the right to object because you were asked.

compendium.name: Tokenism
compendium.what: Including one person or a small number from a group as a visible gesture, without giving them the voice or authority that inclusion seems to promise.
looks: One seat at the table, no vote.
Diversity in the photo, uniformity in the decisions.
nots: A first step toward inclusion that is sincere and has a visible plan for more seats and more influence.
A new role whose authority is still being defined and is growing in practice.
Being asked for your perspective on something you know well, when it is one voice among many and not a stand-in for a whole group.
A small team where everyone, including the newest member, has limited influence for ordinary reasons of seniority.
An organization that says honestly what the role can and cannot decide right now.
sounds: "We have a woman on our leadership page, so that criticism isn't fair."
"You're the only one here from that background, so what would your community think?"
A photo of the one new member of color placed at the front of the annual report.
"We'd love to have you at the table." The table has no vote for you and your suggestions are "noted."
"Look, we hired one already," said when someone asks why there are no others.
A panel invitation framed as an honor, with the speaking slot cut to five minutes.
compendium.why: Your presence gets used as the reply to the very criticism you were brought in to raise, and pushing back makes you look ungrateful for the seat. You can end up carrying the group's image while holding none of its power.

compendium.name: Individualization of Systemic Issues
compendium.what: Presenting a problem caused by workload, staffing or structure as a personal weakness that the individual is expected to fix.
looks: Burnout answered with wellness webinars instead of workload review.
'Have you tried a gratitude journal?' as a response to understaffing.
nots: A skill gap that coaching really would close, offered alongside a look at the workload.
A manager who says plainly that the staffing cannot change this year, and offers help coping in the meantime. That is a limit stated honestly.
A wellness program offered in addition to, and not instead of, a review of workloads.
