One person's difficulty that, when examined, is specific to their own approach and not shared by colleagues.
Advice from a friend about habits, given with no authority over your conditions.
sounds: "Have you tried blocking out time on your calendar?" in reply to being given three people's workload.
"Our wellness webinar on stress is Thursday, and all staff are welcome." The staffing request is not mentioned.
"Everyone else manages. Maybe it's about your boundaries."
A clinic told that waiting times are down to "patient attitudes," with no one examining appointment slots.
"We just need everyone to take more ownership of their stress levels."
A parent told the school problem would ease if the child were more motivated, though six other families report the same issue.
compendium.why: You add self-improvement to an already unsustainable load, and you conclude the shortfall is in your own resilience instead of in the conditions. Meanwhile the thing that is actually broken stays unexamined and keeps hurting the next person too.

compendium.name: Diffusion of Responsibility
compendium.what: Spreading a decision or a harm across so many people and steps that nobody can be found who is answerable for it.
looks: 'That's not my department' forming a perfect circle.
Decisions with consequences but no author.
nots: Large organizations dividing work among specialists, where someone can still tell you who owns your case.
Legitimate delegation to a person with more relevant expertise, who then answers for the result.
Honest confusion after a restructure, when staff really do not know who inherited a responsibility and are trying to find out.
A genuine referral to the correct office, which then takes the case.
A decision that many people shaped, but where a named person signs off and can explain it.
sounds: "That's not my department. You'll want billing." Billing says the account team, and the account team says billing.
"I only processed what the previous team sent me."
"The system generated that letter. No one reviewed it individually."
"The committee decided. I can't speak for the committee."
"I just followed the procedure, and the procedure came from head office."
A call transferred four times, each agent saying the previous one should have handled it.
compendium.why: The harm is real and nobody is answerable for it, so you have nowhere to take it, no one to ask for repair, and no way to stop it recurring. Hours go into being transferred, and the problem stays where it started.

compendium.name: Deepfakes
compendium.what: Fabricated images, video or audio made to show a real person doing or saying something they never did.
looks: Media of you that you know is fabricated, used to threaten, humiliate, or extort.
nots: Genuine footage that shows something embarrassing. Unflattering is not fake, and a real recording calls for a different response.
Satire or parody clearly labeled as such, where viewers are not meant to take it as a record.
Ordinary retouching, filters, color correction or dubbing that the person knowingly agreed to.
A low-resolution clip that looks strange because of how it was saved and re-shared many times.
A real photo with a false caption, where nothing was synthesized but the framing misleads.
A lookalike or impersonator filmed in real life, which is a different problem from synthetic media.
sounds: A clip or image of you circulating that shows a place, act or statement you know never occurred.
People you know reacting to something you have no memory of, and asking why you did it.
A sexual image carrying your face that you never posed for, posted to a forum or sent to your contacts.
A message demanding money, more images or silence, with a sample of the fabricated media attached as a reminder of what could be shared.
A video with no original upload, no named source, and a caption urging viewers to pass it along quickly.
Audio in your voice saying words you have never said, or a face and mouth that look slightly out of step, though a good fake may show neither flaw.
Posters who answer questions about where the footage came from with insults instead of a source.
compendium.why: The target is left disproving something that never happened, to people who have already seen it, and a denial can sound like what anyone caught would say. Shame and speed of sharing do much of the damage.

compendium.name: AI Voice Cloning
compendium.what: Software-made copies of a real person's voice, used to impersonate them in calls, messages or recordings.
looks: Calls or voice notes that sound like someone you know, saying things they deny — often paired with urgent money requests.
nots: A real call from a real person who is stressed, ill or in a noisy place and so sounds unlike themselves.
A human impression or prank by someone with a good ear.
An openly labeled automated voice, such as a clinic's appointment reminder.
A bad phone line, compression or Bluetooth echo that distorts a genuine voice.
A genuine recording that is unwelcome. Hearing yourself say something you regret is not proof it was cloned.
A voice copy that a person agreed to and disclosed, for example for audiobooks or accessibility.
sounds: A call in a voice that sounds like a relative's, describing an emergency that needs money right now.
A voice note from a boss or colleague asking for gift cards, a transfer or a login code, outside their usual habits.
A caller who resists being phoned back, or insists you stay on the line and tell no one.
The real person, reached another way, knowing nothing about the call.
A recording of someone supposedly admitting something, with no date, no setting and no one else on it.
Flat emotion, odd pauses or repeated phrasing in an otherwise convincing voice, though a clone may show none of these.
A voice-only request from someone who normally writes.
compendium.why: A voice you have trusted all your life stops being evidence of anything, and checking each unexpected call through a second channel becomes a permanent tax on ordinary contact. People can lose money or be blamed for words they never spoke.

compendium.name: Doxxing
compendium.what: Publishing a person's private details, such as a home address or workplace, so others can find or harass them.
looks: Your private details appearing in public threads alongside hostile framing.
nots: Information you chose to make public, such as your own business address on your website.
Naming a public official in connection with their public role, where office contact details are listed openly for that purpose.
A news report that names someone and describes a public act without personal contact details.
A neighbor knowing where you live, or a friend mentioning your employer to someone who also knows you.
Harsh criticism of your public statements or work.
A court or property record that has always been public. It can feel invasive, but its existence is not an invitation to harass.
sounds: A post that lists your address, employer or family names beside an angry account of something you are said to have done.
Strangers messaging or phoning you about a dispute, using your real name.
Deliveries, calls or visitors you did not request arriving at your home or workplace.
A thread where people trade more details about you and congratulate each other for finding them.
Your real name suddenly attached to an account you kept anonymous.
A photo of your house or street shared with a comment.
An employer or landlord receiving complaints that name you right after an online dispute.
compendium.why: Risk moves offline and out of your hands: your home, workplace and family become reachable by strangers who have no tie to the original dispute, and the exposure cannot be fully undone.

compendium.name: Sock Puppets
compendium.what: Fake accounts run by one person or a small group to pass as independent people, creating false agreement or pile-ons.
looks: Multiple 'strangers' with thin histories arriving in unison to support one person's version.
nots: Real people who share an opinion and post around the same time because a news story or a famous account prompted them.
A person's disclosed alternate accounts, such as a work account and a personal one.
A group openly organizing supporters under its real name.
New accounts made by people who joined just to follow a breaking event.
A fan community whose members repeat the same slogans and memes.
Automated bot accounts, which can look similar but are not one person pretending to be many.
sounds: Several new accounts with thin histories appearing together under a post to defend one person.
Replies that echo the same unusual phrase or talking point within minutes.
Accounts that praise or back each other and rarely talk to anyone else.
A witness who turns up to confirm a story and has no posts before the dispute.
Generic or stock-looking profile photos and handles ending in long strings of digits.
A set of accounts that are all active at the same odd hours.
A new account that knows details of a private argument it should not have seen.
compendium.why: You argue against what looks like a consensus and decide you are the outlier, when the numbers on the other side were never real. The same trick can make a pile-on feel like the verdict of many.

compendium.name: Fabricated Evidence
compendium.what: Presenting made-up or altered messages, images or documents as genuine proof of something that did not happen or was not said.
looks: 'Receipts' of things you never wrote, shown to third parties.
nots: A real screenshot cropped for brevity, with its meaning intact. Cropping is not forging.
Confusion about which conversation or time frame an image comes from. People mix up threads constantly.
Authentic images that look different because of another device, language setting or app update.
A genuine message quoted out of context. That can mislead, but the record itself is real, which is a different problem from invented content.
A sincere misremembering of what was written, from someone who shows what they honestly believe the message said.
A real record with a phone number or name blacked out for privacy, labeled as such, with the rest untouched.
sounds: 'Here are the receipts', followed by a screenshot of words you have no memory of writing.
A thread shown to your employer or friends that does not match the same conversation on your own phone.
A message under your name, with phrasing or punctuation you never use.
Timestamps, contact names or dates that do not fit when you were actually in touch, or an app layout that does not match the app it claims to come from.
A screenshot with no way to see the surrounding messages, and a refusal to produce the original phone or an export.
A document that cites an agreement, policy or payment you have never seen or signed.
'I don't need to show you the original. The picture says it all.'
compendium.why: Screenshots and documents are widely accepted as proof, so disproving a fake means asking people to doubt evidence they normally trust. Meanwhile your own account can start to look like the lie, and the harm can reach work, school or court before anyone checks the item.

compendium.name: Coordinated Reporting
compendium.what: Organized mass reporting of an account or post, often on false grounds, to get a platform to remove or restrict it.
looks: Accounts or posts removed in waves right after conflict with one person or group.
nots: Many independent people reporting a post that really breaks the rules.
A single mistaken removal by an automated filter.
A platform enforcing a rule you did not know about.
A follower reporting something harmful on their own.
A group openly flagging a real scam, where the reports match what is actually posted.
A platform outage or policy change that affects many accounts at once.
sounds: A sudden warning, strike or suspension arriving right after a public dispute.
A notice citing a rule that does not match what you posted.
Several posts removed within an hour for different stated reasons.
Followers telling you a thread or group is circulating your handle with encouragement to report it.
An account locked while the appeal sits unanswered.
Removal alerts arriving in bursts at similar times of day.
compendium.why: You can lose your account, your audience or your income through a system built to protect people, and appeals against decisions made on volume can be slow and hard to reach.

compendium.name: Credential-Costuming
compendium.what: Presenting invented, stretched or borrowed titles and affiliations so that a claim or request carries more authority than the person's real qualifications support.
nots: An unfamiliar credential is not a false one. Many genuine titles mean nothing outside their field, and a modest person may describe real experience in a way that sounds grand.
Honorary degrees, titles from other countries, and professional bodies that differ in how they name qualifications.
Titles that really belong to the person but are used loosely in conversation, such as calling a research fellow 'professor'. This is sloppy, and not necessarily invented.
Self-taught expertise, which can be real and deep with no certificate behind it, and which is not a costume if the person says so.
A job title that sounds big because a small company hands out large titles, which is a company habit.
sounds: As a top-university-trained strategist, I can tell you this won't work. (the university has no record of a degree)
I sit on the board of several major organizations, so I know how this goes.
You wouldn't understand the details. That's why people hire someone with my credentials.
A bio listing 'Doctor' and 'Professor' with no field, institution or year.
A website showing the logos of well-known companies under 'As seen in', where no article can be found.
A certificate image whose issuing body has no website, or one that does not list the person.
I've been advising the government on this for years, but I can't say who.
compendium.why: You defer to standing that is not there, and the questions you would otherwise ask start to feel out of place. Decisions, such as money, health or hiring choices, can then rest on the look of expertise instead of anything that was tested.

compendium.name: Identity Performances
compendium.what: Presenting a built persona, with claimed experiences and traits, that earns trust or access the person's real circumstances would not support.
nots: Everyone presents differently in different rooms. Someone rebuilding or still working out who they are is changing, not fabricating.
Code-switching, where a person shifts vocabulary or tone to fit a community without changing any facts about their life.
Privacy: leaving out painful details, or keeping an ex's name private, is not inventing false ones.
Exaggeration in a funny story, which listeners understand as storytelling.
People using a pen name or an online handle to keep their work life and personal life apart.
sounds: I went through the exact same thing, so I know just how you feel. (later, no part of the history fits)
A profile with photos that reverse-image search places on a stranger's account.
A person who is a nurse to one group, a former soldier to another, and has no record in either.
I can't video call because my camera is broken, again.
My family all passed away, so you're really all I have. (a sibling is later mentioned in passing)
Telling a support circle a severe personal story that a family member says never took place.
A new colleague whose past employers cannot recall them, and whose references are all one phone number.
compendium.why: You extend trust to a version of someone that does not exist, so your read on the relationship rests on facts that were supplied to you and never observed. When the gap appears, you can doubt your judgment as well as the person.

compendium.name: Social Engineering
compendium.what: Getting information, access or action out of someone by exploiting trust, urgency or social habits, usually under a false pretext such as a claimed role or emergency.
nots: Genuinely urgent, legitimate requests exist, and real IT or security staff follow processes that most people have never met. Checking back through a channel you already trust costs an honest request nothing, which makes it the cheap test here and not suspicion of the person.
A real colleague who is rushed and informal and writes a short, blunt email with no pretext at all.
Marketing or sales outreach that is pushy but honest about who is calling and what they want.
A friend or relative who actually has an emergency, which can be confirmed by calling them on their usual number.
A security drill run by your own employer that has been announced through official channels.
sounds: This is the fraud team at your bank. Someone is draining your account right now, and I need you to read me the code we just sent.
Hi, it's Dana from the CEO's office. I'm in a meeting and can't talk. Can you buy gift cards for a client and send me the numbers?
A text saying a package is held, with a link and a one-hour deadline.
IT here. We're locking your account in ten minutes unless you confirm your password.
Grandma, it's me, I'm in trouble. Please don't tell Mom. I need money wired today.
A visitor in a work vest, holding a box, who asks you to hold the door because they left their badge inside.
An email from a familiar name with a slightly different address, asking you to change where an invoice is paid.
compendium.why: What gets used is ordinary decency: being helpful, deferring to apparent authority, not wanting to make a fuss. So the loss afterwards, of money, access or privacy, can feel like a personal failing and not something that was done to you.

compendium.name: Performative Allyship / False Solidarity
compendium.what: Declaring support for a cause or group in public while private actions and choices do not match the words, so the support earns trust it has not backed up.
nots: Many people are further along in their stated values than in their practice and are genuinely, if unevenly, catching up.
Quiet support that is never announced anywhere is the reverse of this pattern, not a mild version of it.
Someone who supports a cause but is limited by real constraints, such as a precarious job, and says so honestly.
A newcomer to an issue who is learning, makes mistakes, and takes correction well.
A person who disagrees with one tactic of a movement while backing its aims.
sounds: I'm so proud to stand with you. You can always count on me. (and in the meeting, silence)
A manager who posts about inclusion on Friday and turns down the flexible-hours request on Monday.
I'm one of the good ones. I've read all the books.
I'd say something publicly, but it's complicated. You understand, right?
A group chat full of supportive emojis when the topic is trending, and no reply when you ask for a favor.
Look how much I've done for your community. How could you say I let you down?
Colleagues who endorse your cause in a team meeting and vote against it in private.
compendium.why: Trust is given on the strength of stated values, and the gap only becomes visible when support would have cost something, which is usually the moment you most needed it. The let-down then lands as a betrayal and can make future trust harder.

compendium.name: Premature Exclusivity
compendium.what: Pressing for an exclusive, serious commitment before the other person has had time to learn enough about you to choose freely.
nots: Two people who both feel a strong pull and both choose exclusivity gladly. The speed is shared and nobody is being pushed.
A person who prefers clarity early and says so once, then accepts that you need a slower pace.
Pacing norms that differ by culture, faith or age, where earlier commitment is simply expected.
An honest statement of what someone wants, such as 'I am only looking for something exclusive', which lets you decide to step away.
A person who is eager and a little clumsy about it, and relaxes once you say you need time.
sounds: I've never felt this way. Why would we wait?
If you really cared, you wouldn't need time to think.
I deleted the apps last night. I assumed you would too.
We've been seeing each other for three weeks. Are you telling me you still want to date other people?
Everyone else I've met was a waste of time. You're different, so say yes.
I need an answer by Friday, because I can't keep guessing.
compendium.why: You commit before you have the information the decision needed, and once you have said yes you have often let go of the other options you would have compared it with. Doubts that arrive later can feel like breaking a promise.

compendium.name: Confirmation Bias Exploitation
compendium.what: Supplying enough good moments that your own habit of favoring the kinder reading does the work of discounting the harm.
nots: A relationship that really is mostly good, where holding on to the good parts is accurate and not denial.
Someone who has a bad day, behaves badly once, apologizes sincerely, and changes how they act.
A normal hopeful reading of ambiguous behavior, with no cycle of harm and reward behind it.
Genuine growth, where kindness lasts and the harm becomes rarer and then stops, not returning after each peak.
A friend or family member reminding you of a person's real strengths because they know the whole history.
sounds: I don't know what came over me. You know I'm not like that.
Look at everything I did for you this week.
Remember our trip? That's who I really am.
He was exhausted, that's all, and he's been so sweet since.
I told my sister about the argument, then remembered the flowers and felt silly for telling her.
Every time I decide it's too much, something lovely happens and I put the thought away.
compendium.why: Your own hope becomes the thing that keeps you in place, and the pattern stays hidden from the one person best placed to see it. You may defend someone to others and to yourself while privately keeping count.

compendium.name: Halo Effect Exploitation
compendium.what: Pointing to someone's impressive achievement, talent or reputation as the answer to a concern that has nothing to do with it.
nots: A person whose long, consistent record of good conduct makes a first complaint worth checking carefully, though it settles nothing by itself.
A colleague who says a person was excellent in a role and also agrees the specific complaint needs to be investigated.
Sincere admiration for a skill that is not offered as an answer to anything.
A character reference given to a court or panel as one input among others, which then examines the facts.
An honest surprise that someone you know well did something out of character.
sounds: She's the best surgeon in the region. She would never mistreat a nurse.
He has raised thousands for charity. You can't mean that.
Do you know how many people he has mentored?
Our founder built this place from nothing. A bit of temper is the cost of that.
Everyone loves him. Maybe it's you.
I kept thinking about his award and told myself my complaint had to be small.
compendium.why: A concern gets weighed against a reputation instead of against the evidence for it, and you learn not to raise it before anyone else has even heard it. Other people with similar worries may stay silent because you did.

compendium.name: Covert Contracts
compendium.what: Holding someone to rules or debts they never agreed to and were never told about, then punishing or shaming them when they fall short.
nots: Some expectations are shared widely enough that most people would recognize them unstated, such as telling a housemate you will be out overnight. Someone who adjusts readily once told the rule was never communicated is having a miscommunication, not enforcing one.
Long relationships build genuine mutual obligations that both people would describe the same way if asked separately.
Honest hurt that an assumed closeness was not there, said once as hurt and not as a charge.
A spoken or written promise that was forgotten or dropped. That is a broken agreement, not a hidden one.
A family or cultural custom you know about and have chosen to honor, even when it costs you.
sounds: I shouldn't have to ask. You should just know.
After everything I've done for you, this is the least you owe me.
We never talked about it, but I assumed you understood how we do things.
Why would I have to tell you to call me first? It's obvious.
A good daughter wouldn't even ask whether she has to come.
Once you're part of this group, you don't need to be asked to show up.
You find out about a rule only when you are met with a week of silence for breaking it.
compendium.why: You are judged against a standard you were never shown, so effort never buys safety: there is always another rule you have not been told. Questioning a supposed debt gets treated as disloyalty, not as a fair question about what you agreed to.

compendium.name: Financial Dependence by Design
compendium.what: Arranging money, work and access to accounts so that one person cannot manage without the other, whatever either of them feels about the relationship.
nots: A household that divides earning and caring by shared agreement, where each person understands the money and can reach it.
Caregiving, illness, a disability or a poor job market limiting independence without anyone arranging it.
A partner who handles the bills because they like it and who shows you everything when you ask.
A couple pooling money by agreement and keeping separate access for emergencies.
A budget that is tight for both people, with both people affected equally by it.
sounds: You don't need to work. I'll take care of everything.
Why would you need your own account? Ours is fine.
Receipts, please. I want to see where every dollar went.
If you take that course, who is going to look after the house?
Don't worry about the bills. It's too complicated for you.
My card was declined and I realized I didn't know which accounts I was on.
compendium.why: Leaving becomes a question of survival and not of judgment, so whatever you conclude about the relationship, the conclusion cannot change anything. Fear about housing, food and children can keep a person in place for years.

compendium.name: Platform Migration
compendium.what: Steering a conversation from messages or email onto calls, disappearing-message apps or in-person talk when the topic is one that might later be quoted back.
nots: A person who prefers voice or in-person talk for anything weighty and applies that to every topic, including dull ones.
A privacy concern about a particular app or a workplace policy that really does restrict written channels.
A call that is followed by a written summary from either side, such as 'to confirm what we agreed'.
Someone who finds written arguments escalate and wants to speak to defuse them.
An organization where sensitive matters go to a formal meeting by rule, with minutes kept.
sounds: Let's not get into this over text. Call me.
Can we switch to the other app? This one is a bit slow.
I'd rather explain in person than put it in an email.
I don't do messages for things like this. It's easier to talk.
Delete that thread, it's getting messy.
After our call, I realized there was nothing I could point to for what he promised.
compendium.why: You lose the record, so any later dispute about what was said becomes your word against someone else's, with the whole burden of remembering exactly falling on you. Promises that were never written down are easy to dispute.

compendium.name: "Sacred Duty" Manipulation
compendium.what: Presenting an ordinary request as a spiritual, moral or ancestral obligation, so that saying no is treated as a sin or a betrayal.
nots: A person speaking sincerely about their own faith and obligations without expecting you to act on them.
A shared tradition you also hold and freely choose to honor, such as caring for elders or tithing.
A religious leader or relative who gives guidance, hears your disagreement, and accepts that you may decide differently.
A cultural expectation of family support that applies to everyone and that you were able to talk about openly.
A moral appeal that you find persuasive on its merits after thinking it over.
sounds: God has asked this of you, and you are saying no?
Our ancestors gave up everything. The least you can do is give up this job.
A good daughter does not question her mother.
It's your duty to forgive and stay. That's what a faithful wife does.
If you really believed, you wouldn't need to think about it.
I said no and felt as if I had committed a sin, even though I didn't know what I had done wrong.
compendium.why: Refusal stops being a preference and becomes a moral failure, so you cannot decline without feeling you have done something wrong, and you often cannot appeal to anyone inside your own community.

compendium.name: Shame-as-Governance Disguised as Advice
compendium.what: Criticism of a person's character, offered as helpful guidance, that leaves them feeling smaller and makes objecting sound ungrateful.
nots: Feedback that is unwelcome in the moment but names one specific behavior and a way to change it.
A clumsy delivery from someone who cares and adjusts once they hear how it landed.
A mentor or manager giving a hard assessment of your work in a setting where that is expected.
A friend saying 'I'm worried about how much you're drinking' and then listening to your answer.
Advice you asked for, even when the honest answer hurt.
The usable test is what you are left holding afterwards: something to do, or only something to feel.
sounds: I'm only telling you this because I care, but a responsible mother wouldn't have let it get that far.
No offense, but people like you never learn until someone is blunt with them.
I'm saying this for your own good: you're careless with money and everyone can see it.
Why are you so defensive? I was trying to help.
Somebody has to say it. You've really let yourself go.
You should be grateful I'm honest with you.
compendium.why: You come away smaller instead of better equipped, and your objection is answered before you make it, because it was only ever offered as help. Over time you may stop bringing things to them, or start hearing their voice in your own head.

compendium.name: PIP Weaponization
compendium.what: A formal performance improvement plan that, in practice, sets goals the person cannot meet and builds a record toward their exit.
nots: A genuine performance gap handled properly: clear goals, real support and honest timelines are how formal plans are meant to work.
A plan that follows several documented earlier conversations about the same gap.
Timing that happens to follow a complaint but rests on problems recorded beforehand and reviewed by someone independent.
A short informal coaching note, which is not a formal plan.
A plan applied in the same way to others in the same role with the same gap.
A hard but fair target where your own work log shows the shortfall.
sounds: We want you to succeed, so we're putting some expectations in writing. Please sign here.
The goal is to improve your communication. We'll know it when we see it.
That target was updated last week. You'll be measured against the new figure.
Your last update was late, so we're logging that.
We can't share what others on the team are held to.
Your manager's notes from the first three weeks reach you today, nine days before the review.
HR advised that this is the standard process.
compendium.why: You are set a target you may not be able to hit while a record of your exit is being assembled. Defending yourself means arguing against a document that already exists, and your income and references may depend on the outcome.

compendium.name: Credit Laundering
compendium.what: Passing a person's idea or work through several hands, each slightly rewording it, until nobody can trace it back to them.
nots: Ideas do improve as they pass through people, and the later version may truly belong to the group.
Large workplaces spread information with nobody steering it, and the first thought gets lost without anyone choosing that.
Two people sometimes reach the same thought separately, especially when working on the same problem.
A colleague who credits you in the room, forgets to in the written summary, and fixes it when reminded.
Team-level credit that a workplace gives to everybody equally by policy, including for senior people's work.
Your own memory that an idea began with you when no message or draft shows it. It may be true, and it cannot be told apart from outside.
sounds: Great point, Priya. (Two days later, to the director:) Our team has been thinking about this approach.
The deck going to the board carries the department head's name and no mention of the analysis that came from your desk.
I think someone mentioned it in a meeting a while back.
Where did this come from? It's just kind of been in the air.
It's a team effort, so we don't list names on this one.
A forwarded email chain is cut down to its last message, which no longer shows your original proposal.
The announcement thanks 'everyone involved' and names the three people who presented it.
compendium.why: You watch your own work succeed without you and cannot point to a moment when it was taken. That makes raising it feel like sour grapes, even to you, while promotions and trust go to others.

compendium.name: The "Good Woman Program"
compendium.what: A set of unspoken social rules that reward women for compliance and self-sacrifice and charge a price for directness, boundaries or taking up space.
nots: Kindness and consideration are values many people hold for themselves, with nothing imposed.
Some people are accommodating by temperament, content and consistent about it.
A family or culture that expects everyone, men included, to put others first. The unevenness is what marks this pattern.
A single colleague who found your tone abrupt, with no sign they would say that to someone else.
A faith or community norm of service that you have chosen and can step back from without a penalty.
sounds: You're so easy to work with. Don't change.
She's a bit sharp, isn't she? (said of a woman who asked a direct question)
Why can't you just be nice about it?
A good wife wouldn't make a fuss.
Be the bigger person. (said to you in every dispute)
I'd never ask her to say no. She's always so helpful.
I feel guilty even asking for what I'm entitled to. (said to yourself)
compendium.why: The same conduct costs you more than it costs others, so a proportionate no draws a penalty. Over time, discomfort with taking up space can feel like a personal trait when it is partly a response learned from that penalty.

compendium.name: Objectification
compendium.what: Treating a person as a tool, a body or a source of output, so that only what they supply seems to count about them.
nots: A frankly transactional relationship both people understand, such as with a contractor or a supplier.
Valuing a skill, such as asking the best cook to cater, while still knowing and caring about the person.
Focus on a task for the moment, like a surgeon concentrating on the operation, without contempt.
A colleague who only asks for help this week and asks about you afterwards.
Admiration of your appearance that you welcome and that sits beside real interest in you.
The test is whether anything about the person registers at the moments when the useful part is not needed.
sounds: You're the only one who can do the spreadsheets, so I'll leave that with you.
Where's the person who fixes the printer?
I only call when I need something, you know that.
You look good in the photos, so you're coming to the launch.
Why would I ask how your week went? You're here to run the event.
Don't bring your problems into it. Just do what you do best.
She's just the receptionist.
compendium.why: Your worth seems to rise and fall with how useful you are, so the parts of you that are not useful go unseen. When attention withdraws, it can feel like something you failed to supply.

compendium.name: Dehumanization
compendium.what: Reducing a person to a label, a number or a problem, so that decisions are made about them without room for their own point of view.
nots: Formal, clinical and bureaucratic language, which exists for good reasons and is applied to everybody in some settings. The test is whether the reductive framing is used selectively for one person.
Professional detachment in triage, where speed matters more than conversation, which is not contempt.
Shorthand between staff, such as ward or ticket numbers, while the person is still addressed by name and heard.
Someone with a blunt or cold style who treats everyone the same way.
A privacy practice, such as using ID codes in a study or file to protect people rather than remove them.
sounds: Bed fourteen needs moving. (said about a patient who is listening)
She's a difficult case. Don't bother asking what she wants.
We'll tell him what's been decided when it's been decided.
Those people never understand the rules.
Next. Number forty-two.
He's a flight risk, so we'll handle him accordingly.
Just process her and move on.
Is the problem tenant still on the third floor?
compendium.why: Decisions are made about you in language that has no place for your view, so there is no point at which your own account could plausibly be asked for. It can wear down your sense that your voice counts.

compendium.name: Overcorrection Demands
compendium.what: Demanding an apology, payment or gesture far larger than a small lapse warrants, so the repair is shaped more by who sets the terms than by the harm.
nots: What looked minor turned out to have caused real damage, such as a missed payment with fees, and a bigger repair is fair.
Expectations around apology vary across families and cultures, and elaborate ones can be sincere. The revealing moment is what happens when the disproportion is named out loud.
A person who asks for more than is needed at first, hears 'that's too much', and agrees to something smaller.
A formal process, such as a settlement or workplace policy, that sets consequences by rule for everyone.
Your own sense of guilt, which can run larger than anything anyone is asking for.
A request to fix the actual problem, such as paying for what you broke.
sounds: A text apology isn't enough. I want you to say it to my face, in front of your family.
You forgot my birthday dinner, so you can cover the whole trip.
That's not a real sorry. Do it again, and mean it this time.
Write it out, three paragraphs, and I'll decide if it's good enough.
You'll stay out of the group chat for a month, and we'll see.
Questioning the size of the apology is one more thing you'll need to make up for.
Now you owe me for how you reacted to being asked.
compendium.why: Repair stops being achievable and becomes a performance of submission, and you learn that small mistakes carry costs you cannot predict. You may start over-apologizing, or hiding mistakes, to avoid the bill.

compendium.name: Toxic Positivity / Weaponized Optimism
compendium.what: Insisting on a cheerful outlook in answer to real pain or a real complaint, so that the feeling becomes the problem and its cause goes unexamined.
nots: Encouragement that arrives alongside real acknowledgement of the difficulty.
Optimism by temperament, shared without requiring anyone to match it.
Perspective offered once about a genuinely small setback and not insisted on.
A friend who says 'that's awful' first and, when you are ready, mentions something hopeful.
A workplace that asks for solutions after it has heard and logged the problem.
A gratitude practice you have chosen for yourself.
sounds: Just stay positive. It could be worse.
Everything happens for a reason.
At least you have your health.
We don't do negativity on this team.
You'd feel better if you were more grateful.
I don't want to hear problems, only solutions.
Good vibes only.
Why are you bringing the mood down?
compendium.why: Your dissatisfaction becomes the thing that needs fixing, so whatever caused it goes unexamined, and saying it again costs you standing in the room.

compendium.name: Credibility Theft
compendium.what: Casting doubt on someone's reliability in advance, so whatever they later report is heard as doubtful before they have said it.
nots: A documented record of inaccuracy reasonably affects how much weight an account carries, and doubting one particular claim is not a campaign. The separation is between doubt about a claim and doubt installed in advance about the person.
A colleague saying 'I'm not sure about that date, can we check the email?'
Mutual wariness between two people who have each been caught out before.
A private word to you, from someone who cares, that you seem overwhelmed lately.
An investigator or judge testing a witness's account, which is their job.
Someone honestly disagreeing with what you said and telling you so in the open.
sounds: You know how she exaggerates.
I'm not saying he's lying, just that he gets confused about dates.
Take what she says with a pinch of salt, she's been going through a lot.
Don't be surprised if he tells you a different story; he does that.
Your manager has already been told you 'tend to misread situations' before you raise your concern.
When you report something, the reply opens with 'is this another one of your situations?'
A relative tells the others, 'She'll probably bring that up again, just be kind about it.'
compendium.why: Your account is discounted before you give it, so whatever you later report meets people who have already been prepared not to believe it, and you may never find out why. Asking for help becomes hardest exactly when you most need it.

compendium.name: Projection
compendium.what: Charging someone with a behavior or motive that the exchange shows more clearly in the person making the charge.
nots: An accusation can be accurate even when it also describes the accuser, and in most conflicts both people contribute some of the same behavior. Someone naming a pattern they share, and owning their half, is doing the opposite.
A counter-complaint that is specific, dated and checkable, even if it is uncomfortable to hear.
A genuine mirror, where both of you do the thing and each can see it.
A flash of defensiveness that the person admits an hour later.
Honest self-reflection such as 'I think I'm stressed, and I may be hearing criticism where there is none.'
sounds: You're the one who's controlling, said by someone who has just told you whom you may see.
I'm not angry, you're angry, said loudly.
You're always accusing me of lying. You're the liar here.
You're being so defensive! said in reply to a calm question.
You're obsessed with money, said by a person who has just reviewed every receipt.
I'm not the one who doesn't trust you. You're the one who doesn't trust me.
An email answers your note about missed deadlines with a list of deadlines you supposedly missed, none of them dated.
compendium.why: You spend the conversation defending yourself against the very thing you came to name, which makes the source of the harm hard to see, and harder to describe to anyone else. The conflict ends in a tie instead of an answer.

compendium.name: Authority Hijack
compendium.what: Insisting you know what another person really feels, thinks or meant better than they do, and treating their own account as the thing to be corrected.
nots: People who know you well sometimes offer a reading you had not considered, and in therapy that questioning is invited, not imposed; a clarifying question is not a counter-claim. The difference is whether your own account is still allowed to be the last word.
A friend saying 'I wonder if you're more tired than angry' and then accepting 'no, I'm angry.'
Someone noticing your behavior has changed and asking what is going on.
A guess at your mood from a visible sign, such as asking if you are cold when you are shivering.
A coach or teacher pointing out a habit you had not noticed, like rushing your answers.
A formal assessment you agreed to, in which a professional describes patterns in your answers.
sounds: You don't actually feel that, you just think you do.
I know what you really meant.
You're not upset about the meeting. You're upset about your mother.
Deep down you want me to say sorry.
I understand you better than you understand yourself.
You say you're fine, but I can tell you aren't, and I know why.
A supervisor's feedback form lists your 'real motivation' for a decision you explained in writing.
compendium.why: You end up arguing the case for your own feelings, and simply being taken at your word is no longer on offer. Over time you may start checking your inner states against someone else's reading before you trust them.

compendium.name: Accountability Evasion via Diagnosis
compendium.what: Answering a complaint about someone's conduct by suggesting the complainant has a condition, so the complaint is treated as a symptom.
nots: A real condition can be part of the picture, and someone qualified raising it with care is doing their job. The question is whether the original report ever gets answered by anybody, or whether the diagnosis is where the matter ends.
A manager who offers support resources and also investigates your complaint.
A person who tells you they are worried about your sleep because they noticed you are not sleeping.
A clinician explaining a diagnosis you asked about.
A friend who suggests therapy and also hears you out.
A review that found the complaint was not supported by the facts and said so plainly, with reasons.
sounds: Have you thought about seeing someone about how you've been feeling?
I think this is your anxiety making it seem worse than it was.
We're just worried about your mental health, that's all.
A reply to a harassment complaint says only that 'we recommend our employee assistance program.'
A clinic answers a complaint about treatment with 'perhaps your distress is part of why it felt that way.'
Maybe you're not coping well with stress right now, and that's why you saw it that way.
A school letter on your report of bullying discusses your child's 'sensitivities' and says nothing about the incident.
compendium.why: The complaint is never answered. It is converted into a symptom, and you are sent to seek help for a reaction to someone else's conduct. What happened stays unexamined, and you carry both the harm and the label.

compendium.name: Spiritual Bypassing
compendium.what: Using spiritual or wellness ideas, such as forgiveness, positivity or karma, to avoid answering for a harm and to shame the hurt person's pain.
nots: Many people hold these beliefs sincerely and apply them first to their own lives. A faith or practice that someone lives by is not an attack on you.
Spiritual perspective offered alongside a real acknowledgement of what happened. It is the ordering that matters: letting go requested before anything is admitted.
A grieving friend leaning on 'everything happens for a reason' to cope with a loss that has nothing to do with you.
A chaplain, counselor or elder who sits with your pain first and mentions forgiveness only if and when you ask.
You choosing to forgive in your own time and your own words. That is your decision, not something done to you.
sounds: "Everything happens for a reason. There's no point dwelling on what I said at the party."
"Anger is just fear wearing a mask. Maybe sit with that instead of with me."
"Forgiveness sets you free. Holding on to this is hurting you more than it hurts me."
"Someone who had really done the work wouldn't still be upset about this."
"I released it weeks ago, so I don't see why you haven't."
"You keep attracting this because you stay in a low place."
"We're all on our own path. I can't take on your reaction."
compendium.why: Your anger gets judged as a spiritual shortcoming, and forgiveness is requested before anything has been acknowledged. The harm is closed off without being repaired, and you may start to feel that the hurt itself was the mistake.

compendium.name: Burden of Proof Shifting
compendium.what: Arranging an exchange so the person raising a concern must prove they were harmed, are innocent, or deserve ordinary decent treatment.
nots: A dispute where a fact is truly contested, such as who paid a bill, and where a receipt would end the argument for both sides.
A court, school hearing or HR process that asks everyone involved for evidence under the same rules.
Someone asking 'can you give me an example?' because they honestly do not understand what you mean and want to fix it.
A reasonable request to confirm a plan in writing that applies to both people equally.
A person who needs time to check their calendar or records before agreeing that something happened.
sounds: "Prove it. Show me where I said that."
"If it was really bothering you, you'd have mentioned it with dates."
"I need you to give me three specific examples before I'll even consider changing."
"Where's your evidence that I ignored you? Feelings aren't facts."
"Unless you can show me, it didn't happen."
"Convince me you really need the weekend off."
"You're asking me to change my behavior. The least you can do is justify it properly."
compendium.why: You have to build a case for ordinary treatment, and the work of proving becomes the price of asking. Most people eventually stop asking, not because things are fine but because the cost is too high.

compendium.name: Gish Gallop
compendium.what: Overwhelming a rival in live debate with a rapid stream of claims, many weak or false, too many to answer one by one.
nots: Well-prepared people cover ground fast because they are prepared, and enthusiasm makes people talk quickly.
A dispute that really does contain many separate, valid points, such as a long list of faults in a contract.
A person who is anxious and says everything at once because they fear being cut off.
A summary of a topic given at speed to a class or colleague where questions are welcomed afterwards.
A strong case with several supporting reasons, where each one holds up when you check it.
sounds: "Okay, but what about the 2019 report, and the survey in Ohio, and the guy at the hospital, and the budget numbers, and the fact that nobody ever answers this one?"
"You haven't addressed point four, or seven, or nine. I'll take that as a concession."
"I could list twenty more examples, but let's start with these eleven."
"You spent all that time on one thing. What about the other things I said?"
"Just answer the question. Any of the questions. I asked forty."
A post with a long list of bullet points, each one a separate claim with a link that has no clear relation to it.
compendium.why: You lose on speed rather than on substance, and the fact that you could not answer everything gets treated as evidence that you could not answer anything. Onlookers and you yourself may count the loss as real.

compendium.name: Limited Hangout
compendium.what: Admitting a smaller wrong or sharing part of the truth so the matter seems fully disclosed, while the larger part stays hidden.
nots: People often disclose in stages as they find the nerve, or because they genuinely do not yet know the full scope of what they did.
Leading with the largest thing and filling in details later is a natural order, not a suspicious one.
A person who tells you something small and truthful, and then answers every question you ask after that.
A lawyer or manager who limits what they share for legal or privacy reasons and says so openly.
Keeping something private that is not your business, which is different from hiding something you are entitled to know.
sounds: "Fine, I did go for a drink with her. That's all it was. I've been honest with you now."
"I'll admit the invoice was late. Let's not go digging for more."
"I already told you about the loan. Why are you still asking questions?"
"I made one mistake and I've owned it. Isn't that enough?"
"We're releasing the first set of emails today in the interest of transparency."
"Okay, yes, I spent some of it. Happy now?"
compendium.why: You close the matter believing you now have the full picture, and the smaller admission is afterwards used as proof that there was nothing more to tell. When the rest surfaces, you may feel you should have known, and trust becomes harder.

compendium.name: Pseudo-Profundity / Intellectual Intimidation
compendium.what: Using grand, technical or abstract language that sounds deep but explains little, so questioning it feels like admitting you are not clever enough.
nots: Some subjects genuinely need specialist vocabulary, and real experts are frequently poor at translating what they know into plain language.
Asking for a simpler version usually separates them: genuine expertise can be restated, and hollow language cannot.
A genuinely hard idea, such as a maths proof or a legal doctrine, that takes time and effort to learn.
Poetry, scripture or philosophy that is deliberately open-ended and does not claim to settle a factual question.
A person who is nervous and over-explains with long words, and who relaxes once you ask a simple question.
sounds: "It's really about the ontological reframing of the value proposition."
"If you have to ask what it means, you haven't yet reached the level where it makes sense."
"The truth is paradoxical; to see it you have to stop looking for it."
"I would explain, but it requires a grounding in the literature that you may not have."
"It's a synergistic holistic framework that transcends the usual binaries."
"Most people don't have the intellectual patience for this, which is fine."
Asked to say it simply, they reply with a longer sentence using the same words.
compendium.why: You are left unable to challenge a conclusion you never understood, and you read your own confusion as a shortfall in yourself rather than in the explanation. Decisions about money, health or work may then be made on words nobody checked.

compendium.name: Semantic Erosion / Meaning Dilution
compendium.what: Stretching a serious word or accusation across so many trivial cases that it stops carrying weight when someone needs it for a real one.
nots: Words drift for ordinary cultural reasons all the time, loosened by thousands of unconnected people using them casually.
A sincere, good-faith argument about where a concept's edges lie, such as when a word applies and when it does not.
A person gently pointing out that a term you used is stronger than the situation you described.
Hyperbole in everyday speech, like 'I'm starving' or 'that's a disaster', which most listeners understand without confusion.
A legal or clinical term with a defined meaning, where checking the definition is a fair thing to do.
sounds: "If that's harassment, then so is asking someone to pass the salt."
"Everyone is traumatised these days. It's just a word people use."
"I've been called abusive for burning toast. The word means nothing anymore."
"You're saying I stole it? Everything is theft to you people."
"That's what you're calling a crisis? We all have bad days."
"You said 'gaslighting' about a missed call. How can I take it seriously now?"
The same strong word used in ads, memes and arguments about trivial matters until it sounds like a joke.
compendium.why: You lose the accurate word for your own situation, so describing it plainly now sounds like exaggeration, to other people and often to you. Without the word, it can be harder to find support or to be believed.

compendium.name: Dog Whistling / Coded Signaling
compendium.what: Using words that sound ordinary to most listeners but carry a different, often threatening or exclusionary message to those who know the code.
nots: Private references and inside jokes are ordinary and usually harmless, and a phrase can land on something painful entirely by accident.
Because the meaning is by design invisible to observers, this is one to hold especially loosely: no onlooker, and no tool, can confirm it from the words alone.
A real request for information, like asking which way you drive home because they want to offer a lift.
Slang or symbols that a group uses openly to show belonging, with no message aimed at a target.
Your own heightened alertness after a past threat, where an unrelated phrase recalls something painful.
sounds: A cheerful remark about your route home that you know refers to something they once said they could find out.
"Nice family you have. It would be a shame if anything happened to the dog," said lightly, with a smile.
A particular phrase that, every time it is used, comes shortly before a punishment or a withdrawal.
A manager saying they want people who are a 'good fit' for the team, directed at one colleague in the same breath as a remark about their accent.
A seemingly harmless number or symbol in an online profile that a group uses to recognize each other.
Everyone else laughs at a comment, while you and one other person go quiet because you know where it comes from.
compendium.why: You react to something real that nobody else in the room can see, so your reaction becomes the visible event while the message itself stays deniable. Being the only one who flinches is isolating, and it can make you doubt what you heard.

compendium.name: Information Cascades
compendium.what: A belief or reputation that spreads because each person sees others accepting it, so agreement stands in for anyone checking whether it is true.
nots: A widely held belief that is simply correct. Popularity and truth overlap far more often than they split.
Relying on a source with a real track record, such as a physician or a reference book, rather than re-checking everything yourself.
A group where people each tested the claim by different methods and reached the same result, like several labs repeating a measurement.
One loud person repeating a claim, which is persuasion by a single voice and not a chain of followers.
A cautious group that says openly, "we are going by the expert's word", and can name the expert.
Someone changing their mind after hearing others' reasons. The marker here is people citing each other's numbers in place of anything independent.
sounds: "Everyone's saying it, so there must be something to it."
"I didn't look into it myself, but three people I trust believe it."
"Why question this? The whole team already agrees."
A group chat where each new message points to the message before it instead of to a document or a firsthand account.
"Well, I heard it from Dana, and Dana heard it from the people in accounting."
A new hire's reputation arriving in rooms before they do, repeated in the same words each time.
Silence after someone asks "where did this come from?", followed by a change of subject.
compendium.why: Someone can end up judged on a belief nobody actually checked, and correcting it means pushing against a whole group's momentum instead of answering one person's claim. A reputation or rumor that has hardened this way can be very hard to undo.

compendium.name: Interruption Patterns
compendium.what: Repeatedly cutting off the same people in group conversations so their points never get finished, while other speakers finish theirs freely.
nots: A talkative, overlapping culture, such as a loud family dinner, where everyone cuts in on everyone and nobody minds. The test is distribution: spread across the room, or concentrated on the same voices.
One burst of enthusiasm from someone excited, followed by an apology.
A chair who stops long speeches to keep an agenda moving and does it to every speaker.
Interrupting to ask a clarifying question and then letting the speaker resume.
Cross-talk from call lag, where two people honestly start at once and both back off.
A cut-off after a long stretch of rambling, which differs from being stopped after a few seconds.
sounds: "Right, right, but what I think is..." said before the other person reaches the end of a sentence.
"Let me stop you there," aimed at the same colleague in most meetings.
"What she's trying to say is..." followed by a different version of her point.
"We're short on time," said only when one particular person has the floor.
A video call where someone else unmutes over one person every time they begin on the budget.
"Sorry, go ahead," followed by a second interruption within a sentence.
"Anyway," and a switch of topic the moment they take a breath.
compendium.why: Their points never reach completion, so their contribution gets judged on fragments, and in time they start shortening themselves before anyone has cut in. People in the room may remember them as unclear when the cutting-off was the cause.

compendium.name: Idea Theft in Real Time
compendium.what: Someone repeats a point you just made, moments later, and the room gives them the credit or response your version did not get.
nots: Two people reaching the same idea within minutes of each other, which happens often in teams working on one problem. Once is coincidence; it is the repetition that registers.
Someone who did not register your version and honestly believes theirs is new.
A restatement that adds something substantive, such as a number, a timeline or a fix, and has earned its own credit.
A chair who sums up the room's points without naming speakers, for everyone.
A person who repeats your point to confirm they understood it and says "as you said".
An idea that is common knowledge in the field, where nobody owns the first mention.
sounds: "Here's what I think we should do...", repeating what you proposed five minutes ago.
"Oh, great idea!" from the chair, who said nothing when you said it.
"That's basically what I was saying," after you point it out.
"I'm not sure that's quite what you said, though."
"We're all on the same page. Does it matter who said it first?"
A written summary that credits your proposal to the person who repeated it.
A chat thread where your message gets no reply and the same suggestion posted ten minutes later gets three.
compendium.why: Your contribution counts for somebody else, and the only way to claim it back risks making you look petty in the very moment it happens. Over repeated meetings, this can quietly shape who is seen as the source of ideas.

compendium.name: Gatekeeping
compendium.what: Controlling who can reach certain people, information, resources or opportunities, so that some people must ask permission while others get access without asking.
nots: Managing access as the actual job. Receptionists, editors, registrars and records officers do this openly, and so do many managers.
Published criteria applied to everyone, such as a minimum certification or a posted application window.
Someone slow to make an introduction because they are busy.
Privacy protections that restrict access for everybody, such as medical records or children's information.
A safety rule, such as training before using equipment, applied to every user alike.
A friend group that is simply full, with no pattern in who gets turned away.
sounds: "Send it to me first and I'll see if it's the right time."
"That's not how we do things here," when nothing is written down.
"You need an introduction from someone senior," while newer colleagues are simply given access.
"We'll let you know," followed by silence, while others got the same access right away.
A shared folder or group chat that everyone else was added to automatically.
"I'd love to connect you, I'm just swamped," repeated across several months.
"Let's wait until you've proven yourself," with no description of what proving means.
compendium.why: You need permission that others do not, and because the criteria move, there is no way of asking correctly that reliably works. Time and effort go into passing a test that keeps changing, and you may start to doubt your own qualifications.

compendium.name: Punishment by Proxy
compendium.what: Difficulty, coldness or harm falling on someone you care about after a disagreement, in a way that leaves you absorbing the cost without a direct attack on you.
nots: Coincidence. Timing overlaps happen far more often than intuition expects, and a bad week for your friend may have nothing to do with you.
A third person's own history with the same people, such as an old feud that predates your dispute.
An ordinary side effect of your conflict that reaches others, such as a team being reassigned after a complaint.
Someone venting to mutual friends, which spreads an argument without aiming at anyone.
A reorganization, policy change or audit that affects your relative and has nothing to do with you.
Your own worry, which is real but is not evidence about what caused the difficulty. This is among the easiest patterns to over-read and the least safe to act on from timing alone.
sounds: "Things have been tough for your sister at work lately. Maybe it's worth thinking about that."
A friend stops being invited to events a few days after your disagreement with the host.
"I'm only being honest: people are asking questions about your mother now."
A teacher, landlord or manager who was fine with your relative's work begins to find fault soon after your complaint.
"It isn't only you who feels this," said about the third person's new troubles.
A child's lessons, a friend's access or a relative's money changes right after you refuse something.
"Look what your attitude has caused."
compendium.why: Your own boundaries start to carry a cost for someone you care about, so protecting yourself means exposing them, which is often enough to make you stop. Because the link is rarely provable, you may carry the guilt and the doubt on your own.

compendium.name: Weaponized Inclusion / Strategic Containment
compendium.what: Placing someone inside a group or process where they stay closely visible and have little real influence, so inclusion replaces independent action.
nots: Real inclusion where your input changes outcomes. From outside it looks the same until you see what changed, and a new structure may not yet have mechanisms that make input count.
Having less influence because of seniority, experience or role limits that are stated openly.
Confidentiality or collective-responsibility rules that bind every board member equally.
A role you asked for and know to be advisory, accepted with eyes open.
A group that heard your suggestion, declined it and explained why, which is a lost argument and not containment.
A newcomer who is slowly given more responsibility, with a clear path to a vote.
sounds: "We want you on the steering group, because your perspective matters." There is no vote.
"You were in the room when we decided this."
"If you have concerns, bring them to the working group, not outside it."
"Why go public? You have a seat at the table."
Minutes that list the person as a contributor to decisions they argued against.
A task force that meets monthly, with recommendations never mentioned in any later decision.
"We can't have the committee look divided, can we?"
"You helped build this, so you can't really criticize it now."
compendium.why: Your independent options close as the formal ones open, and any objection is answered with the fact that you were included. You can end up co-owning decisions you never shaped, with less room to act outside them.

compendium.name: Controlled Opposition
compendium.what: A protest group, critic or movement that is secretly funded, steered or shaped by the very power it appears to oppose, so dissent goes somewhere harmless.
nots: Movements argue about tactics all the time. A moderate wing and a radical wing can both be sincere.
A critic who is cautious by temperament or conviction is not a plant. Mildness is not evidence of control.
Overlap between a critic's positions and the interests of those they criticize is common and usually coincidental.
Accepting a meeting, a grant or a seat at a table can be a real strategy, and sometimes it wins concessions.
A group that fails to win is usually just weak or outnumbered. Losing does not prove it was set up to lose.
A group that takes public money for a narrow, openly stated purpose is not secretly steered.
sounds: The petition got a million names and a meeting with the minister, and then a statement that the minister 'heard the concerns'.
A spokesperson thunders about waste and rudeness in the agency, but never mentions the contract that actually decides things.
Funding records show the 'grassroots' watchdog's biggest donor is the company it reports on.
The group's leader meets the people in charge in private, then returns and asks followers to calm down and wait.
Every consultation ends the same way: a thank-you, a report, and no change to the plan.
The rival campaign that proposed a harder demand was ignored by the 'main' opposition and called unrealistic.
The march route, slogans and speakers were all approved by the authorities in advance.
compendium.why: If you pour your energy into a channel built to absorb it, you can spend years believing you are pushing for change while nothing moves. It can also make you distrust real allies. Asking for evidence protects you from both mistakes.

compendium.name: Reputation Laundering
compendium.what: Passing a damaging or flattering claim about a person through enough retellings that it loses its source and starts to feel like common knowledge.
nots: Reputations are often earned. 'Everyone says that' is sometimes simply true.
Several people with similar first-hand experiences who compare notes are corroborating each other. The line to draw is between people who met the person and people who only met the story.
A warning from one colleague who worked with someone and tells you what happened is a report, not laundering.
A person's reputation changing after a documented event, such as a verdict or public statement, is a normal response to news.
A story that is vague because the teller does not remember the details is ordinary gossip.
A formal reference check that asks former managers what they saw.
sounds: I don't know the details, but everyone says she's difficult to work with.
That's just what people say about him, there must be something to it.
Three different people warned me about you before I even met you.
I heard it from someone who heard it from the team, so I assume it's true.
It doesn't matter where it started. The reputation is what it is.
Ask anyone in the department. They'll tell you the same thing.
He's got a reputation, so I'd keep your distance.
compendium.why: The target has to argue against a portrayal with no traceable origin, while each person repeating it treats everyone else's repetition as their evidence for it. You cannot rebut a source that has vanished.

compendium.name: Maternal Gatekeeping
compendium.what: A mother's habit of correcting, redoing or limiting the other parent's or caregiver's care of a child until they lose confidence and step back.
nots: One specific safety concern, raised constructively, is not this. Examples are a sleeping position, a car seat strap or an allergy.
Two caregivers can have genuinely different methods that both work. Choosing one routine for consistency is not control.
Someone still learning a skill can be given proportionate guidance without their competence being the target.
A breastfeeding mother who needs to be the one to settle a baby for practical reasons.
A parent recovering from birth or ill health who is anxious and over-protective, and relaxes once reassured.
A child with medical needs whose care really does require specific steps.
sounds: No, give her to me, you're holding her wrong.
I'll just do it, it's quicker than explaining.
You did put his socks on inside out. I'll fix it.
Don't take her to the park without me, you don't know her signals.
That's not how we do bedtime. Here, let me.
You can babysit him on Saturday, but I've written down exactly what to do.
He only settles for me, so there's no point you trying.
compendium.why: The corrected caregiver's confidence erodes until they step back, and the stepping back is then read as proof they were never really willing. Both the child and that caregiver can lose time and closeness.

compendium.name: Echo Chamber Construction
compendium.what: Arranging what another person reads, hears and talks about so that they mostly meet one view, and come to see every other source as unreliable.
nots: People form affinity groups on their own, and recommending sources you honestly rate is not curating somebody else's world.
The distinguishing feature is active discouragement of everything else, not enthusiasm for something in particular.
A parent who limits a young child's screen content is making an age-appropriate choice.
A recommendation algorithm that serves more of the same is how the platform works, and this does not show what anyone meant.
A hobby group, faith community or fan club that shares a strong view but welcomes questions and outside friends.
A friend who says a particular source is unreliable and gives their reasons for you to check.
sounds: Don't bother with that site, they're all lying anyway.
Your sister would only confuse you. She doesn't understand what we know.
Here, watch this one. It explains everything the others hide.
If you hear them out, they'll just twist your words.
Real friends would see this the way we do.
You don't need other opinions. You've got us.
Anyone who disagrees hasn't done the research.
compendium.why: The target loses the outside views that would let them sense-check their own situation, and the narrowing arrives feeling like a preference they chose. It is hard to notice what you are no longer hearing.

compendium.name: Stochastic Harassment Direction
compendium.what: Repeatedly describing a named person in inflammatory terms to a large audience, so some listeners predictably harass them although the speaker never gives an instruction.
nots: Proportionate public criticism of someone's public actions is legitimate, even when a third party overreacts to it.
Reporting real wrongdoing through proper channels is not incitement.
What is described here is repeated inflammatory portrayal aimed at an audience, not criticism as such.
A single harsh review or angry post that happens to go viral, with no pattern of repeated targeting.
A news outlet reporting accurately on a public figure, and some readers reacting badly.
A group of people independently angry about the same documented event.
sounds: Posts that name the person, say what a disgrace they are, and tag their employer or school.
Followers' messages that quote the speaker's exact phrase: 'You are exactly what he said you are.'
The speaker's reply to complaints: 'I never told anyone to contact her. I only said what she did.'
A flood of one-star reviews, calls to the workplace or anonymous emails within hours of a post.
Repeated hints such as 'someone should do something about this person' with no instruction attached.
The target's address, workplace or family showing up in comments after a post, posted by strangers.
New accounts appearing in the target's inbox with the same few insults.
compendium.why: The target absorbs harassment from many people at once while the portrayal that produced it stays technically deniable, so there is no single act to report and no one to hold to it. It can feel as if the whole world has turned on you.

compendium.name: Information Laundering
compendium.what: Passing a false or unverified claim through a series of apparently credible sources until it looks like established fact and its origin can no longer be seen.
nots: Responsible journalism legitimately cites and builds on other credible reporting.
A claim that several outlets each confirmed separately is corroborated rather than laundered.
The thing to trace is whether any link in the chain did original verification work.
A well-known idea being cited in a textbook that has itself been properly checked.
An honest error that spreads because busy reporters trusted a reputable source that was wrong.
A source quoting an unnamed person whom the outlet has vetted and stands behind.
sounds: A headline that says 'according to reports' and links to another article that says the same.
A footnote that cites a blog, which cites a forum post, which cites nothing.
An expert on a panel quoting 'a widely reported figure' that cannot be traced to a study.
A news story built on a screenshot that no one has authenticated.
A statistic that appears in many places, all with the same rounding, and none with the underlying data.
An article that is later cited as a source by the site that supplied the original tip.
A correction posted at the original place that does not follow the claim to the places it spread.
compendium.why: The target is contradicted by something that now looks well-sourced, and disproving it means unpicking a chain of citations rather than a single claim. By then, the claim has been quoted in so many places that it feels settled.

compendium.name: Emotion Control
compendium.what: Rewarding the feelings a person is allowed to show and punishing or shaming the rest, until they perform emotions instead of reporting them.
nots: A household or workplace with norms about how feelings get expressed, such as no shouting at the table. Cultures differ widely, and a difference in emotional style is not a tactic.
A norm that falls evenly on everyone in the room, including the person who set it, instead of landing on one person as a penalty for particular feelings.
Someone asking for a calmer tone in the middle of a heated argument, then coming back to hear you out.
A person who finds sadness or anger hard to be near, says so, and does not punish you for having it.
A job that asks for steady composure with customers while leaving room to be human elsewhere.
One kind attempt to cheer you up that you are free to turn down.
sounds: Smile. Nobody wants to see that face at dinner.
You have so much to be grateful for. Why are you crying?
Go on, tell me how you really feel. (Later:) So you admit you resent me.
Don't you dare raise your voice in this house.
We don't do negativity here.
I'll talk to you when you're in a better mood.
Look how lovely you are when you're not complaining.
compendium.why: When only some feelings are safe to show, you stop reporting the rest and may eventually stop noticing them. What is left of your emotional life is the part that was permitted.

compendium.name: Ritualized Exhaustion
compendium.what: A relentless run of schedules, demands and lost sleep that keeps a person too depleted to think clearly, weigh options or push back.
nots: A hard stretch with a real, disclosed end point, such as a launch, a new baby or a family crisis. A demanding period that ends is different from an open-ended schedule that never gives rest back.
Choosing a punishing schedule yourself because you love the project or are training for something.
Shift work, on-call duty or night nursing, where hours are tough but agreed, paid and followed by recovery.
A chaotic household or office where nobody is rested, including the person making the demands.
Insomnia, anxiety or a health condition wearing you down without anyone imposing a schedule.
Caring for a sick relative, where the demands come from the illness itself.
sounds: You can sleep when the work is done.
If you were really committed, you wouldn't need eight hours.
Just one more thing before you go to bed.
Everyone else manages fine.
A message or task lands at 2 a.m. and a reply is expected within minutes.
A rota with no free day, and a day off that gets filled at the last minute.
Being told you look tired, followed by another task.
compendium.why: Depletion that runs for months narrows the ability to think, weigh options and push back, and once that is gone, noticing its absence gets harder too.

compendium.name: Nonverbal Dominance
