A mutual friend saying, "I just don't think you realize how much you've hurt them." (about the person who raised the complaint)
"I guess I'm just a terrible person, then. Is that what you want me to say?"
"I can't handle this right now. I need you to be supportive."
You, a few minutes after you were the one wronged: "I'm sorry I brought it up."
Tearful silence and withdrawal as soon as the complaint is named, followed by you finding yourself offering a hug.
nots: Two people who were both hurt in the same conflict, each with a fair claim to be heard.
Someone overcome by guilt who cries or goes quiet but still hears you out and acknowledges what they did.
A person who is also going through something painful and separate, such as a loss, an illness or a job crisis, and says so without using it to close the topic.
Mutual reassurance after a conflict, which is a normal part of making up when the harm has been named first.
A person who is overwhelmed, steps away briefly and returns to deal with what happened.
compendium.why: Sympathy that should have gone to the person harmed goes elsewhere, and the person harmed ends up soothing and apologizing. Onlookers form an impression that is very hard to correct later, and the person harmed may start doubting whether they have the right to be upset.

compendium.name: Preemptive Accusation
compendium.what: Accusing someone of a fault before they have spoken, often the same fault that is about to be raised about the accuser, so their later account sounds like a copy.
sounds: "I just want you to know I've noticed how you talk about people behind their backs." (said before you have said a word about them)
"I'm sure you're going to say I'm the difficult one, but it's you who always makes things hard."
"Funny, she's going to tell you I ignored her. She's the one who never replies to anything."
"That's what they said I would say, so I'm telling you first: she lies about this stuff." (to a mutual friend)
When you do raise it: "See, this is exactly what I said you'd do."
"Don't be surprised if she twists this. She did it to me last year."
nots: A real concern someone raises early because they noticed first. Being first to speak does not make a claim false or strategic.
A person who braces for a hard talk by saying 'I know this may sound defensive, but...' while still engaging with your point.
Two people with true complaints about each other that happen to land in the same week.
A manager or friend giving advance feedback about a pattern they have actually seen.
An honest guess about what someone will say, based on a long history of a fight, followed by real listening.
compendium.why: By the time the other person speaks, the ground has been prepared. An accurate account arrives sounding like retaliation for one already made, and the person raising it spends their effort defending their motives.

compendium.name: Complaint Weaponization
compendium.what: Using a formal or informal complaint, often filed first, to shape how a later and truthful report from the other person will be received.
sounds: "I've already spoken to HR about the way you treated me." (said before you have contacted anyone)
A manager telling you, "There's already a complaint about you on file. Anything you raise now will be looked at in that light."
"Funny that you're only bringing this up now, after I reported you."
A mutual friend saying, "She told the group leader first, so I'm not sure it's wise to push this."
A formal letter listing your faults, sent a day after a heated argument with no earlier warning.
"I had to protect myself. Someone had to go to them first."
nots: Reporting a real problem quickly through the right channel, which is exactly what people are told to do.
Someone who files first because they are frightened and have never faced a process like this before.
Both people filing independently around the same time, each unaware of the other's report.
A complaint that is accurate, even if it is unwelcome and was filed before yours.
A person asking a supervisor for advice about a conflict without making any formal charge.
compendium.why: Whichever account reaches the record first tends to set the frame, so a truthful second report is read as a response rather than as information. The person harmed may lose time, credibility, a job or standing before being heard.

compendium.name: Counterfeit Calm
compendium.what: Putting on an unbothered, composed manner so that someone's honest upset looks irrational or excessive by comparison.
sounds: "I'm not upset at all. I just think you're getting a bit worked up."
"Let's take a breath. I'm happy to talk when you're ready to be reasonable."
"I'm just trying to keep things peaceful. Why are you so angry?"
A slow, quiet "Okay." in answer to a long, painful explanation.
"I'm not going to argue. I'll wait until you've calmed down."
A gentle smile and a glance at others in the room as your voice rises.
nots: A naturally even-tempered person who is just as steady in every situation, including ones that concern them.
A person who keeps their voice low to cool a heated moment and says they want to return to the issue, which they then do.
A cultural or family style where raised voices are seen as disrespectful and calm is the norm.
A person who is calm because they are not very affected, and who says so plainly without implying you should feel the same.
A trained professional such as a nurse or mediator keeping a steady voice because the job calls for it.
compendium.why: A proportionate emotional response gets read as instability by contrast. A person is left choosing between being upset and being believed, and may start suppressing real feelings to be taken seriously.

compendium.name: Double Binds
compendium.what: Giving someone demands that contradict each other, so that whatever they choose, they are told they chose wrong.
sounds: "Be more independent." Then, when you decide something alone: "You never include me."
"Just tell me what's wrong." Then, when you do: "I can't believe you'd say that to me."
"You never take initiative." Then: "Now you're just doing it because I complained."
"Take your time with it." Followed by irritation that it is not finished.
"I want your honest opinion." Followed by silence or anger if the opinion differs.
"Don't be so sensitive." And then: "Why don't you care how this affects me?"
nots: Feedback on two different matters that happen to pull in opposite directions, such as 'be more concise' on emails and 'be thorough' on reports.
A person whose preferences honestly change over time and who has not noticed the shift.
A hard job with competing real demands, such as a manager asked by their own boss for speed and perfection.
General dissatisfaction from someone stressed, without any trap in the structure.
A mixed message that is acknowledged and fixed once pointed out.
compendium.why: Every available response is wrong, so effort produces fault whatever is chosen. A person begins to conclude that the problem must be themselves, and may stop trying or become hypervigilant.

compendium.name: Sarcasm as Weapon
compendium.what: Using a mocking tone to deliver real criticism or contempt, so that any objection can be answered with "it was a joke."
sounds: "Wow, great parking. Was that a goal of yours?"
"Oh, sure, because you're the expert on everything."
"Nice of you to finally join us."
"No, please, tell me more about your amazing career."
"I'm kidding! God, you take everything so seriously."
"Thanks for the help. Really, I could not have done it without you ruining it."
nots: Mutual, affectionate teasing that both people enjoy is not this, and a generally sarcastic style applied evenly to everyone has no particular target.
One sharp remark in a bad moment, acknowledged and not repeated, is friction rather than a pattern.
Dry humor in a team that roasts everyone, including the boss, and where anyone can say it is too much and be heard.
Sarcasm directed at an idea or a situation, such as a broken printer, rather than at a person.
A habit the speaker is honestly unaware of, who stops when told and thanks you for saying so.
compendium.why: Criticism lands in full while objecting to it means arguing about a joke, so the hurt has nowhere to go.

compendium.name: Public Humiliation
compendium.what: Embarrassing or belittling a person in front of others, or putting their private matters on show, so the audience adds to the sting.
sounds: "Let me show everyone how it should have been done."
"Tell them what you did last weekend. Go on, it's hilarious."
A manager reading out your error on a team call, with your name attached.
"Oh, don't mind her, she never gets the details right."
A group chat message that quotes something private you said, followed by laughing faces.
"Do you want to tell them, or shall I?"
"Since we're all here, we might as well go through your review."
nots: Necessary, time-sensitive feedback that has to be given where others happen to be, such as a safety problem in a room full of people.
Settings where feedback is normal and applied evenly to everybody, such as a design critique, which humiliate nobody.
An awkward moment that was only poor timing, or carelessness with something private, such as an offhand mention at a party.
A public award or roast that the person agreed to and enjoys.
Information that is public for a real, disclosed reason, such as a published result or a minuted decision.
A story told with affection that the person is happy to have told, and might tell themselves.
compendium.why: An audience makes the injury durable in a way private criticism is not: everyone present carries a version of it afterwards, including the person it was about. It cannot be taken back privately later, and it can change how the group treats you.

compendium.name: Labeling as Identity Warfare
compendium.what: Pinning a fixed defect label on a person, such as 'the difficult one', until others read everything they do through it.
sounds: Oh, that's just Dana being Dana.
Careful with him, he's the difficult one.
She seems fine today, but you know how unstable she can be.
A new hire is introduced to you as 'our resident troublemaker', with a laugh.
Your polite email is called passive-aggressive and your direct one is called aggressive.
Of course you'd say that. That's exactly what someone like you would say.
A meeting note files your three questions under the heading 'attitude'.
nots: An unflattering description that is accurate, such as calling a colleague who has missed every deadline for a year unreliable.
A reputation that formed because many people independently had similar experiences with you.
Specific feedback about one act, such as 'you interrupted three times today', that leaves the rest of you alone.
A nickname you chose, or gladly accept, because it is affectionate.
A role word like 'the newest member', which describes a position and not a defect.
compendium.why: Once a label sticks, ordinary behavior is read as confirming it, so nothing you do can count as evidence against it. You may start managing how you appear instead of simply acting, and people who never met you can arrive already holding the verdict.

compendium.name: Rage as Control
compendium.what: Explosive anger that, whatever lies behind it, reliably ends a disagreement because the people around it learn to give way.
sounds: Don't you dare bring that up again! shouted, followed by a slammed door.
Look what you made me do, said over a broken plate.
A fist on the table and 'We're done talking about this.'
Jaw tight, voice low: 'Go ahead. Keep pushing.'
You know how I get. Why do you do this?
Others in the home whispering 'not tonight, they're in a mood'.
Everyone going quiet at the sound of keys in the door.
nots: Proportionate anger at something truly upsetting that is voiced, heard, and followed by a conversation that can still change the outcome.
Someone working on regulating anger who slips, owns it the same day, and uses an agreed break afterwards.
One blow-up during a crisis such as a bereavement, acknowledged afterwards.
A family or friend group where everyone raises their voice and everyone carries on with the topic.
Panic or overwhelm that looks like rage, where the person needs to leave the room and comes back to resume the subject.
compendium.why: People around an outburst learn to put calming things down ahead of whatever started it, so topics stop being raised long before anyone decides to stop raising them. Over time one person's temper quietly sets the limits of a household or workplace.

compendium.name: Credit Theft
compendium.what: Presenting another person's work, idea or effort as one's own, or letting the credit drift away from the person who produced it.
sounds: As I was saying, opening a point you made in the last meeting.
I put together a draft, about a draft you wrote.
The team came up with this, and your name is missing from every slide.
A thank-you sent to you privately while the all-staff message names someone else.
The byline order changes after you have sent the final file.
On a client call, your report is called 'my analysis'.
You don't mind, do you? It's all one team anyway, said after the fact.
nots: Two people reaching the same idea independently, which happens often in shared fields.
A team product where credit is spread by agreement without erasing anyone.
An honest oversight in a list of names, corrected once it is pointed out.
Work done on behalf of an organization or client by agreement, such as ghostwriting or staff writing under a department name.
A manager saying 'my team shipped this', which claims the group and not your piece.
Someone building openly on your idea and naming you as its start.
compendium.why: Work continues while recognition accrues elsewhere, and by the time the pattern is visible the original attribution is hard to prove. Pay, promotion, references and your own sense of competence can all follow the credit rather than the work.

compendium.name: Sabotaging Success
compendium.what: A run of setbacks, such as a canceled lift, a lost message or a sudden crisis, that keeps landing just as someone is about to advance.
sounds: I know your exam's tomorrow, but I really need to talk about us tonight.
Oh, I forgot to tell you the recruiter rang.
I can't do pickup after all, so you'll just have to miss the interview.
Do you really think you're ready for that course? It'll only end in tears.
Keys, charger or paperwork go missing on the morning of the interview, and nobody knows where.
We can't afford the fee this year, maybe next, said each time you sign up.
A crisis in their life on the eve of your milestone, for the third time this year.
nots: Plain coincidence. Unrelated trouble does cluster around big days, partly because those are the days you are watching.
A person who is unreliable about everything, not only around your milestones.
Genuinely competing demands, such as shift work or a sick relative, that clash with your timeline.
A worried 'Are you sure?' from someone who says it once, names the cost to you, and helps anyway.
Your own nerves or avoidance before big moments producing mishaps that are then blamed on someone else.
Self-sabotage, which has a different cause and a different remedy.
compendium.why: Progress keeps stalling for reasons that each look like bad luck, so you start doubting your own competence rather than the timing. Over months, chances to earn, learn or move out can quietly pass, which matters most where you depend on one person for money or a home.

compendium.name: Setting Up to Fail
compendium.what: Giving someone a task or a standard they are unlikely to meet under the conditions provided, then treating the shortfall as proof of their inadequacy.
sounds: "I know it's due Friday and the data isn't in yet, but I have faith in you."
"There's no budget for that, just make it work."
"You don't need to see the client brief. Just draft it."
"Hit ninety-five percent and we'll talk." Then, once you do: "Now we need ninety-eight."
"It just needs to be more polished," with no description of what polished means.
"I want it fast, perfect and cheap, and I'm not discussing which one gives."
"Why did you let it fail? I gave you everything you needed."
"Remember the Henderson project? That's why I can't trust you with this."
nots: Hard tasks with real constraints, which are ordinary work, and resources that are unavailable to everyone rather than withheld from you.
Something that turned out harder than anyone anticipated, with nobody having arranged it.
A stretch goal or pilot framed openly as aspirational, with a fallback in place, so a miss is understood to be fine.
A demanding bar that others in your role have met under the same conditions, or that you have cleared before.
Clumsy delegation by someone who underestimated the task and revises the plan when told.
Hard but specific performance management, with written criteria and support.
compendium.why: Conditions disappear from the account and only the outcome remains, so a predictable failure becomes durable evidence about the person who was handed it. Effort rises while the record of misses grows, and that record can be quoted in reviews and decisions about you long after the conditions are forgotten.

compendium.name: Scapegoating
compendium.what: Placing blame for a shared, systemic or leadership failure on one individual, who then absorbs the consequences while the cause stays in place.
sounds: We found the problem. It's Priya.
If it weren't for him, we'd all be fine.
A report names one junior employee as sole cause and leaves out the sign-off chain.
She's always the one who stirs things up, said in a family after a group row.
Let's not look backward. The person responsible has been dealt with.
The group chat turns on one member after a mistake everyone shared.
The organization says one individual acted outside procedures, while the procedures stay unchanged.
nots: A case where one person did make the consequential mistake.
A situation where shared responsibility really does concentrate in one person's decisions.
Accountability that matches the person's real authority, which can feel harsh and still be proportionate.
A fair investigation that names an individual among several findings and also addresses the system.
Group frustration that fades once the cause is discussed, without anyone being punished.
A leader who owns a group's failure publicly instead of pushing it down.
compendium.why: One person absorbs consequences out of proportion to a collective failure, and the conditions that produced it stay exactly as they were, because the matter has been declared solved. The person blamed can lose standing, income or belonging, while the same problem waits for the next name.

compendium.name: Flying Monkeys
compendium.what: Friends, relatives or colleagues drawn in to carry pressure or criticism to someone, or to report back on them, for another person who stays out of the room.
sounds: I'm not taking sides, but they're really hurting. Can't you just call them?
They asked me to talk to you. I don't want to be the bad guy, but somebody has to say it.
I only know what they've told me, but you need to hear this.
I promised I'd pass this on, so please don't shoot the messenger.
How are you doing? Where are you staying these days?
Three different people have rung me about you this week, and they're all saying the same things.
They said you wouldn't pick up their calls, so I thought I'd try.
A cousin you rarely hear from repeats a phrase you first heard from the other person.
nots: Friends noticing things on their own and reaching out unprompted, and family members who discuss shared worries and reach similar views.
Asking a mutual friend how to approach a hard conversation, which is different from asking them to have it for you.
A go-between set up openly where direct contact is not safe or possible, such as a mediator or a lawyer.
Someone who hears about a conflict and decides by themselves to raise it, speaking for themselves.
A relative who relays a message because both people asked them to, and who is clear about whose message it is.
Someone checking in out of their own long relationship with you.
compendium.why: Pressure arrives from several directions at once, from people who believe they are acting on their own concern, which makes it nearly impossible to answer without appearing to attack them. The person whose concern it is never has to stand behind what is being demanded.

compendium.name: Smear Campaign
compendium.what: Spreading distorted or false accounts of a person to those who matter to them, so they are doubted, shunned or not believed before they have spoken.
sounds: I probably shouldn't say this, but I've always worried about how stable they are.
I'm only telling you because I care what happens to you.
I'm not saying they're lying, but I'd check everything they tell you.
I heard you were the reason the last team fell apart.
Oh, I was warned about you.
A reference you expected to be glowing is lukewarm, and the person says they 'heard some things'.
Friends who were warm go quiet, and one lets slip a phrase you have never said yourself.
You wouldn't believe what they put me through. I don't like to talk about it.
nots: Venting honestly to a close friend after a painful break-up, with no follow-up and no spread.
Independent, accurate criticism from several people who each have their own basis for it.
A specific, warranted concern passed to someone who genuinely needs it, such as an employer checking a documented problem.
Ordinary gossip that nobody started and nobody steers.
Social circles thinning out after a separation, with no account being pushed.
A public dispute in which both sides sincerely believe their own version.
compendium.why: The account travels faster than any correction, and it often reaches people before you know there is anything to correct. When you finally speak, you may be heard as proof of what they were warned about, and you can lose work, friends or standing without a single conversation to point to.

compendium.name: Silent Coalitions
compendium.what: A group quietly agreeing, without any open discussion, to keep one person on the margins so that no clear incident ever exists.
sounds: A group chat that quietly moves to a new thread without you, and no one mentions it.
Plans mentioned on Monday that you learn about only after they happened.
Replies to your messages that are polite but shorter and later than the replies others get.
When you ask whether something is going on, several people say 'no, of course not' in similar words.
Your suggestions in meetings get a pause, then the same idea is picked up when someone else says it.
People who are friendly one-on-one are distant in a group.
nots: Social anxiety can produce the same feeling with nothing at all behind it, and some groups are simply less inclusive as a general dynamic rather than towards one individual.
A low period colors ordinary social gaps and makes a pattern out of them.
A tight friend group that has history together and is not hostile to new people, only slow to open up.
A busy season in which everyone is slow to reply, including to each other.
Drifting apart because interests, schedules or life stages have changed.
compendium.why: There is no incident to point at, only a consistent absence, which turns the search for an explanation inward. The person ends up blaming themselves for something nobody will admit to.

compendium.name: Group Consolidation
compendium.what: Publicly punishing one person harshly enough that everyone watching learns what disagreement will cost them.
sounds: A person who questioned a plan is called out by name at the all-hands, with a long list of past mistakes.
A leader says 'let this be a lesson to everyone' after a minor error.
A group chat member who disagreed is removed, and the rest are told it was 'for the good of the group'.
A dismissal is announced to the whole department the same day, with no private conversation first.
After a public dressing-down, the room goes quiet and the next meeting has no questions.
A relative who disagreed at a family dinner is mocked in front of the table, and others laugh nervously.
nots: Proportionate accountability can be visible simply because of the setting, such as an open-plan office, a meeting or a family gathering.
A genuinely serious matter can warrant a visible response on its own merits.
Consequences applied consistently and announced as policy are not calibrated to an audience.
A leader explaining why a rule was enforced so that others understand the standard, without humiliating the person.
A group removing someone who harassed other members, where the removal protects people and is in proportion.
compendium.why: Everyone watching learns the price of dissent without being told, and the lesson outlasts the person it was demonstrated on.

compendium.name: Pile-Ons
compendium.what: Many people pile criticism onto one person in a short span, so the sheer volume becomes the problem.
sounds: Did you really say that? Everyone is talking about you.
A reply thread where the first twenty responses are the same sentence in different words.
I haven't read the whole thread but wow.
A group chat where people who had been quiet each type 'same' under a complaint about you.
Ratio'd. Just delete your account.
Notifications arriving faster than you can open them.
nots: A serious concern genuinely shared by many people. When many people independently say a statement was harmful, that is feedback, not a pile-on.
Proportionate public criticism of a public figure for a public statement.
Varied, independent responses that disagree with each other and include some support.
Several friends each raising the same worry with you privately, at different times.
Customers all complaining about the same real defect in a product.
Critics who quote you accurately and answer what you actually said, even if there are many of them.
compendium.why: Fifty versions of the same criticism land as something different from one, and there is no way to answer them at the scale they arrive. The person may lose sleep, leave a platform or stop speaking up, even when a few of the points were fair.

compendium.name: Ostracism
compendium.what: Leaving a person out of invitations, conversations, decisions or information until they end up on the outside of their own group.
sounds: Oh, we figured you were busy. (said after plans you were never told about)
It was just a small get-together, we didn't think to invite everyone.
Didn't you see the group chat? (when you were never added)
Nothing's wrong, we just didn't think of you.
A team calendar where every colleague on your project is invited to the planning meeting except you.
A room that goes quiet when you walk in and picks up again when you leave.
nots: One forgotten invitation with nothing following it is an oversight.
A group drifting apart because jobs, moves and children changed everyone's schedules.
Someone who has quietly opted out of events themselves and now seems excluded when they chose it.
A private gathering of a few close friends that was never meant to be group-wide.
A manager limiting a meeting to the people with a role in the decision, and telling you why.
Space that you or others asked for, such as a friend needing time alone after a loss.
compendium.why: Exclusion from information and decisions has practical consequences well beyond the social ones, and each omission is small enough to be explained away. A person can miss deadlines, a promotion or a friend's news, and then be blamed for being out of touch.

compendium.name: Mobbing
compendium.what: Sustained harassment of one person by a group over weeks or months, most often at work or in a community, wearing down their standing.
sounds: Everyone has noticed it, not just me.
You're being very sensitive. No one is out to get you.
We've had several people raise concerns about you. (with no names and no examples)
Did you see what she did in the meeting? Again.
If you were easier to work with, this wouldn't be happening.
A manager's file with half a dozen vague complaints from different people, none dated or specific.
Colleagues who go silent when you walk by, then are friendly when alone with you.
nots: Separate conflicts with different people that happen to land in the same month.
One serious dispute with a colleague that others have taken sides on, which is contentious rather than orchestrated.
A documented instance where the person really was responsible and others responded to it.
Several people giving direct, specific feedback because each saw the same lapse.
A tense stretch around a deadline or reorganization when everyone is short with everyone.
One meeting where several people disagreed with your proposal.
compendium.why: Attempts to address it get absorbed as further evidence, so the ordinary responses open to someone under sustained group pressure tend to make the position worse. Over months the person can lose work, references or standing, and their account is doubted because so many people seem to disagree.

compendium.name: Splitting
compendium.what: Seeing a person or group as all good or all bad, with no middle ground, and flipping that view suddenly after a minor event.
sounds: You're the only person who truly gets me.
I thought you were different. You're just like all the rest.
She's perfect, I can't believe how lucky we are. (weeks later) I can't believe I ever trusted her.
After all that, you did one thing wrong, so I'm done.
Everyone in that department is useless.
You were never my friend. You were pretending the whole time.
I'm a complete failure, there's nothing good in me.
nots: A serious breach of trust that permanently changes how someone is seen is a proportionate reassessment, not a swing.
Gradual disillusionment as you get to know a person better is ordinary.
Someone more reactive during a hard period who still sees nuance when calmer.
Strong enthusiasm for a new friend or hero that mellows over months into a balanced view.
A person describing a bad experience with one organization without generalizing to everyone in it.
A firm opinion about someone's conduct that stays tied to specific events.
compendium.why: Standing shifts without reference to anything actually done, so there is no behavior available that reliably keeps a person in favor. You can end up walking on eggshells, and watching others around them be built up and torn down in turn.

compendium.name: Golden Child Elevation
compendium.what: Holding up one family member as the model of excellence, and using that standard to measure everyone else and find them short.
sounds: Why can't you be more like your brother?
Your sister never needed reminding.
Look what Daniel did this year. Now that's someone who takes things seriously.
She's just going through a phase. You, on the other hand, should know better.
We never had to worry about him.
A parent toasts one child's promotion at a family dinner and skips another's.
nots: Pride in a specific achievement, expressed without reference to anyone else, is just pride.
Different family members having different strengths celebrated differently is not a ranking.
A parent venting their own stress may land comparatively without the comparison being the point.
A parent giving extra help to a child with greater needs, such as an illness or a disability.
A sibling who really is thriving, noticed with warmth rather than used as a yardstick.
A coach pointing to a teammate's technique as an example of one specific skill.
compendium.why: Achievement by one family member becomes the measure applied to the rest, so nothing they accomplish arrives without a comparison attached. Over years, people can grow up believing they are the disappointing one, while the favored one fears losing their place.

compendium.name: Social Proof Pressure
compendium.what: Using the claim that everyone else already agrees to push one person into going along, whether or not the agreement is real.
sounds: Everyone else has already signed off. You're the only one holding things up.
People have noticed you've been difficult lately.
All the other parents agreed. I don't see why you need to be different.
Nobody else has a problem with this.
We talked about it as a group and it was unanimous.
Everyone thinks you've been unfair about this.
Most people in your position just do it.
A screenshot of a group chat is shown with only the agreeing messages in view.
nots: A genuinely unanimous decision, accurately described, that you happen to disagree with.
Social proof offered openly as one input among several, such as 'most people book early, but it's up to you'.
Groups reaching quick, real consensus on something straightforward.
A friend telling you, with names, that several people raised the same worry, so you can ask them yourself.
Summarizing a truly shared concern without naming each person, which people do in good faith.
Workplace or cultural habits of speaking in 'we' language as a courtesy.
compendium.why: A judgment that felt sound a minute earlier starts to feel eccentric. Disagreeing seems to mean disagreeing with everyone, and the claim is vague enough that there is no one to check it with, so the decision gets made against an apparent majority and not on its merits.

compendium.name: Divide and Conquer
compendium.what: Distance or distrust between people who might otherwise support one another, so that they do not compare notes or act together.
sounds: I probably shouldn't tell you this, but here's what Priya really said about you.
You know what they really think of you, right?
Let's keep this between us. The others wouldn't understand.
You're the only one I can trust with this.
I wouldn't bring it up with her. It will only make things worse.
A group chat goes quiet after one person has spoken privately to each member.
Two coworkers are each told they were the one picked for a project, and each is asked not to mention it.
nots: Miscommunication between two people that has nothing to do with anyone else.
Relationships drifting apart for unrelated reasons such as distance, new jobs or new children.
Someone relaying a conversation inaccurately because they remembered it badly.
A person sharing a confidence with one friend because that friend is the one they trust.
A manager meeting employees one at a time for routine reviews.
Two people who simply do not get along and would be at odds with or without a go-between.
compendium.why: Two people who might have compared notes stop speaking, and each carries a version of the other that neither gets the chance to correct. Meanwhile no one is in a position to say that something is wrong, because each person is dealing with it alone.

compendium.name: Foot-in-the-Door
compendium.what: Winning a small yes first, then using it to secure a larger one, so each agreement makes the next harder to refuse.
sounds: Could you just look over this one page? It'll take two minutes.
You already helped with the first part, so it makes sense for you to finish it.
You said yes to the trial, so signing the full contract is really just the next step.
It's only a small change from what we did last time.
Since you covered one shift, could you take the whole weekend?
We've come this far together. You wouldn't back out now.
A free gift is handed over, and the request for a donation that follows mentions the gift.
nots: Small favors that grow into larger ones naturally and mutually, with real consent at each stage, are how most relationships work.
Someone who asks for something small, gets it, and only later finds they need something bigger, with no sequence in mind.
A large request that stands on its own merits whatever came before it.
A trial whose price and cancellation terms were shown clearly before you began.
A role that grows as trust is earned, with each increase named out loud and agreed.
Volunteering for more because you enjoy the work.
compendium.why: The larger request is judged against what you already agreed to, not on its own terms. You can end up carrying an obligation you never chose at any single moment, and refusing starts to feel like going back on your word.

compendium.name: Door-in-the-Face
compendium.what: Making a big request that is likely to be refused so that the smaller request that follows seems modest and hard to turn down.
sounds: "Could you take the whole month of shifts? No? Okay, then how about just next weekend?"
"Would you lend me ten thousand? That's too much, I get it. Could you do two?"
"I met you halfway, so now it's your turn to meet me."
"Fine, forget the donation. Surely you can sign up for the monthly plan?"
"I was going to ask you to move in for a year, but a few weeks would be okay."
"I came down a lot. The least you can do is say yes to this."
nots: Ordinary negotiation, where both sides know the opening position is high and expect to settle in the middle.
Someone who truly wanted the larger thing, asked for it, and then settled for less in good faith.
A person who learns your limits from your first answer and then asks for something that fits them.
Two separate requests that happen to arrive close together.
A reasonable request that you find uncomfortable only because it follows a stressful one.
compendium.why: Relief at the smaller ask stands in for judging it. The second request gets measured against the first, not against what is fair, and a yes given to feel gracious can leave you carrying more than you chose.

compendium.name: Anchoring
compendium.what: Putting forward a first number, price or claim that then shapes how every later figure and offer is judged.
sounds: "The listing price is four hundred, but for you, three-fifty."
"People with your experience usually ask for much more than that." (said before any figure is mentioned)
"We're thinking about forty thousand for this role." (when the going rate is well above)
"Everyone else in the family gave a hundred, but give what you can."
A 'was $199, now $89' tag on an item that was never sold for $199.
"The other side wants a million. I think we can get them down to six hundred thousand."
nots: An honest opening position in a bargain, where both sides know the first number is a starting point.
A real price list, rate card or pay scale that states what something costs.
Someone with little experience of pricing blurting out a high number without any strategy behind it.
A reference you picked yourself, such as the price you saw last week at another shop.
Natural comparison: noticing one thing is cheaper than another is just using information.
compendium.why: Everything that follows gets measured against a figure or framing that was never justified, so an offer that would look unreasonable on its own can seem fair, and you may feel you won something when you did not.

compendium.name: Choice Restriction
compendium.what: Closing off or hiding realistic alternatives one by one, so that a single outcome ends up looking like the only sensible choice.
sounds: You don't really have a choice here.
You could do the second one, but you'd lose your whole routine and it never works out. The first is simple.
I already booked the one that works. You just need to sign.
There's no point looking at other places. I called around and they're all full.
The third option? Honestly, nobody sensible picks that.
I have the forms for this one ready. The others take weeks of paperwork.
Only one form is on the table, already filled in, and the other routes are never mentioned.
Looking back, every path I was offered ended in the same place.
nots: Options are often truly limited by outside constraints nobody arranged, such as a tight budget, a small town or a full calendar.
Honest advice about which of several real options is best, with the others left available to you.
A sensible default set for practical reasons, like a standard meeting time you can change.
A person who only knows a few options, shares them, and welcomes the others when you find them.
A menu of fixed packages shown openly with prices side by side.
Circumstances narrowing over time, as a lease ends or a workplace closes, with nobody steering.
compendium.why: No demand is made, so there is nothing to push back on. By the time you notice, you may have agreed to something you never really picked, with no single moment to point to when you ask how you got here.

compendium.name: Emotional Flooding
compendium.what: Pouring on emotion so fast and so hard that the other person cannot think, and speed or intensity is mistaken for closeness.
sounds: "I've never felt this way about anyone. I know you're the one." (said in the first week)
"I can't breathe when you're not here. Please don't leave me tonight."
A midnight fight, a dawn apology and a gift by noon, repeated most weeks.
"If you really cared, you would have dropped everything."
"I'm in pieces. I need you to fix this right now."
Dozens of long, intense messages a day, swinging between adoration and despair.
nots: The early excitement of a new relationship, which can be intense and then settle into something steadier.
A person in a real crisis, such as a death or job loss, who is overwhelmed because the situation is.
A naturally expressive person whose feelings are big and quickly shown, with nothing engineered behind it.
A single heated argument that left both of you shaken.
Your own flooding in a hard talk. Anyone's thinking narrows when they are overwhelmed.
compendium.why: Sustained intensity leaves no quiet stretch in which to assess anything. Speed gets mistaken for depth, and there is no calm vantage point from which to notice what you are agreeing to.

compendium.name: Cognitive Overload
compendium.what: Burying someone in more information, steps or demands than they can take in, so they cannot judge a decision clearly.
sounds: A forty-page agreement handed over at the signing table with 'it's all standard, just initial here.'
"There are twelve things I need to go through with you, and we are going to do them all tonight."
"I've sent you the whole file, and I need your answer by the morning."
"Do you want me to explain the policy? It will take an hour, and most people just sign."
A long email with seven different questions and a note that all must be answered today.
"If you had read the terms, you would know this."
nots: A decision that is truly complex, such as a mortgage or a medical consent, which does need a lot of real information.
An anxious person who explains everything because they want to be thorough, with no wish to hurry you.
A busy period at work when many real tasks pile up, with nobody designing it.
Plain jargon from someone who forgot you are not an expert in their field.
Your own tiredness or stress, which lowers how much you can take in on any day.
compendium.why: Agreement becomes the fastest way out of the overwhelm, so the decision that results was never really weighed, and you may find later that you consented to things you did not understand.

compendium.name: Bait and Switch
compendium.what: Advertising or promising an appealing deal, then swapping in a worse one after the person is committed or has given something up.
sounds: "That model just sold out, but I can offer you this one for a bit more."
"The role turned out to be different from what we discussed, but you'll grow into it."
"The price I gave you did not include the fees. Everyone pays them."
"I know I said we would live near your family, but this place makes more sense."
"The flat is gone, but there is another one, slightly further out and pricier."
"That's not what I meant. You must have misunderstood."
nots: A real change in circumstances that is explained openly and renegotiated fairly.
An honest error in a quote that the person corrects as soon as they notice, without leaning on you to accept it.
Terms that were clearly described as tentative or subject to approval at the time.
An item that actually sold out, where the seller truly has nothing else and says so.
Your own memory or hope shaping what was said. Writing things down is the only way to know.
compendium.why: By the time the terms change, you have often given something up: a deposit, another offer, a move, a plan. Walking away costs more than accepting, and that cost is what makes a worse deal acceptable.

compendium.name: Pre-Punishment
compendium.what: Shutting yourself down before anyone else can, by not applying, speaking or trying, because past experience taught you that being seen gets punished.
sounds: "There's no point applying. They would only laugh."
"If I speak up in the meeting, they will tear it apart."
"I'd rather not send it. Then no one can say it is bad."
"If I do well, they will expect more, and then I will be punished when I cannot keep it up."
Writing an email, rereading it eleven times and deleting it.
"Who do I think I am?" (in your own voice, before you have done anything)
nots: A realistic judgment that the odds are poor, such as not applying for a job whose requirements you clearly do not meet.
Ordinary caution or humility, which needs no painful history behind it.
Choosing not to pursue something because of competing priorities, such as family, health or money.
Introversion or a preference for staying out of the spotlight, if it brings you no distress.
A needed rest. Pulling back during a hard season can be healthy.
compendium.why: Opportunities close before anyone else has the chance to refuse them. The cost, which includes jobs not applied for and things not said, stays invisible because nothing happened, and your life can narrow without anyone noticing.

compendium.name: Lying
compendium.what: Saying something the speaker knows to be untrue so that another person will believe it and act on it.
sounds: I was at work until nine.
I never got your message.
The payment went through last week.
I haven't spoken to her in years.
It wasn't me who told them.
That's the first I'm hearing of it.
nots: An honest mistake stated sincerely. A rounded or simplified figure that is not technically precise may carry no deception at all, and someone who corrects their account because they later remembered better is doing the right thing.
A prediction or opinion that turned out wrong, such as 'it'll be fine'.
A refusal to share, such as 'I can't discuss that', which declines to answer and states nothing false.
A cover story for a surprise party that everyone laughs about afterwards.
A child's imaginative story told as play.
compendium.why: You decide things with false information, and finding out costs more than one belief. It makes you doubt everything else that person has told you, including the parts that were true.

compendium.name: Lying by Omission
compendium.what: Leaving out information the other person needs for an accurate understanding, while everything that is said stays technically true.
sounds: 'I never said that wasn't true.'
'I told you about it.' (a passing remark, months ago, in a different conversation)
'You never asked.'
'It didn't seem relevant.' (said about the one detail the decision turned on)
A version of a story that includes everything favoring one side and nothing that complicates it.
'Why would I bring that up? It wasn't your business.' (after you had to deal with its effects)
You learn from someone else a fact they had known all along and never mentioned.
nots: Not thinking to mention something that did not seem relevant at the time is ordinary.
Plenty of information is legitimately nobody else's business, such as a friend's confidence or a person's private medical history.
A gap held briefly, with a plan to close it once the timing is right, such as waiting for test results before telling the family. That is a delay, not a concealment.
Context can be missing because the speaker never had it, which is a gap and not a filter.
Sharing what you know as you learn it, across several conversations, differs from choosing in advance which facts another person gets.
A short summary that drops detail for length and would readily expand if asked.
compendium.why: Nothing said was false, so there is no untruth to point at, only a conclusion you reached on grounds you did not know were incomplete. The missing piece usually appears too late to change what you chose, and you may blame yourself for not asking.

compendium.name: Strategic Incompleteness
compendium.what: Giving someone enough information to take the next step but never enough to see the whole picture, so they keep coming back for more.
sounds: Just do this part for now, I'll explain the rest later.
You don't need to worry about that yet.
Trust me, I'll handle that side.
I'll send you the next step once you've finished this one.
I'll walk you through that when we get there.
We'll cross that bridge when we come to it.
nots: Genuinely complex things are often explained in stages because that is the only comprehensible order. Someone who does not yet have the full picture can only pass on what they have, and need-to-know structures exist for reasons unconnected to any one person.
A mentor who holds back advanced material until the basics are learned, and says so.
A project whose later phases genuinely have not been decided yet.
A surprise being planned, where the holder of the plan is open about keeping it.
A safety or legal rule that limits who may receive which information.
compendium.why: You can act, but you can't act well, so every step sends you back to the same source, and independence never arrives.

compendium.name: Catfishing
compendium.what: Building a relationship, usually online, behind a made-up identity such as borrowed photos or an invented life story, so the other person bonds with someone who does not exist.
sounds: Photos that, on a reverse image search, belong to a different name or a model's portfolio.
'My camera is broken' or 'bad signal' every time a video call is planned.
A glamorous remote job, such as offshore work or overseas service, that explains being out of reach.
Life details that clash across chats: a hometown, a sibling or a timeline that changes.
'I've never felt this way about anyone', said within days of meeting.
A sudden emergency that needs money from someone met only online.
No friends or family who ever comment, appear in photos or can be introduced.
nots: Reasonable caution about identifying details early in an online relationship is not a fabricated identity.
Outdated photos and flattering presentation fall short of accurate without being wholesale invention.
Reluctance about video calls or meeting in person is frequently social anxiety.
A username or pseudonym used for privacy, with the real name shared as trust grows.
A person with safety or health reasons, such as someone hiding their location from a former partner, who wants control over what they show.
Role-play in a game or fiction community where everyone knows the characters are invented.
compendium.why: Everything built on the connection rests on ground that was never there, so what is lost on discovery includes the relationship's entire history, not merely its ending.

compendium.name: Half-Truth Framing
compendium.what: Choosing and arranging statements that are each true so that the listener ends up with a false overall picture.
sounds: 'Did the repair pass inspection?' / 'The inspector spent an hour at the house.'
'Were you out with anyone last night?' / 'I was at the pub until eleven.' (the question was who)
'But everything I said was true.' offered after you discover the gap.
'The company has never missed a payroll.' (said of a firm about to close)
'I never told her she was fired. I only said her role was changing.'
'Sales are up 20 percent this month.' (after a 40 percent drop the month before, left unsaid)
Asked a direct question, they answer fully and warmly, about something next to it.
nots: An accurate summary necessarily omits detail for length.
People often present facts in whatever order those facts occurred to them, with no steer in mind.
A genuinely different, honestly held interpretation of the same true facts is disagreement rather than arrangement.
Careful, precise people answer exactly what was asked and nothing more. That can sound evasive without steering anyone anywhere.
An honest answer given with an incomplete picture, because that was all the speaker had.
Things people are entitled not to disclose at all, such as medical history, where they say it is private and do not imply something else.
compendium.why: Every fact checks out, so a careful listener who verifies still reaches the wrong conclusion. When you object you are told, correctly, that nothing false was said, which can leave you doubting your own reasonable inference instead of the account.

compendium.name: False Reports
compendium.what: Filing complaints or accusations with an employer, school, agency or police that contain claims the filer knows are untrue, so the target must answer for something that never happened.
sounds: A letter from HR describing a meeting you can show you did not attend.
A welfare check or investigation notice triggered by a claim you can disprove.
A complaint that names a date when you were provably elsewhere.
Details in the report that match an argument you had, but nothing that actually happened.
Several agencies receiving similar reports from the same source within weeks.
nots: A genuine report that characterises events in a way the subject disputes still reflects the reporter's honest perception. Institutions also make their own errors in processing legitimate reports.
Two people who disagree factually about what happened, where neither is inventing anything.
A report made in good faith and found unsubstantiated. Unproven is not the same as false.
A mandated reporter, such as a teacher or nurse, passing on a concern as their role requires.
A true complaint that is also embarrassing or inconvenient for the person it concerns.
compendium.why: A fabricated complaint puts a real job, license or family arrangement in jeopardy, and the person has to answer for something that did not happen before anyone establishes whether it did.

compendium.name: Paper-Trail Traps
compendium.what: Creating or shaping written records, such as write-ups, emails and notes, that build a one-sided case against someone who does not know it is being assembled.
sounds: Just to confirm what we discussed... followed by a version you do not recognize.
A review that cites 'several previous concerns' no one raised with you.
An email thread about problems with your work that copied you in late, or not at all.
It's all documented, in reply to a question about a concern you have never heard.
A file containing small events from months ago, such as a late arrival or a tone of voice.
A folder of screenshots shown at a meeting, picked to show one side of a long exchange.
nots: Standard documentation applied to everyone is not targeting. A genuine record of concerns that were actually raised with the person is legitimate even if they wish it did not exist.
Someone keeping notes on their own experience for their own reference.
Meeting minutes circulated to all attendees with a chance to correct them.
Records required by law or policy in regulated settings such as care or finance.
A manager who writes an informal summary to help them remember, and shares it when asked.
compendium.why: A record accumulates that the person has no opportunity to answer as it is built, and by the time they see it, it reads as damning.

compendium.name: Compartmentalization
compendium.what: Keeping information in separate pockets, with different people knowing different parts, so that nobody can see enough to notice a problem or ask the right question.
sounds: Don't mention this to your brother, he'd only worry.
That's between you and me.
You don't need to talk to finance about that, I'll sort it.
I've told Mom the dates and Dad the cost, there's no need for them to compare.
Why are you asking her? I said I'd handle it.
Please don't discuss this with the other team.
nots: Confidentiality and need-to-know structures exist for good reasons in most organizations, and information silos form naturally in any large family or workplace. Someone who simply did not think to pass something on has partitioned nothing.
A surprise being planned, where the planner is open about keeping it.
Medical or client privacy that is stated and fits the situation.
Keeping your own private matters from some relatives.
Role-based access required by law, such as patient records.
compendium.why: No single person can see enough to raise a question, so accountability fails not because anyone refused it but because nobody had the view required to ask for it.

compendium.name: Thought Control
compendium.what: Controlling the words, explanations and conclusions a person may use, so doubt is labeled a symptom and one reading of events counts as the only acceptable one.
sounds: Asking that question shows how far you have drifted.
That's just the negativity talking. Everyone goes through it.
We don't use that word here. We say it this way.
People who leave always say things like that. They were never really committed.
If you read what they write, you'll only be confused. Let us tell you what they mean.
Your doubts are normal for someone at your stage. Keep going and they will pass.
You aren't thinking clearly right now. Let's go back over the lessons.
nots: Shared shorthand, which every family, profession and fan community develops over time and which is normal rather than controlling.
A belief you hold independently and can explain in your own words, including to someone who disagrees.
Passionate, sincere conviction, which is different from a mechanism that suppresses dissent.
A teacher or coach insisting on one method for a while so you can learn it, while you stay free to question it afterwards.
Someone disagreeing with you firmly and giving reasons, which is argument and not control.
A religious or political community with strong norms that welcomes questions and lets people leave without penalty.
compendium.why: The words you would use to examine the situation are supplied from inside it, so doubt arrives already labeled as a symptom. Questions that cannot be asked cannot be answered, and you may lose a way to check your own thinking.

compendium.name: Phobia Indoctrination
compendium.what: Intense, out-of-proportion dread attached to particular actions such as leaving, disagreeing or trusting outsiders, until avoiding them is a bodily reflex rather than a reasoned choice.
sounds: You have no idea what happens to people who go out there alone.
Do you know what happened to her after she left? I won't even say.
Don't tell your friends our business. You don't know who they really are.
I'm only saying this because I love you. People like that eat you alive.
I feel sick just thinking about taking that job in another city.
Every time I pick up the phone to call my sister, my hands shake and I put it back down.
He told me I would be nothing and nobody would hire me. I know that isn't true, but I feel it.
nots: Proportionate warnings about real risks from someone with relevant experience, which are useful information.
Pre-existing anxiety or trauma responses that belong to you and may have nothing to do with anyone currently present.
Cautious family or cultural norms that restrict you without having been built to frighten anyone.
A specific phobia, such as fear of flying or of dogs, which has its own causes and its own treatment.
A friend or relative who worries aloud, overstates a risk once, and is happy to be corrected.
Healthy caution after a bad experience of your own.
compendium.why: Avoidance becomes bodily rather than reasoned, so options stay ruled out by a fear response that persists even after you have concluded the fear was unwarranted. Choices that should be open stay shut.

compendium.name: Administrative Escalation
compendium.what: Turning a small, informal concern into a formal complaint, report or legal step whose weight is out of proportion to what happened.
sounds: "I've tried to resolve this, but I'm going to have to take it to HR." No earlier attempt had been made.
A formal written warning arriving three days after you asked for a change to your schedule.
"This is now on the record." The incident was a disagreement in a hallway.
A letter from a lawyer about a fence dispute that began as a chat over the hedge.
"I'm documenting this." A note is placed in your file for a late reply to one email.
A complaint to the housing association the week after you asked about a repair.
nots: A serious issue that rightly goes straight to formal process, whoever raised a concern first.
A workplace or family where formalizing things is the usual practice for everyone, applied to all alike.
Someone who did not know an informal route existed and escalated for lack of another way to be heard.
A formal complaint made after informal attempts truly failed and the problem continued.
A required report, such as a safety incident that staff must file by law or policy.
compendium.why: Defending against a process that is out of scale takes time, money and attention however it ends, and your next concern may go unraised for that reason alone. Even a case that is dismissed leaves a record you did not expect to have.

compendium.name: Paper Terrorism
compendium.what: Overwhelming a person with a steady stream of filings, motions, complaints and requests whose combined burden drains their time, money and energy.
sounds: A fifth motion arriving in six weeks on a point the judge already ruled on.
A records request, a complaint to the licensing board and a new lawsuit all landing in the same month.
A notice that a hearing has been rescheduled again, with a new response due in days.
Letters from three different agencies, each opening a file on a complaint about you with the same wording.
A filing described as a "final notice" followed by another one the next week.
Mailbox and inbox filling with formal papers, each demanding a response within a short window.
nots: A genuinely complex dispute that needs many legitimate filings to resolve, such as an estate, a business split or a multi-party case.
A lawyer being thorough and generating volume as a by-product of diligence.
An institution's own procedures producing a large amount of paperwork, whoever the parties are.
Someone without legal training filing repeatedly because they do not understand how to bring a matter to an end.
A series of separate legitimate complaints about separate real problems.
compendium.why: The burden builds across filings and does not sit in any one of them. Answering all of them costs time and money whether or not a single one has merit, and the cost can force settlements, missed deadlines or default judgments.

compendium.name: Brigading
compendium.what: A group converging on one person's posts, account or message at once, usually after a shared call to do so, so the volume itself overwhelms them.
sounds: Within minutes of a screenshot being shared in another group, your mentions fill with replies that use the same phrases.
Go and look at what this person said, posted in a group chat, followed by a stream of new commenters.
A run of one-star ratings on your shop page within an hour, none from a buyer.
Replies quoting a screenshot of your post that you cannot find a link to.
Report this account, plus a link, repeated by many users.
Dozens of near-identical replies such as 'Wow. Unbelievable.' from accounts with no history with you.
nots: Virality is not coordination: a post that spreads on its own draws unconnected people who arrived by different routes. What marks brigading is convergence traceable to one rallying post or thread, and friends reacting independently to the same post is not that.
Heavy criticism of a public statement from people who each saw it for themselves, in their own words.
An openly announced campaign of letters or calls about a public decision, organized but done in the open under people's own names.
A group of supporters replying warmly to a friend's post, which is coordinated but not an attack.
Real customers leaving many bad reviews after a product actually failed or was recalled.
compendium.why: Volume arriving at once removes any chance of answering the way you could answer a single message, and the platform itself becomes unusable for as long as it lasts. Notifications pile up faster than anyone can read, and a calm reply is buried.

compendium.name: Context Collapse Exploitation
compendium.what: Passing on a statement or image without the surrounding material that gave it its meaning, so viewers read something different from what was meant where it began.
sounds: A cropped screenshot of one angry-looking reply, captioned: Look how this person talks to people.
A quote that stops at 'I don't think any of us should have to' when the line went on to say 'be afraid to ask for help'.
Here's what they said in 2016. Nothing has changed.
A twelve-second clip of a laugh, captioned as mockery of someone grieving, with the minute before it left out.
A group chat joke posted to a public thread with the line: This is what they really think.
Comments from viewers who saw only the clip: I thought they seemed so nice.
nots: People misunderstand context themselves and pass things on innocently, believing the piece they have is complete.
Headlines and short excerpts truncate longer statements as a matter of format, with no attempt to change what was said.
Careless sharing: forwarding something without checking where it came from is a lapse, not a plan.
A fair short quote that does reflect the whole, since all reporting excerpts.
A dated old post pointed out because the person has said the same thing again since.
A screenshot of something that is bad on its own and stays bad when the full thread is read.
compendium.why: The version that circulates is the stripped one, and restoring the context means reaching an audience that has already reacted. By then the first impression has often set, and a correction may not travel as far as the clip did.

codex_completed.name: Gaslighting
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Repeatedly denying what someone saw, heard or remembers until they stop trusting their own account of events.
codex_completed.short_definition: Repeatedly denying what someone saw, heard or remembers until they stop trusting their own account of events.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Gaslighting is a pattern of contradicting a person's memory or perception, often about things that clearly happened, so that they begin to defer to the other person's version of events. One denial means little. The pattern shows when the contradiction repeats, targets things the person has good reason to be sure of, and follows moments when they raised a concern. Over time the person may start double-checking themselves instead of the situation.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone keeps telling you that what you clearly remember didn't happen, until you start wondering whether you can trust your own mind.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: When you can't rely on your own memory, you lose the ability to say what happened, notice a pattern, or ask for change. Naming the pattern accurately, without overclaiming, usually helps more than either ignoring it or assuming the worst.
what_it_is: Contradicting something you witnessed or lived through, flatly, with no room left for an honest mistake.
Recasting your reaction as the problem: you are too sensitive, too emotional, or confused.
Repeating this across many topics and many weeks, so doubt builds up instead of being settled.
Aimed most often at the moments you raise a concern or point to evidence, such as a saved message or something said in front of others.
what_it_sounds_like: That never happened.
You're imagining things again.
I never said that. You're making it up.
You're remembering it all wrong.
You know how you get. You always twist things.
Everyone else agrees with me. You're the only one who sees it that way.
I'm worried about you. You've been so confused lately.
what_it_is_not: Two people recalling a long-ago conversation differently, and both willing to check a text or ask someone else.
A single correction of a small detail, such as which night a dinner was or who said what at a party.
Someone saying 'I see it differently' about how an event felt, which is a difference of view and not a denial of the facts.
Plain forgetting. Memory fades and merges events, and an honest 'I don't remember that' is not an attack on yours.
Disagreeing with your explanation of why something happened while accepting that it did happen.
this_may_be_it_when: The thing being denied is something you can back up with a message, a receipt, or a witness.
The denial arrives with a comment about you: your memory, your stability, or your habit of exaggerating.
It happens when you raise a complaint and almost never when the topic is neutral.
An offer to look at the evidence together is refused or turned into an argument.
You have started keeping notes or screenshots, not to use them, but to reassure yourself that you are not wrong.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The topic is something neither of you recorded, and both of you admit you may be mixing it up.
They suggest looking at the message or asking a third person, and then accept what it shows.
It happened once, in a stressful week, and has not come back.
The doubt is about your interpretation of an event, not about whether it took place.
They correct themselves too, with something like 'I got that wrong earlier'.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Stress, tiredness and a crowded week blur memory for everyone, including you.
Two people notice different parts of the same scene and honestly describe different events.
Someone defensive in the moment may deny something and then admit it hours later.
common_false_positives: A friend who corrects the date of a trip once, and is happy to be shown otherwise.
A partner who truly does not recall a conversation that took place while they were distracted or half asleep.
A family argument in which each side retells a past event with the details that suit their feelings, and nobody is trying to shake anyone else's grip on reality.
discernment_questions: Is there something you could both look at, such as a message or a calendar entry, and would they agree to look?
When the evidence is shown, does the denial change, or does the subject?
Does the doubt attach to your memory in general, or to one disputed detail?
Do you feel less sure of yourself with this person than with others who knew the same events?
Would a neutral person who saw the same evidence side with their version or yours?
less_concerning_if: The disagreement is about something genuinely unrecorded, and both of you stay open to being wrong.
They accept the evidence when it is shown, even grudgingly.
You feel as confident about your memory around other people as you do around this one.
more_concerning_if: The denial covers things with clear proof and carries on after the proof is shown.
Your confidence has dropped across areas of life, not only in this relationship.
They tell other people that you have been confused or unwell, so that your account is discounted before you give it.
pattern_over_time_signs: You rehearse what you will say before raising anything, because you expect to be told it did not happen.
You check your memory against screenshots or notes more often than you used to.
You apologize first, even when you are not sure what for.
Friends or family who knew you before have remarked that you seem less sure of yourself.
codex_completed.repair_check: After you show the evidence, what happens next tells you. If they say plainly that you were right about that, and answer differently the next time it comes up, something has changed. One apology followed by the same denial next week has not.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask to look at the message together and watch what follows. Someone who respects the request opens it with you. Someone who does not turns the conversation toward whether you can be trusted to remember anything.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Repeated contradiction can move where a person places their trust, from their own sense of what happened to the other person's account. It tends to work best where the person depends on the other for approval, housing or belonging, and when the denial arrives calmly and with apparent concern. Over time, checking the other person's version can become a habit.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe second-guessing themselves, keeping private records, avoiding the disputed topic, and finding it harder to make decisions. Some describe relief on learning the pattern has a name, and some describe anger at how long it went unnamed.

response_options.soft_clarification: State what you remember in one sentence and ask for a shared check: 'I remember it differently. Can we look at the thread together?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to debate whether your memory works: 'I'm not going to argue about whether I remember my own life correctly. I'm happy to look at what we wrote.'
response_options.disengagement: End the conversation when it moves from the event to you, and return to the subject only in writing or with a third person present.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe two or three specific examples to someone who knew you before this relationship and see whether your account rings true to them. An outside view helps you test your own.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, confirm decisions in writing right after meetings ('To confirm what we agreed...') so a shared record exists, and keep dated notes you could show a manager or HR.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I remember it differently, and I'm confident enough in my memory to say so. Let's look at the message. If we still disagree after that, I'd rather leave it there than be told I'm imagining things."
codex_completed.safety_note: Being told your memory is wrong is not a physical-safety signal in itself. It becomes one when it travels with threats, monitoring, cutting off money or contact, or fear of what happens when you disagree. If any of that is present, talk to someone outside the relationship, such as a domestic abuse advocate, a counselor or a trusted friend, before confronting anything.
misuse_warning: Calling a one-off disagreement about a detail 'gaslighting' can shut down honest correction. The word fits a repeated pattern, not a single clash.
Using the label to win an argument or to wound someone turns a description of a pattern into a verdict.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Countering puts forward a rival version of events to win a point; gaslighting works on your trust in your own memory. Trivializing shrinks the importance of what you felt but accepts that it happened. Selective Memory is forgetting convenient facts, often passively, while gaslighting asserts the facts did not occur. If the live question is 'did this happen at all?', you are closer to gaslighting than to the others.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Actively matched against pasted text by this tool, at low confidence. Phrase matching can flag wording, but it cannot know intent, tone, history, context, or whether the claim is even true — an innocent reading is always attached to every match. Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Countering
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Flatly contradicting someone's account of an event, again and again, so that no shared version of what happened can ever be settled.
codex_completed.short_definition: Flatly contradicting someone's account of an event, again and again, so that no shared version of what happened can ever be settled.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Countering is the reflex of answering what you say happened with a flat 'no, it didn't', before any checking has been done. It differs from a plain factual dispute because the contradiction comes fast, comes with certainty, and does not move when a message or a witness points the other way. Once, it is just disagreement. When it becomes the usual reply to your account, you can end up arguing about the past in every conversation and never reaching the actual subject.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You say what happened, and the answer is an instant, sure 'no it didn't', every time, so you never get to the real issue because you are stuck arguing over the facts.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Constant contradiction makes shared reality impossible to establish. If every account you give is overruled on the spot, you lose the ability to settle even small facts, and the problem you meant to raise never gets heard.
what_it_is: An immediate denial of your version of events, delivered before anyone has looked at a message, a calendar or a receipt.
Contradiction as the default reply to your account, whatever the topic, so the argument is always about the past and never about what to do next.
A stance of certainty with no room for 'maybe I have it wrong', which is what separates it from an honest difference in recall.
Often paired with accusations that you are distorting things, such as 'you're twisting my words', which turns your report into the thing on trial.
Different from the healthier move of saying 'my memory of that is different, let's check the messages', which keeps the door to evidence open.
what_it_sounds_like: "That's not what happened."
"You're remembering it wrong."
"That's not what happened and you know it."
"That's not how it happened at all."
"You're twisting my words."
"You're putting words in my mouth."
"No. I didn't say that. Stop making things up."
what_it_is_not: A real factual dispute where the person truly believes their version and will look at a text or ask a witness to settle it.
Someone saying 'that's not how I experienced it', which speaks about their own view and does not overrule yours.
A correction of a small detail, such as the day of the week, that is dropped once the calendar is checked.
Honest confusion between two similar events, such as last month's argument and this month's.
Pushback on an exaggeration, like 'you always do this', when the person is objecting to the word 'always' and not to the event.
this_may_be_it_when: Your account is contradicted in the first sentence of the reply, before any question about details.
The denial stays in place after you show a message or name someone who was there.
It happens on many topics, not just the one where you disagree about what was said.
You have started opening conversations with proof in hand because you expect to be overruled.
Your careful wording is itself called 'twisting', so describing events becomes risky.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They say 'let me check' and come back with a correction to their own memory.
The disagreement is about a thing neither of you wrote down, and both of you say you could be wrong.
