They contradict you on a point of fact but stay curious about why you remember it differently.
It happens in one heated argument and not in calmer talks.
They accept the evidence the moment it is shown, even if they are annoyed.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Defensiveness in the moment can make 'that's not true' come out before the person has thought, and a calmer answer may follow later.
People often hold firmly to a memory that feels vivid, even when it is wrong.
Some families and workplaces argue in a blunt, contradicting style with everyone, and no one is hurt by it.
A person who feels accused may deny the whole account to avoid blame, then soften once the heat has passed.
common_false_positives: A sibling who insists the family trip was in July, and laughs and gives in when shown the photos.
A colleague who says 'that's not what the contract says' and then reads the clause aloud with you.
A friend who disputes your retelling of a story at a party because they remember the punchline differently.
discernment_questions: When I offer to check a message or ask a third person, do they agree to that check?
Does their denial change when the evidence appears, or does it just move to a new objection?
Do they contradict me about facts only on certain sensitive topics, or about almost everything?
Have I started avoiding saying what I remember, in order to avoid the fight?
Do other people who were there tend to side with my account or theirs?
less_concerning_if: They contradict you as bluntly as they contradict everyone else, and drop it when shown wrong.
The disputed point is trivial and you can both laugh about it afterward.
You still feel free to say 'I remember it differently' and be heard.
more_concerning_if: Your account is overruled even when you hold written proof, and the proof is waved away.
The contradiction is paired with remarks about your memory, stability or honesty.
You find yourself agreeing with their version just to end the conversation, and then doubting yourself afterward.
pattern_over_time_signs: You stop bringing up concerns because the first ten minutes will be spent on what was or was not said.
You keep a private record, such as screenshots or notes, mainly to reassure yourself.
Arguments become about the past in every case, and decisions about the future get postponed.
You begin phrasing everything as a question, such as 'didn't you say...', to soften the expected denial.
codex_completed.repair_check: A change shows up when they pause before denying. They say something like 'let me check before I answer', and they accept what the message shows. A one-time 'sorry' followed by the same instant 'that's not what happened' next week is not that change.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: When you propose checking a record together, does the offer get taken up or turned into a fresh argument? Someone respecting it opens the thread with you, even reluctantly. Someone who is not may contest the very idea of checking.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Being overruled over and over can teach a person that stating a memory is costly. Some people respond by going quiet, some by arguing harder to defend their account, and some by doubting what they recall to keep the peace. A steady stream of 'no, it didn't' tends to shift attention from the issue to the defense of one's own memory.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe rehearsing what they will say, gathering evidence before conversations, and feeling worn out by arguments that never leave the question of what was said. Some say they stopped raising problems because nothing could be settled. Others describe relief when a friend simply believed their account.

response_options.soft_clarification: Offer a way to settle it without a fight: 'We remember this differently. Could we look at the messages and see?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline the loop on the facts: 'I've told you what I remember. I'm not going to go round again on whether it happened.'
response_options.disengagement: When each reply is a flat denial, stop for now and move the topic to a written message, where what each of you said stays visible.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend who was around at the time what you remember and ask what they recall. A second memory tests yours without a fight.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Follow a conversation with a short email: 'Confirming what we discussed on Tuesday...', so a dated record exists if the account is later disputed.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I've said what I remember, and you've said what you remember. I'm not willing to keep arguing about who is right. If it matters, let's check the messages together, and if they don't settle it, we can leave it as a difference."
codex_completed.safety_note: Contradicting your account is not a physical-safety sign by itself. It becomes more serious if disagreeing brings anger that frightens you, if you are punished for your version, or if the denial covers events involving threats or injury. In that case, write down what happened privately and talk to a counselor or an advocate before raising it again.
misuse_warning: Labeling every disagreement about a fact as 'countering' can punish someone for honestly remembering differently. The word fits an instant, repeated, evidence-proof denial, not a single clash.
Using the label to avoid checking whether you yourself remembered correctly turns a useful term into a way to win.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Countering is the flat 'that didn't happen' aimed at your account on the spot. Selective Memory is claiming not to recall, so there is nothing to argue with, only a blank. Deflection does not contest the facts at all; it moves to a new subject. Gaslighting goes further than any one contradiction: it works over time to make you distrust your own mind, while countering can leave your confidence intact.

codex_completed.name: Selective Memory
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Claiming not to remember what was said or agreed, but only when the forgotten item would cost the person something to remember.
codex_completed.short_definition: Claiming not to remember what was said or agreed, but only when the forgotten item would cost the person something to remember.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Selective memory is forgetting that seems to land only on inconvenient things. The same person may recall a favor they did down to the day, yet draw a blank on a promise they made. Everyone forgets, and nobody can see inside another person's head, so one lapse proves nothing. The pattern is in the shape: what gets forgotten tends to be what was promised, what was apologized for or what would require them to act, and the blank does not shift when you remind them.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone keeps 'not remembering' the promises, deals or apologies that would cost them something, while remembering everything that helps their side.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Agreements only work if both people carry them. When one side's memory conveniently fails, the other ends up holding every promise alone, re-asking, re-proving and eventually giving up on getting things done.
what_it_is: A pattern of blanks that fall on promises, deadlines, agreed chores or apologies, rather than spread evenly across everything.
Sharp recall for a grievance or a favor they did, next to a vague 'I don't recall' about what they owe.
Forgetting that is not fixed by reminders: the same item has to be re-raised again and again.
Often phrased as a confusion on your side, such as 'you must be thinking of someone else', which sounds like a memory gap on the speaker's part but moves the doubt onto you.
Different from a plain memory lapse, which is scattered, regretted and corrected once reminded.
what_it_sounds_like: "I never said that."
"You must be confusing me with someone else."
"I have no memory of saying that."
"Hmm, I don't remember agreeing to that."
"That was a long time ago, how would I know?"
"Did we actually say Friday? I don't think so."
"I told you I'd think about it, I never said yes."
what_it_is_not: Ordinary forgetting. Busy, stressed, sleep-deprived people lose track of things and are embarrassed when they remember.
Memory problems linked to health, medication, grief or age, which may reach every topic, not just the costly ones.
A truly ambiguous exchange, such as a casual 'maybe we should', that each person heard differently.
A person who forgot the plan and then took responsibility as soon as you reminded them.
Someone who has forgotten because the promise was made in a conversation they were not really present for, such as while distracted.
this_may_be_it_when: The forgetting lands on obligations and apologies but never on favors, grievances or things that benefit them.
The same commitment has to be reminded repeatedly and keeps vanishing.
Reminders are met with 'you never told me' instead of a simple 'oh, sorry, I forgot'.
A written record is dismissed as 'out of context' or 'not what I meant'.
The blanks have a tidy fit with what would be inconvenient if remembered.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They forget across the board, including things that would have helped them.
They are visibly embarrassed and want to put it right once reminded.
They set up their own reminders or a shared list and then follow through.
A health or sleep problem, or a very heavy month, could plausibly explain it.
The item was never clearly agreed, and they say so honestly.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Memory is selective for everyone: we hold on to what matters to us and let routine things fade, and that can look unfair from outside.
Stress and overload can wipe out agreements made on the way out the door.
Some people truly never registered a throwaway comment as a commitment.
Illness, poor sleep or grief can make recent promises vanish.
common_false_positives: A partner who forgets the dentist appointment but also forgets their own tasks that week.
A coworker who has no memory of a hallway chat they treated as chitchat.
A parent with a growing memory problem who forgets many things, favors and promises alike.
discernment_questions: Do the gaps fall mostly on what costs them, or are they spread evenly?
Do they remember the details of what they did for me, or of what I did wrong?
When reminded with a record, do they accept it or argue with the record?
Is there a health, sleep or workload reason that could explain the gaps?
Does the same promise have to be rebuilt from scratch more than once?
less_concerning_if: The forgetting is scattered across topics, including ones that would have helped them.
They accept a reminder and carry out the thing without a fight.
A shared note, calendar or list brings the lapses down.
more_concerning_if: The blanks cover promises about money, safety, children or care, where forgetting does real harm.
They remember exact words from your past mistakes while having no memory of their own commitments.
When you show a record, the response is anger at you for keeping one.
pattern_over_time_signs: You begin to write down every agreement, then feel guilty or petty for doing it.
You end up carrying the follow-up on every promise, because you know it will not return on its own.
You stop trusting verbal agreements and ask for texts, then are accused of not trusting them.
The list of things you are 'confusing' grows, and you feel less sure of your own recall.
codex_completed.repair_check: Notice what happens to the item itself once it is raised. When something has really changed, the forgotten commitment gets done, and the person finds their own way to hold on to it, such as a note or alarm. A warm 'you're right, sorry' while the promise stays undone is not that.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: After you ask for agreements to be written down, watch how that request is received. Does it get used, with texts sent and read? Or is it called controlling, and do the same blanks continue despite the written record?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When one person's memory seems to fail only where it is costly, the other can slip into a role of keeper of the record. That job is tiring, and it can make a person doubt whether they are remembering correctly, especially when 'you must be confusing me with someone else' is said with a calm face. The doubt can pull attention from the broken promise toward their own reliability.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe keeping screenshots and notes they hate having to keep, and feeling petty for asking for things in writing. Some say they stopped relying on the person for anything that mattered. Others describe a creeping unease about their own accuracy after being told many times they had it wrong.

response_options.soft_clarification: Offer a record as help, not accusation: 'I want us both to be sure. Can I send a quick text with what we decided?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say plainly what keeps happening: 'I have had to remind you of three promises now. From here on I need these in writing.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop depending on the person for the thing that keeps being dropped, and arrange another way, such as doing it yourself or using a service.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask someone who was present for an agreement what they recall, so you can tell whether your memory or the lapse is the problem.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Send a follow-up note after every meeting listing decisions, owners and dates, and keep those emails so commitments can be pointed to later.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I remember us agreeing to this, and you remember it differently, so let's write down what we decide now. I'll send a text after we talk, and you can correct anything you think I got wrong."
codex_completed.safety_note: Forgetting a chore or plan is rarely a danger signal. That changes when the forgotten items involve money you depend on, a child's care, shared housing, or legal or medical commitments, or when asking for them to be remembered brings anger or punishment. Keep your own copies of important agreements, and consider a counselor, legal aid or an advocate if your income or housing depends on it.
misuse_warning: Accusing someone of 'selective memory' whenever they forget something can turn normal lapses into a character charge. Ask whether the forgetting tracks inconvenience before the label is used.
Using the term to win an argument about who said what can turn two honest memories into a trial.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: A claimed blank, 'I don't recall', leaves nothing contested but also nothing owed, which is what marks selective memory. Countering says it did not happen, a firm contradiction of what you said. Moving Goalposts accepts the deal existed but changes what counts as meeting it. Minimization admits the event and shrinks its weight. Gaslighting works on your trust in your own mind, where this one mostly lets the person off the hook.

codex_completed.name: Moving Goalposts
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Changing what counts as success after you have met the standard that was set, so that you can never quite finish.
codex_completed.short_definition: Changing what counts as success after you have met the standard that was set, so that you can never quite finish.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Moving goalposts happens when a target is named, you reach it, and the target quietly shifts further away. The bar might be a clean house, a work project, a way of apologizing or a level of closeness. A bar that really has to change, because new facts arrived, is ordinary life. The pattern is a bar that moves only after you meet it, never gets written down and always lands just beyond reach, so the effort never earns the result it was promised.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You do what was asked, and then the request changes, again and again, so that you can never reach the point of being done or good enough.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: When success keeps moving, effort stops buying anything. You can work harder for months and still be told it is not enough, which wears down confidence and makes you chase approval you cannot earn.
what_it_is: A standard that is named, met by you, and then replaced by a stricter one the moment you reach it.
Rewards, such as approval, a raise, forgiveness or a promotion, that always sit one step beyond the work done.
Criteria that stay vague at the start, which leaves room to say afterward 'that is not what I meant'.
Often shows up at work, in school, in family expectations and in how an apology is judged.
Different from a bar that rises for a reason you can name and plan around, such as new requirements, a changed budget or a different client.
what_it_sounds_like: "That's still not good enough."
"Now do it properly this time."
"That doesn't count."
"You should have done more."
"That was the bare minimum."
"Now do it again."
"I never said that would be enough."
what_it_is_not: A real change in the requirements, with an explanation of what changed, such as a client who revised the brief.
Feedback that raises the quality bar once, with clear criteria, so that you know when the work will be accepted.
A reasonable ask for more once you have shown you can do the basic version, for instance a manager giving harder tasks as you grow.
Honest disagreement about what 'done' meant, where a written brief would have prevented the confusion.
Your own perfectionism, where nobody else has moved anything but you keep raising the line yourself.
this_may_be_it_when: Each time you finish what was asked, a new and different requirement is named.
The goal was never put in writing, and the person disputes what was agreed once you meet it.
The standard has moved several times and always in the direction of more.
Nobody can say what 'finished' would look like, even when you ask.
Others doing the same task are told they are fine, while you are not.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The bar changed because of a new fact, and the person said so plainly at the time.
There is a written spec or rubric, and you are being held to it.
They can describe what 'done' looks like and sign off when you reach it.
The extra work is a separate, new request that is offered, not demanded.
You are the one adding conditions to your own goal.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Projects change as information arrives, and a good-faith manager may revise a deliverable without meaning to leave you chasing.
A person may not know what they want until they see a first attempt, and refine it.
Quality bars sometimes rise in a competitive setting for everyone at once.
A vague request may seem clear to the person asking and open to a different reading by you.
common_false_positives: A teacher who adds a requirement to the whole class after seeing weak first drafts.
A client who finds a new priority after a launch and asks for a second round, with a new quote.
A partner who asked you to tidy the kitchen and then, once it is done, asks for the garage, as a separate and willing request.
discernment_questions: Was the standard clear and written down before I started, or only after?
If I reach it, is there any version of 'done' they would accept?
Are other people held to the same shifting line, or just me?
Did I get a reason for the change, or only a new demand?
Is the bar rising, or am I the one who keeps raising it?
less_concerning_if: The new requirement comes with a reason and is treated as a new task.
You can ask 'what would make this complete?' and get a straight answer.
The standard stays put once it is agreed and written.
more_concerning_if: The bar moves each time you meet it, and the move always lands just out of reach.
Approval, money, housing or access to something you need depends on a goal that never closes.
Questioning the change is met with accusation, such as 'you're never satisfied' or 'you're being difficult'.
pattern_over_time_signs: You work longer hours or do more for the same recognition, and recognition never comes.
You stop believing the finish line exists and begin to expect to be told 'not yet'.
You pre-emptively over-deliver to avoid hearing it, and still hear it.
You describe your worth in terms of the other person's last verdict.
codex_completed.repair_check: Look for a standard that stays fixed after it is raised. That would mean a stated finish line, written down and honored when you reach it, with changes only for a reason and before the work, not after. An apology for 'being demanding' with no fixed line leaves you where you started.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: What happens when you ask 'what exactly would make this complete?' Does it get a concrete answer you can write down, or does the answer vary each time you ask? A fixed finish line is respect. Another sliding one is the pattern again.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When effort stops producing reward on a predictable schedule, a person can keep trying harder in the hope that the next attempt will be the one. The uncertainty can make approval feel more valuable, and the repeated shortfall can be taken as proof of personal failure rather than as a feature of the arrangement. A hazy target tends to leave the person judging themselves instead of the target.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe working harder and harder with less and less sense of achievement, replaying tasks to find what they missed, and feeling anxious as a deadline approaches or passes. Some say they began to see themselves as never quite good enough. Others describe feeling suddenly lighter when they saw the target had moved and not their ability.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the finish line: 'Before I start, can we write down what a finished version looks like, so we both agree?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold to the first agreement: 'We agreed on this standard, and I met it. If there's a new request, I'm happy to talk about it as a new request.'
response_options.disengagement: If every attempt is met with a new bar, stop investing extra effort in that goal and put it in goals where progress shows.
response_options.support_seeking: Show a trusted colleague or friend the original request and what you delivered, and ask whether they would call it met.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Get criteria in writing at the start, confirm by email when you deliver ('Delivered as per the brief of 4 March'), and keep copies for a manager or HR.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I did what we agreed on. If you want something different now, that's a new request, and I'd like to talk about what it involves and how long it will take before I start."
codex_completed.safety_note: A shifting standard is usually a stress and self-worth problem, not a danger. That changes if the goal controls something you cannot do without, such as a job, a visa, a place to live, or access to your children or money, or if failing the standard brings threats or punishment. If so, keep dated copies of what was asked and delivered, and seek legal aid, a union rep or an advocate.
misuse_warning: Calling every revision 'moving the goalposts' can excuse poor work and make fair feedback sound like abuse. Ask whether a reason was given and whether the bar rose before or after the work.

codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Moving Goalposts accepts that you met the first standard and then raises it. Countering says you did not do what you claim. Deflection changes the subject so that no standard is discussed. Gaslighting denies what was agreed at all, while this tactic can admit the agreement and still put the reward out of reach. The difference is a standard that existed, was met, and then was replaced.

codex_completed.name: Thought-Stopping Clichés
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Stock phrases, said in a closing tone, that end a conversation about a problem before anything in it has been examined.
codex_completed.short_definition: Stock phrases, said in a closing tone, that end a conversation about a problem before anything in it has been examined.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A thought-stopping cliché is a ready-made saying, such as 'it is what it is', used in the place of an answer. Sayings like these can be kind: sometimes people truly need to let a thing go. The pattern is when the phrase arrives each time you raise the same concern, closes the topic, and leaves your question unanswered. The saying may be common wisdom, but used as a door shut on your question, it replaces the conversation instead of continuing it.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Every time you raise a worry, you get a familiar saying, like 'don't overthink it', that closes the topic without answering anything you asked.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A concern that is shut down by a slogan does not go away; it goes underground. You may start to feel that wanting an answer is itself the fault, and stop raising things that need attention.
what_it_is: A well-worn saying used as the whole reply to a real concern, such as 'everything happens for a reason'.
A phrase that sounds wise, so that arguing with it feels petty and leaves the speaker looking calm.
A shift of focus from the problem to your reaction to it, with 'you're dwelling on it' in the place of an answer.
Common in families, workplaces and faith or self-help settings, where the sayings carry shared authority.
Different from comfort that stays with you in the problem, which may use the same words but invites you to say more.

"Everything happens for a reason, stop dwelling."
"Don't overthink it."
"Just let it go already."
"You're blowing this out of proportion."
"Just stay positive."
"We don't talk about that."
what_it_is_not: Comfort offered in grief, where the speaker sits with you and the saying is one small part of the support.
Sensible advice to let go of something that is truly over and cannot be changed, offered kindly and with room to talk.
A friend's clumsy attempt to cheer you up that stops when you say 'I'd rather talk about it'.
A cultural or religious phrase that is a normal part of how a person speaks, with no intent to end your question.
A tired person saying 'let's drop it for tonight' who agrees to return to the topic tomorrow.
this_may_be_it_when: The same phrase turns up every time you bring up one particular issue.
After the phrase, the topic is closed and cannot be returned to.
Your attempt to say more is met with a further saying, not an answer.
You are made to feel foolish, ungrateful or negative for asking.
The phrase answers a practical question, such as who will pay, with a platitude.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They use the phrase and then ask how you are really doing.
A time to talk is named, such as 'not now, but this weekend', and kept.
The phrase is offered about something that cannot be fixed, and they remain with you in it.
They stop saying it when you say it does not help.
Everyone around you talks in sayings, and they apply to every topic equally.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people use idioms when they feel helpless and do not know what else to say.
Someone may use a saying because they have been taught that dwelling on things makes them worse.
A busy or overwhelmed person may reach for a short phrase to get through a moment.
Some cultures and families use proverbs as a form of affection and wisdom, not dismissal.
common_false_positives: A neighbor who says 'everything happens for a reason' at a funeral and then brings food.
A friend who says 'don't overthink it' before a job interview, to calm you.
A coach who says 'let it go' after a missed shot, to help you move on to the next play.
discernment_questions: Does the phrase come with any attention to what I actually said?
Can I come back to the topic later, or is it sealed?
If I say 'that doesn't help', does the speaker change approach?
Is the saying used to end only the topics that are awkward for them?
After one of these exchanges, do I feel heard, or do I feel silenced?
less_concerning_if: The phrase is followed by a question or an offer to talk later.
They change what they say once you tell them it is not helping.
It is used about things that cannot be changed, not about things you are asking them to do.
more_concerning_if: Concerns about safety, money, treatment of you or your children are answered only with a slogan.
Raising the same issue again earns you a label such as 'negative', 'ungrateful' or 'dramatic'.
Others in the group repeat the phrases, so that no member can raise a problem.
pattern_over_time_signs: You stop raising issues, because you can predict the phrase and the feeling it leaves.
Problems pile up unspoken, and small ones become large.
You catch yourself using the phrases on yourself, to shut down your own worries.
You begin to feel that having a concern at all is a flaw.
codex_completed.repair_check: Notice whether the closed topics can reopen. Something real shows up as a named time to talk, and a phrase dropped for plain answers when you ask. Someone who apologizes for 'being dismissive' and then answers the next worry with 'it is what it is' has not yet changed.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: When you say that a saying does not help, what is the next sentence? A response that moves toward your question is respect. A response that repeats the phrase louder, or says you can't take advice, shows that the topic was closed, not heard.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A familiar saying carries borrowed authority, so contesting it can feel like arguing with wisdom itself. When it is used again and again to end a topic, it can teach a person to treat their own questions as the problem. Over time some people begin to say the phrases to themselves, which can mute concerns that might have been worth acting on.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Feeling silly for wanting an answer is common, as is swallowing worries until they grow, and a flat tiredness at being met with slogans. Some people say they started to hear the phrases in their own head. Others describe a quiet anger they could not explain, since the phrase sounded so reasonable.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name what you need: 'I'm not looking to be cheered up. I'd like to be heard for five minutes on this.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say the phrase does not close the topic: 'That saying doesn't answer my question. I still need an answer about who is handling this.'
response_options.disengagement: Take the concern to someone who engages with it, and leave the topic with this person if every attempt returns the same line.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk it over with a friend, counselor or peer group where you can say the whole worry and hear it taken seriously.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: When a manager answers a concern with a slogan, send it by email with a specific question, such as 'Could you confirm who owns this task by Friday?', so an answer is on record.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I know you may mean that kindly, but a saying isn't an answer to what I asked. I'm not going to drop it. Can we set aside ten minutes this week to talk about it properly?"
codex_completed.safety_note: A slogan in place of an answer is usually a communication problem. It matters more when it covers reports of harm, such as pain, abuse, unsafe work conditions or a child's distress, or when a group uses these phrases so that no one can report a problem. If that is the case, take the concern outside the group, to a doctor, a regulator, a trusted professional or an advocate.
misuse_warning: Treating every comforting saying as manipulation makes kind people look like opponents. Most uses of these phrases are clumsy care.
Using the label to avoid hearing 'let it go' advice that is actually wise can keep a person stuck.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Thought-stopping clichés end the conversation with a saying and leave the facts alone. Deflection answers with a new subject or a counter-question. Minimization shrinks the problem by calling it small. Countering denies your account. A cliché does none of those: it does not argue, change the topic or shrink the harm in words, and it just closes the door with a phrase that sounds like wisdom.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Actively matched against pasted text by this tool, at low confidence. Phrase matching can flag wording, but it cannot know intent, tone, history, context, or whether the claim is even true — an innocent reading is always attached to every match. Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Normalization
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Presenting harmful or hurtful treatment as ordinary, expected and not worth questioning, so that objecting to it seems like the problem.
codex_completed.short_definition: Presenting harmful or hurtful treatment as ordinary, expected and not worth questioning, so that objecting to it seems like the problem.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Normalization tells you that what hurt you is simply how things are. It can come from one person ('every couple fights like this'), a family ('this is how we are') or a whole workplace ('everyone puts up with it'). Sometimes it is true, and the comparison gives useful perspective. The pattern is when the comparison is offered to end the talk, when it is unchecked against what you can see, and when it is aimed at the exact thing you are trying to name as harmful.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: When you say something hurt, you are told it is normal and everyone goes through it, so it feels like you are wrong to mind.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: If harmful treatment is called normal, you lose the language to describe it. People can put up with something painful for years because they had been taught that it was simply what relationships, work or family life were like.
what_it_is: A statement that the treatment you object to is typical, such as 'all couples fight like this' or 'every boss yells'.
A comparison to a vague 'everyone' that cannot be checked and does not use your own situation.
A move that places the problem in your reaction, as in 'you are too sensitive', and the behavior stays unquestioned.
Found in families, couples, workplaces, schools and teams, where long habit can make unhealthy things feel standard.
Different from real perspective, which compares honestly and leaves room for the idea that something may still need to change.
what_it_sounds_like: "Every couple fights like this."
"This is just how families are."
"That's just how it is."
"Everyone does it."
"All men are like this."
"This is just normal, so stop."
"I went through the same thing, and I turned out fine."
what_it_is_not: A real, accurate comparison, such as a friend who says that many new parents argue about chores, and who still listens to the details.
A genuine cultural or family norm that is shared by everyone involved and comfortable for them, even though it differs from yours.
Reassurance from an older person who has been through something similar and says so to comfort you, not to close the topic.
Realism about a job that is hard in known ways, such as long hours in a busy kitchen, when pay and terms were agreed beforehand.
A person's own habit of treating a hurt as normal because they were raised that way, with no one else pushing it.
this_may_be_it_when: The comparison is used when you describe being hurt, not in other conversations.
'Everyone' is never named, and you cannot find a single person who agrees when you ask.
After the comparison, the person asks you to stop talking about it.
Your feeling of unease remains while you are being told it is nothing.
The behavior itself is never discussed, only whether people in general put up with it.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They offer a comparison and then ask what you want to change.
Someone you trust who knows your situation says it sounds common and still takes the hurt seriously.
The treatment stops or changes after it is raised.
The thing is a standard feature of a role that you accepted with open eyes.
They agree that it is common but not good, and that it can still be addressed.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many difficulties are in fact common, and hearing so can bring relief and proportion.
A person who grew up in a rough home may truly believe the behavior is normal, with no wish to excuse it.
People often try to comfort by saying 'you're not alone', which can come out sounding like dismissal.
A new parent or new employee may be genuinely unsure what is typical, and a friend may be offering honest information.
common_false_positives: A friend who says every new parent is sleep-deprived and snappy, and brings dinner.
A coworker who says that busy season is rough for everyone, and covers your shift.
A relative who says teenagers slam doors, about a door slam and not about being called names.
discernment_questions: Does the 'everyone' include a person I can actually check with?
Would I think this was normal if it were done to a friend of mine?
Is the statement about the behavior, or just about my reaction to it?
Did my sense that something was wrong exist before anyone told me it was normal?
Has this been normal since the start, or did it change over time?
less_concerning_if: The comparison is accurate, checkable and offered with real interest in how you are.
The behavior stops or softens once you say it hurts.
You feel free to disagree that it is normal without penalty.
more_concerning_if: What is being called normal involves fear, physical harm, control of money or being kept from others.
You are told that objecting means something is wrong with you.
Several people around you say the same phrases, so no one outside the pattern is ever heard.
pattern_over_time_signs: You stop describing what happens to others, because you expect to be told it is normal.
You catch yourself telling friends 'it's fine, it's just how we are'.
Your idea of what is acceptable shifts, a little at a time, toward what once would have alarmed you.
A friend or relative from outside reacts with concern to something you thought was ordinary.
codex_completed.repair_check: Something real shows when the behavior is treated as open to question, either by a change in what happens or by willingness to talk about whether it is okay. An 'I hear you' followed by the same 'it's just how it is' leaves the old message in place.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: What do you hear when you say 'I know others deal with this, but I am not okay with it'? A response that accepts your limit is one thing. A response that goes back to comparing you with 'everyone' shows that the limit is being weighed against a norm, not respected.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People often work out what is acceptable by looking at what those around them accept. When the people close to you insist that something is ordinary, your own alarm can start to seem like an error. Hearing it repeatedly, especially from someone you trust, can slowly shift your sense of what counts as normal, and you may begin to apply the same line to yourself.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Some feel oversensitive for having minded, and short of words for what was happening. Others stayed in painful situations for longer because they had been told it was typical. A few describe a jolt on hearing an outsider say 'that is not normal', followed by grief or relief.

response_options.soft_clarification: Separate common from okay: 'Maybe lots of people deal with this. I'm still telling you it hurts me.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline the comparison as an answer: 'Whether it's normal isn't what I'm asking. I'm asking you to stop doing it.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop trying to prove it to someone who keeps ruling it normal, and take the question to a person outside the situation.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe the specifics, not the label, to a counselor or a trusted person who is not part of the group, and ask whether it sounds ordinary to them.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, check the written policy or code of conduct, and ask HR or a union rep whether what you described is acceptable, instead of relying on what colleagues say is usual.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "You may be right that other people put up with this. I'm telling you that it isn't okay with me. I'd like us to talk about this specific thing, and not about what everyone else does."
codex_completed.safety_note: Calling hurtful treatment normal can hide more serious problems. It becomes a danger signal when the treatment involves physical force, threats, control of money, being kept from friends or being afraid at home. If any of that is true, tell someone outside the relationship, such as a domestic violence advocate, a doctor or a trusted friend, and treat the 'it's normal' message as information about the person saying it, not a fact.
misuse_warning: Hearing 'that's normal' does not always mean someone is hiding harm. Treating every reassurance as suspicious can push away people who are trying to help.
Using the label to avoid ordinary friction, such as in any relationship, can turn small disagreements into a charge.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Normalization says the treatment is typical and so not worth questioning; it points to everyone else. Minimization says this particular incident was small. Countering says it did not happen the way you said. Deflection moves the topic. Gaslighting works on whether you can trust your own mind. Normalization leaves the facts alone and rules your objection out of bounds.

Phrase matching can flag wording, but it cannot know intent, tone, history, context, or whether the claim is even true — an innocent reading is always attached to every match. Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Guilt-Tripping
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Using guilt about past help, sacrifice or hurt feelings to make saying no feel like a moral failing.
codex_completed.short_definition: Using guilt about past help, sacrifice or hurt feelings to make saying no feel like a moral failing.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Guilt-tripping turns your conscience against your own decision. The pressure comes from reminders of what was given, what it cost, or how hurt someone is, so that refusing feels like a debt unpaid. Obligation Hooks is what some people call this when the sense of owing is vague and ever-present rather than tied to one favor; it is not a different tactic. One sigh and one 'after all I've done' means little. A pattern shows when the reminder arrives whenever you decline, and the specifics fade.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone reminds you of what they have done, given up or feel, so that saying no seems selfish or cruel, even when your answer was reasonable.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Guilt that is attached to ordinary refusals makes your own limits feel wrong. Over time you may agree to things you do not want to avoid the sting, and stop being able to tell real obligations from pressure.
what_it_is: Reminders of past sacrifice or help brought up to settle a current, unrelated request.
A general, undefined sense of owing, where no single gift or favor can be pointed to but any refusal still feels wrong.
Hurt feelings presented as proof you did something wrong by deciding as you did.
Often delivered quietly, as sadness or a sigh, so that anger is not needed for it to work.
Found in families, partnerships, friendships, volunteer groups and workplaces that lean on loyalty.
what_it_sounds_like: After everything I've done for you.
I never ask you for anything.
I sacrificed everything for you kids.
I guess I just don't matter to you any more.
If you really cared about me, you would.
How could you do this to me?
You owe me.
No, it's fine. Don't worry about me. I'll manage on my own.
what_it_is_not: Honest disappointment said once, with the decision left to you: 'I'm sad you can't come, and I understand.'
Real reciprocity in a long relationship, where each of you has given and received and both feel it.
Telling someone how their choice affected you, once, as information and not a lever.
A person who feels guilty easily on their own, with nobody applying pressure.
Cultural norms of family duty that are mutual, openly discussed and open to negotiation.
A direct request for the favor to be returned that accepts a 'no' without a penalty.
this_may_be_it_when: Past help is brought up only when you refuse, and never otherwise.
The reminder is about something unrelated to the request being made.
The sense of owing cannot be traced to anything you could list.
Declining is followed by hurt, sighs or withdrawal that fade as soon as you agree.
The same lines come out every time, whatever the request.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They state the disappointment once and then accept your answer.
A fair accounting of give and take shows real debt running both ways, and they acknowledge your side of it.
They ask you to help with something that truly cannot be done without you, and say what is at stake.
Your guilt shows up even when nobody has said or implied anything.
They thank you for past help without attaching it to a request.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Someone who has really given up a lot may be hurt, and speak about it without wanting to coerce.
A person who is anxious about being left may say 'you never have time for me' as an awkward request for contact.
Gratitude in a long relationship can feel like obligation without anyone installing it.
common_false_positives: A parent saying once that they were sad you missed the family event.
A friend who says they felt let down, then asks what could work next time.
A relationship with a long record of giving in both directions where each remembers it kindly.
Your own tendency to feel guilty, which would be there with other people too.
discernment_questions: Does the disappointment leave my decision standing, or work to reverse it?
Is 'after everything I've done' tied to the present request or just a general reminder?
Can I list what each of us has actually given?
Does guilt show up with this person even when I have declined something small?
Does the guilt vanish as soon as I agree?
less_concerning_if: Hurt is voiced once and your answer is then respected.
A fair look at give and take shows real reciprocity both ways.
You feel free to say no and the relationship carries on afterwards.
more_concerning_if: Past help is cited more and more often, and the debts it covers keep growing.
Refusing brings anger or withdrawal over a period of days.
Other people are told you are ungrateful or selfish when you decline.
pattern_over_time_signs: You say yes before you have thought about whether you want to.
You keep your own news small, so they have less to feel excluded from.
You feel a rush of guilt at a refusal that others in your position would not feel.
You apologize first, even when you cannot say what for.
codex_completed.repair_check: In this tactic, repair is a refusal that no longer costs you. They accept a no with a 'that's fine, I'll sort something out', and do not bring up old favors as leverage. A gift or warm gesture straight after the guilt, followed by the same line next month, is not it.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Watch what happens the next time you say no to something small. If they take it in stride, even with a flicker of sadness, your limit is being respected. If the reminder of what you owe returns, the guilt is still doing the work of the request.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Most people want to be fair and to repay kindness. Pressure that links that wish to every refusal can make a no feel like cheating a creditor. A vague, ever-present sense of owing is hard to argue with because there is no specific claim to check, so the only way to ease the discomfort tends to be to comply.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe chronic guilt, difficulty saying no, and a belief that their own needs are selfish. Some keep a mental ledger of who owes what and feel they can never finish paying it. Others describe relief on realizing that saying no had a cost they were never told about, and anger at how long it went unseen.

response_options.soft_clarification: Acknowledge the feeling without taking on the debt: 'I can hear you're hurt, and I'm still not able to do that. Can we find something that works for both of us?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold the answer and decline the ledger: 'I appreciate what you've done, and my answer is still no. Past help doesn't mean I can't say it.'
response_options.disengagement: When the list of past sacrifices begins, say you have heard it and step out of the conversation. Do not argue the accounts line by line.
response_options.support_seeking: Write out what each of you has given and ask a friend outside the family whether the balance looks the way you have been told it does.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager cites past loyalty to get unpaid extra work, ask for the request and its hours in writing, and keep a dated record of what has been agreed.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "When I say no and the answer is a list of what you've done, I start to feel I can't decide anything for myself. I am grateful, and the answer is still no."
codex_completed.safety_note: Being made to feel guilty is painful but not a physical danger. It matters more when you depend on the person for housing or income, or when it comes with threats or anger after refusal. If so, talk to a counselor or advocate before you push back, and keep the plan to yourself until it is ready.
misuse_warning: Hurt feelings are not always guilt-tripping. People may say how a decision affected them, and calling that manipulation can silence an honest request.
Using the label on someone who is grieving or struggling can turn a cry for contact into an accusation.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Martyrdom Display advertises sacrifice to build obligation and need not make any request, whereas guilt-tripping uses it to push against a specific refusal. Demand for Gratitude asks for thanks as payment for help given, and Duty Scripts invoke role expectations such as 'a good daughter would'. Guilt-tripping works through your sense of owing and does not need a role.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Actively matched against pasted text by this tool, at low confidence. Phrase matching can flag wording, but it cannot know intent, tone, history, context, or whether the claim is even true — an innocent reading is always attached to every match. Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Emotional Blackmail
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Making love, closeness or the relationship itself depend on doing what someone wants, so that saying no feels like risking the bond.
codex_completed.short_definition: Making love, closeness or the relationship itself depend on doing what someone wants, so that saying no feels like risking the bond.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Emotional blackmail ties a request to the relationship: do this, or the closeness, affection or the relationship ends, or something worse follows. Conditional Love goes by a different name but describes this very pattern; it is not a distinct tactic. The condition can be a threat to leave, an exposure, a cold withdrawal or a self-harm warning, or the quiet kind where warmth rises and falls with your compliance. One angry line in a bad fight means little. A pattern shows when affection is tied to a specific yes, again and again.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone makes their love, their company or their goodwill depend on you giving in, so saying no feels like putting the whole relationship at risk.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: When affection is held hostage, a choice made under threat is no longer a free one. You may give in to keep the bond, then lose track of what you wanted, and learn to scan for the other person's mood before you speak.
what_it_is: Linking a specific request to what happens to the bond: loving, staying, speaking, or being kind.
Threat of loss or exposure: 'Leave, and everyone will know what you did.'
Quiet versions with no threat spoken at all, where warmth is plentiful after yes and thin after no.
Found between partners, between parents and children of any age, among friends, and with bosses who go cold on dissent.
A consequence aimed at your choice, rather than a feeling shared about it.
what_it_sounds_like: If you really loved me, you'd stay.
Leave, and everyone will know what you did.
Do it, or don't bother coming back.
I could love you so much more if you'd just lose the attitude.
Be sweet like before and we'll be fine.
Prove you love me by dropping that friend.
When you do it my way, we're great. Why can't it always be like that?
You'll be sorry if you go through with this.
what_it_is_not: A real boundary: 'I can't stay in a relationship where lying keeps happening' states what the speaker will do, not a price for your compliance.
Honest hurt about a decision, said once and leaving the choice with you: 'I'm sad about this, and it's your call.'
A heated line said in the middle of a fight and taken back soon after, with warmth continuing.
A parent enforcing a rule and still showing the child affection.
A person asking for time apart after being hurt, who says so and comes back whether or not you give in.
A reasonable expectation such as honesty, where stepping back is protection and not a bargain.
this_may_be_it_when: The condition names a specific act: stay, drop a friend, sign, apologize.
Affection returns quickly and fully after you comply.
Declining is met with silence, cold distance or a threat aimed at what you value, not an honest 'no' back.
Your agreeing is described as proof of love, and declining as proof of the opposite.
You have begun deciding things in advance to keep the peace.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They say they are upset and also say they are staying, and mean it.
The hard line they set is about their own conduct, and they apply it to themselves too.
A threat was said once, in the worst minute of a fight, and withdrawn without being asked.
You say no and the relationship carries on, perhaps after a difficult talk.
The request has a real reason, such as your safety or a shared bill.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Fear of losing someone can come out clumsily as 'I don't know what I'd do without you' with no wish to compel anything.
A frightened or hurt person may say extreme things they do not mean and regret straight away.
Couples sometimes state real dealbreakers early, such as wanting children, which is information and not leverage.
common_false_positives: A friend annoyed that you canceled three times who says so and stays your friend.
A partner stating a dealbreaker once, calmly, and leaving the decision to you.
Someone grieving a possible loss who describes how much it hurts without asking you to change.
A parent firm about homework who is affectionate at bedtime.
discernment_questions: If I said no, would the relationship be at risk, or only the mood for a while?
Is the condition spoken, or only felt in how warmth changes?
Is a specific act being named as the price of staying close?
Do I decide things in advance to avoid a withdrawal?
Does the same standard apply to them?
less_concerning_if: Disappointment is voiced, the decision stands, and warmth continues.
The expectations placed on you are ones they hold for themselves.
When you say no, the next conversation is ordinary and nothing is held back.
more_concerning_if: The threat involves exposing you, hurting themselves, or taking away money, housing or children.
The conditions grow to cover friends, clothes, work or where you go.
Other people are told you are cold or cruel whenever you refuse.
pattern_over_time_signs: The list of things you no longer say or do grows quietly.
You rehearse requests and apologies before raising anything.
Good days follow compliance, so you read warmth as a grade.
People who knew you earlier say you argued more, or laughed more, in the past.
codex_completed.repair_check: Look for warmth that stops rising and falling with your answers. They disagree with you without a chill, accept a no without a penalty, and hold the same line a month later. A big loving gesture straight after you gave in only restarts the cycle.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: After you decline once, does the closeness come back by itself in a day or two, or does it wait for your apology? The pause itself is ordinary. What matters is whether anything is still being withheld until you reverse.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A wish to stay connected is one of the strongest pulls most people have, so tying that connection to a yes can make declining feel like a danger. When closeness comes and goes with compliance, behavior can adjust quickly to protect it, and a person may start to treat their own preferences as a risk to the bond.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe walking on eggshells, becoming expert at reading moods, and feeling guilty for having needs. Some say they could not tell whether they were loved or only well managed. After threats of exposure or loss, people describe dread and a habit of rehearsing everything they say.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name the link without blame: 'It sounds like my answer decides whether we're okay. I'd like us to be able to disagree and still be close.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say what the condition does to you: 'When my answer is tied to whether we stay together, I can't tell what I actually think. I want to answer without that attached.'
response_options.disengagement: When the chill or threat starts, do not chase it. Keep your own plans for the evening and pick the subject up again when both of you are calmer, or in writing.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe two or three specific episodes to a counselor or friend who knows both of you, and ask whether the link between your choices and their warmth looks as clear to them as it does to you.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a boss rewards agreement and goes cold on dissent, confine feedback to work content in writing, keep dated notes, and use a mentor outside the reporting line.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I care about you, and I want to think about this properly, which I can't do while our relationship feels like it depends on my answer. Can we stop here and come back to it tomorrow?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Watch for threats to hurt themselves, to expose you, to take children, money or housing, or fear of what follows if you refuse. Those turn a painful pattern into a safety matter, and even asking for a pause could raise the danger. If any of that is present, call a domestic abuse advocate or crisis line first, from a phone they cannot check, and let them help you plan any change.
misuse_warning: Every relationship has expectations, and an honest limit such as 'I need faithfulness' is not blackmail. The label fits a condition used to force a particular answer.
Calling someone's pain at a possible loss 'blackmail' can dismiss real grief and cut off an honest conversation.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Guilt-Tripping works on your conscience, telling you refusal is morally wrong, and does not put the relationship itself on the line. Self-Harm Threats as Leverage makes the stake the speaker's own safety, while emotional blackmail can name any loss at all. Silent Treatment goes quiet to force a reply, and it can be one delivery method for the withdrawal, but needs no tie to a specific demand.

codex_completed.name: Self-Harm Threats as Leverage
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Saying one will hurt or kill oneself if the other person leaves or refuses, which ties their decision to the speaker's survival.
codex_completed.short_definition: Saying one will hurt or kill oneself if the other person leaves or refuses, which ties their decision to the speaker's survival.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: These are statements about suicide or self-injury that are tied to a particular choice the other person is making: leaving, ending a call, saying no. The same words can come from real despair, and from the outside the two can look identical, so every such statement deserves a serious response. The link to a demand is the tell: the statements arrive when a boundary does, and the person hearing them ends up responsible for another person's life.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone says they will hurt themselves if you go or say no, and your choice suddenly feels like it carries their life. The fear and the crisis can both be real.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Hearing that your decision could cost a life is one of the heaviest things a person can carry. Many people stop making ordinary choices, like ending an evening or taking a trip, because the stakes feel too high, while the underlying distress goes unaddressed.
what_it_is: Statements about suicide or self-injury that arrive just as you move toward a separation, a refusal or a plan of your own.
A link drawn between your choice and the speaker's safety, so that one answer feels like the only safe one.
Sometimes said once on a terrible night, sometimes repeated each time a boundary is tried.
Often followed by a request for reassurance, a promise or a canceled plan, and not by a step toward getting help.
Said face to face, in a late-night text or in a voicemail left after you have gone.
Hard to read from outside, because the same sentence can be a plea for rescue. That is why it is never brushed off.
what_it_sounds_like: If you walk out that door tonight, I don't know what I'll do to myself.
I'll end it. Then you'll be free of me.
You're the only reason I'm still here, so if you go, that's it.
Go ahead and sleep at your sister's. You'll find out in the morning.
I swear I'll do it this time.
I'm not safe right now, and it's because of you.
Answer me in five minutes or you'll have my death on your hands.
what_it_is_not: A person in real crisis who says they are thinking of suicide, with no link to anything you are doing. That calls for care, not analysis.
Telling a friend or counselor 'I've been having dark thoughts' in order to get help, with no demand attached.
A safety plan made with a therapist, where the person texts you a code word when they are struggling.
Flat exhaustion after a loss, such as 'I can't do this any more', that signals depletion and not a plan.
A statement of hopelessness made on a day when you were not leaving or refusing anything.
Someone overwhelmed at a breakup who blurts out the biggest words they have because they cannot find another way to say how bad it is.
this_may_be_it_when: The statement arrives within minutes of you saying you are leaving, declining or ending a conversation.
It names you as the cause, or as the only person who can prevent it.
Offers of a crisis line, a doctor or a relative are waved off in favor of your presence.
The same kind of statement has followed several separate disagreements, each time attached to something you wanted.
The talk of harm fades once you agree to stay or cancel, and returns at the next decision.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They bring it up on a calm day and ask for help finding a therapist or doctor.
They accept help from other people and are not asking you to be the only thing keeping them safe.
The statements have no link to any decision you made.
They tell you ahead of a hard anniversary or appointment so you can check in, without asking you to change your plans.
They already have treatment or a safety plan and are using it.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Despair can peak in the middle of a breakup, and people reach for the biggest words they have.
Someone who has had suicidal thoughts before may truly believe that a loss would be unsurvivable.
A person who never learned to ask for comfort directly may state the feeling in its most extreme form.
Alcohol or exhaustion can turn sadness into something louder late at night.
common_false_positives: A friend confiding that they have thought about ending their life, which is a disclosure and not a demand.
A teenager who says 'I want to die' about an embarrassing moment and laughs. It still deserves a gentle check, but it is not a lever.
A partner in treatment who tells you they are having a bad week and wants you to know.
discernment_questions: Does the statement come with a request about what I should do, or with a request for help?
When I suggested a counselor, a crisis line or a relative, was that accepted or pushed aside?
Has my own plan, such as seeing a friend or taking a job, changed more than once because of these statements?
Do I feel I am the only person who knows, and the only one who can keep them safe?
Who outside this situation could help me tell fear for them apart from being steered?
less_concerning_if: The distress is shared on ordinary days, with no demand tied to it.
They take up professional or family help when it is offered.
Your choices have stayed your own even while they struggle.
more_concerning_if: The statements come with a plan, a method close at hand, a recent attempt or goodbye messages. That needs urgent help whatever else is going on.
The threats grow more frequent or more specific as your independence grows.
They also monitor you, turn up unannounced or physically block you when you try to go.
pattern_over_time_signs: You have stopped saying plans out loud, in case the answer turns into a crisis.
You carry your phone everywhere and check it in the middle of events, afraid of missing a message.
Friends and family see less of you because evenings keep being cut short.
You feel guilty about ordinary things, like switching your phone off to sleep.
codex_completed.repair_check: The plan does not run through you alone: a clinician, a written safety plan, a relative they trust, and the person actually using them when they struggle. Repair also means they can hear 'no' on an ordinary day without the subject returning to their life or death. Tearful apologies alone do not show it.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice whether your wish to bring in a third person is welcomed or fought. When someone is in danger from their own thoughts, an extra helper often brings relief. If every route except you gets refused, that is worth noting, privately and with someone you trust.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Threats like this can fuse two fears: that the person will die, and that you will be the cause. Compassion and responsibility are strong, and once one choice is framed as life or death, weighing your own needs can seem cruel. The effect can outlast the crisis, since you learn that a no may carry a price.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Constant alertness comes up often, as does a sense of being responsible for another adult's life, plans dropped to stay near the phone, and guilt whether you stay or step away. Numbness is reported, or relief mixed with shame once a crisis passes. Many kept it secret in case the person got into trouble.

response_options.soft_clarification: Stay with the feeling first: 'I can hear how much pain you're in, and I take it seriously.' Then ask the plain question: 'Are you thinking of hurting yourself tonight?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold that you are one support and not the only one: 'I care about you, and I can't be the only thing keeping you safe. Let's call a crisis line together.'
response_options.disengagement: If a threat arrives while you are apart, you do not have to argue it out by text. Send a crisis number, or ask a relative nearby to check in on them, and keep your own reply short and kind.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell one person you trust what was said, in the actual words, and ask a counselor or a domestic abuse advocate how to respond. You should not carry this by yourself.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If the messages arrive during work hours, you can tell a manager you have a personal emergency without giving detail, and ask whether your employer offers a counseling program.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I believe it hurts, and I'm taking what you said seriously. I can't be the only one who helps you stay safe, so I'd like us to call a crisis line together right now. Would it help if I rang your brother to come over?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Any talk of suicide deserves a real response, whatever lies behind it. Danger signs are a stated plan, a method at hand, a recent attempt or goodbye messages. If you see them, contact local emergency services or a crisis line (988 in the United States) on their behalf. Separately, if the threats rise whenever you try to be independent, an advocate can help you plan privately. Your next step is to bring in one outside helper.
misuse_warning: Do not treat every expression of despair as manipulation. If you cannot tell which it is, treat it as real danger and get help; the pattern can be sorted out later.
Telling others that someone was 'only threatening' can leave a person who is in real crisis without help.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Emotional Blackmail attaches many possible losses, such as withdrawn love, exposure or anger, to a refusal; here the stake is the speaker's own life. Pity Plays end in comfort and a change of subject, but they do not tie your decision to survival. Guilt-Tripping stays with blame and conscience and holds no threat of actual harm. This is the entry where your choice is linked to whether someone lives.
