codex_completed.name: Pity Plays
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Answering a concern with displays of helplessness or victimhood, so the person who raised it ends up offering comfort and the concern is dropped.
codex_completed.short_definition: Answering a concern with displays of helplessness or victimhood, so the person who raised it ends up offering comfort and the concern is dropped.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Pity plays are moments when a complaint, a question or a request for change is answered with collapse: tears, 'nobody loves me', 'I'm hopeless at everything'. The original subject gets lost as the person who raised it moves into comforting. Real pain can look exactly the same, and one tearful night after a hard conversation proves nothing. Timing is what counts. The distress appears at the moment of accountability, the issue is not returned to, and over time bringing anything up begins to seem cruel.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You bring up something that bothered you, and the conversation turns into you reassuring them. The original problem never gets looked at.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: When every concern ends in reassurance, the problem stays where it was and your need to be heard shrinks. Over time you may stop raising things at all, which makes the relationship quieter but no more honest.
what_it_is: A reaction that grows as the complaint gets more specific: a calm 'you forgot' meets sobbing, silence or 'I'm a terrible person'.
Sweeping statements about oneself, like 'I always ruin things', that are too large to answer, so comfort is the only reply left.
A swap of roles in mid-conversation: the person who raised the issue is soon the one hugging, apologizing or backing down.
A topic that is not picked up again once the person has calmed.
Seen between partners, but also parents and adult children, friends and coworkers.
what_it_sounds_like: Fine, I'm just a terrible friend. Everyone's better off without me.
You'd abandon me too, like everyone else.
I can't do anything right, can I.
After the week I've had, this is what you bring up?
I'm always the bad guy, aren't I.
Look at me, I'm shaking. Are you happy now?
Never mind. I'll stop talking about anything.
what_it_is_not: Depression or low self-worth speaking, which shows up outside conflict too and calls for care.
Someone overwhelmed by shame who cries and goes quiet, then comes back the next day and talks it through.
A grieving or exhausted person who truly cannot have the conversation tonight and says so plainly.
A person who says 'that hurts to hear' and then listens to the rest.
A family style of speaking in strong emotional terms about everything, not only when challenged.
A request for comfort in a moment unrelated to anything you asked of them.
this_may_be_it_when: Distress rises sharply when you ask for a specific change and is absent on neutral topics.
Their statements about themselves are global ('always', 'never', 'everyone') and not about the incident.
Your original point is not mentioned again, and you are the one who apologizes.
Comfort is needed until they are visibly better, with the concern still unresolved.
A similar scene has followed each time you raised something about the same issue.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They cry, then say 'I want to come back to what you said', and do.
Their sadness is about something else entirely, and they ask for support for that alone.
The distress fits the size of what happened, and the concern still gets addressed.
They show the same vulnerability when nobody has asked anything of them.
They accept 'I can listen to you and still need to talk about this' without a further collapse.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Criticism lands on some people as a verdict on their whole worth, so tears come before thoughts.
Someone raised in a home where mistakes brought anger may freeze or collapse when told of one.
Tiredness, grief or illness can make an ordinary complaint hit much harder than usual.
Some people can only process by crying first and talking second.
common_false_positives: A friend who breaks down after hard feedback, then thanks you the next day and makes the change.
A relative with ongoing depression who says bleak things in all kinds of conversations.
A young child who dissolves into tears after being corrected, which is development and not performance.
discernment_questions: After I raised the concern, did we ever go back to it?
Is the sadness about what happened, or about the fact that I said something?
Do I leave these conversations having apologized or comforted, with nothing resolved?
Do they show the same low moments on days when I have asked for nothing?
Have I stopped mentioning things because I know how it will go?
less_concerning_if: The low feeling is spoken about in general, not only when you ask for something.
The original concern is picked up again once the emotion settles.
They can tell you what they need, such as an hour, and then come back.
more_concerning_if: You now check your words in advance to avoid setting off a collapse.
Concerns about money, safety or health stay unresolved because every scene ends in comfort.
Other people who raise concerns with them describe the same scene.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your list of unspoken concerns keeps growing.
You have become the manager of their moods.
Disagreements get shorter because you drop your point early.
You think of them as fragile and of yourself as the sturdy one, with no room to be upset.
codex_completed.repair_check: What counts is whether the dropped concern comes back. Once they have steadied, they open with it themselves: 'I want to go back to what you said about the money.' Reassurance in the moment, with no later return to the subject, leaves the pattern where it was.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself: when I say 'I care how you feel, and I still need an answer', does one arrive within a day or two? Watch whether the answer eventually comes, or whether each attempt starts the same scene again.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Most people are quick to soothe someone who is crying, and that instinct tends to fire before we have thought about what we were saying. Visible distress can move attention from the concern to the person's wellbeing, and raise doubt about whether you had the right to speak. Repeated, this can teach the one raising concerns that doing so causes harm.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Conversations become careful: complaints get softened in advance, speaking up brings a flash of cruelty, and talks end with you more drained than when they started. Doubt creeps in about whether your concerns were fair. Resentment can build quietly over issues nobody answered, followed by guilt for feeling it.

response_options.soft_clarification: Hold both things aloud: 'I can see you're hurting, and I still need us to finish talking about this.' Offer a break with a time to return, such as tomorrow evening.
response_options.firm_boundary: Name the loop gently and stay on the subject: 'When I raise something, we end up talking about how you feel and never about what I said. I'd like us to do both.'
response_options.disengagement: Comfort them briefly, then step out of the room until the emotion has settled, and bring the topic back the next day in a short conversation or message.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe two recent scenes to a friend or counselor and ask whether your concerns were reasonable. It is hard to tell from inside, since the distress is real.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, put the concern in an email with a specific request and a date, so it does not depend on how a conversation goes, and ask a manager to attend if talks keep stalling.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I can see how much this hurts, and I'm not trying to make it worse. I also need us to talk about what I raised. Take as long as you need, and we'll pick it up tomorrow after dinner."
codex_completed.safety_note: Pity plays on their own are not usually a danger signal. What would change that is distress that turns into threats against yourself or them, or into monitoring and blocking contact when you step away. If the sadness ever comes with talk of ending their life, treat that as its own matter and read the entry on self-harm threats. A first step is to write down, privately, which concerns are still unanswered.
misuse_warning: Tears are not proof of a tactic. Calling real grief a 'pity play' can dismiss the pain of someone who is genuinely struggling.
Take care with this label for a person with depression or a trauma history, whose distress may be entirely sincere and who may still need the conversation to happen later.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Martyrdom Display advertises sacrifice already made ('after all I do'), while pity plays voice present helplessness and the exchange ends in comfort. Self-Harm Threats tie a choice of yours to the speaker's survival; pity plays express hopelessness without a link to what you decide. Guilt-Tripping blames you for a harm, whereas here the speaker is the one harmed. The difference is which story takes the stage: your concern, or their suffering.

codex_completed.name: Martyrdom Display
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Pointing out one's own unrewarded effort and sacrifice in a way that leaves the other person feeling indebted and unable to say no.
codex_completed.short_definition: Pointing out one's own unrewarded effort and sacrifice in a way that leaves the other person feeling indebted and unable to say no.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Martyrdom display is the habit of making effort and self-denial visible: the sighs, the 'don't mind me', the list of what has been given up. Help is not asked for directly. Instead the sacrifice sits in the room until someone offers to fix it. One tired remark after a long week is ordinary. The pattern is the same scene each time help is wanted, and a running debt that grows whether or not you agreed to the cost.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone makes their sacrifices obvious instead of asking for help, so you feel you owe them. A plain request would have been easier to answer.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A debt you never agreed to is hard to pay, because the total keeps changing. You may give more time or help than you wanted and then resent it, while the real need for support never gets spoken.
what_it_is: Doing a task loudly, with clattering dishes or heavy sighs, so the effort is seen though nobody asked for it.
Turning down help with 'no, I'll do it', then reminding you later that nobody helped.
Keeping a mental ledger of sacrifices and bringing out entries in unrelated arguments.
Avoiding a direct request for what is needed, so the only answer open to you is to offer.
Found in families, workplaces, caregiving and partnerships where one person does more of the visible work.
what_it_sounds_like: Don't mind me, I'll sit here alone.
I guess I'll just do it myself like always.
I gave up my whole twenties for this family, but sure, go.
No, no, go and enjoy yourself. I'll be fine with the dishes.
I haven't sat down since six this morning. Not that anyone noticed.
I'd never ask you for anything.
Twelve hours on my feet, and I'm not complaining.
what_it_is_not: Honest tiredness said once, such as 'I'm worn out tonight', that asks you to do nothing.
Someone who truly carries an unfair load and is clumsily trying to say so. They may need a better way to ask, not a label.
A direct request: 'I'm overloaded. Could you do the school run on Thursdays?'
A caregiver describing the facts of their week to a friend who asked.
A person who gives generously and does not mention it or expect a return.
A team meeting where everyone lists what they have finished.
this_may_be_it_when: Offers of help are refused, and then the lack of help is mentioned.
The sacrifice is listed just as you are about to do something for yourself.
No direct request has been made, yet you feel you must offer.
The same phrases come back in many different situations.
Your decision to say no is met with days of silence or sighing, and not with a conversation.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They accept help gladly when it is offered and say thank you.
They ask for what they need in a single sentence.
The effort is mentioned once, and nothing in their tone expects a reply.
They are happy for you to go out and do not make you pay for it later.
They are able to say no to other people as well.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Some people learned in childhood that asking for help brings rejection, so they hint and hope.
In some families, quiet self-sacrifice is how love is shown, and mentioning it is how it gets said.
Exhaustion can make a person say more than they mean, and the words land like a bill.
A person may truly not know how to ask, and think that mentioning the work is the same as asking.
common_false_positives: A friend who says 'I'm wiped, I've been up with the baby' and expects nothing in return.
A relative who quietly does a great deal of unpaid caring and is not acknowledged by the rest of the family.
A coworker who lists what they have finished at a stand-up meeting.
discernment_questions: If I offered help right now, would it be accepted?
Was a direct request ever made, or have I been left to guess?
Is the sacrifice mentioned when I am about to do something I want?
Do I feel I owe something I never agreed to carry?
Is there a genuinely uneven load here that I could see without being shown it?
less_concerning_if: The tiredness is mentioned and followed by a simple request.
Help, when given, is thanked and then forgotten.
The person can say how much they have done without it turning into what you owe.
more_concerning_if: A refusal is followed by days of coldness or sighing.
Past sacrifices are brought up when you raise unrelated needs of your own.
The total owed seems to rise whatever you give.
pattern_over_time_signs: You volunteer for tasks before being asked, to avoid the sighs.
You feel a flicker of dread before telling them your plans.
Your own plans shrink to the ones that are easy to defend.
You resent someone you also feel sorry for.
codex_completed.repair_check: Watch what happens to the requests. A change looks like a plain 'I need help with Saturday', help accepted without commentary, and a refusal received without days of quiet. Thanks for one day's help followed by sighing through the next refusal has not changed the part that matters.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Try a small test: say yes to part of a request and no to the rest. Notice whether the part you gave is received with thanks or with a list of what you did not do. The reaction to the 'no' says more than the reaction to the 'yes'.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Visible sacrifice creates a felt debt without any request, and since nothing was asked, there is nothing to refuse. Reciprocity is a strong social habit, and owing something is uncomfortable. With no direct request to answer, a no lands as turning down a plea that was never spoken.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Guilt with no clear source, a sense of never doing enough, help offered out of dread more than willingness, and resentment that then brings its own shame are all reported. Avoidance follows for some: dreading holidays and chores because even kind acts seemed to add to the tally.

response_options.soft_clarification: Turn the hint into a request you can answer: 'It sounds like a lot is on you. What would help most this week?' Then do what you can, and say what you cannot.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline the debt, not the person: 'I'm happy to do Thursdays. I won't take on the rest because of how the week has looked.'
response_options.disengagement: When the sighing starts, you can leave the room or change the subject without trying to repair the mood, and carry on with the plan you had.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask a sibling, friend or counselor whether the split of work in your household looks fair from outside, and what a fair split might be.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, bring workload questions to the team in a shared list with names and hours, so effort is visible to everyone and not held as private leverage.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I can see you've been doing a lot, and I want to help in a way that works for both of us. I can take Thursdays. I can't take on everything just because it's been hard. Can we write down who does what?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Martyrdom display on its own carries no particular danger. What would change that is sacrifice used to control where you go, whom you see or how you spend money, or any hint of retaliation when you decline. If that appears, write down specific examples and talk to a counselor or advocate before changing the arrangement. A practical first step is a written split of tasks.
misuse_warning: A person who really does carry far more than their share may sound like this when worn out. Calling it a tactic can excuse everyone else from the work.
Be careful with the label for elders and carers, whose self-sacrifice is often real and unseen.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Pity Plays focus on present helplessness and end in comfort; martyrdom display lists sacrifices already made and ends in owing. Demand for Gratitude asks outright for thanks after help, while martyrdom display usually asks for nothing aloud and lets the effort speak. Guilt-Tripping blames you for something you did, whereas here the claim is about what the speaker has done for you. The difference is a ledger of the speaker's effort, kept in view but never itemised as a bill.

Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Duty Scripts
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Using a role such as daughter, son or parent as an unarguable rule for what one must do, so refusing sounds like failing at the role.
codex_completed.short_definition: Using a role such as daughter, son or parent as an unarguable rule for what one must do, so refusing sounds like failing at the role.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Duty scripts take a family or social role and turn it into a rulebook that only one person gets to read. 'A good daughter would...' leaves no space to ask whether the role really requires this, or whether it is the speaker's place to judge. Values about family and respect are real and deeply held in many cultures, so invoking one is not the problem. The pattern is the role used to end a discussion: the request is not argued on its merits, and saying no is treated as a failure of who you are.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone says what a good son, daughter, parent or friend would do, and the request stops being a request. Saying no starts to look like a flaw in you.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: When 'what a good daughter does' replaces 'what do you think', your own judgment about your life is outranked by a rule you did not write. People can lose track of what they want, and the relationship starts to feel like a test they can fail.
what_it_is: A request dressed as a rule about a role: 'a good son visits', 'a mother's word is final'.
A definition of the role that only the speaker may set and that can shift to fit the request.
Arguments that skip the practical questions (can you, is it fair?) and go straight to what kind of person you are.
Often tied to family hierarchy, age, culture or religion, though not unique to any of them.
Heard at weddings, caregiving crises, inheritance talks and holidays, when a family is deciding who does what.
what_it_sounds_like: A good daughter would never say that.
Family comes first. You owe us this.
I didn't raise you to talk back to your father.
It's your duty as the eldest.
You're a mother now. Your own plans don't count.
Because I am your mother, that's why.
A real friend would have been there.
Who's going to look after her if not you?
what_it_is_not: A family or cultural value stated as one consideration, with room to say 'I see it differently' and still be loved.
An honest 'we are counting on you for Sunday', which names a need and accepts a no.
A relative sharing what duty meant to their own generation without requiring the same of you.
Obligations you chose, such as caring for your child or keeping a promise, where the duty is plain and shared.
Religious or community teaching about duty given in a sermon or lesson, not aimed at a particular decision.
A parent setting house rules for a young child.
this_may_be_it_when: Your reasons for declining are never answered, only the role you are failing.
The meaning of the role shifts to fit each new request.
Siblings who hold the same role are not held to the same standard.
The phrase is used at the moment you try to decide something for yourself.
A question like 'what do you think?' would feel out of place in the conversation.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They ask about your situation and adjust.
Several people share the duty equally.
The expectation was known when you took on the role, and applies to the speaker too.
You can say 'I can't do this one' and the relationship stays warm.
The talk of duty is about the speaker's own choices and not yours.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many families express love through duty language, and those may be the only words available.
Someone worried about an aging parent may reach for the strongest phrase they know.
A speaker may truly believe the rule they quote and be repeating what was said to them.
common_false_positives: A parent telling a seven-year-old that in this house we say thank you.
A sibling saying 'we all agreed to split Mom's care', reminding you of a commitment you made.
A faith leader teaching about family responsibility to the whole congregation.
discernment_questions: Who defined this role, and was I ever asked?
Do the same expectations apply to the people saying this?
Does the speaker want to hear my reasons, or only whether I will comply?
If the request had been made as a request, would I have said yes?
Am I being judged by a rulebook I could not have read in advance?
less_concerning_if: The expectation is open to discussion, and you can say what you are able to give.
The speaker holds themselves to the same rule.
Duty is mentioned as a value and not used at the moment of a decision.
more_concerning_if: Declining brings exclusion from family events or being spoken of as a disgrace.
The role is used to control your education, relationships, money or where you live.
Other relatives are asked to enforce the script and pass on its judgments.
pattern_over_time_signs: You hear the script in your own head when you think of saying no.
You decide things by asking what you are supposed to do, not what you want.
You feel something close to shame at ordinary boundaries.
You have stopped telling certain relatives your plans until they are settled.
codex_completed.repair_check: Start with whether the role stops being the argument. A shift would sound like 'what do you think you can manage?', with the rule left out, and a refusal that leaves your standing in the family unchanged. A warm apology followed by 'a good son would' at the next decision has changed only the tone.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice what changes after you say 'I can't do that, and I am still your daughter.' Is your place at the table the same? Pay attention to whether invitations, calls and warmth continue, or whether something quietly goes cold.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Roles carry heavy moral weight, and many people take on their family's idea of a good son, daughter or parent early in life. With a request attached to that identity, refusing registers as failing at who you are, not as choosing between options. The rule is never written down, so it cannot be checked, and it can stretch to cover new situations.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Being split between what the family expects and what you want is the usual report, along with deciding like a child would and carrying shame at choosing for yourself. Some could not tell what they wanted for years. Others are left with distance from relatives they love, and grief at what saying no has cost.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask which part of the request matters most, and what the person is most worried about: 'Tell me what you need on Sunday, and I'll tell you what I can do.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Separate the role from the request: 'I am your daughter, and I can't take this on. Please ask me as a question, not as a rule.'
response_options.disengagement: When the script begins, say you will talk about the practical side later and move to another topic, without defending what a good daughter does.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk to someone outside the family who respects your background, such as a cousin, a faith counselor or a therapist familiar with your culture, about where duty ends and pressure starts.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, when a role like 'team player' is used to justify unpaid extras, ask what the written duties are and answer the request in terms of hours and scope.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I take being a good son seriously, and that is why I'm being honest that I can't do this one. It isn't that I don't care about the family. The answer is no. Let's talk about what I can do instead."
codex_completed.safety_note: Role pressure is usually painful rather than dangerous. It changes when refusing brings threats, confiscated phones or papers, being kept in, a forced marriage or travel plan, or talk of family honor tied to harm. Those call for specialist help, such as a forced marriage or domestic abuse service, or legal aid. A first step is to find that service quietly, before any family conversation.
misuse_warning: Cultural or religious duty is not itself a form of pressure. Applying this label to a whole family's values dismisses traditions many people hold dear.
A relative saying 'family comes first' may be asking, not scripting. Check for the pattern before naming it.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Guilt-Tripping blames you for a harm already done, while duty scripts rest on a role you hold, so the claim is about who you are supposed to be. Emotional Blackmail attaches a loss, such as love or approval, to a decision; duty scripts need no threat, only the role's authority. Demand for Gratitude says you owe thanks for help given, but duty scripts say you owe compliance because of a bond. The difference is where the authority is claimed: a rulebook of roles, not a record of acts.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Actively matched against pasted text by this tool, at low confidence. Phrase matching can flag wording, but it cannot know intent, tone, history, context, or whether the claim is even true — an innocent reading is always attached to every match. Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Demand for Gratitude
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Expecting thanks on demand, in the right words or amount, as the price of help given, so that generosity ends up with conditions attached.
codex_completed.short_definition: Expecting thanks on demand, in the right words or amount, as the price of help given, so that generosity ends up with conditions attached.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Demand for gratitude turns help into something that must be repaid in visible thanks. The help may be real: a lift, a loan, a roof, a favor. What changes is that thanks is asked for, measured and chased. A single 'a thank-you would be nice' after a long day is a human feeling. Look for thanks that must come in particular forms, gratitude raised again weeks later, and a helped person made to feel lower for having been helped.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You were helped, and now you are expected to keep showing how thankful you are, in the right way, or be reminded of it. Help turns into a cost.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: When thanks is required, help stops being a gift and starts to feel like a loan with interest. People can start to avoid accepting help, even when they need it, or hide small wins so nobody feels unappreciated.
what_it_is: Thanks asked for out loud ('Where's my thank you?') or counted ('You only said it once').
A specific form demanded, such as a card, a public mention, a visit or a particular tone.
A change of mood when thanks seems too small: a cooler voice, a shorter visit, a withdrawn offer.
Help given in a way that makes the amount of thanks owed obvious, with a mention of cost, effort or time.
Seen between parents and adult children, hosts and guests, employers and workers, and friends.
what_it_sounds_like: A thank-you would be nice for once.
After everything I did to get you that job, not even a card?
I'm still waiting to hear thank you.
You said thanks, but you didn't sound like you meant it.
Other people would be on their knees thanking me.
I don't ask for much. Just a little appreciation.
Did you thank her properly? Look how much she's done for you.
what_it_is_not: Hurt feelings that help went unmentioned, said once and kindly: 'It would mean a lot to hear that it helped.'
Teaching a child to say please and thank you, a normal part of manners.
A charity or club that thanks donors publicly, with the acknowledgement agreed in advance.
Close friends who say thanks for small things as a habit both of them enjoy.
A person who gave a great deal, is worn thin and wants to be seen, which is different from wanting to be repaid.
A workplace that recognizes effort in a review.
this_may_be_it_when: The thanks is checked afterwards: how it was said, when, and in front of whom.
A thank-you from you has to be repeated or made bigger to count.
Not thanking in the preferred way is met with a cooler tone or less help afterwards.
Help arrives with a mention of what it cost, before you have said anything.
You receive reminders of your ingratitude weeks after the help.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They say 'you're welcome' and move on.
They said they were hurt once and did not need it repeated or performed.
Help continues on the same terms whether you thank them loudly, quietly or not at all.
Both of you can say thanks and receive it with ease.
They say the help came with no strings and behave that way.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People who rarely received thanks growing up may feel its absence sharply.
A busy, tired helper may ask for acknowledgement simply because it has been a long week.
Cultures differ in how much thanks is expected, and what looks cold in one looks polite in another.
Receivers often forget to say thanks in a crisis, and the helper's hurt is then genuine.
common_false_positives: A parent reminding a teenager to thank their grandmother for a gift.
A friend who says 'I felt unseen when I helped you move, and wanted you to know.'
A group where each member sends thanks after a shared meal as an agreed custom.
discernment_questions: Was this help offered freely, or did it come with expectations I did not hear?
Is the thanks I give ever enough, or does the bar keep moving?
What happens when I do not show gratitude in the way they expected?
Do I keep up the thanks because I feel it, or because I fear what happens if I stop?
Would I still accept this help if I knew how much repayment it carried?
less_concerning_if: A wish to hear thanks is stated once, kindly, and does not return.
The helper stays warm when thanks is brief or late.
Help is offered again later on the same terms.
more_concerning_if: Thanks is demanded in front of other people, or in a way that embarrasses you.
Help is withdrawn, or threatened, when thanks falls short.
The help being held up as owed is a basic such as housing, rides or money.
pattern_over_time_signs: You over-thank, or rehearse your thank-yous, to avoid friction.
You hide good news or skip asking for help to stay out of debt.
You flinch at a gift, wondering what it will cost.
Visits and calls start to feel like repayments.
codex_completed.repair_check: The moment thanks arrives shows it. A shift sounds like a simple 'glad I could help', then no follow-up check, and a later offer given without a reminder. Another speech about how much has been done, even a warm one, keeps the meter running.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Tell them you are grateful and that you would like help between you to be given freely or not at all. Then see how the next offer arrives: with fewer conditions, or with a longer reminder of the last one?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Gratitude is a real and valuable feeling, and most people want to repay kindness. When thanks is demanded, that feeling can be treated as a payment due, and a person who is slow to produce it may feel ungenerous. Because the amount owed is never fixed, the debt rarely feels settled, and staying quietly agreeable can seem easier.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Never having thanked enough is a frequent feeling, with discomfort at accepting gifts, rehearsed thank-yous, and hiding anything that might look ungrateful. Asking for help can stop altogether, since it would add to the account. A slow dislike can grow toward someone the person has real reason to appreciate.

response_options.soft_clarification: Offer thanks that is true and specific: 'The lift got me to the interview on time, and I appreciated it.' Then notice whether it lands, or whether more is expected.
response_options.firm_boundary: Tell them the way thanks is being asked for is hard for you: 'I am grateful, and I can't be asked for it every time we talk.'
response_options.disengagement: If a meeting turns into a review of your gratitude, close that part with one 'thank you again' and move on, without adding more.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask a friend, relative or counselor whether help like this would normally come with this much accounting, or whether you are missing something.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager or mentor keeps referring to what they did for your career, thank them once in writing, then keep the working relationship on tasks and agreements.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "What you did mattered, and I mean that. I'd like help between us to work without a scorecard. If it comes with a need for more thanks, I would rather manage on my own."
codex_completed.safety_note: Demand for gratitude is not usually dangerous in itself. The picture changes when the help is housing, money or papers and thanks becomes a condition of keeping them, or when refusing brings a threat of being put out. In that case, quietly look up tenant advice, legal aid or a relevant advocate before changing the arrangement, and keep copies of anything that is yours.
misuse_warning: Wanting appreciation is human. Using this label every time someone mentions that they helped would silence honest feelings.
Do not apply it to a child learning manners, or to someone who was truly not thanked after a big effort.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Martyrdom Display shows sacrifice through sighs and 'don't mind me' and asks for nothing aloud; demand for gratitude names the thanks it expects. Duty Scripts claim you owe obedience because of a role, while here you owe acknowledgement because of help given. Guilt-Tripping makes you feel at fault for a harm, and demand for gratitude makes you feel at fault for not feeling thankful enough. The difference is the object: your thanks, in a particular form, as the thing being collected.

Phrase matching can flag wording, but it cannot know intent, tone, history, context, or whether the claim is even true — an innocent reading is always attached to every match. Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Favor Debt
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Citing past gifts, money or support as the reason someone must agree to a present request, so past kindness is treated like a signed contract.
codex_completed.short_definition: Citing past gifts, money or support as the reason someone must agree to a present request, so past kindness is treated like a signed contract.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Favor debt is the habit of citing what one has given, such as school fees, a loan, a place to stay or a favor, as the reason you must say yes to something now. Mutual support is part of nearly every close relationship, and mentioning it is not a problem. The pattern is when old help becomes a lever on a particular decision, can be cited again and again, and has no end point: whatever you give, the balance stays open.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone reminds you of everything they gave you and uses it to get a yes now. Whatever you do, the balance never seems paid off.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A debt you never agreed to has no settlement date, so you can be asked to pay it over and over. People may stay in jobs, relationships or cities they would have left, or hand over money they cannot spare, because refusing feels like taking from someone who helped.
what_it_is: A past gift or support used as the reason for a present request: 'After I paid your rent, you can do this.'
A balance that is never closed: whatever you give back, the original help is still cited.
Help given earlier and described afterwards as a loan, though nobody said so at the time.
Covers money, favors, time, introductions, housing or a career opening.
Found in families, friendships, workplaces and partnerships where one person has more resources.
what_it_sounds_like: Remember who paid for your school.
You owe me after everything.
Everything you have is because of me.
I put a roof over your head when nobody else would.
Who do you think got you that interview?
I covered your rent for a year. The least you can do is cover for me.
After what I spent on your wedding, you can host us.
what_it_is_not: A friend saying 'I lent you money in March, can we talk about when you might pay it back?', which is an openly agreed loan.
Mutual support in a long relationship mentioned honestly: 'We have always helped each other.'
A request for help after helping, offered as a request that accepts a no.
A written agreement to repay, such as a mortgage or family loan, and a reminder of its terms.
A parent saying once, while sad, what they gave up for a child, with no demand attached.
Proper credit within a team for work that helped you.
this_may_be_it_when: Help from years ago is cited when you are asked for something today.
No terms of repayment were stated at the time, but now there are some.
Whatever you do to give back is called too little.
A reminder of the debt arrives at the moment you hesitate.
Declining a request is treated as ingratitude toward the person who helped.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Terms of repayment were agreed at the time, in words or writing.
The helper says 'you owe me nothing' and acts that way when you decline.
Both of you have helped each other, and either can ask.
Your 'no' is accepted without a reminder.
The debt is a plain sum with an end.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Someone who helped at real cost may feel hurt when things now seem one-sided.
People under financial strain may remember exactly who gave what, because every pound counts.
Some families treat generosity as a loan that is expected to come back, and see that as normal.
A person may mention past help to explain why they are asking, with no thought of compelling you.
common_false_positives: A sibling who repaid you last month and now asks for a return favor, describing the arrangement as mutual.
A mentor who asks you once to help a new employee as they helped you, and takes a no kindly.
A friend who mentions a past loan because they are short this month and wants to agree a repayment plan.
discernment_questions: Were there terms when the help was given, or did they appear later?
Is this a request I can decline, or has it been framed as something I cannot?
Does anything I give back ever count as enough?
Does the reminder arrive whenever I hesitate over something unrelated to the original help?
Does help run in both directions in this relationship?
less_concerning_if: Earlier help is mentioned as context while the current request stays optional.
A repayment has been named, and it can be completed.
Both sides can count what the other has done without turning it against each other.
more_concerning_if: The debt is used on decisions about your own life: where you live, whom you marry, what job you take.
Money is involved and your name is on loans, accounts or papers you did not choose.
Saying no brings a cut-off of help you depend on, such as housing, tuition or childcare.
pattern_over_time_signs: You track what you have been given and feel a sting when the person is generous again.
You turn down help you need, to avoid being in someone's debt.
You have said yes to requests you would rather have refused, simply to settle the balance.
The list of what you owe keeps growing, though nothing new has been given.
codex_completed.repair_check: A different pattern shows up as terms: help is named as a gift, or as a loan with a sum and a date, and past help stops being cited when you decline something. A change of tone followed by the same reminder at the next 'no' leaves the account open.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask whether the debt can be named and closed. If you offer to repay a specific sum or to thank them in a specific way, notice whether they accept it as settled. A reaction that raises the amount, or keeps the sum vague, tells you the account cannot be closed from your side.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A strong pull to return favors is useful in healthy relationships. When help is later described as a debt, that sense of fairness can be pointed at a request with no link to the original help. The sum is never fixed, so repaying is never finished, and refusing can seem like taking from someone who gave.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Being trapped by one's own history is a common report, along with avoiding gifts for fear of the cost and agreeing to things disliked just to quiet the reminder. The mix is often bitter: real gratitude alongside anger. Some stayed in a place or a job longer than they wanted.

response_options.soft_clarification: Acknowledge the help and ask to separate it from the request: 'I'm grateful for what you did for my schooling. Can we talk about this request on its own?'
response_options.firm_boundary: State that thanks and agreement are different things: 'I will always appreciate what you did. That doesn't mean I can say yes to this.'
response_options.disengagement: When the reminder comes, you can decline to go through the list again and return to the question in front of you, or end the call.
response_options.support_seeking: Write down what was given and what was agreed at the time, and take it to a friend, an accountant or a legal aid adviser if money or property is involved.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a mentor or boss cites past favors, ask for any commitments in writing and keep decisions about your role tied to your duties, not to who sponsored your career.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I haven't forgotten what you did for me, and I'm still grateful. I can't pay it back by agreeing to this one. Tell me a way to thank you that I can really do."
codex_completed.safety_note: Favor debt becomes a safety matter when the debt is financial or legal: loans in your name, a sponsored visa or housing tied to compliance, or threats to cut off what you depend on. Keep copies of any papers you have signed, and get independent advice from legal aid or a tenant or immigration adviser before changing anything.
misuse_warning: Mentioning past help is not always a lever. Calling every reminder of support 'favor debt' can brush aside people who really did give a lot and are asking fairly.
Do not use the label to avoid repaying a loan that was clearly agreed.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Duty Scripts rest on a role (a good son would) and need no past act; favor debt rests on something that was actually given, such as fees or rent. Emotional Blackmail threatens a loss of love or approval if you refuse, while favor debt points back at what has already been provided. Guilt-Tripping blames you for a hurt you caused, but favor debt claims you are in arrears for a kindness. The difference is the ledger: a specific past gift cited as payment due now.

Phrase matching can flag wording, but it cannot know intent, tone, history, context, or whether the claim is even true — an innocent reading is always attached to every match. Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Catastrophizing as Control
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Predicting that someone will fall into ruin, loneliness or disaster if they act independently, so that leaving or choosing differently begins to feel unsafe.
codex_completed.short_definition: Predicting that someone will fall into ruin, loneliness or disaster if they act independently, so that leaving or choosing differently begins to feel unsafe.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Catastrophizing as control means painting the future in worst-case terms whenever the other person is about to make a choice of their own: a job, a move, a friendship, an end to the relationship. The predictions come as facts, not worries, and they usually cast the speaker as the one thing keeping disaster away. Worry about someone you love is normal, and a frank warning can be a kindness. The pattern is predictions that outsize the real risk, return at each step toward independence, and leave you less able to trust your own plans.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: When you move toward something of your own, someone predicts you will end up broke, alone or ruined without them, until managing alone feels impossible.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Fear of the future can keep a person in place more firmly than any rule. When every independent step is described as the start of ruin, you may stop trying, stay where you are, and lose confidence that you could cope.
what_it_is: Forecasts of disaster delivered as certainties: 'you will lose the house', not 'I am worried about the house'.
A prediction that you personally will fail without the speaker, whatever the plan is.
Disaster linked to many different choices: a job, a course, a move, a friend, a decision to leave.
A forecast that does not change when you show a plan, savings or support.
Sometimes passed through others ('your mother is frightened for you') or backed by selected stories of people who failed.
what_it_sounds_like: If you take that job, this family falls apart.
You'll end up alone and broke without me.
No one else will put up with you the way I do.
You can't survive out there. You've never even paid a bill.
You'll lose the kids, the house, everything, and then who will take you in?
Everyone who tried that ended up on the street.
You won't last a month in that city.
what_it_is_not: Worry named as one's own: 'I'm anxious about the move, and I know it's your decision.'
An accurate warning about a real risk, such as a lease with penalties, with figures you can check.
A friend or relative asking hard questions about a plan, then helping you test it.
A financial adviser or lawyer laying out the realistic downsides of a risky choice.
A person with an anxiety condition who sees danger in most changes, including their own.
Advice you can verify that still leaves the choice with you.
this_may_be_it_when: The predicted outcome is far worse than the actual risk, and nobody explains how it would come about.
The warning appears when you take a step toward independence and rarely otherwise.
Your plans, savings and backup are brushed aside without being examined.
The prediction casts the speaker as the only safeguard.
You are told that no one else would help you or accept you.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They go through your plan with you, point out gaps, and then say the decision is yours.
Their worry is about specific, checkable risks.
They are just as anxious about their own changes.
They help you prepare for the risks they name.
A trusted third person independently sees the same risk.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Anxiety makes some people picture the worst, and they say it aloud to relieve themselves.
A parent who has seen things go wrong may want to protect an adult child without noticing the effect.
A person afraid of losing you may reach for the biggest warnings they can find.
People who had hard times themselves may assume yours will go the same way.
common_false_positives: A partner who says 'I'm scared about our finances if we both leave our jobs' and asks to make a plan.
A friend who warns you about an investment that looks like a scam, with details to check.
A relative who is nervous about you moving abroad but helps with the paperwork.
discernment_questions: Is this an account of a specific risk, or a general sense that I cannot cope?
Has anyone outside this relationship seen my plan and the risks?
Do these warnings come only when I move toward something of my own?
Have earlier predictions that came true been as bad as they were described?
What would I think if a friend were told the same thing about their plan?
less_concerning_if: Warnings include specifics you can check and a way to reduce the risk.
The speaker is as willing to hear that the plan might work as that it might fail.
Support continues after you decide, even if they would have chosen differently.
more_concerning_if: Predictions come with reduced access to money, papers, a phone, or contact with friends and family.
The warnings escalate to claims that you would lose children, home or safety if you left.
Earlier predictions did not come true, yet the same ones keep returning.
pattern_over_time_signs: You have stopped telling the person about your hopes and plans.
You have put off applying, studying, saving or moving.
You hear their predictions in your own voice when you think about change.
People close to you say you used to be more confident.
codex_completed.repair_check: Pay attention to whether the forecasts turn into plans. A change sounds like 'I'm worried about money, can we look at the numbers together?', followed by the person supporting a choice that carries risk. A softer tone, with the prediction repeated whenever you move forward, leaves the fear installed.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice what happens when you ask to look at the actual risk together, with figures on paper. Is the conversation turned toward what could be done, or does the prediction grow? Also watch whether anything about your access to money, phone or friends changes afterwards.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Fear of loss is strong, and a confident forecast from someone close can sound like inside knowledge. Repeated, it can replace your own estimate of what you can handle, and uncertainty tends to get settled by staying put. When you are already unsure or financially dependent, the forecast fills the gap, and each step not taken makes the prediction feel truer.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Feeling smaller, doubting your own competence, putting plans off and hearing a warning voice long after the conversation are all reported. Some felt unable to leave a job, a home or a relationship even when they wanted to. Others found out later that they managed far better than predicted, and felt anger and grief for the lost time.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the mechanics: 'What exactly do you think would go wrong, and what would help?' A specific worry can be checked, and a vague one tells you something too.
response_options.firm_boundary: Say how the predictions land: 'When you tell me I will fail, I feel less able to think. I'd like us to look at the facts instead.'
response_options.disengagement: You do not have to answer every prediction. A short 'I've heard you' lets the conversation move on, and you can work on your plans privately with someone you trust.
response_options.support_seeking: Show your plan, with the figures, to someone outside the relationship, such as a friend, a financial counselor or an advocate, and ask for an honest read of the risks. Keep a copy with a person the other party does not control.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, if a colleague or manager forecasts disaster whenever you apply for a role or take a project, ask for the specific risk in writing and seek an outside view from a mentor or HR.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I've heard that you're worried, and I want to understand the real risks. Can we write down what could go wrong and what would help with each one? I want to talk it over with my sister as well."
codex_completed.safety_note: Predictions of ruin become a safety concern when they travel with control of money, papers, phones or transport, with monitoring, or with claims that you would lose children or housing if you left. Those can be signs of coercive control. A next step specific to this tactic: talk through your real options with a domestic abuse advocate or legal aid service, who can help you plan privately, before anything changes.
misuse_warning: A frank warning about a risky plan is not control. Labeling honest caution as a tactic can lead you to ignore real risks.
Do not use this label to dismiss an anxious relative who is trying, clumsily, to say that they care.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Emotional Blackmail attaches a penalty the speaker will impose, such as withdrawn love, if you do not comply; catastrophizing as control predicts a disaster that will arrive on its own. Guilt-Tripping looks back at blame for a harm already done, while this looks ahead to a ruin that has not happened. Pity Plays make the speaker the one who is suffering, where here you are the one forecast to fall. The difference is direction: a forecast about your future, offered as fact.

codex_completed.name: Love Bombing
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Flooding someone with intense affection, praise and attention very early, at a pace that outruns how well the two people actually know each other.
codex_completed.short_definition: Flooding someone with intense affection, praise and attention very early, at a pace that outruns how well the two people actually know each other.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Love bombing is a burst of adoration at the start of a relationship: constant messages, big declarations, gifts, plans for a shared life, all arriving within days or weeks. Plenty of people fall fast and say so, so speed alone proves little. What marks the pattern is that the intensity is out of step with real knowledge of you, is hard to slow down, and later shifts into coolness, criticism or demands once you have come to depend on it.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone showers you with love, praise and big promises far faster than they could really know you, and the warmth later turns out to come with strings.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A rush of being adored can feel like finally being seen, so it is easy to let other parts of life shrink around it. If the warmth later cools or gets conditional, you may chase the early version and blame yourself for losing it.
what_it_is: A rapid climb in affection: daily or hourly contact, grand declarations and compliments within the first days or weeks.
Praise that is sweeping rather than specific, such as 'perfect' or 'soulmate', before the person has seen you on a bad day.
Gifts, trips or future plans offered faster than the relationship has had time to earn.
Often paired with a feeling that slowing down would hurt or insult the other person.
Most recognizable in hindsight, when the early intensity is compared with what came after it.
what_it_sounds_like: I knew the first night we talked that you were the one.
I've never felt this way about anyone. Nobody else has ever come close.
Let's get away this weekend, just us. I already booked it.
You don't need to see your friends tonight. Stay with me, I miss you too much.
I think we should move in together. Why wait when we both know?
You're literally perfect. I can't believe you're real.
I'll text you all day, I just can't help myself.
what_it_is_not: Two people who fall quickly and openly for each other, both comfortable with the pace and both able to say 'a bit slower' without it landing as rejection.
A naturally effusive person who is warm and generous with everyone, and has been for years.
A long-distance or whirlwind romance in which fast contact reflects circumstance, such as time zones or a short trip, rather than pressure.
Genuine enthusiasm that settles into steady, ordinary care once the novelty passes, instead of flipping to coldness.
A cultural or family style in which grand romantic language is simply how love is spoken.
this_may_be_it_when: The affection arrives in a rush, then drops sharply after you commit, relax or push back on the pace.
Your attempts to slow down are met with hurt, sulking or the suggestion that you do not feel as deeply as they do.
The praise is generic enough that it could be said to anyone, and it does not change as they learn who you are.
Gifts or sacrifices are mentioned later as a debt you owe.
Your time with friends, family or work quietly shrinks because the contact is so constant.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You can say 'I need to go slower' and the answer is a calm 'okay, thanks for telling me'.
The warmth stays roughly the same through arguments, bad weeks and ordinary boredom.
Their compliments are about particular things you have actually done or said.
Your friendships, hobbies and sleep are intact and they ask about them with interest.
They are equally open about their own flaws and do not treat you as flawless.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Early infatuation is a normal, chemical-feeling stage, and many lasting couples remember it as intense and fast.
Some people text a lot and plan big gestures because that is how they show care.
A person coming out of loneliness may pour out affection with no plan behind it at all.
common_false_positives: A first-love or second-chance romance in which both people are swept up and say so out loud.
A friend who is generous with compliments to everyone in the group.
A partner who was ardent at the start and has since become steadier, which is a usual settling and not a reversal.
discernment_questions: Does the pace feel mutual, or am I mostly trying to keep up with it?
If I asked for a slower speed, what would the reaction tell me?
Do the compliments describe me, or could they describe anybody?
Has this closeness cost me time with other people I care about?
Is the warmth the same on days when I disappoint them?
Would I accept this level of declaration from a coworker I had known for three weeks?
less_concerning_if: You both feel carried along at about the same speed and can talk about it.
Asking for space produces understanding rather than a visible drop in warmth.
The relationship stays steady after the first wave of excitement fades.
more_concerning_if: Big gestures are followed by pressure to commit, move in, share money or drop other plans.
The adoration disappears or turns critical when you set a limit or take time for yourself.
Others who care about you have noticed you pulling away from them since this began.
pattern_over_time_signs: The first weeks are recalled as the best of the relationship, and you find yourself trying to bring them back.
Praise becomes sparser and more tied to what you do for them.
The speed that was exciting at the start now feels like being rushed through decisions.
You keep a mental tally of what they gave you early on, and it makes it harder to object now.
codex_completed.repair_check: Affection that continues at a livable level, interest in who you really are, and room for your other relationships would show a change in pace that you did not have to fight for. A promise to 'go back to how it was in the beginning' is not that.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself what happens in the days after you request more space or a slower timeline. If the warmth stays and the request is simply followed, that is a good sign. If it is followed by coldness, guilt or a bigger gesture meant to win you back, note that.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Intense early attention is unusually rewarding, and expectations often rise to match it. When the warmth later drops or turns conditional, the gap can leave someone working to win back the earlier feeling, while a sense of owing gratitude makes objecting feel ungrateful. Fast closeness also leaves little time for ordinary checking, such as meeting friends or seeing how a partner handles disagreement.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Some recall being swept off their feet, then feeling bewildered when the tone changed and blaming themselves for the shift. Missing the early weeks the way one misses a place is a common account, as is feeling unable to leave something that once felt like rescue. Embarrassment at having believed it can delay telling friends.

response_options.soft_clarification: Mention the pace without judging it: 'I really like you, and this is moving faster than I'm used to. I'd like us to see each other a couple of times a week for now.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold the limit even after a sad or grand reaction: 'I'm not moving in this year. That isn't about how much I care.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop accepting gifts, trips or big commitments for a while, and reply to messages on your own schedule instead of instantly.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend or relative who knew you before this relationship what has been happening, and ask what they have noticed about you since it began.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager, client or colleague showers you with sudden praise and favors, note the dates, keep requests in writing, and ask a mentor whether the attention is ordinary for your workplace.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'm enjoying getting to know you, and I want to keep it at a pace where I can still see my friends and sleep normally. Seeing each other twice a week is what works for me right now."
codex_completed.safety_note: Rapid intensity becomes a safety concern when it comes with pressure to cut off friends, share a home or money, hand over passwords, or when your no is met with anger or threats. Keep your own housing, income and phone access in place early on, and talk to a domestic abuse advocate if anything starts to feel like you cannot say no safely.
misuse_warning: Calling every enthusiastic new partner a love bomber can make ordinary, happy infatuation sound sinister, and it can chill people who are simply open with their feelings.
The label describes a pace and a later change. It is not a way to read someone's motives from their first few weeks of texts.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Exclusive Meaning is a specific claim that only this person understands you, which slowly makes other relationships seem lesser, while love bombing is the overall surge of praise and attention. Future Faking centers on promises about what is coming, rather than on affection in the present. Hoovering happens after distance or a breakup, but love bombing arrives at the start of a connection.

codex_completed.name: Exclusive Meaning
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Claiming that only this one person truly understands you, which gradually makes everyone else in your life seem less worthy of your trust.
codex_completed.short_definition: Claiming that only this one person truly understands you, which gradually makes everyone else in your life seem less worthy of your trust.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Exclusive meaning is the repeated message that you are understood by one person alone, and that other people, however close, cannot do it. Said once by a moved partner, it is a romantic line. As a pattern it tends to sit beside small put-downs of your friends or family, and it leaves you with one place to bring your troubles. The difference is whether closeness is described as something added to your life or as a replacement for the rest of it.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: One person keeps telling you that nobody else gets you the way they do, and over time your friends and family start to feel like they do not count.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: If one person becomes the only one who seems to understand you, your other relationships lose weight. That leaves you with fewer people to check reality with, and less ability to leave or disagree safely.
what_it_is: A repeated claim to a special, unmatched understanding of who you are and what you need.
A comparison, stated or implied, in which your other people come out worse: shallow, jealous, not on your side.
Often built from real moments of feeling understood, which makes the claim believable.
Shows up in romance, but also in friendships, mentorships, workplaces and groups with a charismatic leader.
Works gradually, through small remarks, and rarely as one dramatic demand to drop people.
what_it_sounds_like: Your friends don't actually get you. I do.
Nobody has ever listened to you the way I do. You can tell me things you'd never tell your mother.
Why would you talk to her about this? She'll only judge you.
I'm the only person who's ever seen the real you.
They love the version of you that's easy for them. I love all of you.
What we have is on a different level. Other people just can't reach it.
what_it_is_not: Telling someone 'I feel so understood by you', which describes a feeling of closeness without ranking anyone else.
A close confidant, like a best friend or counselor, whom you rely on heavily while still keeping other ties alive and welcome.
A new couple's enthusiasm in the first months, expressed once or twice and then left alone.
Honest concern about a particular friend's behavior, specific and open to your own view of that friend.
A therapist or mentor whose role is to hear you, where the limited scope is clear and everyone else is not put down.
this_may_be_it_when: The remarks about being the only one who gets you come with remarks about specific people who supposedly do not.
You notice you are sharing less with friends because they 'would not see it', in the other person's words.
Your outside relationships are described as threats, competitors or bad influences.
Being understood by them starts to feel like something you must keep earning by staying close.
When you mention a friend's support, the reply is flat, wounded or quickly redirected to themselves.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They encourage you to talk to other people, and are pleased when you feel supported elsewhere.
Their praise for your closeness is a fact about a moment, not a claim that rivals cannot compare.
They speak well of your friends, and ask after them.
You still bring different things to different people and none of it feels guarded.
Their comments about someone in your life are specific, based on something that happened, and not a general verdict.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Early infatuation often produces sentences like 'no one has ever got me like you do' with no hidden aim.
Someone who truly has few friends of their own may overstate how central you are to them out of loneliness.
A deep connection through shared history, such as an illness or a loss, can feel unique and be described that way.
common_false_positives: A spouse of many years who says 'you know me better than anyone', and also gets on well with your sister.
A support group in which people feel understood by others with the same experience, without being told outsiders are lesser.
A teenager and a best friend who say 'only you get me' as part of ordinary adolescence.
discernment_questions: When I say a friend or relative has helped me, how do they respond?
Have I stopped telling others things I used to tell them, and whose idea was that?
Does this person ever suggest another person I could talk to about something?
Is my sense of being understood tied to staying close, agreeing, or avoiding certain people?
If I imagined this person being wrong about my friends, could I say so out loud to them?
less_concerning_if: They are glad when you have other sources of comfort and make room for them.
Compliments about understanding you do not come with criticism of anyone else.
You can disagree with their reading of you and the conversation stays friendly.
more_concerning_if: Specific people in your life are repeatedly described as harmful, with no real examples.
Contact with those people has dropped and you feel unable to bring it back up.
They become distressed or angry when you confide in anyone else.
pattern_over_time_signs: The circle of people you talk to about important things gets smaller month by month.
Your friends remark that they hardly see you, or that you have started echoing the other person's opinions of them.
You begin to censor what you say to others to avoid a cold response at home.
Moments of feeling understood become less frequent, while the claim of understanding gets louder.
codex_completed.repair_check: Watch whether they begin to treat your other relationships as normal and good, such as asking about your friends, supporting plans with them, and withdrawing earlier digs. An apology that leaves you still expected to bring everything to them has not changed the shape.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Think about how your last plan with someone else was received. When you set the limit 'I will keep seeing my friends', a respectful answer is simply to let it stand. Sighs, a sudden illness, or a list of that friend's faults are the response worth noticing.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Feeling deeply understood is one of the most rewarding things in a relationship, so a person may begin to organize their life around the source of it. If the same source also casts other people as lesser, outside views can start to look unreliable, and the person has fewer places to test whether the claim is true. Over time that can narrow where support is sought.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A pleasant early relief at being known is often followed, in accounts of this pattern, by a quiet loneliness as old friendships thin out. Explaining the relationship to anyone can feel impossible, because each concern seems to confirm that outsiders do not understand. Grief can arrive later, on seeing how much of a life had gone quiet.

response_options.soft_clarification: Say what you notice, once, kindly: 'I like that you get me. I also need my friends, and it hurts when you talk about them as if they don't count.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep your plans and your confidences open: 'I'm going to keep talking to my sister about this. You're important to me, and so is she.'
response_options.disengagement: Quietly rebuild contact with one person you have drifted from, even a short call, and notice how the other person reacts to that.
response_options.support_seeking: Pick a friend or relative you have missed and tell them honestly that you have been less in touch than you wanted, and that you would like to change that.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a boss or mentor insists they alone appreciate you, keep up your relationships with peers and other mentors, and ask a trusted colleague what they think of your work.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "It means a lot that you understand me. I'm still going to spend time with my friends and tell them what's going on in my life, and I'd like that to be okay with you."
codex_completed.safety_note: Narrowing the people you confide in can be an early part of coercive control, especially when it comes with checking your phone, deciding who you see, or anger when you make plans. Keep at least one outside contact who knows your real situation, and if you are afraid of the reaction, call a domestic violence hotline to talk through options privately.
misuse_warning: Treating any deeply close partner or friend as isolating can punish ordinary intimacy. The question is whether others are being demoted and your access to them reduced, not how close the bond is.
Telling a friend that their partner is doing this, with only a few comments to go on, may make the friend defensive and cut the very connection that helps.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: The Exception Script tells you that you, unlike everyone around you, are special, which works through flattering comparison to your peers. Exclusive Meaning is about the other person being the sole one who understands you. Love Bombing is the early flood of attention, while exclusive meaning can continue long after the early weeks and grows through small put-downs of the rest of your world.
