codex_completed.name: Hoovering
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Reaching out to draw someone back into a relationship after they have pulled away or ended it, often with promises that things will change.
codex_completed.short_definition: Reaching out to draw someone back into a relationship after they have pulled away or ended it, often with promises that things will change.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Hoovering, named for the vacuum cleaner, is the pull-back that comes after distance or a breakup: messages, apologies, gifts, sudden crises or declarations of change, sent to restart contact. People do sincerely change and ask for another chance, so a single approach means little. It becomes a pattern when the contact returns after each separation, uses whatever has worked before, and ends up with the old dynamics once you are back.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: After you pull away or break up, the other person reaches out with promises, apologies or emergencies that draw you back, and the old pattern restarts.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Each return restarts hope and resets the cycle. You may go back repeatedly, losing time and confidence, and may feel guilty or foolish when it falls apart again.
what_it_is: Contact that arrives after distance or a break, often on or around moments when you have started to settle.
Promises, apologies or declarations of change aimed at the relationship resuming, not at the earlier problem.
Can take many shapes: nostalgic messages, a sudden need for help, a mutual friend carrying a note, a gift, or a claim of illness.
Often repeated across several separations, with the same kinds of approach each time.
Seen mainly in romantic breakups, but also in friendships, family estrangements and former work or group ties.
what_it_sounds_like: I've been in therapy. I'm a different person now. Just let me show you.
I found your old jacket, and the memories came flooding back.
I can't eat or sleep without you. I don't know what I'll do.
Everyone says we belong together. Even my mother asked about you.
I know I messed up. One coffee, that's all I'm asking.
It's your birthday, and I wanted to be the first to say it. Can we talk?
I have something of yours and need to return it. Are you home?
what_it_is_not: A person who truly changed over many months, did the work, and asks once, respectfully, for a chance, then accepts your answer.
Contact required to sort out kids, shared property, a lease or money after a split.
A kind check-in from an ex who marks a loss or a birthday and leaves the response to you.
Reconciliation that both people choose with open eyes and clear terms.
A single message sent in a lonely hour that the person regrets and does not repeat.
this_may_be_it_when: The messages begin soon after you stopped replying, as if timed to the distance.
A no is followed by a new approach through a different route: another number, a friend, a gift to your work.
The promise is about feelings and future, with few concrete steps you can check.
After you return, the earlier problems come back and the promise is no longer mentioned.
The approaches switch between affection, guilt and anger depending on which gets a reply.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They back off when you say you do not want contact.
Evidence of change, such as treatment, steady work on the problem, or months of consistent behavior, comes before any request.
The reason for contact is practical and specific, and ends once handled.
They admit what went wrong in plain terms and do not ask you to forget it.
You decide freely whether and when to respond, and nothing is lost if you do not.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People miss each other after a breakup and may reach out in a weak moment, without calculation.
Some couples do part, reflect, and come back stronger after both put in real work.
Grief and loneliness can produce contact that looks like a pull-back and is simply sadness.
common_false_positives: A former partner who texts once on an anniversary and accepts silence as the reply.
A co-parent contacting you repeatedly about pick-up times.
A friend who drifted away, apologizes sincerely for neglecting you, and lets you choose how much to reconnect.
discernment_questions: Has anything changed that I can see and check, or only what I am told?
How did they respond the last time I said I needed space?
Does the contact come when I seem to be moving on?
Are the same reasons I left still present in how they talk to me now?
What would I decide if I had never been promised anything?
less_concerning_if: They stop when asked and do not send others in their place.
Any change they describe is already visible in their actions over a long time.
The reason for contact is practical and finishes when the task does.
more_concerning_if: The approaches continue after a clear no, or escalate to showing up at your home or workplace.
They rely on your guilt, pity or fear, such as threats of self-harm, to get a reply.
Friends, family or coworkers are being used to pass messages or pressure you.
pattern_over_time_signs: You have separated and reunited several times, each time with a fresh promise.
Each return follows a near-identical script, down to the opening line.
The good stretch after each reunion gets shorter.
You can predict, almost to the week, when the next message will arrive.
codex_completed.repair_check: Real change here is slow and shows up before the request, not after it: months of different behavior, specific accountability for what happened, and no pressure about your timing. A big emotional message with a deadline is the pull itself, not evidence of repair.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: A no is the test. Contact that stops when you say you want none is a very different thing from contact that changes channel, tone or messenger. Pay attention to what follows the first clear 'please do not contact me'.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Hope for a better version of someone you care about is powerful, and a sincere-sounding apology can set off relief and attachment even when little has changed. Contact that arrives unpredictably, mixing warmth with distress, can keep attention fixed on the relationship and make a calm decision harder to hold.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A stomach-drop each time a certain name appears on the screen is a common account, along with doubt about whether leaving was right and tiredness from deciding again and again. Going back can bring a sense of having been weak or foolish. After finally not answering, some report a slow calm mixed with grief.

response_options.soft_clarification: State your decision briefly and leave it there: 'I've thought about it and I'm not getting back together. Please don't contact me about this again.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Block or mute the channels they use, and tell mutual friends you will not be relaying messages in either direction.
response_options.disengagement: Do not reply to the emotional content of a message, and do not set a reply time in your head. Silence can be your whole answer.
response_options.support_seeking: Keep a short log of dates and messages and share it with someone who knows the history, so you do not have to re-argue your decision alone each time.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If an ex or former colleague keeps contacting you at work, tell your manager or HR, give them copies of the messages, and ask that the contact be handled through them.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I read your message. My answer is no, and it won't change with more messages. If there's something practical we need to settle, email me about that only."
codex_completed.safety_note: Repeated unwanted contact after a breakup can slide into stalking, and threats, showing up where you live or work, or messages that mention hurting themselves or you are all danger signals. Save every message, tell someone you trust, and contact a domestic violence advocate or the police if you feel unsafe.
misuse_warning: A former partner who truly has changed and writes once is not hoovering, and branding every attempt at contact that way can shut out honest repair or necessary co-parenting talks.
Labeling a person this way based on one message treats a sad moment as a strategy, which the pattern cannot show.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Future Faking keeps you waiting inside a relationship that is still going, using promises about what is coming, whereas hoovering reaches for you after you have left or pulled away. Love Bombing floods a new connection with praise. Conditional Love is affection offered only for compliance within the relationship, with no break required.

codex_completed.name: Future Faking
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Making vivid promises about a better future together that keep you invested in the present, while the promised things never seem to arrive.
codex_completed.short_definition: Making vivid promises about a better future together that keep you invested in the present, while the promised things never seem to arrive.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Future faking uses promised milestones, such as marriage, a home, a trip, a changed habit or a finished project, to keep a person patient with how things are now. Real plans do slip, and honest people miss dates. Concern grows when the promises are large and detailed, the dates keep moving, nothing small gets done meanwhile, and your waiting is asked to stand in for the thing itself.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone describes a wonderful future with you in detail, so you keep waiting and putting up with the present, but the promises keep sliding away.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Waiting on a promise can use up years, savings or other options. When the future never comes, you may also doubt your own judgment for having believed it, which makes the next decision harder.
what_it_is: Specific, appealing promises about a future that depends on you staying: a wedding, children, a move, a job, a change in the other person.
A pattern where the date keeps shifting, and each delay arrives with a fresh reason and a fresh promise.
Stands in for present action: talk about the house rather than saving for it, talk about quitting drinking rather than seeking help.
Most convincing when it touches the thing you most want.
Appears in romance, but also in jobs ('a promotion is coming'), friendships and business ventures.
what_it_sounds_like: Once the divorce is final, we'll get married. I promise it won't be long.
We'll buy the house by next spring. I've already picked out the street.
After this project, I'll have time for us. Just hang in there.
I'm going to quit drinking after the holidays. This time I mean it.
Give it a year and you'll see. I'm going to make it all up to you.
I'll introduce you to my family once things calm down.
We'll have the baby when the money situation is sorted.
what_it_is_not: A sincere plan delayed by a layoff, illness or family emergency, where the person says so honestly and adjusts the plan with you.
A hopeful dream shared in conversation that was never offered as a promise or a reason for you to wait.
A couple jointly deciding to put off a goal until they can afford it, with both agreeing on the timeline.
A person who keeps small promises each week and also speaks about larger hopes for the years ahead.
A promise that does come true, even later than first hoped.
this_may_be_it_when: The promised date has moved more than once, each time with a new explanation.
There are no visible steps toward the promise, only talk about it.
The promise comes up most when you voice doubt, complain or talk about leaving.
You are being asked to give up something real now, such as time, money or an opportunity, on the strength of it.
Small commitments today, like returning a call or showing up on time, are also not kept.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You can see real progress, like savings accounts opened, applications filed, or treatment attended.
They tell you plainly when a plan has slipped and what that means for you.
You are not asked to put anything on hold while waiting.
They are open to you deciding not to wait and do not use the promise to discourage this.
Outside events that anyone could verify explain the delay.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Optimistic people underestimate how long things take and promise in good faith.
Hard circumstances, such as visa waits, court dates, illness or job loss, can push back real plans.
People sometimes say big, warm things in the moment out of affection, without having planned the details.
common_false_positives: A partner who says they want to marry you, saves for the ring, and sets a date together with you.
A manager who says a promotion depends on budget approval, and tells you when the decision is made.
A friend who says 'we should travel someday' and does not mean it as a pledge.
discernment_questions: What have they actually done toward this promise in the past six months?
What am I being asked to give up or wait for while it happens?
How many times has the date changed?
Do they keep small promises, like showing up when they said they would?
If nothing ever changed from today, would I still want to be here?
less_concerning_if: The delay has a real, checkable cause and you were told promptly.
Concrete steps are happening in view, alongside the talk.
You are free to make your own plans without being talked out of them.
more_concerning_if: You have made major life decisions, like leaving a job or lending money, based on the promise.
Questions about the timeline are met with irritation, hurt or the suggestion that you do not trust them.
The promise grows bigger exactly when you are close to leaving.
pattern_over_time_signs: You can list several promised milestones, none of which has arrived.
The explanations vary but the outcome is the same.
You stop asking about the date because the answer is always 'soon'.
Your own plans, savings or opportunities have been shelved to leave room for theirs.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair means the promise becomes smaller, dated and checkable: one concrete step done this month, and an honest account of what was not done before. A fresh, bigger vision of the future given after you complain is more of the same.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask for a specific step and a date, then watch what comes next. A person may be unable to deliver, yet still work out a first step with you. A reply made entirely of warm words about how much you matter, with the step left out, is a different response.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A vivid, hoped-for future can feel almost real, and the more of it has been imagined and told to others, the harder it is to stop investing. Each new promise can reset the wait. The more time or money already spent, the harder it gets to stop and count the cost.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe years of 'almost', holding their breath for a date, and anger at themselves when it passes. Some talk about having postponed their own education, children, or moves for someone else's timetable. Others say the hardest part was grieving a future that existed only in conversation.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for specifics, kindly: 'I like that picture. What is the first step, and when do you think it can happen?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Tie your own decisions to what has already happened: 'I'm not going to leave my job or sign anything until the plan is in motion.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop adjusting your life around the promise. Put your own plans and savings back on your own calendar.
response_options.support_seeking: Write down the promises with dates and show them to someone you trust, asking what they notice when they see the list as a whole.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a promotion or raise keeps being deferred, ask for the terms in an email, and keep that email. Check what the written policy or contract says.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I believe you want that future. I need to see the first step before I change anything in my own plans. Can we agree on one thing you'll do this month?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Future faking is usually a slow drain rather than a danger. It becomes a serious concern when the promise is tied to marriage for immigration status, a loan, a shared lease, or signing over money or property. In those cases, talk to a legal aid service or financial counselor before you commit anything in writing.
misuse_warning: Delayed plans are common, so calling every unmet promise 'future faking' treats a hard year as a con. The label needs a record of shifting dates and missing steps.
Using it to guess that someone never meant a promise claims knowledge of their mind that nobody outside it has.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Hoovering pulls you back after you have left, using promises, whereas future faking keeps you in a relationship that is still going. Love Bombing floods the present with affection and praise; future faking mostly talks about a later time. Conditional Love ties affection to obedience, and future faking ties your patience to a payoff that never comes.

codex_completed.name: Negging
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Slipping in a subtle insult, wrapped as a compliment or a joke, so that you feel a little smaller and a little more eager for approval.
codex_completed.short_definition: Slipping in a subtle insult, wrapped as a compliment or a joke, so that you feel a little smaller and a little more eager for approval.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A neg is a remark that looks like praise but carries a dig: a compliment with a catch, surprise that you did well, a joke about a feature you are sensitive about. Awkward people and teasing friends say clumsy things too, so one comment tells you little. Repetition is what changes things: digs that come regularly, land on insecure spots, are followed by warmth, and leave you working harder for a better one.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone mixes small put-downs into their compliments, so you end up feeling a bit worse about yourself and a bit more eager to win their approval.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Small digs add up. Over weeks you may begin to trust the other person's opinion of you above your own, and work hard for compliments that always come with a sting.
what_it_is: A remark that praises and cuts in the same sentence, often with a 'for you' or 'considering' attached.
Aimed at something you are already unsure of, such as looks, intelligence, class, age or career.
Delivered in a light, joking or even affectionate tone, which makes objecting feel petty.
Often followed by real warmth, so that approval feels precious and a bit unpredictable.
Common in dating and flirting, but also seen at work, in families and among friends.
what_it_sounds_like: You're pretty smart for someone who didn't go to college.
That dress is bold. Most people couldn't pull it off, but you do you.
I'm surprised you finished that so fast. Good for you!
You'd be gorgeous if you smiled more. Seriously, it's a shame.
Wow, you actually cooked this? Not bad!
I like that you don't care what people think of how you look.
Not many guys with your job would be this thoughtful.
what_it_is_not: Mutual, playful teasing between people who both enjoy it and would both stop if one asked.
An awkward compliment from someone who is clumsy with words and winces when you point it out.
Honest, kind feedback about a mistake, aimed at the work and offered to help.
A cultural or family style of ribbing that everyone in the group takes in fun.
A compliment that surprised you because it was higher than you expected from yourself, not because of a dig.
this_may_be_it_when: The sting always lands on a tender spot you have mentioned or shown.
The compliment only works if you accept a small insult with it.
When you react, you are told you are too sensitive or cannot take a joke.
You notice a pull to prove them wrong, followed by relief when they approve.
The comments are mostly made in front of others, or when you were doing well.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They stop and apologize when you say a comment stung.
They tease themselves in the same way.
Their praise, when it comes, has no tag line.
The same remark would have been fine from a friend of equal standing and you find it funny too.
It happened once and has not come up again.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people are bad at giving compliments and tack on qualifiers out of nerves.
Banter between close friends often includes teasing that is meant and received as affection.
Surprise at your success can be a plain expression of admiration, clumsily put.
common_false_positives: A sibling who has roasted you since childhood and cheers loudest at your wedding.
A colleague whose blunt phrasing, such as 'that's better than I expected', is how they praise everyone.
A date who jokes about their own flaws and then jokes about yours, lightly, while both of you laugh.
discernment_questions: After this person compliments me, do I feel better or slightly worse?
If a friend told me the same words, would I hear a compliment?
Do the digs land on things I have said I am sensitive about?
Do I find myself working harder to hear something kind from them?
When I say it hurt, is it taken seriously?
less_concerning_if: The comment came once, and they changed course when told.
The teasing flows both ways and is about a variety of subjects.
You leave most conversations feeling at least as good about yourself as when you arrived.
more_concerning_if: The remarks come steadily and cluster around your most insecure points.
Objecting is treated as proof that you are fragile.
Your confidence and your wish for their approval have both risen noticeably since you met.
pattern_over_time_signs: You start double-checking your outfit, answers or work before you see them.
You tell a story of their approval as a prize you won last week.
Friends comment that you seem more nervous or self-critical lately.
You laugh at jokes about yourself that you would not have accepted a year ago.
codex_completed.repair_check: The comments stop landing on the same spots, plain compliments arrive that need no footnote, and they take it seriously when you say a remark hurt. Switching to heavier praise for a while after you object is not the same as changing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice the next remark once you have called a comment a dig. If it is quieter, kinder and not repeated, the message got through. If you hear 'I was only joking' followed by a similar line, the boundary was heard and set aside.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Mixed messages, a lift and a drop in the same sentence, hold attention longer than plain praise or plain criticism. A slightly unsure person may then work to secure approval that has been made to seem scarce. Because the sting is phrased as a joke, objecting can look like the bigger offense.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe replaying a comment for days, wondering whether they were being silly to mind, and slowly starting to dress, speak or work for one person's reaction. Some say they became quieter around that person, or began checking themselves in mirrors. Others recall laughing along while feeling a small drop in their stomach.

response_options.soft_clarification: Reflect the comment back lightly: 'Did you mean that as a compliment? It sounded like there was a catch.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Draw a line without raising your voice: 'I don't like jokes about my appearance. Please skip those.'
response_options.disengagement: Respond to a backhanded line with a flat 'okay' and a new topic, and spend less time in settings where it is a regular feature.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend the exact words used and ask how they sound. A second reader often hears the sting you have been explaining away.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a colleague or boss makes digs in meetings, note dates and words, respond to the work content only, and bring repeated remarks to HR or a manager you trust.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "When you say I'm smart for someone like me, it doesn't sound like a compliment to me. If you want to compliment me, just say the nice part."
codex_completed.safety_note: Negging by itself is a corrosive habit rather than a danger. It would change if the remarks escalate to threats, to comments about your body that become touching you without consent, or to attempts to make you dependent on someone with power over your job or housing. In that case, document what was said and speak to HR, a union rep or a trusted advocate.
misuse_warning: Ordinary teasing and clumsy compliments are common, and calling each one a neg can end friendly banter or make an awkward person seem sinister.
The word is also a name from pickup-artist culture, so using it about someone you know as a charge of scheming goes beyond what the words alone can show.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Conditional Love holds back warmth until you comply, while negging delivers digs and warmth at the same time. Exclusive Meaning tells you only they understand you, a message of closeness; negging lowers your standing. The Exception Script flatters by setting you above others, while negging lowers you in the same breath as it praises you.

Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Silent Treatment
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Withholding all communication, warmth or answers from someone, with no stated end, until they apologize or give way to what the other person wants.
codex_completed.short_definition: Withholding all communication, warmth or answers from someone, with no stated end, until they apologize or give way to what the other person wants.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: The silent treatment is a stretch of sustained non-response: no answers, no eye contact, messages left unread, a person in the room treated as absent. Stonewalling and withholding are other names for this one behavior, not separate tactics. It can also reach beyond talk to affection, plans, money or practical information. Everyone goes quiet sometimes. What changes the meaning is a silence with no end date, aimed at one person, that lifts only when that person apologizes or complies.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone stops talking to you, or takes away warmth and information, with no end in sight, until you apologize or give in. The quiet itself is the pressure.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Being frozen out hurts in a way the body treats as real pain. The open-ended wait can leave you desperate to end it at any cost. Ordinary things like a reply or basic warmth turn into rewards, and the issue itself is never resolved.
what_it_is: A sustained stop to talking, replying or acknowledging someone, with no stated end.
Often shows up as ignored texts, one-word answers, leaving the room, or speaking to everyone else but you.
Can reach past talk to affection, plans, shared-account details or household information, held back until you give way.
Ends when the other person apologizes, gives in, or performs some act of making up, usually without the original issue being discussed.
Appears in couples, families, friendships and workplaces, and can last hours, days or weeks.
what_it_sounds_like: Nothing. No reply for two days after you asked a question.
I'm not talking to you until you admit what you did.
A flat 'fine' and a walk out of the room, then no words for the evening.
Don't speak to me. You know what you did.
Messages read, with no answer, while they chat happily with others.
Talking to the dog and the kids but never to you.
No reply to texts for two days after you said no to something, then a cheerful message once you changed your mind.
A partner who stops sharing the plan for the week, or the state of the shared accounts, after you disagreed.
what_it_is_not: Saying 'I'm too angry to talk about this right now. Can we pick it up after dinner?', which has a reason and a return time.
A person who goes quiet from shutting down, depression or overwhelm, and who is silent with everyone and not just you.
A break agreed on by both people during a heated argument, with a time to return.
Not sharing information because it is private, such as a friend's confidence or a medical matter that is theirs to keep.
Quiet from someone whose communication style is slow or private, and who has always been that way.
A cultural or family style of cooling off that everyone practices and that is not aimed at one person.
this_may_be_it_when: The silence starts right after you disagree or set a limit, and never has a stated end.
They speak normally to everyone else in the room.
It ends only after you apologize, bring a peace offering, or drop the issue.
You are expected to work out what you did wrong without being told.
Practical information, money or access is held back along with warmth.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They said they needed time and gave a time when they would return, and did.
The quiet is not specific to you and shows up in all their relationships.
They come back to talk the issue through, and do not require an apology first.
You feel free to approach them and they answer, even if briefly.
They are unwell, grieving or exhausted, and the quiet is clearly about that.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people need quiet to settle down after conflict, and may not have the words yet.
Some people shut down when flooded with emotion and cannot talk, whatever their wish.
Some people were raised in homes where silence was how conflict was handled, and repeat it without noticing.
Phones die, work gets busy, and a slow reply is often just a slow reply.
common_false_positives: A partner who says 'I need an hour' and then returns to talk.
A teenager who gives short answers for a week while stressed about school, and does so with everyone.
A colleague who does not share early drafts because that is how they work with everyone.
discernment_questions: Was a reason or a return time given, or did it simply start?
Does the silence lift only when I apologize or give in?
Do they speak freely to others during the same period?
Once talk resumes, do we ever address what the silence was about?
Is practical information or money held back, or only warmth?
Do I find myself apologizing for things I do not believe I did wrong, just to end it?
less_concerning_if: The quiet is brief, announced and followed by a real conversation.
It is not aimed at you alone and does not need your apology to end.
You can still get what you need, such as money, information and a basic reply, while they cool off.
more_concerning_if: It lasts days or weeks and cuts off practical things, like telling you about money, children or housing.
They control access to money, transport, documents or your children as part of the withdrawal.
It comes with other signs of control, like checking where you are or anger when you try to reach them.
pattern_over_time_signs: You can predict that a disagreement about a certain subject will end in days of silence.
You avoid raising issues, and hold back requests and opinions, because of what will follow.
You feel a surge of relief and gratitude when they speak to you again, and you are the one who always breaks the silence first.
The stretches get longer, or happen with smaller triggers than before.
codex_completed.repair_check: Afterward they talk with you about the silence itself, say what they needed, and next time give a reason and a time to return. Warmth that simply resumes the moment you apologize, with the issue untouched, leaves the pattern as it was.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Over several rounds, one question tells you more than any single reply. When you have said you will talk but do not want to be ignored for days, does the next fight end with a spoken pause and a return, or with another stretch of nothing?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Being ignored by someone you depend on can set off a strong threat response, and the urge to end that discomfort quickly can override your own view. Without information about why or for how long, the mind may fill in the worst, and apologizing can start to feel like the only exit. Because nothing openly harmful was said, you may also doubt your own distress.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A knot in the stomach, constant phone checking, rehearsed apologies and a feeling of being invisible come up often in accounts of being frozen out. Some start to doubt whether they did something terrible, and some say they came to dread the quiet more than an open argument. Many describe walking on eggshells and agreeing to things to stop the next freeze.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the topic, not the warmth: 'You've gone quiet since Saturday. Can you tell me what's on your mind, or when you'll be ready to talk?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Separate pausing from punishing: 'I'm fine with space. I'm not fine with being ignored until I give in. Please tell me when we can talk.'
response_options.disengagement: Do not chase, plead or send a stream of messages. Keep your routines, send one calm message, and answer normally when contact resumes.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe a recent silence to a friend or counselor, including what ended it. Hearing it out loud helps check whether it lasted until you gave way.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager or co-worker holds back information you need to do your job, ask for it in writing and copy the request to someone senior, so a record exists.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "If you're upset, I'll listen and I do want to hear it. Going quiet until I give in doesn't help us fix anything, though. If you need time, tell me roughly how long, and we can pick it up then."
codex_completed.safety_note: Silence alone is painful pressure, not a physical threat. It matters more when you depend on the person for housing, money or care and the freeze cuts off practical information, or when it alternates with intimidation. Keep copies of your identity papers and account details somewhere private, and speak to a domestic abuse advocate or legal aid about your options.
misuse_warning: Needing space is healthy and many people go quiet from overwhelm, so labeling any pause as the silent treatment can punish someone for self-regulating, especially someone with a shutdown response.
Demanding an immediate response and then calling its absence abuse can become a form of pressure of its own.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Emotional Blackmail spells out what you will lose if you do not comply; the silent treatment lets the quiet imply it. Hoovering is contact that returns after a break, with promises of change, while the silent treatment is contact withdrawn inside a relationship that continues. Negging keeps up contact and lowers your confidence through digs, whereas here the contact itself is the thing taken away.

Phrase matching can flag wording, but it cannot know intent, tone, history, context, or whether the claim is even true — an innocent reading is always attached to every match. Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Isolation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Steadily cutting a person off from friends, family and other outside support until one relationship is the only one left.
codex_completed.short_definition: Steadily cutting a person off from friends, family and other outside support until one relationship is the only one left.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Isolation is a gradual shrinking of someone's world. Friends are described as a bad influence, visits to family end in arguments, and plans with other people are met with sulking, interrogation or a sudden crisis. Sometimes the squeeze is practical: no car, no phone credit, no free evening. One complaint about one friend is ordinary. What tips it over is a list of people you still see that keeps getting shorter, with each loss following a comment or a scene. Outside people are often the first to notice that something has changed in you.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Over time, the people who used to support you drop out of your life, and you end up with only one person left to turn to.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: With fewer people around, nobody is left to say 'that doesn't sound right' or to help when things go badly. A small circle can make a hard situation feel like the only one available, and it makes asking for help much harder.
what_it_is: Criticism of nearly every friend or relative, each one failing some test, rather than a worry about one named person.
Making contact costly: a cold silence, an interrogation or an argument after every outing, until staying home feels easier.
Practical blocks, such as control of the car keys, the phone plan or the weekend schedule, that make visits hard to arrange.
Discouraging the new connections that could replace old ones: a class, a team, a coworker who wants to be friends.
Often worded as closeness or loyalty ('we don't need anyone else'), which makes it hard to object to without sounding cold.
what_it_sounds_like: Your sister only calls when she wants something. I don't know why you bother.
Fine, go. I'll just sit here on my own again.
Do you really need to see them again this weekend?
Nobody understands us the way we understand each other.
Why would you tell Dana about our argument? That stays between us.
Every time you come back from your mom's you're in a mood with me.
I just want you to myself. Is that so terrible?
what_it_is_not: A single worry about one friend who really is a bad fit, such as someone who pushes you to drink, raised once and then left alone.
A new baby, a long commute, illness or a house move, any of which can shrink a social life with nobody pushing.
A couple choosing a quiet season mostly together, both content, with friends still welcome.
A partner saying 'I miss you when you're out so much' as a feeling, with no attempt to stop you going.
A person who has always had a small circle and likes it that way.
A decision you made yourself to step back from relatives who hurt you.
this_may_be_it_when: Friendships fade soon after a run of remarks about them, not on their own slow schedule.
Making plans with someone else brings questioning, a cold silence or a crisis that appears just as you are about to go.
You have started lying about where you have been, just to avoid the fallout.
The criticism covers many people in turn, and the reasons change from one person to the next.
Contact is limited by practical means, such as holding the keys, the phone or the money.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You see friends freely and get asked about them with real interest.
The worry names one person and one behavior, and drops once you have answered it.
The drift started with something outside the relationship, such as a move or a new shift pattern.
You are the one who chose to pull back, and you can explain why.
Your friends and family are invited in and included, not merely tolerated.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: In the first year of a relationship, many couples see their friends less, and both people drift a little.
Someone with few friends of their own may feel left out and say so clumsily.
Tension with your family may have existed before this relationship, and your partner may simply be echoing it.
common_false_positives: A partner who dislikes one friend's drinking and tells you once.
A parent limiting a young teenager's time with a particular group.
Two people who agree together to cut back on socializing during a stressful stretch, and who plan to return to it.
discernment_questions: Who did you see regularly a year ago that you rarely see now, and what happened in between?
When you mention plans with other people, do you feel relaxed or braced?
Have you stopped talking about certain friends to avoid a reaction?
Is there anyone outside this relationship who could ask you how things are, in private?
If you made a new friend tomorrow, how do you think it would be received?
less_concerning_if: You can still arrange time with other people without a negotiation.
The shrinking of your social life has a plain external cause that you both acknowledge.
Your friends still feel free to contact you, and you feel free to answer.
more_concerning_if: You have no one left, or only one person, who knows how things really are at home.
Phone, car, money or paperwork are held in a way that makes seeing others impractical.
You are afraid of what will happen if someone from outside contacts you.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your calendar gets emptier, one canceled plan at a time, with an argument or a mood behind most of them.
Old friends stop inviting you because you have declined so often, and you feel too embarrassed to reach back.
You find yourself reporting on your day in advance so there will be no row afterwards.
People who knew you before comment that they have not seen you in months.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair here shows up in your diary. You can see a friend without a debrief afterwards, your phone and car are yours again, and your people are welcome in the house. An apology that leaves the old rules in place, or a warm week followed by the same questions, has repaired nothing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Spend an evening with a friend and look at the next day. Is it ordinary, or is there a cold shoulder or a cross-examination waiting? A boundary about your friendships is being respected when keeping it stops costing you something.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Close friends and family are where most people check their sense of what is normal. When those voices fall away, one person's view can become the main reference point, and rules that would once have raised eyebrows can start to seem reasonable. Depending on one person for company, money or transport can make each skipped outing feel easier than the argument that follows.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe loneliness, shame about having let friends slip, and embarrassment about getting back in touch. Some say they were not sure when it began, only that one day nobody was left to call. Some describe a sense of being unable to judge what is normal in their own home. Many say a simple reply from an old friend meant a great deal.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name the feeling and make a small, specific request: 'I really miss my friends. Could we find a way for me to see them once a week?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep one standing commitment, such as a regular call with a sibling, and treat it as ordinary, without defending it each time.
response_options.disengagement: Keep contact alive in small, quiet ways, such as a message to a friend or a chat with a neighbor, without announcing it or arguing about it.
response_options.support_seeking: Pick one person outside the relationship, such as a friend, a doctor or a coworker, and tell them more than you usually would. Ask them to check in with you.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If work is your remaining outside contact, keep it: go to the lunch, keep the colleague friendships, and consider telling HR or a counselor if getting to work is being obstructed.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I miss my friends. Can we work out a little time with them each week that suits both of us?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Watch for signs that isolation is turning into control: your phone, keys or papers are taken, you are punished for going out, or you feel afraid of the reaction when you come home. Keep at least one outside contact alive, such as a doctor, a coworker or a relative, and talk to a domestic abuse advocate about planning, using a device the other person cannot see.
misuse_warning: Calling every sulk about weekend plans 'isolation' turns an ordinary disagreement about time into an accusation. The word fits a widening pattern, not one grumpy evening.
Telling a worried friend or relative that they are 'isolating' you when they have simply raised a concern can push away people who care about you.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Behavior Control sets rules about what you wear, where you go and what you do, while isolation targets who is in your life. Monitoring & Surveillance checks up on you, and a person can be monitored while still having friends. Punishment of Boundaries answers one particular limit you set with a penalty; isolation is the slower loss of people over many months, with no single refusal behind it.

codex_completed.name: Monitoring & Surveillance
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Demanding constant access to a person's phone, messages and movements, so that every part of their day has to be explained.
codex_completed.short_definition: Demanding constant access to a person's phone, messages and movements, so that every part of their day has to be explained.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: These two names describe one family of behaviors on a scale. Monitoring is the open end: asking for a running account, reading your messages, checking when you were last online. Surveillance is the watching end, which can also happen without you being told. In both, the person lives under inspection rather than trust. A worried question after a scare is ordinary. It becomes a concern when checking turns routine, grows after each answer, and no answer ever settles it.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone expects to see your phone, your messages and your whereabouts on demand, and nothing you show them ever makes the checking stop.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Living under audit changes how you behave, even when you have done nothing wrong. You may start editing what you say, deleting harmless messages, or avoiding people, simply to avoid the next round of questions.
what_it_is: Open demands: unlocking your phone on request, handing over passwords, or reading your messages as a condition of calm.
Running accounts of your time, with questions about gaps, delays and who else was there.
Watching that you may not know about, such as reading your accounts or devices behind your back, which you may only find out about by accident.
A cycle in which each check produces a new question, so proof never settles anything.
Often described as honesty or closeness, which makes saying no feel like confessing to something.
what_it_sounds_like: Who was that? Let me see the message.
You were online at two in the morning. Who were you talking to?
Send me a picture right now of where you are.
Why did it take you forty minutes to answer?
Hand me your phone. If there's nothing there, it won't be a problem.
Couples don't keep secrets. Give me your passwords.
I only looked because you've been acting strange.
what_it_is_not: Two adults who have both chosen to share a calendar or a passcode for practical reasons, and either of whom can stop.
A parent checking a young child's devices in a way that suits the child's age.
Workplace security rules that apply to everyone and are written down.
A one-off request for a text when you arrive home safely, after a frightening evening.
Open questions after a real breach of trust, asked for a limited time with an agreed end, as part of deciding together whether to stay.
this_may_be_it_when: Declining to hand something over leads to accusation, anger or days of silence.
The checking started small and has widened to more apps, more hours and more people.
You have noticed signs that your accounts or devices were opened without your say-so.
Showing the evidence once does not end the question; it only prompts the next one.
You have started deleting harmless messages or avoiding contacts to stay out of arguments.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Both of you share things openly, and either can say no without a penalty.
The request was a single one, tied to a specific scare, and has not come back.
The access is mutual: you can look at theirs as freely as they look at yours.
The checking has an agreed end date and a stated reason, and it ends.
The person accepts your answer and moves on once you have given it.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Anxiety, past betrayal or a bad experience in an earlier relationship can make a person ask for reassurance more than they would like.
Some couples genuinely enjoy sharing everything, and it works because either may stop.
A shared device or family account means some messages are naturally visible to both of you.
common_false_positives: A friend asking you to text when you get home after a late night.
A partner who admits to feeling insecure and asks to talk about it rather than check.
Parents setting limits and reviewing a primary-school child's tablet.
discernment_questions: If you said no to a request to see your phone, what would the next day look like?
Does anything you show ever end the questions, or does it produce more?
Is the access mutual, or does only one of you get checked?
Have you changed who you talk to, or what you say, because you expect to be read?
Do you suspect your accounts or devices are being watched without your knowledge?
less_concerning_if: The checking is open, mutual and can be stopped by either person.
Worry is spoken about as a feeling, and reassurance seems to help.
Declining a request leads to a conversation, not a punishment.
more_concerning_if: The other person seems to know things you have only said in private.
Checking grows after every answer, whatever you show.
A slow reply or a locked phone brings anger that leaves you afraid.
pattern_over_time_signs: You begin to keep your phone within reach and answer fast, to avoid a scene.
You rehearse your explanations for ordinary gaps in the day before they are asked.
Your own privacy stops feeling like something you are allowed.
Passwords you gave once for a practical reason become a permanent entitlement.
codex_completed.repair_check: When this changes, the checking itself stops, or becomes equal. You keep your passcode, your messages are yours, and the worry gets spoken as worry. If they apologize but keep one 'just in case' check, or swap open demands for quieter looking, the audit is still running.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice what a refusal costs you. If a plain 'I'd rather keep my messages private' leads to a conversation about the worry underneath, that is one thing. If it leads to a sulk, a fight or a hunt for evidence, the privacy was never really yours to grant.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Being checked can teach a person to see their own life through the other person's eyes, asking 'how will this look?' before they act. Giving in once to calm a moment can make the next request seem small, and because the proof never satisfies, the demands can grow. Self-censoring can also make a person start to feel guilty even when they have done nothing.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe constant alertness about their phone, a sense of being guilty without having done anything, and shrinking private thoughts. Some say they stopped writing to friends, or deleted harmless things. Some feel exhausted from explaining, and some doubt whether wanting privacy is itself a sign they are hiding something.

response_options.soft_clarification: Say what you notice and ask about the worry underneath: 'It sounds like you're anxious when you can't reach me. What would help with that, besides reading my messages?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep your passcode to yourself where you judge it safe, and offer something else, like telling them about your evening yourself. Think first about how they have reacted before.
response_options.disengagement: Quietly keep sensitive things off a device you believe is being watched, and use a different phone or computer for private matters, without announcing it.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe the specifics to a domestic abuse advocate or a counselor. They can help you check your phone and accounts and plan, using a device the other person cannot reach.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager or coworker demands constant updates beyond the written rules, ask for the expectation in writing and keep a dated record of requests.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I can tell you're worried, and I want to help with that. I would rather tell you about my day than hand over my phone. What has been bothering you?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Watch for checking that comes with anger, threats, or knowing things you never told them. If you think your phone, email or car is being watched, assume the watcher may see what you do on it, including searches for help. Reach a domestic abuse hotline or advocate from a library computer, a friend's phone or a work device, and ask them how to check your devices safely before you change anything.
misuse_warning: Calling any request to see a phone or a text 'surveillance' can dismiss a worry that both people have chosen to handle openly. The pattern is routine, one-sided and growing.
Reading someone else's phone to look for evidence of their monitoring is itself checking up on them. The label should lead to conversation or help, not to more searching.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Location Tracking is the narrower habit of requiring where you are at all times; monitoring and surveillance take in your messages, accounts and whole day. Behavior Control sets rules about what you do, while monitoring checks on what you have done. Isolation reduces who you see; surveillance can sit alongside a full social life and still leave you feeling inspected.

codex_completed.name: Location Tracking
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Requiring a person to keep their live location visible, and treating any gap in it as a problem to be explained.
codex_completed.short_definition: Requiring a person to keep their live location visible, and treating any gap in it as a problem to be explained.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Location tracking is the use of shared maps, location apps or trackers as a rule of the relationship: your dot has to stay on, and a gap needs an explanation. Many couples and families share location because they want to, and can stop. What marks the pattern is that sharing is required, one-way or punished when switched off. One request for your location is ordinary. The line is crossed when stops are questioned, an off switch brings a row, and where you go starts to depend on what you could explain.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone insists on seeing where you are at all times, and turning your location off, or being somewhere unexpected, leads to questions or a fight.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: When every stop might be questioned, ordinary choices start to feel risky. You may drop errands, visits or detours, not because anyone forbade them, but because explaining them has become tiring or frightening.
what_it_is: A requirement to keep live location on, usually from a partner, expressed as a condition of trust or calm.
Questioning of particular stops, such as why you were at a coffee shop for an hour or why the dot was near a friend's house.
Reaction to switched-off location or a flat battery that treats it as proof of something.
One-way flow: your location is visible, and theirs is not offered.
Sometimes extended to vehicles or other devices, not just the phone.
what_it_sounds_like: Why does your dot say you're at Kelly's? You told me the gym.
Your location was off for an hour. What were you hiding?
Keep it on. If you've got nothing to hide, it costs you nothing.
I just want to know you're safe.
Turn it back on. Now.
I saw your car wasn't at work when I went past.
Funny how your phone dies right when I want to check.
what_it_is_not: Mutual location sharing that both people picked, and either can turn off without a row.
A parent using a family-sharing app with a child who knows about it and for whom it suits their age.
A temporary arrangement for something specific, such as a solo hike or a late walk home, that ends afterward.
A workplace fleet tracker that the employer has disclosed and that applies to the job only.
Someone sharing their location with a carer or relative of their own choosing because of a medical condition.
this_may_be_it_when: Switching sharing off leads to accusations, silence or pressure that makes you turn it back on.
Your whereabouts are questioned after the fact, with details that show someone was watching the map.
Only one of you is tracked.
You have started planning routes or stops around what you could justify.
You were told that location sharing is the price of the relationship being peaceful.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You turned it off recently and it was a non-event.
Both of you see each other's location and use it for meeting up and collecting kids.
The sharing was your idea or a shared one, and you still like it.
It was set up for a particular trip or period and has an end.
A question about where you are is answered by your reply, not by the map.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Some people find shared location convenient for pickups and meeting up, and enjoy it.
Someone who has just had a frightening experience may want to see that a partner got home, for a short time.
Families with teens often use it as an agreed safety net and talk about it openly.
common_false_positives: A friend group sharing locations at a festival so nobody gets lost.
A partner asking 'where are you?' when dinner is getting cold, with no follow-up.
A couple who both turn sharing on when traveling and off at home.
discernment_questions: Could you switch your location off tomorrow without a row?
Does sharing run both ways, or are you the only one visible?
Do you pick routes or skip stops because you expect to be asked about them?
Does the person act on what they see, such as turning up where you are or asking about places you did not mention?
If a phone battery went flat, would anyone assume it was an accident?
less_concerning_if: Sharing is mutual, agreed and can be turned off.
The reason is a specific one, such as a trip, and the arrangement ends.
A dot on the map leads to 'did you get there okay?' and no cross-examination.
more_concerning_if: They turn up where you are, or mention places you never told them about.
Turning sharing off is followed by anger or threats, or you fear what it will cause.
You have started staying home or skipping places so you do not have to explain them.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your pauses at shops, friends' houses and appointments start to feel like things you would have to explain.
You carry a charger everywhere, in case a dead phone is read as a sign of guilt.
Places you used to visit freely quietly drop off your routine.
A rule that began as a one-time safety measure becomes permanent without any new conversation.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair looks like the switch actually being yours: sharing optional, off without comment, and questions about stops disappearing. If the app stays on 'for safety' and the questions move to your phone calls or your receipts, the tracking has changed form and not ended.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself how the person behaves in the hour after your location goes off. Calm or curious is one thing. Pressure to turn it back on, a barrage of calls, or an accusation tells you the choice was never really yours.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When a person knows their movements are visible, they can begin to rehearse explanations in advance and to avoid places they would find hard to explain. The self-restriction can come to feel like their own idea. The requirement may also be framed as proof of love or safety, which can make refusing seem like rejecting the relationship itself.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A low hum of anxiety about the phone battery, leaving the phone behind, and feeling watched even when alone are common reports. Some trimmed their day to what could be defended. Some felt guilty about wanting to be unobserved. Others felt relief when a friend or counselor pointed out that a dot on a map is not the same thing as trust.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask about the worry behind it: 'Is there something you're afraid of when you can't see where I am? I'd rather talk about that.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask for a mutual, switchable arrangement: 'I'm happy to share my location when I'm traveling. I'd like it to be something either of us can turn off.' Judge by past reactions whether to ask this now.
response_options.disengagement: Without announcing anything, begin to note which accounts and devices can see your location, and talk with an advocate before changing any of them.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask a domestic abuse advocate how to find out what shares your location and how to change it safely, because a sudden change may be noticed.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If an employer tracks a work vehicle or phone, ask in writing what is collected, when, and whether it ends outside working hours.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'd like location sharing to be something we both choose and either of us can pause. Can we talk about what it's meant to help with?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Treat sudden changes with care: someone who can see your location may notice if it disappears, and a person who turns up where you are, or knows places you never mentioned, is a warning sign. Tracking can also run through cars, family plans and shared accounts, not only one app. Speak with a domestic abuse advocate or hotline before switching anything off, from a device the other person has never used.
misuse_warning: A mutual location-sharing arrangement that both people like is not tracking. Calling it that can dismiss a partner's honest preference for convenience.
Using the label to justify checking on, or tracking, the other person in return repeats the pattern from the other side.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Monitoring & Surveillance covers the whole of your day, such as messages, passwords and accounts; location tracking is the narrower demand to know where you physically are. Behavior Control tells you where you may or may not go, while tracking watches where you went and questions it. Punishment of Boundaries is the penalty that follows when you switch the sharing off.

Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Behavior Control
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Setting rules about what another adult may wear, where they may go and who they may see, and enforcing them.
codex_completed.short_definition: Setting rules about what another adult may wear, where they may go and who they may see, and enforcing them.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Behavior control turns a relationship between equals into one with a rulebook. The rules may be about clothes, social media posts, trips, friends, hours or who you may speak to. They are often stated as facts ('you're not wearing that') rather than as feelings or requests. A single preference is ordinary: most people have views on what their partner wears. Concern rises when the rules multiply, are enforced with anger, silence or cost, and are not open to discussion.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone tells you what you can wear, where you can go or who you can see, and makes you pay if you do not follow their rules.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: When another adult's rules govern your clothes, your outings and your friendships, you can lose the habit of deciding for yourself. Complying quietly can come to feel safer than the conflict that follows, and your sense of what is yours to choose can narrow.
what_it_is: Rules stated as orders, not as feelings or requests: 'you're not going', 'take that down', 'you can't wear that'.
Reach into everyday areas: clothing, makeup, social media posts, what time you come home, which events you attend.
Enforcement through anger, silence, sulking, or loss of something you value, so that breaking a rule costs more than keeping it.
Rules that grow over time, as each one given in to is followed by another.
Often framed as respect, modesty or loyalty, which makes the rule feel like a shared value.
what_it_sounds_like: You're not wearing that.
You're not going unless I say so.
Take that photo down right now.
I forbid you to see him again.
Text me when you get there and when you leave.
Real partners don't go out without each other.
If you cared about me, you wouldn't want to.
what_it_is_not: A partner saying 'that outfit makes me feel insecure, and that's mine to work on', owning the feeling and leaving the choice with you.
Parents setting rules for a minor, which is part of their role.
A dress code at work or a faith community that you joined freely, or house rules that roommates agreed together.
Restrictions set by a doctor, probation officer or court for a stated reason.
Two partners asking each other to dress up or to be home for dinner on a particular night, and being free to say no.
this_may_be_it_when: The statement is an order rather than a request, and 'no' is not an accepted answer.
Breaking a rule leads to a punishment, such as days of silence or anger.
The list of rules has grown over months, and keeps growing.
You have started pre-empting the rules, dressing or acting to avoid a reaction.
The rules apply to you and not to the person making them.
this_may_not_be_it_when: A preference is expressed once, as their own feeling, and you remain free to choose.
Rules are mutual: each of you has the same kind of say in the other's choices.
You can disagree with them and nothing is taken away or punished afterward.
The rule is a shared household agreement made in a calm moment.
It was said in a heated moment and later retracted.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Cultural or family expectations may make a request sound firmer than the person means it.
Someone anxious about a plan, such as a late night out in an unfamiliar place, may state it badly and be glad to talk.
People in love often have opinions about each other's clothes and haircuts, and express them without wanting to control.
common_false_positives: A friend saying 'don't wear that, it's freezing out' on a cold night.
A partner asking you not to post an embarrassing photo of them.
A shared agreement in a household about quiet hours or guests.
discernment_questions: Are you expected to follow a rule, or asked to consider a preference?
What happens when you do something against their wishes?
Do the same rules apply to them?
Has the number of things you have to clear gone up over time?
Are there things you once did freely that you no longer do, and did you choose that?
less_concerning_if: Requests are phrased as feelings and you are free to decline.
The same latitude applies to both of you.
Disagreement is followed by talk, not punishment.
more_concerning_if: Breaking a rule leads to threats, anger that frightens you, or loss of money or access.
The rules reach your work, your family or your religion.
You hide things, such as an outfit, a plan or a friend, to avoid the reaction.
pattern_over_time_signs: Each concession is followed by a new rule that you did not expect.
You check your outfit or plans against their likely reaction before you decide.
Things you used to enjoy, like a hobby, a haircut or a certain friend, fade from your life.
Others who knew you notice you have changed how you dress or where you go.
codex_completed.repair_check: Look for rules being given back to you. If the person asks instead of tells, accepts your no without payback, and loosens one thing without tightening another, that is a change. A promise to be 'less strict' while the same punishments remain only reshuffles the rulebook.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Test a small, safe choice: wear what you like to a low-stakes event and note what follows. A shrug or a question shows a boundary at work. Sulking, interrogation or a new rule shows the limit was being treated as a dare, not as your decision.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Rules enforced by anger or silence can teach a person to anticipate a reaction and avoid it, without anyone repeating the rule. Each accommodation can make the next request look small, so the territory can grow gradually. Calling a rule care, modesty or loyalty can make a person feel it would be unkind or ungrateful to object.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Reports include checking an outfit or a plan against someone else's likely reaction, avoiding people or places that cause arguments, and losing sight of what you like. Some end up enforcing the rules on themselves. Others feel shame at having gone along with it, or feel like a guest in their own life.

response_options.soft_clarification: Separate the feeling from the rule: 'If it bothers you, I'd like to hear that. But what I wear is my decision.' Gauge how they have reacted before choosing to say it.
response_options.firm_boundary: Pick one thing that is clearly yours, such as a friendship or a haircut, and keep it without explaining it every time, if you judge it safe.
response_options.disengagement: Avoid debating each rule. Say little, comply where it is safer, and put your effort into support and a plan, not into winning arguments.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe the rules, one by one, to a trusted friend or counselor, and ask whether they sound ordinary to them. A list on paper often looks different from a mood in the room.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, a manager's rules should match written policy. Ask for any new expectation about dress or conduct to be in writing, and bring HR in if it is applied to you only.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "It bothers you, and I'd like to understand why. This one is my call, though. What's behind it for you?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Rules that are enforced with threats, damage to your things, anger that frightens you or the loss of money, housing or contact with children are signs of coercive control. In that case, avoid direct confrontation about the rules. Contact a domestic abuse advocate or a legal aid service, in private, and talk through a safety plan before you change anything about how you comply.
misuse_warning: Calling any disagreement over clothes or plans 'control' can shut down honest negotiation. Control is rules enforced with a cost, not an opinion voiced.
A family or faith tradition you value is not 'behavior control' just because an outsider finds its rules strict. What matters is whether you can say no and stay in good standing.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Infantilization treats you as unable to manage your affairs and takes tasks over; behavior control leaves the tasks with you and dictates what you may do. "I Know Best" Paternalism gives the rule a caring reason, 'for your own good', whereas behavior control may not bother with one. Punishment of Boundaries is what happens after you refuse; behavior control is the rulebook you refused.
