Phrase matching can flag wording, but it cannot know intent, tone, history, context, or whether the claim is even true — an innocent reading is always attached to every match. Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Infantilization
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Treating a capable adult as if they cannot manage their own money, tasks or decisions, and taking those over.
codex_completed.short_definition: Treating a capable adult as if they cannot manage their own money, tasks or decisions, and taking those over.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Infantilization is treating a grown person like a child who needs supervising: speaking for them, taking over their bills, appointments or paperwork, praising small tasks, or sighing at their mistakes. One offer of help with something new is ordinary. It stands out when the assumption of incompetence is broad, stays in place after you have shown you can do the task, and is hard to refuse. Over time the person can lose both practice and confidence, which then seems to prove the point.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone talks and acts as though you can't handle adult life, takes over your jobs and decisions, and leaves you feeling less able than you are.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Skills and confidence both fade when they are not used. A person who is told often enough that they cannot cope may stop trying, and may end up unable to manage money, paperwork or decisions they once handled well.
what_it_is: Taking over money, bills, appointments or paperwork on the basis that you would get them wrong.
Talking about you or for you, in front of you, such as answering questions put to you at the doctor's.
A tone usually kept for children: pet names, patient sighs, praise for ordinary tasks.
Treating each mistake as proof, while the person's successes go unmentioned.
Taking away your chances to practice, so that the inability seems to become real.
what_it_sounds_like: You can't handle money, sweetie. Let me.
You'd be lost without me organizing your life.
Give me that. You'll only mess it up.
You wouldn't understand anyway.
She's very sensitive, so I deal with the paperwork.
Don't worry your head about it.
Look at you, you did it all by yourself!
what_it_is_not: An offer of help with something you have not done before, which you can accept or decline.
Carers of an adult with a real impairment who still ask them, explain things and include them in decisions.
Parents who have not caught up with the fact that their grown child has changed, and who respond when told.
A partner who is simply better at spreadsheets and takes them on by agreement, and would hand them back if asked.
A temporary need for extra help during illness, grief or a crisis.
this_may_be_it_when: The assumption that you can't cope covers many areas of your life, not just one skill.
You have shown competence and the assumption stays the same.
You are talked over or spoken for in front of other people.
Your requests to do something yourself are brushed aside or met with a sigh.
You have been shut out of money, accounts or documents that affect you.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You can ask for a task back and get it, with no fuss.
The help is for a specific, unfamiliar job and ends when you are ready.
You are included in the decision and your opinion counts.
You and the other person split the household's jobs by agreement, and either of you can change the split.
There is a real health reason for support, and your preferences still steer it.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A partner who enjoys being useful may not notice they are taking over until you tell them.
Older relatives often keep an out-of-date picture of what you can do.
Habit: whoever started handling the bills years ago may simply have carried on.
common_false_positives: A friend offering to help you set up a new phone.
A parent doing a household task for a teenager during exam time, by agreement.
A carer or relative stepping in for a limited period after surgery.
discernment_questions: Could you take back a task you have been relieved of, and would you be allowed?
Do you know where your documents are and what your accounts say?
Does this person speak to you or for you when other people are present?
Has your confidence in tasks you used to manage dropped since they were taken over?
Would the same assumption be made about someone else in your position?
less_concerning_if: Help is offered, not imposed, and you can say 'I've got it'.
You know where your money and papers are and have access to them.
The arrangement can be renegotiated and has been.
more_concerning_if: You cannot see or reach your own bank accounts, ID or medical records.
Your wishes are overruled on matters that are yours, such as your health or your money.
You are told, or begin to believe, that you could not manage without them.
pattern_over_time_signs: Tasks you once did, such as paying a bill or booking an appointment, quietly become theirs.
You hesitate before making ordinary decisions and check with them first.
You hear yourself calling yourself useless, using words that first came from them.
Friends or relatives notice you deferring on things you used to decide easily.
codex_completed.repair_check: Watch for tasks and information coming back to you: the login, the folder, the appointment. A person who changes will hand them over and let you do it your way, even badly. Praise, an apology and a promise to 'let you try' while still hovering, only restyles the supervision.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask to do one thing yourself, start to finish. Does it stay with you if the result is imperfect, or do they step in, correct it or take it back? The way a small mistake is treated shows whether the request was accepted.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People partly learn what they can do from how others treat them. Being repeatedly told you cannot, and having tasks removed, can lead to less practice, and the resulting mistakes or avoidance can then be pointed to as proof. Dependence can also make the arrangement feel necessary, even when it began as an offer of help.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Reports include losing confidence in things once done easily, such as banking, driving or choosing what to eat, and embarrassment in front of others. Some apologize constantly or stop trying new things. Some are surprised, on getting a task back, to find they can still do it.

response_options.soft_clarification: Offer a concrete picture of what you want: 'I'd like to handle the electricity bill myself this month. Could you show me where the login is?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask for something you are entitled to, such as access to your accounts or papers, plainly and calmly, and without having to prove you can be trusted with it first. Think about how they have reacted before.
response_options.disengagement: Practice quietly: take on small tasks of your own, such as booking your own appointments, and build the record of what you can do.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone who knows you well which areas of your life have been taken over, and ask them what they remember you managing. If your money or papers are held back, a legal aid service can explain your rights.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work or with professionals, speak for yourself: ask doctors, bankers or officials to address you directly, and ask for written summaries you can keep.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Wanting to help is kind of you. I want to do this one myself, and I'll ask if I get stuck. Could you show me where everything is?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Take extra care if you cannot see or reach your own money, ID, medication or documents, or if you are told you are not allowed to decide. These can lead to loss of income, housing or independence, particularly for older adults and people with disabilities. Reach an advocate, adult protective services where they exist, or a legal aid service, and make copies of your key documents somewhere the other person cannot get to.
misuse_warning: Calling every offer of help 'infantilizing' can punish people who are simply trying to be useful, and can push away real support during illness or grief.
Using the label about care for someone with a real impairment can overlook their need for assistance. The test is whether they are still included, not whether help is given.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: "I Know Best" Paternalism overrides a particular choice you have made, with the reason that it is for your good; infantilization assumes you cannot make choices at all, and takes the tasks over. Behavior Control dictates what you may do and wear; infantilization takes over what you would do yourself. Isolation cuts your contacts; infantilization leaves you in company but doubting that you can act.

codex_completed.name: "I Know Best" Paternalism
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Overriding another adult's choices in the name of what is good for them, and expecting them to be grateful.
codex_completed.short_definition: Overriding another adult's choices in the name of what is good for them, and expecting them to be grateful.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: This is the habit of deciding for another adult what is good for them and acting on it, often alongside real affection. Advice turns into steering, steering into pressure, and a decision you made is quietly undone or ignored. One piece of advice is ordinary, and a person who knows more than you may be right. It stands out when your refusal is not accepted, when your choice is reversed behind your back, or when the relationship cools if you decide differently.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone says they are acting for your good, but does not accept your decision when you say no, and keeps pushing or working around you.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Care that cannot accept your no is hard to turn down, because refusing can feel ungrateful. Over time you may stop trusting your own judgment, or stop telling the person what you are deciding.
what_it_is: Advice that does not stop after you have decided, and returns until you give in.
Reasons that appeal to your own good, your future or what others would say, rather than to a preference the person admits is theirs.
Acting around your choice, such as rebooking, canceling or arranging something without telling you.
Expecting thanks, or reading your disagreement as ingratitude.
More common in families, workplaces and care settings, where one person has more seniority, age or experience.
what_it_sounds_like: I know what's best for you.
Trust me, I know better than you do.
You'll thank me later.
I've already moved your appointment. It's for your own good.
After everything I've done for you, the least you can do is listen.
You're making a mistake, and I won't let you.
One day you'll understand why I did this.
what_it_is_not: Advice offered once, with a plain 'it's your decision', and support afterward whatever you pick.
An elder who really does know better on a specific matter, such as a roofer on roofs, whose view you can weigh.
A mentor, doctor or teacher whose guidance you sought and whose expertise you expect to carry weight.
Fear for your safety, such as a parent worried about a risky plan, voiced openly while leaving the choice with you.
A strongly argued disagreement between equals, where each can concede.
this_may_be_it_when: You said no, and the topic keeps returning until you give in.
Your decision was reversed or worked around without your being told.
Disagreement is described as ungrateful, naive or hurtful to them.
The warmth of the relationship seems to depend on your choosing as they would.
You have started concealing decisions to avoid the argument.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They say their piece once and then back whatever you decide.
You asked for their opinion first, so the advice is something you wanted.
They can accept that you chose differently and the relationship stays warm.
Their concern is about a specific danger and they say so plainly.
The decision really does belong to both of you, such as joint finances, and both of you are weighing it.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People who care often find it hard to watch someone make a choice they fear will hurt them, and speak too strongly.
Parents and grandparents often keep the habit of deciding for you long after you've grown.
In some families, strong advice is a normal way of showing love.
common_false_positives: A friend who tells you they are worried about a risky plan, once, and then asks how it went.
A doctor recommending a treatment and respecting your decision to decline it.
A boss giving direction in an area where they are accountable for results.
discernment_questions: After you decided, did the person accept it, or did the conversation return?
Have your decisions ever been changed without your knowledge?
Does this person ever say 'it's your call' and mean it?
Does your disagreement bring a warm response or a cool one?
Do you tell this person less than you used to about your plans?
less_concerning_if: Concern is stated once and your final decision is supported afterward.
They are open about the fact that it is their own worry, not a fact about your life.
You can disagree without the relationship cooling.
more_concerning_if: They take actions around your decision, such as canceling, rebooking, or speaking on your behalf.
Refusing is followed by withdrawal of money, help, contact or approval.
They have control over something you depend on, like housing, income or care.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find you are deciding less, and sharing less, to avoid the debate.
Past choices that went your way are not mentioned, while the ones that went wrong are.
Their advice arrives earlier and earlier, before you have asked or decided.
You feel a sinking feeling before telling them news, because you expect disapproval.
codex_completed.repair_check: Next time you decide something they disagree with, their response tells you. If they say their worry once and then help you carry out your choice, that is a different pattern. A warm apology followed by another quiet reversal is the same thing in a softer voice.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Is the decision still standing a week later? That is the test. A boundary about your choices is respected when nothing is rebooked, redone or relitigated, and when disagreement does not change how you are treated.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Care and control can sound alike, and a person may sincerely believe they are helping. For the receiver, an objection can feel like turning down affection, and the cost of saying no rises. When someone is repeatedly told their choices are mistakes, they can start to defer, or to hide decisions until they are already done.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe guilt for refusing someone who 'means well', frustration at not being heard, and hesitation to share news in case it is overruled. Some say they began making decisions in secret. Some describe doubting their judgment, especially when the person was often right. Some feel grief at a relationship that only works when they agree.

response_options.soft_clarification: Acknowledge the care and keep the decision: 'I know you're worried because you care. I've thought it through, and I'm going ahead.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say you will not discuss the choice again, and then do not: 'I've made my decision, and I'm not going to go over it again. I'd love to talk about anything else.'
response_options.disengagement: Move to topics other than the decision, and share news after it is done, not before, if the debates drain you.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask someone who knows both of you whether your decision seems reasonable. An outside view can check your judgment without handing it over.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: When a supervisor or professional overrides you, ask for the reasons and the alternatives in writing, and say clearly which decisions belong to you.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I know you're telling me this because you care, and I've heard it. My decision is made, and I'm asking you to trust me with it. Let's talk about something else."
codex_completed.safety_note: Unwanted help from people who love you is usually a family or friendship strain, not a danger. It changes if refusing is followed by cut-off money, housing or care, if documents or medication are withheld, or if threats appear. If any of that is true, treat it as coercion and speak to a legal aid service or an advocate before you confront the person.
misuse_warning: Labeling every piece of strong advice as paternalism can shut out people who are right to be worried. The test is whether your no is accepted, not whether you were advised.
Using the label to dismiss a doctor, a supervisor or an older relative who knows more than you can mean ignoring good information. You can weigh their view and still decide.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Behavior Control gives orders with no pretense of care, such as 'you're not wearing that'. Paternalism says 'it's for your own good', and often means it. Infantilization assumes you cannot do ordinary adult tasks; paternalism accepts you can, and overrides one choice. Punishment of Boundaries is the cold shoulder or penalty that follows your no, which may come after either.

Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Punishment of Boundaries
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Answering a limit someone has set with a penalty, such as coldness, withdrawn help or a taken-away privilege, until saying no starts to feel costly.
codex_completed.short_definition: Answering a limit someone has set with a penalty, such as coldness, withdrawn help or a taken-away privilege, until saying no starts to feel costly.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Punishment of Boundaries is a reply to a stated limit that makes the limit expensive. After someone says no, asks for space or changes an arrangement, a cost follows: days of silence, a lift that is no longer offered, a sudden cold tone, a favor pulled back, a story told to mutual friends about how difficult they have become. Hurt feelings about a new limit are ordinary, and one sour evening says little. What marks it is a cost that arrives every time a limit is set and lifts only when the limit does.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You say no or ask for space, and something you value goes cold or goes missing until you take it back.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: People learn from what a no costs. When every limit is followed by a chill, a lost favor or a week of silence, many stop setting limits at all, and the relationship quietly shrinks to whatever the other person will accept.
what_it_is: A cost attached to a limit: the silence, the sharper tone or the withdrawn favor begins after the limit is set and ends when it is dropped.
Penalties come in many sizes, from a cold shoulder and sarcasm to canceled plans, held-back money or a smear among mutual friends.
Tied to the act of saying no or asking for space, whatever the limit was actually about.
Often followed by full warmth the moment the person gives in, so the contrast does the teaching.
Found between partners, parents and grown children, bosses and staff, and close friends.
what_it_sounds_like: Fine. Have your 'boundary.' See how the weekend goes.
Oh, you need space? Enjoy the silence, then.
Oh, so now you have boundaries.
If you can't do Sunday dinner, don't bother coming at all.
I drove you everywhere for years, and this is what I get.
Don't ask me for anything this week.
Go ahead, take the night off. Don't expect me to cover for you next time.
what_it_is_not: A quick hurt reaction to a new limit, such as 'that stings', that settles within a day and ends in acceptance.
A natural consequence that comes with the limit itself: if you won't drive on Fridays, you can't also be the Friday driver.
Someone needing a few hours alone to absorb a no, and saying so, without making you pay for it.
Two people renegotiating a shared arrangement, each saying what they can still offer.
A policy that applies to everyone, such as a workplace rule on canceled shifts, applied to you as it is to others.
Sadness about a limit that is spoken as sadness, with no penalty added.
this_may_be_it_when: The chill starts within hours of your no and lifts soon after you back down.
The penalty falls on something you rely on, such as lifts, childcare, money or invitations.
Warmth returns in full when you give in, which makes the contrast stand out.
Other people hear how unreasonable your limit was before you have spoken to them yourself.
The cost is out of proportion to the size of what you asked.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They told you honestly that it hurts, and then did what you asked.
The mood is brief and ordinary contact resumes without you giving anything up.
What you lost is a direct, unavoidable result of your limit, and nobody added to it.
They are in the middle of something large, such as grief or illness, and would have reacted to almost any change.
They ask what the limit is for and then adjust.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Being turned down stings, and a short awkward mood is part of getting used to a new arrangement.
Someone who depended on your help may be scrambling to cover for it, which can sound sharp.
People who never heard a no growing up can react clumsily to a first limit and improve after talking.
common_false_positives: A friend who is quiet for an evening after you cancel, then calls to say they were disappointed.
A manager who has to reassign a shift after you decline it and sounds rushed about it.
A relative who says 'I'll miss you at Christmas' once and then makes other plans without fuss.
discernment_questions: What happens in the days after I say no, and does it differ from what happens when I say yes?
Does the cost land on something unrelated to the limit, like affection, time with the kids or help I rely on?
Have I stopped asking for things because of what the last request cost?
Does the relationship go back to normal only when I withdraw the limit?
Is the response the same size for a small limit as for a large one?
less_concerning_if: The reaction is spoken as a feeling, and no consequence follows it.
Contact and help carry on at their usual level once the first awkward day has passed.
They have adjusted to at least some of your limits over time.
more_concerning_if: The penalties grow each time, from silence to withdrawn money or access to people you care about.
You have begun to say yes in advance to avoid what a no would bring.
The penalty includes pressure about your safety, your children, your housing or your income.
pattern_over_time_signs: You time requests for good moods and put off the ones that might cost you.
Your list of limits gets shorter, and you can't remember the last one that stuck.
Friends say you used to say no more easily.
Warmth and chill seem to track whether you complied, more than anything else going on.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair shows up as the next limit going differently. They name the freeze or the withdrawn favor as theirs, the limit holds without a penalty, and later ones hold too. An apology that arrives only once you have given ground is not about the limit.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Watch the days after a limit, not the minutes. Is anything taken away, and does it come back only when you reverse yourself? A limit that is respected leaves help, warmth and contact where they were, even if the person is sad about it.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Behavior changes fast around whatever follows it. When a no is followed by coldness or loss and a yes by warmth, the person may start to avoid the penalty by not asking, and the limit disappears without anyone having argued against it. Fear of losing something they depend on, such as closeness or money, can make the lesson stick faster.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe walking on eggshells before saying no, rehearsing how a request will land, and feeling guilty about needs that are ordinary. Some carry out favors resentfully rather than risk the fallout. Some find the habit has spread to work or friendships, where they now hesitate to refuse anything.

response_options.soft_clarification: Describe the sequence in your own terms and ask what it is about: 'When I said I couldn't come on Sunday, we didn't speak until Wednesday. I'd like to understand what that was.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold the limit without adding to it: 'I've said I can't do Sundays. I'm still glad to see you on Saturdays.' You don't need to defend it again each time it comes up.
response_options.disengagement: When the silence or sarcasm starts, let it sit and carry on with your day, rather than rushing to restore the old closeness by reversing your answer.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone outside the relationship what happened after your last two limits, and ask whether it sounds like a proportionate reaction to them.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a declined overtime shift is followed by worse rotas or sharp treatment, keep dated notes of the request, your answer and what changed, and take them to HR or a union representative.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I know it was disappointing to hear no. I'd like us to talk about it, and I'd like us to keep treating each other the same way while we do."
codex_completed.safety_note: Penalties become a safety matter when they include threats, damage to your belongings, using the children's time as a lever, cutting off money or housing, or following and watching you after a no. If a refusal brings fear, tell one trusted person or a domestic abuse advocate about the pattern before you set the next limit, and ask how to plan it safely.
misuse_warning: Calling any sulk after a refusal 'punishment' ignores that disappointment is normal. The label needs a repeating cost tied to the limit.
Using it to cast someone as vindictive can close a conversation in which they might simply have said that it hurt.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Isolation works to cut you off from other people so you depend on one person, while this answers one particular no, whoever it concerned. Behavior Control sets rules in advance about what you may do; Punishment of Boundaries arrives afterwards, once you have acted on your own. Monitoring & Surveillance asks for constant accounting, whereas here the other person may ask nothing until you decline something.

Phrase matching can flag wording, but it cannot know intent, tone, history, context, or whether the claim is even true — an innocent reading is always attached to every match. Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: DARVO
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A three-part reply to being confronted: deny it happened, attack the person raising it, then claim to be the one who was wronged.
codex_completed.short_definition: A three-part reply to being confronted: deny it happened, attack the person raising it, then claim to be the one who was wronged.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: DARVO stands for Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender. Psychologist Jennifer Freyd named it in the late 1990s. Someone is told their behavior hurt another person. They say it did not happen, turn on the person who spoke up, and end up describing themselves as the one under attack. The listener then spends the talk defending themselves, and the first complaint is never answered. One defensive flash after a surprising accusation is common. The pattern shows when all three moves arrive together and come back each time.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You bring up something that hurt you, and within minutes you are the one apologizing, because the other person has made themselves the injured party.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: People who raise a hard subject often do it at real cost. When the reply turns them into the accused, they can leave convinced the original problem was never real, or that speaking up is not worth the price.
what_it_is: A sequence of three moves, not one: refusing the facts, going after the person who raised them, and then taking the role of the hurt party.
It often shows up after someone describes harm directly, such as in a confrontation, a complaint to a manager, or a public accusation.
The attack usually borrows from the complaint itself, so the words 'hurt', 'abuse' or 'lied' get handed back to the person who said them.
The reversal can be sincere on the speaker's side. Someone can feel truly wronged by being accused, and the pattern is still visible in the exchange.
what_it_sounds_like: That never happened, and I can't believe you'd say it.
Oh, so now I'm the villain?
After everything I've put up with from you, you have the nerve to accuse me?
You're the one who's been cruel to me.
I'm the real victim here, and you know it.
I'm getting hurt just listening to this.
You always twist things so you look innocent.
what_it_is_not: A person who is falsely accused and says, with specifics, which part is wrong. Disputing a claim is different from reversing the roles.
A two-sided conflict in which both people carry real grievances and each gets a turn to be heard.
Visible hurt or tears from someone told they caused harm. Feeling wounded is not the same as flipping the blame.
A first, defensive burst of denial that settles into 'let me think about what you said' after a few minutes or a day.
A counter-complaint that is raised after the first one has been answered, and is treated as a separate matter.
this_may_be_it_when: Within the same conversation, you go from raising a concern to defending your own character.
The other person describes you as the abusive, cruel or dishonest one, using the same words you used about them.
The original complaint is not mentioned again once the argument turns to your behavior.
The same reversal follows each time you raise something similar, whatever the topic.
You leave feeling you owe an apology for having spoken at all.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They answer your complaint point by point first, and only then raise something of their own.
Their counter-claim has real support, such as a message or a witness, and is open to the same checking as yours.
The denial concerns one fact they can show is wrong, with no attack on you attached.
Both of you are able to say 'I hurt you' and 'you hurt me' within the same talk.
They come back later and take up your original point without being asked.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Being accused of something hurtful is painful, and people often lash out in the first minute before they can think clearly.
The accusation may have been delivered in a harsh or public way that made self-protection feel urgent.
Some people were raised in homes where admitting fault brought punishment, so denial is a learned reflex and not a plan.
They may truly remember the event differently, and be as sure of their memory as you are of yours.
common_false_positives: A coworker falsely accused of a mistake who says 'that wasn't me, here is the log', and then asks why you thought it was.
A couple fighting where each person feels unheard, and both say 'you are the one hurting me'.
A friend who snaps back in the moment and sends an apology the next morning that deals with the actual issue.
discernment_questions: Did anyone answer what I first raised, even once, before the talk moved to my behavior?
Are the three moves (denial, attack, role reversal) all present, or is it only a short flash of defensiveness?
Does this reversal happen each time I bring up this kind of subject?
If someone else heard a recording of this conversation, would they say the complaint was ever addressed?
Is there anything in their counter-accusation that is checkable and true, which I should take seriously?
less_concerning_if: The reversal fades once things calm down, and the original subject is picked up again.
The counter-complaint is specific, supportable and discussed as a second matter.
They can say 'I felt attacked' without also saying 'so you are the problem'.
more_concerning_if: They tell other people you are the one who has been abusive, before or after you have spoken up.
They threaten to report you, take your children or involve your employer in response to your complaint.
You have started to rehearse apologies before you raise anything, or to drop subjects entirely.
pattern_over_time_signs: Complaints you once raised openly are now kept to yourself because they end in a fight about you.
You keep a list of your own past mistakes close at hand, ready for when the reversal comes.
Mutual friends or family have heard their account of events more than yours.
Months later you cannot say what your first complaint was, only that you ended up sorry.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair here would mean going back to the first complaint and answering it, including the part they dispute, before any counter-claim gets a turn. Warning signs are a general 'sorry things got heated' that never touches the original point, or an apology that arrives only after you have apologized.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Watch what happens to your original concern after you ask to finish it first. Does it get a reply, a date to continue, or a promise to return to it? Or does the conversation snap back to your character within a minute or two?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Psychologist Jennifer Freyd named DARVO in the 1990s, and later research by Harsey, Zurbriggen and Freyd (2017) linked exposure to it with people blaming themselves more. Being cast as the wrongdoer right after speaking up can pull attention onto clearing your own name, and the first complaint tends to slide out of view.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe leaving a confrontation feeling guilty and confused, sometimes apologizing for the very thing they came to raise. Some go quiet about later problems, because the last time cost too much. Others replay the conversation for days trying to find where it turned.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name the order of events calmly: 'I came to talk about the missed payment, and now we are talking about me. Can we finish the first subject?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Refuse to defend yourself against the counter-charge until the first matter is answered: 'I will listen to your concern next, but I need an answer on mine first.'
response_options.disengagement: When the talk has turned to your character, end it for now, say you will return to the original point, and put that point in writing so it does not get lost.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a trusted person what you originally raised and what happened next. Hearing 'that is not what you came to talk about' from someone outside can restore your footing.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Put the original complaint in writing with dates before any meeting, and ask HR or a manager to keep the discussion on that record when a counter-complaint appears.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "What I said hurt you, and I will talk about that. But I came here to talk about the missed dinner and the lie about it. Can we stay on that first, and then take your concerns right after?"
codex_completed.safety_note: DARVO can show up alongside abuse, where a person who reports harm is then described to others as the one who caused the harm. Watch for threats to report you, to call your employer, or to claim custody, and for fear of what happens if you push back. Domestic violence advocates and legal aid can help you plan. If the counter-accusations are joined by threats of violence, call your local emergency number instead of waiting to see how it plays out.
misuse_warning: Anyone who is angry at being accused can sound like this for a minute. Naming DARVO after one defensive reply shuts down a conversation that might have recovered.
People who really have caused harm sometimes say 'that is DARVO' about any pushback they receive. The word does not settle who is right.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Blame-Shifting puts the cause of the act on you but does not necessarily claim to be injured. Whataboutism answers with a different past complaint and does not deny or attack. Denial only refuses the facts. DARVO ends by casting the accuser as the wrongdoer and the accused as the victim.

codex_completed.name: Blame-Shifting
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Placing the cause of your own action on the other person, so that your choice is described as something they did to you.
codex_completed.short_definition: Placing the cause of your own action on the other person, so that your choice is described as something they did to you.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Blame-shifting takes a real action, such as a shout, a missed promise or a broken thing, and moves its cause onto someone else. 'I did it' becomes 'you made me do it.' Context does matter in real conflicts, and naming it once is not the problem. The pattern appears when the other person's behavior is offered as a complete explanation, leaving no room for the speaker's own choice, and when this repeats across different events. The person who was harmed ends up holding both the injury and the fault.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone does something hurtful, then explains it as your doing. By the end you are apologizing for causing what they chose to do.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: If every hurtful act is explained as a reaction to you, you can end up policing your own behavior to head off theirs. That is a heavy job nobody can do, and it keeps the real problem from ever being talked about.
what_it_is: An explanation that treats the speaker's choice as if it were forced on them by what you said or did.
It usually follows a specific act: raised voices, a forgotten task, a broken agreement, or a mistake at work.
The cause sits in the past tense of your behavior, such as 'if you had called', and the speaker's own option to act differently is missing.
It tends to include a list of your faults offered as proof, whether or not those faults relate to what happened.
what_it_sounds_like: Look what you made me do.
I wouldn't have yelled if you had just answered the phone.
You drove me to it.
If you hadn't brought up money, none of this would have happened.
You know how I get when you do that, so this is on you.
I only lied because you would have overreacted.
You brought this on yourself.
what_it_is_not: Honestly describing a real trigger, such as 'I was exhausted and your comment landed badly', while still owning the response.
A mutual conflict where both people admit what they added and neither claims to be the only cause.
A true statement of fact about timing, such as 'I was late because the train was canceled'.
A child or very stressed adult who blames the nearest person in the heat of the moment, then settles and takes responsibility.
Explaining your reasons for a decision without claiming the other person left you no option.
this_may_be_it_when: Every time something goes wrong, the explanation leads back to something you did or did not do.
The phrase 'you made me' or 'you forced me' is used for actions that were clearly a choice.
You find yourself changing your behavior to prevent their reactions, such as speaking less, hiding purchases or avoiding certain subjects.
Their own part, even a small one, is never named, even after you raise it calmly.
An apology from you is expected before anything is discussed.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They name your part and theirs in the same breath, with something like 'I shouldn't have said that, though I was hurt'.
The explanation is limited to one real event and is not repeated across different ones.
They accept that you could not have predicted how they would respond.
You can point to something you did that really did contribute, and they do not inflate it.
Afterwards, they change what they do, not what you do.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People under heavy stress often grab for an outside cause first and find their own part only later.
Some families teach that anger is always caused by someone else, so the habit is inherited rather than chosen.
Your own behavior may truly have been unkind, and the explanation is partly accurate even if incomplete.
common_false_positives: A friend who says 'I snapped because I was waiting on that message all day' and then apologizes for snapping.
A manager who points out that a deadline slipped because a handoff was late, while still taking responsibility for the plan.
Two siblings arguing about who started it, each partly right, with no one using it to avoid owning their own part.
discernment_questions: Did they do something that was within their own control to do differently?
Does the explanation leave any share at all for their own choice?
Has my behavior changed to avoid setting them off, and has that helped?
Does this explanation appear after most conflicts, or just this one?
If a friend of mine did the same thing and gave the same reason, would I accept it as a full account?
less_concerning_if: They add 'that was still my choice' to the sentence, even grudgingly.
They are able to describe their own part once things have cooled.
The reason they offer is a fact about the situation and not about your character.
more_concerning_if: The blame is attached to anger, shoving, damaged belongings or threats, and it is used to explain these.
You have started to apologize for their outbursts as if you had caused them.
Other people around you have begun repeating that you are the cause of their moods.
pattern_over_time_signs: You keep a mental checklist of things not to say, and the list grows rather than shrinks.
Their outbursts persist even after you have changed what they said set them off.
You notice you are apologizing for events that happened before you arrived.
Friends comment that you seem to walk on eggshells around them.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair would sound like 'that was my decision' with no 'but' attached, and it would show the next time the same trigger appears: the shout, the lie or the slammed door does not happen, and you are not asked to prevent it. A list of what you did to cause it is the opposite.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: After you say the reaction was theirs to choose, notice whether they pause and engage with that, or whether a new charge arrives, such as being cold, unfair or unwilling to take any responsibility yourself. The blame may have only moved to a new place.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Many people accept responsibility quickly, especially for someone they care about or after being told they are difficult. Repeated, confident blame can draw on that readiness, so the receiver starts auditing their own conduct before the event itself, and the other person's choice drops out of the picture.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe constantly monitoring what they say, apologizing for outbursts they did not cause, and losing track of where their own responsibility starts and ends. Some grow quieter or more anxious around the person, and some begin hiding things to avoid setting off a reaction.

response_options.soft_clarification: Separate the trigger from the choice: 'I can see that I upset you, and you were still the one who decided to throw the plate.'
response_options.firm_boundary: State where your responsibility ends: 'I will own what I said. I will not own what you did in response.'
response_options.disengagement: When the explanation turns to your faults, leave the room or end the call, and say you will return once the subject is what happened and not who is to blame.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe a specific incident to someone outside the relationship and ask whether the cause they hear sounds like yours. Outsiders often notice the shift in blame before you do.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Record what happened in neutral terms, with dates and who did what, and ask for the discussion to cover each person's actions separately, not who caused whom.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I can see that I upset you, and I am willing to talk about my part. What you did next was your decision. I'm not going to accept being told I made you do it."
codex_completed.safety_note: Blame placed on you for shouting, breaking things or physical force can be part of a pattern of control, in which you are made responsible for managing someone else's anger. Warning signs include fear of their reaction, injury, or being told you deserve it. A domestic abuse advocate or trusted person can help you plan. If you are hurt, or afraid for your life, during one of these blame episodes, that is an emergency: call the emergency number where you live.
misuse_warning: People are sometimes accused of blame-shifting for mentioning any context at all. Explaining what led up to something is fair. The concern is explanations that leave no room for the speaker's own choice.
Using the label to avoid hearing a legitimate point about your own contribution turns it into a way of dodging.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: DARVO adds a denial and an attack, then makes the speaker the victim. Blame-Shifting can come with a calm admission of the act, so long as its cause is placed on you. Whataboutism points to a separate wrong of yours instead. Denial refuses that the act happened at all.

codex_completed.name: Whataboutism
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Answering a complaint by raising a different wrong from the other side, so that the original issue goes unanswered.
codex_completed.short_definition: Answering a complaint by raising a different wrong from the other side, so that the original issue goes unanswered.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Whataboutism meets a complaint with a counter-complaint about something else, usually older or from a different topic. 'What about the time you forgot my birthday?' The tit-for-tat can feel fair, because both things may be real. The problem is the swap. The first concern is set aside as if the two cancel out, and the talk ends in a draw with nothing resolved. Raising your own grievance is reasonable. It becomes this pattern when it replaces the answer instead of following it.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You raise a problem, and instead of a reply you get a different problem about you. Both end up unsolved, and the talk feels like a tie.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: When each complaint is met with another one, nothing is ever finished. Real issues pile up unresolved, and the person who raised the first one starts to wonder if it was fair to speak at all.
what_it_is: A reply that sets one wrong beside another instead of answering the first.
The counter-point is often from a different time or subject, such as an old argument or an unrelated mistake.
It often arrives as a question, which makes it hard to answer without being pulled off course.
It differs from a related issue raised later, because here the new point takes the place of a response.
what_it_sounds_like: What about that time you forgot?
And you've never been late once in your life?
Well, what about when you left me waiting at the airport?
You did the exact same thing last year.
Funny that you bring it up, given how you treated my mother.
If we are keeping score, I could list yours too.
what_it_is_not: Pointing out a true double standard and then returning to the original issue to answer it.
Asking to talk about a related concern after the first one has been dealt with, as a separate conversation.
A comparison that helps explain the point, such as 'I was late too last week, so I understand how it happens'.
A reasonable request that both people apply the same rule, made while still engaging with the complaint.
Two people with overlapping grievances who agree to take turns and keep to it.
this_may_be_it_when: The counter-point is raised before your complaint has had any response.
The topic they raise has no clear connection with what you brought up.
Your complaint is never returned to, even after the other matter has been talked through.
Every complaint you raise is met by one from the past, drawn from a ready list.
You end up defending an old event instead of discussing the new one.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They say 'that is fair, and I would also like to talk about something from my side afterwards'.
The point they raise is directly relevant, such as the same rule being applied unevenly.
Your complaint gets an answer first, even a short one.
The two of you have agreed to cover one subject at a time, and they follow that agreement.
The counter-complaint is not a repeat from earlier arguments but something new to them.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People who feel a long-standing grievance has gone unheard may bring it up at any chance because it is on their mind.
A person raised in a household where arguments were fought by trading points may know no other way to disagree.
They may hear your complaint as unfair because of something they remember, and mention it to show that, not to dodge.
common_false_positives: A roommate who says 'I will do the dishes tonight, and can we also talk about the bathroom schedule tomorrow?'
A partner who answers your complaint about lateness with 'you are right, and I felt the same when you were late last month', then discusses both.
An employee who notes that a rule applies to everyone and asks whether it will be enforced evenly.
discernment_questions: Was my original point responded to before the other point came up?
Is what they raise connected to what I said, or is it a different subject?
Does the conversation end with either issue settled?
Do I have a similar list of their faults, and am I tempted to use it the same way?
Would we both agree to deal with one at a time, and stick to it?
less_concerning_if: The counter-point is held for afterwards and actually gets its turn.
They respond to your complaint in a sentence before bringing up their own.
Both of you leave with at least one of the two issues settled.
more_concerning_if: Your complaints are consistently answered with a catalog of your past faults.
The older grievance they raise has already been apologized for and settled.
Raising anything has begun to feel like it will cost you an equal and opposite attack.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find yourself holding back complaints because you expect the answer to be a worse one about you.
The same few old events appear in arguments about unrelated subjects.
Issues you raised a year ago are still open, along with theirs.
You start tracking your own past mistakes so you can defend them quickly.
codex_completed.repair_check: Your complaint gets an actual answer first, and theirs gets a separate time set aside. A mutual 'we both have faults' that closes the topic leaves your first point exactly as unanswered as before, and may be followed by the same swap next time.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Try asking for one subject at a time and see what follows. Do they answer the first point, then hold their own for later? Or does the same counter-point come back, louder, as if the order of the conversation were not up for discussion?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A counter-complaint appeals to a fairness instinct: if you have made mistakes too, pressing your own point can feel unfair. That discomfort can pull attention away from the first complaint, and it tends to work best when the counter-point is true.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe feeling that raising anything is pointless because it will be matched with something else. Small issues pile up unspoken. Some begin to feel they owe a running debt of past wrongs, and keep a quick defense of old events ready.

response_options.soft_clarification: Acknowledge the new point and keep the order: 'That sounds like it matters. Can we deal with the dishes first, and then set time for the birthday?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say you will not trade grievances: 'I am willing to talk about your concern. I am not willing to treat it as the answer to mine.'
response_options.disengagement: If each point gets a new one back, stop and say you will return with a single written issue, so only one thing is on the table.
response_options.support_seeking: Write both lists out and show them to a neutral person. They can often tell whether each concern is fair and whether they were ever answered.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In a meeting, ask for an agenda with one item at a time and note whose item is being discussed, so that a counter-point is placed on the list and not used to replace the first.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "You may be right about what happened at the airport, and I want to talk about it. I would like an answer on the money first, and then we can give your issue the same time."
codex_completed.safety_note: Whataboutism on its own carries no physical danger. It would change if the counter-accusations turn into threats to expose old mistakes, to report you somewhere, or to punish you for raising anything. In that case, write down what is said and speak to someone you trust, or to an advocate or lawyer.
misuse_warning: Calling every counter-point whataboutism can silence a person who truly has a fair, related grievance. The test is whether your complaint gets answered at all.
In public debates the word is sometimes used to wave away a relevant comparison. A fair comparison deserves a real reply.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: DARVO denies the act, attacks you and casts the speaker as the victim. Whataboutism simply sets a different wrong beside yours. Blame-Shifting says your behavior caused the act at issue, while whataboutism leaves that act alone and talks about another. Denial claims nothing happened, which whataboutism does not.

codex_completed.name: Non-Apology Apology
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A statement that sounds like an apology but regrets your reaction or feelings, not the thing that was actually done.
codex_completed.short_definition: A statement that sounds like an apology but regrets your reaction or feelings, not the thing that was actually done.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A non-apology apology uses the word 'sorry' but does not own the action. The regret is aimed at your feelings, your reaction, or the situation, so the speaker never has to say 'I did that.' Common forms use an 'if', a 'but', or a 'you feel' to move the weight across. Some people were never taught how to apologize and sincerely think this counts. What matters is whether the action is named. A weak apology that does name it is still different from one that never does.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone says sorry, but the sorry is about how you took it, not what they did. You are left feeling that nothing was admitted.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: An apology is how people close a wound and rebuild trust. When the form is there and the substance is not, the hurt stays open and you may feel unreasonable for still being upset after being told sorry.
what_it_is: A statement of regret that points at your reaction or feelings, not at the act itself.
It often contains a hinge word: 'if' you were hurt, 'but' you started it, 'that you feel' this way.
It can be fluent and warm in tone, which makes it hard to explain why it feels empty.
It ends the conversation in the speaker's favor, because after 'sorry' you are expected to move on.
what_it_sounds_like: I'm sorry you feel that way.
I'm sorry if you were offended.
I'm sorry, but you started it.
I apologize that you took it the wrong way.
Sorry you're so upset about this.
I'm sorry you chose to be hurt by it.
Mistakes were made, and I'm sorry it came to this.
what_it_is_not: An imperfect apology that clearly names what was done, such as 'I'm sorry I forgot, that was careless of me'.
A speaker who does not yet understand why something hurt and says honestly, 'I'm sorry it hurt, and I want to understand what I did'.
A sincere expression of sympathy for how someone feels, offered where no wrongdoing is involved, such as at a loss.
A clumsy first attempt from someone who has not learned to apologize, followed by a better one once they are shown how.
An apology in a language or culture where regret is expressed through the situation instead of the person.
this_may_be_it_when: The sentence would still make sense if you removed the action from it entirely.
The word 'if' or 'but' sits right after 'sorry'.
Your reaction is described as the thing to be regretted.
You are expected to say it is fine as soon as it has been said.
The same thing happens again soon after, with the same kind of apology.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The speaker names the specific act, even awkwardly, in the same sentence.
They ask what they could do to put it right and then listen.
The first attempt falls short and they accept correction without defensiveness.
The behavior changes afterwards, whatever the wording.
The regret is about something outside their control, such as bad news, and no one is blamed.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people learned these phrases as children and use them without noticing what they leave out.
Fear of being shamed can make a person reach for vague wording that feels safer than naming the act.
Some formal or professional settings, such as customer service scripts or legal advice, push people toward cautious wording.
common_false_positives: A colleague who says 'I'm sorry this has been such a rough week for you' after a delay that was no one's fault.
A shy teenager who mumbles 'sorry about before' and means the specific thing you both know about.
A company statement that is vague because lawyers wrote it, from a person who privately apologizes properly later.
discernment_questions: Does the apology say what was done, in words that name the action?
Is the regret about my feelings or about their behavior?
Does the sentence have an 'if' or a 'but' that changes its meaning?
What changed after the apology, if anything?
If I explain what was missing, do they take it in or defend the original wording?
less_concerning_if: A second, fuller apology follows once you say what was missing.
The wording is clumsy, but the behavior shifts right away.
They can state back to you what they did and why it hurt.
more_concerning_if: You are told you must accept the apology and are pressured when you do not.
The apology is given with a reminder of your past mistakes, as a trade.
The same act, and the same sort of sorry, come around on a regular schedule.
pattern_over_time_signs: You have heard the same apology wording more than once for the same kind of event.
You have stopped asking for apologies because they never include the part you need.
You find yourself saying 'it's okay' without feeling that it is.
Old hurts stay open because nothing was ever acknowledged enough to close them.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair would include the action named in plain words, an acknowledgment that it was theirs, and something that changes afterwards, with nothing asked of you in return. An apology that asks you to feel better, mentions what you did, or repeats unchanged soon after does not close anything.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: What do they do when you ask for the action to be named? A second attempt that says what happened suggests it was heard. Being told you are impossible to please turns the request into a fault in you.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: The word 'sorry' carries social weight, and people tend to forgive on hearing it. A sentence with the shape of an apology but not its content can draw on that habit, so declining it feels rude, and attention shifts from what was done to how you respond.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe feeling dismissed even after being told sorry, unsure whether they may stay upset, and sometimes accepting the apology just to end the tension. Over time some stop expecting acknowledgment at all, and old hurts stay open because nothing closed them.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the missing piece: 'Thank you for saying sorry. Could you tell me what you are sorry for? I would like to hear the action named.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say plainly that it does not count yet: 'I appreciate the attempt, but that apology is about my feelings. I need one about what happened.'
response_options.disengagement: You do not have to accept an apology you did not receive. You can say 'I hear you' and leave it there until something more real arrives.
response_options.support_seeking: Read the apology aloud to a friend and ask what it admits. Hearing it from outside can confirm what felt missing and reduce self-doubt.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you need a record, ask in writing for a confirmation of what happened and what will change. Vague apologies in a workplace can be followed up with a specific, dated request.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Moving forward is what I want too. What I need is to hear what you did and that it was wrong, not that I feel upset. Can you try saying it that way?"
codex_completed.safety_note: A hollow apology is not itself a safety signal. It would matter more if it sits in a cycle where harm is followed by sorry, then by harm again, or if refusing to accept it brings anger or threats. In that case, speak to a trusted person or a domestic abuse advocate about the larger pattern.
misuse_warning: Marking every imperfect apology as a non-apology can punish people who are trying and failing at a hard skill. Check whether they name the act and change course.
Demanding exact words from someone, then rejecting each attempt, turns the label into a test no one can pass.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Blame-Shifting says your behavior caused theirs, while this tactic need not blame you at all: it regrets your feelings. DARVO denies, attacks and reverses roles. Denial refuses any wrongdoing, whereas here something like a concession is offered and then emptied of the one thing it should contain, the act.
