codex_completed.name: Shame Installation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Treating a person's mistake as proof that something is wrong with them as a whole, so shame replaces guilt.
codex_completed.short_definition: Treating a person's mistake as proof that something is wrong with them as a whole, so shame replaces guilt.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Guilt says 'I did something bad'. Shame says 'I am bad'. Shame installation is the repeated move from the first to the second: a mistake is treated as a verdict on the whole person, until the shame lives inside them and starts working without the other person present. One harsh 'what is wrong with you' on a bad day is common. The pattern is when every error becomes proof of a deep flaw.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A mistake gets treated as proof that something is wrong with you as a person, until the shame stays with you even when the other person is not there.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Guilt can lead to an apology and a repair. Shame often leads to hiding, which makes repair less likely. A person who believes they are the problem can find it hard to ask for help or to trust their own judgment.
what_it_is: Turning a particular action into a statement about the person's character or basic worth.
Delivered as moral disappointment or alarm, often in a heavy, serious voice rather than a sneer.
Reaching into the past, so old mistakes get brought back as evidence.
Can be aimed at needs, bodies, desires or history, such as asking for help, being sexual, or having had a hard childhood.
Different from honest criticism because it offers no way to put things right.
what_it_sounds_like: You should be ashamed of yourself.
What is wrong with you?
How can you even live with yourself?
Any normal person would know better.
I don't know who raised you.
After everything, this is who you really are.
Shame on you.
what_it_is_not: 'What's wrong with you?' as an exasperated idiom, said about a spilled drink and gone a minute later.
Guilt that comes from your own conscience after you really did hurt someone, which can be healthy.
A clear, serious statement that what you did was wrong, with an invitation to make amends.
A community or family naming a harm and expecting accountability for it.
A mentor being blunt about a serious professional error while still saying you can do better.
this_may_be_it_when: The criticism moves from what you did to what you are.
Old failures are listed as proof every time something new happens.
There is no stated way to repair it, only more disappointment.
You feel dirty or defective, not just sorry, after a conversation.
Ordinary needs or traits get treated as moral failings.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They say what was wrong, say what they'd like to see, and move on once it's done.
The disapproval is about a real harm and you agree it was one.
They put it in terms of the act, such as 'that was not okay'.
They are equally hard on their own errors in the same moral language.
You feel sorry and motivated to fix it, not diminished.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Some religious or cultural settings use strong moral language about conduct, which can feel shaming without being aimed at the person's worth.
A frightened parent may blurt harsh words when a child is in danger.
A friend who feels betrayed may lash out in the moment.
common_false_positives: A teacher firmly telling a student that cheating is wrong and that they are expected to do better.
Your own guilty conscience after you forgot something important.
A hurt friend saying 'that really hurt me', which describes impact and does not judge your worth.
discernment_questions: After the conversation, do I think 'I did something wrong' or 'I am something wrong'?
Is there something I could do to make it right, and would that be accepted?
Are old mistakes brought up as proof of who I am?
Do I feel the shame later when no one is saying it?
Would I speak this way to someone I loved who made the same mistake?
less_concerning_if: They name the act, say how it affected them, and let it go once addressed.
Your past errors are not used as ammunition in new disputes.
You can disagree with them without being told you are a bad person.
more_concerning_if: Shame is used to stop you from asking for things, like help, space or money.
It targets parts of you that cannot be changed, such as your body, background or sexuality.
You find yourself hiding ordinary things out of fear of how they will be judged.
pattern_over_time_signs: You apologize for existing, taking up room, or having needs.
You hear the critical voice when the person is not around.
You hide mistakes rather than risk the reaction.
You find it harder to accept kindness because you feel you do not deserve it.
codex_completed.repair_check: Watch whether past errors stay in the past. When something has shifted, a mistake gets talked about as a mistake, a way to fix it is offered, and the topic closes. An apology that is followed by 'but this is exactly what I'd expect from you' has just moved the shame to the next sentence.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: When you say you will answer for what you did but not for who you are, notice whether the conversation can stay on the act. Can they say what they want from you without a verdict? If each request ends with a statement about your character, the limit hasn't taken hold.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Shame is a social emotion and strongly tied to belonging, so being told you are fundamentally flawed can register as a threat to your place with the person. Because shame pushes people to hide and be small, it can weaken the very responses, such as explaining and repairing, that would resolve the matter. Repeated, the inner voice can carry the message on alone.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A heavy, physical sense of being defective is a common report, along with hiding mistakes, avoiding eye contact, and taking on blame in situations that were shared. Some become very hard on themselves. Others describe an unexpected relief when the difference between doing something wrong and being wrong was named, as though a weight had been put in the right place.

response_options.soft_clarification: Separate the act from the person: 'I can hear that what I did upset you. I'd like to talk about that, not about whether I'm a bad person.'
response_options.firm_boundary: State the limit on verdicts: 'I'll take responsibility for what I did. I won't agree that something is wrong with me as a person.'
response_options.disengagement: When it shifts to your character, stop defending yourself point by point. Let silence or a topic change signal that the conversation stays on actions.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a trusted person what was said word for word and ask how it sounds to them. A counselor can also help separate fair guilt from borrowed shame.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask for feedback in terms of specific tasks and examples, and write down remarks about your character or worth, with dates, if they continue.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I did get that wrong, and I'm willing to fix it. What I won't do is accept that the mistake says something terrible about who I am. Let's talk about what happened and what would make it right."
codex_completed.safety_note: Shaming alone is a harm to self-worth rather than physical danger, but it deserves care if you are starting to believe you deserve mistreatment or have thoughts of hurting yourself. In that case, contact a crisis line or a mental health professional promptly. It also changes if shaming is paired with threats, isolation or control of money.
misuse_warning: Calling every strong moral disapproval 'shaming' can excuse real wrongdoing from being named. Accountability for an act is different from an attack on your worth.
Telling someone 'you are shaming me' to deflect a legitimate complaint turns the label into a way to avoid hearing it.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Contempt shows scorn and superiority, often in a sneer, while shame installation speaks in the language of moral failure and disappointment. Emotional Invalidation disputes your feelings; shame installation disputes your worth. Comparative Devaluation holds you against another person, but here the standard is not a person but a vague idea of what a decent human would be.

codex_completed.name: Intimidation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Using a hint or open warning of unwelcome consequences to push someone toward giving in or staying quiet.
codex_completed.short_definition: Using a hint or open warning of unwelcome consequences to push someone toward giving in or staying quiet.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Intimidation works through fear of what might happen next. The threat can be spoken ('you'll regret this'), hinted at ('you know what I'm capable of'), or carried by body and surroundings, such as standing over you or blocking a door. The consequence is often left vague, which does more work than any detail would. A person who is only upset is not doing this. The pattern is fear attached to your saying no or disagreeing.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone makes you afraid of what will happen if you disagree or say no, whether by saying it outright or by hinting at it.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: When you comply out of fear, the other person may never learn whether you agree, and you may stop saying what you think at all. The fear can also grow, because the unspoken consequence never needs to be tested to keep working.
what_it_is: A stated or implied warning of unwelcome consequences, tied to what you decide or say.
Often vague, such as 'you'll see', and a vague threat leaves the imagination to fill in the worst.
Can be carried by posture and objects: standing close, slamming things, blocking the doorway, driving aggressively.
Can be social or practical as well as physical, such as hints about your job, immigration status, children or reputation.
Different from anger, because it is about making you afraid to continue.
what_it_sounds_like: You don't want to see me angry.
Keep pushing and find out what happens.
You'll regret this.
You don't know what I might do.
Nice life you've got here. It would be a shame if something happened to it.
A hand slammed on the table, then a quiet 'say that again'.
I know where you work and what time you leave.
what_it_is_not: A plain statement of a real consequence, said without heat, such as 'if the rent isn't paid, the landlord will start eviction.'
A person saying they are very angry and need to leave the room to calm down.
A prediction of how someone else will react: 'if you tell your boss that way, you'll regret it.'
A firm boundary with an ordinary consequence, such as 'I won't ride with you if you've been drinking.'
Someone venting a frightening-sounding sentence during a rage and then horrified by it afterward, which is still serious but different from a campaign to control you.
this_may_be_it_when: The warning comes just when you say no, push back, or ask a question.
You change what you do because of what might happen, not because you agree.
Their body, voice or surroundings are used to make a point, such as blocking, looming, or breaking things.
The consequence is left vague but you feel the weight of it.
Others have noticed you go quiet or defer around this person.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The 'consequence' is something they have no part in and they said it as information.
They are visibly frightened or upset by their own words and take them back.
You can disagree and nothing about their behavior toward you changes.
The warning is something they would equally apply to themselves.
No one is afraid at the end of the conversation, including you.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People use dramatic phrases in anger that they would not follow through on, though they can still frighten.
A person who sets a normal consequence, like ending a lease, may sound harsh without any intent to scare.
Cultural or family styles of loud talk can sound threatening to outsiders.
common_false_positives: A parent saying 'if you don't wear a coat, you'll be cold'.
A manager reminding staff that missing the deadline has contract penalties.
A friend saying 'I'm so angry I could scream', which is about feeling, not about you.
discernment_questions: Am I afraid of what will happen if I disagree, or just uncomfortable with the disagreement?
Do I change my decisions because of what this person might do?
Is the consequence ever spelled out, or does the vagueness itself carry the message?
Have I felt unsafe in my body around this person, such as when they stand close or block a path?
Would a friend hearing this exchange be alarmed?
less_concerning_if: The consequence named is a normal, specific one that applies to everyone involved.
You can say no and nothing changes in how you are treated.
They notice your fear, stop, and ask what is going on.
more_concerning_if: The hints concern something you cannot easily replace, such as your home, children, status or income.
There has been any physical act, such as throwing, grabbing or cornering, alongside the words.
The warnings are getting more specific, or the person knows details about where you go and when.
pattern_over_time_signs: You scan their mood on arrival and adjust what you say before speaking.
You agree to things you do not want in order to avoid the build-up.
You have stopped bringing up certain subjects at all.
Friends or family notice that you seem on edge or have become quieter.
codex_completed.repair_check: Real change here is visible in how disagreement is handled: you can say no, and the person stays calm and takes it. Gifts, tears and promises made after a scare do not show that, and a pattern that also includes control of your phone, money or movement needs outside help, not a private agreement.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Because the reaction may be unsafe, look back at earlier times you disagreed and judge the risk from that. A past of calm acceptance is reassuring. A past of fear, sulking, retaliation or damage should be taken seriously before you test a limit directly.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Fear narrows attention and pushes people toward whatever feels safest in the moment, often giving in or going quiet. A vague warning can be especially effective because the mind fills in the worst. When compliance is followed by relief, people can learn to avoid triggering the warning, which means the threat works even when it is not repeated.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Many report living on alert: a racing heart when a certain tone appears, rehearsing how to avoid setting someone off, and giving up preferences they once had. Some feel ashamed of 'letting' it happen, though going along with a threat is a common response to fear. Trouble sleeping or concentrating, and a habit of checking exits, are also mentioned.

response_options.soft_clarification: Stay inside the conversation and keep it calm: 'I want to hear what you need. Can you tell me what you'd like me to do?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Name the effect without accusing: 'I find it hard to think when the conversation feels like a warning. Can we slow down and take this one point at a time?'
response_options.disengagement: Ask for a pause in ordinary terms, such as a drink of water or a call to a friend, and use that time to think about your safety. Decide privately, with an advocate, what comes next.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a trusted person or a domestic violence advocate exactly what was said and done, and ask them to help you think about safety before the next conflict.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work or in a professional setting, write down the date, words and witnesses, keep copies, and report to HR, a union rep or a regulator rather than confronting the person alone.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "My thinking is getting cloudy, and I want to keep talking about this. Could we take a short break and come back to it, or could someone else sit in with us?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Threats, blocked doors, damaged property, or hints about knowing where you go can sit alongside physical danger. Keep a private record, tell someone you trust, and avoid announcing plans to leave or confronting the person. A domestic violence advocate can help you plan safely, and if you are in immediate danger, call your local emergency number.
misuse_warning: Calling any stated consequence a threat can make honest warnings, like a landlord's notice or a parent's rule, look sinister. Look for fear attached to your saying no.
Labeling someone as a person who intimidates, rather than describing what was said, can escalate a situation. Describe the words and actions you saw.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Baiting provokes you so that your reaction can be used against you, while intimidation works through fear to stop or steer you. Contempt looks down on you and need not threaten anything. Shame Installation attacks your worth; intimidation points to what might be done to you or taken from you.

codex_completed.name: Triangulation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Bringing a third person, real or invented, into a two-person disagreement so their supposed opinion carries the argument.
codex_completed.short_definition: Bringing a third person, real or invented, into a two-person disagreement so their supposed opinion carries the argument.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Triangulation turns a disagreement between two people into a contest with an audience. The speaker quotes a mother, a coworker, a friend or an unnamed 'everyone' as backing, so the other person faces a crowd instead of a single complaint. The third person may be real, exaggerated or made up, and often does not know their words are being used. One mention of someone else's view means little. It becomes a habit when outside voices keep arriving in place of the speaker's own position.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Instead of saying what they think, someone keeps telling you that other people agree with them, so a two-person problem starts to feel like you against a group.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You end up arguing with people who are not in the room and cannot be questioned. It becomes hard to know what anyone actually said, and relationships with the people being quoted can sour without a word being exchanged with them.
what_it_is: Citing a named person's opinion of you as proof in an argument, such as 'Even your sister thinks so'.
Reporting what a third person said about you in a way that sets the two of you against each other.
Using an unnamed crowd ('people are saying', 'everyone has noticed') that cannot be checked or asked.
Carrying messages back and forth so that two other people form a view of one another through the middle person.
what_it_sounds_like: Even your mother thinks you were out of line.
Dana told me what you said about me at lunch.
I've talked to the whole team and none of them see it your way.
Ask anyone. They'll all tell you the same thing.
Your brother called me last night, and he agrees with me.
I'm not the only one who feels this way, you know.
Marcus says you've been talking behind my back.
what_it_is_not: A person who says 'I talked this over with my sister and she gave me a useful angle' while owning the view as their own.
A group conversation, such as a family meeting, that everyone knowingly joined to settle something together.
A caring group raising a worry directly and openly with someone, for example friends speaking up about a risky situation.
Venting to a close friend after a hard day, with no plan to bring the friend's opinion back as proof.
A mediator or manager who is brought in by agreement and hears both sides.
this_may_be_it_when: Other people's views are announced to you as a verdict rather than offered as one perspective.
The quoted third person, when you ask them, says they never said it or were told something different.
The speaker avoids saying what they personally want and keeps pointing to what others think.
You learn a mutual friend or relative has been given a one-sided account before you were told there was a problem.
Two people who used to get along start distrusting each other after both talked to the same go-between.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They name the person, say what was actually said, and invite you to ask that person yourself.
The third person raised the concern on their own, and the speaker is passing it along because it matters.
They state their own view first and mention another's only as a side note.
The other people involved are openly present and speaking for themselves.
It was a single mention during a heated moment and was not repeated or used again.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People often seek advice from family and friends, and it is natural to mention what they said.
Someone who feels outnumbered or unsure of themselves may reach for others' views to feel steadier.
A group of people may truly share a concern, and one person ends up as the messenger without any plan.
common_false_positives: A parent who says 'your grandmother and I are both worried' about a real problem and then asks what you need.
Coworkers who have each separately mentioned the same missed deadline to a lead who then raises it with you.
A friend who admits 'I asked my roommate for a second opinion' and tells you exactly what was said.
discernment_questions: If you asked the third person directly, would they confirm what was said and how it was meant?
Does the speaker ever say what they themselves think and want, or only what others think?
Were those other people invited into the matter, or recruited after it began?
Does the outside opinion arrive as one view among several, or as the final word?
Has a relationship with a mutual friend or relative cooled because of things relayed through someone else?
less_concerning_if: The speaker is happy for you to speak with the people they mention.
Other people's views come up rarely and as context, not as proof you must accept.
When it turns out a quote was wrong, they correct it and drop the point.
more_concerning_if: The quoted people turn out to have been misrepresented, or never existed.
You are cut off from the people mentioned, so their side cannot be checked.
Several relationships in your circle have been shaped by one person's retelling.
pattern_over_time_signs: Arguments increasingly start with 'we all think' instead of 'I feel'.
You learn of conflicts between you and others that you did not know existed until a go-between brought them up.
You start preparing for every disagreement as though facing a panel instead of one person.
Friends or relatives report hearing a version of events from the speaker that you have never heard yourself.
codex_completed.repair_check: A real change shows up when they begin speaking for themselves and stop citing a chorus. Checking a quote with the person who supposedly said it, and correcting it if wrong, is a meaningful step. An apology that still ends with 'but everyone agrees with me' is not.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask the speaker to keep this between the two of you, and then see whether a mutual friend brings it up with you a week later. Honoring the request looks like quiet. Going around it looks like the same message arriving through someone else.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A group's apparent opinion tends to carry weight, and standing alone against several voices is uncomfortable. Opinions relayed secondhand are hard to test, so the receiver may defer rather than risk being the odd one out. It can also strain the bond between the receiver and the people quoted, leaving the speaker as the only trusted source.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Being outnumbered in a conversation that was meant for two is what many describe. Some feel a rush of dread when a friend's name is mentioned, some grow wary of relatives they once trusted, and some stop raising problems at all because they expect to meet a crowd in reply.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the speaker's own position: 'I'd like to hear what you think, separate from what other people said. What is bothering you?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to argue against people who are absent: 'I'm not going to debate what someone else supposedly said. If it matters, I'll ask them directly.'
response_options.disengagement: Pause the conversation when the list of other people's opinions begins, and return to it only if the speaker is willing to talk about their own view.
response_options.support_seeking: Check a quoted statement by asking the person it came from, in a neutral way. Confirming or correcting it for yourself restores your footing.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask that feedback be given directly and in writing with specific examples, instead of 'the team feels', and ask who is raising the concern.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I want to hear your concern, but I can't answer for what other people think. Tell me what bothers you, and if someone else's view matters here, I'll ask them myself."
codex_completed.safety_note: Being quoted against by a crowd is distressing but is not a physical-safety signal alone. It changes if the recruited group is used to track where you are, to keep you from leaving a house or a job, or to pressure you about money or children. In that case, speak with an advocate or a legal aid service before replying to anyone.
misuse_warning: Labeling any mention of a friend's opinion as triangulation can shut down normal advice-seeking. The label fits when outside voices replace a person's own position, not whenever others are consulted.
Assuming a quoted third party is lying, without asking them, can create the very distrust the pattern is known for.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Flying Monkeys are third parties who act, such as pressing or watching you, often without knowing why; triangulation uses their words as evidence against you. Forced Teaming claims a shared 'we' that binds you and needs no third voice at all. Concern Trolling uses worry as the vehicle. Triangulation stands apart because the argument is carried by someone who is not in the room.

Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Forced Teaming
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Declaring a shared 'we' that the other person never agreed to, so a separate choice starts to look like betrayal.
codex_completed.short_definition: Declaring a shared 'we' that the other person never agreed to, so a separate choice starts to look like betrayal.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Forced Teaming means announcing a partnership, a shared cause or a common enemy and then treating the other person as already enrolled. Once 'we' is established, saying no feels like deserting the team, and obligations attach that nobody asked you about. Healthy teams form by invitation and can be declined. A single 'we' in conversation is ordinary speech. It becomes forced when the 'we' arrives first, the request follows, and your own preference is treated as disloyalty.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone says 'we' for you, such as 'we need to deal with this', and then acts as if you have already signed up, so saying no feels like letting the team down.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Obligations you never accepted can pile up under a word that sounds warm. Declining then costs you the belonging you were offered, so people often go along to avoid being cast out of the 'we'.
what_it_is: Announcing a joint project or shared problem before the other person has said yes.
Treating a quick act of kindness as proof that you have joined a long-term alliance.
Building a shared enemy, such as 'us against them', so that dissent feels like crossing sides.
Using 'we' to assign tasks, costs or secrecy without discussing them first.
what_it_sounds_like: We're in this together whether you like it or not.
People like us have to stick together.
It's us against the world.
We both know what we have to do about this.
After everything we've been through, you can't back out now.
We've decided to handle this ourselves, so don't mention it to anyone.
Come on, we're a team. Teams don't ask questions.
what_it_is_not: A genuine invitation such as 'Would you like to work on this with me?', where a no is welcome.
Ordinary team language at a shared job, where roles were assigned openly and everyone knows what they signed up for.
A couple or friends who use 'we' because they actually decided something jointly.
An enthusiastic person who says 'we should do this' as a suggestion and drops it when you are not keen.
A coach or organizer who builds team spirit, but allows people to leave or opt out of particular tasks.
this_may_be_it_when: The 'we' is stated as a fact before you were asked anything.
Your reluctance is described as selfishness, disloyalty or abandonment of the group.
The shared cause grows to include a list of things you are expected to do, give or keep quiet about.
A common outsider is named, and questioning the plan is treated as siding with them.
You notice you rarely get to be asked first and mostly learn about commitments after they are made.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You were asked, you said yes, and you can still say no to specific parts.
The group's goals, costs and roles were laid out openly before anyone committed.
Your hesitation is met with questions about what would make it work for you.
The shared 'we' is a figure of speech and nothing is demanded in its name.
Others in the group also decline things and nothing bad follows.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Enthusiastic people often say 'we' loosely when they mean 'I would love it if we did'.
Close families and long-term couples really do share many obligations, and the language reflects that.
Some cultures and workplaces use collective speech as a warm default, with no pressure behind it.
common_false_positives: A manager who says 'we need to finish by Friday' about a deadline that really does belong to the whole team.
A friend who says 'we should move in together' as a hopeful idea and is fine when you want to wait.
A sports captain who rallies the squad with 'we win together' while excusing a player who needs a break.
discernment_questions: Did anyone ask whether you wanted to join, or was the 'we' simply announced?
Can you decline one part of the plan without being treated as leaving the whole group?
Who gains from the joint effort, and who carries most of the cost?
Is there a shared enemy, and does disagreeing with the plan get described as taking that enemy's side?
Do you find yourself saying yes to avoid being called disloyal?
less_concerning_if: The invitation is open and a refusal changes nothing in how you are treated.
The costs and expectations of the joint effort were explained up front.
Several members freely opt out of parts without any penalty.
more_concerning_if: The 'we' is used to keep secrets, move money or make promises on your behalf.
Dropping out is described as a betrayal that others will hear about.
The shared cause narrows your contact with people outside it.
pattern_over_time_signs: More and more of your time and money goes to causes you only joined by default.
You start checking in with the other person before making small decisions of your own.
Past kindnesses are cited as proof that you owe loyalty now.
Friendships outside the 'team' have thinned, and mentioning them draws sarcasm.
codex_completed.repair_check: Change looks like asking before assigning, and accepting a no without sulking. If the next joint plan begins with a question and ends without a penalty when you decline, something shifted. A warm speech about how much you mean to the team does not count.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Try declining one specific task while staying friendly. Does the 'we' stretch to include your no, or does the mood turn cold until you comply? How the temperature changes in the hours after tells you more than the words said at the time.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Belonging is a strong human need, and being offered a place in a close pair or group is a gift. Being welcomed in first may make a later refusal seem like handing that gift back. Naming a common enemy can raise the felt cost of disagreeing, because dissent starts to look like switching sides.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe saying yes and resenting it later, feeling bound by promises they cannot remember making, and a quiet guilt whenever they want something separate. Some say they stopped being able to tell their own wishes from the team's, and some describe relief when a team they never chose finally let them go.

response_options.soft_clarification: Separate the invitation from the assumption: 'I didn't realize we'd agreed on this. Can you tell me what you're hoping I'll do?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline the part you do not want and leave the relationship intact: 'I'm glad to help with that piece, but I'm not signing up for the rest.'
response_options.disengagement: Step back from the shared project or group chat for a while without explaining your whole case, and see whether the 'we' still stands without you.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend outside the group exactly what you were expected to do and ask if it sounds like something you agreed to.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask for roles, deadlines and decision rights in writing before taking on shared work, and note in an email what you accepted and what you did not.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I like working with you, and I also need to be asked before I'm counted in. I'm in for this part. I'm not agreeing to the rest, and I'd like us to talk about it as two separate people."
codex_completed.safety_note: A forced 'we' alone is not usually dangerous. It becomes serious when the shared cause is used to get access to your money, accounts, home or immigration papers, or to keep you from outside contact. If joint finances or secrecy are involved, a legal aid service or a financial counselor can help you review the arrangement before signing anything more.
misuse_warning: Calling any enthusiastic 'we' manipulation can make you suspicious of normal teamwork and of people who are simply eager.
Using the label to avoid commitments you did agree to turns a real pattern into an excuse.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: "We're Family" Erasure leans on a blood or marriage tie to override your answer, while forced teaming can be built with strangers, coworkers or new friends. Triangulation brings in a third voice as proof, and forced teaming needs only the word 'we'. Flying Monkeys carry out someone's wishes on their behalf, whereas forced teaming makes you the one expected to carry them.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Actively matched against pasted text by this tool, at low confidence. Phrase matching can flag wording, but it cannot know intent, tone, history, context, or whether the claim is even true — an innocent reading is always attached to every match. Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: "We're Family" Erasure
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Invoking family loyalty so that fairness, limits and the right to say no no longer seem to apply between relatives.
codex_completed.short_definition: Invoking family loyalty so that fairness, limits and the right to say no no longer seem to apply between relatives.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: This pattern uses the word 'family' as a trump card. A request for money, labor, time or silence is made, and a limit is answered with 'but we're family', as though the bond cancels the limit. Family can mean real generosity, and giving freely to relatives is common and good. It becomes erasure when the bond is invoked mainly to override a no, when the giving runs one way, and when asking for fairness is treated as proof you do not love them.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A relative says 'we're family' to shut down your limit or your sense of what is fair, so the closeness becomes a reason you cannot say no.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The people you love most can be the hardest to refuse. When the family bond is used to cancel every limit, you may give up money, time and peace, and feel guilty for even wanting fairness.
what_it_is: Answering a limit, such as a price, a schedule or a boundary, with a reminder of blood or marriage ties.
Expecting free work, loans or childcare from relatives while treating payment or a repayment plan as an insult.
Treating privacy, personal space or a decision about your own life as something that family has a right to override.
Making giving flow in one direction, with some members always providing and others always receiving.
what_it_sounds_like: We're family, so you can't say no.
Family doesn't need boundaries.
You can't charge your own cousin.
Blood is thicker than water.
I can't believe you'd make your own mother ask twice.
In this family we don't keep score.
After all we've done for you, this is how you repay us?
what_it_is_not: A relative who says 'we're family, I'd love to help' and genuinely accepts it if you cannot.
A family where help flows in every direction over the years and everyone knows it evens out.
A relative who is truly in a crisis and asks once for help, with openness about what they can do in return.
A cultural or religious tradition of shared duty that everyone in the household values and chooses to honor.
An older relative who feels hurt by distance and says so, without demanding that you drop your limits.
this_may_be_it_when: 'Family' is mentioned right after you state a limit and almost never in other conversations.
You are expected to provide money or time, but your own needs get no matching attention.
Your request for a written agreement, repayment date or fair split is taken as an accusation of not caring.
Others who have given less are never asked to give more.
You find yourself paying for peace, and feeling guilty about the cost.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They accept a no calmly and still treat you warmly afterward.
The family has talked about what each person gives, and everyone agreed to the arrangement.
Family loyalty is mentioned warmly as a value and not as an answer to your objection.
Your relative returns favors, even if not in the same currency.
You honestly want to help and the discomfort is about your own limits, which they have not pushed against.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: In many families, sharing resources without counting is a cherished norm that works well for those involved.
A relative may be asking out of real need and not know how else to phrase it.
Grief, an illness or a family event can raise the emotional stakes of a request that is otherwise ordinary.
common_false_positives: An aunt who asks you to help move and says 'that's what family is for', but thanks you and does the same for you.
Siblings who share the cost of a parent's care by an arrangement they all made.
A grandparent who asks for more visits, is told you are busy this month, and says 'I understand, call when you can'.
discernment_questions: When you state a limit, does 'family' come up as the answer?
Does giving go both ways, or have you always been the one who gives?
Would the same request feel fair if a friend or neighbor made it?
Can you ask for repayment, a schedule or a written agreement without being called cold?
Do other relatives face the same expectations, or are you the one who is always asked?
less_concerning_if: A relative can hear 'not this time' without it turning into a family crisis.
Help is offered back when you are the one who needs it.
The family talks about fairness openly and adjusts when someone is stretched.
more_concerning_if: Your money, home, legal signature or children are drawn in under the banner of loyalty.
Saying no leads to other relatives being enlisted to pressure you.
You are warned that you will be left out of the family if you hold your ground.
pattern_over_time_signs: The same relatives get the same yes from you year after year, and the cost keeps increasing.
Loans to family are never mentioned again, and asking about them gets a cold reaction.
Holidays and family events become occasions to be asked for something.
You rehearse excuses so that you do not have to say 'no' to a relative's face.
codex_completed.repair_check: Look for a relative who asks first, accepts a no, and then pays back or reciprocates without being chased. Agreeing to put a loan in writing counts. A tearful 'I only did it because I love you' that ends with the same request does not.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: State the limit once and notice what happens at the next gathering. Are you still welcome at the table and treated normally, or is there a coolness, a guilt-laden remark or a relative sent to talk you round? Respect shows in how ordinary things stay.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Most people are taught early that family is where loyalty is supposed to be unconditional, and that teaching can be strong enough that a limit feels like a betrayal of who you are. When the word is attached to a request, refusing it can feel less like a choice and more like breaking a moral rule. Guilt does much of the work.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe giving until they are exhausted and resentful, then feeling ashamed of the resentment. Some say they dread phone calls from certain relatives, and some say they cannot tell whether they actually want to help or simply cannot bear the guilt. Grief for the family they hoped for is common.

response_options.soft_clarification: Say what you can offer and what you cannot: 'I love you, and I can lend a hand on Saturday. I can't lend money this time.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold the limit without arguing about loyalty: 'Being family doesn't change what I can afford. My answer is still no, and I'm glad to see you at dinner.'
response_options.disengagement: Take a break from calls or gatherings where the request will come up, and let your answer stay as it was without repeating it.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk with a sibling, cousin or friend who has seen the pattern, or a counselor who works with families, and check whether your limits sound fair to them.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If relatives are in your business or workplace, put pay, roles and hours in writing, and separate family events from work matters.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I do love you, and being family doesn't change what I'm able to give. I can't do this one, and I'd rather say so plainly than say yes and resent it. Let's find something that works for both of us."
codex_completed.safety_note: Usually this is a painful family dynamic and not an emergency. It turns more serious when 'family' is used to get your signature on loans or property, to take your income, or to put children or housing at stake. Before signing anything, speak with a legal aid service or a financial counselor, and keep copies of what you were asked to sign.
misuse_warning: Calling every family request 'erasure' can leave you cut off from relatives who simply need help and ask in a clumsy way.
Using the phrase to cover a limit you could have discussed gently can harden a conflict that a calm talk might settle.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Forced Teaming builds a 'we' out of nothing, between people who may barely know each other, while this pattern borrows an existing bond to cancel a limit. Triangulation uses a third person's opinion as the weight, and here the weight is the relationship itself. Concern Trolling wraps a directive in worry, and this one wraps it in duty.

Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Concern Trolling
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Voicing worry for someone's wellbeing as the cover for telling them what to do, so refusing the advice looks like harming themselves.
codex_completed.short_definition: Voicing worry for someone's wellbeing as the cover for telling them what to do, so refusing the advice looks like harming themselves.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Concern Trolling wraps a directive in the language of care. The speaker says they are worried, and the worry always leads to a specific instruction about your job, your body, your partner or your choices. If you decline, you are told that you are being reckless or in denial, which makes it hard to push back without looking careless. Real concern is offered once and leaves the decision with you. Here the worry keeps pointing toward what the speaker wants.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone says they are worried about you, but the worry always ends in an order, and if you say no, they act as if you are hurting yourself.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Care is hard to argue with, so a directive dressed as care leaves you with two bad choices: comply, or be treated as someone who cannot look after themselves. Over time you may stop trusting your own judgment.
what_it_is: Expressing worry that always ends with the same recommendation, such as quitting, ending a friendship or changing how you look.
Describing your decisions as signs that you are not coping, which makes the advice look like a rescue.
Mentioning that 'everyone has noticed' or is 'concerned' to make the worry seem widespread.
Treating each refusal as new evidence that you need to be helped.
what_it_sounds_like: I'm only saying this because I worry about you.
As your friend, I have to say everyone's noticed.
I'm just worried, which is why you really should quit that job.
As someone who cares about you, I can't watch you do this.
You've seemed so off lately. I think you need to cut her out.
If you cared about your health you'd listen to me.
I'd hate for you to regret this. Please just trust me on it.
what_it_is_not: A friend who says 'I'm worried about you' once, asks if you want advice, and accepts it if you say no.
A doctor, therapist or other professional giving health guidance as part of their role.
Family members raising a serious worry together, such as a safety concern, and asking what you want from them.
Someone who offers practical help, such as a ride or a meal, without attaching conditions.
A worry that is repeated because the situation is truly getting worse and is still offered as concern, not as an order.
this_may_be_it_when: The worry is always followed by the same instruction, whatever the topic.
When you say no, the concern grows louder or turns to 'you are in denial'.
The person never asks what you think or what you need.
The suggested fix happens to benefit the speaker, such as ending a friendship they dislike.
Your reasons are dismissed as symptoms of the problem the speaker is worried about.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The person asks 'do you want input or just a listener?' and honors your answer.
They raise the worry once and let it go when you say you have heard it.
The advice does not benefit them in any way and they offer to help whichever way you decide.
Their worry is about a risk you also see, and the conversation is about options and not orders.
They tell you what they noticed and leave out any claim about what is wrong with you.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People who care often fumble the delivery, and an awkward 'you should' can come from fear and love.
Some cultures and families express affection through direct advice, which can sound pushy and be meant kindly.
A friend who has been through the same thing may be speaking from hard experience.
common_false_positives: A coworker who says 'you've been working late all month, are you OK?' and leaves it there.
A sibling who says 'I'm worried about your drinking' once, with specifics, and offers to go with you to a doctor.
A friend who disagrees with your partner choice, says so kindly one time, and then stays supportive.
discernment_questions: Does the worry come with a specific instruction, and does it point the same way each time?
What happens when you decline the advice: respect, or a heavier dose of worry?
Does the person ask what you want from the conversation?
Would the speaker gain something if you did what they suggest?
Can you picture saying 'I've heard you, and I'm choosing differently' and the matter ending there?
less_concerning_if: The concern is stated once, with specifics, and then left with you.
The person keeps being kind after you choose differently.
They ask what would help instead of what you should do.
more_concerning_if: The worry is shared with others so that your choices are discussed without you.
Refusal is met with threats to withdraw support, contact, or approval.
The concern targets your friends, your money or your movements.
pattern_over_time_signs: The same worry returns every few weeks, a little louder each time.
You start hiding decisions from this person so that you do not have to hear the concern.
Other people begin to repeat the same worry, and you suspect it came from one source.
You notice that you second-guess ordinary choices because you expect the response.
codex_completed.repair_check: Look for concern that changes shape once you name it: a question replaces the directive, and your answer is allowed to stand. Someone who says 'I get it, it's your call' and then stops has changed. A new round of worry framed as an apology has not.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: What happens in the week after you say 'thanks, I've got it'? Does the topic rest, or does it come back through a different door, such as a mutual friend or a gentle email? Respect leaves the matter alone.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Concern is hard to push against because refusing it seems ungrateful. When worry is attached to an instruction, saying no may sound like admitting the speaker is right about you. Repeated worry can also plant a seed of doubt, so you begin to wonder whether you really are not coping, which makes the directive easier to accept.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Cornered by kindness, unable to say no without seeming defensive: that is how many put it. Some start hiding choices to avoid the speech, some feel guilty for being annoyed at someone who 'only cares', and some begin to doubt whether their own judgment can be trusted at all.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask what they need from you: 'Thanks for caring. Are you telling me what you've noticed, or asking me to do something specific?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Acknowledge the care and decline the instruction: 'I know you mean well. I've heard you, and I've decided. Please don't bring it up again.'
response_options.disengagement: Change the subject or end the call when the worry begins again, and do it kindly, without debating whether you are fine.
response_options.support_seeking: Share the specific advice with someone you trust and ask whether it matches your own view, or whether you are reacting to pressure.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a colleague or manager frames direction as worry, ask for feedback in terms of work expectations and put any agreed changes in writing.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I can tell you care, and I'm grateful. I've thought about what you said, and I'm making a different choice. I'd like you to trust me with it, and I'll tell you if I want your help."
codex_completed.safety_note: Worry about someone is normally harmless. Take it more seriously if the 'concern' is used to justify checking your phone, controlling your money, deciding who you see, or escalating when you decline. If that begins, talk with someone outside the relationship, such as a counselor or a domestic abuse advocate, about what you are experiencing.
misuse_warning: Dismissing every worried friend as a concern troll can leave you ignoring a warning you needed to hear. Real concern is common.
Using the label to wave off a doctor, therapist or someone with relevant experience can cost you good advice.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Flying Monkeys carry pressure on someone else's behalf; concern trolling is delivered by the person who wants the outcome. Triangulation brings in outside voices as proof, and concern trolling may use one voice, the speaker's own, and call it care. "We're Family" Erasure cancels a limit by appeal to duty, and this one cancels it by appeal to worry for your own good.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Actively matched against pasted text by this tool, at low confidence. Phrase matching can flag wording, but it cannot know intent, tone, history, context, or whether the claim is even true — an innocent reading is always attached to every match. Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Ultimatums
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Demanding that someone pick one of two outcomes immediately, with a loss attached to the option the speaker does not want.
codex_completed.short_definition: Demanding that someone pick one of two outcomes immediately, with a loss attached to the option the speaker does not want.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: An ultimatum states a demand and names what will be lost if it is not met, often with a deadline or no room to reply. Honest limits can be worded this way too, so the form alone proves little. What marks the pattern is that the choice is sprung suddenly, the loss is aimed at you rather than at the speaker's own wellbeing, and other options are kept out of view. Repeated use can teach a household that every disagreement ends in a deal-or-else.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone hands you two choices, one of them painful, and expects an answer on the spot instead of a conversation.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A decision made with a loss hanging over it is rarely a free one. You may agree to things you would have weighed differently, and you may stop raising concerns at all, because every concern risks turning into a showdown.
what_it_is: A demand paired with a named loss, such as the end of a friendship, a job offer, a move, or a relationship.
Often delivered at the peak of an argument, when neither person is thinking clearly.
Aimed at what you are asked to give up or do, rather than at what the speaker will do to look after themselves.
Frequently arrives with a clock: tonight, by Friday, before the party.
Sometimes dressed up as a question, as in 'So what is it going to be?'
what_it_sounds_like: It's me or your sister. Pick.
Quit the band by Friday or we're done.
Hand over your password or don't bother coming home.
This is your last chance. Last one.
Either you sign it tonight or I'm telling everyone why.
I'm not asking twice. Yes or no.
Choose: your mother or me.
what_it_is_not: A boundary about the speaker's own wellbeing, such as 'I can't stay in the room while there is shouting, so I'm going to step out.'
A deadline set by the outside world, such as a lease renewal, a job offer that expires, or a visa date.
A dealbreaker stated calmly after long thought, with room to talk about it, such as 'I do not want children, and I need to know where you stand.'
A parent or manager naming a real consequence that follows from a rule everyone already knew.
A heated 'I can't take this anymore' said once in tears and taken back or explained afterward.
this_may_be_it_when: The demand concerns your friends, family, work, or phone rather than anything the speaker does themselves.
The loss named is out of proportion to the issue, such as ending a marriage over a weekend plan.
You are given hours, or minutes, to answer a question that would normally take weeks.
Asking for a day to think is treated as a refusal.
The threatened loss has been named before in earlier fights without being carried out, and used again anyway.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The speaker is describing what they will do for their own safety or peace, and asks nothing of you in return.
You are free to say no and the conversation goes on afterward.
The deadline comes from a third party and both of you are under it.
They offer to talk it through before you have to answer.
The limit was told to you well in advance, in a calm moment, and has not changed.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A person at the end of their rope may blurt out a hard line they do not fully mean, then walk it back.
Some people who have been ignored for a long time reach for a firm statement because earlier requests did not land.
A real dealbreaker, such as wanting children or moving cities, can sound like an ultimatum even when it is stated honestly.
common_false_positives: A friend saying 'I can't keep covering your rent, so this is the last month I can do it.'
An employer saying the position closes on a set date and the offer will lapse after it.
A partner who says 'I need us to see a counselor, or I think I will struggle to stay,' after months of trying other things.
discernment_questions: Is the loss being named something the speaker will do for their own wellbeing, or something meant to pressure you?
If I asked for a few days, would the answer be yes?
Were there other options that nobody mentioned because the demand was shaped as two doors only?
Has this same kind of demand shown up in earlier fights, and what happened after I gave in?
Would I be making this choice if the loss were not hanging over it?
less_concerning_if: The limit is stated once, calmly, and the speaker is willing to discuss how to get there.
The deadline belongs to the outside world and both of you are working against it.
They accept a 'not yet' without punishing it.
more_concerning_if: The ultimatums grow more frequent and more extreme over time, covering contact with family, money, or your phone.
The named loss is something you depend on, such as housing, children, income, or your standing in a community.
Refusing leads to the loss actually being inflicted, which teaches that the next demand is real too.
pattern_over_time_signs: You have stopped bringing up disagreements because you can predict how they will end.
Concessions pile up that you made at the deadline and later regretted.
The size of what is demanded creeps up, from small chores to bigger life choices.
You catch yourself scanning for the signs of a coming showdown before you walk in the door.
codex_completed.repair_check: Notice whether the demand itself is taken back, not just the tone. Someone repairing this brings the underlying need to the table as a request and accepts 'let me think'. An apology for how loudly it was said, with the same demand still standing, leaves the structure in place.

Sometimes a whole emergency, such as a crisis only you can fix right now, built from something small through tone and framing.
Works by removing the chance to sleep on it, read the fine print or phone someone.
Seen in sales, scams, workplaces, families and relationships, from last-chance offers to late-night talks that must be settled now.
Usually stated by one side only, in a form you cannot easily check.

If you call anyone, it will be too late.

Everyone else has already agreed. We're only waiting on you.
Answer me now. I can't wait until tomorrow.
A countdown timer on a checkout page that starts over when you reload it.
what_it_is_not: Real deadlines exist, such as a sale end date or a flight boarding time. Ask what actually happens if you take one more day.
Real emergencies feel exactly like this from the inside, and a burst pipe does need a call now.
Someone anxious who voices urgency because they feel it, with no view about how you decide.
An honest request for an answer by Friday because the venue needs a headcount, with the reason given.

codex_completed.core_meaning: Describing a situation as having only two possible answers when more exist, so that the person feels pushed toward one.
codex_completed.short_definition: Describing a situation as having only two possible answers when more exist, so that the person feels pushed toward one.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A false dilemma squeezes a messy situation into two choices, usually one that suits the speaker and one that sounds unbearable. Often one option is made to sound reasonable and the other unthinkable.
Common in sales, politics, family arguments, and workplace decisions.

Different from an ultimatum because it need not threaten a loss; it only hides the exits.

You're with us or you're against us.
If you're not paying for the premium plan, you clearly don't care about your data.

There's no middle ground here. It's all or nothing.
You can be honest, or you can be nice. You can't be both.
We either do it my way or we do nothing.
what_it_is_not: A situation that really does come down to two options, such as accepting a job offer or turning it down.

A simplified choice offered by someone who invites you to add what they missed, as in 'I see two options. Is there a third?'
A narrow question set openly in a quiz, a poll, or a debate class, where everyone knows the format.
Someone's honest belief that no middle path exists, held without any intent to steer you and dropped when shown otherwise.
this_may_be_it_when: You name a third option and it is dismissed without discussion.
The two choices are unequal, with one framed as obviously the sensible one.
Total words such as always, never, and everything crop up in the framing.
Choosing neither is treated as a hostile act.
The same either-or framing returns across unrelated topics.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The speaker readily adds options when you bring them up.
There are truly only two outcomes, such as signing a contract or not signing it.
The tone is tired or flustered, and the framing softens after a break.
A neutral person looking at the same facts also sees only two realistic paths.
They ask what you see as alternatives and then actually discuss them.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Under stress, many people reduce a decision to two options simply because they cannot think of more.

Binary phrasing is a common habit of speech and does not always signal an effort to steer.
common_false_positives: A doctor explaining that a procedure either gets done this week or waits for the next opening.
A friend who says 'we can eat here or go home' at a place where nothing else is open.
A teacher setting a yes-or-no question on an exam.
discernment_questions: Can I name at least one option that was left out of the list I was given?
When I raise another option, is it discussed or brushed aside?
Is one of the two choices clearly presented as the unthinkable one?
Would a trusted friend looking at the same situation see only two doors?
Do I feel allowed to say 'neither' or 'not yet'?
less_concerning_if: The person updates their framing the moment another option is mentioned.
The choice really is limited by facts such as a deadline set by an outside body.
The binary shows up once, in a rushed moment, and not as a habit.
more_concerning_if: Declining both options is treated as betrayal or as proof of a character flaw.
The narrow frame is used on matters that affect your relationships, money, or housing.
Third options you raised in the past were mocked, ignored, or held against you later.
pattern_over_time_signs: Disagreements keep arriving as loyalty tests, with sides already chosen.
You find yourself mentally arguing against an either-or even before it is spoken.

Friends outside the situation keep naming options that you had stopped seeing.

codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People under pressure tend to take the options in front of them rather than invent new ones, because generating alternatives takes effort that stress leaves little room for. codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Feeling cornered without being able to say why is common in accounts of this, doubting that they ever had a real say, and getting stuck in decisions where every route feels like a betrayal. codex_completed.name: Sunk Cost Exploitation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Pointing to the time, money or effort already spent as a reason you cannot stop, change course or leave now.
codex_completed.short_definition: Pointing to the time, money or effort already spent as a reason you cannot stop, change course or leave now.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: People often keep going with something because they have already put so much into it. Sunk cost exploitation takes that ordinary pull and leans on it, whatever the reason, so past investment becomes the main reason to stay. It differs from honest grief about a shared history because the past is cited at the moment you consider leaving, and it substitutes for any case about the present. Different from honest sadness about a shared past, which accepts that you may still choose differently.

Do you know what I sacrificed to get us here?

Leaving is described as a waste or a betrayal of what you both gave.

this_may_not_be_it_when: They also talk about the present and what could improve, not only the past.

codex_completed.core_meaning: Treating the time taken to answer a message as a failing that must be explained, so you feel permanently on call.
codex_completed.short_definition: Treating the time taken to answer a message as a failing that must be explained, so you feel permanently on call.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Everyone has felt a flicker of worry when a text goes unanswered. codex_completed.why_this_matters: If every delay needs a defense, your attention is no longer fully yours. You may carry your phone like a leash, cut things short with other people, and feel guilty for being away from it, even when you were doing nothing wrong.
