A rule that runs one way: your delays are noted and theirs are not.
Often escalating from a single message to multiple calls, follow-ups, and a rising tone.
what_it_sounds_like: I can see you read it at 3:41. It's now 4:20. Where were you?
Why did it take two hours to answer me?
You were online and you didn't text back. Who else was on your phone?
If you cared, you'd have answered right away.
Seven missed calls. What could possibly be more important?
Left me on read again. Nice.
Next time, text me the second you arrive. I mean it.
what_it_is_not: A worried 'just checking you got home safe' sent once, with no reproach if you were asleep.
A shared agreement, such as parents and teens texting arrival times, applied to both sides.
A reasonable expectation at work or in an emergency role, such as on-call nursing, that is written down and shared.
Disappointment said once, such as 'I missed hearing from you today', with no demand attached.
Real anxiety after a loss or a scare, such as an accident, where a person asks for more contact and accepts a limit.
this_may_be_it_when: A late reply is followed by a demand for an account of where you were and who with.
Your own long silences from them are met with no questions.
The expected reply time keeps shortening over weeks.
Explaining does not settle it, because a new gap soon draws the same charge.
You have started to reply from places and times where you would not choose to, such as the bathroom or a meeting.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You both agreed to the check-in rule and it applies equally.
A missed message prompts a single worried question rather than a demand.
The urgency comes from a real situation, such as a sick relative or a shared deadline.
They tell you what they are feeling instead of asking you to account for yourself.
They accept 'I was busy' without pressing further.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People with anxiety, or who have lost someone suddenly, may check more often than others and be reassured easily.
Couples in different time zones may feel each gap more sharply because their windows are short.
A person whose messages usually get fast replies may simply be surprised by a silence, and curious, rather than accusing.
common_false_positives: A parent asking a teen to text when they arrive at a friend's house, and calmly accepting a late text.
A teammate pinging during a live project because a decision cannot wait.
A new partner who texts a lot early in a relationship and settles into a rhythm as comfort grows.
discernment_questions: Does a late reply lead to a question about me, or to a demand for a defense?
Do the same expectations apply to the other person?
Has the time I am expected to reply in become shorter over the weeks?
Do I feel free to turn my phone off for a dinner, a nap, or a day?
When I explain a gap, is the explanation accepted, or does the questioning move on to the next thing?
less_concerning_if: The expectation is shared, written down or spoken, and applies in both directions.
A slow reply gets a short, warm check-in and nothing more.
The person can say what they are feeling and let you explain later without a trial.
more_concerning_if: Delays bring anger, accusations of cheating, or the silent treatment.
The checking extends to your location, your phone contents, or who you were with.
You have begun to cut off other people or activities to stay reachable.
pattern_over_time_signs: You carry your phone everywhere, and notice dread when it buzzes.
You pre-explain absences before they happen, such as 'I'll be out of signal at the gym.'
The windows you are allowed to be unreachable have shrunk to almost nothing.
Time with friends has become shorter or skipped because of the fallout from a missed message.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair is visible in what happens to the clock, not only in words. When the other person stops asking for an accounting of delays, accepts a late reply without comment, and states their own worry as their own, the pressure is lessening. An apology that comes with a new, stricter check-in rule has only moved the problem.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Tell them when you will usually be reachable and when you will not, then watch the week that follows. Does the next gap pass without a charge? Or do the questions return in a different wrapping, such as jokes, sulking, or a suddenly cold tone?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Being told that silence is a sign of how much you care can make delay feel like a moral failing rather than an ordinary part of a busy day. Answering fast becomes a relief from the discomfort of being questioned, and each quick reply tends to reinforce the expectation. Over time, anticipating the next message can occupy attention even when the phone is quiet.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A tight feeling when the phone buzzes comes up often, apologizing for delays that were not their fault, and cutting short meals, meetings, or sleep to answer. Some say they stopped telling anyone where they were going, because the explanations never ended the questioning. Others describe being unable to put the phone down even once the demands eased.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name the gap without apologizing for it: 'I was in a meeting and couldn't look at my phone. I'm happy to tell you when I'll be free next.'
response_options.firm_boundary: State your availability plainly: 'I'm not able to answer within minutes during the day. I'll reply when I can, and I'd like us to trust that.'
response_options.disengagement: Silence your notifications for set blocks of time and answer when you are ready, rather than in the middle of a demand.
response_options.support_seeking: Show a friend the actual message thread, with the time stamps, and ask whether the response times look unreasonable to them.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager expects instant replies, ask for the expectation in writing, including hours when you are off, and raise it with HR if it grows.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'm not ignoring you when I don't answer right away. I'll reply when I can, and I'm not going to explain every gap. If something is urgent, call me and I'll pick up."
codex_completed.safety_note: Reply-time rules become a safety concern when they turn into tracking: location sharing you did not choose, going through your phone, checking who you were with, or anger or threats after a delay. If a missed text brings fear rather than annoyance, speak to a domestic abuse advocate, who can help you plan privately, away from the monitored device.
misuse_warning: Labeling an anxious partner's reasonable worry as policing can leave real needs for contact unheard.
Treating slow replies as proof of anything about the other person is the mirror mistake; delays alone say nothing about intent.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Interrogation demands justification for anything you did or said, while this tactic is specific to the gap before you reply. An ultimatum names a loss if you fail to comply; here the penalty is usually mood, guilt, or questioning. Urgency manufacturing makes a decision feel rushed, whereas this one makes your availability feel owed. The identifying feature is the clock running on your reply.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Actively matched against pasted text by this tool, at low confidence. Phrase matching can flag wording, but it cannot know intent, tone, history, context, or whether the claim is even true — an innocent reading is always attached to every match. Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Exaggeration
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Stretching a claim with words like always, never, everyone or nothing, so it sounds bigger and harder to answer than the facts support.
codex_completed.short_definition: Stretching a claim with words like always, never, everyone or nothing, so it sounds bigger and harder to answer than the facts support.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Exaggeration here means inflating a claim with absolutes and extremes: always, never, everyone, nothing, completely ruined. Nearly everyone does this when upset, so a single 'you never listen' says little. What matters is whether the stretched word is the main charge, whether one counterexample is waved away, and whether the talk gets stuck on 'always' while the real complaint, which may be partly fair, goes unanswered.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone turns a specific problem into a sweeping one, with words like 'you never' and 'you always', so you end up arguing about the word instead of the thing that happened.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A stretched claim is hard to answer. Defending yourself against 'never' can make you look petty for listing the one time, and a fair point buried inside the claim gets lost along with the exaggeration.
what_it_is: Words like always, never, everyone, nothing or ruined standing in for a count that would be closer to 'twice this month'.
A claim about a person's character rather than one event: 'you are always late' instead of 'you were late on Tuesday'.
Sometimes spoken about a group: 'the whole team hates this idea' when two people said so.
A small lapse presented at the scale of a betrayal, so any reply sounds either too small or too defensive.
Usually built around a true core, which is what makes it hard to dismiss.
what_it_sounds_like: You ALWAYS do this.
You never listen to me.
Nobody on the team agrees with you.
Every single time I ask for one thing, it turns into a fight.
You've ruined the whole trip.
You haven't called me once this month.
what_it_is_not: Ordinary venting, such as 'ugh, you always leave the cupboards open' said with a sigh and a half-smile.
A claim that is close to literally true because the thing really has happened nearly every time.
Casual rounding, like 'I've told you a hundred times' when the number is five.
Strong feeling put into big words by someone tired or hurt, who steps back when asked for an example.
Enthusiastic overstatement such as 'best day ever', which is mood rather than a charge against anyone.
A real disagreement over how often something happens, where both people are counting honestly.
this_may_be_it_when: Asked for an example, the person repeats the absolute more loudly instead of naming a date.
A counterexample you offer is brushed off as 'that doesn't count'.
The sweeping word turns up in nearly every complaint, whatever the subject.
The claim grows between tellings: 'a few times' on Monday, 'always' by Friday.
The conversation ends up about whether 'never' is accurate, and the original request is never answered.
this_may_not_be_it_when: When asked for an example, they give one and the claim shrinks to fit: 'Okay, not always, but the last three times.'
The big word is followed by a specific request you can act on.
They use absolutes about themselves too, as in 'I always mess this up'.
You can count, and it really is nearly every time.
They laugh or soften when you point out it isn't literally true.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Tired or hurt people often reach for big words because small ones feel too weak for what they feel.
Some families and cultures talk in strong, dramatic terms as an everyday style.
A person who has made the same request many times may feel 'never' is true even if you remember two exceptions.
People speaking a second language may use absolutes for lack of softer words.
common_false_positives: A friend's 'you're always late' after you have been late the last six times.
A teenager's 'it's the worst day ever', which describes a mood and charges nobody.
A line like 'we never get time alone' that sums up a long stretch and is broadly accurate.
A rule such as 'never share your password', which is policy and not a stretched claim.
discernment_questions: If I count the actual occasions, how many are there?
When I ask for an example, does the claim get smaller or louder?
Is there a fair point inside the big claim that I am tempted to dismiss because of its wording?
Does every disagreement with this person come in absolutes, or only the heated ones?
Am I listing exceptions to defend myself instead of hearing the complaint?
less_concerning_if: A specific example arrives as soon as you ask for one.
They soften the word once you point out it isn't literal.
Big words are simply how this person talks in every mood and about every topic.
more_concerning_if: The sweeping claim is about your character and is used to decide what you may ask for.
The same stretched claim is told to other people, so your side arrives already discounted.
Asking for specifics is answered with 'See, you always do this', treating the request as proof.
pattern_over_time_signs: You start answering absolutes with lists of dates, and the lists never settle anything.
You soften your own requests in advance so they can't be blown up.
Old small lapses are cited again as part of a history that grows in each retelling.
You begin to describe yourself in their words, as someone who 'never' gets anything right.
codex_completed.repair_check: Watch what the claim does once an example is on the table. Someone repairing says the number out loud, 'it was twice, not always', and keeps the complaint alive. A change of wording that quietly drops the issue has fixed nothing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself: after I said I would talk about specific times, did the talk get more specific? A later argument that still has sweeping words but also a date or two suggests the request landed. Sentences that all still begin with 'always' suggest it did not.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A sweeping claim can shift the listener's job from understanding to defending. Because one exception technically refutes 'never', people often reach for exceptions, and the exchange becomes about accuracy. Strong words also tend to be remembered longer than the details around them, so the label can stay with you after the facts fade.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Being summed up unfairly is the usual report, along with keeping a mental tally of the times you did help, and wearing out in arguments that never reach the real issue. Some hear big words in every piece of feedback, even gentle ones, and some start to believe the sweeping version of themselves.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the count without disputing the feeling: 'It feels like never to you. Can you tell me about the last time, so I understand what you mean?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to debate the word and steer to one event: 'I will talk about specific times. I won't argue about whether always is true, so pick the one that bothers you most.'
response_options.disengagement: If the argument becomes a contest of counterexamples, stop listing them. Say you will come back to it once it is down to one event, and take a break first.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend who knows you both what was said and what you think the real count is. Saying it aloud can show whether there is a fair point inside the 'always'.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask for feedback with dates and examples ('Which meetings do you mean?') so you can reply to the facts instead of the adjective.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Hearing what's wrong is what I want, and a real example is how I can do it. Can you tell me about one time this week? Then we can talk about that, instead of always and never."
codex_completed.safety_note: Stretched wording is an everyday habit and rarely a safety signal alone. That changes if sweeping charges come with threats, if you fear the reaction when you ask for an example, or if the same claims about you are repeated to others in ways that cut you off from them. Write down what was said and when, and show it to someone you trust before the next argument.
misuse_warning: Labeling a frustrated 'you never' as manipulation can make it harder for the person to say anything strongly, and leaves the fair core of the complaint unheard.
Counting up someone's 'always' statements as evidence against them turns a speech habit into a verdict.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Vague Allegations refers to unnamed critics or unspecified charges, while exaggeration names a real event and stretches its size. Lying states something false; exaggeration usually has a true core that has been blown up. Fabricated Evidence invents proof. Exaggeration needs none, only a word like 'always' that cannot be checked and that one example from you can puncture.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Actively matched against pasted text by this tool, at low confidence. Phrase matching can flag wording, but it cannot know intent, tone, history, context, or whether the claim is even true — an innocent reading is always attached to every match. Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Vague Allegations
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Hinting that unnamed people have unspecified complaints about someone, so the claim cannot be checked, answered or corrected.
codex_completed.short_definition: Hinting that unnamed people have unspecified complaints about someone, so the claim cannot be checked, answered or corrected.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Vague allegations are accusations with the details removed: no names, no dates, no description of what was said or done. 'People are talking' or 'I've heard things' hands the listener something heavy and nothing to respond to. Sometimes a person is honestly protecting a source or has only a hazy impression, and one such remark says little. Concern grows when specifics are always unavailable and yet the claim is treated as settled.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone says there are complaints about you but won't say who, what or when, so you can't answer them and are left to imagine the worst.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You can't correct what you can't see. People hit by a vague claim often spend weeks searching their memory and scanning faces for who knows what, while their standing with others may shift without a word being said to them.
what_it_is: A claim about what others think or say, with the who, what and when left out.
Hints dropped in meetings, family gatherings, group chats and reviews, such as 'there have been concerns'.
A statement that cannot be proved false, because with no detail there is nothing to disprove.
Often delivered as friendly concern or a warning, so declining to guess feels rude.
A gap the listener fills in alone, usually with something worse than any real complaint.
what_it_sounds_like: People are talking about you.
I've heard things, and I'm not going to say from whom.
There have been concerns about your attitude.
Everyone knows what you're really like.
Word is going around.
I'm not the only one who feels this way.
what_it_is_not: A colleague who says 'a few people struggled with the handover' and then offers specifics when asked.

A manager under a formal confidentiality process who cannot name a complainant but describes the behavior and offers a way to respond. Awkwardly protecting a source while relaying a real concern is not the same as hiding the concern.
A friend who says 'I might be wrong, but I got the impression you upset Sam' and is open to hearing your side.
A summary of feedback from many people, such as a 360 review, that reports themes without names and gives examples of behavior.
A person who honestly has only secondhand talk and says so.
this_may_be_it_when: Asking 'who?' or 'what did they say?' gets 'I can't say' every time, and the claim still stands.
The statement is presented as settled fact: 'everyone knows'.
The remark arrives soon after you disagree, ask for something or raise a complaint.
You are told to change but not told what to change.
The details shift or vanish when you probe.
this_may_not_be_it_when: When you ask what behavior is meant, they describe one, even if they won't say who raised it.
They say plainly it is only their impression and invite your side.
The concern is formally recorded and you are given a process to respond.
They come back later with specifics.
It was said once, and they looked surprised to be pressed.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People who hear talk secondhand often lack the details too and pass it on as heard.
Someone in HR, counseling or a similar role may be bound by confidentiality and say less than they would like.
Some people cannot bring themselves to say a hard thing plainly, so they hint.
A person may fear the one who raised it would suffer if named.
common_false_positives: An anonymous course evaluation summary reporting that students found lectures unclear.
A relative who says 'your aunt seemed upset after dinner' without knowing why.
A friend who says 'something is off between you and Sam, I think', honestly guessing and open to hearing more.
discernment_questions: If I ask for one example of behavior, is one given, even without a name?
Is the claim presented as fact, or as an impression?
Has anything actually changed in how others treat me, or am I filling in blanks?
Is there a process where I can see a concern and answer it?
How much of my worry comes from what was said, and how much from what I have imagined to fill the gap?
less_concerning_if: A reason for the vagueness is given and the behavior is described.
The speaker offers to find out more and returns with an answer.
You are invited to give your own account.
more_concerning_if: The same unnamed 'concerns' follow you from one setting to another.
Other people repeat the hints to you and no one can say where they came from.
Your requests for specifics are treated as proof of the problem: 'see how defensive you are'.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find yourself reviewing old conversations for a slip-up that might explain it.
You grow wary of group chats and rooms where people go quiet when you arrive.
The same phrases come back attached to new topics.
You start apologizing for unspecified things and adjusting your behavior to fit guesses.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair looks like a name or a description arriving: either the actual behavior ('Tuesday's meeting, the way the budget was challenged') or an honest 'I have no specifics and I shouldn't have said it that way'. A softer repeat of the same hint in a warmer tone is not that.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice what happens to your question, 'Can you tell me what was said?' A respectful reply gives something, or says honestly why it can't. If the question itself is treated as proof that something is wrong with you, the boundary was not respected.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: An unspecific accusation leaves a gap, and the mind often fills gaps with its own worst fears. With nothing concrete to check, it can keep searching and turn ordinary events into possible clues. Not knowing who is involved can make everyone in the room a possible source, which may lead to withdrawing from the people who could have helped.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe rereading old messages, replaying conversations and watching coworkers' faces for signs. Some change their behavior to fit guesses about the complaint, and some pull back from groups where they think the talk is happening. Feeling judged without a hearing can be painful in its own right.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for one piece of detail: 'Can you tell me what was said, or what it was about? Even without names, I'd like to know what to look at.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Name the gap once, then stop guessing: 'Hints are hard for me to act on. Until there is something specific, I'm going to carry on as I am.'
response_options.disengagement: If every request for detail meets 'I can't say', you don't have to keep guessing. Let the topic rest until specifics exist, and don't volunteer apologies for things nobody has named.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask someone you trust who sees you in the same group what they have actually observed, separating what was seen from what was passed along.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask for the concern in writing with examples and dates, and for the chance to respond. Note the date you asked and what you were told.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I take it seriously if people have concerns. I can't respond to something I haven't been told, though. If you can describe what happened, even without names, I'll listen and answer it properly."
codex_completed.safety_note: A vague claim alone is mostly a reputational and emotional strain. It becomes more serious if it is tied to consequences you can't see coming, such as a looming dismissal, a custody dispute or a housing review. Then ask in writing what is being claimed, and bring a union representative, employment adviser or lawyer in before any meeting where you are expected to answer.
misuse_warning: Calling every cautious or confidential remark a 'vague allegation' can punish people who are protecting a source for good reason.
Demanding names from someone relaying a real concern can put the person who raised it at risk.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Exaggeration stretches a real event; vague allegations offer no event at all. Fabricated Evidence produces a screenshot or document you can at least examine and challenge, whereas a vague allegation gives you nothing to hold. Lying by Omission leaves a fact out of an otherwise concrete account; here the account itself is what is missing.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Actively matched against pasted text by this tool, at low confidence. Phrase matching can flag wording, but it cannot know intent, tone, history, context, or whether the claim is even true — an innocent reading is always attached to every match. Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Identity Hooking
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Claiming that someone's identity, skills or successes belong to you, so that standing apart from you means giving up the self they have built.
codex_completed.short_definition: Claiming that someone's identity, skills or successes belong to you, so that standing apart from you means giving up the self they have built.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Identity Hooking is credit-taking that grows into ownership. Help given in the past, such as a loan, a teacher's time, a parent's sacrifice or a boss's early break, is restated as the whole reason the person is who they are. Gratitude is normal and often deserved. The telling detail is a claim raised mostly at moments of separation or independence, and when it leaves the person feeling that any success of theirs still counts as someone else's.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone insists that who you are and what you have achieved are really theirs, so that moving on from them feels like erasing yourself.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: If you are told you were made by someone, walking away may seem to mean disowning your own history. Wins stop feeling like yours, and independence starts to look like ingratitude or self-destruction.
what_it_is: Turning real help from the past into a claim over the person's present self, talents and results.
Often raised at a turning point: a job offer, a move, a new partner, a decision to study something else.
Retelling the person's story with the speaker at the center, so that their own effort and luck drop out of it.
Different from taking pride: pride says 'I watched you grow', ownership says 'you are my work'.
what_it_sounds_like: I made you who you are.
Everything you have, you have because of me.
Without me you would still be waiting tables.
That promotion is really mine. Who do you think taught you to speak up?
Go ahead and leave, but whatever you build, remember whose idea you were.
People only listen to you because of the name I gave you.
You're nothing without me.
what_it_is_not: A mentor, coach or parent saying they are proud and glad to have helped, while still treating your choices as yours.
Someone accurately noting that a past favor mattered, such as a reference letter or tuition money, without tying it to what you owe now.
A founder, teacher or relative who feels hurt when you move on and says so, without claiming your accomplishments.
An exaggerated boast made once in a heated argument, then taken back when things cool.
A culture or family where credit is shared by tradition, and everyone, including you, claims credit for the group's successes.
this_may_be_it_when: The claim of ownership comes up mainly when you mention leaving, a new opportunity, or a bigger life.
Your achievements get retold as the other person's achievements, even in front of others.
Thanking them is never enough; the debt is described as total and permanent.
Your own part in what you have done is waved away as luck or as something they handed you.
You catch yourself downplaying your wins around them to avoid the speech about who made you.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They are glad about your plans and the credit they mention stays in proportion to what they did.
The comment about their role came once, with visible hurt, and was followed by a plain 'it is your life'.
You are the one who feels obliged, and nobody has told you that you are.
They ask for something specific in return, such as help for a few weeks, rather than claiming your identity.
Others who were there confirm the help was real, and nobody is using it as a leash.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A teacher or parent who invested years in someone can sound possessive when they are really afraid of losing closeness.
Praise like 'I always knew you had it in you' can be warmth, not a claim of authorship.
Some families speak in sweeping, dramatic sentences that nobody means literally.
common_false_positives: A coach who says 'I'm proud I helped you get here' and then cheers when you sign elsewhere.
A grandparent who paid for school and sometimes brings it up out of pride, but never makes it a condition.
A business partner stating who contributed what in an honest dispute about credit or ownership of a project.
discernment_questions: When they talk about helping you, does it end in 'and I am glad' or in 'and so you owe me'?
Does the language of making you appear mainly when you are about to go somewhere without them?
Can you tell your own good news without bracing for a speech about their part in it?
Do you have a version of your story in which your own work and choices appear, and could you say it aloud to them?
Would a fair outsider say the credit being claimed matches what was actually given?
less_concerning_if: The credit claimed is proportionate and sits beside real acknowledgment of your own effort.
Your plans for independence are met with mixed feelings but no claim over you.
The topic comes up occasionally in a warm voice and never as a condition.
more_concerning_if: The ownership claim grows louder each time you take a step toward independence.
Your successes are publicly retold as theirs, and correcting them leads to anger or silence.
Your sense that your skills are real has begun to wobble, and you credit them to someone else by reflex.
pattern_over_time_signs: You stop sharing good news with this person because it triggers a speech about who deserves the credit.
You begin answering compliments from others with 'it was really thanks to them', even when it was not.
Plans for school, work or moving get delayed, and the reason you give yourself is a feeling of owing.
Friends notice that you describe your own accomplishments in the third person or with a shrug.
codex_completed.repair_check: Look at how your next piece of good news is received. When someone has taken in what you said about the claim, they can be glad with you and leave your credit alone. An apology that arrives with a reminder of everything they did for you has moved the claim, not dropped it.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Do you get to keep your credit after you state it? Someone respecting the boundary might wince, then let you tell the story your way. Someone who is not respecting it may list their sacrifices again, or treat your request as proof of ingratitude.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When a person's competence and sense of self are repeatedly described as someone else's creation, the story can sink in as a fact about them. Gratitude, a normal and decent feeling, may then get used as the lever, because refusing the claim starts to register as betraying a real kindness. Separation then registers as self-erasure.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Some readers report being unable to enjoy their own successes, feeling like impostors in their own careers, or postponing a move because leaving seemed like giving up their own origin. Others recall feeling guilty for wanting credit at all. Over time, a few notice that they have begun saying the line themselves before anyone else can.

response_options.soft_clarification: Acknowledge the real part and keep the rest: 'You helped me a lot and I am grateful. The work after that was mine too, and I want that said.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline the ownership frame while keeping the thanks: 'I will always thank you for that year. I will not agree that I am your work.'
response_options.disengagement: When the speech starts, you can let it run its course without arguing, change the subject, and share future news only with people who enjoy it.
response_options.support_seeking: Write out your own timeline: what you did, what others gave, what you earned. Show it to someone who knew you at the time and ask whether it matches.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager or supervisor claims your work, keep dated drafts and send a short summary of your contribution to the team in writing, so credit is on the record.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I am glad you helped me, and I will keep saying so. I also did the work, and the choices ahead are mine. Let's talk about my plans without that coming up."
codex_completed.safety_note: Being told who you really are is pressure on your sense of self, not a danger signal. It changes if the claim of ownership starts to come with warnings about what happens to you when you pursue independence, with attempts to control your money or movements, or with threats. Then speak to a counselor or advocate before you act on any plan to separate.
misuse_warning: Calling every proud mentor or parent an identity hooker can turn real, healthy gratitude into suspicion. The test is ownership and obligation, not pride.
Using this label to explain away a stranger's or colleague's unfair credit-taking blurs two different problems.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Conditional Worth ties your value to what you do for the other person at present, while Identity Hooking ties it to what they supposedly did for you in the past. Learned Helplessness insists you cannot cope, where Identity Hooking insists you did not do it yourself. Identity Erosion is what you may notice inside after years of either; Identity Hooking is the claim made out loud.

codex_completed.name: Conditional Worth
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Treating a person's value as something that rises and falls with their usefulness and their willingness to comply.
codex_completed.short_definition: Treating a person's value as something that rises and falls with their usefulness and their willingness to comply.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Conditional Worth is a gauge of approval that the other person holds. Warmth, respect and even a place at the table go up when you perform, obey or produce, and drop when you do not. A request is fine; a rating of your whole self is the pattern. What matters is that the message is about who you are, not about the task, and that it comes back across different kinds of requests, so you learn to read the gauge before you speak.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone makes you feel that you matter only while you are helpful or agreeable, and that your place shrinks when you are not.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A worth meter held by someone else makes rest feel like failure and a no feel dangerous. You can end up working harder for a feeling of acceptance that keeps moving away.
what_it_is: Approval handed out in proportion to usefulness, obedience or results, then pulled back when those dip.
A verdict on the whole person ('you are lazy', 'you are no use') in place of a comment on one task.
Often visible in how affection changes: warmth after a favor, coolness after a refusal.
Found in families, couples, workplaces and teams where being needed is the only way to be valued.
what_it_sounds_like: You're only worth something when you're useful.
Earn your place in this family.
I'll be nice to you once you've done what I asked.
What do you even bring to this house?
Funny how I only hear from you when you want something, and funnier how I only like you when you're handy.
Good girl. See, that's the version of you I like.
You were great last week. Today you're a disappointment.
what_it_is_not: A direct request such as 'I need you to pick up your brother today', which asks for a task and says nothing about your worth.
Reasonable performance standards at work, where a bad quarter leads to a coaching talk rather than contempt.
Someone who is stressed and curt for a day but returns to ordinary warmth afterward.
Clear house rules or chores in a family, applied fairly and without suggesting anyone's place is at stake.
A person saying 'I felt let down by that' and still treating you as a full member of the relationship.
this_may_be_it_when: The warmth you get tracks what you did for them that week, and falls off when you rest or say no.
Criticism of a missed task turns into a statement about your character.
You are praised mainly when you are producing, serving or agreeing.
Your needs, illness or tiredness are met with irritation instead of care.
You catch yourself calculating what you have done lately to deserve kind treatment.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Disappointment about a task passes without affecting how you are treated afterward.
You can be unproductive, ill or unhelpful for a while and still be welcomed without a price.
The expectation is applied equally to everyone in the household or team, including the speaker.
They thank you for help without making the thanks a precondition for friendliness.
The standard is set by a role, such as an employer's job description, and not by a personal verdict.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Anyone can feel more affection toward someone who has just done them a kindness; that is not a ledger.
Workplaces, teams and sports squads often reward results, and people can confuse that with being loved.
A person raised in a home where love had strings may repeat it without noticing.
common_false_positives: A manager who gives bad reviews for missed targets but is courteous and fair to you as a person.
A tired parent who says 'I need your help tonight' and thanks you warmly afterward.
A friend who is quiet for a few days after you cancel on them, then picks things up again as normal.
discernment_questions: Does the way they treat you change depending on what you did for them recently?
When you cannot help, are you met with understanding or with a drop in respect?
Is the criticism about the task, or does it sweep up your whole character?
Is there anyone, here or elsewhere, who values you on days you produce nothing?
Would you apply the same standard to someone you love, or to a friend in your position?
less_concerning_if: Standards are applied fairly to everyone and are tied to a role, not to personal worth.
Care continues even when you are unhelpful, sick or in need.
The remarks about usefulness are rare and are followed by warmth.
more_concerning_if: Basic things such as affection, a seat at the table or a place to live are made to depend on your obedience.
You are compared to others who are more useful, or told that you are replaceable.
You no longer ask for anything because every ask is tallied against you.
pattern_over_time_signs: You overwork or over-give and find rest uncomfortable, because pausing starts to feel like losing your place.
You scan faces and moods before asking for anything.
Compliments arrive after sacrifices and vanish after refusals, so you learn the pattern without being told.
You say sorry for being tired, sick or busy.
codex_completed.repair_check: Pay attention to a day when you cannot give anything. Care that continues anyway counts, and so does a retraction of the worth comments that is more than a single sentence. A sudden burst of praise after a bad week is not the same thing, because it still depends on what you are doing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice what a refusal costs. If you say 'I cannot do that today' and the reply is a disappointed but ordinary 'okay', the boundary is being respected. If affection cools until you give in, the boundary is being priced.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Acceptance is a basic human need, so when it is given and withdrawn according to performance, the person tends to learn what earns it and organize themselves around it. The gauge moves inside the person, which is why it can keep running when the other person says nothing. Self-worth starts to rise and fall with output.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Some people report that they cannot relax without guilt, that they say yes before they think, or that they feel hollow after being praised, since the praise was for the work. A few find that a sick day or a failure sets off a rush of shame far larger than the event itself.

response_options.soft_clarification: Separate the request from the verdict: 'I can help with that. I am not okay with being told I am worthless when I cannot.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold the line on the task without trading worth for it: 'I am not available today. That does not change what I am worth to you.'
response_options.disengagement: When warmth is being offered only in return for compliance, you can decline to bargain for it and spend your energy where care is not conditional.
response_options.support_seeking: Name a few moments to someone who sees you unproductive and still likes you, such as a friend or counselor, and notice how it feels to be valued while doing nothing.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask for expectations in writing, with measures that apply to the job. Keep performance feedback and character comments apart, and raise any contempt with HR or a mentor.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Are you asking me for something, or telling me what I am worth? I am glad to talk about the request. My value to you is not up for negotiation each time I say no."
codex_completed.safety_note: Worth tied to usefulness is a heavy pressure but not a danger signal in itself. It carries more risk when a place to live, money, your children or your safety is also made to depend on your compliance. If that is happening, speak to a counselor, legal aid service or domestic abuse advocate about your options before you push back.
misuse_warning: Treating every disappointed reaction or fair work standard as conditional worth can make ordinary accountability look like harm. The label fits a pattern about your value, not a task.
Applying it to someone who is simply overwhelmed or burned out can turn their exhaustion into an accusation.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Identity Hooking claims credit for who you already are; Conditional Worth rates you now, by what you provide. Fawning is your own appeasing reflex, while Conditional Worth is the pricing that can set it off. Loyalty Binds treats disagreement as betrayal; Conditional Worth treats any shortfall in usefulness as a loss of standing.

codex_completed.name: Learned Helplessness
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Repeatedly telling someone they could not cope alone, until they start to believe it and stop trying.
codex_completed.short_definition: Repeatedly telling someone they could not cope alone, until they start to believe it and stop trying.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: In this entry the term means a communication pattern, not a clinical finding: someone keeps stating, in many forms, that you are incapable of managing life without them. Warnings about money, driving, work or health are delivered as facts. Tasks may also be taken away 'to help'. A single worried remark is common. The pattern is the steady repetition across topics and the way your own attempts get discouraged, so that doing less starts to look like the safest option.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone keeps telling you that you cannot cope alone, and takes tasks off your hands, until you stop trusting your own ability to manage.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Abilities shrink when they go unused. If you are told often enough that you cannot manage, you may stop trying, and then the lack of practice looks like proof that they were right.
what_it_is: Broad statements of incapacity ('you can't manage money', 'you'd get lost') that cover more than one real difficulty.
Taking over tasks, such as bills, calls or driving, with the explanation that you will only make a mess of them.
Remarks that grow louder when you mention a course, a job, a trip or a move.
Sometimes delivered kindly and with concern, which makes it harder to name as a pattern.
what_it_sounds_like: You can't survive without me.
You'd fall apart in a week on your own.
Let me handle the bank. You'll only get it wrong.
Nobody else would put up with how scattered you are.
You know you can't drive on the motorway. Just stay home.
I'm only doing this because I know you can't.
Remember what happened last time you tried? Exactly.
what_it_is_not: Honest worry about one specific, real limit, such as a medical condition or a lack of experience with a task, stated once and with offers to help you learn.
A caregiver doing more for someone who really is ill, injured or newly bereaved, and planning with them to get abilities back.
Over-protectiveness from a parent or partner who is anxious and says unhelpful things, but is glad when you succeed.
Someone sharing out chores by who is quicker at what, not by who is deemed hopeless.
A warning given once because a plan really did look risky, followed by respect for your decision.
this_may_be_it_when: The claim of incapacity covers many unrelated areas, not one skill.
Your successes are ignored or explained away, while your mistakes are replayed.
Tasks you used to do have been taken from you without being asked for.
Mentioning independence, such as a job or a trip, brings out a fresh round of warnings.
You now doubt skills that others who know you still see as plain.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The concern is limited to one clear area where you have asked for help.
They teach you the task instead of removing it, and celebrate when you manage it.
Illness or a crisis really does limit what you can do right now, and everyone agrees it is temporary.
Others who know you would also say the specific warning was reasonable.
You can still say 'I want to try' and be given the chance.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Parents of anxious children and partners of people with health conditions often over-help from love and habit.
Someone may take on a task simply because they are better at it or enjoy it.
A person who has seen you struggle before may voice worry in clumsy words, without any wish to hold you back.
common_false_positives: A spouse who handles the taxes because they like spreadsheets, and happily explains how if you ask.
A friend who says 'are you sure you can do that alone?' about a hard move, then helps once you say yes.
An adult child taking over some tasks for a parent with early memory loss, in agreement with the parent and their doctor.
discernment_questions: Is the claim that you cannot cope tied to one real limit, or does it spread across everything?
When you succeed at something, does anyone say so, or does it get explained away?
Have you stopped doing things you could do a few years ago, and who decided that?
What happens when you propose handling a task yourself, even if imperfectly?
Do people who know you outside this relationship describe your abilities the same way?
less_concerning_if: The limits mentioned are specific, accurate and come with offers to help you build the skill.
Your attempts at independence are welcomed, even when worry is expressed.
Tasks taken over are handed back when you want them.
more_concerning_if: You have lost access to your own money, transport, phone or paperwork on the grounds that you cannot handle them.
Others are told that you are incapable, so that your own account is discounted.
Your confidence has dropped sharply in areas where you used to be competent.
pattern_over_time_signs: You ask permission or reassurance for decisions that used to be routine.
You avoid trying new tasks because you expect to fail, and you cannot say when that began.
Skills you once had, such as budgeting or navigating, feel rusty.
People who knew you earlier remark that you used to be more sure of yourself.
codex_completed.repair_check: A change shows up in the tasks, not the words. Look for jobs being handed back, mistakes met with teaching and not with a summary of your failures, and your own plans treated as plans. A kind sentence about your abilities that leaves every responsibility where it was is not much.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Try taking back one small job and see what happens. When the boundary is respected, you get to do it badly, then better, without a running commentary. When it is not, the commentary arrives and the job drifts back to the other person.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Skills tend to be maintained by use and by feedback. When attempts are discouraged, tasks are removed and failures are replayed, a person may lose both practice and confidence, and the resulting hesitation can then seem to confirm the claim. The belief begins to work as a forecast the person helps bring about, even with nobody pushing.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Some report hesitating over choices they used to make easily, dreading a task they once did without thought, or asking for sign-off on small matters. Others describe being surprised, after time away, at what they could still do. A few feel anger at how long they went along with it.

response_options.soft_clarification: Say which part is true and which is not: 'I do need help with the tax form. I do not need help with everything else, and I would like to try.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask to keep one task in your hands: 'I would like to try making that call myself, and we can look at how it went afterward.'
response_options.disengagement: Rather than debating whether you are capable, keep a few skills in practice in private ways, such as a budget saved on your own phone or a route you learn, without needing anyone's agreement.
response_options.support_seeking: List five things you handled in the past year and ask a friend, relative or counselor who knows you to read it with you. Their reaction is a useful second opinion.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask a manager for a stretch task with written feedback, and keep a record of finished tasks so that your own track record stays visible to you.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I know you worry about me. I would like to handle the electricity bill this month, and afterward we can look at how it went."
codex_completed.safety_note: Watch for the claim of incapacity coming together with control of your money, documents, phone, transport or contact with others, or with fear of what happens if you try something alone. These can signal coercive control. A domestic abuse advocate or legal aid service can help you plan privately, including how to keep copies of key papers safe.
misuse_warning: Using this label for a caregiver who is helping someone who truly cannot do a task can shame people who are doing difficult, loving work.
Applying it to anyone who ever expresses worry makes ordinary concern look like control. The test is breadth and repetition, not a single warning.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Conditional Worth rates your value by what you provide; Learned Helplessness rates your ability to manage at all. Identity Erosion is the loss of your tastes and friends over time, whereas Learned Helplessness takes away your confidence in doing things. Self-Gaslighting Induction is doubt about your memory and perception; Learned Helplessness is doubt about your competence and capacity.

codex_completed.name: Loyalty Binds
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Defining loyalty as obedience and silence, so that disagreeing, asking questions or telling outsiders counts as betrayal.
codex_completed.short_definition: Defining loyalty as obedience and silence, so that disagreeing, asking questions or telling outsiders counts as betrayal.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Loyalty Binds attach a moral price to speaking. The group, family or person is given an idea of loyalty in which questioning, objecting, keeping a friend outside the circle or seeking help counts as disloyalty. Loyalty itself is a real value, and bounded privacy is normal. The pattern is a definition with no room for honest dissent, so the only way to count as good is to stay quiet and go along, even when something is wrong.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Being loyal gets defined as never disagreeing or telling anyone, so speaking up about a problem makes you the traitor and the problem stays hidden.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: When disagreeing means betrayal, problems stay inside the group. You may carry something heavy alone, because getting help would feel like a breach of loyalty, and the guilt can outlast the situation.
what_it_is: A definition of loyalty that leaves out disagreement, so that any objection is treated as an attack.
Rules about secrecy that cover things that harm someone, such as money trouble, drinking, cruelty or abuse.
A moral frame around speech: the person who tells is bad, and the person who caused the problem recedes.
Found in families, close friendships, teams, religious groups and workplaces.
what_it_sounds_like: If you tell anyone, you're betraying this family.
What happens in this house stays in this house.
A real friend wouldn't go around questioning me.
I never thought you'd take their side over mine.
Loyalty means never questioning.
After everything this team did for you, you go to HR?
If you really loved us you wouldn't make us look bad.
what_it_is_not: A request to keep one specific private matter private, such as a medical diagnosis or a surprise, while you stay free to disagree on everything else.
A professional duty of confidentiality, for instance for therapists or lawyers, which has stated limits and a purpose.
Real hurt from a friend who felt you did not stand by them, said once and open to your side of it.
A family or team culture of pulling together under stress that still allows questions and objections.
Your own strong commitment to someone, which you have chosen and can still examine.
this_may_be_it_when: Disagreeing, even politely, is described as betrayal.
Secrecy is demanded about things that hurt someone, not just private matters.
Asking an outsider for advice is treated as proof that you are disloyal.
Your loyalty is tested with favors or silence and never matched by the same loyalty to you.
Others in the group have learned to stay quiet, and the quiet itself is praised.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The request for confidentiality covers one matter, with a reason, and you can say what you think about everything else.
Disagreement is met with discussion, even heated, and the relationship carries on.
The loyalty runs both ways, so the speaker also keeps your confidences and takes your objections seriously.
You can talk to people outside the circle without a cost.
The rules about discretion stop short of covering harm or danger.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Families often keep matters private out of shame or pride, without meaning to silence anyone.
A person who has been betrayed before may be especially sensitive to what looks like disloyalty.
Teams in tough situations, such as emergency services, may lean on tight bonds that are healthy when disagreement is still possible.
common_false_positives: A friend who asks you not to share their health news, and is fine with you telling your partner or a counselor if you need support.
A family that is close and protective of its reputation, but lets members voice disagreement at the table.
A manager who asks that unreleased plans stay inside the team, and still welcomes internal objections.
discernment_questions: Can I disagree with this person or group and still count as loyal to them?
Is the secrecy about something private, or about something that is hurting someone?
Is loyalty owed to me in the same way, or does it run one way?
What happens when someone speaks to an outsider about a concern?
If a friend described this rule to me about their own family, what would I tell them?
less_concerning_if: The privacy asked for is narrow, explained and time-limited.
Questions and objections get a hearing, even if they are unwelcome.
Asking for outside advice is tolerated, and you can name the problem in your own words.
more_concerning_if: The silence is demanded about harm to a child, a partner, a worker or yourself.
People who spoke up were shunned, blamed or described as traitors.
Contact with outsiders has narrowed because it is labeled disloyal.
pattern_over_time_signs: You edit what you say to relatives, friends or colleagues so that nothing outside the group gets said.
You feel a rush of guilt just from thinking critically about the person or group.
Disagreements go unspoken and build into resentment, but you keep acting as if all is well.
People who left or voiced concerns are no longer mentioned, or are mentioned only with contempt.
codex_completed.repair_check: Compare how a later disagreement is treated. Where something has really shifted, you can say 'I see this differently' and the relationship holds. A tearful apology for having called you disloyal, followed by a fresh round of secrecy rules, has changed the tone, not the rule.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: What happens if you tell someone outside the group that you are stressed? Notice whether the reaction is curiosity or punishment. Where a boundary is respected, your talking to a friend is allowed to stand. Where it is not, you are quizzed on what you said and to whom.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Loyalty, belonging and a sense of being a good person are strong motivators, and tying them to silence can turn the person's own conscience against speaking. Guilt then works as an internal guard, so the rule keeps running even when nobody is watching. Fear of being excluded from the group can reinforce it.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Some report carrying a secret for years, feeling sick with guilt after talking to a counselor, or going quiet at family gatherings. Others describe splitting into two selves: the one who says everything is fine, and the one who knows it is not. A few say that being believed by one outsider was a relief.

response_options.soft_clarification: Separate care from silence: 'I care about this family. I also need to be able to say when something worries me.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Offer the bounded kind of confidence: 'Your private news stays private with me. Other things, I would like to be free to talk about.'
response_options.disengagement: You can listen to the loyalty speech without agreeing, answer briefly, and then seek out a conversation with someone outside the group on your own time.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a counselor, doctor, faith leader outside the group, or a trusted friend what you have been asked to keep quiet. Many services treat what you tell them as confidential.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If your team calls reporting a concern disloyal, look up your organization's whistleblower or ethics channel and the rules on confidentiality, and keep notes of what you saw.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I care about this family, and I am not trying to hurt it. I am finding it hard that disagreeing seems to count as betrayal. Can we talk about that?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Take extra care when the secrecy covers physical harm, threats, money you are being made to hide, or danger to a child. Reporting can feel like betrayal and can also carry real risk. A child protection service, domestic abuse advocate or legal aid line can talk through options without asking you to commit to anything, and can advise how to stay safe while doing it.
misuse_warning: Calling any request for privacy a loyalty bind may treat legitimate confidentiality, such as a friend's diagnosis, as a trap. Look for a rule that forbids disagreement and covers harm.
Using the label to dismiss a group's grief or pride can ignore the real bonds that hold people together.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Conditional Worth ties your value to your usefulness, while Loyalty Binds ties your goodness to your silence. Identity Hooking claims credit for who you have become; Loyalty Binds claims your voice. Fawning is the appeasing reflex you may carry, and a loyalty bind can be one of the things that sets it off.
