Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Medical Gaslighting
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Dismissing, minimizing or reattributing a patient's symptoms or pain in a medical setting until the patient is left doubting what their own body is telling them.
codex_completed.short_definition: Dismissing, minimizing or reattributing a patient's symptoms or pain in a medical setting until the patient is left doubting what their own body is telling them.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Medical gaslighting is a name patients use when clinicians treat their account of symptoms or pain as unreliable, minor or imagined, and explain it away without fully looking into it. A wrong guess is not it, because every clinician is wrong sometimes. The pattern is in how the report is handled: pain is discounted, requests for tests go unanswered, and notes describe what the patient said differently from how they said it. It is not a formal diagnosis or a legal term. People with symptoms that are hard to see or measure often describe it.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A doctor or clinic keeps telling you that what you feel is nothing, or all in your head, and you start to wonder whether your own body can be trusted.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Dismissal delays diagnosis and treatment, and it teaches people, especially those from groups that medicine has often disbelieved, to distrust their own symptoms and to avoid seeking help the next time something is wrong.
what_it_is: Symptoms or pain explained away as stress, anxiety, weight, age, hormones or 'just life' before other causes have been looked at.
A report that goes unrecorded or is recorded in a different form, such as 'complains of' where you described a fact.
Requests for tests, imaging or a referral declined without a reason you can understand.
Repeated across visits or clinicians, so that the same dismissal follows you.
Different from a missed diagnosis: the issue is how your account is treated, not that the answer is still unknown.
what_it_sounds_like: It's probably just anxiety.
There's nothing medically wrong with you.
Have you thought about losing a little weight?
Lots of women your age feel like this.
Pain isn't something we can measure, so I can't do much.
You're young and healthy. It's stress.
I'm not going to order that. It won't change anything.
Maybe you're just more sensitive to pain than most.
what_it_is_not: A clinician who thinks anxiety or stress is the most likely cause, says why, and agrees to look further if symptoms continue.
A diagnostic work-up that is still in progress and has not yet produced an answer.
A wrong diagnosis made in good faith and corrected when new information appears.
A decision not to order a test because guidelines do not support it for this symptom, explained to you plainly.
A brisk appointment in an overloaded clinic where the pace, not disbelief, limited what could be done.
An accurate assessment that the symptom is minor, with a plan to review it if it changes.
this_may_be_it_when: Your account is questioned or reworded instead of explored with questions.
A psychological cause is named before physical ones are checked.
You ask for a test or referral and no reason for declining is given.
Different providers write down different versions of what you said.
Your symptoms are discussed as a matter of personality, weight or mood rather than as information.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They ask detailed questions and examine you before suggesting a cause.
A less serious cause is proposed along with a clear plan for follow-up if you are not better.
Your account appears accurately in the visit summary.
If you ask for a second opinion or a test, they discuss it as a reasonable thing to do.
The explanation matches what a second clinician later says.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many symptoms really do have a common, harmless cause, and clinicians start with what is most likely.
Time pressure can make a clinician sound abrupt without disbelieving you.
Providers still searching for an answer may say 'I don't know' in ways that feel like a brush-off.
common_false_positives: A first visit that ends in 'let's wait and see', with a follow-up booked.
A test result that turns out normal after a thorough work-up.
A specialist who says the problem is outside their field and refers you onward.
A doctor who declines to prescribe a specific medication or scan you asked for, and explains why.
discernment_questions: Did anyone ask me detailed questions about the symptom, or only tell me what it was?
Was a physical cause actually checked, or only ruled out by suggestion?
When I asked for a test or second opinion, was it treated as reasonable?
Does the record match what I said?
Have I heard the same dismissal from more than one clinician, or only one?
less_concerning_if: The explanation is paired with a follow-up date and an open invitation to come back.
Different clinicians who see you reach compatible conclusions and explain them.
You can see your notes and they match your account.
more_concerning_if: Symptoms worsen or new ones appear while the same explanation is repeated.
You are told that asking for a second opinion or a copy of your records is a problem.
The explanation is tied to your weight, gender, race, age or disability and not to any examination.
pattern_over_time_signs: You begin arriving with a written list in case you are cut off.
You play down symptoms in the exam room to avoid being labeled.
You wait longer to seek care and put off visits for new problems.
A diagnosis, when it comes, arrives after years of the same answer from several people.
codex_completed.repair_check: A clinician who returns to your original account, says what they missed, orders the test or referral you asked about, and writes your symptoms down in your words has changed something. A 'sorry you felt that way' that leaves the plan as it was has not.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask that your symptoms be written in the chart in your own words, then see what follows. Does the entry appear, and does the plan address it? Compare the visit summary with your own notes before deciding how the request was taken.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Pain and fatigue cannot be seen, so clinicians rely on what patients say, and a clinician with limited time may reach for a familiar explanation. Once a psychological or lifestyle explanation is in the notes, later clinicians can read the chart through it. Patients who have been dismissed before may soften their reports, which makes dismissal easier still.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe leaving visits feeling foolish, then going home and doubting whether the pain is real. Symptoms may go unmentioned, care may be delayed, and appointments may start to feel like something to brace for. A diagnosis, when it comes, can bring relief alongside grief and anger at how long it took, and a lasting wariness of waiting rooms.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the clinician to walk you through their reasoning: 'What else could cause this, and how would we rule those out?' A real answer shows the thinking.
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask for the refusal to be written down: 'If you're not ordering that test, could you note that I asked and why it was declined?'
response_options.disengagement: If the visit is not going anywhere, end it politely and book with another clinician or clinic, bringing your notes along.
response_options.support_seeking: Bring someone to appointments, join a group for your symptom or condition, and ask a patient advocate how to request a second opinion.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you must show an employer or school what you are dealing with, ask the clinician to put your symptoms and limits in a letter, and keep copies of every visit summary.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'm still having this pain and it's affecting my work and sleep. What else could it be, and what do you suggest if it doesn't improve? Could you also record in my chart that I asked for further tests?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Dismissed symptoms are most dangerous when they signal something time-critical: pain that is sudden and severe, symptoms that are rapidly worsening, a fever with a stiff neck or confusion, or signs of a stroke. Do not wait for a better appointment for those; go to an emergency department and describe what you told earlier clinicians. For anything slower, request your own records and book a second opinion.
misuse_warning: Using the label for any visit that did not end in the answer or treatment you wanted can overlook honest uncertainty and make good clinicians harder to reach.
Telling a person that their doctor 'gaslit' them, before they have asked about the reasoning, can push them away from care they still need.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Clinical Tone Policing criticizes how you express distress, while medical gaslighting is about whether your symptoms are believed at all. Trash-Can Diagnosis hands out a mental health label as an insult, and Weaponized Therapy-Speak uses clinical words in arguments between people. Medical gaslighting happens inside a care relationship, where the thing being discounted is your account of your own body.

Phrase matching can flag wording, but it cannot know intent, tone, history, context, or whether the claim is even true — an innocent reading is always attached to every match. Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Sexual Coercion
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Using pressure, guilt, obligation or implied consequences to push someone into sexual activity without their free consent.
codex_completed.short_definition: Using pressure, guilt, obligation or implied consequences to push someone into sexual activity without their free consent.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Sexual coercion covers the many ways, short of physical force, that a person can be pushed into sex or sexual acts: repeated asking after a no, sulking or anger, guilt about what is owed, threats to end something, or leaning on a difference in power. Consent that is given to avoid a penalty, or to stop the asking, is not free consent. A single moment of disappointment is not coercion. The pattern shows when a no carries a cost, and the costs push the answer toward yes.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone makes saying no costly, through guilt, anger, pressure or threats, until agreeing feels easier than refusing.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Saying yes under pressure is not the same as wanting to, and living with the difference can leave real marks: shame, numbness, loss of trust in your own signals. You are not to blame for what pressure made you do. Naming it can help restore your sense of your own limits.
what_it_is: Pressure to engage in a sexual act, delivered through guilt, anger, sulking, or repeated asking.
Consequences attached to a no, whether spoken or implied: a cold shoulder, a threat to leave, a withdrawal of money or help.
Can be linked to a power gap, such as age, employment, money, or immigration status.
Includes pushing for acts you have already declined, and pressing during moments when you are tired, intoxicated or afraid.
Often hard to name from the inside because no force was used.
what_it_sounds_like: You owe me this after everything I've done for you.
If you really loved me, you would.
Everyone else does it. What is wrong with you?
Fine. I guess I'll find someone who will.
I'll be in a terrible mood all week if you say no again.
Don't be so dramatic. Just give in and get it over with.
You said you wanted to keep this job, didn't you?
what_it_is_not: Telling a partner honestly that you feel disappointed or want more closeness, and then accepting 'not tonight' without a penalty.
Flirting and asking once, with the other person free to decline and no change in the mood afterwards.
Partners who talk openly about a mismatch in desire and work out together what to do about it.
Changing your mind in the moment and saying so, with the other person stopping straight away.
Your own mixed feelings after saying yes, which can be worth talking over with a counselor but do not by themselves show that pressure occurred.
this_may_be_it_when: A no is followed by sulking, anger, guilt, or a threat, rather than acceptance.
The asking continues after a clear refusal, or arrives at times you are least able to resist.
Something you need, such as housing, a job, or affection, seems tied to the answer.
You say yes mainly to end the pressure or to avoid what will happen if you do not.
You find yourself planning how to avoid being alone with this person.
this_may_not_be_it_when: A no is met with acceptance, even if there is visible disappointment.
Both of you can raise desire openly and neither feels owed anything.
Nothing in your life depends on the answer, and the mood does not change if you decline.
They ask once, hear your answer, and move on.
You feel free to start, stop, or change your mind during intimacy.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Partners often differ in how much they want sex, and voicing that difference does not equal pressure.
A person can feel hurt by a refusal without trying to override it.
Shared, honest talk about intimacy may sound intense without being coercive, if every no is honored.
common_false_positives: A partner who says 'I miss you, and I'd love to be close tonight', and then fully accepts 'not tonight.'
A couple negotiating how often to be intimate, each free to say what they want and to say no.
Sadness or a quiet evening after a refusal, without blame or consequence attached.
discernment_questions: If I said no, would the answer be respected without a cost to me?
Am I agreeing because I want to, or to stop the pressure or avoid a consequence?
Does the other person take my no as an answer, or as the start of a negotiation?
Is anything I rely on, such as my home, money, job, or the peace in the house, linked to the answer?
Would I feel able to change my mind halfway through?
less_concerning_if: A decline is accepted with only brief, honest disappointment and no penalty.
The topic can be raised by either person without fear.
Nothing tangible depends on what you say.
more_concerning_if: Saying no leads to threats, withdrawal of money or housing, or intimidation.
There is a big gap in power, such as an employer, a teacher, or someone you depend on for immigration status.
You are pressed when you are asleep, intoxicated, ill, or afraid, or after you have already said no.
pattern_over_time_signs: You say yes more often to prevent a bad mood than because you want to.
You plan your evenings to avoid being alone with this person, or go to bed at different times.
You feel dread, numbness, or relief when the other person is away.
Refusals have become rare because you have learned what they cost.
codex_completed.repair_check: Where there has been pressure, repair starts with the person accepting a no with no sulking and no later reminder of it. Pay attention to whether they take responsibility for the pressure itself rather than for your reaction, and whether your no stays free of cost for weeks afterwards. Words alone, followed by more asking, are not it.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself one thing after a no: did the mood, the money, or the manners toward you change afterwards? A respected no leaves the relationship as it was, perhaps with some disappointment. A no that is punished, argued with, or raised again the next day was treated as an opening bid.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When a refusal carries a cost, the mind may start to weigh the cost of saying no against the cost of going along, and tiredness, fear or dependence can tip that scale. Going along repeatedly can blur the line in your own head between what you chose and what you gave in to, which can make it hard to trust your own signals afterwards.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Numbness, shame, going quiet during intimacy, going quiet during intimacy, dreading evenings and doubting whether they ever really wanted something are all described. Some say they only later realized they had been pressed, and struggled with whether it 'counted'. Many describe a loss of trust in their own judgment about what they want.

response_options.soft_clarification: Say your answer once, plainly, and stay in the conversation: 'I'm saying no, and I need that to be enough. I'd like to talk about what closeness looks like for us.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep to the answer without giving reasons: 'My answer is no, and it doesn't need a reason. I'd like you to stop asking tonight.'
response_options.disengagement: If you can, change location or ask to pause the conversation until tomorrow, and use that time to think about who you can speak to privately. Do not announce plans.
response_options.support_seeking: Speak to a sexual assault or domestic abuse advocate, a counselor, or a trusted friend; many services answer by phone or chat and can help you think through what happened without pressure to act.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If it happens at work or school, write down dates, words and witnesses, and speak to HR, an ombuds, a union representative, or legal aid about a confidential report.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "My answer is no, and I'd like that to be enough. I'm not able to talk about this right now. Can we pause and pick up the conversation tomorrow, with someone we both trust if you want?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Sexual pressure can sit alongside threats, stalking, control of money or housing, or force that escalates when a no is given. Warning signs include fear of what happens if you refuse, being cornered, and threats about images or reputation. Contact a sexual assault or domestic abuse hotline or an advocate to plan privately; call emergency services if you are in immediate danger.
misuse_warning: Applying this label to a partner's honest disappointment, or to a single clumsy ask that was dropped at once, can blur it with serious harm and leave real cases harder to name.
Only the person on the receiving end can say what they did or did not freely agree to; outsiders and the label itself cannot decide it for them.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: An ultimatum demands a choice and names a loss, while sexual coercion applies pressure to a specific intimate decision, often with the cost unspoken. Interrogation presses for explanations; here the pressure is for compliance. Urgency squeezes the time to decide, which may be one part of it. A false dilemma limits options. This tactic is the one aimed at consent itself.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Actively matched against pasted text by this tool, at low confidence. Phrase matching can flag wording, but it cannot know intent, tone, history, context, or whether the claim is even true — an innocent reading is always attached to every match. Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Financial Control
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can flag phrasings matching this tactic directly in pasted text, at low confidence, always alongside an innocent reading. A single flagged line is never proof — repetition, context, and the whole conversation matter far more than any one sentence.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Restricting someone's access to money, financial information or earning, or using money and assets as leverage, so that they depend on one person.
codex_completed.short_definition: Restricting someone's access to money, financial information or earning, or using money and assets as leverage, so that they depend on one person.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Financial control is limiting what a person can see, spend, earn or own, or tying money and assets to behavior, so that disagreeing or leaving becomes costly. Financial enmeshment names this same lever, money and assets tied to compliance, so one entry covers both. Shared budgets and one-earner households are ordinary. The concern is money used as a lever: access given or withdrawn depending on compliance, information kept out of sight, and one name on everything.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: One person decides what money you can see, spend or earn, and access shifts with how you behave, which makes it hard to disagree or to leave.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Money decides whether a person can pay rent, buy food, hire a lawyer or leave a bad situation. When access depends on compliance, every disagreement carries a price, and the practical options narrow without anyone saying so out loud.
what_it_is: Limiting access to bank accounts, cards, statements or tax papers, so one person cannot see the household's real position.
Controlling earning: discouraging or forbidding work, or interfering with a job, a shift or a pay check.
Putting the home, the car, the accounts and the debts in one person's name only.
Handing out money as an allowance, a reward or a punishment, with asking required each time.
Finding loans, cards or debts in your name that you did not know about or agree to.
The opposite of transparent shared finances, where both people can see everything and neither can lock the other out.
what_it_sounds_like: "You don't need your own bank account."
"I'll decide what you get to spend."
"You're not allowed to work."
"My money, my rules."
"You'll get your allowance when you behave."
"Ask me for permission before you spend."
"Everything here is in my name."
"I'll cut off your card."
what_it_is_not: Agreed household budgeting where one person tracks the books and the other can see everything and change the arrangement.
A temporary arrangement during real hardship, discussed openly and with an end in sight.
A one-earner household with shared rules, where both people have access to the money.
Long-term financial interdependence built through a mutual relationship, which is common and not used as leverage.
A couple who agree to run big purchases past each other, in both directions.
A parent or guardian managing a minor's money, or an adult's money under a formal legal or care arrangement.
this_may_be_it_when: You cannot see statements or balances, or you are told you would not understand them.
Money for groceries, medicine or transport has to be requested, and may be refused after a disagreement.
Your earnings are taken over, or work is discouraged or interfered with.
Accounts, loans or signatures exist in your name that you never knowingly agreed to.
Money comes up in arguments as something you owe or could lose.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Both of you can see every account and change the arrangement whenever you like.
You chose the split for your own reasons and can spend your share without asking.
A restriction is time-limited and openly agreed, such as repaying a debt you both took on.
You have your own account or cash, and nothing is said when you use it.
When you ask to see papers, they are shown without fuss.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People differ in how they earn, spend and save, and a gap in style is not a gap in fairness.
One partner may simply be more comfortable with paperwork, and the other happy to leave it to them while seeing everything.
Family or cultural habits may have one person handle the money by long-standing, mutual agreement.
common_false_positives: A transparent shared budget in which both people can see everything and have a real say.
"My money, my rules" said as a joke inside a system where both people have access.
A couple living tightly while paying down a debt they chose together.
discernment_questions: Can I see every account, bill and loan I am named on, today, without asking permission?
If I wanted to spend a small amount on myself, would I need to explain or ask?
Could I cover rent and food for a month on my own if I needed to?
Does money come up in arguments as something that can be given or taken away?
Has anything been opened, borrowed or signed in my name that I did not agree to?
less_concerning_if: Both people can see all accounts, and the arrangement was chosen by both.
You have money of your own that nobody comments on.
Questions about money get answers and papers, not annoyance.
more_concerning_if: Money is withheld or granted depending on how you behave in an argument.
Work, school or contact with friends is discouraged in ways that leave you without income of your own.
Debts, loans or legal documents exist in your name without your informed agreement.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your own savings, income or credit shrink over time without a decision.
You ask for small amounts and keep track of what you have been given.
You rehearse how to raise a purchase, or put it off.
Documents you need, such as ID or bank cards, end up in someone else's keeping.
codex_completed.repair_check: Look for access that no longer depends on mood: your name on the accounts, statements you can open yourself, income that stays yours, and a way to see the whole picture. An apology after a hard conversation that leaves the same arrangement in place has changed the tone, not the control.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask a small, practical question about money, such as to see last month's statement, and notice what comes next. Is the paper produced and the question treated as ordinary? Or does the answer turn to your tone, your motives, or what you owe?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When a person cannot pay for food, travel or a lawyer without permission, going along can become the practical path of least resistance. Access that is granted and withdrawn can also teach a person to anticipate moods and avoid asking. Over time the narrowing of options can feel like a fact of life instead of an arrangement that someone could change.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe asking permission for small purchases, hiding receipts, feeling like a child in their own home, and a sinking sense that leaving is not affordable. Some find out about debts only when a letter arrives. Others say the money was never the whole story, and that the loss of choices was what wore them down.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask an ordinary question in an ordinary tone: "Could we look at the statements together this weekend? I'd like to understand where we stand." If asking could make things worse, skip this step.
response_options.firm_boundary: Name the pattern once, calmly, without blame: "When money depends on how I behave, it is hard for me to speak up. Could we change that?"
response_options.disengagement: If a money conversation turns to what you owe or could lose, you can ask to pause it: "I need some time to think. Can we come back to this?" Use your own judgment about whether pausing is safe.
response_options.support_seeking: Speak to a domestic abuse advocate, a financial counselor or a legal aid service. Many can talk privately about economic abuse and help with documents, accounts and credit without the other person knowing.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If someone else controls your pay, ask payroll or HR in writing, when it is safe, whether wages can go to an account in your sole name. A legal aid or employment advice service can explain your rights.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Could we go through the accounts together this weekend? I'd like both of us to be able to see what we have and agree who decides what."
codex_completed.safety_note: Warning signs include being cut off from money after you disagree, losing hold of your ID, phone or transport, debts opened in your name, or being kept from work. Quietly note what you know, and talk to a domestic abuse advocate or legal aid service about protecting income, documents and credit before you raise any change with the other person.
misuse_warning: Calling a tight budget, or one partner paying the bills, financial control can turn an agreed arrangement into an accusation. The test is whether the other person can see it and change it.
Using the label on a parent or guardian who manages a minor's or dependent adult's money under a formal arrangement mistakes protection for control.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Infantilization treats you as unable to run your affairs in general, while financial control is specifically about who holds the money and the papers. "I Know Best" Paternalism overrides your choices for your own good and needs a stated reason; here the rule can be simply that the money is theirs. Isolation undermines your other relationships, whereas this limits the money needed to pay, travel or stay.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Actively matched against pasted text by this tool, at low confidence. Phrase matching can flag wording, but it cannot know intent, tone, history, context, or whether the claim is even true — an innocent reading is always attached to every match. Guards (sarcasm, quotation, hypothetical framing, reported speech, and others) can reduce or nullify a match. Severity only contributes to the overall index above the detection floor.

codex_completed.name: Weaponized Incompetence
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can technically match phrasing linked to this tactic, but text alone cannot reliably establish intent here — the same words are too easily produced by an innocent explanation. It is shown as low-signal information only and is never scored.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A pattern in which someone seems unable to do an unwanted task, so that it falls to another person for good.
codex_completed.short_definition: A pattern in which someone seems unable to do an unwanted task, so that it falls to another person for good.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A task is done badly, or a person says they just cannot do it, and soon it is given to someone else. It happens most often in households and workplaces over chores such as laundry, school forms or booking appointments. This entry does not claim to know why anyone struggles with a task, and skill gaps, disability and honest confusion are common. What stands out is a task that never gets learned and always lands with the same person.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A chore gets done so badly, or is said to be so hard, that you take it over for good, and it never comes back to them.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The task lands permanently on one person, along with the work of noticing it, asking about it, and eventually giving up on asking. Raising it also makes them sound as if they are complaining about help they were offered.
what_it_is: A task handed back to one person after a failed or half-hearted try, until it quietly becomes theirs.
Found mostly in unseen work: remembering birthdays, tracking appointments, restocking supplies, handling forms.
It often comes with praise, like 'you're just so much better at this', which makes the shift feel like a compliment.
The person taking on the extra load also carries the mental effort of watching for what has been missed.
what_it_sounds_like: You're just better at it than I am.
I'll only do it wrong, and then you'll be annoyed.
I loaded the dishwasher and now nothing fits. You'd better do it.
I can't work out that form. Could you handle it?
You do it so much faster. It makes sense for you to keep doing it.
Don't ask me, I never know where anything goes.
A shirt returned pink from the wash, with the remark 'well, I tried'.
what_it_is_not: A real gap in skill, such as someone who never learned to cook, who is willing to be taught and does improve.
Disability, ADHD, chronic illness or exhaustion, which can make some tasks truly harder, in ways that are not a choice.
A division of labor you both chose after talking it over, where the other person takes tasks of equal weight elsewhere.
A person new to a task who fumbles at first and gets better with each go.
One bad attempt on a day when someone was sick or distracted.
this_may_be_it_when: The person manages equally hard tasks at work or in hobbies, but not this one.
Offers to teach them are put off or brushed aside.
The same unwanted jobs, and not the pleasant ones, are the ones they cannot seem to do.
After each failed attempt, you take the task back and they do not try again.
You do the planning and remembering for a job that they call shared.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They ask for instruction, practice and get better over weeks.
They take on another job of similar weight and handle it reliably.
The difficulty is linked to a known health condition and you have agreed together on how to cope.
They check in on how the shared load feels to you, and adjust.
The task is one they do carry out, only to a different standard than yours.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People often have unequal standards about what 'clean' or 'done' means, which can look like incompetence from the other side.
Someone who grew up never doing a given job may feel truly lost and embarrassed, and hide it by avoiding it.
Fear of being criticized can lead a person to avoid a task that they are afraid of doing wrong.
common_false_positives: A new parent still learning how to handle a feeding or bath routine, who asks questions and improves each week.
A partner with a disability who does tasks in a different way or at a different time, by agreement.
A coworker who is honestly out of their depth in a new system and is asking for training.
discernment_questions: Does the skill seem to appear for tasks they like and vanish for those they do not?
When you offer to teach, is the offer taken up?
Have they ever got better at this task, even slowly?
Who carries the job of remembering that the task exists?
If the roles were swapped, would you be allowed to say 'I can't, you do it'?
less_concerning_if: They take up teaching and visibly improve, even if it is slow.
The overall load, counting unseen work, is shared in a way both of you call fair.
The difficulty is stated openly, along with an agreed way to deal with it.
more_concerning_if: The tasks avoided involve money, children's needs or health appointments, where mistakes cost real harm and someone else must clean up.
Your complaints are met with annoyance or sulking, so you stop raising them.
You have taken on the work to protect them from being upset.
pattern_over_time_signs: The list of things only you do grows, and nothing comes off it.
You start doing jobs before they are needed so as to avoid the flawed version.
You carry a running mental list of what has to be done, and they carry none.
You feel more like a manager than a partner or colleague.
codex_completed.repair_check: Watch what happens with the task itself, not what is said about it. Change looks like them learning it, doing it unprompted, and taking over the remembering too. A warm apology followed by another handback the next week leaves the work where it was.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Hand the task back with a clear date and no rescue, then see what follows. Does it get done, imperfectly but sincerely? Or does it quietly come back to you, with a reason? Your answer shows whether the new split is being kept.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A person who gets quick relief from an unwanted job after a poor attempt can come to expect that outcome again. Meanwhile, the one who takes the job over often does so to avoid delay or conflict, and that reinforces the split. Over time the extra work can come to seem like a trait of the person who does it, rather than a division that formed gradually.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe resentment building quietly, tiredness from managing the household or team on top of their own tasks, and guilt about feeling resentful. Some say they felt silly raising something that sounded like 'I do too much laundry'. Others describe feeling like a parent to another adult and losing the sense of being partners.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name the specific task and the gap: 'I notice the school forms always end up with me. Can we work out how you take them on?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hand the job back with a date: 'This one is yours now, start to finish, including remembering it. I'll show you once, and then I won't redo it.'
response_options.disengagement: Let a low-stakes task stay undone or done imperfectly rather than rescuing it, and see whether the other person takes it up.
response_options.support_seeking: Write out all the recurring tasks, including the unseen ones, and go through the list with someone who knows both of you, to check your sense of the balance.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask for tasks to be assigned in writing, with an owner and a date, and rotate the unpopular jobs on a shared schedule.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'm happy to show you how I do the school forms once. After that they're yours to track and finish, including remembering the deadlines. If it turns out to be really hard for you, tell me and we'll work out a swap of equal weight."
codex_completed.safety_note: This is a fairness and workload issue, not usually a safety one. It changes if the avoided tasks involve a child's medical care or safety, or if you are being punished for handing a task back, or if you control no money and cannot leave a bad split. In those cases, speak to a family doctor, a mediator or legal aid about the specific job at stake.
misuse_warning: Applying this label to anyone who does a chore differently from you can punish people who are honestly learning or who have a disability. Check whether they improve and whether the load really is uneven.
Using it as an accusation of laziness ends the conversation. This entry is about a pattern in the work, not what anyone intends.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Blame-Shifting is about responsibility for something already done wrong, while Weaponized Incompetence is about who ends up with future work. Minimization shrinks your complaint, saying it is only a chore, whereas the pattern here is the quiet handover of the chore itself. Denial refuses that anything is wrong; this one often involves cheerful agreement that they are bad at the task.
codex_completed.detection_notes: A phrasing pattern exists in this tool's library for this tactic, but it is deliberately capped below the scoring threshold: this signal is too context-dependent and too easily produced innocently for text alone to establish intent. It is never scored.

codex_completed.name: Strategic Apathy
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can technically match phrasing linked to this tactic, but text alone cannot reliably establish intent here — the same words are too easily produced by an innocent explanation. It is shown as low-signal information only and is never scored.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Declaring 'I don't care' or 'whatever you want' at decision points, then criticizing whichever choice the other person makes.
codex_completed.short_definition: Declaring 'I don't care' or 'whatever you want' at decision points, then criticizing whichever choice the other person makes.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A choice has to be made: a restaurant, a school, a holiday, a house. One person says 'you pick, I don't mind', and the other picks. Later the choice is picked apart. The first person carries no risk, while the second carries all of it. This entry does not claim to know why someone says they do not care, and real indifference is common. What stands out is a shrug at the moment of choosing and strong views afterward.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You are told 'I don't care, you decide', and then whatever you choose turns out to be wrong.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: One person makes every decision alone and then carries the criticism for whichever way it went. Over time, deciding stops feeling like having a say and starts feeling like exposure.
what_it_is: A refusal to state any preference at the moment a decision is due, even when asked directly.
Followed by disappointment, sighs or complaints once the other person has chosen.
Seen with small choices, such as dinner, and with large ones, such as moving or how to raise children.
It leaves one person with all the responsibility and none of the agreement, since a choice they never shared in cannot be fully theirs.
what_it_sounds_like: I don't care, you decide.
Whatever you want is fine with me.
Do what you want, you always do anyway.
It's your call. Don't blame me if it goes wrong.
(After the choice) Well, I wouldn't have picked that one.
(After the choice) I said I didn't mind, but I didn't think you'd pick that.
I'm not the one who chose it.
what_it_is_not: Honest indifference about a small thing, with no later complaint about the outcome.
Depression, burnout or decision fatigue, where choosing really does feel impossible and the person says so openly.
A couple who agreed that one of them handles certain kinds of decisions, such as holidays or finances, and who trust each other's judgment.
Someone from a family or culture where deferring to the host or the other person is polite, and who means it.
A person who truly has no strong feeling on the matter and is happy with any result.
this_may_be_it_when: The 'I don't care' always comes on matters that carry some risk of a poor outcome.
Preferences appear after the decision is made, often as criticism.
You are asked to decide, then told you should have known what they wanted.
When a decision goes well, you hear no credit, and when it goes badly, you hear all of the blame.
You have started guessing at their preferences rather than choosing for yourself.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They accept the result cheerfully, whatever it is.
They tell you plainly that they are overwhelmed and need you to take this one.
They share responsibility afterward, saying 'we chose that, let's fix it'.
The pattern is only on small, low-stakes choices.
Their indifference is the same across the decisions that affect only them.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People who often get overruled can learn to stop stating a preference at all, which looks like apathy from outside.
Someone anxious about choosing wrong may hand the choice off, then feel a mix of relief and regret.
Many people truly have no strong view about ordinary things like where to eat, and just want to be done.
common_false_positives: A friend who says 'anywhere is fine' about dinner, and enjoys wherever you end up.
A partner coping with a heavy period at work who asks you to run the planning for now, and thanks you.
A teenager who shrugs about a family outing and then has a good time.
discernment_questions: After the decision, do you hear a preference you were never told?
Does the indifference appear only when something could go wrong?
If you pick what you think they would like, is it still wrong?
Does the person ever take responsibility for a choice you made together?
Can you name a time they were glad about what you chose?
less_concerning_if: A mix of decisions are made by each of you, and there is no running commentary on the outcome.
When asked, they can say what matters to them, even if it is just one thing.
The indifference is stated as it is, like 'I'm worn out, I'll go with whatever you pick', and held to.
more_concerning_if: The decisions involve things with high stakes, like moving, money or children, and you are left to carry them alone.
You are blamed for outcomes outside your control, such as a delayed flight on the trip you chose.
Asking for their input leads to anger or silence, so you stop asking.
pattern_over_time_signs: You stall or put off decisions because you dread the aftermath.
You over-research every option to be able to defend your pick.
You rehearse justifications before committing to even a small choice.
Joint decisions have turned into your decisions, and you cannot say when that happened.
codex_completed.repair_check: At the next decision, change either shows or it does not. Change shows in them naming a preference up front, even a small one, and standing by the outcome afterward. Saying 'I know I leave it all to you' and then going back to 'whatever' with the next choice is not that.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Try this: say that you'll choose once they have given one preference, and wait. Does a preference arrive? Or does the wait itself get blamed, as in 'now you're making a big deal of it'? What fills that silence shows how the request is landing.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Making a choice exposes a person to being wrong. When one person declines to take part, they avoid that exposure, while the other takes on all of it. If criticism follows, the decision-maker may begin to try to predict the other's hidden preferences, a task that has no stable answer and can wear down confidence in their own judgment.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe dreading ordinary choices, feeling alone in a partnership, and second-guessing themselves long after a decision is made. Some say they started to avoid deciding altogether, or to make safe, dull choices. Others describe feeling like a manager of someone else's life, tired of carrying the blame as well as the work.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for one small input: 'I'd really like to hear one thing you'd want here, even if it's minor.' The reply shows if a preference exists.
response_options.firm_boundary: Share the outcome as well as the decision: 'If you leave this to me, then it's my choice and I won't hear it picked apart afterward.'
response_options.disengagement: On low-stakes choices, pick quickly without seeking approval and move on. Save your energy for the ones that really need two voices.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask a friend how they handle shared decisions, to find out what a balanced split looks like, then compare it with your own.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager says 'your call' and later objects, ask for the decision criteria in writing before you act, and send a one-line note confirming what you chose.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "If you tell me to decide, I'll decide, and then it's decided. I'd like one thing from you before I do. What matters most to you about this? If you really have no preference, I'll go ahead without hearing about it afterward."
codex_completed.safety_note: Strategic Apathy is a pattern about decisions, not a danger in itself. What would change that is blame for outcomes escalating to anger, threats, or punishment, or being left to bear the cost of decisions about money, housing or children with no access to the accounts or papers. If that is happening, collect copies of key documents and speak with a financial counselor or legal aid service about your position.
misuse_warning: Reading every 'I don't mind' as a trap can make you miss someone who truly is easygoing. Look for the later criticism, not the shrug.
Pushing a tired or depressed person to state preferences can add to their burden. Ask first whether they are struggling.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Blame-Shifting moves fault for something that went wrong onto you after the fact, while Strategic Apathy sets up the position beforehand by leaving you as the only decider. Minimization says your concern is small; here the person says their own opinion is. Denial refuses to admit a problem, and this one does not even stake out a position that could be denied.

codex_completed.name: Reverse Psychology
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can technically match phrasing linked to this tactic, but text alone cannot reliably establish intent here — the same words are too easily produced by an innocent explanation. It is shown as low-signal information only and is never scored.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Arguing against the outcome you actually want, so that the other person's wish to resist or prove you wrong carries them to it.
codex_completed.short_definition: Arguing against the outcome you actually want, so that the other person's wish to resist or prove you wrong carries them to it.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Reverse psychology is the play of saying the opposite of what you want, hoping contrary feelings do the work. Used lightly, it is a familiar game with children, friends and in jokes. In a manipulative form, doubt or a dare is aimed at a person's pride or independence, so the choice they believe they made on their own was steered. Text alone cannot show which is happening, and a speaker may be honestly doubtful, which is why this is a watch-only entry and never a verdict.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone talks you out of something they actually want you to do, hoping you will argue back and choose it yourself.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The target's own resistance is what does the deciding, so a choice that felt like their own defiance may not have been theirs at all. Over time you might lose track of which of your decisions were really yours.
what_it_is: Arguing for the opposite of the wanted result, so that your resistance leads to it.
Often delivered as doubt, a dare, or mock indifference, such as 'you probably could not do it.'
Works by aiming at pride, independence, or the wish to prove someone wrong.
Overlaps with playful teasing and with honest doubt, so it cannot be read from the words alone.
Only clear in hindsight, when the outcome matches what the speaker quietly wanted all along.
what_it_sounds_like: You probably couldn't handle it anyway.
Fine, don't come. I'm sure you have better things to do.
I wouldn't ask you to take on that project. It might be too much for you.
Oh, you wouldn't want to move in with me. It would cramp your style.
Don't apply for it. They'd never pick you anyway.
You can say no. I'm sure you will.
what_it_is_not: Playful teasing between friends who both know it is a game, such as 'you will never beat me at chess.'
Honest doubt about your readiness, voiced out of concern, that the speaker would accept if you agreed with it.
A parent's mild trick with a toddler about eating vegetables, which is a common and openly understood game.
A coach challenging you to prove yourself, with the goal stated openly and your success wanted either way.
Plain reluctance to push you, in which the speaker truly would be fine with whichever way you choose.
this_may_be_it_when: The doubt appears just before a commitment the speaker obviously wants.
You notice the speaker's mood brightens when you push back and prove them wrong.
The discouraging line is repeated in similar words before different decisions.
If you take the discouragement at face value, the speaker seems unexpectedly disappointed.
Looking back, several choices that felt like your own defiance ended up serving the speaker.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The speaker would be genuinely content if you said 'you are right, I won't.'
The doubt is specific, reasoned, and open to discussion.
It is part of a game or joke you both play and enjoy.
The speaker has nothing to gain from either outcome.
There is no outcome the speaker seems to be waiting for.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A person who truly is unsure about your plan may voice doubt, without any aim of provoking a reaction.
Teasing and challenges are an ordinary part of many friendships and families.
Someone reluctant to pressure you may speak in a low-key way that sounds like discouragement but is simply respect for your freedom.
common_false_positives: A friend saying 'you will never finish that marathon' as a running joke, who cheers loudest at the finish line.
A relative who honestly worries about a risky plan and says so, and accepts your decision to go ahead.
A colleague who says 'it's a hard role, I'm not sure it suits you' because they care about your wellbeing.
discernment_questions: Would the speaker accept it if I simply agreed with their doubt?
Does the discouragement line up neatly with what they wanted me to do?
Have I noticed this move before, before other decisions?
Do I feel pushed to prove something rather than to decide something?
Would I have chosen this without the dare?
less_concerning_if: The doubt is explained with reasons you can weigh.
The speaker is relaxed whichever way you go.
It is a known game, played by both of you.
more_concerning_if: The dares attach to decisions with real stakes, such as money, moving, or ending a relationship.
The speaker pushes back or sulks when you accept the discouragement.
You notice that your pride is the main thing being used.
pattern_over_time_signs: You realize several 'independent' decisions all ended in the same outcome for the same person.
You find yourself reacting to the doubt before hearing the reasons.
You have started second-guessing whether your own motives are really your own.
A friend points out that you tend to do the exact thing you are told you will not.
codex_completed.repair_check: Once you have named it, the useful change is that the speaker says what they want straight out and lets you answer. They may feel awkward saying it. If the dares simply change wording, or the teasing becomes more sophisticated after you raise it, the same approach has been repackaged.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Try replying 'you may be right, I'll pass' and see what happens. If the response is relaxed, there was likely no hidden aim. If the speaker suddenly argues in favor of the very thing they discouraged, the doubt was probably serving a purpose.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People often resist feeling told what to do, a reaction sometimes called reactance, and a challenge to our ability can sharpen the urge to prove it wrong. Reverse psychology tends to lean on those habits, so that the decision feels like independence even when it has been shaped from outside. It is likely to land best where pride or rivalry is already in play.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe an uneasy sense that choices they were proud of had been anticipated, doubt about which of their decisions were truly their own, and, afterward, irritation at having been steered. Some say they started second-guessing even sincere encouragement, and found it hard to trust kind words without searching for a motive.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the speaker to say it directly: 'What do you actually want me to do here? I'd rather hear it straight.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to rise to it: 'I don't make decisions to prove a point. I'll decide based on what I want.'
response_options.disengagement: If a dare lands, pause before replying. Let a day pass before agreeing to anything that was set up as a challenge.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe the exchange to someone who knows both of you and ask whether they would have heard it as honest doubt or as a nudge.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: When a manager discourages you in a way that might be provocation, ask for the actual expectation and the reasoning, and confirm any decision in writing.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "If you'd like me to do this, say so plainly and I'll consider it. I'm not going to decide anything based on a dare, and I'm happy to hear honest reasons either way."
codex_completed.safety_note: On its own this is a low-stakes move. It becomes worrying when the provocation steers you toward real risk to your money, health, or safety, or toward actions that give someone control of your housing, work or finances. If a pattern of dares has left you committed to something costly, a trusted adviser or legal aid can help you review it.
misuse_warning: Because honest doubt and playful teasing look the same in text, accusing someone of reverse psychology on a single remark can wrongly cast a caring comment as scheming.
Treating every discouragement as a trick can make it hard to accept genuine advice.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: An ultimatum forces a choice under threat; reverse psychology threatens nothing and pretends to hold back. A false dilemma narrows your options, while this tactic makes one option feel like your own idea. Interrogation demands answers and is openly forceful. Here the speaker seems to step back, which is what lets the push go unnoticed. The pull in this tactic comes from your resistance.

codex_completed.name: Malicious Compliance
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can technically match phrasing linked to this tactic, but text alone cannot reliably establish intent here — the same words are too easily produced by an innocent explanation. It is shown as low-signal information only and is never scored.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Doing exactly what was asked, to the letter, in a way that predictably defeats the point of the request.
codex_completed.short_definition: Doing exactly what was asked, to the letter, in a way that predictably defeats the point of the request.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Malicious compliance is carrying out an instruction so literally that the result fails the purpose behind it, while the person can still say they did as told. It tends to show up in workplaces and households after a disagreement, an unwelcome order or a criticism. The same outcome can come from an honest literal reading, a badly worded request or a rule that really does produce a bad result, so one case says little about why it happened. A pattern is the literal reading being chosen again and again, soon after friction.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You asked for something, you got exactly those words and nothing more, and the result is useless. It is hard to complain because the instruction was followed.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The person on the receiving end absorbs the failure with no clear grievance to name. The instruction was followed, so pointing at anything risks sounding unreasonable, and they are left wondering whether they asked badly.
what_it_is: Meeting the exact wording of a request while its obvious purpose goes unmet.
Often appears after an order the person disagreed with, a rebuke, or a change they were not consulted on.
Can involve rules as well as requests, such as applying every written procedure to the letter when everyone knows a shortcut would have worked.
Leaves the asker holding a result that is correct on paper and wrong in practice.
Hard to dispute, because the person can point to the instruction exactly as it was given.
what_it_sounds_like: You said to send it to everyone on the list, so I did. All four hundred of them.
You told me to wait for your sign-off before ordering anything, so we've been without supplies all week.
You asked me to wash the dishes. You didn't say to dry them or put them away.
You said 'by Friday.' It's Friday, 11:58 at night.
I just did it the way you told me to, said flatly after something goes wrong.
Happy to. Just tell me every single step and I'll do exactly those steps.
A colleague follows a new procedure line by line for a job that used to take ten minutes, and it now takes the whole afternoon.
what_it_is_not: Genuine literal-mindedness. Many people, including many autistic people, take words at face value, and the result can look the same with no hostility behind it.
A declared work-to-rule action, where a team announces openly that it will follow every rule strictly as a protest. That is stated, not hidden.
A vague request that was met exactly as phrased. The gap may be in the instruction.
Declining to do unpaid or out-of-scope extras after being refused fair terms, which is a boundary about the job.
Following a safety or legal rule that is inconvenient but real.
Weak results from someone who lacked the context or skill and tried their best.
this_may_be_it_when: The literal reading is one almost nobody would choose, from a person who usually understands unspoken context well.
It begins soon after a disagreement, a criticism, or an order they objected to.
When the result fails, the person seems pleased or flatly satisfied rather than puzzled.
After you explain the purpose plainly, the next result is still literal in the same way, or in a new way.
The cost of the failure falls mostly on the person who gave the instruction.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The person asks 'do you mean this or that?' before starting, and then does what you clarified.
Once the purpose is stated, the next result fits it.
They tell you what they are doing as they go: 'I'll do exactly this unless you want more.'
The task was new to them and they had nobody to ask.
They read similar requests sensibly with other people and in calmer weeks.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Someone new to a role may follow instructions tightly out of caution, afraid of overstepping.
A person who was blamed for earlier judgment calls may now prefer exactness, because exactness feels safer.
The same words mean different things in different workplaces and families, so 'tidy up' can differ from house to house.
Tiredness or overload can reduce anyone to the literal minimum.
common_false_positives: A new employee who follows the checklist exactly because nobody said which steps could be skipped.
A team that announces in the open that it will follow every rule strictly during a pay dispute.
A child told to 'clean your room' who shoves everything under the bed, having finished the task as they understood it.
discernment_questions: If I had said the purpose out loud in one sentence, would the outcome have been different?
With other tasks, does this person usually grasp what I mean without it being spelled out?
Did the literal reading start after a disagreement or after I said no to something?
Have they been blamed before for guessing wrong, so that exactness now feels safer to them?
When the result failed, did they seem sorry, puzzled, or pleased?
less_concerning_if: The outcome follows the exact words, and the person fixes it quickly once the purpose is explained.
They asked what you meant before they started.
It happened once, in a rushed week, off a rushed instruction.
more_concerning_if: The person reads instructions loosely and sensibly when it suits them, and rigidly only on tasks they objected to.
The failures land at the moments where they cost the most, such as the hour before a deadline.
Asking for clarification gets 'you said what you said', and the next request goes the same way.
pattern_over_time_signs: You start writing instructions like contracts, listing every step and every exception.
You take the task back or do it yourself to avoid the outcome.
Routine requests begin to need follow-up checks that they never needed before.
You build up a set of 'I did what you asked' exchanges that are hard to describe to anyone else.
codex_completed.repair_check: Once you have explained a task's purpose, the next one comes back sensibly done, together with a plain acknowledgment of what went wrong the last time. Quick agreement to every instruction, followed by the same exact-words result, means the pattern is still running.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself what changes after you say you want the purpose honored as well as the wording. Do tasks begin arriving fit for use, or does the answer become 'then say so next time'?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: An instruction can be treated as a contract, and meeting its words gives a person cover. Disagreement can then be expressed through the outcome instead of through a conversation. This can happen when someone feels unable to refuse openly, felt unheard when they objected, or was blamed for earlier judgment calls. The asker then sees only a failed task, not the disagreement beneath it.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe becoming stiff and over-specific in how they ask, wondering whether they phrased something badly, and carrying the cost of the failed work themselves. Some start to dread delegating or hold back from making requests. Others describe feeling oddly unable to complain, since the instruction was carried out.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name the purpose, not only the task: 'What I need is a handout people can use tonight. Will this do that?' Then see whether the next version fits.
response_options.firm_boundary: State the standard you expect: 'I need the work to meet the goal, not just the wording. If a step won't get us there, tell me before you do it.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop writing longer and longer instructions to close each loophole. Give the goal, check the result once, and move the task elsewhere if it keeps failing.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe two or three of the instructions and results to a colleague or friend who knows both of you, and ask whether they would have read your request the way you meant it.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Put the goal and deadline in writing and invite questions up front. If it recurs, take dated examples of outcomes to your manager, and leave guesses about motive out of it.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "When I ask for something, I need it to do the job, not just match my words. If my wording is unclear, ask me before you start. If you disagree with the request, tell me, and we can sort it out."
codex_completed.safety_note: Sloppy work done to spite you is friction over work or chores, not a danger signal. That changes if the failures involve a skipped safety step, a missed medication, or work that puts your job at risk without being traceable to you. Then record dates and outcomes, and report the safety step to a supervisor, safety officer or union rep.
misuse_warning: Calling a literal reading 'malicious' assumes a motive you cannot see. Someone who takes words at face value, or who was burned for guessing, can be accused of sabotage when they are being careful.
The label can excuse a vague request. If you never said what you wanted, the problem may sit in the instruction.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Blame-Shifting turns the fault toward you once something goes wrong; here the fault is pre-assigned to your own wording. Minimization plays a harm down after it is raised, while here the harm is built into the work itself. Denial contests what happened, but nothing is contested here: the request was met, just very narrowly.

codex_completed.name: Moral Licensing
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can technically match phrasing linked to this tactic, but text alone cannot reliably establish intent here — the same words are too easily produced by an innocent explanation. It is shown as low-signal information only and is never scored.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Pointing to a good character or past good deeds as a reason the present complaint does not need an answer.
codex_completed.short_definition: Pointing to a good character or past good deeds as a reason the present complaint does not need an answer.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: As used here, moral licensing is offering someone's good reputation or earlier kindness in place of an answer to what is being raised now. Psychologists also use the term for a tendency to feel freer to act badly after doing something good, which can happen quietly with no conversation at all. In an exchange it shows when a complaint about Tuesday is met with a list of what was done for years. One mention of a record is ordinary context. The pattern is the record regularly taking the place of the answer.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Instead of talking about what you raised, the other person reminds you how good they are or what they have done for you, and your complaint is left sitting there.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A specific, current complaint goes unanswered because the conversation turns into a ruling on someone's overall goodness. The person who raised it never asked that question and cannot win it, and the original problem stays exactly where it was.
what_it_is: A swap: a record of past good conduct is placed where an answer to the current complaint should be.
Draws on many kinds of credit, such as years of service, donations, a clean record, belonging to a respected group, or favors done for you.
Can come from others who vouch for the person, as in 'he would never do that'.
Sets up a false choice, where agreeing the complaint is fair seems to mean calling the person bad.
Different from the research finding, which describes a private shift in behavior rather than something said aloud.
what_it_sounds_like: I have given up so much for this family. You're really going to bring this up now?
I volunteer every weekend. Ask anyone who knows me.
Do you know how many people I've helped? I'm not that kind of person.
In twenty years I've never had a single complaint.
After all the favors I've done for you, I'd expect a little trust.
I've always supported equality. I'd never say something like that.
A manager points to their leadership award when an employee reports how a meeting went.
what_it_is_not: Relevant context given alongside an answer: 'I know that stung and I was wrong about the deadline. I hope the last two years count for something.'
Someone hurt that an accusation overlooks years of effort, who says so while still engaging with the complaint.
A character witness in a formal process such as a hearing, where track record is relevant by design.
Genuine surprise: 'That doesn't sound like me. Tell me more about what happened.'
The private tendency, described in research, to relax standards after doing good. That is not a conversational move and cannot be seen in one exchange.
Two people in a long relationship reminding each other of their shared history with honesty and goodwill.
this_may_be_it_when: A complaint about one event is answered with praise for the person's whole life.
The list of good deeds gets longer each time you return to the subject, while the event itself is never described.
Your complaint is framed as ungrateful, as though what you owe cancels what you raised.
Other people are asked to vouch ('ask anyone'), and their testimony replaces the facts.
Agreeing with the complaint is treated as a statement that the person is bad.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The track record is mentioned in a sentence, and then the specific issue is addressed.
They own what they did and also say it is out of character for them.
They ask you to look at the facts of this one event, not at their reputation.
The history comes up because you asked whether this has happened before.
The conversation ends on a concrete change, even a small one.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Hurt at being misjudged can make anyone reach for their best moments.
People sometimes cite their history because they sincerely believe it shows this was a mistake and not typical.
In some workplaces and cultures, reputation and standing are the normal way to discuss someone's conduct.
common_false_positives: A character reference in a formal setting, such as a hearing or a reference check, where track record is the question.
A friend you complained about who says 'I'd hate to think I've let you down after all this time', and then asks what happened.
Someone speaking warmly about a person accused in public, who has nothing to dodge themselves.
discernment_questions: After the good deeds were listed, was the specific thing I raised ever discussed?
Would my complaint still be fair if every one of those good deeds were true?
Do they bring up their record only when I raise a problem?
Am I being asked to weigh their whole life against one event?
Does it feel safe to say that both things can be true?
less_concerning_if: The person says in one breath that they do a lot and that they got this wrong.
The record comes up when you ask about it, not in reply to the complaint.
The specific event is settled before the conversation ends.
more_concerning_if: Questioning their conduct is treated as a betrayal or an insult to their service.
Other people are recruited to speak for their character before you have finished explaining.
Their standing gives them an exemption from rules that others follow, in a workplace, congregation or family.
pattern_over_time_signs: You expect the reminder before you speak, and begin to wrap complaints in praise to soften them.
You find yourself defending your own record of kindness to them.
Small issues pile up unsaid, because raising them feels like arguing against someone's entire character.
Others in the group start to treat the person as beyond question.
codex_completed.repair_check: Their own words name the specific event back to you before any mention of their record. If history comes in afterwards as context and the event still gets addressed, the exchange has moved. A longer list of credentials on the second try has not changed anything.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice whether saying 'I'm asking about Tuesday, not about your whole character' changes their next reply. Watch for a move from the list to the event, or for the list getting longer along with a hint that you are being unfair to ask.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A person's good standing can work as a shortcut for deciding what is likely: someone kind seems unlikely to have done harm. Listeners may discount a complaint, and the person making it, before checking the facts. The speaker can also be reassured by their own record, which may make an uncomfortable complaint feel like an error rather than information.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Accounts of this often include guilt for raising something real, and extra caution about raising it again. Some doubt whether they have the right to complain, given what the person has done for them. Others are left with a small, specific problem that was never discussed and a large, vague sense of having been ungrateful.

response_options.soft_clarification: Acknowledge the record and return to the point: 'I know you've done a lot, and that's not what I'm asking about. I'm asking about what happened on Tuesday.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Refuse to let the complaint become a vote on their character: 'I'm not asking you to be a bad person. I'm asking you to answer this one thing.'
response_options.disengagement: If the list of achievements begins, stop competing with it. Say you will leave it there for now, then return later in writing with the one specific request.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask someone who knows you both whether they can hold two things at once: that this person has done real good, and that this event still needs an answer.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Describe the event and its effect factually, leave their reputation out of it, and ask for the specific action you need, so a good name has nothing to answer.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I believe you've done a lot of good, and I'm not asking you to prove it. I'm asking about one thing that happened. Can we talk about that first, and then talk about everything else if you like?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Not a danger signal alone. It deserves more care where good standing is itself the source of power: a respected leader, clergy member, coach or senior colleague whose reputation makes complaints unlikely to be believed. There, keep dated notes and take the complaint to an outside body, such as an ombuds, regulator or independent reporting line, instead of to the person's own circle.
misuse_warning: Not every mention of a good record is an evasion. Using the label on someone sincerely hurt by an accusation can shut them out of a fair hearing.
Someone's real history can be relevant evidence. Waving it away as 'licensing' discards context that may matter.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: A flat Denial says the thing did not occur; licensing can concede there is a complaint and answer it with reputation. Blame-Shifting hands the fault to you, while licensing leaves fault unmentioned and puts the speaker's goodness on the table, which can leave you feeling in debt. Minimization makes the harm small, whereas licensing swaps in a different question: are they a good person?

codex_completed.name: Strategic Self-Deprecation / Performed Humility
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can technically match phrasing linked to this tactic, but text alone cannot reliably establish intent here — the same words are too easily produced by an innocent explanation. It is shown as low-signal information only and is never scored.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Putting yourself down or sounding modest at the moment criticism is due, so the other person ends up comforting you instead of raising their concern.
codex_completed.short_definition: Putting yourself down or sounding modest at the moment criticism is due, so the other person ends up comforting you instead of raising their concern.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Strategic self-deprecation and performed humility are two names for one behavior: harsh self-criticism or modest talk that lands just as a concern is about to be raised. The listener turns to reassure, and the concern goes unsaid. Self-criticism is common and often sincere, so one instance says little about timing. What stands out is repetition at the same moment, a concern that never gets its turn, and a listener who keeps leaving as the comforter. It describes how an exchange looks, not what anyone feels inside.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Just as you start to bring up a problem, the other person says how awful or hopeless they are, and you end up cheering them up while the problem goes unmentioned.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You arrive with a concern and leave having given reassurance. The thing you came to say never gets said, and you may feel unkind for having wanted to say it. Over months, small concerns can pile up unspoken.
what_it_is: Self-criticism or modest talk that appears right when a complaint, question or piece of feedback is about to be voiced.
Two labels for the same move: 'self-deprecation' stresses the putting-down, 'performed humility' stresses the modest tone, and both show up in the same spot in the conversation.
A turn in the conversation where the person who came with a concern becomes the helper, offering comfort or a compliment instead.
Found at work in review meetings, in couples when a chore or promise is raised, and among friends when a late reply or a missed event comes up.
Judged by where it falls and what follows, since the same sentence in a calm moment can be plain honesty.
what_it_sounds_like: Oh, I know, I'm hopeless. I forget everything. You must be sick of me.
Go ahead, tell me what I did wrong this time. I'm sure it's terrible.
