I'm such a bad friend. I don't even know why you put up with me.
Honestly, I'm not good enough for this job. I keep letting the whole team down.
You're so patient with me. I really don't deserve you.
I'm the worst at this, so whatever you were going to say, you're probably right.
Never mind, it's fine, I'm just a mess. Can you tell me it's okay?
what_it_is_not: Genuine humility and self-aware humor. Plenty of people joke about their flaws with no concern waiting to be raised, and the joke changes nothing about what happens next.
Someone who is truly ashamed and spirals when a mistake is pointed out. Their distress is real, and it can still be a reason to slow the conversation rather than a sign of strategy.
A person who takes responsibility, such as 'I dropped the ball, here's what I'll change.' Naming a fault and then dealing with it is the opposite of deflecting.
Modest talk from someone raised to avoid sounding proud, who plays down real achievements in every setting.
Depression or low self-esteem, where harsh self-talk shows up all day and not only when feedback is due.
this_may_be_it_when: The self-criticism arrives within a sentence or two of you starting a hard subject.
You end the talk having reassured them, and your own point was never made.
The self-blame is large and general ('I'm useless') while the specific thing you raised goes unmentioned.
Nothing changes afterwards, even though they agreed so thoroughly that they were at fault.
You have started to soften or skip concerns because you expect to spend the conversation consoling.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They put themselves down in all kinds of moments, including happy and neutral ones.
After the reassurance, they ask 'now, what did you want to tell me?' and listen.
The self-criticism is specific, such as 'I missed the deadline because I took on too much', and leads to a plan.
They are visibly distressed and ask for a pause, then come back to the subject later.
You raised a concern and got a calm answer, and the self-criticism only came up later in a different talk.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Some people cope with embarrassment by joking about themselves first, which is a habit and not a tactic.
A person anxious about being criticized may over-apologize before anyone has said a word.
In some families and workplaces, downplaying yourself is the polite norm and is not meant to steer anyone.
common_false_positives: A colleague who says 'I'm terrible at spreadsheets' and then asks for help with them.
A friend going through a rough patch whose self-criticism has increased everywhere, not only around feedback.
An apology that includes real self-blame and is followed by a change in behavior.
discernment_questions: When I start to raise something, how soon does the self-criticism come, and does it come at other times too?
At the end of the conversation, whose feelings did we spend the time on?
Did my original concern ever get an answer, even a short one?
Do I find myself editing what I say, or staying quiet, to avoid setting off the self-criticism?
Does the self-blame lead to something concrete, or does it fade once I have reassured them?
less_concerning_if: The self-criticism is steady across all kinds of moments and does not cluster around feedback.
Your concern is heard once the reassurance is over.
They can hear a specific complaint without first describing themselves as hopeless.
more_concerning_if: Each attempt to raise a concern ends with you comforting them, over many months.
The self-blame grows more dramatic the more specific your concern is.
Raising anything now feels cruel to you, and you have stopped trying.
pattern_over_time_signs: A list of unspoken concerns builds up that you have never found the right moment to mention.
You rehearse how to phrase a point so gently that it barely counts as a point.
The same issue returns because the earlier talks ended in reassurance and not in a decision.
You feel guilty after conversations that you started to fix something.
codex_completed.repair_check: Once you raise the concern again, it gets its turn: the person listens to the whole thing, says what they will do differently, and does it. A warm exchange where you do the soothing and nothing changes has not repaired anything.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Try saying 'I'd like to finish my point first.' Someone who can sit with their discomfort while you talk is honoring it. A louder self-criticism, or a question about why you are being so harsh, means the point is still blocked.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Most people feel pulled to comfort someone who sounds hurt, and many feel unkind pressing a point against visible distress. Self-criticism can set off that pull: arguing with it feels like kicking someone, so the listener's attention moves from the concern to the person's feelings. Repeated, the listener may learn to avoid the subject in advance.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe leaving conversations feeling oddly guilty, holding concerns for weeks because the right moment never comes, and doubting whether their complaint was fair. Some find themselves praising someone to stop their distress, then feel resentful afterwards and unsure why.

response_options.soft_clarification: Acknowledge the feeling, then return to the point: 'I can tell this is hard to hear. I still need to say one thing, and then we can talk about how you're feeling.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say you will not take on the comforting role right now: 'I care about you, and I'm not going to reassure you before I've said what I came to say.'
response_options.disengagement: If the self-criticism keeps filling the whole conversation, put your concern in a short message or note, so it can be read without any performance around it.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend you trust what you wanted to raise and ask them to check whether it sounds fair. It helps you see that the concern was reasonable all along.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In reviews, write feedback down in advance and send it as well as saying it, and ask for one agreed next step at the end of the meeting.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "You feel awful, and I'm not dismissing that. I'd still like to say what I came to say first. After that, I'm glad to talk about how you're feeling."
codex_completed.safety_note: Constant self-criticism from someone else is an uncomfortable habit and not a danger signal. It would change if the self-criticism becomes threats of self-harm whenever you raise something, which needs real support: stay with the person if you can, and contact a crisis line or someone close to them so you are not the only one responding.
misuse_warning: Treating any self-critical person as a schemer punishes people who are anxious, ashamed or depressed. Check the timing across many moments before using this label.
Telling someone 'you're only putting yourself down to avoid criticism' in the middle of their distress is itself a way of closing the conversation.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Identity Performances builds a whole persona for an audience, while this is a single move at a single moment. Performative Allyship / False Solidarity uses stated values, not stated flaws, to deflect scrutiny. Credential-Costuming raises someone's standing to stop questions, whereas self-deprecation lowers it to the same end. Here the signature is the other person turning into the comforter.
codex_completed.detection_notes: A phrasing pattern exists in this tool's library for this tactic, but it is deliberately capped below the scoring threshold: this signal is too context-dependent and too easily produced innocently for text alone to establish intent. It is never scored.

codex_completed.name: Priming / Narrative Seeding
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can technically match phrasing linked to this tactic, but text alone cannot reliably establish intent here — the same words are too easily produced by an innocent explanation. It is shown as low-signal information only and is never scored.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Planting an interpretation of a person or event in someone's mind ahead of time, so that what they later see gets read through it.
codex_completed.short_definition: Planting an interpretation of a person or event in someone's mind ahead of time, so that what they later see gets read through it.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Priming, or narrative seeding, is the quiet handing over of a conclusion before the evidence arrives. A remark in the hallway, a story told before a visit, a heads-up before a meeting: each sets a lens, and the later event is read through it. One warning from a friend who cares may be only that. What makes it worth noticing is the order, with the frame placed first and the facts second, and later events that keep landing on the same reading. From one message you usually cannot tell, because you cannot see what was said before.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone tells you what to think about a person or event before you have seen it yourself, and then what you see seems to prove it.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You read an event through a lens you never chose and mistake a supplied conclusion for your own judgment. The frame is hardest to question because it arrived before the evidence did, so by the time you look, you already know what you expect to see.
what_it_is: A remark placed just before an encounter: 'Just so you know, she can get prickly' said as you walk into a meeting with her.
A story told before a visit, hearing, interview or first date that tells you how to read the person you are about to meet.
A matter of order: the interpretation comes first, so ordinary behavior afterward gets sorted as confirming it.
Aimed at a person, a group, a decision or an incident, and it can be flattering as well as unflattering.
Often invisible to the person it works on, who remembers forming the opinion themselves.
Different from a briefing, which hands over facts and leaves the reading to you.
what_it_sounds_like: Not to prejudice you, but you'll see what I mean when you meet him.
Just a heads-up before the meeting: she tends to take things personally.
I'm sure it's nothing, but keep an eye on how he reacts when money comes up.
You'll notice she goes quiet when something is off.
A relative describes your partner to the whole family before the first dinner, in a tone of concern.
A new manager's first week opens with a colleague's three-minute account of who to be careful around.
Everyone says the last team lead was awful, so watch how this one handles it.
what_it_is_not: A briefing that gives you facts you can check, such as a colleague telling you the client moved the deadline twice last month.
A sincere warning from someone who had a bad experience and presents it as their experience, not as a fact about the person.
Reading someone through your own history with them, which is memory and not a frame handed to you.
A reputation that formed because many people independently reported the same thing.
A hunch you formed yourself from earlier meetings.
Ordinary scene-setting, such as a host mentioning that Grandpa is hard of hearing so you speak up.
this_may_be_it_when: The comment arrives just before an encounter, instead of when something relevant came up.
It tells you how to interpret behavior ('watch how she reacts') rather than describing something that happened.
Afterward you notice exactly the behavior you were told to expect, and little else.
The same advance word is given to several people who will all be in the room.
Asked what the comment was based on, the speaker has no specific event to point to.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The speaker can describe a specific event, with a date, and you can check it yourself.
They tell you in the same breath what the other person does well.
They say 'ignore me if it turns out differently' and then actually let it.
You had formed the same impression on your own before hearing anything.
The remark is practical information about the setting, such as parking, deadlines or who has authority to decide.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People pass on context because they care about you and want the first meeting to go smoothly.
Someone nervous about an encounter may rehearse their own worries aloud, and the listener hears a verdict.
Gossip travels through habit as much as design, and the speaker may not notice how it shapes the listener.
Many workplaces hand over notes about people as routine, so a heads-up may be a handover habit.
common_false_positives: A nurse's shift handover noting that a patient was agitated overnight, shared so the next shift can help.
A friend warning you that the restaurant you picked is very loud, so you can set your expectations.
Your own past with someone coloring how you read their next message, with nobody having said a word.
discernment_questions: What did I know about this person or event before I saw it, and who told me?
Would I have reached this reading if I had arrived with no advance word?
Was the comment a fact I could check, or an instruction about how to interpret?
Does everything I have seen since fit so neatly that I have stopped looking for anything that does not?
Did the person who told me also say what they were basing it on?
less_concerning_if: The advance word named something specific and checkable, and you checked it.
The speaker also offered the other side, or said they might be wrong.
You went in curious, and your impression changed once you met the person.
more_concerning_if: The same advance word is delivered to everyone who will meet the person, before they meet.
Anyone who reports something different from the frame is told they are being naive.
The person being described never learns what was said about them, though decisions about them follow.
pattern_over_time_signs: Before each new encounter with the same person, a similar piece of advance commentary appears.
New people join a group already holding a view of someone they have never spoken to.
The person described meets wariness they cannot trace to anything they did.
Your own impression has drifted toward the advance description, and you can no longer say which part came from experience.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair here means going back to the people who were given the frame and correcting it: saying what was opinion, what was fact, and what is not known. Quietly dropping the subject, while the earlier framing stays in everyone's head, leaves the lens in place.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself what happens when you say you would like to form your own view. A reply like 'fair enough', followed by a change in how they talk, suggests the request was heard. More advance commentary, now with a note that you are naive, suggests it was not.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People tend to look for what they were told to expect. Once a story is in place, ambiguous behavior can be sorted into it and contrary behavior explained away as an exception. Because the story arrived as information and not as pressure, the listener may remember adopting it freely. It tends to work better when the source is trusted and the encounter is unfamiliar.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe walking into a room already wary, then feeling puzzled at how readily a stranger's behavior seemed to match the warning. Some say they later realized their first impression had never really been tested. A person described in advance can meet coolness they cannot explain, and may start changing how they act to shake it off.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask where it comes from: 'What did you see that makes you say that?' A specific answer is something you can weigh, and a vague one tells you how much weight to give it.
response_options.firm_boundary: Say you will form your own view: 'Thanks, but I'd rather meet him without a briefing.'
response_options.disengagement: Change the subject when advance commentary starts, and let the meeting itself be the first evidence you collect.
response_options.support_seeking: If you are the one being described, ask a trusted colleague or friend what has been said about you and who said it, so you know what to expect before you arrive.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask for facts in writing before a meeting about a person: dates, documents, who was there. Raise it with a manager or HR if opinions about someone are circulating before they can respond.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I appreciate the heads-up, but I'd like to meet her without it. If something specific happened, tell me what and when, and I'll weigh it myself. Otherwise I'll make up my own mind."
codex_completed.safety_note: Rarely a safety concern alone. It changes when advance word is aimed at people who control something you depend on, such as a landlord, an employer, a custody evaluator or an immigration officer, or arrives with threats or isolation. Then write down what was said and by whom, and take it to a legal aid service or an advocate before you respond.
misuse_warning: Any advance warning can be called seeding. Treating every heads-up as a plot leaves you unable to take sincere advice, and the label cannot show what anyone meant.
Suspecting that someone primed your friends can become its own lens, in which every cool reception proves the plot.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Credibility Theft aims advance word at one thing, whether you can be believed as a witness; priming can set any interpretation, including of an event, and does not need to attack anyone's honesty. Frame Assassination swaps out a frame in the middle of a conversation, while priming places one before the conversation starts. Authority Hijack tells you what you feel, whereas priming tells you what you will see in someone else.
codex_completed.detection_notes: A phrasing pattern exists in this tool's library for this tactic, but it is deliberately capped below the scoring threshold: this signal is too context-dependent and too easily produced innocently for text alone to establish intent. It is never scored.

codex_completed.name: Push-Pull
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot detect this from a single line. It only becomes visible as a shape across a whole conversation over time (rhythm, cycles, timing) — repeated context is required. It is never scored and never raises the index on its own.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Swinging between closeness and distance in repeating cycles, so the other person keeps working to get back to the warm stretch.
codex_completed.short_definition: Swinging between closeness and distance in repeating cycles, so the other person keeps working to get back to the warm stretch.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Push-pull is a rhythm in a close relationship: a run of attention, plans and affection, then a sudden cooling with no clear reason, then a return to warmth. One cold week means little, since everyone has them. What marks it is a swing that repeats, a cold phase that tends to start right after you got close or asked for something, and a warm phase that comes back mainly when you pull away or work harder.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone is very close, then suddenly distant, then close again, and you end up spending your energy trying to get back to the good part.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You start organizing your attention around a temperature you cannot predict, and you tend to read every cold spell as something you must have caused. That can crowd out your own plans, friendships and sleep.
what_it_is: A repeating swing between a warm phase (daily contact, future talk, tenderness) and a cool phase (short replies, vague plans, slow answers).
Cool phases that arrive without a stated reason, so you are left guessing what you did.
Warmth that tends to come back when you pull away, make other plans, or stop asking for more.
A rhythm that runs across months, which is what separates it from one bad week.
what_it_sounds_like: Three days of good-morning texts and plans for the weekend, then no reply until Thursday night.
"I've just been really busy," said with no mention of the plans that were dropped.
"I missed you so much," arriving the day after you finally went out with friends.
"I'm not sure what I want right now," followed two weeks later by "Why are you being so distant?"
A warm voice call at midnight after a week of one-word texts, and no mention of the week.
"Don't read into it. I'm just like this sometimes."
what_it_is_not: A person who goes quiet under real pressure, such as a death in the family, an illness, or a work crunch, and tells you so.
An introvert who needs regular solitary time and says so plainly, with a predictable rhythm you can plan around.
Two people early in dating who are still working out how much contact suits each of them.
Ambivalence that is stated openly: 'I'm unsure about this' is hard to hear but is an honest message, not a cycle.
A relationship with a real distance difference, such as shift work or time zones, where the gaps follow the schedule.
this_may_be_it_when: The cool phases start soon after a moment of real closeness, such as an intimate talk or a weekend away.
Warmth returns in step with your pulling back, not in step with anything happening in their life.
You can tell the day's mood from the first message, and you plan your own week around it.
Asking what changed gets 'nothing' or 'you're overthinking', and the cycle begins again.
You have been through at least three or four full swings, not one.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The quiet spells line up with something you can see, such as a work deadline or a family event.
They tell you ahead of time: 'I'll be off my phone this week, I'll call Sunday.' And they call.
The swings are small, and both of you move through them with no one chasing.
When you name the gap, they explain it and the next one is shorter or better flagged.
You are the one who tends to go cold, and they are simply responding to that.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Someone managing depression, anxiety or burnout can swing in how much contact they can manage, without being aware of the effect on you.
A person afraid of commitment may approach and retreat out of their own fear, which is painful for you even though it is not about controlling you.
Life events such as a new job, a child, or a sick parent legitimately change availability from week to week.
common_false_positives: Early dating where one of you is slower to commit and the contact is uneven for a few weeks.
A long-distance relationship in which busy periods at work thin out the calls.
A friend who disappears for months at a time because that is how they treat everyone, not only you.
discernment_questions: Can you predict when the cool phase will start, and does it follow closeness or following a request from you?
Does the warmth return because something changed for them, or because you backed off?
Do you spend more time decoding their silence than doing the things you used to enjoy?
When you ask directly about a cold spell, do you get an answer you can use?
Would you describe the relationship to a friend as one steady thing, or as a series of weathers?
less_concerning_if: They name their own pattern and say what they are doing about it, such as asking for notice before they go quiet.
The cool phases are short and the closeness comes back without you chasing.
You can tell them it unsettles you and they are curious about that, not irritated.
more_concerning_if: The cold phases grow longer or sharper each cycle, and the warm ones need more effort from you.
Cooling follows your attempts to see other people or spend time on your own plans.
The distance is combined with criticism, comparisons, or hints that someone else would be easier.
pattern_over_time_signs: You stop making plans more than a day ahead, since you do not know which version of them will turn up.
You send more messages in the cold phases and fewer in the warm ones, as if on a leash.
Friends comment that you check your phone constantly or seem anxious in a way you did not before.
The warm stretches are shorter than they used to be, yet they still feel worth waiting for.
codex_completed.repair_check: Change here looks like steadier contact over months, plus a straight answer whenever they do need space: when they will be back in touch and why. A passionate reunion that resets everything, with the silence still unmentioned, only restarts the loop.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: A week on from asking for steadier contact, what does the calendar show? Contact that really steadies is a good sign. Warmth that lasts only while you keep quiet, with the cool phase creeping back as you ease off, is an answer to your request too.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Closeness that comes and goes can make people watch for signs of the next change. When warmth returns after a gap, the relief can feel stronger than steady kindness would, which may tie a person more tightly to the one who gave it. Uncertainty tends to keep attention fixed on the relationship, and people often fill the unexplained gaps with self-blame.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe constant low-level alertness around their phone, rehearsing messages, and putting friends and hobbies aside in case the warm phase arrives. Some say they began to feel they were too much when closeness was offered and not enough when it was taken away. Many describe confusion about whether the good moments or the bad ones were the real relationship.

response_options.soft_clarification: Describe what you notice without guessing at reasons: 'Some weeks we talk every day and some weeks I hear nothing. Can you tell me what's going on at your end?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say what you will and will not do: 'I'm not available to wait through silences. If you need space, tell me how long, or I'll take it as an answer.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop replying within minutes during cool phases, return to your own plans, and notice how you feel when no one is setting the pace.
response_options.support_seeking: Show a friend the last two months of messages and ask what shape they see. Outsiders often spot the rhythm quicker than the person inside it.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If this is a colleague or supervisor who is friendly one week and cold the next, keep a dated note of what was said and ask in writing for clear expectations on your projects.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I like you, and I can't do the hot-and-cold. Talking every few days at an ordinary pace works for me, and so does a heads-up when you need a break. If that doesn't suit you, I'll step back."
codex_completed.safety_note: Alone, this rhythm is a source of distress, not physical danger. It becomes more serious if cold phases turn into threats, if you are told you will be abandoned for ordinary things such as seeing family, or if money or housing depends on their mood. Then tell one trusted person what is happening and speak to a counselor about making a plan that does not rely on their moods.
misuse_warning: Pinning the label on someone who is slow to text or who has real ambivalence can turn an honest 'I'm unsure' into a charge of manipulation.
Naming it in the middle of an argument as proof of a hidden game tends to shut down the very conversation that would clarify things.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Compared with Love Bombing, which front-loads affection and need never cool, this has real distance in it. Hoovering comes after a split or a long gap, when someone reappears with promises. Breadcrumbing is thin, steady scraps with no warm phase at all. Push-pull has both: real stretches of closeness, then real distance, again and again.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched line-by-line. This requires repeated context or a recognizable sequence across a long enough thread to mean anything — a single message is never sufficient. Never scored.

codex_completed.name: Intermittent Reinforcement
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot detect this from a single line. It only becomes visible as a shape across a whole conversation over time (rhythm, cycles, timing) — repeated context is required. It is never scored and never raises the index on its own.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Handing out affection, praise or kindness unpredictably and rarely, so that the few good moments hold a person more tightly than steady warmth would.
codex_completed.short_definition: Handing out affection, praise or kindness unpredictably and rarely, so that the few good moments hold a person more tightly than steady warmth would.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: The name comes from learning research on reward schedules, where rewards that arrive on an unpredictable timetable tend to produce persistent effort. In a relationship, it describes long stretches of criticism, indifference or flat routine broken by occasional real warmth or praise. Every relationship has good and bad days, so the pattern is judged by ratio and timing: how rare the good moments are, how much you do to earn them, and how hard they are to predict.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Kindness shows up only now and then, with no way of knowing when, so you keep working for the next bit and it becomes hard to leave.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Effort goes up while the returns go down. The rarity of the good moments is what makes them feel worth waiting for, so the loop can feed itself, and you may end up measuring the whole relationship by its best hour.
what_it_is: A relationship where approval or tenderness arrives on no schedule you can learn, while criticism or neglect fills the gaps.
Rewards that are real but small in number, such as a compliment, a surprise visit, or a night when they are fully attentive.
A rising effort on your side: more chores, more patience, more worry about getting it right.
A pattern that can occur at home, at work, in friendships, and in families.
what_it_sounds_like: Weeks of 'fine' and 'whatever you want,' then one evening of "You're the best thing in my life."
A supervisor who ignores your reports for months and then praises you in front of the team.
"See, this is how it could always be, if you tried a bit harder."
A parent who is cold through most of a visit and then hugs you tightly at the door.
Silence when you do well, and a thank-you only when you stay late or give up something you wanted.
"I do love you. You just don't see it."
what_it_is_not: A relationship with ordinary variation in mood, where kind days are still the large majority.
A partner or boss who is consistently reserved, and shows appreciation in small, steady ways that do not look like praise.
A season of grief, illness or overwhelm in which the other person has less warmth to give.
A family culture that rarely says 'I love you' aloud but shows it reliably through actions.
A pleasant surprise after a difficult period of real conflict, with an honest conversation attached.
this_may_be_it_when: You cannot guess which of your actions earns the good moment, or whether any of them do.
The warm episodes are far outnumbered by cold or critical ones, and you still describe the relationship by the warm ones.
You find yourself doing more and more, for rewards that stay the same size or shrink.
Praise tends to come when you are on the edge of leaving, going quiet, or giving up.
You feel a rush of relief and gratitude at small kindnesses that would barely register elsewhere.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You can state what they appreciate, and when you do it, they respond with warmth.
The good moments are common enough that you could plan around them.
Dry spells match visible reasons such as their illness, travel or workload.
Your effort is steady, and you do not feel a pull to do more to earn the next kind word.
You feel as free to relax around them as around other people you trust.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Some people simply express warmth rarely and unevenly, and feel more than they show.
Stress or low mood can flatten someone's expression of care for a season.
Workplaces with overloaded managers often hand out praise at random, which feels like a pattern but is only disorganisation.
common_false_positives: A friend whose attention is strong when you meet and thin between meetings, which suits both of you.
A new job where feedback is rare because everyone is busy, not because anyone is rationing it.
A relationship in therapy or recovery where good and hard weeks both come as part of real change.
discernment_questions: Roughly how many days out of ten would you call warm, and how many hurt or empty?
What would it take for the good moments to become predictable, and have you asked?
Do you work harder for approval now than when the relationship began?
Does a small kindness make you forget a month of coldness?
Would you ask a friend in your position to stay, if you heard this described?
less_concerning_if: When you ask for more consistent warmth, there is a visible effort to provide it.
The unevenness is tied to circumstances you can see and that pass.
Your life outside the relationship stays full and steady, with your own friends and goals.
more_concerning_if: The long gaps are filled with criticism and comparison, not just neutrality.
Warmth returns reliably when you threaten to leave, then fades once you stay.
You have started to doubt that you deserve more than the occasional good day.
pattern_over_time_signs: You keep a mental list of the good moments and replay them when things are bad.
You lower what you hope for, and treat a quiet evening as a win.
Friends see you give a great deal while receiving little, and say so.
Your own interests slip, because you save energy for the chance of the next warm episode.
codex_completed.repair_check: Look at whether the good treatment spreads out. Real change makes kindness frequent and ordinary, something you can count on a Tuesday. A bigger gesture after your complaint, with the gaps just as long between, is the same schedule at higher volume.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Tell them what regular warmth would look like for you, and see what the next month holds. Are the good moments still rare and arriving as rewards, or do they turn into a daily baseline you no longer have to earn?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Learning research has long found that rewards arriving unpredictably can keep behavior going longer than rewards that come every time. In a relationship, this may mean that uncertainty about when warmth will come keeps attention and effort fixed on the other person. The rare good moments may feel much larger against the background of the gaps, which can make leaving feel like giving up the one thing worth having.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe a kind of hunger for the next warm moment, replaying old kind words, and pushing their own needs aside to stay in the other person's favor. Some say they feel grateful for crumbs, then ashamed of being grateful. Others describe trouble recognizing steady kindness from other people, because it seems flat beside the highs.

response_options.soft_clarification: Say what helps in plain terms: 'When you tell me what I did well, I feel like I can relax. Could we try noticing the small things as they happen?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decide what level of regular care you need and say it: 'I won't keep working for rare praise. I need basic kindness as the normal state, not a prize.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop trying to earn the next warm moment. Keep your effort level the same for a month and see what is offered without it.
response_options.support_seeking: Share the ratio with someone neutral, for example by writing down a month of days marked warm, neutral or cold, and show a counselor or friend the tally.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager's praise comes only now and then, ask for regular check-ins with specific criteria, and keep your own record of completed work to measure against.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I've noticed I only hear good things from you once in a while, and I work very hard for those moments. I need steadier warmth, even on ordinary days. If that isn't something you can offer, I'll need to rethink how much I put in."
codex_completed.safety_note: By itself this is a painful emotional pattern, not a physical danger. Take it more seriously if the gaps are filled with threats, if the warm moments come only after a scare, or if you are tied to the person by money, housing or children. Then keep a record of the cycle and speak to a counselor or advocate who can help you plan your next steps while you still have your own income and contacts.
misuse_warning: Using the term to describe any uneven mood in a partner can make you read ordinary moodiness as a campaign.
Calling someone's occasional kindness 'just a reward schedule' can dismiss warmth that was real.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Compared with Love Bombing, a heavy early flood of affection, the affection here is scarce and unpredictable. Conditional Love states the terms, such as 'I'll be warm if you obey', while this pattern never says what earns the reward. Negging mixes in insults that wear down confidence. Push-Pull swings in regular cycles of closeness and distance; this one is mostly lean, with rare warm bursts.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched line-by-line. This requires repeated context or a recognizable sequence across a long enough thread to mean anything — a single message is never sufficient. Never scored.

codex_completed.name: Breadcrumbing
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot detect this from a single line. It only becomes visible as a shape across a whole conversation over time (rhythm, cycles, timing) — repeated context is required. It is never scored and never raises the index on its own.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Sending just enough sporadic attention to keep someone hopeful and available, while the contact never turns into real plans or commitment.
codex_completed.short_definition: Sending just enough sporadic attention to keep someone hopeful and available, while the contact never turns into real plans or commitment.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Breadcrumbing is small, low-cost contact that keeps a person interested without moving forward: a like, a 'thinking of you', a message after weeks of silence. It is also called benching, and the two are the same tactic under different names. Benching stresses the person being kept in reserve while others are pursued. Anyone can be a poor texter, so one slow stretch proves nothing. The pattern is thin bursts that never become a plan and appear just as you drift away.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone gives you tiny scraps of attention now and then, enough to keep you waiting in reserve, but the contact never becomes a date, a plan, or a real relationship.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You may hold a place open for a relationship that never arrives, on the strength of contact that costs almost nothing to send. Time, other opportunities and your sense of what you are worth can quietly drain away.
what_it_is: Brief, low-effort contact such as a reaction to your story, a meme, or a 'hey you' that asks for nothing.
Warm words with no follow-through: 'we should get dinner sometime' that never gets a date.
Bursts of attention that come after long silences, often when you have gone quiet.
An arrangement where you do the work of arranging meetings, and plans fall through or go unanswered.
A status that is never stated: you are kept available as an option while the other person is free to pursue other things.
what_it_sounds_like: "Hey stranger" after six weeks of nothing.
A heart on your photo and no reply to your actual message.
"We need to catch up soon!" and then no day suggested.
"Sorry, work has been insane. Let's talk this week," repeated each month.
A late-night text that says only "thinking of you."
Plans that are agreed in principle and then 'let's see how the week goes' when you propose a date.
Messages that become frequent and warm right after their other plans fall through, then thin out again.
A direct question about where this is going gets a compliment, an emoji, or a new subject.
what_it_is_not: A person who is busy in a demanding season and is honestly slow, but makes real plans when they are free.
A mutual casual connection in which both of you know what it is and neither expects more.
Someone shy or anxious who sends small signals because bigger ones feel risky, and who speeds up when you reach out.
A friendship that runs on occasional contact and is fine with that on both sides.
A new connection that is honestly still undefined, where both of you are working out what you want.
this_may_be_it_when: Over months, nothing becomes a plan, even though warm words keep arriving.
Contact picks up when you seem to be losing interest or seeing someone else.
You are the only one proposing times, and your proposals get vague replies.
When you ask where this is going, you get a compliment or a change of subject.
You feel more hopeful after each message and more empty a day later.
this_may_not_be_it_when: When you suggest a date, they pick one and show up.
They have said clearly what they can offer, and you are choosing to accept that.
The gaps match their life, such as exams, shifts, or a sick relative.
They also make effort to reach you, with real questions and follow-up.
You never actually asked for more, so they may not know you want it.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people are poor at keeping in touch and treat everyone the same way.
Someone coming out of a bad relationship may be unsure about moving forward but still enjoy your company.
Messaging apps make it easy to tap a reaction without meaning anything beyond 'I saw this'.
common_false_positives: A long-distance friendship where you speak a few times a year and both like that.
Someone busy with a new baby who sends short messages because that is all they have energy for.
A person who is slow-burn interested and gets bolder once you signal clearly that you want to see them.
discernment_questions: In the last two months, how many plans did we actually make and keep?
Who reaches out first, and who does the arranging?
Have I told them directly what I want, and what did they say?
Does their contact rise when I step back, then fade when I engage?
If a friend described this, would I think they were being offered a relationship or a reminder?
less_concerning_if: A direct question about plans gets a real answer, even if it is a no.
Both of you know the contact is casual and are content with that.
Their attention is steady in small ways and matches how they treat other friends.
more_concerning_if: They imply a future ('someday we'll...') while never acting on it.
You are asked to keep things quiet or low-key while they show interest in private.
Their contact increases specifically when you start dating someone else, then stops.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your phone becomes something you check for one particular name.
You turn down other invitations, in case they finally suggest something.
The same sentence ('let's catch up soon') appears again and again, without a date.
Months in, you know very little about their daily life, and they know a great deal about yours.
codex_completed.repair_check: A change here is visible in the calendar. Once you raise it, look for an actual date proposed by them and kept, and a clear statement of what they want. A heartfelt apology for being 'bad at this', followed by another round of crumbs, is the same pattern with better manners.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: State the kind of contact you want and observe what they do next. Do they offer a concrete plan or say honestly that it is not what they want? Or do they send a warm message that skirts the question and the same thin contact resumes?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Hope is a strong motivator, and small signs of interest can be enough to keep it alive. When contact is rare and uncertain, ambiguous signals often get read in the most favourable light, and waiting for more is a common response. Because each message is easy to explain away, it can be hard to say what exactly is wrong, and so hard to stop waiting.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe putting dating and friendships on hold, replaying short messages for hidden meaning, and feeling foolish for hoping. Some say that the lack of any clear 'no' made it harder to grieve than an ordinary break-up. Others describe a drop in confidence after months of being kept at arm's length.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for a specific thing and see what comes back: 'I'd love to see you. Are you free Saturday at 6 for dinner?' A reply with a yes or no is information.
response_options.firm_boundary: Tell them what you need: 'I'm looking for someone who makes plans. If that's not you right now, I'd rather know.' Then act on the answer you get.
response_options.disengagement: Stop replying to low-effort pings that carry no invitation. Put the energy into people who meet you halfway, and notice who that is.
response_options.support_seeking: Show a friend the thread, or screenshots of the dates and gaps, and ask what they would expect from someone who was truly interested.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a colleague or mentor keeps promising a project, introduction or promotion in passing, ask for a date and put the commitment in writing by email.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I enjoy hearing from you, but a message every few weeks isn't enough for me. If you want to see me, pick a day this week. If you don't, that's okay, and I'd prefer you tell me."
codex_completed.safety_note: Breadcrumbing is not usually a physical-safety concern. It deserves more care if the person controls something you depend on, such as your job, immigration sponsorship or housing, or if their attention is accompanied by pressure for secrecy or sexual contact. Then do not rely on their promises; get any commitment written down and talk to someone outside the situation.
misuse_warning: Calling every slow replier a breadcrumber can make you read ordinary busyness as contempt and discourage honest, awkward people.
Using the word to describe someone who told you plainly they were casual puts a harm on them that they never promised to prevent.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Future Faking paints a detailed, specific future to keep you invested; breadcrumbing offers almost no picture at all, only small contact. Hoovering follows a break or an exit and tries to pull you back; breadcrumbing runs while you are still hovering. Next to the intensity of Love Bombing, this is the opposite: very thin attention, never a surge of it.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched line-by-line. This requires repeated context or a recognizable sequence across a long enough thread to mean anything — a single message is never sufficient. Never scored.

codex_completed.name: Trauma Bonding
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot detect this from a single line. It only becomes visible as a shape across a whole conversation over time (rhythm, cycles, timing) — repeated context is required. It is never scored and never raises the index on its own.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A strong attachment that forms through cycles of hurt followed by comfort from the same person, so that fear and closeness become tangled together.
codex_completed.short_definition: A strong attachment that forms through cycles of hurt followed by comfort from the same person, so that fear and closeness become tangled together.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Trauma bonding describes an attachment that grows in a relationship where harm and relief come from the same source. After a frightening or painful episode, the person who caused it is also the one who apologizes, soothes or becomes tender, and that comfort can feel unusually intense. Ordinary couples fight and make up, so a single quarrel is not this. The pattern is a repeating cycle in which the closeness after the pain is taken as proof of how deep the bond is.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You feel most attached to the person right after they hurt you, because the same person who caused the pain is the one who comforts you.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Relief and harm come from the same person, so your strongest feeling of closeness can arrive just after the worst treatment, and then becomes a reason to stay. Knowing this can help you tell the strength of a feeling from the safety of a relationship.
what_it_is: A cycle in which a hurtful episode is followed by apology, tenderness, gifts or a heartfelt reunion from the person who caused it.
A bond that feels stronger after the worst episodes than it did before them.
A relationship where the comforter and the source of fear are one person, so there is nowhere else to turn for relief.
A shared sense that 'what we go through together proves our love', which makes the harm part of the story of the bond.
what_it_sounds_like: "I've never felt closer to anyone than I do right now," said the night after a screaming match.
"Nobody understands us. We've been through so much."
A tearful apology, a long hug and a promise, a few hours after you were threatened or humiliated.
Your own voice saying, "It's not always like this. You should see how good it is when it's good."
"If I didn't love you this much, I wouldn't get this upset."
A friend asking why you stay, and your sense that they could not understand the part after the fight.
what_it_is_not: Two people bonded by shared hardship from outside, such as caring for a sick child or surviving a disaster, where neither is the source of the pain.
A couple who quarrel loudly, apologize honestly and change something afterwards, so the same fight does not repeat.
Ordinary attachment to someone you love who has hurt you once, and who has since taken full responsibility.
The strong loyalty of family members who have been through difficult years together, with no one inflicting the harm.
A person's long-standing attachment style, which may make partings painful without anyone causing the pain.
this_may_be_it_when: The reconciliations after bad episodes feel like the most intense moments of the relationship.
You find yourself defending the person to friends while also being afraid of them.
The same kind of harm returns, and the same kind of comfort follows it.
Leaving brings a sharp physical longing, even though you know how things have been.
The person who hurt you is the only one you want when you are upset.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The hard moments are honestly acknowledged and the behavior changes afterwards.
Comfort and support come from several people, not only from the one involved in the conflict.
The hurtful incidents were few, real repair followed, and months have passed without a repeat.
Your feelings of closeness are steady and do not spike after conflict.
You feel free to leave a conversation or a room without being afraid of what follows.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people feel unusually close after an emotional reconciliation, even in healthy relationships, because strong feelings are being shared.
Grief and shared loss can bring people together in a way that feels intense and is not harmful.
Staying through a hard stretch can come from loyalty, love and practical limits such as money or children, not only from a bond to the harm.
common_false_positives: A couple in counseling who feel raw and close after an honest session about a real problem.
Soldiers, nurses or siblings who bonded through a shared ordeal.
A single serious argument, followed by sincere change, that left the relationship stronger.
discernment_questions: Do I feel closest to this person right after they have hurt me?
Is the person who comforts me the same person who caused the distress?
Has this cycle of harm and reconciliation happened more than a couple of times?
When I tell friends the good parts, do I leave out the other parts?
If someone I loved described this relationship, how worried would I be?
less_concerning_if: Harm has stopped, and the closeness has remained steady without needing a crisis.
You have other people you turn to for comfort, and you do turn to them.
The person has acknowledged specific hurts and shown lasting change.
more_concerning_if: The harm includes fear for your physical safety, threats, or humiliation in front of others.
Reconciliation follows each episode quickly and keeps you from speaking to anyone else.
You cannot picture life without the person, and the prospect of leaving brings panic.
pattern_over_time_signs: Each cycle seems to cost a bit more, and the make-up comes with higher stakes or bigger gestures.
You pull away from people who express concern, because they do not seem to see the good side.
You have left or tried to leave more than once and returned during a warm period.
Your idea of what counts as a normal bad day has shifted over time.
codex_completed.repair_check: Real change here is dull and visible: the harmful episodes stop altogether, and closeness no longer depends on a crisis first. Intense reconciliation scenes that follow each new incident, with the underlying behavior unchanged, are the cycle itself and not the end of it.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Consider what the apology is asked to do. When you say you need the harmful behavior to stop, is the answer a different way of acting, or another emotional reunion that leaves you grateful and quiet? The second keeps the loop closed.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Fear and distress can heighten the need for comfort, and if comfort is available from only one person, attachment to them may deepen. Relief after a threat can feel especially strong and can be mistaken for love. Cut off from other sources of support, a person may find it harder to see the cycle, and the strength of the feeling may seem to prove the relationship is right.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Reported experiences include being torn between dread and longing, being unable to explain to others why you stay, and shame about missing the person who hurt you. Some say they felt addicted to the reconciliation. Many describe a long period after leaving when the pull stayed strong, which surprised them and which they took, wrongly, as a sign that leaving was a mistake.

response_options.soft_clarification: If it is safe to speak, name the cycle in one sentence: 'I notice we are closest right after we have hurt each other. I want closeness without the hurt first.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decide privately, with an advocate and not with the other person, what you would do if it happened again. Announcing a deadline or a consequence to someone who may react badly can raise the risk, so keep that plan to yourself and the people helping you.
response_options.disengagement: Plan any exit with care: gather documents, pick a safe place to go, and tell someone beforehand. Expect the pull to be strongest in the first weeks.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk to a counselor or advocate trained in relationship harm, and keep up contact with at least one person outside the relationship who knows the whole story.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a boss, teacher or mentor alternates harsh treatment with warmth and you feel tied to them, speak to HR, an ombuds or a mentor elsewhere before the next cycle.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I know you're sorry, and I can tell how much you mean it right now. What I need is for the apology to be followed by something different. I'd like us to talk with someone else in the room, a counselor or someone we both trust, about how these cycles go."
codex_completed.safety_note: This pattern can accompany physical violence, threats, stalking, and control over money or contact, and the days around leaving are often the riskiest. Watch for escalation, strangulation, threats to kill or to harm children or pets, and weapons. Ask a domestic violence advocate to help you build a leaving plan, including where your documents, a spare phone and a go-bag will be kept.
misuse_warning: Telling someone in a hard relationship that they are 'just trauma bonded' can dismiss their real love, real reasons and practical constraints, and push them away.
Using the term for any intense make-up after a quarrel mislabels ordinary couple life as something sinister.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Relief Bait is the move itself: kindness placed right after harm to reset what you will tolerate. Trauma bonding is the attachment that can result when this is repeated. Intermittent Reinforcement concerns the unpredictable timing of rewards, whether or not pain precedes them. Conditional Love sets out terms; here the terms are never stated, and the bond is felt as love.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched line-by-line. This requires repeated context or a recognizable sequence across a long enough thread to mean anything — a single message is never sufficient. Never scored.

codex_completed.name: Relief Bait
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot detect this from a single line. It only becomes visible as a shape across a whole conversation over time (rhythm, cycles, timing) — repeated context is required. It is never scored and never raises the index on its own.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A burst of kindness placed right after hurtful treatment, so that relief takes the place of an honest reckoning with what happened.
codex_completed.short_definition: A burst of kindness placed right after hurtful treatment, so that relief takes the place of an honest reckoning with what happened.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Relief bait is the sweetness that follows a harsh moment: the gift, the soft voice, the sudden tenderness after contempt or a cold shutdown. Genuine apologies also bring kindness, so the key is what is missing. In this pattern the kindness arrives instead of naming the harm, the harm repeats, and the relief makes the next episode a little easier to absorb. One kind gesture after a quarrel proves nothing; the repeating order of hurt, then sweetness, then hurt does.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Something hurtful happens, and soon afterward comes unusual kindness that never talks about what happened, so you feel relieved and let it go.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Each round of kindness resets what you will put up with, so the level of treatment you accept can drop without you noticing it move. You also lose the chance to have the original harm discussed.
what_it_is: Warmth, gifts or affection that arrive within hours or a day of a hurtful act, without any acknowledgment of it.
Kindness that is out of step with the way the person usually treats you, so it feels like sudden mercy.
A sequence that repeats: sharpness, then softness, then settled quiet, and then sharpness again.
A way of closing a subject by making it feel ungrateful to reopen it.
what_it_sounds_like: A bunch of flowers and "Let's not fight anymore, okay?" the morning after being called useless.
"Come here. I'm making your favorite dinner." with no mention of what was said at lunchtime.
A sudden "I booked us a weekend away!" the day after a week of silence.
"Why bring it up now? We were having such a nice evening."
A gentle back rub, a joke, and "See? We're fine."
A sweet message at 9 p.m. after a harsh one at noon, with no reference to it.
what_it_is_not: A sincere apology that names what was done, explains what will change, and comes with a gift or a kind act as an addition.
A couple who often comfort each other after tension and do so with open acknowledgement of what was said.
A person who is warm by nature and offers kindness as a gesture of care at many different times, not only after hurting you.
A move to lighten the mood after a minor disagreement that both of you consider settled.
Reaching out after an argument because they cannot bear the distance, followed by a talk the next day.
this_may_be_it_when: The kindness comes at a consistent distance after harm and is rarely seen at other times.
The hurtful behavior is never mentioned by name afterwards.
Raising the earlier incident is met with 'but I was so nice to you after'.
You notice you are grateful for ordinary decency, and the gratitude feels out of proportion.
The same kind of hurt has happened several times, each followed by the same kind of sweetness.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They name what they did before or while being kind, in specific terms.
The hurtful behavior changes, so there is less to follow with relief.
The tenderness is part of a steady pattern of warmth, not clustered around bad moments.
You can still raise the earlier incident later and have it discussed.
The harm was a single incident they have since owned up to.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People often feel guilty after a harsh moment and show it through action first, planning to talk about it when they have calmed down.
Some families and cultures repair through shared food or small favors, not words.
A person embarrassed by their own behavior may find the words difficult and offer kindness as a clumsy first step.
common_false_positives: A parent who snapped at a child and then reads them a bedtime story, and later apologizes in words.
A friend who cooks you dinner after a falling out, and then talks it over at the table.
A partner whose habit of buying small gifts has nothing to do with conflict.
discernment_questions: Does the kindness come with any words about what happened?
If I bring up the earlier moment after the kindness, is it welcome or resented?
Is the sweetness more common after bad moments than at other times?
Has the hurtful behavior actually changed since the first time?
Do I feel relief, or do I feel settled and respected?
less_concerning_if: The gesture was accompanied by a plain acknowledgment, and the same hurt has not returned.
The kindness is part of how they treat you at ordinary moments too.
They are willing to discuss the incident when you raise it, even if it is uncomfortable.
more_concerning_if: The harm is getting sharper while the gestures are getting bigger.
Raising the incident after the kindness is treated as ingratitude or as ruining the mood.
The hurt includes threats, intimidation or damage to your belongings, followed by tenderness.
pattern_over_time_signs: You can tell, in the middle of the hurt, that sweetness is coming, and you may find yourself waiting for it.
Your threshold for what counts as acceptable treatment has quietly moved.
Gifts and gestures pile up while the issues behind them stay unresolved.
You find it hard to remember what the original fight was about, only how good the making-up felt.
codex_completed.repair_check: The kindness itself tells you little, and what it is attached to tells you more. When there is change, the incident is named, in words, by them, and the behavior stops. Where only the flowers, the dinner or the soft tone appear and the hurtful act gets repeated, the gift has stood in for the repair.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: After you ask them to talk about the hurtful moment before any treat or gesture, what happens? Do they sit with the topic, or does the warmth become more insistent, turning your request into the thing that spoils a nice day?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Relief after distress can feel stronger than steady comfort would, and a person may link the relief to whoever provides it. When kindness comes straight after the harm, it can blur the sense that the two events belong together, and it can make raising the harm feel mean. Repeated rounds tend to raise what feels tolerable, because the bad moments are always followed by good ones.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Common accounts include guilt about staying upset when the other person is being so nice, losing track of how often it has happened, and not knowing whether to trust the gifts. Some say they began to flinch at kindness, waiting for what it covered. Others could not explain to friends what was wrong, since each good moment looked so generous from outside.

response_options.soft_clarification: Thank them for the gesture and name the missing step: 'That was kind. I'd still like to talk about what you said on Monday before we move on.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Put the order in plain terms: 'Please don't answer a hurtful moment with a gift. I'd rather you tell me what you did, and we go from there.'
response_options.disengagement: Take the gift or the gesture if you want it, but leave the conversation about the incident marked as unfinished, and step out of the evening if the subject keeps being closed.
response_options.support_seeking: Write down the last three incidents and what followed each one. Show the list to a counselor or trusted friend and ask whether the order looks as odd to them as it does to you.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager follows harsh criticism with praise or perks, ask for the criticism in writing with specifics, and keep your own record of both.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I appreciate the dinner. But it doesn't fix what you said to me earlier, and I don't want the nice evening to be where that gets dropped. Can we talk about it first? Then I'll enjoy the dinner."
codex_completed.safety_note: Kindness that regularly follows intimidation, shoving, destroyed property or threats can be part of a controlling cycle in which things get worse over time. Watch for fear of their moods, harm that is getting more frequent, and apologies that come with pressure not to tell anyone. A domestic violence advocate can help you judge the risk and plan around it, starting with a written list of the incidents and their dates.
misuse_warning: Treating every apology gift as bait can leave you unable to accept sincere repair, and punishes people who say sorry with actions.
Telling a partner that their kindness is 'just relief bait' during a fight hands them no way to be forgiven, and can end a conversation that might have worked.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Apology Without Repair says sorry in words and changes nothing; relief bait often skips words and uses warmth. Intermittent Reinforcement is about rare, unpredictable rewards, whereas here the reward comes at a predictable moment, just after hurt. Trauma Bonding is the attachment that may grow over many cycles; relief bait is one move inside the cycle. Hoovering pulls you back after you have left, while this happens inside the relationship.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched line-by-line. This requires repeated context or a recognizable sequence across a long enough thread to mean anything — a single message is never sufficient. Never scored.

codex_completed.name: Dr. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot detect this from a single line. It only becomes visible as a shape across a whole conversation over time (rhythm, cycles, timing) — repeated context is required. It is never scored and never raises the index on its own.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Showing one warm, admired face to the world and another harsh one to a particular person, which leaves nobody else seeing the treatment that person receives.
codex_completed.short_definition: Showing one warm, admired face to the world and another harsh one to a particular person, which leaves nobody else seeing the treatment that person receives.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: The name comes from a well-known story about one man with two opposite selves. In everyday life it describes a split between behavior in front of others and behavior alone with one person. Performative public affection is another label for this same split. Everyone is a little different in public and private, so that alone means little. It deserves a closer look when the private side is harsh, the public side is admired, and the gap leaves the receiving person with no one who would believe them. The pattern does not show what anyone meant by it.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Everyone outside the home sees a kind, attentive person. Alone with you, they are cold, controlling or cruel. Because no one else sees it, you wonder who will believe you.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You have no witnesses. The version other people know makes your account of the other version sound implausible, including to yourself, and anyone you might turn to has only seen the public one.
what_it_is: A sharp gap between conduct in front of others and conduct in private, aimed at one person or a small circle.
Affection or attentiveness that rises when an audience is present, and is described by others as helpful, funny, generous, reliable.
Harder to name when good phases between the harsh ones feel like proof that the harsh phases were a mistake.
Seen in couples, parents and children, bosses and employees, and religious or community leaders.
An effect created by the gap itself: the more admired the public side, the less likely the private side is to be believed.
what_it_sounds_like: A friend says, "But he's so lovely whenever I see him. Are you sure?"
In front of guests: "Isn't she wonderful? I'd be lost without her." At home, hours later, a cold silence.
"No one is going to believe you. Look how everyone sees me."
A pleasant, joking voice at the party; a flat, hostile one on the drive home.
"You've got everyone fooled into thinking I'm the bad one."
Warm texts to your family, curt and critical ones to you.
Affectionate posts and public compliments that rise on the days the private mood is worst.
what_it_is_not: A shy or tired person who is quiet at home and animated at work, with no harshness toward anyone in either place.
A professional who is polished with clients and grumpy after a long day, but who owns it and repairs it.
Someone with a hard private temper who is open about it, so others also know and can judge.
A relationship where outsiders simply have not seen ordinary arguments, which many couples keep to themselves.
A person who is guarded in public but relaxed and kind at home, which is the reverse of this split.
Someone whose public warmth is genuine and consistent with, if more understated than, their private behavior.
this_may_be_it_when: How they treat you when others are around is so different that you are unsure which one is real.
The hostile side shows up only where nobody else would see or hear it.
Friends or relatives have said they find the person lovely, and you have stopped bringing it up.
The kindness shows up after the harshness, in a way that makes you doubt your memory of it.
They have said, or you believe, that no one would take your word over theirs.
this_may_not_be_it_when: People close to you have also seen the harsh side and do not find your account surprising.
The private behavior is irritable but not cruel, and gets owned and apologized for.
The difference is one of volume or formality, such as being relaxed at home and polite at work.
A specific, understandable conflict sits behind the tension, and both of you can talk about it.
The warm public manner is also how they treat you when you are alone together.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People do act more formally in public, so a warmer social manner does not hide anything by itself.
Stress from work or health can make home the place where someone's patience runs out.
A person may hold back private arguments from friends out of embarrassment or loyalty.
Ordinary conflict is often invisible to outsiders without anyone concealing it on purpose.
common_false_positives: A teenager who is chatty with friends and withdrawn at the dinner table.
A teacher who is relaxed with students and strict in staff meetings.
Two partners with different moods after the children are asleep, both of them tired and frayed.
discernment_questions: Would people who know them be shocked, or just surprised, to hear how they speak to you in private?
Is the harshness reserved for the times when no one can hear it?
Does the warmth rise noticeably when there is an audience?
Have you stopped telling anyone because you expect not to be believed?
Do you hold dated notes, messages or recordings that show the other side, and do you feel you need them?
less_concerning_if: The difference is mostly in volume and formality, and nothing in private is hurtful.
Close friends or family have seen both sides and are not surprised by your account.
Hard moments in private are named and repaired afterward, and do not return in the same form.
more_concerning_if: You have been told directly that you would not be believed, or that you would look unstable if you spoke.
The private harshness comes with monitoring of your phone, money or movements.
They contact your friends or family to describe you as difficult before you speak to them.
pattern_over_time_signs: You decide what to share with others by how likely they are to say, "But he seems so nice."
Photos and posts show a happy home that does not match your own account of it.
Your sense of which version is real keeps flipping with the weather in the house.
You have started to keep your own record of events because nobody else holds one.
codex_completed.repair_check: Change would look like the harsh side no longer needing a hiding place: they treat you the same when unobserved, do not object when you speak to others about what happened, and stop asking you to keep the private version private. A kinder week with the public face intact shows only a pleasant phase.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice whether your request is honored when nobody is watching. A boundary kept only in front of guests and dropped at home tells you what it is worth. Compare early weeks with later ones: do the private behaviors continue, even once the public manner has softened?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When most people see only the pleasant version, a person on the receiving end can start weighing their own account against everyone else's, and tends to lose. Good phases may feed hope that the harsh phases were not real, while the private ones leave no proof. Doubt about what happened, and about who would listen, can keep a person quiet.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe isolation that feels odd because they are surrounded by people who admire the other person. Some report rehearsing their account for years without telling it, and feeling an odd guilt for describing someone others like. Others say they came to dread praise of the person, and found it hardest to be congratulated for having such a partner.

response_options.soft_clarification: Say what you notice without arguing about character: 'You were gentle with my sister today, and this morning you spoke to me very differently. I'd like to understand that.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Pause the conversation when the harshness starts: 'I'm not going to continue while I'm being spoken to like this. We can try again when it is calmer.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop trying to prove the private side to people who like the public one, and keep your own dated notes where the other person cannot read them.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell one person who can listen without trying to fix or defend, such as a counselor, a domestic abuse advocate, or a friend outside the shared circle.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, write down dates, words and witnesses, and bring the record to HR or an ombuds, since a charming manner in meetings will not show up on its own.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'd like us to speak to each other at home the way we do in front of other people. I'm not asking you to agree about the past, only about how we talk from here."
codex_completed.safety_note: A split like this can sit alongside controlling behavior, threats, or physical harm that stays hidden from outsiders. Warning signs are fear of what happens after guests go home, being told you would not be believed, or having your phone, money or contacts checked. Tell a domestic abuse advocate first, and keep your records somewhere private and out of the home.
misuse_warning: Calling a person a Jekyll and Hyde because they were short with you after a hard day makes ordinary mood shifts into a case against their character. The label needs a sustained gap, not a bad evening.
Using it to tell friends that a well-liked person is secretly cruel, on the basis of your side alone, can spread a verdict that the evidence cannot yet support.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Contempt is disgust toward you and can show in public and private alike; this one depends on a gap between the two. Intimidation implies a cost for not complying and needs no split of faces. Flying Monkeys are third parties enlisted to pressure you, while here the audience usually has no idea, and is simply charmed. What is distinctive is that you have no witness who knows the private version.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched line-by-line. This requires repeated context or a recognizable sequence across a long enough thread to mean anything — a single message is never sufficient. Never scored.

codex_completed.name: Ambient Abuse
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot detect this from a single line. It only becomes visible as a shape across a whole conversation over time (rhythm, cycles, timing) — repeated context is required. It is never scored and never raises the index on its own.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A steady climate of tension, criticism and unpredictability in which no single moment looks serious but the whole leaves a person worn down.
codex_completed.short_definition: A steady climate of tension, criticism and unpredictability in which no single moment looks serious but the whole leaves a person worn down.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Instead of a few clear incidents, this is a background mood that a person lives inside: sighs, corrections, changeable tempers, and a sense that something will go wrong soon. Taken one at a time, each moment can be explained away. What marks it is the total effect, the constant bracing, and the way the mood seems to follow one person's moods or approval. Ordinary stressful periods can look similar for a while.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: There is no big fight to point to. It is the sighs, the sharp tone, the sense of having to guess the mood, until you are tired all the time and cannot say why.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: There is nothing to quote, so the exhaustion has no justification the target can offer to anyone, themselves included. They stay braced without being able to say what for.
what_it_is: A climate rather than an event: the effect builds from many small moments, not one that stands out.
Usually built from low-level criticism, shifting moods, silence, sighing, and rules that seem to change without notice.
Often leaves the person monitoring another person's face, footsteps and tone as a way to predict the evening.
Hard to describe to outsiders because each example, told alone, sounds trivial.
