codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot detect this from a single line. It only becomes visible as a shape across a whole conversation over time (rhythm, cycles, timing) — repeated context is required. It is never scored and never raises the index on its own.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A sexually charged or menacing atmosphere around a person, kept alive through repeated small signals, so they stay on guard with nothing definite to report.
codex_completed.short_definition: A sexually charged or menacing atmosphere around a person, kept alive through repeated small signals, so they stay on guard with nothing definite to report.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: This describes a climate rather than a single act: remarks about your body, lingering looks, jokes with a sexual edge, someone appearing near you more often than seems accidental. Any one of these can be explained as clumsiness or humor. The pattern is in the total effect, where a person begins to rearrange their route, schedule or clothing around someone. It does not show what anyone intended, only what the surroundings feel like to the person in them.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Nothing happens that you could report, but you are always aware of one person, adjusting where you go, when you leave and who is with you, because of how they make a space feel.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The target reorganises their movements, schedule and attention around one person while holding nothing concrete enough to report, or even to explain to a friend.
what_it_is: A repeated set of small signals, such as comments on your appearance, jokes with a sexual edge, or proximity, that add up to unease.
Different from a single act in that each piece is easy to deny or dismiss, and the effect lives in the repetition.
Seen at work, in schools, in shared housing, in congregations, and in families and friend groups.
Often leaves a person planning around it: taking another stairwell, bringing a friend, avoiding a room.
what_it_sounds_like: "You look good in that. Don't tell anyone I said so."
A running joke about what you would be like in bed, said in front of others.
"Relax, I'm only kidding. You're no fun."
Appearing at the edge of the break room, again, when you are alone.
A look from across the room, held a beat too long, on more days than not.
"I always know where you are." said with a smile.
what_it_is_not: A single clumsy compliment or off-color joke that the person took back as soon as it was pointed out.
A friendly colleague who greets everyone warmly and has no pattern of focusing on you.
A culture of bawdy humor shared evenly by everyone who takes part, where nobody is uncomfortable and anyone could opt out.
Your own feeling of unease with someone whose behavior has not changed and who has done nothing you can describe, which is worth taking seriously but does not prove a pattern.
A partner or date whose sexual remarks are welcomed and reciprocal.
this_may_be_it_when: The remarks or looks come from the same person across weeks, and keep coming after you showed discomfort.
You have changed your route, your clothes or your hours to avoid them.
Others have noticed and said things like "he is just like that", which has not made it stop.
You are often left alone with them in situations that did not need to be one-on-one.
When you object, you are told you are uptight, and the behavior goes on.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They stopped as soon as you said it bothered you, and apologized without making it awkward.
The comments are directed at everyone in the group, are mutual, and no one has said they feel uneasy.
Your unease comes from a single moment that you can explain to yourself in ordinary terms, such as a misread tone.
Contact is limited and public, and the person is rarely near you without others present.
The person has a known manner, such as being very direct about everything, that you have seen with nonsexual topics too.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Misjudged jokes and compliments are common, and most people stop when they find out they landed badly.
Some people stand close or hold eye contact longer as a habit of their culture or personality.
A person new to a workplace may copy the humor around them without seeing its effect.
common_false_positives: A coworker who greeted you twice in a hallway on the same day.
A friend who teases you about a crush, which you also find funny.
A mutual flirtation between two adults who both wanted it, which later turned sour.
discernment_questions: Have the remarks or looks continued after you showed discomfort, even slightly?
Are you changing where you go, who you are with or what you wear to avoid this person?
Is this person like this with everyone, or is it focused on you or a few others?
Could you describe three separate moments, even small ones, to someone who has not met them?
Do you feel safe if you are alone with them, and what makes you say so either way?
less_concerning_if: The behavior ended when it was pointed out and has not come back.
The setting is public, mutual and open, and everyone involved is comfortable.
You can describe a specific misunderstanding that accounts for the unease.
more_concerning_if: The person finds ways to be alone with you, or learns your schedule and location without being told.
The behavior comes with a difference in power, such as a supervisor, teacher or landlord.
Anything touches your body, belongings or space without your agreement, or your refusal is met with anger or silence.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your routes, hours and seating gradually shift to avoid one person.
You start to dread places you used to like, such as a gym, a break room or a family gathering.
You find yourself telling friends small, odd details because each one on its own is embarrassing to repeat.
A sense of being watched stays with you after the person has left the room.
codex_completed.repair_check: Change would mean the signals stop completely and stay stopped, with no testing of how far you will go along. An apology paired with fresh jokes, or with "I thought we were joking around", has not touched the underlying pattern, since the effect on you stays the same.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Once you have asked for the remarks or the looks to stop, watch what the following weeks hold. A person who respects it simply stops and does not make it awkward. Distance followed by sudden coldness, or the same behavior returning in a new form, answers the question the other way.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When a situation is ambiguous, a person tends to scan it for danger and to act on that scan before they can prove anything. A background of small signals keeps that scanning switched on, and the lack of a clear event makes it hard to justify the strain, even to oneself. Wondering whether you are overreacting can add to it.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe taking longer routes, leaving early, dressing to draw less attention, and feeling embarrassed that they cannot explain it. Some talk about doubting their own read, and about the tiredness of staying watchful in places that should be ordinary. Others describe anger at having to plan their day around another person's presence.

response_options.soft_clarification: If you feel safe, say one thing plainly and briefly: "Comments about my body make me uncomfortable." You do not need to argue the point.
response_options.firm_boundary: State it once without softening, and write down the date and the words you used: "I do not want comments about my appearance. Please stop."
response_options.disengagement: Where you can, avoid being alone with them, bring a colleague or friend, and use routes and times that keep other people around.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone you trust what you have noticed, even if it sounds small, and ask them to keep a record with you of dates and what was said.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Write down each incident with date, place, words and witnesses, and bring the record to HR, a union rep, a school office or an ombuds, as a pattern rather than separate incidents.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Please stop commenting on my appearance. I would like to keep our conversations about the work."
codex_completed.safety_note: Signals that raise concern are the person learning your schedule, turning up where you are, touching you without agreement, being in a position of power over you, or reacting to a refusal with anger. Keep dated records, tell someone you trust where you are going, and contact a sexual assault or domestic violence advocate or the police if you feel in immediate danger.
misuse_warning: Reading a pattern into a single awkward remark can wrongly mark a person as a threat. The label needs repetition and a continued focus on one person.
Your discomfort is real information, but it does not show what the other person means, and a report is best made on specific dated behaviors, not on a verdict about their character.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Intimidation carries an implied consequence for non-compliance, and this one stays suggestive and deniable. Contempt is disgust toward you, whereas here the signals are sexual or watchful in character and may be wrapped in friendliness. Emotional Invalidation answers your feelings once you voice them. This is attention aimed at you that makes you feel watched before you say anything.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched line-by-line. This requires repeated context or a recognizable sequence across a long enough thread to mean anything — a single message is never sufficient. Never scored.

codex_completed.name: "Polite Hostile" Environments
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot detect this from a single line. It only becomes visible as a shape across a whole conversation over time (rhythm, cycles, timing) — repeated context is required. It is never scored and never raises the index on its own.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A workplace or social setting that stays courteous on the surface while quietly penalizing anyone who speaks plainly or disagrees.
codex_completed.short_definition: A workplace or social setting that stays courteous on the surface while quietly penalizing anyone who speaks plainly or disagrees.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: In a polite hostile environment, nobody raises their voice and every email is warm, yet raising a real problem is followed by cooler treatment: left off invitations, passed over for projects, or described as 'not a culture fit'. Because nothing rude happened, there is nothing to report. One slow promotion or one cold week proves little. What marks it is the record across months and several people, when honesty and dissent are repeatedly followed by quiet losses.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Everyone is nice to your face, but people who speak up about real problems slowly get shut out, so you learn to stay quiet.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Nothing that happens is documentable, so whoever spoke up carries the cost alone, with no evidence to present. Everyone watching learns that silence is the sensible option, and the place slowly loses its honest voices.
what_it_is: A setting where courtesy is strictly kept and honest disagreement is quietly punished.
Penalties that arrive as small omissions: dropped from a meeting list, a project given to someone else, a slower reply.
Feedback that is vague and warm, such as 'we love your energy', followed by exclusion that is never explained.
A shared understanding among staff or members that certain topics, though never forbidden, cost you something to raise.
what_it_sounds_like: Every formal exchange is warm, and raising a real concern is followed by weeks of cooler replies.
A manager says 'thanks for flagging this, really valuable' and the next project goes to a colleague.
Staff describe a 'vibe' that no one can name in official terms.
Someone who questioned a decision is described as 'not quite aligned with the team'.
A review lists no problems, yet the person is repeatedly left off planning meetings after speaking up.
Colleagues say privately 'you can think that, just don't say it in the meeting'.
Invitations to informal events stop arriving after a complaint, with no one ever saying why.
what_it_is_not: A workplace where politeness is a real norm and people who disagree respectfully are still heard and promoted.
A company going through budget cuts, where several people's projects stall for stated business reasons.
A single raised concern that went nowhere because the issue was weighed and judged minor.
A reserved culture where people are formal with everyone, not only with those who spoke up.
Honest feedback about how a concern was delivered, which may be fair even when it stings.
this_may_be_it_when: Two or more people who raised real concerns describe similar quiet consequences afterward.
The pattern is visible in outcomes, such as who gets projects, but never in words anyone said.
Staff warn newcomers informally about which subjects to avoid.
Official channels for complaints exist, but people who use them are later treated differently.
Praise for 'communication style' coexists with exclusion of those who communicate directly.
this_may_not_be_it_when: People who disagree openly are still included, and your own slower progress has a stated reason.
Concerns raised lead to visible change or a clear explanation of why not.
The cooler treatment began before you spoke up, or applies to everyone in your role.
Colleagues who raised issues say they were treated fairly afterward.
A manager gives concrete feedback you can act on, even if it is hard to hear.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Organizations that value tact may simply expect disagreement to be handled privately and kindly.
A cold period after a tense meeting may be awkwardness and not a punishment.
Opportunities stall for reasons unrelated to anyone's honesty, such as budgets, timing and reorganizations.
common_false_positives: A team that has been polite throughout a hiring freeze, where no one is getting promoted.
A manager who is formal and reserved with everyone and cooler to you after a real performance problem.
A group that feels clique-ish because its members have worked together for years and are slow to include newcomers.
discernment_questions: Looking back over several months, does speaking up reliably come before a loss of opportunity?
Has anyone else who raised a concern experienced something similar?
Can you name any employee who disagreed openly and was treated well afterward?
Is the exclusion explained anywhere, or does it only exist as an absence?
Do you have a record, such as dates and outcomes, that you could review calmly with an outside person?
less_concerning_if: At least some people who disagree openly continue to advance.
When you raise a problem, you get a real answer or an honest reason for no change.
Cooler treatment applies to everyone equally and has a plain explanation.
more_concerning_if: A series of quiet losses is following several different people who each raised the same kind of issue.
Your pay, hours, references or job security begin to slip after you spoke.
Formal complaint channels exist and everyone knows that using them carries a cost.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find yourself editing your comments in meetings until they say nothing.
People you trust tell you privately that they agree, and never say so publicly.
Colleagues who once spoke freely have become quiet or have left.
Your own record of dates and outcomes shows a consistent gap after each time you spoke up.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair here is structural, not a personal apology: an honest account of what happened to people who raised concerns, a visible change in who gets opportunities, and a channel where speaking up stops costing something. A friendly all-hands about 'psychological safety' with no change in outcomes does not count.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: A useful test is what happens to the next person who disagrees in public. If the response is curiosity and a decision, the space can hold dissent. If they are warmly thanked and quietly sidelined, your own boundary or concern will probably meet the same fate.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People learn quickly what is safe to say by watching what happens to others. When the cost of honesty is delayed and deniable, a person may not link the loss to the remark, and may blame themselves instead. Seeing a colleague quietly sidelined can teach a whole group to stay silent without any rule being stated.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe self-doubt, because nothing rude ever happened that they could point to. Some say they became overly careful with their words, some felt isolated from colleagues who stayed quiet, and some began to dread work without being able to say what was wrong. Leaving the place can bring relief and grief at once.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask a plain question in private: 'After I raised that issue, I noticed I wasn't included in the planning meetings. Is there a reason I should know about?'
response_options.firm_boundary: State what you will continue to do: 'I will keep raising problems I see, in writing, so there is a clear record of what was said and when.'
response_options.disengagement: Put your energy into the people and work that are still open to you, and stop investing in channels where candor has been punished.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk with a mentor outside the organization, a professional association or an employment advisor about what you have seen, and compare your timeline with their experience.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Keep a dated log of what you raised, who responded and what changed afterward. Bring it to HR, an ombuds office or an employment lawyer if the consequences are tangible.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I appreciate how respectful this team is, and raising concerns is part of doing my job well. Let's put them in writing so we can all see what was raised and what was decided."
codex_completed.safety_note: This pattern is mostly about status and opportunity, not physical danger. It changes if consequences reach your pay, your hours, your references or your immigration or housing status, since a job loss then has serious effects. Document quickly, and speak with an employment lawyer, a union representative or a legal aid service before the situation moves.
misuse_warning: Applying this label to any workplace where you did not get a promotion can turn a real pattern into a way of avoiding honest feedback.
Describing a whole organization as hostile on the strength of one bad manager can overlook colleagues who are acting in good faith.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Concern Trolling is personal and aimed at one person's choices, while a polite hostile environment is a climate that touches many people. Forced Teaming demands loyalty to a 'we' by name, and here the loyalty is unspoken and enforced through omission. Triangulation uses specific third parties as ammunition, whereas this one needs no individual messenger at all.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched line-by-line. This requires repeated context or a recognizable sequence across a long enough thread to mean anything — a single message is never sufficient. Never scored.

codex_completed.name: Self-Gaslighting Induction
codex_completed.detectability_note: This describes an internal state in the person reading a result, not the other party in a conversation. This tool never detects or scores this about its user — doing so would mean diagnosing the person using the tool, which it will not do. It is here purely so you can recognize the state in yourself and seek support if it resonates.
codex_completed.core_meaning: The habit of doubting your own memory and perception on reflex, long after anyone else has needed to challenge it.
codex_completed.short_definition: The habit of doubting your own memory and perception on reflex, long after anyone else has needed to challenge it.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Self-Gaslighting Induction describes what can remain after a long stretch of having your memory or perception contradicted. The doubting now comes from inside. You may quietly correct your own account, assume you misread things and edit what you say before anyone has pushed back. Ordinary uncertainty and open-mindedness are healthy. The pattern is a reflex that overrides clear memories, and that tends to side with someone else's version of events.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: After being told for long enough that you misremember, you start doubting yourself automatically, even when nobody is arguing with you and you are sure.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The doubting continues with nobody present to do it. You discount things you clearly remember and edit your own account before anyone has even challenged it.
what_it_is: A reflex of second-guessing your memory that fires before any disagreement has been voiced.
A habit that may have formed after repeated denial of your account in a relationship, family or workplace.
Self-editing, such as softening or dropping the part of a story you are sure about.
Not a defect of memory: it is how you treat your memory, and it can ease with time and support.
what_it_sounds_like: Catching yourself saying 'maybe I'm remembering it wrong' about something you wrote down at the time.
Rehearsing an account that matches someone else's version before you have said what you remember.
Feeling a jolt of uncertainty about an event you can picture clearly.
Opening a sentence with 'I'm probably overreacting, but...' about something that plainly upset you.
Rereading your own saved messages to see whether you are allowed to be upset.
Telling a friend the story and then adding 'but I might have it wrong' unprompted.
what_it_is_not: Everyday epistemic humility: checking a calendar or admitting an error is healthy and shows an open mind.
Honest haziness about something long ago or something you only half noticed.
Updating your view after credible new evidence, which is an ordinary use of reasoning.
A normal memory slip under stress, tiredness or distraction, which happens to everyone.
A medical memory problem, which has its own causes and needs a doctor, not a pattern label.
this_may_be_it_when: You doubt clear memories, even ones backed by messages, receipts or witnesses.
The doubt shows up quickly, before anyone has disagreed.
You edit your account to match another person's, without being convinced.
You feel more certain about the same type of memory when the person is not around.
You need outside confirmation before trusting a plain perception.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The memory really is fuzzy, and you hold it loosely for that reason.
You changed your mind because someone showed you a reason, and the new view makes sense to you.
You doubt yourself equally in every area, in a way that a doctor or therapist is already exploring.
Your doubt lifts as soon as you check the record, and stays lifted.
It is a short phase of stress or sleep loss that eases once things calm down.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Memory blends and fades for everyone, so some uncertainty does not need a story behind it.
A cautious person may say 'I could be wrong' as a habit of speech that does not reflect real doubt.
Anxiety and depression, among other things, can undermine confidence in memory without any relationship being involved.
common_false_positives: Checking your notes before a meeting because the details matter and you want to be accurate.
Honestly reconsidering a story after a sibling remembers a detail you had forgotten.
Feeling unsure about a conversation from years ago that you never thought about again.
discernment_questions: Do I doubt things I clearly remember, or only things that are really hazy?
Does the doubt arrive before anyone has said I am wrong?
Does it ease when I am away from a particular person or place?
Whose version do I tend to adopt when mine differs?
If a friend told me this story, would I find it plausible, and why do I not extend that to myself?
less_concerning_if: The doubt is limited to hazy memories and fades when you check.
You can hold your own account calmly when someone disagrees.
Updating your view happens because of evidence you found convincing.
more_concerning_if: You doubt events you have documented, and the doubt does not ease once you see the proof.
The reflex now spreads to decisions about work, money and health.
It comes with distress, sleeplessness or dread about saying what you remember.
pattern_over_time_signs: You check your memory against saved messages more often than before.
You apologize first in disagreements, before working out what happened.
You say 'I don't know, maybe' to questions you can in fact answer.
Friends comment that you used to trust your own account more.
codex_completed.repair_check: Watch for small moments when the old reflex does not fire, such as telling a story as you remember it without adding a hedge. Change tends to arrive as repeated, small choices to believe yourself, helped by people who confirm what you saw, rather than as one big realisation.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice what happens when you give yourself permission to pause before deciding what you think. Does the permission hold, or does the old habit override it within seconds? A boundary here is a promise to yourself, and it is kept in small, repeated acts.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When your account is contradicted again and again, especially by someone you rely on, you can learn that your read of events is the thing most likely to be wrong. The doubt then gets moved inside, so it can fire quickly and quietly as a way of avoiding conflict. Over time, it may pass for a personal trait.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Some report hedging every sentence, keeping notes to prove they are not wrong, and feeling lost when asked what they want. Others describe tiredness from constant checking, or surprise at how clear their memory felt once they were away from the person who contradicted it.

response_options.soft_clarification: To someone who asks what happened, try giving your account first and the hedge second, or not at all: 'Here is what I remember.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Treat your own notes as legitimate: 'I wrote it down at the time, and I am going to trust that record.'
response_options.disengagement: When the urge to retract arrives, you can postpone the decision. Close the conversation, give yourself an hour, and come back to the facts as you see them.
response_options.support_seeking: A therapist or counselor who works with people leaving controlling relationships can help you test your memories and rebuild trust in them. A friend who was around at the time can help too.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, writing short same-day notes after meetings gives you a record that does not depend on anyone agreeing, and it can help you hold your ground.

codex_completed.boundary_script: Self-support script: "I am allowed to trust my own read of things. I do not have to decide how I feel about this right now, and I can check what I wrote down before I change my account."
codex_completed.safety_note: This entry describes a habit you carry, not a threat from someone else. If the person whose version you doubt is still in your life and you feel afraid of them, or if the doubt comes with low mood that does not lift, a counselor, doctor or domestic abuse advocate can help, and you can start with a private conversation.
misuse_warning: This is a way to understand yourself, not a label to hand to someone else ('you are self-gaslighting') or to treat as proof that your memory is unreliable.
Treating every moment of doubt as a symptom can make healthy caution feel like damage. Some doubt is just good thinking.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Identity Erosion is the slow loss of tastes, opinions and friendships, while Self-Gaslighting Induction is distrust of your memory and perception. Fawning is appeasing a person in the moment, but this habit continues when the person is not there. Learned Helplessness is doubt about whether you can manage tasks; this one is doubt about what you saw and remember.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored, by design. This tool never evaluates its own user's internal state — doing so would mean diagnosing the person using the tool.

codex_completed.name: Fawning
codex_completed.detectability_note: This describes an internal state in the person reading a result, not the other party in a conversation. This tool never detects or scores this about its user — doing so would mean diagnosing the person using the tool, which it will not do. It is here purely so you can recognize the state in yourself and seek support if it resonates.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Responding to a threatening person by pleasing, agreeing and shrinking yourself, as an automatic way of staying safe.
codex_completed.short_definition: Responding to a threatening person by pleasing, agreeing and shrinking yourself, as an automatic way of staying safe.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Fawning is a safety response, listed alongside fight, flight and freeze in many accounts of how people react to threat. Facing someone who feels dangerous or unpredictable, the person agrees quickly, flatters, apologizes, anticipates needs and sets their own opinion aside. It usually forms because it worked once. It is different from kindness: the driver is fear, and the pattern may continue after the danger has gone.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: When someone feels threatening, you go into automatic pleasing mode, agreeing, apologizing and hiding what you think, because it once kept you safe.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Safety is bought with the target's own position: they apologize for things done to them, and lose track of what they actually think while they are still saying it.
what_it_is: A quick, automatic move toward agreement, flattery or apology when a particular person seems unsafe.
Often learned in childhood homes or relationships where calm depended on keeping someone else happy.
A reaction shaped by fear, not character, and one that can happen without any decision.
Can carry on with new people who remind the body of the old one, even when no real threat is there.
what_it_sounds_like: Apologizing for something that was done to you, before anyone asks.
Hearing yourself say 'you're right, I'm sorry' while privately thinking you are not wrong.
Laughing along with a cruel joke because the room feels tense.
Feeling your opinion drain away mid-sentence when someone's face changes.
Noticing you have already rehearsed an apology for something you do not think you did.
Telling someone what they want to hear, then feeling sick afterward.
Offering help before being asked, to read their mood.
what_it_is_not: Everyday kindness, tact or good manners in which you choose to be agreeable and could do otherwise.
Cultural norms of respect or deference toward elders, which are about values and not about fear.
Fair compromise between two people who each give something up and neither is afraid.
A preference for peace or a dislike of conflict that shows up in safe relationships too.
Professional courtesy to a customer or boss, which follows the job and not a sense of danger.
this_may_be_it_when: The urge to please is strongest around one person or type of situation that feels unsafe.
There is a physical feel of dread or tightness just before you agree.
You apologize in advance for things that are not your fault.
You track their mood closely and adjust before they have said anything.
You agree out loud while privately holding a different view, and cannot say why you did not speak.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You are accommodating because you care and feel free to say no to this person.
The pleasing eases or disappears around people who feel safe.
The agreement follows genuine reflection and you still hold it afterward.
You feel neutral or warm, not afraid, when you go along with the group.
The deference is part of a shared cultural custom you value.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Politeness, shyness and a wish to avoid pointless arguments are common and carry no threat behind them.
Wanting to be liked by a new boss or in-law is normal social behavior.
Some people are simply more agreeable by nature, in every setting.
common_false_positives: Going along with a restaurant choice because you honestly do not mind.
Smoothing over a tense meeting by being diplomatic, then speaking up in private afterward.
Bowing to an elder in a culture where it is the normal sign of respect.
discernment_questions: Does the urge to please strike mostly around people who feel unpredictable or unsafe?
Is there fear underneath it, or is it more of a preference for harmony?
Does it ease with people who treat you kindly?
Do you find yourself apologizing for things you did not do?
Could you say no to this person, and what do you picture happening if you did?
less_concerning_if: The pleasing is occasional, chosen and comes with an ability to say no.
You go back to your own opinions easily once the moment passes.
You feel at ease with most people and keep the habit for rare tense moments.
more_concerning_if: The pleasing is a daily survival strategy around someone who frightens you.
You no longer know what you like or want when that person is near.
You feel intense dread at the thought of disagreeing with them.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find it hard to say what you want in restaurants, shops or decisions, even with safe people.
You apologize automatically, including to furniture or strangers.
Friends notice you seem different, quieter or more agreeable, around one person.
You feel tired after social contact because of how much mood-reading you do.
codex_completed.repair_check: Look for moments when the automatic yes loosens, such as taking a beat before answering or saying a small no to a safe person and surviving it. Change tends to build through many small experiences of staying safe while disagreeing, not through a decision to stop.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: When you give yourself time to answer, does the pause hold, or does the old reflex override it in seconds? Treat this as information about your nervous system, not about your character, and note which settings let the pause last.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When a person has learned that someone's anger or disapproval brings real costs, agreement and appeasement can become a quick, practiced way to lower the threat. Because it often worked, it tends to run automatically and without thought. The response can stay active in later situations that echo the first, even when the danger is gone.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Some report not knowing what they think until they are alone, feeling shame about things they agreed to, or being worn out from constant mood-reading. Others notice that with kind people they feel strangely blank when asked what they want. Many describe relief on learning that this has a name and a reason.

response_options.soft_clarification: With someone safe, you can name the habit lightly: 'I tend to say yes fast. Can I think about that and tell you tomorrow?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Practice small refusals in low-stakes settings first, such as choosing the film or the food, to build the experience of staying safe while holding a preference.
response_options.disengagement: If a person or place sets off the reflex, it is fine to keep contact brief, choose calmer settings where you can, and recover afterward somewhere quiet.
response_options.support_seeking: A therapist who understands trauma responses can help you work out when fawning protects you and when it costs you. Tell them about the specific people it happens around.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a boss triggers it, keep decisions in writing and give yourself a rule of answering after a day on anything large, so your yes is not made under pressure.

codex_completed.boundary_script: Self-support script: "This quick yes is a safety habit. I can notice it without acting on it yet, and I can take my time deciding what I actually think."
codex_completed.safety_note: Fawning usually points to a situation where someone feels frightening. If that person is threatening you, monitoring you or controlling your money or movements, plan with a domestic violence advocate or hotline rather than alone, and keep your plans private. If the reflex is mostly from the past, a trauma-informed therapist is a good next step.
misuse_warning: Do not use this label for someone who is just polite, agreeable or accommodating. Fawning is about fear, and applying it to ordinary kindness makes kindness look like damage.
It describes a response, not a flaw in the person, and should never be used to blame someone for how they coped.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Self-Gaslighting Induction is doubt about your memory and perception, while Fawning is pleasing to keep the peace. Identity Erosion is the long loss of your tastes and friends; Fawning is the moment-to-moment response that may feed it. Conditional Worth is the pricing someone else applies to you, which can be one of the things that sets this reflex off.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored, by design. This tool never evaluates its own user's internal state — doing so would mean diagnosing the person using the tool.

codex_completed.name: Identity Erosion
codex_completed.detectability_note: This describes an internal state in the person reading a result, not the other party in a conversation. This tool never detects or scores this about its user — doing so would mean diagnosing the person using the tool, which it will not do. It is here purely so you can recognize the state in yourself and seek support if it resonates.
codex_completed.core_meaning: The slow loss of your own tastes, opinions, limits and friendships inside a relationship, until the person you were earlier is hard to find.
codex_completed.short_definition: The slow loss of your own tastes, opinions, limits and friendships inside a relationship, until the person you were earlier is hard to find.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Identity erosion is something a person carries rather than something done in a single moment. Over months or years, preferences narrow toward what someone else likes, old friendships fade, and your own needs and limits are set aside to keep the peace. Self-abandonment names this very pattern from the inside, so this entry covers both. Everyone changes in a close relationship, and some of it is welcome. The concern is change that runs one way, that you did not choose, and that leaves you unsure what you would pick alone.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You look up and cannot say what you like, what you think or where your limits are, because most of it has been bent around keeping someone else content.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You can say what would keep the peace far more readily than what you want, and your own limits stop being information you are willing to act on. That makes it harder to judge a situation, to describe what you need, or to reach the people who could help.

Agreeing to things you promised yourself beforehand you would not agree to, then treating your own tiredness or need for rest as something to hide.
A shrinking circle, in which friends and family are seen less because there is less room or less welcome for them.
Often a run of small accommodations, each reasonable alone, that add up to a different life.
A state felt from the inside, usually noticed later when a song or a photo shows the gap.

"I used to love painting, but I haven't picked up a brush in years."
"I haven't seen my college friends since we moved in together. It just sort of happened."
"What do I think about it? I'd have to check what we think."
"I can tell you what would keep things calm. I can't tell you what I want."

"I swore I would not say yes to that again, and I just said yes."
"I can't remember what I wore before I met them."

Falling out of an old hobby because you lost interest, with nobody encouraging that.

Your own exhaustion, limits or wishes feel like problems to hide rather than information to use.
Imagining a day entirely on your own leaves you unsure what you would do with it.

Your old friends are still in your life, though you see them less because of distance.
You have taken on your partner's hobby and still do things that only you enjoy.
Your views have shifted because you thought them through, and you can argue for them.
Changes are matched by your partner's own changes, and both of you say the relationship has made you more yourself.

A busy stage of life, with young children or demanding work, pushes out hobbies and friendships for reasons that involve nobody's influence.
Someone coming out of a difficult stretch may be rebuilding their sense of self slowly.

Choosing a quieter life after years of being very social, and being glad of it.

If you were making plans only for yourself, what would you pick?

codex_completed.name: Internalized Conditioning
codex_completed.detectability_note: This describes an internal state in the person reading a result, not the other party in a conversation. This tool never detects or scores this about its user — doing so would mean diagnosing the person using the tool, which it will not do. It is here purely so you can recognize the state in yourself and seek support if it resonates.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Following rules and reactions that once came from another person, now enforced from inside your own head even when that person is nowhere near.
codex_completed.short_definition: Following rules and reactions that once came from another person, now enforced from inside your own head even when that person is nowhere near.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Internalized conditioning is what remains after someone else's rules, moods and judgments have been absorbed so fully that you apply them to yourself. A voice comments on your choices, or a flinch arrives before anyone has reacted, and nobody has to be in the room. One borrowed rule means little, since everyone carries habits from the people who raised them. What marks it is a rule that traces back to one person, overrides what you would choose, and keeps running after the relationship is over or far away. It was learned, so it can be unlearned.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: The rules of someone who once controlled the room now play inside your own head, so you police yourself even when they are gone.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The rules keep running when the other person is gone, so distance, even the end of the relationship, does not bring the relief you expected. You can leave the room and still find yourself obeying.

Guilt or dread that arrives before any reaction, as if a penalty has already been handed out.
A rule traced to one household or relationship that you still follow in places where that person has no say, such as a new job or a new home.
Often noticed only after distance, when the outside enforcement has stopped and the rule keeps operating.
Different from a value you chose, and the test is whether you would keep the rule if that person's opinion were taken out of the picture.

I haven't told anyone yet and I already feel like I'm in trouble.
I can't eat that in front of people. Nobody has said a word, I just can't.
Why am I rehearsing an apology for something nobody is angry about?
I know he isn't here. I still keep my voice down on the phone.
It's my own apartment and I still scrub the counters the second I get home, because otherwise I hear him.
I turned down the offer before I even asked myself whether I wanted it.
what_it_is_not: A conscience or personal values. Values you have examined and would choose again are yours, even if a parent first taught them.
Thinking about how a partner or friend will feel before you act. That is care, and it is one input among several.
Ordinary habits picked up from the family you grew up in, such as how you load a dishwasher or when you say thank you.
A loved person's remembered advice that comforts you and leaves the decision with you.
Anxiety or perfectionism with no single origin in one person, which has its own causes and its own treatments.
Respect for a workplace or faith rule that you understand and accept.
this_may_be_it_when: You can name the person whose phrasing the inner voice uses.
The penalty you brace for is one that person once handed out, though no one else in your life would.
The rule switches on in settings that person never visits.
Your preference and the rule point in opposite directions and the rule wins without a debate.
Their absence brought less relief than you expected, and the rules sometimes feel louder.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You can explain the rule's reasons in your own words and would pick it again.
The voice sounds like a mentor whose advice you test and sometimes ignore.
Breaking the rule leaves you uneasy for a minute, not dreading for days.
The standard applies to everyone in your life and is not tied to one person's disapproval.
It shows up only in a stressful stretch and fades when the stress does.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Children copy the habits and sayings of the adults around them, and many of those are kind.
Grief can make a lost parent's voice louder in your head for a while.
A cultural or religious upbringing shapes conscience, and conscience is not conditioning.
common_false_positives: Hearing a grandmother's advice about money and choosing to follow it.
Feeling nervous before a hard conversation, which almost everyone does.
Following your family's table manners at a holiday meal out of habit.
discernment_questions: Whose voice is this, and would I follow the same rule if that person had never existed?
Does the dread arrive before any real reaction, or only after one?
Where does the rule switch on, and where does it stay quiet?
When I act against it once, what actually happens, and how does that compare with what the voice predicted?
Does this rule protect something I care about, or does it only keep an old peace?
less_concerning_if: The rule is one you have looked at and still endorse.
It eases when you are rested, among people you trust, or far from old triggers.
You can break it sometimes without a spike of dread.
more_concerning_if: The inner voice calls you names or predicts punishment in terms that match what was once said to you.
It limits food, money, friendships or medical care in ways that harm you.
Even a small step against it brings panic, shaking or a sense of danger.
pattern_over_time_signs: You keep catching the same borrowed phrases in your own self-talk.
New relationships start to be treated as if they enforce the old rules.
Time away does not quiet the voice, and in some seasons it seems to sharpen it.
Small experiments, such as skipping a rule, go slightly easier each time.

codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Try pausing before you obey the voice and ask what you would do with nobody watching. Does the pause hold, or does the old rule sweep it aside within seconds? How quickly permission gets withdrawn is useful information, and it usually slows with practice.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Rules that were enforced again and again, with real consequences attached, can be stored as part of how a person monitors themselves. codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Tension can show up in places that should be safe, such as a new home or a quiet evening. response_options.firm_boundary: Pick one small, low-stakes rule and break it this week, then write down what actually happened beside what the voice said would happen.
response_options.disengagement: When the voice gets loud, step out of the decision itself: walk, drink some water, and hold any answer until the next day.
response_options.support_seeking: Say the rule aloud to a therapist or to a friend who knew you before. Hearing it outside your head often shows how specific and how borrowed it is.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If the rule follows you to work, as dread of any feedback, ask for expectations in writing so that a real standard stands where the old one did.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "That is an old rule from someone else, and I am allowed to pause before I follow it. I can work out what I want first."
codex_completed.safety_note: Rules you now enforce on yourself are a pattern inside your head, not a danger signal. In either case, bring the voice itself to a therapist or a crisis line this week.

Fawning is appeasing a person who is present, whereas here the enforcer is missing and the flinch comes anyway.

codex_completed.name: Silence Installation

codex_completed.core_meaning: A learned inability to speak about specific things, where the thought of naming them brings dread because raising them has repeatedly cost more than staying quiet.
codex_completed.short_definition: A learned inability to speak about specific things, where the thought of naming them brings dread because raising them has repeatedly cost more than staying quiet.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Silence installation is a learned block around particular subjects. The words may be clear in your head, even rehearsed for weeks, but when the moment comes the body shuts down: the throat tightens, the mind blanks, the topic changes. It usually follows a history in which naming the problem brought anger, ridicule or a worse week. A single awkward silence proves nothing. What stands out is a specific topic that stays unspeakable for years, tied to a memory of what speaking cost. It is a protective habit, not a flaw.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: There are things you cannot make yourself say, because the earlier times you tried went badly. The silence is protection you learned, not weakness.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The problems most in need of raising become the ones you physically cannot raise, so they go unaddressed and quietly grow. Meanwhile other people may read your silence as agreement, or as proof that all is well.

A bodily response such as a closing throat, a blank mind or a sudden need to leave the room.
A reaction built from earlier costs, when raising the subject was met with anger, mockery, sulking or a turned back.
Narrow rather than general, so you can talk freely about many things and freeze on this one.
A block that can outlast the relationship that taught it, showing up with a doctor, a boss or a new partner.

I opened my mouth and nothing came out.
It's not worth bringing up. It never goes well.
The sentence is ready in my head, and then my chest locks.
Every time I almost mention the money, I end up talking about the weather.
I told my friend everything was fine again. I don't know why I keep doing that.
Please don't ask me about it. I can't.
what_it_is_not: Privacy or discretion, which is a choice made with a clear head about who needs to know.
Waiting for a better moment, such as holding a hard topic until after a deadline or a funeral.
Shyness or introversion that shows up across every subject and not around particular ones.
A cultural habit of not discussing certain topics at the table, where leaving them unspoken costs you nothing.
Social anxiety or selective mutism, which are separate conditions with their own clinical assessment.
Not being ready to talk about a loss, where silence is part of coping and was never a response to penalties.
this_may_be_it_when: You can trace the freeze to a specific time when speaking up was punished or mocked.
The block appears around the same person or topic even when you are calm.
You rehearse again and again and still skip it when the moment comes.
Others mention that you seem fine because you never raise anything, while you are not fine.
The dread arrives before you have even decided whether the issue is worth raising.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You stay quiet for a few days, then bring it up on your own terms.
You can say it to a friend or counselor, even if saying it to one particular person is hard.
The reluctance is about choosing a good time and not about expecting consequences.
The topic is simply private, and you are at peace with that.
The freeze belongs to a wider anxiety that appears in every setting and that a professional is already helping with.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Most people find some conversations harder than others, such as money, health or grief.
Fear of a hurtful reaction is reasonable even when the other person has never reacted badly.
People raised in families that avoid direct talk may simply never have practiced it.
common_false_positives: Putting off a hard conversation until after a family wedding.
Not telling coworkers about a diagnosis, which is a personal decision.
A shy person who freezes in a large meeting but speaks easily one-on-one.
discernment_questions: Is there a particular topic that locks me up while others do not?
What happened the last time I said it, or something like it?
Do I freeze with everyone, or mostly with one person or one kind of person?
Could I write it down, or say it to someone safe, even if I cannot say it to the person it concerns?
What do I imagine will happen if I speak, and does that picture match anything that has actually happened?
less_concerning_if: Writing the message down, or saying it to a trusted listener, comes easily.
The block loosens when circumstances change, such as a new setting or a calmer week.
You choose silence on some topics and feel fine about the choice.
more_concerning_if: The topic involves your safety, health, money or your children.
The block is spreading, so more topics become unspeakable over time.
Speaking up was once followed by punishment that you still fear.
pattern_over_time_signs: A rehearsed sentence stays unsaid for months or years.
The list of topics you avoid gets longer.
You answer 'fine' to questions that deserve a longer answer.
People close to you are surprised when you finally say it.

codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When speaking has repeatedly been followed by a bad outcome, the mind can learn to predict that outcome at the first hint of the topic. codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Rehearsed sentences pile up unsaid. Some lie awake over a conversation they could not start, or feel invisible when others assume all is well. response_options.firm_boundary: If someone talks over you or mocks the attempt, you can say 'I need to finish this sentence' and carry on at your own pace.
response_options.disengagement: If the topic stays locked in the moment, put it in a note, a text or a letter instead. Writing sidesteps the throat-closing part and leaves a record.
response_options.support_seeking: Say the sentence first to someone with no stake in your answer, such as a counselor, a helpline volunteer or a friend from outside the family.

Self-Gaslighting Induction is doubting whether what you saw was real, but with silence you know exactly what you saw and cannot say it.

codex_completed.short_definition: Coming to depend on one person's approval, often built through warmth that comes and goes unpredictably, until their reaction counts for more than your own judgment.

I only feel proud of something once they've said it was good.

codex_completed.repair_check: Look at how the next cold spell goes. If the person turns steady, says in words what is bothering them, and keeps warmth and coolness predictable, the pull has less to feed on. If praise simply returns after a stretch of distance, the swing is still in place. For you, change starts with noticing your own verdict first.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Try giving an opinion before asking for theirs, and watch what follows. Does a different view get heard, or does the room go cold? Watch your own reaction as well, and whether you can tolerate the quiet without rushing to fix it.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Rewards that arrive at unpredictable intervals tend to be chased harder than rewards that come steadily, and approval can work this way. Each warm moment feels like relief after a cold one, which raises its value. As attention shifts to forecasting the other person's reaction, practice at consulting your own taste and judgment can fade.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A good day can come to hang on a face or a text. Some go numb about their own opinions, cannot enjoy an achievement until someone confirms it, or feel oddly empty when the person is pleased. Others notice that old interests slipped away without any decision to drop them.

response_options.soft_clarification: Try pausing before you ask what they think: 'Let me tell you what I thought first.' It restores the order of whose view comes first.
response_options.firm_boundary: State a preference without waiting for a verdict, such as 'I'm going with the blue one,' and then leave the silence alone instead of filling it.
response_options.disengagement: When the guessing starts, step away from the phone or the room for ten minutes and write down your own view of how things went.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask a friend who sees you in other settings whether you seem different around this person. An outside read helps you recalibrate.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask a manager for specific criteria for good work, such as three measurable goals, so approval rests on shared standards and not on mood.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Give me a day to write down my own view first. After that we can compare notes."
codex_completed.safety_note: Not a safety issue by itself. That shifts when approval is tied to housing, income or immigration status, or when withdrawn warmth turns into threats or surveillance, because displeasing the person then has practical stakes. In that case, talk through options with an advocate or counselor in private before changing anything in the relationship.
misuse_warning: Calling someone's warmth 'cultivation' turns any run of hot and cold moods into an accusation, when moods swing for countless ordinary reasons.
Reading every wish to please as an addiction can make normal love and care look like illness.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Conditional Worth states, openly or by implication, that you matter only when useful, while approval dependence is leaning on one person's reaction for your sense of how you are doing. Fawning is appeasement driven by fear of a threatening person, whereas here the pull is toward their warmth. Identity Hooking has them claim your achievements as theirs, but here the achievement stays yours and only the verdict is outsourced.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored, by design. This tool never evaluates its own user's internal state — doing so would mean diagnosing the person using the tool.

codex_completed.name: Parentification
codex_completed.detectability_note: This describes an internal state in the person reading a result, not the other party in a conversation. This tool never detects or scores this about its user — doing so would mean diagnosing the person using the tool, which it will not do. It is here purely so you can recognize the state in yourself and seek support if it resonates.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Being placed, as a child or partner, in the permanent role of caring for an adult's emotions, practical needs and crises, at the cost of your own development.
codex_completed.short_definition: Being placed, as a child or partner, in the permanent role of caring for an adult's emotions, practical needs and crises, at the cost of your own development.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Parentification is a role reversal in which a child, or sometimes a partner, ends up looking after the adult: soothing their moods, handling bills or siblings, fielding their crises. Chores and a hard season of helping are normal in families. It becomes parentification when the caretaking is constant, beyond what the child could be expected to handle, and nobody looks after the child in return. Many people only see the role once they are adults, because as children it simply looked like what a family was.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Instead of being looked after, you became the one who looked after a parent or partner, handling their feelings and problems long before you should have had to.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You come to treat your own needs as an imposition, and the growing-up that was postponed to keep an adult afloat does not happen later on its own. Resting may seem like neglecting someone.
what_it_is: A child who calms a parent's tears, mediates their arguments or listens to adult worries no child should carry.
Practical work beyond the child's age, such as managing money, cooking for siblings or reminding a parent about medicine.
A role that stays when circumstances improve, instead of ending with the crisis.
Care that flows one way, with the child tending to the adult's needs and the adult rarely asking about the child's.
Something that can also appear between adult partners, where one becomes the manager of the other's moods, calendar and crises.
Often praised as maturity ('so responsible for your age'), which makes the cost harder to see.
what_it_sounds_like: You're the only one I can talk to. Sit down, I need to tell you about your father.
I don't know what I'd do without you. You're my rock.
Can you call the landlord? You're better at this than I am.
Don't upset your mother, you know how she gets.
You are so mature for your age.
Go and see if he's okay. I can't deal with him tonight.
If I take one evening off, I think everything will fall apart.
what_it_is_not: Age-appropriate chores, such as setting the table or looking after a pet, which teach skill without displacing a child's needs.
A short season of extra help during illness, job loss or a death, which eases when the crisis does.
Caring for a sick or disabled relative as a free adult choice, with support and a way to step back.
Families where older children help raise siblings as a shared, supported arrangement and still receive care themselves.
A parent saying 'I'm sad today' once, without handing the child the job of fixing it.
Adult children helping aging parents, which is a normal turn in the life cycle.
this_may_be_it_when: As a child you handled things like bills, siblings or an adult's moods that no one your age should.
Your own upset got less attention than theirs, or was treated as an extra burden.
The household seemed to wobble when you were absent or unwell.
You were praised for being mature and also scolded for any sign of being a kid.
Today you feel responsible for other people's feelings in every room, and guilty over resting.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The jobs suited your age and stopped when homework or play began.
An adult also checked in on you, asked about your day and noticed when you were low.
The extra load came during a crisis and ended with it.
You helped by choice, could say no, and nothing bad followed.
You remember being cared for as well, even though you also helped.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Families under strain, such as single parents on long shifts, often depend on older children.
Some cultures treat sibling care as a normal part of growing up.
A parent may lean on a child out of loneliness without having noticed the weight, and that does not show what anyone meant.
common_false_positives: Being asked to wash dishes and watch a younger sibling for an hour after school.
Helping a parent through a hard year, then being released from it.
An adult who chose to become a caregiver and has support.
discernment_questions: How old was I when I started, and what was I handling?
Who looked after me when I was upset or ill?
Did the role stop when the crisis stopped?
If I said no, was it accepted, or treated as abandoning them?
Do I now find it hard to ask for help or to rest?
less_concerning_if: Your responsibilities matched your age and eased when the difficult stretch passed.
Someone was taking care of your needs too.
Saying no was possible and was met without punishment.
more_concerning_if: You carried adult emotional work from a young age with no one looking out for you.
Refusing was treated as betrayal or as proof of being a bad child.
Siblings, money or safety depended on you.
pattern_over_time_signs: Every crisis in the household finds its way to you.
You grow into the person at work and among friends who handles everyone's feelings.
You feel guilty or restless when nobody needs you.
Your own needs go unnamed until they become a crisis, and then you feel ashamed.
codex_completed.repair_check: From an adult who leaned on you, change would sound like noticing the load, taking tasks back, and finding other support for their feelings. For you, it looks like practicing small asks. Praise for how well you coped, with no change in who carries the weight, is not repair.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: When you hand a task back or say you cannot take a call tonight, notice what follows. Does the adult manage, adjust and move on, or does guilt arrive at once, along with a reminder of what they did for you? The response to the first small no is often the clearest answer.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A child who is needed gets attention and a sense of worth from being useful, and may learn that love arrives through caretaking. Tuning in to an adult's moods early can become automatic vigilance. When the role is also praised, it may harden into identity, so putting it down looks like abandoning people and not like resting.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Adults who grew up in this role often report difficulty receiving help, feeling responsible for everyone's mood, and swinging between overworking and collapsing from exhaustion. Some mourn a childhood that they now see was shorter than other people's. Some feel loyalty and resentment at once and are confused by both.

response_options.soft_clarification: If an adult in your life still leans on you, name the load in a neutral way: 'I can listen for ten minutes, but I can't solve this for you.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decide ahead what you will no longer take on, such as being the go-between, and decline that one job each time it comes up, kindly and briefly.
response_options.disengagement: When a crisis call arrives and you have nothing left, let it go to voicemail and reply in writing later. Rest is allowed.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk with a therapist who knows family role patterns, or with a sibling or friend who grew up in the same house, and compare what each of you carried.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, notice if you take on everyone's emotional upkeep or unpaid extras, and practice handing back what belongs to other people.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I love you, and I can talk for a little while tonight. I can't be the one who fixes this, so I'd like you to ask your sister or a counselor for that part."
codex_completed.safety_note: Being the family's caretaker is not, in itself, a danger signal. That changes if the adult's crises involve self-harm threats you are expected to prevent, violence, or loss of housing that you are told is your responsibility. A child or teen in that position needs an adult outside the household, such as a school counselor, a doctor or a relative, to share the weight.
misuse_warning: Calling every childhood chore 'parentification' can erase the real value of contributing to a household.
The label can become a way to blame a struggling parent for everything, while overlooking the illness, poverty or lack of support that shaped the household.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Learned Helplessness is the message that you cannot cope alone, whereas parentification is nearly the reverse, with you treated as the one who must cope for everyone. Loyalty Binds defines love as silence and compliance, but here the demand is for care work. Conditional Worth ties your value to usefulness, which often accompanies the role but can exist without it.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored, by design. This tool never evaluates its own user's internal state — doing so would mean diagnosing the person using the tool.

codex_completed.name: Process Exhaustion
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A process that keeps adding steps, forms, meetings and re-reviews until the person gives up from tiredness, not because their matter was decided.
codex_completed.short_definition: A process that keeps adding steps, forms, meetings and re-reviews until the person gives up from tiredness, not because their matter was decided.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Process exhaustion is when the process itself becomes the obstacle. Each step may be reasonable and follow written rules, but together they restart clocks, ask for the same information again, pass the person between offices, and stretch a simple matter across months. It shows up in insurance claims, benefits, immigration paperwork, workplace complaints, school accommodations and housing disputes. Complex matters do take time. The difference is effort out of proportion to the issue, progress that does not carry from one step to the next, and a withdrawal recorded as though you had chosen it.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Each time you ask for something, a new form, meeting or review begins, and after enough rounds you stop pursuing it, so the matter ends without anyone deciding it.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You lose through depletion instead of a decision, and the record shows it as your choice: you withdrew, you did not follow up, you stopped replying.
what_it_is: A sequence of required steps that keeps lengthening: another form, another office, another review, another waiting period.
Restarted clocks: a new complaint, a changed address or a missing signature sends you back to the beginning.
The same documents requested more than once, by different people, with no sign earlier ones were read.
Rules followed to the letter, which makes it hard to point to any single wrong act.
An ending reached when the person stops, so the file closes as 'withdrawn' or 'no response' instead of with a finding.
Seen in settings where a formal process controls money, status or services.
what_it_sounds_like: We received your form, but we need it on the new version. The review period starts again from today.
That office handles part of this. You'll need to file the other part with them.
Your request was closed because we did not hear back within ten days.
We need those documents again. The earlier ones have been archived.
The review committee meets quarterly. Your case will be considered at the next meeting.
To appeal, first request a reconsideration, then the appeal form, then a hearing date.
Your case manager has changed. Please explain the situation to them from the beginning.
what_it_is_not: A complex matter that really needs several expert steps and a long time, with each step building on the last.
A slow office short of staff, where every applicant waits the same long time.
Required documents and safeguards meant to prevent fraud or protect others, which feel heavy but apply equally to everyone.
An appeals ladder that is long but stated up front, with stage timelines you can plan around.
A delay caused by a real error, such as a lost file, that is then fixed with credit for the time already waited.
Waiting on a third party, such as a lab or a court date, that nobody in the process controls.
this_may_be_it_when: Progress does not carry over: each new step asks for what you have already supplied.
Others with similar matters are decided faster or face fewer hurdles.
The requirements change between steps, in ways that cannot be traced to a stated rule.
The process asks for effort when you can least give it, such as during working hours or after a crisis.
You are told the matter will be settled at the next step, and the next step repeats the same promise.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Every step has a stated purpose and a time, and the schedule is kept.
Information you provide once is used throughout, and status updates match the file.
Others in your position describe the same path and timing.
The long wait ends in a decision with reasons you can appeal.
You have one named contact who can tell you where things stand.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Understaffed offices and older systems that do not share data cause repetition for everyone.
Rules written for the hardest cases can burden the ordinary ones.
Staff turnover can force you to explain again, without anyone meaning the repetition.
common_false_positives: A mortgage or visa application with long documented requirements, all stated at the start.
A court process that is slow because of its calendar, not because of anything about you.
An insurer asking for a missing document that really was missing.
Waiting for an appointment in an overstretched public service.
discernment_questions: Does each step build on the last, or restart from zero?
Is the amount of paperwork proportionate to the size of the question?
Are other people in my position going through the same thing?
Do I have one person who knows where my case stands?
If I stopped replying today, what would the record say about why?
less_concerning_if: The path and timeline were given at the start, and the actual progress matches them.
Delays are explained and credited when the fault lies with the office.
A named person answers questions and can escalate.
more_concerning_if: The matter affects your housing, income, health care or legal status, and the delay itself causes harm.
A deadline for you stays firm while the office's own deadlines slide.
Missing one step closes the case for good, with no way to reopen it.
pattern_over_time_signs: You keep a growing folder of duplicate submissions and confirmations.
Each new round turns out slightly longer than you were told.
You take time off or arrange childcare for steps that could have been done by mail or phone.
Your list of reasons to keep going gets shorter, and the file closes with a note saying you withdrew.
codex_completed.repair_check: Genuine reform means one consolidated file, a single contact, a final timeline in writing and credit for time already waited. Regret paired with yet another form, or a fresh review that starts the clock at day one, repeats the first problem.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice what happens when you ask for a written list of every remaining step, with dates. If it arrives and holds, the process can be planned around. If the list keeps changing, or the request is passed from desk to desk, that tells you something about the process.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Effort and waiting can wear people down in a way that open disagreement does not. Each step asks for a little more time, money or composure, and the cost of continuing grows while the chance of an end stays unclear. Because every step seems reasonable alone, it is hard to point to one moment where things went wrong, which can make complaint feel petty and quitting feel like personal failure.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe dread of letters and calls, losing hours of work to appointments, repeating painful details to a new person each time, and finally giving up on something they were entitled to. Some feel shame at having quit, though the process had asked more than the matter was worth. Others describe the process taking over their free time.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the office for the full list of remaining steps and what each one is for: 'Can you give me everything still needed, in writing, with dates?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold the process to its own record: 'I submitted this on the date shown on my confirmation. I'd like it treated as received then, not restarted.'
response_options.disengagement: Put a limit on your own effort. Pick one day a week for the process and let the rest of the week stay free, so it stops filling every gap.
response_options.support_seeking: Bring in a caseworker, legal aid office, union steward or advocate for your kind of case; they often know which steps are required and which can be combined.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Keep a single dated log of every submission, call and name, and ask in writing for escalation to a supervisor or ombuds office when a step repeats.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I've already provided these documents on the dates shown on my confirmations. Please check the file for them, and let me know in writing what is actually still outstanding and when a decision will be made."
codex_completed.safety_note: Being worn down by forms and deadlines is a fairness and time problem. It becomes more serious when the matter protects your housing, income, health care, immigration status or custody, because a missed step can close the case permanently. If you are close to a hard deadline of that kind, contact legal aid or a caseworker now and ask what the actual cut-off date is, before spending more time on forms.
misuse_warning: Calling any slow or heavy process 'exhaustion' can write off real safeguards and long timelines that apply to everyone, and can make an overloaded office look hostile.
A person who missed deadlines on their own may use the label to explain the loss; a dated log of what actually happened is the check.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Pressure to Sign compresses time to nothing, while process exhaustion stretches it out. Confidentiality as Weapon closes the file to you, whereas here the file is open and the path keeps growing. Legal/Administrative Threats mention an authority as a warning, and nothing in this tactic needs to be said aloud, because the steps themselves wear you down.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: HR Shielding
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A workplace complaints process that in practice protects the organization's reputation and the accused person more than the employee who reported harm.
codex_completed.short_definition: A workplace complaints process that in practice protects the organization's reputation and the accused person more than the employee who reported harm.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: HR shielding is when a complaints function, set up to help employees, ends up serving the organization's exposure to blame: its reputation, its legal risk and the accused person's position.
