Strategic HR Complicity is a second label for this very practice, and covers using a complainant's trust to draw out details that then shape the organization's reply. One slow or disappointing process proves little. What gives it away is what happens to the person who reported compared with the person reported.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You report harm to HR, and the process seems to protect the company and the person you named while you are the one who feels the strain.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Someone brings a complaint believing they are speaking to a protector, and finds that what they said has been used to shape the response against them. They absorb the disruption while the situation continues, and colleagues learn what reporting costs.
what_it_is: A complaints, grievance or investigation process that looks correct on paper: forms filed, meetings held, letters sent.
Information a complainant gave in trust being passed to managers or lawyers and used to prepare the organization's position.
Attention fixed on the organization's exposure, such as reputation, legal risk and how things look, more than on what happened.
Friction landing on the person who reported, such as new scrutiny or a cooler team, while the accused carries on as before.
Found in workplaces, schools, universities and other bodies that run their own internal complaints office.
what_it_sounds_like: We want to make sure this doesn't get blown out of proportion.
Let's think about how this looks for the team.
Before we go further, can you tell me everything, including who else you have spoken to?
I can't share the outcome with you. It's confidential.
Your manager knows the details of your report before you have been told what happens next.
The case is closed as 'no further action' without the witnesses you named being interviewed.
You are offered a move to another team, while the person you reported stays where they are.
A performance review that was fine last year now lists new concerns about you.
what_it_is_not: Due process protects the accused too. A fair process lets them respond and limits who learns the details, which can feel one-sided to the person who reported.
HR staff who explain the limits of confidentiality at the start, follow a policy that disappoints you, or reach a conclusion you disagree with are doing the job as designed, not colluding.
A finding of 'not substantiated' means the evidence did not meet the standard. It is not the same as being disbelieved.
An under-trained or overloaded HR team producing a slow, clumsy process through lack of capacity.
HR advising a manager on how to handle a case, done openly and fairly to both sides, which is part of the role.
this_may_be_it_when: What you told HR in confidence shows up in how managers or lawyers respond to you.
Questions in meetings focus on your conduct, your motives or who you told, more than on the events you reported.
You see no sign that anyone spoke to the witnesses or collected the records you pointed to.
You face new criticism or changes to your role after reporting, while the accused is untouched.
You are told to wait or stay quiet, and no timeline or outcome is shared.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You were told at the start who would see what you said, and that matches what happened.
Witnesses were interviewed and records collected, even though the finding went against you.
The delay has a stated reason, and the process keeps moving in stages you are told about.
Interim steps, such as changed seating or schedules, apply to both of you.
Changes to your work come from a documented business reason that predates your report.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Confidentiality rules often stop HR from sharing outcomes or discipline, so silence can look like protection when it is a legal limit.
HR teams are often small and handle complaints beside hiring and payroll, so a slow reply may be capacity.
A manager may have to be told something so that people can be kept apart, which can feel like exposure.
common_false_positives: An investigation that took months and ended without a finding in your favor, but was thorough and explained to you.
An HR officer who said at the outset that they work for the organization and cannot act as your advocate.
A complaint about a policy decision rather than about harm, where HR correctly explained that the policy applied.
discernment_questions: Were the people and records I named actually looked at?
Who has been told what I said in confidence?
Since I reported, has my own treatment changed more than theirs?
Can I get a written account of each step, the standard used and the reason for the outcome?
Would an outside reviewer, such as a union representative or employment adviser, read the process as fair on its face?
less_concerning_if: You were told early who can see your report, and nothing contradicts that.
Delays come with updates and a stated next step.
Steps that affect you apply to the accused as well.
more_concerning_if: Your report becomes a reason for discipline, a transfer or a performance plan aimed at you.
You are pressed to withdraw the complaint or accept an agreement before you have had advice.
The harm you reported is ongoing or involves safety, sexual harassment, discrimination or your income, and the process has not touched it.
pattern_over_time_signs: Replies to you get shorter and further apart, while the organization's file on the case grows.
Colleagues who saw what happened go quiet, having watched what followed your report.
You keep your own notes of every conversation because what was said in meetings does not match what is later written.
You learn that earlier complaints about the same person ended the same way, or that those who made them left.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair would show in the process itself: witnesses interviewed, a written reason for the outcome, protection from retaliation put in place, and what you shared no longer used against you. A warm meeting and an offer of a transfer, with the case itself untouched, only changes the mood.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask whether your request for the process to be explained led to an explanation. A written answer to who has seen your report and what happens next shows the request was respected. Being told it is confidential, or that your questions are slowing things down, suggests it was handled as a nuisance.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People usually bring complaints to HR trusting that it is neutral, so they share more than they otherwise would. A process can then be shaped by liability concerns while using the language of fairness, which can make unfair treatment look like routine policy. Because each step is defensible alone, the person may end up blaming their own handling of the case.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Many say they felt betrayed by the one place they were told to go, and regret at having shared details. Some say they stopped trusting any internal process, wondered whether they imagined the harm, or dreaded going to work. Others describe losing sleep over each email and weighing whether to push further or leave a job they need.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask in writing for the steps and who will see your report: 'Could you confirm the stages, the expected dates and who has access to what I submitted?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask for your concerns about how the process is running to be recorded in the case file, in writing, along with a copy of the procedure being followed.
response_options.disengagement: Keep what you tell HR to facts and dates, in writing where possible, and avoid offering extra detail in informal chats until you have outside advice.
response_options.support_seeking: Speak to a union representative, an employment advice service or a legal aid clinic before the next meeting, and ask whether a companion may attend with you.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask whether there is an ombuds office, a second-level reviewer or an external body for complaints about the process, and request that route in writing.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Before we go on, could you tell me in writing who has seen what I reported, what the next steps are, and when I will hear back? I would also like to ask whether I can bring a support person to the next meeting."
codex_completed.safety_note: Watch for retaliation after you report: changed hours, lost shifts, a sudden performance plan or pressure to sign something, since these can put your income or immigration status at stake. If the original harm involves threats, stalking or sexual violence, tell someone outside work as well. Keep dated copies of your own messages and notes, and ask an employment lawyer or legal aid clinic about time limits before signing anything.
misuse_warning: A disappointing outcome is not proof the process was rigged. Treating every unfavourable result as shielding can erode trust in a process that may have been fair.
Pinning this label on one HR worker can personalise a problem that usually sits in how the process is built and whom it answers to.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Confidentiality as Weapon uses secrecy to keep you from seeing the accusations or evidence, while HR shielding is wider, covering the whole complaint process and where its effort goes. Pressure to Sign is a single push to accept a document on the spot, and may appear inside this pattern. Institutional Betrayal names the harm of being failed by a body you depend on; this names one route to it, a complaints function turned toward protecting the organization.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Pseudo-Consultation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Asking for opinions, feedback or comment after the decision is already settled, so the input has nothing left to change.
codex_completed.short_definition: Asking for opinions, feedback or comment after the decision is already settled, so the input has nothing left to change.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Pseudo-Consultation is a consultation that happens in form but not in function. A survey, town hall, comment period or feedback session is held, people give their views, and the outcome turns out to have been fixed beforehand. The decision is then described as shaped by those who took part. One disappointing consultation proves little, since honest ones also end in decisions people dislike. What gives it away is timing: the contract was signed, the vendor chosen or the announcement drafted before the first person spoke.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You are invited to have your say about something already decided, and afterward it gets described as a choice you took part in.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You spend real effort and real candor on input that could never have changed anything, and the decision is afterwards described as shared with you. Next time you may speak up less, or feel you gave up the right to object because you were asked.
what_it_is: A feedback step placed after the point where a decision can still be reversed, such as after a lease, contract or restructure has been signed.
Input gathered in public and then summarized in a way that thanks people without saying what, if anything, changed.
Questions that only offer choices among options already picked, like the color of the new logo but not whether to rebrand.
A record of participation (attendance sheets, survey counts) later cited as evidence that the people affected agreed.
what_it_sounds_like: "We value your input. The new schedule starts Monday, and we'd love to hear how you feel about it."
A town hall where the slides already show the final floor plan, and the sign-in sheet is collected at the door.
"Thank you all for your feedback, which has been carefully noted." Nothing in the next announcement differs from the draft you saw before the meeting.
A survey with a comment box, closing the day after the vendor contract was announced.
"The consultation showed broad support" cited in a report, when most people at the session objected out loud.
A staff meeting where the manager says, "Nothing is set in stone," and the new policy is in the handbook by the end of the week.
what_it_is_not: A consultation that says up front what is fixed, for example, "The budget is set, but you can shape how it is spent." Honest limits are not staged influence.
Feedback on how to carry out a decision that really is final, when that narrower scope is stated plainly.
A real consultation where the decision went against most of the people who spoke. Losing a fair process is not the same as never having had one.
A legal requirement to hold a comment period that the body treats seriously, even if the final text changes only a little.
A leader who listened, weighed everything and kept the original plan, and can say why.
this_may_be_it_when: Documents show the decision, purchase or hire was complete before the consultation opened.
No one can say what happened to the comments, or the summary leaves out every objection.
The consultation closes at a point where the plan could no longer be changed without cost or embarrassment.
People who gave detailed input find the final plan identical to the version circulated beforehand.
Participation is later cited as proof of agreement, even from people who voiced strong doubts.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Earlier drafts and the final plan differ in ways that trace back to what people said.
The organizers explain which suggestions were not used and why.
The consultation covered only a stated slice of the decision, and the slice did move.
The decision was delayed or reopened after the feedback came in.
You only suspect the outcome was fixed because you dislike it, and have no timeline or record pointing that way.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Organizers sometimes consult late because a deadline, funder or regulator left them little room, and then say so.
A leader may have a strong preference, listen honestly, and still end up where they started.
Consultations often gather more suggestions than a project can absorb, so many are filed for later without being dismissed.
common_false_positives: A public hearing on a zoning change where the council votes against the majority of speakers after weighing legal limits.
A workplace survey about a launched system where only the training schedule can still be changed, and the notice says so.
A design review in which the lead adopts two ideas out of thirty and keeps the rest of the plan.
discernment_questions: Do dates, contracts or announcements show when the decision was actually made compared with when you were asked?
Can anyone point to one thing that changed because of what people said?
Were you told in advance which parts were open and which were not?
If nobody had attended or answered, would the outcome have been any different?
Is the reply to objections an explanation, or a thank-you that avoids the point?
less_concerning_if: The limits on what can change are stated at the start and the process stays inside them.
A written summary shows which input was used, which was not, and the reasons.
The organizers reopen a point when someone raises a fact they had missed.
more_concerning_if: The same format is repeated on decision after decision without a single visible change.
People who object during the session are later described in the record as having supported the plan.
The consultation is held to meet a duty to consult, and its date falls after the plan became irreversible.
pattern_over_time_signs: Attendance drops at each new session because people have seen that earlier ones led nowhere.
The people who do keep speaking up are treated as difficult for expecting a response.
Final outcomes keep matching the earliest draft, whatever was said in between.
Reports cite 'extensive consultation' as a credential for decisions nobody remembers influencing.
codex_completed.repair_check: Change shows up as a seat at an earlier stage, a published account of what input did and did not alter, and at least one decision reopened. An apology that leaves next year's process the same does not count.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask in writing what remains open and who decides. A straight answer, even a disappointing one, shows respect for the question. Watch whether you get reassurance and a thank-you instead of dates and names.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Being heard calms objections even when nothing changes, and a person who took part in a process often feels more bound by its result. A consultation held after the fact can borrow that effect, and a record of attendance can later stand in for consent. Raising a late objection then feels like going back on your own word.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe effort wasted on long written submissions, followed by embarrassment at having believed it mattered. Some stop attending or answering anything. Others feel quietly implicated, as though they agreed because they showed up, and hesitate to object to the decision later.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask a neutral question before investing time: 'Which parts of this are still open, and when is the final decision being made?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say you will give input once you have been told what it can change, and that you want a written reply showing what was done with it afterward.
response_options.disengagement: Skip the survey or session if the decision is visibly final, and send a short written objection for the record instead of a performance of enthusiasm.
response_options.support_seeking: Compare notes with others who took part. If several of you saw the same fixed outcome, a joint letter or a conversation with a representative carries more weight.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Keep the dates of the invitation, the draft and the announcement. If a formal consultation duty applies, a union rep, ombuds office or regulator can tell you what was required.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Before I give feedback, which parts can still change? If you can send me the decision date, and tell me afterward what happened to the comments, I'll write something thorough."
codex_completed.safety_note: This tactic is a process problem, not a danger signal. It becomes more serious when the decision at stake involves your housing, pay, care or immigration status and a deadline to object is quietly running. In that case, find out the appeal window now and ask a tenants' union, legal aid office or employee representative about it.
misuse_warning: Calling any unwelcome decision a sham consultation dismisses leaders who listened and still disagreed. The label needs a timeline or record, not just disappointment.
Using it to refuse all later participation can leave you with no voice on the next decision, which may be a real one.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Tone policing answers your distress by calling it excessive, whereas Pseudo-Consultation answers your input with thanks and no change. Legal threats name an authority to frighten you into silence; here nobody threatens you, and the invitation to speak is the whole exchange. Only this one asks you to take part first and then points to your taking part afterward.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Tokenism
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Including one person or a small number from a group as a visible gesture, without giving them the voice or authority that inclusion seems to promise.
codex_completed.short_definition: Including one person or a small number from a group as a visible gesture, without giving them the voice or authority that inclusion seems to promise.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Tokenism is inclusion that exists mainly to be seen. One member of a group is given a title, a seat on a panel, a spot in a photograph, and then is expected to stand for everyone like them. Their presence is mentioned more often than their views are asked for. A first hire from an underrepresented group is not tokenism by itself, since every change starts somewhere. It becomes tokenism when visibility stays high and influence stays near zero, and the person's presence is offered as the answer to questions about representation.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A person holds a seat, a title or a spot in the photo that makes the group look inclusive, while their opinions carry little weight in real decisions.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Your presence gets used as the reply to the very criticism you were brought in to raise, and pushing back makes you look ungrateful for the seat. You can end up carrying the group's image while holding none of its power.
what_it_is: A single representative placed on a committee, board or team with no vote, no budget or no say in the agenda.
A person asked to speak for an entire community, as if one account covered millions of different lives.
A presence that is more visible on a website or brochure than in the meetings where decisions are made.
A role whose job description sounds senior but whose decisions are reviewed and reversed by others.
what_it_sounds_like: "We have a woman on our leadership page, so that criticism isn't fair."
"You're the only one here from that background, so what would your community think?"
A photo of the one new member of color placed at the front of the annual report.
"We'd love to have you at the table." The table has no vote for you and your suggestions are "noted."
"Look, we hired one already," said when someone asks why there are no others.
A panel invitation framed as an honor, with the speaking slot cut to five minutes.
what_it_is_not: A first step toward inclusion that is sincere and has a visible plan for more seats and more influence.
A new role whose authority is still being defined and is growing in practice.
Being asked for your perspective on something you know well, when it is one voice among many and not a stand-in for a whole group.
A small team where everyone, including the newest member, has limited influence for ordinary reasons of seniority.
An organization that says honestly what the role can and cannot decide right now.
this_may_be_it_when: The person's seat carries no vote, veto or budget, and everyone knows it.
Their presence is cited whenever representation is questioned, but their proposals are rarely adopted.
They are asked to speak for everyone like them, while colleagues are asked for individual expertise.
Nothing about who gets hired, promoted or heard has changed since they arrived.
Raising concerns about the role itself is met with reminders of how lucky they are to be included.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The person's decisions stand, and others have been added since their arrival.
They hold a real portfolio, a vote or a budget that others respect.
The organization is small, and the limited influence applies to every junior member.
A written plan lists further hires or seats with dates, and some have already happened.
The person themselves describes the role as meaningful and chose it with full knowledge of its limits.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A newly created role often needs months to earn influence, whoever fills it.
A group may have very few qualified candidates at first and be working to widen the pipeline.
Someone invited to represent a community may truly want that visibility and use it well.
common_false_positives: The only junior engineer on a team being overruled on architecture decisions, for reasons of experience and not background.
A board adding its first member from a user community and asking that member for candid advice.
A person choosing to take a public-facing ambassador role knowing it is symbolic.
discernment_questions: Can you name a decision that went a different way because of this person?
Is their presence mentioned more often than their ideas are?
Do they get the same access to information, budget and meetings as peers at their level?
Is there a visible plan for further inclusion, or does one seat stand as the whole answer?
Is this person asked as an individual expert, or as a spokesperson for an entire group?
less_concerning_if: The role's authority is stated clearly and is expanding in visible steps.
The person was consulted about the role and chose it.
Others from the same group have been brought in since.
more_concerning_if: The person's disagreement with how the role is used is treated as ingratitude.
Their name and image appear in outside messaging far more often than their work appears in decisions.
When the person leaves, the seat is left empty or refilled with no change in how decisions are made.
pattern_over_time_signs: The same single person is pictured in every brochure while their proposals vanish from the minutes.
Departures from this role repeat, each described as a surprise.
Questions about representation are met by gesturing at the existing member each time.
The person starts to downplay their own views to avoid being seen as the difficult one.
codex_completed.repair_check: A vote, a budget line or a deciding role appears that did not exist before, and a second person joins so one voice is no longer asked to carry a group. A new title or a thank-you event leaves the work untouched.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Tell them which decisions you need a hand in. Notice whether your next meeting differs: are you now on the agenda, copied on drafts, present before the decision? Praise for your contribution that comes with the same limits shows nothing changed.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A lone member of a group in a larger one tends to be noticed more and to feel watched, which can make criticism feel risky. Being offered a visible role can create gratitude and a sense of obligation, and speaking about the limits of the role can then feel like biting the hand that offered it.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People in this position describe feeling like a poster instead of a colleague, carrying pressure to speak for everyone like them, and doubt about whether their work was hired for or merely displayed. Some say they hold back criticism to protect a role they fear losing.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask what the role can decide: 'Which decisions will I have a vote or final say in, and which are advisory?' A clear answer helps either way.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to speak for a whole community, and speak only for your own experience and expertise when asked.
response_options.disengagement: Turn down appearances, photos or panels that show you in a role you do not hold, until the role itself changes.
response_options.support_seeking: Speak with others who have held similar seats elsewhere, or a mentor outside the organization, to test whether your read of the role is fair.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask for the role's authority and budget in writing, raise representation with HR or a diversity office if one exists, and keep a dated record of proposals you made and what became of them.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I can share my own experience, but I can't speak for everyone from my background. Can we agree on what I actually get to decide in this role, so my presence here counts for something?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Tokenism in itself brings no physical danger. It can carry career risk if raising it is answered with threats to your position or reference. If that begins, keep a dated record of the exchange and ask an employment lawyer, union representative or ombuds office what protection applies before you press further.
misuse_warning: Calling someone a token can wound the very person who earned the seat, and it can hide that they are doing real work. The word describes a role's design, not a person's worth.
Applying the label to any early step toward inclusion can discourage organizations that are sincerely trying.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Tone policing reframes your distress as excessive, whereas Tokenism points to your presence as proof nothing is wrong. Legal threats use authorities as leverage against you, while here the institution rewards you with visibility and withholds power. A token sits in the room and sees the decision made, but does not make it.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Individualization of Systemic Issues
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Presenting a problem caused by workload, staffing or structure as a personal weakness that the individual is expected to fix.
codex_completed.short_definition: Presenting a problem caused by workload, staffing or structure as a personal weakness that the individual is expected to fix.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Individualization of Systemic Issues treats a shared, structural problem as a private shortcoming. A team is understaffed, deadlines are unrealistic or the process is broken, and the advice offered is to manage time better, build resilience or practice self-care. Personal habits do matter, and coaching can help. The trouble is when the individual frame is the only one on offer, even though many people hit the same wall and the conditions never come up for discussion.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: When the real problem is the workload or the system, you are told to fix yourself instead: sleep more, plan better, be more resilient.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You add self-improvement to an already unsustainable load, and you conclude the shortfall is in your own resilience instead of in the conditions. Meanwhile the thing that is actually broken stays unexamined and keeps hurting the next person too.
what_it_is: Offering a wellness class, app or resilience workshop in response to a complaint about workload or staffing.
Giving advice about personal habits to someone describing a problem with the way work or services are organized.
Treating one person's struggle as a performance issue even when colleagues report the same strain.
Describing burnout, errors or lateness as traits of individuals while the policies that produce them go unreviewed.
what_it_sounds_like: "Have you tried blocking out time on your calendar?" in reply to being given three people's workload.
"Our wellness webinar on stress is Thursday, and all staff are welcome." The staffing request is not mentioned.
"Everyone else manages. Maybe it's about your boundaries."
A clinic told that waiting times are down to "patient attitudes," with no one examining appointment slots.
"We just need everyone to take more ownership of their stress levels."
A parent told the school problem would ease if the child were more motivated, though six other families report the same issue.
what_it_is_not: A skill gap that coaching really would close, offered alongside a look at the workload.
A manager who says plainly that the staffing cannot change this year, and offers help coping in the meantime. That is a limit stated honestly.
A wellness program offered in addition to, and not instead of, a review of workloads.
One person's difficulty that, when examined, is specific to their own approach and not shared by colleagues.
Advice from a friend about habits, given with no authority over your conditions.
this_may_be_it_when: Several people raise the same difficulty and each gets personal advice.
The suggested fix would not change the cause even if you followed it perfectly.
Any mention of staffing, tools or deadlines is steered back to your coping.
The same problem returns each quarter with a new training attached.
Declining the fix is read as proof that the problem is you.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The organization has reviewed the workload and shared what it found, even if little can change.
Only you struggle with this task, while peers with the same load do fine.
Personal support is offered together with a concrete change in how work is assigned.
The advice came from someone who asked about the structure first and then moved on to habits.
The problem lies in a specific skill you asked to build.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People who care often reach for advice they have found useful, without thinking about structure.
Training budgets are sometimes the only resource a manager controls, so it is what gets offered.
Some stress really is helped by sleep, exercise or planning, and mentioning them is not an accusation.
common_false_positives: A coworker with a real gap in spreadsheet skills being offered a course while the team load is reasonable.
A manager who cannot add headcount but moves deadlines and then offers a time-management workshop.
A friend suggesting you rest after a hard week, without knowing the workplace details.
discernment_questions: How many other people are facing the same problem, and what were they told?
If I did everything suggested, would the cause of the problem actually be gone?
Has anyone asked about the workload, staffing or process, or only about my coping?
Is there any acknowledgment that conditions play a part?
Does the advice help me carry the problem longer, or remove it?
less_concerning_if: The conditions are discussed openly alongside any personal advice.
The advice is optional and comes with changes to the load.
Others with the same job and load are doing well, which points to something particular about your situation.
more_concerning_if: Colleagues who report the same strain are each handled separately, so no one sees the shared pattern.
Declining the personal fix is recorded in reviews as a lack of effort or attitude.
People leave with the same story and the departures are treated as individual choices.
pattern_over_time_signs: Each cycle of complaints produces a new wellness initiative and no change in staffing or scheduling.
You start to believe the problem is your resilience, and apologize for needing a break.
Colleagues quietly compare notes and find their experiences match.
Exit interviews describe the same pressures while records list reasons as personal.
codex_completed.repair_check: Something has shifted when the workload, tools or staffing are actually examined and a change follows, with someone named as responsible for it. A second webinar or an apology for the tone of the advice leaves the load as it was.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask for the cause itself to be looked at, not just for support, and see what comes back. A response that records your request and returns with a finding is real. One that returns with another coping tip suggests the question has been set aside.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When a problem is named as yours, the natural move is to look inward for the explanation, especially when the advice sounds caring and the speaker has authority. If everyone is handled one at a time, nobody sees that others have the same trouble, so the pattern stays invisible and self-blame can deepen.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe working harder on self-care while feeling worse, a creeping sense of being the weak link, and shame about raising the issue again. Some discover that colleagues were struggling in the same way and feel anger and relief at once. Others leave the job, convinced they failed it.

response_options.soft_clarification: Separate the two layers aloud: 'Habits may help, but even with better habits this volume does not fit the hours. Can we look at the workload?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to treat a structural problem as a personal one: 'I'll try the training, but I'm not willing to record this as my own failing.'
response_options.disengagement: Step back from the self-improvement tasks that eat more of your time than the problem warrants, and protect your rest before taking on another one.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask colleagues quietly whether they hit the same wall. Three people with the same story is a far stronger case than one person asking for help.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Bring numbers, such as hours, caseloads or tickets, with a shared request from several colleagues, to a manager, union steward or health and safety committee.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'm open to tools that help, but my hours and the size of this workload aren't a personal skill issue. Can we look at what is being asked of the team before we talk about what I should change?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Prolonged overload can harm health, so this is more than an irritation when it brings chest symptoms, panic, or thoughts of not wanting to go on. Tell a doctor or counselor about the physical and emotional load, and keep a record of hours worked, since that record may matter if you later seek leave or support.
misuse_warning: Calling every piece of advice about habits 'individualization' can shut out help that is offered kindly and would actually serve you.
Treating all personal difficulty as someone else's fault can leave real skill gaps unaddressed.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Therapy-speak turns clinical vocabulary against you in a specific exchange, while this shifts attention from conditions to your coping, often with no jargon at all. Trash-can labels hand you a mental-health verdict; Individualization only suggests you need to be more resilient. Tone policing treats your distress as excessive, but here the distress is accepted and sent back to you as a problem to solve.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Diffusion of Responsibility
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Spreading a decision or a harm across so many people and steps that nobody can be found who is answerable for it.
codex_completed.short_definition: Spreading a decision or a harm across so many people and steps that nobody can be found who is answerable for it.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Diffusion of Responsibility, as an institutional pattern, is a chain in which each person can truthfully say they only did their part. One drafted it, another approved it, a third carried it out, and a fourth says it is policy from elsewhere. When harm results, tracing it leads in a circle. Large organizations really do share decisions, and shared ownership is not wrongdoing. It becomes a problem when real harm falls on someone and the search for who can fix it keeps ending at another desk.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Everyone points to someone else, so a harm that really happened has no person who owns it or can put it right.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The harm is real and nobody is answerable for it, so you have nowhere to take it, no one to ask for repair, and no way to stop it recurring. Hours go into being transferred, and the problem stays where it started.
what_it_is: A chain of approvals in which each person depends on the previous check and nobody examines the whole outcome.
Referral from desk to desk, department to department, each saying the matter belongs elsewhere.
Decisions credited to a committee, a system or a policy with no named person who can reverse them.
An outcome that everyone describes as unfortunate and nobody describes as theirs to correct.
what_it_sounds_like: "That's not my department. You'll want billing." Billing says the account team, and the account team says billing.
"I only processed what the previous team sent me."
"The system generated that letter. No one reviewed it individually."
"The committee decided. I can't speak for the committee."
"I just followed the procedure, and the procedure came from head office."
A call transferred four times, each agent saying the previous one should have handled it.
what_it_is_not: Large organizations dividing work among specialists, where someone can still tell you who owns your case.
Legitimate delegation to a person with more relevant expertise, who then answers for the result.
Honest confusion after a restructure, when staff really do not know who inherited a responsibility and are trying to find out.
A genuine referral to the correct office, which then takes the case.
A decision that many people shaped, but where a named person signs off and can explain it.
this_may_be_it_when: You have been sent to three or more different people or offices for one problem, and none claims it.
Each person describes their own step as correct, while the combined outcome is clearly harmful.
Nobody can tell you who has the authority to reverse the decision.
Asking for a name or a role title is answered with a department or a policy.
Written replies come from shared inboxes with no signature.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Someone eventually takes ownership, even after a delay, and acts on it.
The organization gives you a named contact and a timeline.
The delays follow a recent merger or staff change, and people are plainly searching for the owner.
The first office you reached was simply the wrong one, and the second was right.
A process owner explains why the outcome happened and offers a route to appeal.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Frontline staff often have no authority to override a rule, and honestly cannot help even when they want to.
After reorganizations, ownership of old processes can be unclear to everyone involved.
Specialization means no single person sees an entire process, which is a feature of size and not a concealment.
common_false_positives: A hospital routing you to the right specialist, where each one tells you the next step honestly.
A bank clerk who cannot change a fee but gives you the manager's direct line.
A group project where several people contributed and the team lead openly takes responsibility for the result.
discernment_questions: When you follow the trail, does it land on a person who can act, or does it loop?
Does every individual have a reasonable account of their own step?
Can anyone tell you who has the authority to reverse this?
Is there any effort to find the point of failure, or do people discourage you from looking?
Would an outside reviewer be able to name who could have prevented it?
less_concerning_if: A named owner or escalation route is given when you ask.
The organization acknowledges the gap and says who is looking into it.
The runaround ends within a reasonable period and the problem is resolved.
more_concerning_if: The loop persists after you have documented each referral and asked for a decision-maker by role.
The harm falls on you in ways you cannot absorb, such as lost pay, lost benefits or missed deadlines.
Staff who try to help are discouraged from naming who is responsible.
pattern_over_time_signs: The same kind of problem recurs for other customers, patients or staff with the same dead ends.
Each time it surfaces, the response is a new apology from a different person who has no authority to act.
Records show a decision was approved by many and authored by none.
People stop complaining because the effort of tracing the problem exceeds what it cost them.
codex_completed.repair_check: A named person takes the case, says what they will do and by when, and the fix is made. A sympathetic call from someone who cannot change anything, or a promise to pass the complaint along, does not count.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask for a single owner by name and a date for the next step. See whether you get both. Notice if the reply restates the process in more detail instead, which leaves your question unanswered.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When many people each hold a small share of a decision, each can feel the outcome is not really theirs, and each check may be treated as someone else's safety net. On the receiving end, repeated transfers tend to wear down persistence, and the effort of tracing the problem can end up larger than the problem.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe retelling their story to a fifth stranger, losing days to hold queues, and a growing sense that they are shouting into a wall. Some give up and absorb the cost. Others turn their anger on individual staff who are as powerless as they are.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask each person who you reach one question: 'Who is the person who can decide this, and can you give me their name or role title?'
response_options.firm_boundary: State that you will keep one written thread open until someone with authority takes ownership, and ask for a reference number to quote each time.
response_options.disengagement: Pause the phone calls, which leave no record, and move to email or letters so each referral is on paper before you invest more time.
response_options.support_seeking: Take the log of who said what to an ombuds office, a consumer or patient advocate, or an elected representative's caseworker, who can often find the owner you cannot.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Within an organization, ask for the process owner or the approving manager for the decision by role, and request a written account of how the decision was reached.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I understand that your step was done correctly. I still need the name or job title of the person who has the authority to reverse this, and I'll keep a written record of each person who points me elsewhere."
codex_completed.safety_note: The runaround itself is not dangerous, but the stakes can be. Where the harm affects medication, benefits, housing or a legal deadline, the clock matters more than finding the owner. Contact a patient advocate, legal aid or the relevant regulator for the deadline first, and chase the responsible person second.
misuse_warning: Assuming a bureaucratic runaround was arranged can make you hostile to staff who are as stuck as you are. The pattern is about structure, and it does not reveal anyone's motives.
Calling every referral a dodge can overlook the real case where you were sent to the right place.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Legal threats name an authority to frighten you, whereas Diffusion of Responsibility gives you no one to address, threatening or otherwise. Tone policing meets your distress with a person who calls it excessive; here no single person stays long enough to say anything. Therapy-speak needs a speaker using clinical words, but this runaround often involves none at all.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Deepfakes
codex_completed.detectability_note: This is an evidence-and-reporting matter, not a phrasing question. This tool cannot verify media, hacks, or fabricated content, and does not assign it a severity score. If this is happening to you, the practical steps are preservation and reporting, not text analysis.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Fabricated images, video or audio made to show a real person doing or saying something they never did.
codex_completed.short_definition: Fabricated images, video or audio made to show a real person doing or saying something they never did.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A deepfake is media made or altered with software so that it shows a real person in a situation that never happened: a face placed on another body, a mouth made to speak new words, or a staged scene that looks recorded. It is used to humiliate, extort, defraud or damage a reputation. A polished look proves nothing either way. What matters is whether the person shown, and independent records, say it happened.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A fake picture, video or recording that looks real and shows you doing or saying something you never did. How real it looks is not a reliable test.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The target is left disproving something that never happened, to people who have already seen it, and a denial can sound like what anyone caught would say. Shame and speed of sharing do much of the damage.
what_it_is: A fabricated image, clip or recording of a real person, made so it passes as a genuine record.
Often sexual when aimed at private individuals, which makes it a form of intimate-image abuse even though no such photo was ever taken.
Also used in fraud, such as a fake video of a trusted figure, and in smear campaigns against public figures.
Harmful through belief and spread, not quality: a rough fake can still travel far among people ready to believe it.
Set apart from ordinary editing by presenting invented events as unaltered reality.
what_it_sounds_like: A clip or image of you circulating that shows a place, act or statement you know never occurred.
People you know reacting to something you have no memory of, and asking why you did it.
A sexual image carrying your face that you never posed for, posted to a forum or sent to your contacts.
A message demanding money, more images or silence, with a sample of the fabricated media attached as a reminder of what could be shared.
A video with no original upload, no named source, and a caption urging viewers to pass it along quickly.
Audio in your voice saying words you have never said, or a face and mouth that look slightly out of step, though a good fake may show neither flaw.
Posters who answer questions about where the footage came from with insults instead of a source.
what_it_is_not: Genuine footage that shows something embarrassing. Unflattering is not fake, and a real recording calls for a different response.
Satire or parody clearly labeled as such, where viewers are not meant to take it as a record.
Ordinary retouching, filters, color correction or dubbing that the person knowingly agreed to.
A low-resolution clip that looks strange because of how it was saved and re-shared many times.
A real photo with a false caption, where nothing was synthesized but the framing misleads.
A lookalike or impersonator filmed in real life, which is a different problem from synthetic media.
this_may_be_it_when: You can show where you were at the time, and the media claims otherwise.
The content has no original source and first appeared on a new or anonymous account.
It arrived with a demand, a deadline, or a threat to send it to people you know.
A sexual image uses your face, but the body, room or marks on it do not match your own.
People who know you well say it does not look or sound like you, but cannot say why.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You remember being filmed or photographed and can recall the occasion.
The original file can be traced to a device that you or a friend used.
The person who shared it names a real source and takes it down when asked.
The media is clearly labeled as software-made and nobody presents it as real.
Your only reason for doubt is that the content is upsetting to see.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Heavy compression, filters and poor lighting can make genuine faces look waxy or odd.
A relative or coworker may forward a clip in alarm without any idea it is fake.
A joke made with an app among friends can later spread beyond the group without anyone planning that.
Video-call glitches and dropped frames distort faces in real recordings.
common_false_positives: A real clip of a public figure that viewers dislike and therefore call fake.
A dubbed or translated video where the lip movements do not match the new language.
A film or game character built with openly disclosed digital effects.
A genuine voice note with static or clipped words.
discernment_questions: Can I show, from my own records, where I was and what I was doing at the time the media claims?
Is there an original upload, or only copies of copies?
Who first posted it, and what did that account post before?
Is anyone using it to demand something from me?
Am I judging it by how real it looks, which is no longer a safe test?
less_concerning_if: It is labeled as altered and nobody is presenting it as a record.
The person shown agreed to it and knows where it will appear.
It has stayed within a small group, and its maker removed it when asked.
more_concerning_if: It is sexual, or comes paired with a demand for money, images or silence.
It is being sent to your employer, family or school.
Copies reappear on new accounts after takedowns.
pattern_over_time_signs: New versions of the media appear, each posted on a different site or account.
Strangers write to you about content you have not seen.
Friends and coworkers begin treating you differently without saying why.
You search for your own name or face every day and dread the next find.
codex_completed.repair_check: Whether anything improved shows in what comes down and stays down: the media removed from the sites that host it, the account closed, and the maker naming themselves and ending any demands. An apology while copies still circulate repairs nothing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Did the demands or new postings stop after you reported, or only change accounts? A pause that ends when attention moves elsewhere is not the same as the matter being closed.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Eyes and ears get believed before anyone asks where a clip came from, so a realistic fake lands as proof before any thinking starts. Once viewers have seen it, a denial may sound like what anyone caught would say. Shame, fear of exposure and the speed of sharing can push targets toward silence or compliance, which is part of what gives the fabrication its force.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe shock at seeing their own face or voice used, shame they did not earn, dread about who has seen it, and trouble sleeping or going to work or school. Some pull back from social media, friends or public life. Others describe steadier footing once they had a report number, a lawyer or a friend on their side.

response_options.soft_clarification: If someone you trust has seen it, tell them plainly that it is fabricated and that you can show where you were. Then ask them not to forward it.
response_options.firm_boundary: Do not bargain with anyone demanding something in exchange for keeping it private. Keep the demand as it was sent and hand it to the people handling your report.
response_options.disengagement: Stop replying to the sender. Before blocking anyone, save the messages, links and dates so there is a record.
response_options.support_seeking: StopNCII.org and Take It Down are hash-matching services that help block known intimate images on participating platforms. Ask whether they can take your case, and contact a victim advocate or legal aid about options where you live.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If it reaches work or school, give HR or an administrator a short factual note with links and dates and ask for a named contact. You do not have to describe the content in detail.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "This is fabricated media of me. I have saved the links, the dates and every message about it. I am asking you to remove it and to tell me what happens next."
codex_completed.safety_note: Fabricated sexual images, demands for money, and threats to send material to family or an employer are danger signals, as is anyone who seems to know where you live or work. Save everything unaltered, tell someone you trust, and contact a victim advocate, legal aid or a police cybercrime unit. If you fear for your physical safety, call emergency services.
misuse_warning: Calling an unflattering but genuine recording a deepfake is a way of discrediting real evidence, including a real victim's.
Declaring a clip fake from how it looks alone can wrongly accuse an innocent poster and leave the actual question untested.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: AI Voice Cloning fakes sound only, and often arrives as a live call or voice note asking for money; a deepfake fabricates sight, with or without sound. Doxxing publishes things that are true and private, such as an address, while a deepfake invents something false. Sock Puppets invent people who do not exist, not an invented version of a real one.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted text cannot verify or authenticate forensic/evidentiary claims — that requires the actual technical evidence, not conversational text.

codex_completed.name: AI Voice Cloning
codex_completed.detectability_note: This is an evidence-and-reporting matter, not a phrasing question. This tool cannot verify media, hacks, or fabricated content, and does not assign it a severity score. If this is happening to you, the practical steps are preservation and reporting, not text analysis.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Software-made copies of a real person's voice, used to impersonate them in calls, messages or recordings.
codex_completed.short_definition: Software-made copies of a real person's voice, used to impersonate them in calls, messages or recordings.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: AI voice cloning is the use of software to produce speech that sounds like a specific real person, built from recordings of them. It appears as an urgent call from a relative, a voice note from a boss, or a recording offered as proof of what someone said. A familiar sound no longer shows who is speaking. The pattern to notice is a trusted voice paired with pressure to act fast or keep quiet.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A computer-made copy of someone's voice that can say things they never said. It may sound exactly like a person you trust, so the sound alone proves nothing.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A voice you have trusted all your life stops being evidence of anything, and checking each unexpected call through a second channel becomes a permanent tax on ordinary contact. People can lose money or be blamed for words they never spoke.
what_it_is: Speech generated by software to imitate one particular person, including their pitch, pacing and accent.
Used in phone scams where the caller sounds like a child, parent or boss in trouble and asks for money or codes.
Also used to produce fake recordings of someone supposedly confessing, threatening or agreeing, to damage them or win a dispute.
Convincing enough that people who know the person well can be fooled, so a trusted-sounding voice is no longer a safe test.
Different from a human impersonator, because it is software producing the voice rather than a person doing an impression.
what_it_sounds_like: A call in a voice that sounds like a relative's, describing an emergency that needs money right now.
A voice note from a boss or colleague asking for gift cards, a transfer or a login code, outside their usual habits.
A caller who resists being phoned back, or insists you stay on the line and tell no one.
The real person, reached another way, knowing nothing about the call.
A recording of someone supposedly admitting something, with no date, no setting and no one else on it.
Flat emotion, odd pauses or repeated phrasing in an otherwise convincing voice, though a clone may show none of these.
A voice-only request from someone who normally writes.
what_it_is_not: A real call from a real person who is stressed, ill or in a noisy place and so sounds unlike themselves.
A human impression or prank by someone with a good ear.
An openly labeled automated voice, such as a clinic's appointment reminder.
A bad phone line, compression or Bluetooth echo that distorts a genuine voice.
A genuine recording that is unwelcome. Hearing yourself say something you regret is not proof it was cloned.
A voice copy that a person agreed to and disclosed, for example for audiobooks or accessibility.
this_may_be_it_when: The voice is familiar, but the request is unlike anything this person has ever asked.
Urgency and secrecy arrive together: pay now and tell nobody.
The payment route is hard to trace or reverse, such as gift cards, crypto or a wire.
The person cannot be reached by their usual means while the call is happening.
The caller dodges a question that only the real person could answer.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You phoned back on a number you already had and the same person answered.
The request matches what this person has done before, through their usual channel.
Someone who is physically with them confirms the situation.
The caller is fine with delay and welcomes you checking.
The voice sounds different because they are known to be sick, traveling or somewhere loud.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A cold or exhaustion can change a voice a great deal.
People calling from a borrowed phone, a hospital or a station can sound and act unlike themselves.
Family emergencies are real, and a frightened relative may truly ask for money.
Voicemail systems and cheap earbuds flatten voices.
common_false_positives: A friend who sounds robotic on a patchy connection.
An automated voice from a bank or clinic, openly announced as automated.
A relative who asks for help in an odd way because they are embarrassed.
A comedian or actor doing a recognizable impression.
discernment_questions: If I hang up and call this person back on a number I already had, who answers?
Does anyone else who knows them know about this?
Am I being rushed, and told not to tell anyone?
Could I be sure of this voice if I could not see who was speaking?
How is the money supposed to move, and could I get it back?
less_concerning_if: You reached the person on a known number and they confirmed the call.
Nothing about money, codes or secrecy is asked.
The request fits the person's normal habits and channel.
more_concerning_if: The speaker asks for money or codes and says you must not call anyone.
A recording is used as proof against someone, with no known origin.
The same voice shows up making demands to several people in one family or office.
pattern_over_time_signs: Calls or voice notes keep arriving in familiar voices, small asks first and bigger ones later.
Relatives report similar calls that none of them can trace to the real person.
You catch yourself unsure whether to trust even genuine calls from people you love.
A recording attributed to you gets cited in a dispute, and each retelling treats it as settled.
codex_completed.repair_check: Practical steps show repair: the number or account shut down, the bank freezing or reversing a transfer where it can, and everyone who was called told that it was not the real person. Anyone calling it a misunderstanding while the money is still gone has repaired nothing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: When you say you will call back on a number you already have, watch what the caller does. A real person welcomes the check. Pressure to stay on the line is the pattern showing itself.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A familiar voice tends to bypass doubt because we link it to people we love and trust, and a panicked tone can narrow thinking to the emergency in front of us. Urgency, secrecy and fear of being the one who did not help can push people to act before they check. Embarrassment afterward often keeps people from telling anyone.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A drop in the stomach on hearing a loved one in apparent danger is common, followed by shame or anger at oneself after learning it was false. Some people lose savings. Others start doubting real calls or avoid answering the phone. Someone whose voice was copied may feel violated that something so personal was taken.

response_options.soft_clarification: Tell the caller you are going to phone back on the number you already have, then do it. A genuine caller can wait a minute.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to send money, codes or sensitive details on a call you did not start, however urgent it sounds. Say it will be handled through your usual channel.
response_options.disengagement: Hang up and check with the person, or someone near them, by another route. Do not stay on a line that insists you keep going.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell your bank right away if money moved, report the call to the police or your country's fraud reporting service, and let family know so they can be careful.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a voice message from an executive asks for payment or credentials, confirm with that person by a separate known route and report it to your security or finance team.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "A voice is not proof. Before I send anything, I am going to hang up, call this person back on the number I already have, and ask someone who is near them whether any of this is true."
codex_completed.safety_note: Cloned voices are used to claim a relative is in danger and to push money out of savings. If you hear a threat to someone you love, confirm they are safe through a separate channel first. Then contact your bank and the police or a fraud service, and legal aid if a recording is used in a custody, protective order or employment dispute. Call emergency services if anyone is in immediate danger.
misuse_warning: Calling any awkward recording a voice clone can discredit genuine evidence, including a real victim's.
Telling a relative who really phoned for help that they must be a fake can leave a true emergency unanswered. The label calls for a check, not a refusal.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Deepfakes fabricate how someone looks and may also carry their voice; voice cloning is sound only and often arrives as a live call. Sock Puppets are invented personas with no real person behind them, whereas a clone borrows one real person's voice. Doxxing publishes true private details instead of faking a speaker.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted text cannot verify or authenticate forensic/evidentiary claims — that requires the actual technical evidence, not conversational text.

codex_completed.name: Doxxing
codex_completed.detectability_note: This is an evidence-and-reporting matter, not a phrasing question. This tool cannot verify media, hacks, or fabricated content, and does not assign it a severity score. If this is happening to you, the practical steps are preservation and reporting, not text analysis.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Publishing a person's private details, such as a home address or workplace, so others can find or harass them.
codex_completed.short_definition: Publishing a person's private details, such as a home address or workplace, so others can find or harass them.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Doxxing is the release of personal information that was not meant to be public: a home address, phone number, employer, a child's school, or the real name behind an anonymous account. The details often arrive with a hostile story about the person. The exposure itself is the harm, since details once public cannot be fully recalled. Gathering findable facts into one profile can be harmful even if each fact alone was easy to find.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone posts your private details, like where you live or work, where strangers can see them, so you are easier to find and bother.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Risk moves offline and out of your hands: your home, workplace and family become reachable by strangers who have no tie to the original dispute, and the exposure cannot be fully undone.
what_it_is: Posting a home address, phone number, workplace, school or a relative's name where strangers will see it.
Linking an anonymous account to a real name, which can end the safety that anonymity gave.
Combining facts that were each findable alone into one profile, which changes what they can be used for.
Usually paired with a story that casts the person as deserving of anger, so readers feel invited to act.
Set apart from criticism because it targets where a person can be reached, not what they said.
what_it_sounds_like: A post that lists your address, employer or family names beside an angry account of something you are said to have done.
Strangers messaging or phoning you about a dispute, using your real name.
Deliveries, calls or visitors you did not request arriving at your home or workplace.
A thread where people trade more details about you and congratulate each other for finding them.
Your real name suddenly attached to an account you kept anonymous.
A photo of your house or street shared with a comment.
An employer or landlord receiving complaints that name you right after an online dispute.
what_it_is_not: Information you chose to make public, such as your own business address on your website.
Naming a public official in connection with their public role, where office contact details are listed openly for that purpose.
A news report that names someone and describes a public act without personal contact details.
A neighbor knowing where you live, or a friend mentioning your employer to someone who also knows you.
Harsh criticism of your public statements or work.
A court or property record that has always been public. It can feel invasive, but its existence is not an invitation to harass.
this_may_be_it_when: The details were private until a dispute began.
The post pairs them with a call to contact or confront you.
Strangers start reaching you in places you never shared with them.
Your anonymous name and your real name are now linked in public.
Family members or an employer are named, not just you.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The detail is one you posted publicly yourself.
It is a business listing or a public office contact.
There is no hostile framing and no sign anyone is acting on it.
It was shared privately with someone you trust and went no further.
The poster removes it promptly when asked.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A friend may mention your workplace online without realizing it is sensitive.
A tagged photo can reveal your location without anyone having chosen to expose you.
Data brokers and public records may hold your details long before any dispute.
Local news or a school newsletter may name you in a routine way.
common_false_positives: Your business address appearing on a review site.
A tagged check-in that you or a friend posted.
A harsh review of your business under the business's own name.
A spam call from a marketer who bought a contact list.
discernment_questions: Was this detail private before, or have I shared it somewhere myself?
Is it paired with anger or an invitation to contact me?
Are strangers reaching me in ways that follow the posting?
Which details could be used to find me physically, and who else has them?
Is anyone in my household or workplace now exposed too?
less_concerning_if: The detail is already printed in a public place that you chose.
No stranger has contacted you about it, by message, phone or in person.
The poster took it down when you asked.
more_concerning_if: Your home address, a child's school or your daily routine are shown.
People are being urged to visit, call or report you.
The details reappear on new sites after removal.
pattern_over_time_signs: Contact from strangers comes in waves tied to new posts.
More details about you surface over weeks, as if someone keeps adding to a file.
You change routines: routes, hours, phone numbers, social media.
People you know ask whether you are okay after seeing a thread about you.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair shows in what is removed and stays removed: the post and its copies taken down, the publisher confirming in writing that nothing further is kept, and the contact from strangers dying off. An apology while the thread stays up does not count.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: After you report, does the contact slow, or does fresh content turn up on other accounts? Whether the listing stays down is a better measure than anything said to you.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Exposure tends to turn an online dispute into a physical-world worry. Once a person knows strangers could find their door, ordinary acts like answering the phone or walking home can feel risky. Crowds can also spread responsibility thin: each stranger does a small thing and nobody feels like the cause of the whole, which can leave the target feeling watched by everyone.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe fear at home, checking windows and cars, changing numbers, altering children's routines, and dreading every unknown caller. Some take time off work, go offline or move. Others describe shame at being found, or anger that a private life was made public.

response_options.soft_clarification: If a friend or relative may have shared a detail without thinking, ask them privately to remove it, and ask anyone who tagged you to do the same.
response_options.firm_boundary: Report each post to the platform and to the site host, pointing to the page that shows your private details. Ask for removal of the information, not a debate.
response_options.disengagement: Do not reply to the thread or to strangers who contact you. Save what arrives with dates, then limit who can reach you on each account.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone you trust and a victim advocate where the post is, so a second person can help watch. If threats appear, contact the police and, where available, a legal aid clinic.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Alert your employer's security or HR team early so the front desk or phone line is ready for odd calls, and give them a short factual note rather than the thread itself.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "This page shows my home address and workplace, which I never made public. I have saved the link and the date. I am asking that it be removed, and for help reporting any related posts."
codex_completed.safety_note: A home address, a child's school or a daily routine appearing online is a safety signal, as are threats, strangers arriving in person, or anyone who seems to track your movements. Save everything, tell the people you live with, and contact the police and a victim advocate. If someone is at your door or you fear immediate harm, call emergency services.
misuse_warning: Calling a public figure's openly listed office contact doxxing can shield them from legitimate accountability.
Posting someone's details to expose a supposed wrongdoer is the harm itself, whoever the target is and however sure the poster feels.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Deepfakes invent something false about you, while doxxing publishes something true and private. Stalking-by-Notification is watching your online activity and building a case from it, typically by one person, while doxxing hands your location to many. Coordinated Reporting targets your account, while doxxing exposes your doorstep.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted text cannot verify or authenticate forensic/evidentiary claims — that requires the actual technical evidence, not conversational text.

codex_completed.name: Sock Puppets
codex_completed.detectability_note: This is an evidence-and-reporting matter, not a phrasing question. This tool cannot verify media, hacks, or fabricated content, and does not assign it a severity score. If this is happening to you, the practical steps are preservation and reporting, not text analysis.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Fake accounts run by one person or a small group to pass as independent people, creating false agreement or pile-ons.
codex_completed.short_definition: Fake accounts run by one person or a small group to pass as independent people, creating false agreement or pile-ons.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A sock puppet is an account that looks like an independent person but is controlled by someone else, often the same person behind other accounts. Several of them can make a view look widely held, cheer on an argument, vouch for a story, or swarm a target. The deception lies in the appearance of separate people. A single odd account proves little. What stands out is a group that seems independent but behaves as one.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: One person pretending to be many. The accounts seem unconnected, but the crowd of agreement or attack is smaller than it looks.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You argue against what looks like a consensus and decide you are the outlier, when the numbers on the other side were never real. The same trick can make a pile-on feel like the verdict of many.
what_it_is: Accounts presenting as separate people but directed by the same hand.
Used to cheer for one side, back up a person's story, or pile on a target so that a crowd appears.
Often built to look ordinary, with a plausible name, a photo and everyday posts, so the account itself reveals little.
Different from an openly run brand account or a person's disclosed second account.
Harmful through false social proof: you read the numbers as other people's real opinions.
what_it_sounds_like: Several new accounts with thin histories appearing together under a post to defend one person.
Replies that echo the same unusual phrase or talking point within minutes.
Accounts that praise or back each other and rarely talk to anyone else.
A witness who turns up to confirm a story and has no posts before the dispute.
Generic or stock-looking profile photos and handles ending in long strings of digits.
A set of accounts that are all active at the same odd hours.
A new account that knows details of a private argument it should not have seen.
what_it_is_not: Real people who share an opinion and post around the same time because a news story or a famous account prompted them.
A person's disclosed alternate accounts, such as a work account and a personal one.
A group openly organizing supporters under its real name.
New accounts made by people who joined just to follow a breaking event.
A fan community whose members repeat the same slogans and memes.
Automated bot accounts, which can look similar but are not one person pretending to be many.
this_may_be_it_when: Accounts claiming to be strangers show matching phrasing, timing and topics.
A cluster appears the day a conflict starts and vanishes after it.
They never post about anything else.
An account's claims about the dispute contain inside details.
When one is challenged, another steps in with near-identical wording.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The accounts have long, varied histories and talk with many other people.
Their views differ in detail and tone.
The people can be reached and are known offline.
The support is openly announced by an organization.
