The only evidence is that you disagree with them or that there are many.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Members of one community often share slang and arrive together when a link is passed around.
People open new accounts after losing a password or leaving a platform.
Privacy-minded users often keep sparse profiles as a safety habit.
A viral post sends a surge of newcomers to the same thread.
common_false_positives: A fan group rallying after a post by a celebrity.
A company's official accounts posting together, openly.
A person with a main account and a clearly labeled hobby account.
Strangers who agree with you for their own reasons.
discernment_questions: Do these accounts have lives beyond this dispute?
Is the wording alike in ways a shared news story would not explain?
Would I think differently if only two or three voices were saying this?
Did they appear only when this conflict began?
Am I judging them by their opinions, or by their behavior?
less_concerning_if: The accounts have long, varied histories and reply to many unrelated people.
Differences in opinion and style show up among them.
An organization claims the group and names itself.
more_concerning_if: They are used to push a target out or to make threats while appearing unrelated.
Accounts return under new names after being removed.
They quote private information about the person they target.
pattern_over_time_signs: New accounts keep arriving with the same argument whenever the issue returns.
The mass of support or attack drops to nothing once a decision date passes.
The agreement seems to come from a different crowd each time but sounds the same.
You begin to doubt your own views because everyone online seems to disagree.
codex_completed.repair_check: When one operator is found out, repair would mean closing the extra accounts, saying openly that one person ran them, and retracting what they claimed. A fresh batch of accounts after a public apology shows the opposite.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Check whether the pile-on thins after you report or mute, or whether fresh accounts take the same place. A crowd of separate individuals tends to drift away; a staged one tends to be replaced.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Other people's apparent views serve as a guide to what is normal and safe to say, so several seeming strangers agreeing may read as evidence. A crowd also tends to leave a target feeling isolated and outnumbered, and to push bystanders toward silence or the majority side. Since each account looks separate, spotting the link takes effort most readers do not spend.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Feeling outnumbered is a common description, along with doubting a view once held, withdrawing from a forum, or reading a pile-on as proof of being widely disliked when it came from few people. Some feel anger on learning the crowd was thin, and some grow distrustful of every new account that agrees with them.

response_options.soft_clarification: Before answering a crowd, look at whether the accounts have histories and whether their wording matches. A plain question such as whether you have talked before can show a lot.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to argue with accounts you cannot place. Say what you think once, in your own space, and do not answer each reply.
response_options.disengagement: Mute, block or limit replies on the thread and step away until the wave passes. Answering a swarm can feed it.
response_options.support_seeking: Show a few examples to a friend who knows the dispute, or to a moderator or reporter, so a second pair of eyes can say whether the pattern looks real.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If this targets your business or role, collect dated examples, report them through the platform's channel for fake accounts, and tell your communications lead.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Before I react to this crowd: do these accounts have lives of their own, or did they all arrive together? Would I think differently if only three people were saying it?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Sock puppets alone are usually a distortion and a nuisance, not a physical danger. That changes when the accounts threaten you, share your personal details, or show up in your real-world life. Then save screenshots with links and dates, report to the platform, and speak to a victim advocate or the police.
misuse_warning: Calling anyone who disagrees with you a sock puppet dismisses real people and can end an honest discussion.
Naming a particular person as the operator behind accounts, from similar writing alone, can wrongly accuse an innocent user.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Coordinated Reporting uses a crowd, real or fake, that complains in private to a platform; sock puppets speak in public to fake a crowd. Deepfakes fake a real person's actions, while sock puppets fake the existence of other people. Doxxing uses real details about you; a sock puppet's persona is invented.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted text cannot verify or authenticate forensic/evidentiary claims — that requires the actual technical evidence, not conversational text.

codex_completed.name: Fabricated Evidence
codex_completed.detectability_note: This is an evidence-and-reporting matter, not a phrasing question. This tool cannot verify media, hacks, or fabricated content, and does not assign it a severity score. If this is happening to you, the practical steps are preservation and reporting, not text analysis.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Presenting made-up or altered messages, images or documents as genuine proof of something that did not happen or was not said.
codex_completed.short_definition: Presenting made-up or altered messages, images or documents as genuine proof of something that did not happen or was not said.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Fabricated evidence is material that looks like a record but is not one: an edited message thread, a screenshot of a conversation that never took place, a changed date or a forged document, offered as proof. Forged screenshots is simply another name for this: a faked image of a message is one kind of fabricated record. Screenshots are often treated as settled proof, which is why a fake can carry weight. It differs from a real record taken out of context, because here the item itself is not authentic. It is usually shown to a third party, so the harm falls on your credibility.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone shows others a screenshot or document that looks real but was made up or changed, and presents it as proof of something you never wrote, said or did.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Screenshots and documents are widely accepted as proof, so disproving a fake means asking people to doubt evidence they normally trust. Meanwhile your own account can start to look like the lie, and the harm can reach work, school or court before anyone checks the item.
what_it_is: A message, image or document that looks like a record but was edited, assembled or invented, then presented as authentic.
Either a full invention, such as a conversation that never took place, or an alteration of something real, such as a changed word, name, date or amount.
Usually shown to a third party, such as friends, an employer, a school, a platform or a court, and not to you.
Often introduced with a phrase like 'I have receipts', which asks for trust in the look of the thing and not in what it contains.
Found in breakups, custody and workplace disputes, online feuds and disputes with institutions, wherever a record could decide whose account is believed.
It concerns whether the record itself is genuine, which is different from whether someone remembers events correctly.
what_it_sounds_like: 'Here are the receipts', followed by a screenshot of words you have no memory of writing.
A thread shown to your employer or friends that does not match the same conversation on your own phone.
A message under your name, with phrasing or punctuation you never use.
Timestamps, contact names or dates that do not fit when you were actually in touch, or an app layout that does not match the app it claims to come from.
A screenshot with no way to see the surrounding messages, and a refusal to produce the original phone or an export.
A document that cites an agreement, policy or payment you have never seen or signed.
'I don't need to show you the original. The picture says it all.'
what_it_is_not: A real screenshot cropped for brevity, with its meaning intact. Cropping is not forging.
Confusion about which conversation or time frame an image comes from. People mix up threads constantly.
Authentic images that look different because of another device, language setting or app update.
A genuine message quoted out of context. That can mislead, but the record itself is real, which is a different problem from invented content.
A sincere misremembering of what was written, from someone who shows what they honestly believe the message said.
A real record with a phone number or name blacked out for privacy, labeled as such, with the rest untouched.
this_may_be_it_when: The record contradicts your own copy of the same conversation in wording, order or dates.
The phrasing is unlike your own, or it mentions events you never took part in.
Only an image is offered, never the original device, account export or file.
Neither the platform nor anyone else can match the item to a real message.
The item appears just as a decision is being made about you, such as a hearing, review or breakup.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Your own copy of the thread, once you look, matches it.
The difference is a cropped section or a missing earlier message, not changed words.
The platform's own export confirms the messages and dates.
The person who sent it also shares the original and invites you to compare.
The odd formatting is explained by a different phone, language setting or app version.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Memory of an old exchange is often worse than people expect, and a real thread can surprise the person who wrote it.
Messages can come from an old or shared account or device and be forgotten.
Someone who received a forwarded screenshot may repeat it, believing it genuine.
Apps display the same message differently across devices, time zones and language settings.
common_false_positives: A screenshot that looks wrong only because it is cropped on a small screen.
A real message you sent while upset or tired and no longer recall.
A document retyped or reformatted to fit a form, with the same content.
discernment_questions: Do I have my own copy of the same conversation, and does it match word for word?
Can the original be checked on the device, account or platform it is said to come from?
Do the names, times and layout fit the app and the date claimed?
Does the wording sound like how I write, and does it mention things I could not have known?
Who is the item being shown to, and what decision is it meant to influence?
Was anyone else in this conversation who could confirm it?
less_concerning_if: The original can be opened and checked, and it matches what you were shown.
The person corrects the record when shown your copy.
The disagreement is about what a real message meant, not whether it was written.
more_concerning_if: The item is used in a formal complaint, a custody or protective-order matter, or to get you dismissed or shut out of a group.
More than one doubtful item has appeared, or accounts that would hold the originals have become unavailable to you.
The other person has had access to your phone, accounts or cloud backups.
pattern_over_time_signs: More than one doubtful item appears, each shown to a different audience.
Records that could settle the matter, such as old messages, vanish or become unavailable.
Your standing with mutual friends, a workplace or a school drops without your knowing what was said.
You begin exporting or photographing your own conversations regularly to protect yourself.
codex_completed.repair_check: Correction here looks like paperwork: the item withdrawn from everyone who saw it, the original produced and compared, and the audience told it was not genuine. An apology to you alone, while the fake stays in circulation, leaves the damage where it was.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask in writing, calmly, to see the original. Does it appear, can a neutral person examine it, or does the talk move to how you reacted? Whether the item can be examined is the test, not how confident anyone sounds.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A record-shaped object earns trust quickly, and a screenshot has the air of a witness who cannot be argued with. Third parties often have no way to check it, so the first version they see can set their view. The person it targets may start doubting their own memory, which can make the fake feel more believable.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe shock at reading words attributed to them, then a scramble to prove a negative. Some lose standing at work, with friends or in a legal matter before anyone checks the item. Others describe doubting their memory, going silent to avoid more material, and feeling that being believed has turned into a technical problem.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask to see the record in the app it came from, not as an image: 'Can we open that conversation on the phone it came from?' A genuine record can usually survive that request.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to argue about the item with the person who produced it, and move the question to a neutral reviewer, such as a platform, a mediator or HR, who can compare originals.
response_options.disengagement: Stop replying about the item, delete nothing on your side, and do not repost the fake to disprove it, since that spreads it further. Save it with its source and date.
response_options.support_seeking: Bring your saved originals and the suspect item to a lawyer, legal aid clinic or victim services advocate, and ask how originals are authenticated.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If it reached your employer or school, give HR or the conduct office your own export with dates, and ask in writing that the item be checked against originals before anything is decided.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "That does not match my records of this conversation. I have the original with its dates saved, and I'd ask that whoever decides this look at both side by side before drawing a conclusion."
codex_completed.safety_note: A fabricated record used in a custody dispute, a protective-order hearing, a workplace complaint or a threat of exposure can cost you housing, income, children or safety, so treat it as a legal matter and not as an argument. Save originals with their dates, delete nothing, and speak to a lawyer or legal aid before replying to the person who produced it. If you fear for your safety, an advocate can help you plan.
misuse_warning: Calling a damaging screenshot fake is the same move reversed: a real record can be disowned with the word 'forged'. Ask for the original, not a verdict.
Telling others that a named person forged something, without evidence, is itself an accusation. Describe which details do not match instead.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Lying is a false statement in someone's own voice. Fabricated evidence is a false object that borrows the authority of a record, so it can be passed to others and outlive the conversation. Lying by Omission invents nothing and leaves out a piece of a true story. Vague Allegations point to unnamed critics or unspecified accusations with nothing to inspect, while fabricated evidence supplies something concrete to inspect that turns out not to be authentic.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted text cannot verify or authenticate forensic/evidentiary claims — that requires the actual technical evidence, not conversational text.

codex_completed.name: Coordinated Reporting
codex_completed.detectability_note: This is an evidence-and-reporting matter, not a phrasing question. This tool cannot verify media, hacks, or fabricated content, and does not assign it a severity score. If this is happening to you, the practical steps are preservation and reporting, not text analysis.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Organized mass reporting of an account or post, often on false grounds, to get a platform to remove or restrict it.
codex_completed.short_definition: Organized mass reporting of an account or post, often on false grounds, to get a platform to remove or restrict it.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Coordinated reporting is the use of a platform's report buttons by many people at once to get someone suspended, demonetized or removed, whether or not a rule was broken. Platforms may treat the number of reports as a signal, so volume can stand in for evidence. Many honest reports about a real violation are not this. What marks it is organization, a mismatch between the reports and the content, and a target who cannot see why.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Many people file complaints about the same account at the same time, not because of a real problem but to get it shut down.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You can lose your account, your audience or your income through a system built to protect people, and appeals against decisions made on volume can be slow and hard to reach.
what_it_is: Many reports against one account or post, filed close together, often citing a rule the content does not break.
Organized in a group chat, thread or list where people are told whom to report.
Aimed at creators, activists, small sellers and ordinary users, sometimes after they criticized someone.
Can rest on false claims such as spam, impersonation or harm.
Different from legitimate reporting, where independent people flag real violations and the content matches the complaint.
what_it_sounds_like: A sudden warning, strike or suspension arriving right after a public dispute.
A notice citing a rule that does not match what you posted.
Several posts removed within an hour for different stated reasons.
Followers telling you a thread or group is circulating your handle with encouragement to report it.
An account locked while the appeal sits unanswered.
Removal alerts arriving in bursts at similar times of day.
what_it_is_not: Many independent people reporting a post that really breaks the rules.
A single mistaken removal by an automated filter.
A platform enforcing a rule you did not know about.
A follower reporting something harmful on their own.
A group openly flagging a real scam, where the reports match what is actually posted.
A platform outage or policy change that affects many accounts at once.
this_may_be_it_when: Your removal followed a public argument by hours or days.
The rule cited does not fit the post.
People you do not know write to celebrate your suspension.
A thread or chat names your account as a target.
Several of your posts fell at once though nothing else changed.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The post does break a rule once you read the policy.
Only one post was removed, with an explanation that fits.
Other users of similar content were treated the same way.
The platform shows an error or a mass policy change.
Nobody had a dispute with you beforehand.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Automated systems flag posts by keyword, which catches harmless content.
A post may truly have upset many people, who each reported it on their own.
Platforms change rules and enforcement in waves.
A viral post draws more attention and with it more reports, including honest ones.
common_false_positives: A real policy violation that many independent users flagged.
A glitchy removal of many accounts after a platform update.
A temporary restriction that follows ordinary rate limits.
Being muted or blocked by someone, which is not a report.
discernment_questions: Does the rule cited match what I actually posted?
Did this follow a dispute, and who was involved?
Is there any sign, such as a group post or a shared list, that people were organized?
Do I have the notices, dates and screenshots saved?
What appeal route exists, and have I used it?
less_concerning_if: The cited rule fits the content on a fair reading.
Removal came with a clear explanation and a working appeal.
No dispute with others came before it.
more_concerning_if: It repeats after each reinstatement of the account.
It hits your source of income, such as a shop, channel or ad account.
The reporting is paired with harassment, doxxing or threats.
pattern_over_time_signs: Each time you post on one subject, a wave of reports follows.
Appeals meet automated replies while the cycle continues.
Your reach shrinks and you begin to censor yourself.
The same names, or the same kinds of accounts, appear in threads about you before each removal.
codex_completed.repair_check: Reinstatement is only part of it. Repair also means the history and strikes cleared, and the platform confirming the reports were unfounded. An account restored on Monday and hit again by Friday has not been repaired.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Consider whether your appeal gets a human answer that addresses the actual content. Silence, form replies, and a second wave of reports soon after reinstatement all suggest the problem is continuing.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Reporting systems are designed to treat many separate complaints as a sign that something is wrong, so volume can pass for evidence. Automated review, thin staffing and the weight of numbers can carry the decision before a person looks. Targets often censor themselves out of fear of the next strike, which can quiet them even without a removal.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe losing months of work, followers or income in an afternoon, the helplessness of an appeal that goes nowhere, and a creeping habit of watching their words. Some feel anger at being treated as the offender, and some move to other platforms or stop posting about the subject that drew attention.

response_options.soft_clarification: Read the notice closely and write down which rule it cites and which post it points to. A mismatch is useful to state in your appeal.
response_options.firm_boundary: Use the platform's appeal route and state facts only: what you posted, the rule cited, and why they do not match. Keep it short and attach screenshots.
response_options.disengagement: Do not argue with accounts celebrating the suspension or ask them to stop. Keep your records and let the appeal run.
response_options.support_seeking: Contact the platform's creator or business support if you have it, a digital-rights group, or a lawyer if income is at stake. Share the timeline with someone who can help watch the account.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If the account is part of your job, tell your manager early and keep the notices, dates and appeal numbers in one folder so the business can show what happened.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "The rule cited in this notice does not match what I posted. I have saved the notice, the post and the date. I am asking for a review by a person, and for the reports behind it to be looked at together."
codex_completed.safety_note: Mass reports sometimes travel with harassment, doxxing or threats, and with the loss of a business or income. Threats, strangers learning your address, or messages celebrating your harm are signals to take seriously. Keep every notice and thread, tell a trusted person, and reach the police, a victim advocate or legal aid for threats or lost income.
misuse_warning: Calling a legitimate removal a brigade avoids asking whether the post broke a rule.
Naming specific people as the organizers of a report wave without evidence can bring harassment onto the wrong person.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Sock Puppets make a fake crowd that speaks in public; coordinated reporting uses a crowd, real or fake, that complains in private to a platform. Doxxing sends people to your door instead of to your report queue, though the two can travel together. Stalking-by-Notification gathers your activity to use against you, while here the weapon is the platform's own enforcement.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted text cannot verify or authenticate forensic/evidentiary claims — that requires the actual technical evidence, not conversational text.

codex_completed.name: Credential-Costuming
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Presenting invented, stretched or borrowed titles and affiliations so that a claim or request carries more authority than the person's real qualifications support.
codex_completed.short_definition: Presenting invented, stretched or borrowed titles and affiliations so that a claim or request carries more authority than the person's real qualifications support.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Credential-costuming is dressing a claim in a title, degree, affiliation or association that the person does not hold, or holds only in a smaller form. A consultant becomes a 'Dr.', a conference attendee becomes 'a member of the advisory board', one meeting with a famous person becomes 'we work closely together'. The title then does the work that evidence should do. An unfamiliar credential is not a false one, so checking comes before concluding anything.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone leans on a title or affiliation that is invented or inflated, so you stop asking questions you would normally ask.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You defer to standing that is not there, and the questions you would otherwise ask start to feel out of place. Decisions, such as money, health or hiring choices, can then rest on the look of expertise instead of anything that was tested.
what_it_is: Inventing a degree, license or job title, or claiming one from an institution that cannot confirm it.
Stretching something small into something large: a weekend course becomes 'certified', and a freelance gig becomes 'former head of the department'.
Borrowing authority from others, such as logos, photos with notable people, or a name-dropped organization that has no real link to the person.
Leaning on the title where evidence should be, as in 'trust me, I'm a doctor of this' in place of an explanation you can check.
Common in sales pages, social media bios, consulting, wellness and finance advice, and job applications.
what_it_sounds_like: As a top-university-trained strategist, I can tell you this won't work. (the university has no record of a degree)
I sit on the board of several major organizations, so I know how this goes.
You wouldn't understand the details. That's why people hire someone with my credentials.
A bio listing 'Doctor' and 'Professor' with no field, institution or year.
A website showing the logos of well-known companies under 'As seen in', where no article can be found.
A certificate image whose issuing body has no website, or one that does not list the person.
I've been advising the government on this for years, but I can't say who.
what_it_is_not: An unfamiliar credential is not a false one. Many genuine titles mean nothing outside their field, and a modest person may describe real experience in a way that sounds grand.
Honorary degrees, titles from other countries, and professional bodies that differ in how they name qualifications.
Titles that really belong to the person but are used loosely in conversation, such as calling a research fellow 'professor'. This is sloppy, and not necessarily invented.
Self-taught expertise, which can be real and deep with no certificate behind it, and which is not a costume if the person says so.
A job title that sounds big because a small company hands out large titles, which is a company habit.
this_may_be_it_when: The institution or licensing body has no record of the person, or the credential cannot be found in a public register.
The title is used mainly to end questions ('I'm the expert here') and not to support an explanation.
Basic follow-up questions about the claimed field get vague or inconsistent answers.
The details of the credential shift between tellings: different years, different schools, different roles.
The credential is offered in place of evidence precisely when a claim is challenged.
this_may_not_be_it_when: A quick check of the register or the institution confirms the title.
The person explains the credential's limits unprompted, such as 'my degree is in a related field.'
They welcome follow-up questions and answer with working knowledge.
The mismatch is only that you did not recognize the title or the institution.
The claim is small, easy to confirm, and tied to what they are actually asking you to do.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Some qualifications are real but obscure, so a first search finds nothing.
People sometimes round up a title out of nerves in an interview or on a bio, without any plan to deceive.
Cultures and industries differ in how titles are awarded and written.
common_false_positives: A professional with a genuine but regional or unusual qualification that takes a few minutes to look up.
A young specialist with a modest title whose knowledge is deep and checkable.
A practitioner who lists a past role accurately but did not update their bio after leaving it.
discernment_questions: Can I confirm this credential with the body that issued it, using contact details I found myself?
Does the person's knowledge match what the title implies when I ask ordinary follow-up questions?
Is the title being used to answer my question, or to replace an answer?
Do the dates, institutions and roles stay the same each time the person describes them?
What am I being asked to do on the strength of this claim, and what would it cost if it were wrong?
less_concerning_if: The credential checks out when you look it up, and the person's knowledge fits it.
The claim is minor and has no bearing on money, health or safety decisions.
They correct any overstatement as soon as you point it out.
more_concerning_if: You are being asked for money, access or a health or legal decision on the strength of the title alone.
The credential falls apart in the register and the person continues to use it.
Questions about the credential are met with offense or with a reminder of how important the person is.
pattern_over_time_signs: The list of affiliations and titles grows over months without any new evidence appearing.
Each time a claim is questioned, a new credential is offered in answer.
Details about education or past roles quietly change between conversations or profiles.
People who check the claims are told they are being petty or disloyal.
codex_completed.repair_check: Once a gap is found, correction looks like the title being dropped or restated accurately everywhere it appeared, including old profiles and printed material. Reworded claims that sound nearly as grand, or an explanation that blames a misunderstanding by others, leave the costume in place.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask to verify the credential through the issuing body, and watch the answer. Someone with a genuine qualification usually gives the name of the register, and may be pleased you asked. Delay, offense, or a new credential offered in its place is a different signal.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Titles work as shortcuts: it is hard to judge expertise yourself, so people often rely on markers such as degrees and affiliations. That shortcut can make questions feel rude, particularly in front of others or in fields where the listener lacks background. A borrowed marker can carry weight that has not been tested.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe acting on advice they later could not confirm, feeling embarrassed at having deferred, and growing wary of all experts afterwards, including honest ones. Some describe being unsure how they missed it, when the title itself had made checking feel unnecessary.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask a curious, plain question: 'Where did you train for this? I'd like to read about it.' Genuine experts tend to answer easily.
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold your decision until you can verify: 'I make choices like this after I've checked the licensing register myself, so I'll get back to you.'
response_options.disengagement: Step away from the offer, purchase or sign-up until a check is done, and let the delay stand.
response_options.support_seeking: Show the claim to someone who works in the field, or to a librarian or fact-checker, and ask whether the credential and institution look real.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In hiring or vendor choices, confirm degrees, licenses and references directly with the issuing body, and apply the same check to every candidate.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'm sure it's accurate, and I double-check titles for anyone I'm going to rely on. Could you send me the name of the institution and the year, so I can confirm it myself?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Usually this is a trust and money problem, not a physical one. It changes when the claimed credential is medical, legal, financial or about child care and someone acts on it. In that case, check the person against the official licensing register before acting, and report a false claim to that licensing board.
misuse_warning: Accusing someone of faking their credentials because their title is unfamiliar can hurt a real professional. Look it up before saying anything.
Dismissing self-taught or non-traditional experts as costumed ignores real expertise that has no certificate.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Identity Performances is a whole persona tailored to each audience, while credential-costuming is one specific claim about qualifications that can be checked. Strategic Self-Deprecation / Performed Humility lowers standing to block criticism, where this raises it to block questions. Social Engineering often borrows a title as a pretext to get something quickly; here the title is the point.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Identity Performances
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Presenting a built persona, with claimed experiences and traits, that earns trust or access the person's real circumstances would not support.
codex_completed.short_definition: Presenting a built persona, with claimed experiences and traits, that earns trust or access the person's real circumstances would not support.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: An identity performance is a persona assembled for an audience: a backstory, interests, hardships or beliefs that land well with that audience, and told in a way that does not match the facts. It can be a dating profile, a networking pitch, a support-group story or a social media character. Everyone adjusts how they present across settings, so a different manner at work proves nothing. The signal is specific claims that fall apart under ordinary follow-up questions.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone shows you a version of themselves, with a story and traits tailored to you, that turns out not to match the facts.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You extend trust to a version of someone that does not exist, so your read on the relationship rests on facts that were supplied to you and never observed. When the gap appears, you can doubt your judgment as well as the person.
what_it_is: A persona with a backstory, such as a hardship, a career or a past relationship, that is invented or heavily reshaped.
A presentation that shifts with each audience in ways that go beyond tone, so that facts change, not just style.
A story that fits what a particular group would find sympathetic, such as a shared illness, shared faith or shared loss.
Found in online dating, community groups, online forums, workplaces, fundraising and friendships that began online.
Most visible when a claim meets a detail that can be checked, such as a date, a place or a mutual acquaintance.
what_it_sounds_like: I went through the exact same thing, so I know just how you feel. (later, no part of the history fits)
A profile with photos that reverse-image search places on a stranger's account.
A person who is a nurse to one group, a former soldier to another, and has no record in either.
I can't video call because my camera is broken, again.
My family all passed away, so you're really all I have. (a sibling is later mentioned in passing)
Telling a support circle a severe personal story that a family member says never took place.
A new colleague whose past employers cannot recall them, and whose references are all one phone number.
what_it_is_not: Everyone presents differently in different rooms. Someone rebuilding or still working out who they are is changing, not fabricating.
Code-switching, where a person shifts vocabulary or tone to fit a community without changing any facts about their life.
Privacy: leaving out painful details, or keeping an ex's name private, is not inventing false ones.
Exaggeration in a funny story, which listeners understand as storytelling.
People using a pen name or an online handle to keep their work life and personal life apart.
this_may_be_it_when: Specific claims about history, family or work fail when you ask ordinary follow-up questions.
The details of the story change between tellings, or between audiences.
The backstory seems built for you, such as an uncannily close match to your own experiences.
Photos, names or places cannot be matched to anything real when checked.
Offers to meet, call or be seen are repeatedly put off for reasons that keep changing.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The differences are in tone, vocabulary or humor, not in facts.
The person gives plain reasons for caution, such as safety concerns, and still shares verifiable details over time.
A mutual acquaintance or public record confirms the main claims.
The story is incomplete, and not contradictory: they simply have not told you everything yet.
They are open about using a pseudonym or a persona, such as an artist or performer.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People are often more guarded, or more upbeat, with new acquaintances than with old friends.
Someone recovering from a hard chapter might not describe it in full, or might describe it differently at different times.
Shame about a job, a past or a family can lead to softened details without any plan to gain from them.
common_false_positives: A person who is quieter and more formal at work and loud and silly with old friends.
Someone exploring a new identity, such as a new name, a new faith or a new gender expression, whose self-description is changing as they find it.
A friend who tells the same anecdote differently each time because it is a good story, not a record.
discernment_questions: Which specific claims could I check, and when I check them, do they hold?
Do the facts change between audiences, or only the tone?
Does the story seem unusually well matched to what I would find sympathetic?
When I suggest meeting, calling or meeting a friend of theirs, is there a plain, consistent reason for any hesitation?
What am I being asked for, and would I still be willing to give it if I knew the real story?
less_concerning_if: The main facts about work, family and location are consistent and can be confirmed by independent sources.
The differences between settings are tone and style and not details of the person's history.
Nothing is being asked of you that depends on the story being true.
more_concerning_if: The persona comes with requests for money, secrecy, access to your accounts or private images.
Several claims fail a simple check and the explanation changes each time.
You are urged to keep the relationship or the story private from friends and family.
pattern_over_time_signs: New details appear to fit each new need, such as a sudden illness when money comes up.
Old details quietly drop away, and questions about them are met with irritation.
People from different parts of their life have never met and are never introduced.
Your own picture of them has grown from things they told you and not from things you have seen.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair starts with the facts being put right in specific terms: which parts were not true, who was told, and what that cost. A fresh, more moving story to explain the old one, or a plea that you understand why, keeps the performance going.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask to confirm one concrete detail, such as a video call, a mutual contact or a workplace. Is it made easy, or is the answer more story? A genuine person with a reason to be careful will usually offer another way to confirm.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Stories that mirror our own experiences earn trust quickly, and those who seem like us earn warmth. A persona shaped to match can speed up closeness before there are facts to base it on. Because the closeness feels earned, questions can seem disloyal.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe grief when a connection turns out to rest on invented details, shame about having believed it, and doubt about their own judgment in new relationships. Some find it hard to say which parts were real, and mourn those too.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for detail the way a friend would: 'Tell me more about that time. Who else was there?' Consistent, easy answers are reassuring.
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep the relationship at its current depth until something can be verified: 'I'd like to meet in person or on video before I share anything personal.'
response_options.disengagement: Slow your replies and stop sharing personal information, and let the lack of verifiable detail settle the question.
response_options.support_seeking: Show the profile or story to a friend and ask what they see, or run a reverse image search on photos and check what turns up.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: For hires and partners, check employment history and references directly, with numbers you looked up yourself, and treat each candidate the same way.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I like getting to know you. Before I go any deeper, I'd feel better if we could video call, or if I could meet someone who knows you. Would that be okay?"
codex_completed.safety_note: A persona alone is not a safety signal. It becomes one when it comes with requests for money, secrecy, intimate photos or access to your accounts. If it does, stop sending anything, keep the messages, and report the profile to the platform or to your bank's fraud team.
misuse_warning: Accusing someone of 'performing' because they are shy, reserved or private punishes people who simply do not share much.
People with changing identities, new names or pen names are often mislabeled as fake. Look for false facts, not unfamiliar presentation.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Credential-Costuming is one claim about titles and qualifications, while identity performance is a whole constructed person. Performative Allyship / False Solidarity is about stated values that go unpracticed, not invented history. Social Engineering is a pretext for one specific request made quickly, whereas a persona is built up over weeks or months and rests on closeness.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Social Engineering
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Getting information, access or action out of someone by exploiting trust, urgency or social habits, usually under a false pretext such as a claimed role or emergency.
codex_completed.short_definition: Getting information, access or action out of someone by exploiting trust, urgency or social habits, usually under a false pretext such as a claimed role or emergency.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Social engineering is a request that gets past normal checks by working on people instead of on systems. A caller claims to be from the bank, a message appears to be from a boss, someone in a hi-vis vest walks through a door. The request leans on helpfulness, respect for authority or fear of getting it wrong. Real organizations also make urgent requests, so urgency alone settles nothing. The test is whether the request can be verified through a channel you already trust.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone pretends to be a person or organization you would normally help, and uses urgency or authority to get you to hand over information or access before you check.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: What gets used is ordinary decency: being helpful, deferring to apparent authority, not wanting to make a fuss. So the loss afterwards, of money, access or privacy, can feel like a personal failing and not something that was done to you.
what_it_is: A request that arrives with a role attached, such as bank staff, IT support, a manager, a delivery driver or a government agent.
A pretext, meaning a made-up reason, that explains why the usual process must be skipped this once.
Pressure on time or on feelings: a deadline, a threat to an account, a relative in trouble, or embarrassment about asking.
Delivered by phone, text, email, social media, or in person at a front desk or a door.
Aimed at what people can give freely: a code, a password, a payment, a keycard, a favor or a piece of personal information.
what_it_sounds_like: This is the fraud team at your bank. Someone is draining your account right now, and I need you to read me the code we just sent.
Hi, it's Dana from the CEO's office. I'm in a meeting and can't talk. Can you buy gift cards for a client and send me the numbers?
A text saying a package is held, with a link and a one-hour deadline.
IT here. We're locking your account in ten minutes unless you confirm your password.
Grandma, it's me, I'm in trouble. Please don't tell Mom. I need money wired today.
A visitor in a work vest, holding a box, who asks you to hold the door because they left their badge inside.
An email from a familiar name with a slightly different address, asking you to change where an invoice is paid.
what_it_is_not: Genuinely urgent, legitimate requests exist, and real IT or security staff follow processes that most people have never met. Checking back through a channel you already trust costs an honest request nothing, which makes it the cheap test here and not suspicion of the person.
A real colleague who is rushed and informal and writes a short, blunt email with no pretext at all.
Marketing or sales outreach that is pushy but honest about who is calling and what they want.
A friend or relative who actually has an emergency, which can be confirmed by calling them on their usual number.
A security drill run by your own employer that has been announced through official channels.
this_may_be_it_when: The request arrives unexpectedly and asks for a code, password, payment or access.
The contact discourages you from checking, such as 'don't call the bank, they're involved' or 'there's no time'.
The channel is new or slightly off: a different number, a similar-looking address, a new account.
You are asked to move money in unusual ways, such as gift cards, crypto or wire transfers.
The story leans hard on fear, secrecy or the importance of the person asking.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You started the contact, using a number or address you found yourself.
The request fits a process you already know and can confirm through your own channels.
They are happy for you to hang up and call back, or to ask a colleague first.
Nothing sensitive is being asked, such as a code, money, or access.
Your organization announced the request ahead of time through a known route.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Banks, employers and delivery firms do contact people, and sometimes under real time pressure.
A busy manager might write a terse message from a new phone number for a harmless reason.
A new employee might be asked for details by a department that has not yet been introduced.
common_false_positives: A real alert from your bank that you can confirm by logging in through the app yourself.
A colleague you have not met who is genuinely from another office and is following a normal process.
A cold sales call that is annoying but accurate about who is calling.
discernment_questions: Can I confirm this request using a number or address I already trust, and not the one it came from?
Is the person asking me to skip a step that normally exists?
Why is there no time to check, and who benefits from that?
Am I being asked for a code, a payment or access, and what would happen if the request were false?
Is the contact unusual in its channel, wording or timing for this person or organization?
less_concerning_if: You can confirm the request through a channel you chose yourself, and it checks out.
The requester welcomes verification and does not mind a delay.
The request asks for nothing sensitive and can wait.
more_concerning_if: You are told to keep the request secret, or not to call anyone while it is open.
Money has been requested in a hard-to-trace form, or you have already shared a code or password.
Threats are made, such as arrest, loss of an account or harm to a relative, if you do not act right away.
pattern_over_time_signs: Repeated contacts from slightly different names or numbers, each building on the last.
Small, harmless requests come first, then larger ones, once you have said yes.
A growing amount of your personal detail, such as birthdays, addresses and workplaces, appears in the messages.
The pressure escalates each time you delay or ask to check.
codex_completed.repair_check: After a request is found to be false, repair for you is practical: the bank, employer or platform is told, passwords and codes are changed, and the channel that was used is blocked. The genuine organization, if one was imitated, explains what it will never ask for.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask whether you can verify and call back, and watch whether the pace slows. A legitimate caller tends to agree and wait. Pressure that rises, a new reason it cannot wait, or an offer to stay on the line while you check is the signal.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Pressure and borrowed authority can narrow attention to the request, so the habit of checking gets crowded out. Fear of loss or of letting someone down tends to push people to act quickly. Familiar roles, a known name or a plausible detail can lower guard, since most such requests in daily life are honest.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe sudden panic followed by shame, replaying how they missed the signs, and reluctance to tell anyone for fear of being judged. Some become wary of every call and message, and some lose savings, access to accounts or private information.

response_options.soft_clarification: Say you handle such matters yourself: 'I'm going to check this through the official number and come back to you.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to share codes or passwords with anyone who contacts you first: 'I don't give that out in response to a call or message, whoever it is.'
response_options.disengagement: Close the message, end the call without explanation, and then contact the real organization using a number from its official site or the back of your card.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone you trust right away, even if you feel foolish. If money moved or a password was shared, call your bank's fraud line and ask for help securing your accounts.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Report any odd request to your security or IT team, and set up a rule that payments or access changes need a second person to confirm by a known channel.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Thanks for letting me know. I deal with anything like this through the official number, so I'll look it up myself and check. If it's real, it will still be there after I've confirmed it."
codex_completed.safety_note: Watch for threats of arrest, claims that a relative is in danger, demands for secrecy, and pressure to send money in hard-to-trace ways. These can lead to serious loss of savings or access. If you have already sent money or shared a code, phone your bank's fraud line straight away using the number on your card, since speed matters.
misuse_warning: Treating every urgent request as a scam can strain relationships and slow honest work. Verification is the test, not a feeling of suspicion.
Blaming someone who fell for it adds shame to a loss. Good people with good habits get caught by well-built pretexts.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Credential-Costuming is about inflated titles and standing over time, while social engineering is a single request that uses a role to get something now. Identity Performances builds a persona over weeks or months; here the pretext is usually short-lived and aimed at an action. Performative Allyship / False Solidarity trades on shared values, not on urgency or authority.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Performative Allyship / False Solidarity
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Declaring support for a cause or group in public while private actions and choices do not match the words, so the support earns trust it has not backed up.
codex_completed.short_definition: Declaring support for a cause or group in public while private actions and choices do not match the words, so the support earns trust it has not backed up.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Performative allyship and false solidarity are two names for one behavior: public statements of support or shared values that are not matched by anything done when no one is watching. 'Allyship' is the term usually used for social causes and 'solidarity' is used more widely, including at work and among friends. The statement may even be heartfelt. The gap shows when support would cost something, and it quietly disappears.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone says all the right things about standing with you or your cause, but when support would cost them something, it is not there.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Trust is given on the strength of stated values, and the gap only becomes visible when support would have cost something, which is usually the moment you most needed it. The let-down then lands as a betrayal and can make future trust harder.
what_it_is: Public statements, posts, badges or slogans of support that sit beside private choices that point the other way.
Two labels for the same gap: 'allyship' is used in discussions of social justice, 'false solidarity' in workplaces, unions, friendships and movements.
Support that rises with attention, such as around an event or a campaign, and fades when the audience moves on.
A declared alliance used as cover, so that a later criticism is met with 'but I support you'.
Visible most clearly when something concrete is needed, such as a vote, a referral, a speaking-up, a shared cost or a risk.
what_it_sounds_like: I'm so proud to stand with you. You can always count on me. (and in the meeting, silence)
A manager who posts about inclusion on Friday and turns down the flexible-hours request on Monday.
I'm one of the good ones. I've read all the books.
I'd say something publicly, but it's complicated. You understand, right?
A group chat full of supportive emojis when the topic is trending, and no reply when you ask for a favor.
Look how much I've done for your community. How could you say I let you down?
Colleagues who endorse your cause in a team meeting and vote against it in private.
what_it_is_not: Many people are further along in their stated values than in their practice and are genuinely, if unevenly, catching up.
Quiet support that is never announced anywhere is the reverse of this pattern, not a mild version of it.
Someone who supports a cause but is limited by real constraints, such as a precarious job, and says so honestly.
A newcomer to an issue who is learning, makes mistakes, and takes correction well.
A person who disagrees with one tactic of a movement while backing its aims.
this_may_be_it_when: Public support is loud, and nothing happens in private when a real cost arises.
The support appears when many people are watching and drops away when few are.
Your request for something concrete is met with warm words and no action.
The stated alliance is raised in response to a complaint about specific behavior.
The person gains reputation or access from the declared support, and carries none of the cost.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Statements of support are followed by some real action, even if small or imperfect.
The person tells you plainly what they can and cannot do, and does what they said.
They accept criticism of a specific failure and change what they did.
Their support looks the same in public and in private.
The gap is between what they said last year and what they know now, and they say so.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People often sincerely mean a statement and then struggle to act on it when it gets uncomfortable.
Fear of losing a job, a friendship or standing can hold back someone who really does care.
Some people post as a way of processing their feelings and have not yet thought about the next step.
common_false_positives: A friend who supports you privately and never posts about it.
A coworker who has not yet found the right way to help but keeps asking what would be useful.
An organization that makes a public statement and, more slowly, changes its policies.
discernment_questions: What has this person done, as opposed to said, in the last year?
Does the support look the same when nobody is watching?
When help would cost them something, what happened?
Is the stated alliance used to answer specific concerns I have raised?
Are they open about what they can't do, or do they keep up the promise of more?
less_concerning_if: The person is learning, makes mistakes, and acts on correction.
Words of support are followed, even slowly, by concrete steps.
They are straightforward about the limits of what they can offer.
more_concerning_if: The declared support is used to shut down specific criticism or to gain a position of leadership.
They benefit in reputation or income from the cause while the people it is meant for bear the costs.
Those who point out the gap are described as ungrateful or divisive.
pattern_over_time_signs: Each crisis brings strong statements and the same absence when practical help is needed.
Support rises and falls with what is trending.
Your requests for concrete help are met with praise for the cause instead of an answer.
People who were helped in the past quietly stop relying on this person.
codex_completed.repair_check: Mending this shows up as costs accepted: a specific thing done, a decision changed, a seat or credit given up, and a plain acknowledgment of the earlier gap. Another statement of support, however well written, only repeats the gap.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask for one specific, practical thing and see what follows. If it gets done, even imperfectly, the stated support has substance. Another statement of how much they care, or a claim that your request is unfair, is the pattern again.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Stated shared values can lower our guard, because we expect people who say they care to act accordingly. Public statements are cheap and bring social reward, while acting often carries a cost, so the reward can arrive without the cost. A person on the receiving end may then excuse the gap for a long time, hoping for the action.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A particular sting comes when someone who said they stood with you is absent at the critical moment, and you start doubting whether your need was reasonable. Some become wary of every public statement of support, and some keep thanking people who have done little.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name what you need in concrete terms: 'It would really help if you could raise this at Thursday's meeting. Can you do that?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to offer praise or credit in place of action: 'I appreciate the words. I need to see what you will do before I treat it as support.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop relying on this person for the thing they promised, and turn to people who have shown up before.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk with others in the same cause or community about who has actually helped, and build on those relationships.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask for specific commitments in writing, such as a policy change, a date, or an owner, and follow up on them in the next meeting.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Your saying that means something. What would mean even more is one concrete step. Could you tell me what you are able to do this month, and by when?"
codex_completed.safety_note: This is usually a trust and credibility problem and not a danger. It would change if the declared alliance is used to gain access to a vulnerable person, such as in a support group or a youth setting, or to pressure someone into silence. In that case, raise it with the group's organizer or a safeguarding contact.
misuse_warning: Calling every public statement performative discourages people who are sincerely learning and who may act later. Judge by what follows, over time.
Using the label to dismiss someone who disagrees with you turns a description of a gap into a way of ending a debate.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Identity Performances invents a history or persona, while performative allyship leaves the person's real history alone and gaps appear between stated values and actions. Strategic Self-Deprecation / Performed Humility deflects through stated flaws, where this deflects through stated virtue. Social Engineering is a quick request under a pretext, while here the alliance is long-running and the cost is what is left undone.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Premature Exclusivity
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Pressing for an exclusive, serious commitment before the other person has had time to learn enough about you to choose freely.
codex_completed.short_definition: Pressing for an exclusive, serious commitment before the other person has had time to learn enough about you to choose freely.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Premature exclusivity is a push to become a couple, drop other dating or friendships, or label the relationship, at a point when the other person barely knows you. Fast feelings alone prove nothing, since many couples move quickly and are happy. The telling detail is the response to hesitation: wanting time is treated as rejection or a test, so the slower person gives in before the facts are in.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone asks you to be exclusive far sooner than you can know them, and any wish for more time is met with hurt or pressure instead of patience.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You commit before you have the information the decision needed, and once you have said yes you have often let go of the other options you would have compared it with. Doubts that arrive later can feel like breaking a promise.
what_it_is: A request to be exclusive, move in, or call it a relationship that arrives well ahead of the usual pace for those two people.
A push that meets slowness with sadness, accusations of not caring, or a deadline for an answer.
A commitment made before basic facts are known, such as how the person handles conflict, money, or other people in their life.
A sequence in which the yes is treated as binding at once, so backing off later looks like betrayal.
what_it_sounds_like: I've never felt this way. Why would we wait?
If you really cared, you wouldn't need time to think.
I deleted the apps last night. I assumed you would too.
We've been seeing each other for three weeks. Are you telling me you still want to date other people?
Everyone else I've met was a waste of time. You're different, so say yes.
I need an answer by Friday, because I can't keep guessing.
what_it_is_not: Two people who both feel a strong pull and both choose exclusivity gladly. The speed is shared and nobody is being pushed.
A person who prefers clarity early and says so once, then accepts that you need a slower pace.
Pacing norms that differ by culture, faith or age, where earlier commitment is simply expected.
An honest statement of what someone wants, such as 'I am only looking for something exclusive', which lets you decide to step away.
A person who is eager and a little clumsy about it, and relaxes once you say you need time.
this_may_be_it_when: Your request for more time brings sulking, accusations, or sudden coldness.
A deadline is attached to the question of commitment.
You are asked to end other friendships or contacts before you know the person well.
Declarations of how special you are arrive in a rush, and doubt is treated as an insult to them.
You noticed you agreed mainly to end an uncomfortable conversation.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You raised the pace yourself, or you are as keen as they are.
When you ask for time, they say 'okay, take it' and keep seeing you the same way.
The commitment requested is small and easy to revisit, like deleting an app together.
Both of you agreed on the pace afterwards and neither of you feels cornered.
They tell you early and plainly what they want and leave the choice open.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Some people fall quickly, mean it, and ask clumsily because they are nervous.
People coming out of a long gap, or who are older, sometimes have little patience for slow dating.
A person who was hurt by vague arrangements before may ask for clarity sooner than most.
common_false_positives: A whirlwind romance where both people keep choosing each other and neither feels rushed.
A question about exclusivity at a normal moment, accepted calmly when the answer is 'not yet'.
A community where courtship is short by custom and both families and both people expect it.
discernment_questions: Did I say yes because I was sure, or because saying no was going to cost me?
What happens to the mood when I say I need longer?
What do I know about how this person acts when things go wrong, and how did I learn it?
Would I give the same answer if there were no deadline and no hurt look?
Did we set this pace together, or did I get swept along by it?
less_concerning_if: A request for time is met warmly and the relationship carries on at your pace.
The person has been open from the start about what they want and has not asked you to shrink the rest of your life.
Both of you can say the pace is too fast or too slow and the other one adjusts.
more_concerning_if: You are asked to cut contact with friends, family or other partners before you have known them long.
Each delay brings a bigger display of hurt or a new condition.
You have started telling small lies about your plans to avoid the reaction.
pattern_over_time_signs: Each step forward in closeness is announced as already agreed, with your consent assumed.
Your own doubts get quieter because voicing them always costs more than it gains.
You find out, months in, facts about the person that you would have wanted before saying yes.
Plans with other people shrink one at a time, each time with a reason that sounded fair.
codex_completed.repair_check: Look at how time is treated after you raise it. If they slow down, ask what pace suits you, and stay steady when you take it, the push has actually changed. A warm apology that still keeps the deadline in place has not.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself whether the answer 'not yet' is allowed to stay an answer. When it is, they carry on kindly and you can keep exploring. When it gets reopened daily or punished with distance, the boundary is being treated as a hurdle.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A strong early rush of attention and affection can make a person feel they owe something in return, and a yes spoken under that glow tends to feel binding afterwards. People also tend to defend a choice they have already announced. Early commitment can therefore settle the question before the evidence for it is in.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe lingering unease about a decision that never felt fully theirs, embarrassment at having agreed so fast, and a habit of explaining their doubts away. Some say they lost touch with friends in the first weeks and found it awkward to reconnect.

response_options.soft_clarification: Tell them how you feel about the pace and ask what they need: 'I like you, and I need more time before we label anything. Can we keep going as we are for now?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep the answer short and the same each time: 'I'm not ready to be exclusive yet. Asking again won't change it, and I'd like us to stop revisiting it.'
response_options.disengagement: If the subject takes over every meeting, give yourself a few days without contact to hear your own opinion again.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend what you were asked and when, and see whether the timeline sounds as fast to them as it does to you.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If the pressure is from a colleague or manager, keep the matter in writing and decline the personal commitment in a sentence. Report persistent pressure to HR.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I like where this is going, and I'm not ready to be exclusive yet. I'll tell you when that changes. Until then, let's carry on without revisiting it every time we meet."
codex_completed.safety_note: Being rushed into exclusivity is a pacing problem, not a danger signal. It turns more serious if the push comes with demands to hand over your phone, cut off specific people, or move in right away, or if saying no brings threats or rage. Then talk privately with a trusted friend or a relationship abuse advocate before replying.
misuse_warning: Treating every early 'I love you' or fast romance as pressure can make you dismiss someone who is simply keen. Look at how they respond to 'not yet'.
Using the label to accuse a partner who wanted something you did not want, without looking at how they took your answer, turns a mismatch into a charge.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Halo Effect Exploitation leans on someone's impressive reputation to quiet doubts, while this pattern pushes a commitment date and punishes hesitation. Covert Contracts holds you to expectations nobody named, whereas here the request is spoken aloud and the pressure lies in the speed and the penalty for slowness.

codex_completed.name: Confirmation Bias Exploitation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Supplying enough good moments that your own habit of favoring the kinder reading does the work of discounting the harm.
codex_completed.short_definition: Supplying enough good moments that your own habit of favoring the kinder reading does the work of discounting the harm.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Everyone tends to notice evidence that fits what they already believe about someone they love. In this pattern, hurtful incidents are regularly followed by warmth, gifts or promises, and each warm stretch becomes the proof of who the person truly is. The harm does not need hiding; it gets filed as an exception. One kind gesture after a bad day means little. A repeating cycle where the good always arrives right after the harm is what makes it a pattern.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: After something painful, the person is lovely for a while, and you hold on to that as the real them while the painful moments get explained away.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Your own hope becomes the thing that keeps you in place, and the pattern stays hidden from the one person best placed to see it. You may defend someone to others and to yourself while privately keeping count.
what_it_is: A cycle in which a hurtful event is followed within days by unusual warmth, effort or generosity.
A way of talking about the harm as out of character, with the good periods presented as the true person.
A setting where you, not the other person, do the explaining: you find reasons for the incident before anyone offers one.
A pattern that relies on a normal human habit, favoring evidence that fits what we hope, rather than on any special trick.
what_it_sounds_like: I don't know what came over me. You know I'm not like that.
Look at everything I did for you this week.
Remember our trip? That's who I really am.
He was exhausted, that's all, and he's been so sweet since.
I told my sister about the argument, then remembered the flowers and felt silly for telling her.
Every time I decide it's too much, something lovely happens and I put the thought away.
what_it_is_not: A relationship that really is mostly good, where holding on to the good parts is accurate and not denial.
Someone who has a bad day, behaves badly once, apologizes sincerely, and changes how they act.
A normal hopeful reading of ambiguous behavior, with no cycle of harm and reward behind it.
Genuine growth, where kindness lasts and the harm becomes rarer and then stops, not returning after each peak.
A friend or family member reminding you of a person's real strengths because they know the whole history.
this_may_be_it_when: Warm periods follow incidents with a regularity you could predict.
Telling a friend about the incident you notice yourself softening it as you speak.
You keep the good memories close to hand specifically for the moments you doubt.
Raising the harm brings a list of what the person has done for you, instead of a response to what happened.
The kind periods change what is said but not what is done about the cause of the harm.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The kindness is steady and does not rise and fall around incidents.
After a bad moment, the person names what went wrong and the cause is dealt with.
You feel free to describe the incident to anyone without feeling disloyal.
The harm was one event, long ago, and has not returned.
Your doubts get answered and then settle, rather than returning after each sweet spell.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People who love each other usually do try to make up after a hard moment, and that is healthy.
Anyone who cares about someone gives them credit for the good they know.
A rough patch in a stressful season can be followed by real, lasting kindness.
common_false_positives: A long marriage in which the good outweighs the bad and both people work at it.
A friend who stays loyal to someone through one bad year because of a long record of kindness.
A couple making honest progress, where the apologies are followed by changed behavior and the incidents get further apart.
discernment_questions: If I wrote down only the hurtful incidents, in order, what would the list look like?
Does the good behavior arrive soon after harm, or does it arrive on its own, unconnected to anything?
Would a friend who heard the incidents told plainly be as relaxed as I am?
What do I tell myself in the days after an incident, and where did that explanation come from?
Has anything about the cause of the harm changed between cycles?
less_concerning_if: The good periods continue without interruption and the harmful incidents grow rarer.
The person helps you look at what happened and does not need you to forgive it quickly.
You can discuss the hard moments with people close to you without defending the person.
more_concerning_if: The harm gets more serious across cycles while the warm stretches stay the same.
You are keeping the good memories like evidence for a defense case.
Mentioning the harm is answered with a tally of your own faults or of their kindnesses.
pattern_over_time_signs: You can predict the sweet period that follows an incident almost to the day.
Your account of the relationship to others has shrunk to the good parts, or to a story of ups and downs with no explanation.
You have become the person who reassures others that things are better than they sound.
Each time you consider leaving or asking for change, something warm arrives first.
codex_completed.repair_check: Compare what is different after a warm stretch with what was different before it. A change in how the person acts when angry, one that outlasts the sweetness, is repair. A very good week that leaves the cause untouched is only the same cycle again.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Does the good behavior continue after you state a limit, or does it drop away once the point has been made? Warmth that depends on you not raising the matter is a sign your boundary is being paid for with affection.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Attention goes first to facts that match the picture we hold of someone we love, and awkward facts get reread more kindly. Warmth arriving right after harm brings relief, and relief strengthens the hopeful story. The result can be a mind that collects the good evidence and files the harm as a one-off.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe defending the person to friends and then feeling confused at themselves, a private ledger of good days against bad, and a sense that their own instincts cannot be trusted. Some say the hardest part was that the good times were truly good.

response_options.soft_clarification: Say what you noticed and ask a question: 'Last month was hard and this week has been lovely. Can we talk about what is going to be different about the hard part?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Separate the apology from the pattern: 'I'm glad you're being kind. It doesn't change what happened, and I still need the thing that hurt me to stop.'
