response_options.disengagement: When a gift or sweet gesture arrives right after an incident, accept it quietly and do not treat it as having settled the matter. Wait a week before deciding what it means.
response_options.support_seeking: Give a trusted friend or counselor only the list of incidents, without the good moments, and ask for their honest reaction.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, keep a short dated record of the harmful incidents apart from the warm ones, so a manager or HR hears about the events themselves if you report.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I can see you are making an effort, and I appreciate it. I still want to talk about what happened on Saturday, because the kindness now doesn't change that it happened or make it okay."
codex_completed.safety_note: This cycle can sit alongside danger when the harmful incidents include threats, force, or control over where you go and who you see, because hope in the good stretch can make a risk harder to see. If that applies, tell a domestic abuse advocate about the whole cycle, including the good parts, and ask them about a private safety plan.
misuse_warning: Reading every kind act after a quarrel as a strategy punishes ordinary making-up. The cycle only counts as a pattern when harm and warmth keep alternating and the cause never changes.
Telling a friend that they are being exploited because they forgive someone easily can leave them defending the person harder. Describe what you saw, not what you assume about the other person.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Halo Effect Exploitation uses a single impressive trait or reputation, often one that the wider world admires, to excuse conduct in another area, while here the excusing material is the warmth that follows each incident. Premature Exclusivity concerns the speed of commitment at the start; this cycle shows up months or years in. Covert Contracts punishes breaking an unspoken rule, whereas here no rule is involved, only the alternation of harm and affection.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Halo Effect Exploitation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Pointing to someone's impressive achievement, talent or reputation as the answer to a concern that has nothing to do with it.
codex_completed.short_definition: Pointing to someone's impressive achievement, talent or reputation as the answer to a concern that has nothing to do with it.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: The halo effect is the ordinary habit of assuming that a person who is good at one thing is good in other ways too. In this pattern the habit is leaned on: a great reputation, a title, a charitable record or a charming manner gets offered whenever a worry about unrelated conduct is raised. A real track record does earn some benefit of the doubt. The trouble starts when it works as a standing exemption from scrutiny, and the person with the concern learns to keep quiet.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: When you raise a worry about how someone behaves, you are answered with how impressive, successful or well-liked they are, as if that settled it.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A concern gets weighed against a reputation instead of against the evidence for it, and you learn not to raise it before anyone else has even heard it. Other people with similar worries may stay silent because you did.
what_it_is: A reply to a complaint that cites the person's success, fame, kindness elsewhere, or standing instead of addressing what was reported.
A reputation that is real, which is part of why the answer feels persuasive.
A setting where the same person is trusted by many, so the person raising the concern expects to be doubted.
A pattern seen in workplaces, congregations, teams and families, wherever one person is admired by the group.
what_it_sounds_like: She's the best surgeon in the region. She would never mistreat a nurse.
He has raised thousands for charity. You can't mean that.
Do you know how many people he has mentored?
Our founder built this place from nothing. A bit of temper is the cost of that.
Everyone loves him. Maybe it's you.
I kept thinking about his award and told myself my complaint had to be small.
what_it_is_not: A person whose long, consistent record of good conduct makes a first complaint worth checking carefully, though it settles nothing by itself.
A colleague who says a person was excellent in a role and also agrees the specific complaint needs to be investigated.
Sincere admiration for a skill that is not offered as an answer to anything.
A character reference given to a court or panel as one input among others, which then examines the facts.
An honest surprise that someone you know well did something out of character.
this_may_be_it_when: The achievement mentioned has no bearing on the matter you raised.
Your concern is not examined, only met with a list of the person's credits.
People who express doubt are told they do not appreciate what the person has done.
You find yourself hesitating to speak because of how liked the person is.
The same defense appears whenever different people raise different concerns.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The person's record is directly relevant to what you are asking, such as a long safety record when the question is about safety.
People say 'that's a good record, and we are still going to look into this'.
The concern is looked at on its own and the finding is shared with you.
The admiration is expressed once and then drops out of the conversation.
The person admired is also the one asking for the matter to be investigated.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People who are honest in one area often are in others, and some trust is reasonable.
Friends of someone admired may be shocked and need time to take a complaint in.
Someone may mention a person's work because they are trying to give a fuller picture, not to end the discussion.
common_false_positives: A manager who weighs a first complaint against a spotless ten-year record and still opens an inquiry.
A friend who says 'that doesn't sound like her, can you tell me more?' and then listens to the answer.
A hiring panel that lists a candidate's strengths and still asks about the gap in the file.
discernment_questions: If I removed every achievement from the conversation, would my concern still be taken seriously?
Is the quality being praised related to what I reported, or does it belong to a different part of the person's life?
Has the concern itself been looked at by anyone?
Do I feel that raising it makes me ungrateful?
Are there others who share my worry but have kept it to themselves?
less_concerning_if: The person's reputation is mentioned alongside a real look at your concern.
You were able to say what you needed and someone acted on it.
Others who know the person well have heard the concern and taken it seriously.
more_concerning_if: Several people hold the same concern and none of them has said so out loud.
People who raise the concern lose standing, invitations or opportunities.
The person's status is used to decide who counts as a credible witness.
pattern_over_time_signs: Concerns about this person stop being raised because everyone expects the same answer.
New people are warned off criticism before they have any, and told how much the person has given the group.
You notice that you have started rehearsing the person's accomplishments before you speak.
Complaints that were made in the past are remembered as bitterness rather than as complaints.
codex_completed.repair_check: Watch what changes once you raise the matter again. If the achievements drop out and someone examines the specific complaint and tells you what they found, that is a different conversation. If the credentials return with a softer voice, the halo is still doing the work.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Does 'I need this looked at separately from their record' get accepted as a fair request? Respect looks like a promise to examine the matter by itself. Disrespect looks like a reminder of the person's standing, or a hint that you are the one being unfair.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A strong first impression or a standout trait can color the view of everything else about a person, so the admired one is assumed to be good all round. When a whole group shares that admiration, doubt can seem disloyal. That mix can move the burden of proof onto whoever raises a concern.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe doubting their own judgment, feeling isolated among a group that adores the person, and silencing themselves before anyone else can. Some say they watched others get treated well in ways they were not and wondered whether they had misread it.

response_options.soft_clarification: Acknowledge the record and separate it from the question: 'I know how much good she has done. I'm asking about what happened on Tuesday, which is a different thing.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to trade achievements for answers: 'Whatever he has accomplished, it doesn't answer what I reported. I'd like someone to look at that specific incident.'
response_options.disengagement: If a discussion becomes a recital of the person's merits, stop adding to it and take the matter to a different person or a formal channel.
response_options.support_seeking: Find out whether anyone else has had a similar experience, ideally one person at a time and away from the admiring group.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Put the concern in writing with dates and facts only, leave out opinions of the person's character, and send it to a channel that is not run by the admired person's supporters.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'm not questioning the good work. I'm asking for what happened on the third to be looked at by itself. Could someone who isn't close to him go through it with me?"
codex_completed.safety_note: A great reputation can make a report of serious harm, such as violence, abuse of someone vulnerable, or retaliation, harder to make and to have believed. If that is what you are carrying, go outside the group that admires the person: a legal aid service, an independent hotline, or an official body that handles complaints about that kind of role.
misuse_warning: Treating every well-liked, accomplished person with suspicion is a mistake. Reputation proves nothing either way, and the concern still needs to be looked at on its facts.
Dismissing a friend's sincere admiration as 'the halo effect' can silence honest, relevant testimony about someone's character.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Confirmation Bias Exploitation works through the warm, repeated stretches that follow each harmful event in a close relationship, while the halo here comes from standing, talent or reputation that other people share and that has nothing to do with the incident. Premature Exclusivity pushes a quick commitment; the halo is used to quiet doubt about conduct after the fact. Covert Contracts punishes breaking a rule never stated, which is a different problem from being talked out of a concern.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Covert Contracts
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Holding someone to rules or debts they never agreed to and were never told about, then punishing or shaming them when they fall short.
codex_completed.short_definition: Holding someone to rules or debts they never agreed to and were never told about, then punishing or shaming them when they fall short.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A covert contract is an agreement that exists only in one person's head: a rule about how often you call, what you share, or what you owe after past favors. Nobody names it, yet breaking it brings a penalty. Obligation Contracts describes this very thing, stressing debts and loyalty enforced through shame and duty. One misunderstood expectation means little. What stands out is new unwritten rules that keep surfacing only after you break them.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You are expected to follow rules nobody told you, or to repay debts nobody named, and you find out only when you are punished or shamed for missing them.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You are judged against a standard you were never shown, so effort never buys safety: there is always another rule you have not been told. Questioning a supposed debt gets treated as disloyalty, not as a fair question about what you agreed to.
what_it_is: A rule that exists only in one person's expectations, such as answering messages within the hour or never turning down a family event.
A debt assumed from the past: favors, money or sacrifices are counted as owed back, though nobody said they were loans.
Discovered only by breaking it. The first sign of the rule is the anger, the silence or the lecture that follows.
Enforced through shame and duty language rather than a request, so questioning it sounds like betrayal.
Found in families, friendships, couples, teams and communities, anywhere closeness or loyalty is simply assumed.
what_it_sounds_like: I shouldn't have to ask. You should just know.
After everything I've done for you, this is the least you owe me.
We never talked about it, but I assumed you understood how we do things.
Why would I have to tell you to call me first? It's obvious.
A good daughter wouldn't even ask whether she has to come.
Once you're part of this group, you don't need to be asked to show up.
You find out about a rule only when you are met with a week of silence for breaking it.
what_it_is_not: Some expectations are shared widely enough that most people would recognize them unstated, such as telling a housemate you will be out overnight. Someone who adjusts readily once told the rule was never communicated is having a miscommunication, not enforcing one.
Long relationships build genuine mutual obligations that both people would describe the same way if asked separately.
Honest hurt that an assumed closeness was not there, said once as hurt and not as a charge.
A spoken or written promise that was forgotten or dropped. That is a broken agreement, not a hidden one.
A family or cultural custom you know about and have chosen to honor, even when it costs you.
this_may_be_it_when: You learn a rule exists only when you are punished for breaking it.
The rule is unusual or one-sided, and nobody else in your position would have guessed it.
When you ask what was agreed, you get hurt or anger in place of an answer.
Past help is raised as a standing debt, with no total and no end in sight.
Each time you meet one expectation, another appears behind it.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Once the expectation is named, you can discuss it, change it or decline it without a penalty.
They say 'I assumed you knew, sorry' and are open to dropping the assumption.
Most people in your circle would have guessed the expectation without being told.
The favors they mention were offered as gifts and are not brought up again.
Both of you would describe the arrangement the same way if asked separately.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People raised in different families carry different unspoken rules, and each can assume theirs is obvious.
Someone who gave generously may feel unseen and say so clumsily, in the language of debt.
Early in a relationship nobody has said how often to call or how to split chores, so assumptions fill the gap.
common_false_positives: A housemate annoyed that you ate their labeled food, which most households treat as understood.
A friend hurt that you missed their wedding, who accepts your reason and talks it through.
A grandparent's Sunday dinner that you have always known about and can openly decline.
discernment_questions: Could a fair person have guessed this expectation without being told?
Do I learn about these rules only by breaking them?
If I say I never agreed to this, does that start a conversation or count as an offense?
Does the debt have a size and an end, or does it grow with every favor?
Does the person hold themselves to the same rule?
less_concerning_if: The expectation is a reasonable one that you can renegotiate once it is named.
Their annoyance fades once the misunderstanding is explained.
The rule applies to them as well.
more_concerning_if: The penalty comes first and the explanation, if any, comes after.
Declining the expectation brings the loss of help you rely on, such as housing, money or contact with family.
Other people are told you are ungrateful or disloyal before you have had a chance to explain.
pattern_over_time_signs: You start asking permission or checking the mood before doing ordinary things.
The list of what you owe grows, while your own needs are described as selfish.
You scan for the next unwritten rule, and can no longer tell which ones are real.
Past favors resurface in unrelated arguments as the reason you cannot say no.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair starts with the rules being said aloud: what was expected, where it came from, and a plain admission that you were never asked. After that you get a real vote on which ones stay. Being thanked for finally understanding, while the debt stays open, is the same contract in new words.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: When you say you never agreed to something, does the other person ask what you would agree to? Watch what declining costs you afterwards: a cold week, a story told to others, a favor withdrawn. A boundary that is honored leaves the next ordinary day intact.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Shame and duty are strong motivators, and few people want to be the ungrateful one. When rules are never stated, you cannot check them, argue with them, or meet them once and be done. That can keep your attention on guessing what is wanted, and the sense of owing can make saying no feel like a moral failing instead of a choice.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe walking on eggshells, over-explaining ordinary choices, and feeling guilty with no clear reason. Some say they keep paying a debt whose size they never learned. Others describe a late moment of recognition, looking back and seeing that a whole set of expectations had been made on their behalf.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the rule in plain words: 'I didn't know that was expected. Can you tell me what you were hoping for, so we can talk about it?'
response_options.firm_boundary: State what you did and did not agree to: 'I never agreed to that, so I can't treat it as settled. I am willing to talk about what I can offer.'
response_options.disengagement: When the debt is raised again in an unrelated argument, stop that thread, and come back to the original topic later or in writing.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe the expectations to someone outside the relationship and ask whether they would have guessed them. If not, you have learned something about the rule, not about your character.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask for unwritten expectations about hours, availability or duties to be put in writing, and keep the reply with its date.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I didn't know that was something you expected, and I don't think I agreed to it. I'm happy to talk about what I can do, and I want us to say it out loud so we both know where we stand."
codex_completed.safety_note: Unspoken rules you never agreed to are mostly a pressure-and-guilt problem. It changes if refusing a hidden rule brings threats, loss of housing or money, being cut off from other people, or fear. In that case, keep dated notes of what was demanded and what followed, and ask an advocate or legal aid service about your housing or money position before you change anything.
misuse_warning: Calling a friend's disappointment a covert contract can dismiss a fair request. Ask whether the expectation was reasonable and whether they accepted it once it was named.
Using this label to escape obligations you knowingly took on, such as a promise or shared bills, turns a useful term into an excuse.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Premature Exclusivity asks for commitment out loud and early, before you know enough, while a covert contract asks for nothing aloud and is revealed by the penalty, at any stage. Financial Dependence by Design builds real economic reliance, whereas a covert contract works through duty and shame even when no money is involved. Halo Effect Exploitation uses someone's good name to excuse harm; here a person's good deeds are counted as a debt you owe.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Financial Dependence by Design
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Arranging money, work and access to accounts so that one person cannot manage without the other, whatever either of them feels about the relationship.
codex_completed.short_definition: Arranging money, work and access to accounts so that one person cannot manage without the other, whatever either of them feels about the relationship.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: This describes a household or organization where one person ends up with no income of their own, no standing on the accounts, no recent work history or no knowledge of the finances. Many households divide earning and caring by choice, and illness, caregiving or a poor job market can limit independence without anyone arranging it. The concern grows when steps toward independence, such as a job, a course, a card in your own name, meet resistance, and the arrangement makes leaving a matter of survival.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Money, work and accounts are set up so that you could not support yourself if you left, and steps toward your own income or knowledge are discouraged.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Leaving becomes a question of survival and not of judgment, so whatever you conclude about the relationship, the conclusion cannot change anything. Fear about housing, food and children can keep a person in place for years.
what_it_is: An arrangement in which one person has no income, no access to savings, or no name on the accounts and the home.
Discouragement or obstruction of paid work, training, a driving license or a bank account of your own.
A situation where you are given an allowance, asked to account for purchases, or kept unaware of debts and assets.
Found in couples, in families that run a business together, and in some workplaces or communities where pay is withheld or tied to staying.
what_it_sounds_like: You don't need to work. I'll take care of everything.
Why would you need your own account? Ours is fine.
Receipts, please. I want to see where every dollar went.
If you take that course, who is going to look after the house?
Don't worry about the bills. It's too complicated for you.
My card was declined and I realized I didn't know which accounts I was on.
what_it_is_not: A household that divides earning and caring by shared agreement, where each person understands the money and can reach it.
Caregiving, illness, a disability or a poor job market limiting independence without anyone arranging it.
A partner who handles the bills because they like it and who shows you everything when you ask.
A couple pooling money by agreement and keeping separate access for emergencies.
A budget that is tight for both people, with both people affected equally by it.
this_may_be_it_when: Your wish for work or study is met with resistance that is out of proportion to the practical issue.
You are unable to see statements, passwords or the household's debts.
Your wages, benefits or documents are held by someone else.
You could not pay rent and food for a month if the other person stopped contributing.
Asking about money brings anger, silence or a reminder of how much they provide.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You can see and use every account and know where things are kept.
Plans for you to work or study are treated as a practical matter to solve together.
The dependence began because of a health crisis or caregiving and both of you want it to change.
You have your own money and a way to get at it that they know about and accept.
Questions about money are answered plainly, even when the answers are awkward.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Parents at home with young children often rely on one income through a joint decision.
One partner may take on the finances because the other dislikes or struggles with them.
Someone recovering from illness or an immigration delay may be unable to work for a time.
common_false_positives: A single-income household where both people see the accounts and agree about the plan.
A partner who is worried about a risky course or job and says so, but accepts your decision.
A family business where relatives are paid late because of a bad year, and everyone is affected.
discernment_questions: Could I get hold of money, ID and a place to stay tomorrow without anyone's permission?
What happened the last time I talked about getting a job, a course or my own account?
Do I know what we own and owe, and could I find out without a fight?
Has the household got into a position where only one of us can leave?
Is the money arrangement something we chose, or something I found myself in?
less_concerning_if: Both people can see the whole financial picture and either could change the arrangement without penalty.
Steps toward independence are met with practical help and not with obstacles.
The reliance on one income has a plan and an end date that both people made.
more_concerning_if: Money is used to reward, punish or control what you do, who you see or where you go.
Work, school or your own account is discouraged, sabotaged, or paid for with conflict.
You are afraid of what would happen to housing, food or the children if you stopped complying.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your own income, savings and work history get smaller over the years.
More accounts, debts or property arrive in one person's name only.
Each attempt at independence meets a fresh obstacle, such as lost transport, a sudden crisis or a change in the rules.
You find you keep less money, fewer contacts and less information than you once did.
codex_completed.repair_check: Real change shows in access, not apologies: your name on the accounts, your wages in your hands, statements you can read, a job or course you can take without a fight. A promise to do better that leaves everything arranged as before has not altered anything.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice what follows a request about money, such as seeing a statement or keeping some of your pay. When it is handled as an ordinary request, the money is open. When it brings anger, a lecture or a new restriction, the arrangement is defending itself.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When a person has no money, no recent work history and no knowledge of the accounts, the cost of leaving rises with each year, and options that look possible from outside may not be possible in practice. A gradual loss of income and confidence can make dependence feel like a fact about you rather than about the arrangement.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Accounts of this include feeling trapped, ashamed about not earning, anxious about every request for money, and unsure how they would cope alone. Some report that they gave up imagining a different life, because every version needed money they did not have.

response_options.soft_clarification: If you judge it safe, ask for ordinary information in ordinary words, such as 'Could you show me where our money is kept, in case something happens to you?' Notice how the answer is given.
response_options.firm_boundary: If it is safe to do so, keep one small piece of independence, such as a course, a few friends or an account you are named on, and treat it as routine without arguing its merits.
response_options.disengagement: Rather than announcing anything, build options quietly and privately: keep copies of your own ID with someone you trust, and learn what benefits or housing help exists where you live.
response_options.support_seeking: Speak to a domestic abuse or financial abuse advocate, a legal aid service or a credit counselor, and ask about a private plan before you change anything at home.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If pay, housing or documents are tied to a boss or sponsor, keep dated records of hours and payments and contact a labor rights group, union or legal clinic.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I've been thinking I should know more about how our bills and accounts work, in case anything happens to you. Could you show me sometime when it suits you?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Watch for money being used to control where you go, threats to cut off housing, food or children's needs, debts placed in your name without your knowledge, or fear when you ask about finances. A domestic violence advocate can plan privately with you, including how to build savings and records safely. Ask the advocate which phone and email are safe to use for that first contact.
misuse_warning: Describing every division of household income as a trap can insult people who chose it freely and dismiss real caregiving work. Ask who can see the money and what happens when you try to change it.
Telling someone in this position to simply earn their own money overlooks the obstacles that may be in the way and can add shame.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Covert Contracts punishes you for breaking rules nobody told you about, while this pattern is about whether you can get at money and survive on your own. Platform Migration concerns where conversations happen and what record exists. Premature Exclusivity is a quick push to commit; here the commitment may be long made and the issue is that you have no way out of it.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Platform Migration
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Steering a conversation from messages or email onto calls, disappearing-message apps or in-person talk when the topic is one that might later be quoted back.
codex_completed.short_definition: Steering a conversation from messages or email onto calls, disappearing-message apps or in-person talk when the topic is one that might later be quoted back.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Platform migration is the repeated move of a conversation away from anywhere a record is kept. It might be a request to call instead of write, a switch to an app where messages vanish, or an insistence on discussing things in person. Plenty of people prefer to talk by voice, and some platforms have real privacy problems. The pattern is in what moves: ordinary logistics stay in writing, while promises, accusations, money and disputes are the topics steered off the record.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Easy topics stay in text, but the serious ones, like promises or complaints, are moved to a call, a vanishing-message app or a face-to-face talk where nothing is saved.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You lose the record, so any later dispute about what was said becomes your word against someone else's, with the whole burden of remembering exactly falling on you. Promises that were never written down are easy to dispute.
what_it_is: A repeated switch from written messages to calls, voice notes that expire, disappearing-message apps or meetings in person.
A switch that tends to happen at the moment a subject involves a commitment, a complaint, a payment or an agreement.
A pattern that can appear at work, in a landlord or tenant dispute, in a relationship, or between a buyer and a seller.
Something that can be done politely and with a reason, which is why it often passes without notice.
what_it_sounds_like: Let's not get into this over text. Call me.
Can we switch to the other app? This one is a bit slow.
I'd rather explain in person than put it in an email.
I don't do messages for things like this. It's easier to talk.
Delete that thread, it's getting messy.
After our call, I realized there was nothing I could point to for what he promised.
what_it_is_not: A person who prefers voice or in-person talk for anything weighty and applies that to every topic, including dull ones.
A privacy concern about a particular app or a workplace policy that really does restrict written channels.
A call that is followed by a written summary from either side, such as 'to confirm what we agreed'.
Someone who finds written arguments escalate and wants to speak to defuse them.
An organization where sensitive matters go to a formal meeting by rule, with minutes kept.
this_may_be_it_when: Small matters stay in writing while promises and complaints are moved elsewhere.
A request for written confirmation after a call is brushed aside or answered with irritation.
You are asked to delete messages or to use an app with disappearing messages.
The same person has previously denied things you remember being said.
You notice that the only records you have are the ones from before the move.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The person talks to you by voice about everything, trivial or serious.
They are glad to send a written recap after a call and accept your corrections.
The reason given for the move is real and applies to everyone, such as a security rule at their workplace.
You were the one who asked to call, and they readily agreed to a written follow-up.
Nothing in the conversation depends on exactly what was said.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Tone is hard to read in text, so people sometimes call to avoid a misunderstanding.
Some people dislike typing, have poor eyesight, or find writing stressful.
Employers, clinics and security teams often forbid discussing certain matters in unmanaged channels.
common_false_positives: A friend who always phones instead of texting, about everything from lunch to a diagnosis.
A colleague who proposes a short call to resolve a fiddly email thread and then sends notes.
A person who avoids a messaging app after a data breach and has said so for months.
discernment_questions: Does the move happen for every topic, or only the ones I might want proof of later?
What happens if I ask to confirm the call in writing?
Has this person denied or changed something they said before, in a way I could not check?
Is there a real reason for the change that they would give anyone?
What would I lose if this conversation could not be proven later?
less_concerning_if: The preference for calls or in-person talk is consistent across every kind of topic.
A written summary follows the call and neither side objects to it.
The reason for the switch is clearly stated and tied to a real rule or concern.
more_concerning_if: You are asked to delete messages, hand over your phone, or use a channel where records vanish.
Requests for a written summary are met with annoyance or a change of subject.
Matters involving money, housing, work or safety are the ones kept off the record.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your written trail has gaps exactly where the important agreements should be.
Things you recall being promised are described as never having been said.
More of the relationship, dispute or deal is conducted over channels with no history.
You start taking your own notes after calls, because there is nothing else to rely on.
codex_completed.repair_check: A record now exists. If the person agrees to confirm important points in writing, sends the summary, and does not fight when you correct it, the pattern has eased. A promise to be more open that still routes hard topics to calls has not.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: When you say you would like a topic kept in writing, notice what comes next. A reasonable alternative, such as a short recap after the call, shows the request was heard. A sulk, a joke that closes the subject, or a call that happens anyway, tells you the request was not.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Spoken words and vanishing messages leave no shared record, so memory becomes the only evidence, and memory is easy to doubt. When one person is unsure what exactly was said, they may defer to whoever sounds most certain. The loss of a record can therefore shift the weight of any later disagreement toward the person who remembers it their way.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe replaying conversations to check what was promised, taking notes in secret, doubting their memory, and feeling foolish for having no proof. Some say the missing record made it harder to ask anyone else for help because they had nothing to show.

response_options.soft_clarification: Offer a way to have both: 'A call is fine. Could you send me a short message afterwards so I have the details straight?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold your position on specific subjects: 'For anything involving money or dates, I'll need it in writing. I'm happy to talk first.'
response_options.disengagement: If a topic keeps moving off the record, write your own summary of each call and send it the same day, then continue only with what has been confirmed.
response_options.support_seeking: Keep your own dated notes after each call and show them to a trusted friend or adviser who can check whether they match what you remember.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, follow a call with an email beginning 'To confirm what we discussed', and keep a copy outside the workplace system if your policy allows it.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "A phone call works for me. After we hang up I'll send a short note of what we agreed, so we both have the same version. Tell me if I get anything wrong."
codex_completed.safety_note: Moving off the record usually matters for disputes, not for danger. It becomes a concern when it accompanies threats, demands to delete messages, or pressure to use a phone or app the other person can look through. If that happens, keep copies of what you have somewhere safe and talk to an advocate or legal clinic before changing how you communicate.
misuse_warning: Treating any request for a phone call as evasion will make you distrust people who simply prefer to talk. Look at which topics move and how they react to a written recap.
Recording a call secretly may be illegal where you live. Check the rules before relying on it, and write notes instead if unsure.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Covert Contracts holds you to expectations that were never said aloud at all, whereas here something was said and the record of it disappears. Financial Dependence by Design is about control of money and access, while this is about where talk happens. Halo Effect Exploitation answers a concern by pointing to someone's standing in other people's eyes; this one takes away the trail you would need to show those people.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: "Sacred Duty" Manipulation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Presenting an ordinary request as a spiritual, moral or ancestral obligation, so that saying no is treated as a sin or a betrayal.
codex_completed.short_definition: Presenting an ordinary request as a spiritual, moral or ancestral obligation, so that saying no is treated as a sin or a betrayal.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Faith, ancestry and family duty are real values, and a person who speaks from conviction about their own obligations is not doing this. In this pattern the language of the sacred is attached to a request that happens to benefit the person making it, such as caring for them, giving money, staying in a marriage, or giving up a plan. Refusal then reads as a failure of faith or of loyalty, and the usual routes for disagreement are closed. The tell is whether the sacred framing appears for every request or only some.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A request is dressed up as a duty to God, your ancestors or your family, so that saying no feels like a moral failing and not an ordinary choice.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Refusal stops being a preference and becomes a moral failure, so you cannot decline without feeling you have done something wrong, and you often cannot appeal to anyone inside your own community.
what_it_is: A request framed as something God, scripture, ancestors or the community demand of you, when it is also what one person wants.
A moral argument offered in place of a conversation about what you can afford, want or are able to give.
A framing that draws on beliefs you may hold sincerely, which is why it carries weight.
Something that can occur in families, congregations, communities and groups, wherever shared values give a request extra authority.
what_it_sounds_like: God has asked this of you, and you are saying no?
Our ancestors gave up everything. The least you can do is give up this job.
A good daughter does not question her mother.
It's your duty to forgive and stay. That's what a faithful wife does.
If you really believed, you wouldn't need to think about it.
I said no and felt as if I had committed a sin, even though I didn't know what I had done wrong.
what_it_is_not: A person speaking sincerely about their own faith and obligations without expecting you to act on them.
A shared tradition you also hold and freely choose to honor, such as caring for elders or tithing.
A religious leader or relative who gives guidance, hears your disagreement, and accepts that you may decide differently.
A cultural expectation of family support that applies to everyone and that you were able to talk about openly.
A moral appeal that you find persuasive on its merits after thinking it over.
this_may_be_it_when: The sacred language comes up for requests that benefit the speaker but not for others.
Disagreement is answered with questions about your faith or loyalty and not with the substance of what you said.
You are warned about moral or spiritual consequences if you say no.
The obligation is stricter for you than for other members of the same family or community.
You find it hard to describe the request apart from the religious wording.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The same duty is applied to everyone, including the person asking.
They hear your reasons and stay respectful when you decline.
The obligation is one you hold yourself, whether or not anyone mentions it.
Doubt and questions are welcomed in your community, and people who decline are not shunned.
The request is small, open to negotiation, and not tied to your standing.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People who hold deep convictions naturally talk about duty in religious or ancestral terms.
Elders raised in a culture of obligation may sincerely know no other way to ask.
A relative in distress may reach for the vocabulary of faith because it is the one they have.
common_false_positives: A parent who says 'it would mean a lot to me as part of our faith' and accepts your reply.
A congregation that expects regular giving and says so openly, with no penalty for those who cannot.
A family whose custom of caring for aging relatives is shared by all the siblings, who negotiate the details.
discernment_questions: Does this kind of moral language come up for everything, or only for what one person wants?
Can I say no to this request and still be respected in my community?
Do I hold this belief myself, or have I mainly been told I should?
Is anyone else held to the same duty, or is it mine alone?
Would the request look different without the religious or ancestral wording?
less_concerning_if: You share the belief and chose the obligation yourself.
The people who ask also hold themselves to the same duty.
You can decline or adjust the request and keep your place.
more_concerning_if: Saying no costs you your standing, your family's support, or your place in the community.
The duty is used to keep you in a situation where you are being hurt, or to stop you getting help from outside.
Leaders or relatives treat questions about the request as proof of weak faith.
pattern_over_time_signs: The list of things you owe grows, and each addition is put in sacred terms.
You feel guilt or dread before you even say no.
Your own wishes, work, study or friendships have been given up in turn for duties.
People who once declined similar requests are spoken of as having failed.
codex_completed.repair_check: Pay attention to whether the request can be talked about without the sacred language. If the person can state what they need, hear what you can give and accept a smaller answer without calling you faithless, something has changed. A sorry that arrives with a fresh appeal to duty has not.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: What you can learn from a 'no' here is whether your reasons are heard. If they are met with talk about the request itself, that is respect. If the response is a reminder of what God, family or ancestors expect, the boundary is being treated as a spiritual failing.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Beliefs about duty, sin and loyalty often sit deep, are tied to belonging, and are held with feeling. A request carrying that weight can bypass the usual weighing of costs, because declining seems to risk more than the request itself: guilt, rejection, or the loss of your community. Such framing tends to work best where the person's belief is sincere.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe guilt out of proportion to the request, a sense of being split between their own life and their faith or family, and a reluctance to speak to anyone in the community. Some say they came to doubt their own beliefs because of how those beliefs had been invoked, and others say it was painful to separate the belief from the request.

response_options.soft_clarification: Speak from your own faith and separate it from the request: 'I take this seriously, and I don't think it requires me to give up my job. Can we talk about what you actually need?'
response_options.firm_boundary: State the limit without arguing doctrine: 'I can help with groceries on Sundays. I can't take on more than that, and I'd like to leave the question of faith out of it.'
response_options.disengagement: If the conversation turns to your faith or character, you can say you will think about it and take time away before replying.
response_options.support_seeking: Speak to someone you respect in your tradition who is not part of the request, such as another elder or a counselor who understands your faith, and ask what they think the duty requires.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a colleague or supervisor cites religion or culture to ask for extra work, bring it back to the written duties of the job and speak to HR if it continues.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I do care about our family and my faith, and I've thought this through. I can help in the ways I've said. I'm not able to do more, and that doesn't mean I've stopped believing."
codex_completed.safety_note: This is not usually a physical danger on its own. It deserves more care when the duty is used to keep you in a marriage with abuse, to arrange a marriage you do not want, or to cut you off from help, because leaving can then risk your community and home. In those cases, speak privately to an advocate who understands your faith or culture.
misuse_warning: Calling a sincere religious or cultural expectation manipulation can be disrespectful to the person and the tradition. The question is whether you can decline without penalty and whether the framing is used selectively.
Using the label to dismiss anyone who invokes faith overlooks that many people feel their obligations deeply and ask for help in good faith.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Covert Contracts holds you to expectations nobody ever said, but here the expectation is said loudly and given a moral name. Financial Dependence by Design is about control of money and the means to leave, whereas this works through guilt and belonging and may involve no money. Halo Effect Exploitation relies on someone's reputation, while here the authority comes from a shared belief.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Shame-as-Governance Disguised as Advice
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Criticism of a person's character, offered as helpful guidance, that leaves them feeling smaller and makes objecting sound ungrateful.
codex_completed.short_definition: Criticism of a person's character, offered as helpful guidance, that leaves them feeling smaller and makes objecting sound ungrateful.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: This is moral judgment delivered in the voice of help. The advice may be about money, parenting, appearance, work or faith, and it often arrives unasked. What sets it apart is what you are left holding: a verdict on who you are, not something you can do. Because it is framed as care, saying it stung can be answered with 'I was only trying to help.' One clumsy remark means little. Repetition is what matters: the advice keeps landing on your character, and each objection is taken as proof you cannot take guidance.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone gives you advice that is really a judgment of what kind of person you are, and if you flinch, they say they were only helping.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You come away smaller instead of better equipped, and your objection is answered before you make it, because it was only ever offered as help. Over time you may stop bringing things to them, or start hearing their voice in your own head.
what_it_is: Advice with a verdict on character attached, such as 'a more organized person wouldn't have this problem.'
Offered without being asked, often in front of other people or when you are already low.
Framed as concern, so a hurt reaction can be recast as ingratitude or defensiveness.
Tied to a picture of how a good parent, partner, employee or believer behaves, with you falling short of it.
Heard most from people with some standing over you, such as relatives, senior colleagues or community elders, though peers use it too.
what_it_sounds_like: I'm only telling you this because I care, but a responsible mother wouldn't have let it get that far.
No offense, but people like you never learn until someone is blunt with them.
I'm saying this for your own good: you're careless with money and everyone can see it.
Why are you so defensive? I was trying to help.
Somebody has to say it. You've really let yourself go.
You should be grateful I'm honest with you.
what_it_is_not: Feedback that is unwelcome in the moment but names one specific behavior and a way to change it.
A clumsy delivery from someone who cares and adjusts once they hear how it landed.
A mentor or manager giving a hard assessment of your work in a setting where that is expected.
A friend saying 'I'm worried about how much you're drinking' and then listening to your answer.
Advice you asked for, even when the honest answer hurt.
The usable test is what you are left holding afterwards: something to do, or only something to feel.
this_may_be_it_when: After the conversation you have a feeling about yourself but nothing you could actually do next.
The comments describe your character, as lazy, selfish or careless, instead of a behavior or a situation.
The same kind of advice returns on the same topic whether or not anything has changed.
Saying it hurt gets 'I was only trying to help' and the talk turns to your reaction.
The advice is given in front of others, so answering back would make you look prickly.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They name one specific thing and what might help, then leave the choice with you.
You asked for their honest view first.
When you say it landed badly, they ask what they got wrong and change how they put it.
They give the same candid feedback to people they hold in high regard.
You finish the conversation with a clearer next step, even an unpleasant one.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Someone raised in a blunt household may believe harshness is how care sounds.
People often give advice to ease their own worry, and clumsy words can come out of that.
Families and cultures differ on how direct advice may be, and what feels shaming to you may be ordinary to them.
common_false_positives: A performance review that is hard to read but lists specific, fixable points.
A doctor, coach or teacher who is frank about your habits within their role.
A friend who repeats a worry because the thing they worry about is still happening.
discernment_questions: After this advice, do I know one thing I could do, or only that I feel worse?
Is it about something I did, or about what kind of person I am?
When I say it stung, do they get curious, or am I told I'm too sensitive?
Does the advice come with any offer of help, or only with a judgment?
Would they say this in the same words to someone whose opinion they fear?
less_concerning_if: The advice is specific, and you can act on it or decline it without a penalty.
They change their wording when you tell them how it sounded.
You can say no thank you and the relationship stays warm.
more_concerning_if: Turning down the advice is treated as a flaw in you, with disapproval that lingers.
Other people hear about your shortcomings 'out of concern' before you do.
You rehearse before telling them anything about your life, expecting a judgment.
pattern_over_time_signs: You stop sharing news, problems and decisions with them because disclosure leads to a lecture.
Their voice turns up in your head over ordinary choices, such as what to buy or how to word an email.
Advice arrives when you are already struggling and rarely when things go well.
Going along earns warmth, acting independently earns a cooler reception, and you begin to notice the difference.
codex_completed.repair_check: A mended version starts with them asking how the advice sounded from your side, then dropping the commentary on your character and keeping only specifics you can use. A 'sorry you felt that way' followed by the same lecture next month is not that.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Look at the next piece of advice after you said it stung. Is it about a task, and does it come only when you invite it? Then something shifted. If the lectures return in new wording, or you are now told you cannot take guidance, nothing has.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Shame is a social signal that you may be falling out of good standing, and most people are quick to act on it. Criticism aimed at who you are, rather than what you did, can set that signal off without giving you anything to fix. Calling it help can make arguing back feel like proof of the fault.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: After conversations that were meant to help, you may feel smaller and second-guess choices you were comfortable with. Asking for advice can start to feel risky. Some find they scold themselves in the other person's phrasing. The mismatch between kind words and a bad feeling afterwards can be confusing in itself.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask what the advice is meant to help with: 'What would you want me to do differently?' A specific answer can be worked with. A reply about what kind of person you are shows where the conversation is heading.
response_options.firm_boundary: Separate the advice from the verdict: 'I'm willing to hear what you'd suggest. I'm not willing to hear what it says about my character.'
response_options.disengagement: When advice turns into a comment on who you are, change the subject or end the call for the day, and keep that part of your life to yourself for a while.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone outside the relationship what was said, word for word, and ask how it sounds to them. Hearing it in another voice often makes the verdict part easy to spot.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If it comes from a manager, ask for feedback in terms of observable work: 'Can you point to the specific piece, and what good would look like?' Jot down dates and wording afterwards.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I do want input on this. What I can use is something specific about what I did and what you would try. I can't use comments about what kind of person I am. If we stay with the first kind, I'm glad to talk."
codex_completed.safety_note: Advice that shames is a wounding pattern, not a danger signal. That would change if the 'advice' begins to come with control over your money, contacts or movements, or with fear of what happens when you decline it. If so, talk with a counselor or advocate who knows controlling relationships before you decide anything.
misuse_warning: Calling any blunt feedback shaming can excuse you from hearing something true. Ask whether it named a behavior you could change.
Telling someone their well-meant advice is 'shame as governance' hands them a verdict on their motives, which the words on the table cannot show.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: PIP Weaponization puts a formal performance process, with deadlines and paperwork, around the judgment, while this uses friendly advice and leaves nothing written. Overcorrection Demands asks for a large apology or payment after a small lapse; this one offers a lesson and hands you a verdict. What defines this tactic is a judgment of your character dressed as help.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: PIP Weaponization
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A formal performance improvement plan that, in practice, sets goals the person cannot meet and builds a record toward their exit.
codex_completed.short_definition: A formal performance improvement plan that, in practice, sets goals the person cannot meet and builds a record toward their exit.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A performance improvement plan, or PIP, is a written process with goals, a timeline and check-ins. Done well, it gives someone a fair chance to close a real gap. It is also a document that can later be used to justify ending a job. The pattern is seen when goals are vague or keep moving, promised support is missing, feedback arrives too late to act on, and the plan follows a complaint, a medical leave or a request for adjustments. A plan alone means little. What matters is whether it could realistically be passed.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A workplace improvement plan with goals that are hard to meet or keep shifting, so the paperwork ends up supporting a dismissal.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You are set a target you may not be able to hit while a record of your exit is being assembled. Defending yourself means arguing against a document that already exists, and your income and references may depend on the outcome.
what_it_is: A formal, written plan with deadlines, usually presented as a chance to improve.
Goals that are subjective ('improve attitude'), moving, or stricter than those for peers in the same job.
Check-in notes written by one side, which may become the main evidence if the job ends.
Often begins soon after a complaint, a leave of absence, a request for accommodation or a disagreement with a boss.
Sometimes ends in an offer to resign with a package, which leaves the plan's fairness never tested.
what_it_sounds_like: We want you to succeed, so we're putting some expectations in writing. Please sign here.
The goal is to improve your communication. We'll know it when we see it.
That target was updated last week. You'll be measured against the new figure.
Your last update was late, so we're logging that.
We can't share what others on the team are held to.
Your manager's notes from the first three weeks reach you today, nine days before the review.
HR advised that this is the standard process.
what_it_is_not: A genuine performance gap handled properly: clear goals, real support and honest timelines are how formal plans are meant to work.
A plan that follows several documented earlier conversations about the same gap.
Timing that happens to follow a complaint but rests on problems recorded beforehand and reviewed by someone independent.
A short informal coaching note, which is not a formal plan.
A plan applied in the same way to others in the same role with the same gap.
A hard but fair target where your own work log shows the shortfall.
this_may_be_it_when: The plan appeared within weeks of a complaint, a leave or a request for adjustments.
Goals cannot be measured, or change once you start meeting them.
The support promised, such as training or a reduced load, does not appear.
Your reviews were fine until shortly before the plan.
Colleagues in similar roles with similar numbers were not put on one.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The shortfall is documented in earlier reviews, with dates that predate any complaint.
Goals are numbers or tasks you can check yourself, and they stay fixed.
Your manager meets you regularly, gives feedback with time to act, and records progress when you make it.
Peers with comparable gaps have been through the same process.
You privately agree the gap is real and the plan is a fair map of it.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Managers are often told by their HR team to put concerns in writing, even when they hope you will improve.
A new manager may find old problems nobody wrote down and use a plan to make them visible.
Business pressure, such as a lost contract, can sharpen targets for a whole team.
common_false_positives: A coaching plan you asked for after missing a promotion.
A probation review with set targets, which is ordinary in many new jobs.
A written warning about one specific lapse, such as breaking a safety rule, which is not a development plan.
discernment_questions: What happened in the weeks before the plan: a complaint, a leave, a conflict?
Can I say in plain terms what passing looks like?
Have the goals changed since I started meeting them?
Do peers with similar results face the same process?
Is the support described in the plan actually being given?
less_concerning_if: The plan names the gaps in measurable terms and sets a date for review.
Support such as training, mentoring or fewer duties is provided on time.
Other employees in similar situations have been through the same steps, and some have passed.
more_concerning_if: The plan follows a complaint, medical leave, injury or request for adjustment.
Passing seems ruled out, since targets rise as you meet them.
You are asked to sign statements agreeing to facts you dispute, or to resign before the plan ends.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your calendar fills with meetings about the plan, leaving less time for the work being judged.
Small slips that went unrecorded before are now logged.
Colleagues hear less about your projects, or begin to keep their distance.
You start writing down everything you do, in case you need to prove it later.
codex_completed.repair_check: Fair handling shows in changes to the plan itself: goals rewritten so they can be measured, missed support supplied, and credit given when you hit a target. An apology in a meeting, followed by the same moving goalposts, only mends the mood.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Watch what happens when you ask for the goals in measurable terms. If they are rewritten clearly and held still, the request was taken seriously. If the answer is that you are being difficult, or that the plan is standard and cannot change, the question was treated as resistance.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A formal document carries weight because it looks neutral. When a plan lands on someone already worried about their job, fear can narrow attention to the plan and leave less energy for the work itself, which can make the shortfalls it describes more likely. Being measured against shifting goals can also make it hard to know what effort will count.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Dread before each check-in meeting, broken sleep, doubt about work you used to be proud of and a sense of being watched are common accounts. Some start to see themselves through the plan's words. Money worry can crowd out everything else, including the search for a new job.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for clarity in writing: 'Could you spell out what meeting this goal looks like, and how it will be measured?' Their answer gives you both something to hold to.
response_options.firm_boundary: Say plainly that you want to meet the plan, that you need the targets fixed in writing before the next review, and that the support it promises should start.
response_options.disengagement: Keep contact with the person who wrote the plan to scheduled check-ins, and send a short follow-up message afterwards recording what was said, so you are not relying on memory.
response_options.support_seeking: Speak confidentially with a trusted colleague outside your reporting line, a union representative if you have one, or an employment advice service before signing anything. Ask whether the plan looks ordinary for your workplace.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Keep a dated note of what you were asked, what you delivered and any praise, somewhere you can still reach if your access ends, and ask HR how to attach your own comments to the plan file.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Passing this plan is my aim. For that I need each goal written so I can tell when I've reached it, and my comments added to the file after every review. Can we settle that today?"
codex_completed.safety_note: A plan can sit beside real threats to income, housing or immigration status, particularly when a work visa depends on the job. Watch for pressure to resign quickly, to sign away claims, or to keep the plan secret. Before signing anything, ask an employment lawyer, a union representative or a legal aid service what it would mean for you.
misuse_warning: Calling any plan a weaponized PIP can excuse you from a real gap. Check whether the shortfall was recorded before any complaint.
Telling a manager their plan is weaponized claims to know their purpose, which a plan on paper cannot show.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Shame-as-Governance Disguised as Advice works through informal comments about your character with nothing written down; a PIP puts a document and dates around the judgment. Credit Laundering removes your name from successful work, where a PIP builds a record of supposed failure. Overcorrection Demands asks for outsized repair after a small lapse, whereas a PIP tells you to close a gap by a set date.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Credit Laundering
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Passing a person's idea or work through several hands, each slightly rewording it, until nobody can trace it back to them.
codex_completed.short_definition: Passing a person's idea or work through several hands, each slightly rewording it, until nobody can trace it back to them.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Credit Laundering is the slow cousin of simply taking credit. An idea or piece of work moves from person to person, each restating it a little, until it reaches the people who decide things with your name gone from it. No single hand takes it outright, which is why you may never find the moment it happened. One missing name in one meeting is common. Repetition is the tell: your work keeps arriving at the top without its history, and asking about it gets vague answers.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Your idea is repeated by one person, then another, each changing a few words, until it reaches the boss with someone else's name on it.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You watch your own work succeed without you and cannot point to a moment when it was taken. That makes raising it feel like sour grapes, even to you, while promotions and trust go to others.
what_it_is: A chain of two or three retellings, each dropping a bit of the source, so credit thins out gradually.
Most common where work moves up through layers: committees, forwarded email, slide decks, review boards, group chats.
The idea often arrives nearly unchanged, with new phrasing and no footnote.
Different from one person claiming your work in one go, because nobody in the chain has to say anything false.
Costs show up in reviews, promotion decisions and who is invited to the next conversation.
what_it_sounds_like: Great point, Priya. (Two days later, to the director:) Our team has been thinking about this approach.
The deck going to the board carries the department head's name and no mention of the analysis that came from your desk.
I think someone mentioned it in a meeting a while back.
Where did this come from? It's just kind of been in the air.
It's a team effort, so we don't list names on this one.
A forwarded email chain is cut down to its last message, which no longer shows your original proposal.
The announcement thanks 'everyone involved' and names the three people who presented it.
what_it_is_not: Ideas do improve as they pass through people, and the later version may truly belong to the group.
Large workplaces spread information with nobody steering it, and the first thought gets lost without anyone choosing that.
Two people sometimes reach the same thought separately, especially when working on the same problem.
A colleague who credits you in the room, forgets to in the written summary, and fixes it when reminded.
Team-level credit that a workplace gives to everybody equally by policy, including for senior people's work.
Your own memory that an idea began with you when no message or draft shows it. It may be true, and it cannot be told apart from outside.
this_may_be_it_when: You can show an earlier version, such as an email, draft or chat, and the later version is nearly identical.
The idea has passed through three or more people and nobody mentions its first source.
Your name is cut from summaries or forwarded threads at the point where it was last visible.
Questions about where it came from get answers like 'it was in the air.'
This has happened to your work more than once, in more than one meeting.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The later version has changed in substance and carries ideas from others.
A written record shows someone else proposed it first, or at the same time.
Credit is spread equally across the team as standing practice, including for senior people's own ideas.
When you point to the earlier source, the person fixes the record.
You cannot say where you first heard the idea, and neither can anyone else.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People often forget where an idea came from, because ideas absorbed in conversation lose their labels.
Senior people retell ideas in summary form, and brevity can strip out names.
Some organizations present everything as a team product by custom.
common_false_positives: A group brainstorm where the final idea honestly combined several contributions.
A report that cites team members by function and leaves names to an appendix.
A manager who restates your idea to others and says it came from you.
discernment_questions: Can I show the first version, with a date, and does the later one match it?
At which hand-off did my name drop out, and was it at one person or throughout?
Did the idea change in substance, or only in wording?
Is anyone else's work disappearing in the same way, or only mine?
When I mention where it began, is the record corrected or brushed off?
less_concerning_if: The idea changed meaningfully along the way and many people helped shape it.
Someone corrects the record when it is pointed out.
Credit is shared by a stated, consistent team policy that applies to everyone.
more_concerning_if: Attribution disappears repeatedly, and mostly from the same person's work.
Your earlier version is no longer in the shared folder, or you have lost access to the files that showed it.
The people who benefit from the credit decide your reviews or promotions.
pattern_over_time_signs: You are no longer asked into the meetings where your ideas are discussed, since the idea has gone ahead without you.
You start copying more people on emails so there is a dated trail.
People two levels above you are unaware of what you have contributed.
You grow reluctant to share ideas early, since early sharing seems to give them away.
codex_completed.repair_check: When this is handled well, someone with authority names the original source in the same place the credit went astray, such as an updated deck or an email to the same people, and tracing sources becomes routine. A private 'thanks for your input' leaves the public record as it was.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Check whether your name appears the next time the same material is passed along. A request to put sources on shared documents is honored when it becomes routine for everyone. It is not honored when you are told the credit is petty, or the next version quietly leaves you out again.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Credit tends to go to whoever is visible when a good idea lands. Each retelling moves the idea a step further from you in people's memory, and because no one hand removes your name, nobody may feel they did anything unfair. Observers usually remember the last teller, so attribution can fade through ordinary memory habits alone.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A slow resentment that cannot be pinned to any one event is typical, along with hesitation about sharing ideas in progress and worry that raising it will look petty. Some stop speaking up in meetings; some start documenting everything. Careers can stall while the work is praised under other names.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask about origins in a neutral way when the idea comes up again: 'I'm glad this is going forward. Can we note in the deck that it grew out of my proposal?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask that sources be listed on shared documents from now on, for everyone's work: 'Can we add a line for who proposed what on this one?'
response_options.disengagement: Share early ideas in writing with the person who needs them instead of aloud in groups, and hold unfinished work back from open channels until it is dated and filed.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask a colleague who saw the idea develop to confirm the history, and talk it through with a mentor outside your direct line, who can tell you whether this is typical in your field.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: After you share an idea, send a short dated email ('As discussed, I proposed...'), and when the work is presented, ask your manager to say where it began.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "The earliest version of this is my email from the second week of March. Can we put that source on the first slide before it goes to leadership?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Credit Laundering is rarely a personal danger. It would change if raising it brings threats to your job, housing or visa, particularly from someone with power over those. In that case keep dated copies of your own work and speak to an employment advice service or union representative before pushing further.
misuse_warning: Saying 'credit laundering' about an ordinary group process can turn a real conversation about shared authorship into an accusation.
Using the label for an idea that arose in many conversations can claim for one person what belonged to many.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: PIP Weaponization builds a record of supposed failure around someone, while credit laundering builds a record of success that leaves them out. Objectification treats a person as a source of useful output; credit laundering is one way that output can be absorbed without the person being thanked. Shame-as-Governance Disguised as Advice leaves you feeling smaller; here you may feel fine about yourself and still find your work belongs to others.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: The "Good Woman Program"
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A set of unspoken social rules that reward women for compliance and self-sacrifice and charge a price for directness, boundaries or taking up space.
codex_completed.short_definition: A set of unspoken social rules that reward women for compliance and self-sacrifice and charge a price for directness, boundaries or taking up space.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: This is less a tactic used by one person than a background set of expectations absorbed from family, school, media, work and faith.
