The label can also be used to dismiss a mother who has legitimate reasons for restricting contact. Gatekeeping needs the pattern, not just the disagreement.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: General gatekeeping controls access to people or resources of any kind; the maternal form is specifically a caregiver's control of another caregiver's role with a child. Interruption patterns cut someone off in group talk; here the cutting off happens through redone and taken-over tasks. Punishment by proxy harms someone you care about to send a message. Here the target is the caregiving role itself, not a message.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Echo Chamber Construction
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Arranging what another person reads, hears and talks about so that they mostly meet one view, and come to see every other source as unreliable.
codex_completed.short_definition: Arranging what another person reads, hears and talks about so that they mostly meet one view, and come to see every other source as unreliable.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: An echo chamber is a closed circle in which the same views bounce back and outside voices are cast as biased. Construction is the active part: someone feeds a person selected sources, introduces them to one set of friends, and pre-labels outsiders as liars or fools before they have spoken. Sharing links you like is ordinary. The pattern is when other sources are steadily discouraged, and doubt about outsiders is taught in advance.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone slowly fills your information world with one point of view and teaches you in advance to distrust everyone else, so it feels like your own choice.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The target loses the outside views that would let them sense-check their own situation, and the narrowing arrives feeling like a preference they chose. It is hard to notice what you are no longer hearing.
what_it_is: Steady recommendations of the same few channels, authors or forums, with a dismissal of everything else.
Introducing the person to one circle of friends or one online group, and cooling their ties with others.
Describing outsiders in advance as biased, paid or 'asleep', so their views are discounted before they are heard.
Praise for repeating the group's view, and awkward silence for questions.
It differs from simply liking a community. The marker is discouragement of everything else.
what_it_sounds_like: Don't bother with that site, they're all lying anyway.
Your sister would only confuse you. She doesn't understand what we know.
Here, watch this one. It explains everything the others hide.
If you hear them out, they'll just twist your words.
Real friends would see this the way we do.
You don't need other opinions. You've got us.
Anyone who disagrees hasn't done the research.
what_it_is_not: People form affinity groups on their own, and recommending sources you honestly rate is not curating somebody else's world.
The distinguishing feature is active discouragement of everything else, not enthusiasm for something in particular.
A parent who limits a young child's screen content is making an age-appropriate choice.
A recommendation algorithm that serves more of the same is how the platform works, and this does not show what anyone meant.
A hobby group, faith community or fan club that shares a strong view but welcomes questions and outside friends.
A friend who says a particular source is unreliable and gives their reasons for you to check.
this_may_be_it_when: You are told in advance, in general terms, that certain sources or people cannot be trusted.
Questions about the group's view get hurt reactions or a change of subject.
Your time with other friends and family shrinks as time with the one circle grows.
Information that disagrees is described as an attack before you have read it.
You notice you repeat phrases and examples that you first heard from one person.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The person gives reasons for distrusting a source and invites you to check them yourself.
You keep friends, news sources and interests outside the group and nobody objects.
The group answers hard questions with evidence rather than a mood.
You can describe the best case for a view the group rejects.
Leaving the group or disagreeing with it carries no penalty.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People naturally befriend others who think alike, and the circle narrows without anyone planning it.
Platform recommendations feed you more of what you clicked, with no human steering.
A new enthusiast can sound like a convert for a few months and then settle.
common_false_positives: A new member of a club who spends all their free time with it for a season.
A friend who warns you off a site that has really published false stories.
A family that mostly talks politics with relatives who agree, with no pressure on the others.
discernment_questions: When did I last read or hear a serious case against what this circle thinks?
Who told me those sources could not be trusted, and did they show me why?
Do I still have friends outside this group, and has that changed?
What happens when I voice doubt: curiosity, or coolness?
Could I explain the other side's view well enough that they would recognize it?
less_concerning_if: You choose your own sources and the person is relaxed about it.
Outside friendships and views are welcomed, even if teased.
The group changes its mind when shown good evidence.
more_concerning_if: The person asks you to cut contact with people who disagree, or to delete or avoid certain accounts.
Group membership becomes tied to money, housing or a relationship.
You are told that outside people are dangerous or are out to harm you.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your list of trusted sources keeps getting shorter, and each loss comes with a reason.
You start to finish the group's sentences and use its private vocabulary.
Old friends say you have changed, and you feel defensive before they finish speaking.
Reading something the group frowns on makes your stomach tighten.
codex_completed.repair_check: When the narrowing is named, repair looks like the person encouraging you to read widely, backing contact with those you have drifted from, and tolerating your doubts without any penalty. A short pause in the pressure, followed by a return to the same sources and the same warnings, is not that.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Try something small, such as saying you will read a source they dislike, or meet an old friend alone. Does the person accept it, or pay you back with sulking, a lecture or sudden coldness? Accepting without a price suggests the limit is being respected.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Hearing the same view often, from people you like, can make it feel like plain fact. Having your view echoed back can also feel good. If outsiders are described as biased before they speak, their arguments can be dismissed without being weighed. Over time this can make one circle's picture feel like plain reality, and doubt feel like betrayal.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Meeting outsiders can come as a shock, with the world looking different from what the circle said. Some report losing touch with relatives, finding it hard to talk to anyone who disagrees, and feeling embarrassed later about what they once repeated with certainty.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask a mild question when you hear a sweeping claim: 'What is the best argument against that, and where would I read it?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep your own reading and your own friends: 'I'm going to keep seeing my sister and reading more widely, and that doesn't change how I feel about you.'
response_options.disengagement: Reduce time in the closed group chat or forum, and see what changes when you do. Do it quietly, and without a speech.
response_options.support_seeking: Reach out to one person from before and tell them honestly what you have been hearing lately. See whether they remain steady and kind.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If this is a workplace team or professional network, ask for more than one source of information on decisions, and put questions in writing.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I like a lot of what you share, and I also want to hear other views for myself. I'll keep reading widely and keep seeing my friends. If we disagree on something, I'd rather talk it through than be told the other side is lying."
codex_completed.safety_note: Echo chamber construction is not by itself a physical-safety signal. It becomes one if you are told to cut off family, hand over passwords or devices, or if leaving the circle brings threats or loss of housing or income. At that point, reach for an outside person you trust, and for a cult-recovery or domestic abuse service.
misuse_warning: Saying someone is 'in an echo chamber' is a quick way to dismiss their view without engaging with it. Everyone's circle is somewhat narrow.
It can be turned on a loved one who has found a community that suits them, when nobody is steering them and the door is open.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Information cascades spread a belief because agreeing seems safe, and no single person has to run it. Echo chamber construction has someone actively shaping the supply and teaching distrust of the rest. Gatekeeping controls who gets in or out, and here the control is over what gets in to your head. Strategic ambiguity is about vague wording; this is about a narrow diet.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Stochastic Harassment Direction
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Repeatedly describing a named person in inflammatory terms to a large audience, so some listeners predictably harass them although the speaker never gives an instruction.
codex_completed.short_definition: Repeatedly describing a named person in inflammatory terms to a large audience, so some listeners predictably harass them although the speaker never gives an instruction.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Stochastic means 'driven by chance': nobody can say which listener will act, only that with a large enough audience, some probably will. In this pattern, someone repeatedly names a target and describes them in a way that provokes anger, often with their workplace or town, and never gives an instruction. Then a wave of messages, calls or visits arrives. One harsh post means little. The pattern is repeated portrayal, followed by repeated waves that cite the same words.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone keeps painting a particular person as a villain to a large audience, never telling anyone to do anything, and then strangers start harassing that person.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The target absorbs harassment from many people at once while the portrayal that produced it stays technically deniable, so there is no single act to report and no one to hold to it. It can feel as if the whole world has turned on you.
what_it_is: A repeated, inflammatory description of a named individual, often with their job, school or neighbourhood attached.
An audience large and angry enough that a few of its members acting is close to certain.
No direct instruction, only a framing that makes harassment seem justified, so the speaker can say they never asked for it.
Waves of messages, calls or complaints that arrive soon after each post and quote its wording.
It is about foreseeable effect over time, not about one person's anger or one heated post.
what_it_sounds_like: Posts that name the person, say what a disgrace they are, and tag their employer or school.
Followers' messages that quote the speaker's exact phrase: 'You are exactly what he said you are.'
The speaker's reply to complaints: 'I never told anyone to contact her. I only said what she did.'
A flood of one-star reviews, calls to the workplace or anonymous emails within hours of a post.
Repeated hints such as 'someone should do something about this person' with no instruction attached.
The target's address, workplace or family showing up in comments after a post, posted by strangers.
New accounts appearing in the target's inbox with the same few insults.
what_it_is_not: Proportionate public criticism of someone's public actions is legitimate, even when a third party overreacts to it.
Reporting real wrongdoing through proper channels is not incitement.
What is described here is repeated inflammatory portrayal aimed at an audience, not criticism as such.
A single harsh review or angry post that happens to go viral, with no pattern of repeated targeting.
A news outlet reporting accurately on a public figure, and some readers reacting badly.
A group of people independently angry about the same documented event.
this_may_be_it_when: The same person returns to the same target again and again, each time with sharper language.
Waves of harassment follow the speaker's posts closely and quote their phrases.
The speaker names or tags the target's employer, school or home area when it adds nothing to the point being made.
When harassment starts, the speaker disclaims it but keeps going.
Personal details that the speaker never posted begin to circulate among the audience.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The speaker explicitly condemns the harassment and removes or edits the post.
The criticism is about a public act of a public figure, and keeps to that act.
The backlash began before the speaker said anything, from other sources.
The speaker has not referred to the target again since the first post.
The target is a public official or business criticized for what they did in that role.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A writer can be shocked by a post's reach and bewildered by what some readers do with it.
An emotional post written in anger may be regretted, and handled well after a pause.
A story can spread without the original author's input, through other people sharing it.
common_false_positives: A viral complaint about a restaurant that brings in a spike of harsh reviews, with no repeated targeting.
A journalist's report on a politician's record that draws hostile replies.
A reply thread of critics responding to a public statement by a company spokesperson.
discernment_questions: Did the harassment arrive after a specific post, and does it quote that post's words?
Has the speaker returned to this person more than once, and with escalating language?
Did the speaker say anything to calm their audience when the harassment began?
Is the person being named in a way that connects to a public role, or to their private life?
Would the criticism have been just as clear without pointing the audience at their workplace or home?
less_concerning_if: The speaker moves on from the topic, or states plainly that nobody should contact the person.
The criticism concerns something the person did in public, and names no private details.
The reaction is limited to ordinary replies and does not reach the target's work or family.
more_concerning_if: The harassment includes threats, repeated unwanted visits, or the sharing of the person's home address or children's details.
Contact is arriving at the target's workplace, threatening their income.
The speaker keeps posting after the target says they have received threats.
pattern_over_time_signs: Each new burst of harassment follows a new post by a day or two.
The speaker's description gets harsher and the audience's replies get more personal.
New people turn up with the same wording, and the target feels watched in more places.
The target begins to change how they live: locking accounts, varying their routes or leaving their usual places.
codex_completed.repair_check: If the speaker is confronted with the harassment, repair would be them publicly telling the audience to stop, taking down the posts and not naming the person again. A reply that says 'I never asked anyone to do that' and then goes on posting has changed nothing for the target.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask whether, after you or someone else asks that the posts stop, new waves still follow within days. If the posts stop and the waves die down, the request has been honored. If they continue, then the request is being treated as a part of the story.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A large audience can contain a few people who are already angry or looking for a target. A vivid, repeated portrayal can tell them whom to be angry at and make acting feel righteous, while the speaker keeps a sense of distance, since no instruction was given. Responsibility then seems to spread out among many senders, and no one feels it entirely.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe constant alerts, losing sleep, fear when the phone rings, and pulling out of public life. Some lose work because employers get flooded with complaints. Others describe feeling unable to explain it, since no single message looks serious on its own.

response_options.soft_clarification: If you think you may be the audience, ask yourself in private what the speaker is wanting you to do, and whether you would say it to the person's face.
response_options.firm_boundary: Do not reply to the harassers or to the speaker in public. Block, mute and report from your accounts, and keep screenshots with dates and links.
response_options.disengagement: Lock down accounts, remove personal information from public view, and ask trusted people to help you watch messages so you are not alone with them.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a trusted friend or family member what is happening, and ask for help with a record of each message, including a note of when it arrived.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you are the target at work, tell your manager or HR early, give them your record, and ask that the organization handle calls and emails about you.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I am keeping a dated record of every message, and I am not replying to any of them. Will you read through them with me and help me work out who should see them?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Harassment waves can move from messages to threats, doxxing or visits to a home or workplace. Signs to take seriously are your address being shared, threats naming you or your family, or someone appearing in person. Keep dated copies, report each wave to the platform, and take the file to the police or a victim-support service, who can advise on protective orders.
misuse_warning: Treating any pile-on after a post as proof of orchestrated incitement can shield real wrongdoing from public criticism.
Someone who is being criticized may use the label to cast all criticism of themselves as harassment.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Punishment by proxy hits someone the target loves, to send a message, while here the pain lands on the target directly, from many strangers. Information cascades spread a belief because agreeing is safer, and no one aims it at a person. Reputation laundering hides the source of a claim, whereas here the speaker is out in the open and the deniability sits in the lack of any instruction.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Information Laundering
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Passing a false or unverified claim through a series of apparently credible sources until it looks like established fact and its origin can no longer be seen.
codex_completed.short_definition: Passing a false or unverified claim through a series of apparently credible sources until it looks like established fact and its origin can no longer be seen.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Information laundering moves a claim from a weak source, such as an anonymous post or a fabricated document, through a chain of better-looking ones: a blog, a small outlet, a bigger outlet, an expert quoting the outlet. Each step cites the one before and adds a little respectability. Citing earlier reporting is normal. The pattern is when no link in the chain ever checked the claim itself, and the original source fades out of view.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A shaky claim is passed from one source to a more respectable one, and then another, until it looks well-sourced even though nobody ever checked whether it was true.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The target is contradicted by something that now looks well-sourced, and disproving it means unpicking a chain of citations rather than a single claim. By then, the claim has been quoted in so many places that it feels settled.
what_it_is: A claim moved upward through outlets of rising credibility, each citing the last.
A circle of sources that repeat each other, so the number of citations looks like independent confirmation.
A weak original, such as a forged document or an anonymous post, that becomes hard to find once better-known outlets carry it.
Credibility gained from the messenger's reputation, not from any new evidence.
It happens in news, in academic citations, in company reports and in word-of-mouth.
what_it_sounds_like: A headline that says 'according to reports' and links to another article that says the same.
A footnote that cites a blog, which cites a forum post, which cites nothing.
An expert on a panel quoting 'a widely reported figure' that cannot be traced to a study.
A news story built on a screenshot that no one has authenticated.
A statistic that appears in many places, all with the same rounding, and none with the underlying data.
An article that is later cited as a source by the site that supplied the original tip.
A correction posted at the original place that does not follow the claim to the places it spread.
what_it_is_not: Responsible journalism legitimately cites and builds on other credible reporting.
A claim that several outlets each confirmed separately is corroborated rather than laundered.
The thing to trace is whether any link in the chain did original verification work.
A well-known idea being cited in a textbook that has itself been properly checked.
An honest error that spreads because busy reporters trusted a reputable source that was wrong.
A source quoting an unnamed person whom the outlet has vetted and stands behind.
this_may_be_it_when: Following the citations ends in a single anonymous or unverifiable origin.
Every source uses the same wording or the same image, and none adds its own checking.
The claim gets more certain at each step, though no new evidence enters.
The earliest source quietly disappears or gets edited once bigger outlets carry the claim.
People who try to trace it find that the sources only point to each other.
this_may_not_be_it_when: One or more sources in the chain interviewed witnesses, checked records or ran their own analysis.
Independent outlets with different sources arrived at the same claim.
The original source is clearly named and has a track record of accuracy.
Corrections traveled with the claim when a mistake was found.
The claim is tentative at every step, and stays that way.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Time pressure leads reputable editors to trust a wire service or partner without redoing the work.
Authors cite secondary sources because the primary one is hard to reach, and say so.
A mistake in one respected outlet may be copied by others in good faith.
common_false_positives: A science story that cites an earlier news report on a peer-reviewed paper, with a link to the paper.
A rumor in a group chat that turns out to be true because a local reporter confirmed it.
An encyclopedia entry that summarizes several independent studies.
discernment_questions: If I follow each citation back, where does it end, and is that source something I can check?
Did any of these sources add new evidence, or did they each repeat the one before?
Is the original easy to find, or has it been hard to locate since the claim spread?
Do the sources disagree in the details in ways that suggest independent work?
Who benefits from this claim being widely believed?
less_concerning_if: Each source names where it got the claim and links to it.
At least one source in the chain shows its evidence, such as documents or recordings.
Outlets that got it wrong issued visible corrections.
more_concerning_if: The claim concerns a named person or group, and has led to threats, firing or harassment.
The origin appears to be a forged document, edited image or fake account.
Outlets refuse to say where the claim came from when asked.
pattern_over_time_signs: The same unverified claim returns months later, now with a longer list of citations.
Search results fill with articles that quote each other and none the original source.
Attempts to correct the record are answered with 'it has been widely reported'.
Details of the claim harden over time, such as numbers becoming exact, while the evidence stays thin.
codex_completed.repair_check: When a chain is exposed, repair looks like each outlet stating that it relied on an earlier source it did not check, updating the original piece and telling readers who saw the earlier version. Quietly deleting a link while leaving the claim in place does not remove it from circulation.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: When you ask an outlet or colleague where a claim came from, watch how they respond. Naming the source and conceding what they did not check shows that the question was respected. Pointing to the number of other places that ran it avoids the question.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Messenger reputation often does the work that checking should. Readers can judge a claim by how reputable the messenger seems and by how often they have seen it, rather than checking the root. A respectable outlet can lend its reputation to something it did not verify. Seeing a claim in several places can feel like confirmation, even when they all trace to one origin.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe the frustration of facing a claim that seems sourced and cannot be answered in one line. Targets report harm to their name or job from something they never said. Readers describe feeling foolish on learning that the 'many sources' were one.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the person sharing it: 'Where does this first come from, before the article?' Wait for an answer you can check.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to repeat or cite the claim until you have traced it to a source that did its own checking.
response_options.disengagement: Stop engaging with a thread that is only citing itself, and avoid sharing it further, which gives it more reach.
response_options.support_seeking: Send the chain you traced to a fact-checking organization, a librarian or a reporter who covers the topic, and ask them to review it.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you edit, research or cite for work, require a primary source for key claims and note in your records how each source was checked.

codex_completed.boundary_script: Verification script (to yourself, before sharing): "Can I trace this back to someone who actually saw it, measured it or held the document? Or am I looking at five sources that all got it from the same place?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Information laundering is mostly a harm to understanding and reputation. It becomes a safety matter if a laundered claim names a private person and prompts harassment, threats or loss of work. If that happens, save copies of the pages, report to the platforms and outlets, and speak to a lawyer or a media-law advice service.
misuse_warning: Calling a claim 'laundered' just because you dislike it, without tracing it, dismisses honest reporting.
The label can be used to wave away any claim that many outlets carried, even when each one verified it separately.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Information cascades spread a claim because agreeing is safer, and nobody needs to have staged the climb. Information laundering is built to make a weak claim look verified, and the chain matters. Strategic ambiguity keeps meaning vague to avoid being pinned down, while here the claim is specific but its origin is hidden. Reputation laundering does the same to a person's image.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Emotion Control
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Rewarding the feelings a person is allowed to show and punishing or shaming the rest, until they perform emotions instead of reporting them.
codex_completed.short_definition: Rewarding the feelings a person is allowed to show and punishing or shaming the rest, until they perform emotions instead of reporting them.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Emotion control is a pattern in which a household, relationship or group sets which feelings may be shown and enforces it through reactions that differ by feeling. Cheerfulness and gratitude get warmth. Anger, sadness or doubt get coldness, shame or a lecture. Some versions also demand that feelings be confessed on request. One tense reaction to one outburst means little. Weight comes from repetition: the same feelings are penalized every time, whatever the situation, and the person starts editing themselves before anyone has reacted.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Some of your feelings are welcome and others cost you something, so you learn to show only the welcome ones, even at home.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: When only some feelings are safe to show, you stop reporting the rest and may eventually stop noticing them. What is left of your emotional life is the part that was permitted.
what_it_is: Approval handed out for certain feelings (cheerfulness, gratitude, calm) and withdrawn for others (anger, grief, fear, doubt).
Demands for positivity in the middle of a real problem, such as being told to smile or be thankful when something has gone wrong.
Requests to confess how you feel, followed by that confession being kept and used later as proof of a flaw.
Penalties out of scale with the feeling: days of silence, a long lecture, or mockery after a mild complaint.
Found in couples, families, workplaces with mandatory enthusiasm, and tightly run groups.
what_it_sounds_like: Smile. Nobody wants to see that face at dinner.
You have so much to be grateful for. Why are you crying?
Go on, tell me how you really feel. (Later:) So you admit you resent me.
Don't you dare raise your voice in this house.
We don't do negativity here.
I'll talk to you when you're in a better mood.
Look how lovely you are when you're not complaining.
what_it_is_not: A household or workplace with norms about how feelings get expressed, such as no shouting at the table. Cultures differ widely, and a difference in emotional style is not a tactic.
A norm that falls evenly on everyone in the room, including the person who set it, instead of landing on one person as a penalty for particular feelings.
Someone asking for a calmer tone in the middle of a heated argument, then coming back to hear you out.
A person who finds sadness or anger hard to be near, says so, and does not punish you for having it.
A job that asks for steady composure with customers while leaving room to be human elsewhere.
One kind attempt to cheer you up that you are free to turn down.
this_may_be_it_when: The same feeling gets a cold, shaming or angry response on many different days, whatever the topic.
Your good moods are noticed and praised while your low ones are called a phase, a mood or an act.
You rehearse a cheerful face before walking in the door.
A feeling you admitted when asked is quoted back at you in a later argument.
The reaction to a mild feeling is far bigger than the feeling was.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The other person hides anger and tears too, and the rule applies to everyone equally.
Disagreement and upset are welcome as long as they come without contempt or shouting.
A request to pause comes with a promise to return, and they do.
You can name a person or place where the same feeling is received without a cost.
The sensitivity is about one subject, such as a recent death, and not about a whole range of feelings.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Someone raised in a home where feelings were never discussed may simply have no practice receiving them.
A tired or overloaded person can lack room for someone else's upset, which says little about whether the feeling is allowed to exist.
A culture or faith tradition may prize restraint, and the person holding that norm may apply it to themselves as well.
common_false_positives: A friend who says they cannot hear this right now and asks to talk tomorrow, then does.
A team lead who asks for a steady manner in front of clients.
A parent teaching a child not to hit when angry, while still letting the anger itself be spoken.
discernment_questions: Which feelings can I show here without a price, and which ones cost me something?
Do I act out feelings I do not have, and who am I protecting when I do?
Does the other person hide the same feelings, or is it only me who is expected to?
Can I remember a time I said I was sad or angry and was simply heard?
Is the reaction in proportion to what I said, or does it work to shut the feeling down?
less_concerning_if: The norms are stated openly, hold for everyone, and can be talked about.
Anger or sadness is met with a request for a different time or tone, not with withdrawn warmth.
You still have at least one place where you can show your full range.
more_concerning_if: Warmth, money or privileges rise and fall with whether you look cheerful.
Feelings you confessed are stored and brought back as evidence that you are difficult.
When someone asks what you feel, you find you no longer know.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your range narrows: fewer complaints, fewer tears, then fewer reports of delight as well.
You answer 'how are you' with 'fine', even to people who would listen.
You edit messages to remove anything that sounds negative before sending.
Friends say you seem flat, or that you used to be more expressive.
codex_completed.repair_check: The next time you are visibly sad or angry is when it shows. Repair here shows up as the same warmth arriving whether or not you are cheerful. An apology for a harsh reaction, followed by the cold shoulder on your next low day, has not changed the rule.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Think about what it costs to say 'I'm not okay today' a week after asking for room to feel things. If the answer is nothing, the request landed. If the price is back, in sighs, silence or a lecture, it did not.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People adjust what they show in order to keep approval and avoid pain, and the adjustment can become automatic. When warmth reliably follows some feelings and withdrawal follows others, a person can learn to suppress the penalized ones before they surface. Being asked to confess feelings on demand can add a second pressure: anything admitted may be kept. Over time the habit can reach the feeling itself, not just its display.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Accounts include numbness or flatness at home, not knowing what you feel when asked, rehearsing cheerful answers, and crying only when alone. Some report feeling fake in their own family, or noticing that relief at leaving the house was the only strong feeling left. Others are surprised at how quickly anger and grief came back once the penalty was gone.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name the pattern of reaction, not the person: 'When I say I'm sad, the room goes cold. I'd like to be able to say it and have you just listen.'
response_options.firm_boundary: State what you will and won't do tonight: 'I'm not going to pretend to be fine. I'm tired, and that's all I'm saying.'
response_options.disengagement: When a feeling is being ridiculed, take it out of the room for a while: a walk, a bath, a call to a friend who lets you have it.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone who has seen you in many moods what you have stopped saying at home. A counselor can help you test whether your range has narrowed.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Where cheerfulness is part of the job culture, keep your composure with clients, and find one manager or colleague one-to-one where you can say 'this week was hard' plainly.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I can be kind and calm with you, but I can't be cheerful on command. If I'm sad or angry, I want to say so once and have you hear it without a lecture."
codex_completed.safety_note: Being punished for a feeling is pressure on your inner life, not a physical danger. It can change when the penalty for a feeling includes threats, intimidation when you show anger, control of money or contact, or a mood being treated as proof you are unfit or unwell. If a reaction to a feeling ever frightens you, tell a friend, a doctor or a domestic abuse advocate what happens in the minutes after you speak.
misuse_warning: Calling every request for calm 'emotion control' can turn an ordinary ask to lower the volume into an accusation. The label fits when penalties fall repeatedly on particular feelings.
Using it to excuse your own outbursts, as if any limit on how you express anger were control, misreads it.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Nonverbal Dominance uses sighs, stares and eye rolls to unsettle or dismiss you in a single moment. Emotion control is the lasting rule about which feelings may appear at all, and a sigh or a stare may be one way it gets enforced. Ritualized Exhaustion drains your capacity through schedules and lost sleep, while emotion control leaves your energy alone and works on what you show.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Ritualized Exhaustion
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A relentless run of schedules, demands and lost sleep that keeps a person too depleted to think clearly, weigh options or push back.
codex_completed.short_definition: A relentless run of schedules, demands and lost sleep that keeps a person too depleted to think clearly, weigh options or push back.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Ritualized exhaustion is a sustained pattern of fixed routines, constant demands and cut-down sleep that leaves a person chronically worn out instead of briefly busy. It can appear in a household, a workplace, a caregiving arrangement or a tightly run group. A hard week or a launch crunch is not this. What sets it apart is a load with no end date, rest treated as laziness or failure, and a reduced ability to think and object that nobody acknowledges.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You are kept so busy and so short of sleep that you have nothing left for thinking, deciding or saying no.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Depletion that runs for months narrows the ability to think, weigh options and push back, and once that is gone, noticing its absence gets harder too.
what_it_is: Fixed routines, such as early wake-ups, late-night tasks and set check-ins, that crowd out sleep, meals and time alone.
Demands that arrive as fast as the last one is finished, so catching up never happens.
Rest treated as a lapse: tiredness gets called weakness, poor attitude or lack of commitment.
An open-ended quality: nobody can say when the pace will ease.
Seen in households, caregiving, workplaces and tightly run groups where keeping the schedule is part of belonging.
what_it_sounds_like: You can sleep when the work is done.
If you were really committed, you wouldn't need eight hours.
Just one more thing before you go to bed.
Everyone else manages fine.
A message or task lands at 2 a.m. and a reply is expected within minutes.
A rota with no free day, and a day off that gets filled at the last minute.
Being told you look tired, followed by another task.
what_it_is_not: A hard stretch with a real, disclosed end point, such as a launch, a new baby or a family crisis. A demanding period that ends is different from an open-ended schedule that never gives rest back.
Choosing a punishing schedule yourself because you love the project or are training for something.
Shift work, on-call duty or night nursing, where hours are tough but agreed, paid and followed by recovery.
A chaotic household or office where nobody is rested, including the person making the demands.
Insomnia, anxiety or a health condition wearing you down without anyone imposing a schedule.
Caring for a sick relative, where the demands come from the illness itself.
this_may_be_it_when: Nobody can give you a date or a condition for when the load will ease.
Requests for sleep or a day off are answered with doubt about your commitment.
The demands rise after you have shown signs of objecting.
Your errors and slowness get noted, but the hours behind them do not.
You notice you now agree to things you would have refused when rested.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The heavy period has a named end and you can see it coming.
The person setting the pace works the same hours and is exhausted too.
You can refuse a task and the refusal is accepted.
Time off is given back after a crunch.
You chose the load and could change it without penalty.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Seasonal or deadline work can pile hours onto everyone involved.
A newborn, an ill relative or a house move can fill every hour of a home with no one's wish behind it.
Poor planning can produce relentless demands without anyone noticing the cumulative cost.
common_false_positives: A crisis-response week for emergency staff, followed by agreed recovery time.
A founder working punishing hours on their own venture by choice.
Parenting a baby, where broken sleep comes from the baby's needs and not from anyone's rules.
discernment_questions: Is there a date, or a clear condition, when this pace ends?
Is anyone else on the same schedule, including the person setting it?
When I say I'm too tired, is the toll acknowledged or does the pace stay as it was?
Have I noticed my ability to decide or object shrinking as my sleep has?
Do I get any hours that are mine?
less_concerning_if: The pace has an end date and that date is honored.
Rest is protected when you ask for it.
The people setting the pace live under it too.
more_concerning_if: Sleep or meals are directly controlled by others, such as being woken, kept up, or having food timed.
Exhaustion goes together with fear of what happens if you slow down: lost housing, pay or standing.
The schedule keeps you from friends and family, so nobody outside sees the state you are in.
pattern_over_time_signs: Rest days vanish one by one, and each loss is described as temporary.
You make more mistakes, and are then told the mistakes prove you need more structure.
Friends stop hearing from you because you have no hours left.
Small decisions you used to make, like when to eat or sleep, now wait for permission or do not happen.
codex_completed.repair_check: Look for rest that actually returns: a day off that stays off, a schedule that shortens, sleep that is left alone. A promise that things will calm down next month, repeated every month, is another pass of the same schedule.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask for one protected block, such as a full night's sleep before a set hour, and see whether it holds on the third and fourth night as well as the first. A limit respected only when it costs nothing is easy to mistake for one that is kept.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Long sleep loss and constant demand can reduce attention, memory and the ability to plan or weigh consequences. A tired person may take the nearest available option, accept requests they would otherwise refuse, and have little energy left to question the arrangement. The schedule can also use up the very time in which someone might talk to friends, look at alternatives or simply think.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Accounts include fog, irritability, getting sick more often, forgetting simple things, and a feeling of watching one's own life from a distance. Some lose the ability to picture an alternative, or the energy to want one. Others notice how quickly their thinking cleared after a few nights of real sleep.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask about the shape of the load rather than its fairness: 'How long do you expect this pace to last, and what could ease it?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Make one small request in plain terms: 'I do better work when I've slept. Could late-night requests wait until morning?'
response_options.disengagement: Protect small pockets of rest without announcing them or arguing about them: a short walk, a meal eaten sitting down, ten minutes of quiet.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a doctor about your sleep and workload, and a trusted friend or advocate about the schedule itself. If anyone controls when you may sleep or eat, an advocate can help you plan privately.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Write down hours worked and requests received, with dates. A manager, HR contact, union representative or employment advice service can compare them with your agreement or local rules.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "On this little sleep I can't think clearly, and I do want to do this well. Can we agree on which of these things really have to be done tonight, and which can wait until tomorrow?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Forced sleep loss and an unbroken schedule can sit alongside coercive control, exploitative work, or a group that rations rest. Watch for being woken or kept up by others, food or sleep used as reward, punishment for refusing, and shrinking contact with outsiders. A doctor, a labor-rights service or a domestic abuse advocate can help you plan privately, and keeping dated notes somewhere the other person cannot find them helps.
misuse_warning: Describing a busy season or a new baby as ritualized exhaustion mislabels ordinary strain and can sour a relationship over circumstances nobody chose.
Applying the label to an employer's heavy demands without looking at pay, agreement and end date can hide a simple contract dispute that has its own remedies.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Resource Sabotage takes away the tools and support you need so that you fail, while ritualized exhaustion leaves the tools alone and fills your hours. "Managed Out" Through Exhaustion is a loss of purpose and belonging at work over months, so the person ends up sidelined rather than overloaded. Emotion Control works on what you may show, and this one works on how much you have left.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Nonverbal Dominance
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Using posture, stares, sighs, eye rolls or the way a body fills a room to dismiss or pressure someone without saying anything.
codex_completed.short_definition: Using posture, stares, sighs, eye rolls or the way a body fills a room to dismiss or pressure someone without saying anything.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Nonverbal dominance is pressure carried by the body instead of words: a pointed sigh, an eye roll, a long stare, standing over someone who is seated, or taking the head of the table and more room than the moment needs. Postural dominance is simply another name for this, and nothing separates the two. Each signal is easy to deny and hard to quote. One sigh means little. It becomes a pattern when it reliably lands on the moments you disagree, correct something or ask for something, and you start editing yourself around it.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Without saying a word, someone uses sighs, stares, eye rolls or where they stand to make you feel small, so you stop disagreeing. There is nothing you could quote back to them.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Nothing quotable is said, so the experience is hard to explain to anyone else, and you may end up quietly editing yourself around a reaction you could not describe if asked. Being looked down on, literally, works below the level of argument: you feel smaller and cannot point to why.
what_it_is: Signals sent with the face and body: sighs, eye rolls, long stares, a turned back, a slow exhale timed to the end of your sentence.
Positioning that puts you lower or smaller: standing over you while you sit, taking the head of the table, leaning over your desk or your chair.
Wordless, so it leaves nothing to quote and is easy to answer with 'I didn't say anything.'
Found in kitchens, meetings, classrooms and car rides, where the same sigh can carry a very different weight.
What sets it apart from ordinary body language is aim: it lands on disagreement, correction or a request, not on everything that irritates the person.
what_it_sounds_like: A long exhale and an eye roll the moment you say 'I see it differently', and none when you agree.
They stay standing at the counter looking down at you while you explain, and only sit once you stop talking.
Silent staring after you ask for something, held until you say 'never mind'.
You raise a concern in a meeting and a manager leans back with arms folded, eyes on the ceiling, while others speak without that reaction.
When you correct a detail they step closer or lean over your chair.
They turn away or pick up a phone as soon as you mention the budget.
You ask what is wrong and hear: 'Nothing. I didn't say anything.'
what_it_is_not: Faces move on their own: a flash of visible irritation, an expressive manner, a real sigh at the end of a long day. The test is whether the reaction appears whenever something is annoying, or specifically whenever one person disagrees.
Rooms have layouts. A standing desk, a low sofa or a narrow kitchen can put one person above another, and someone standing up is usually just about to leave.
People differ in height, build and posture, and a tall or broad person takes up room without meaning anything by it.
A family or cultural style with long or short eye contact, or comfortable silence, that shows up with everyone.
Tiredness, pain, or a neurological or sensory difference that shapes facial expression and eye contact.
A frown or far-off stare while someone concentrates on what you are saying.
this_may_be_it_when: The sigh, stare or positioning follows disagreement, correction or a request far more often than anything else.
It stops or softens when you give in or go quiet.
Other people in the same room get a different reaction when they say the same thing.
Your body reacts first, by shrinking, going quiet or tightening, before you can say what happened.
If you ask about it, you hear a denial with no other explanation, and the same signal returns next time.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The same expressions show up with everyone, including people with more power than you.
A plain spoken reason comes when you ask, such as 'Sorry, my back hurts, I can't sit.'
It belongs to a hard season, like grief or illness, and eases as that passes.
The positioning is dictated by the room, such as the only free seat or the person nearest the screen.
You can say 'I disagree' and the person engages with what you said.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Chronic pain, a bad night's sleep or a long shift can come out as sighs, frowns and refusing to sit.
Some people sigh to release tension and barely know they are doing it.
Norms about eye contact, personal space and who stands differ across cultures and families, so the same stare can mean something else where the person grew up.
A resting face can look stern or contemptuous when nothing is meant.
common_false_positives: A colleague who stands to talk because they think better on their feet.
A teenager's eye roll that is mostly mood and appears with everyone at home.
Someone who is visibly frustrated by a slow website, a stuck printer and then a disagreement, in the same way each time.
discernment_questions: Does the reaction come when I disagree, ask or correct, or whenever the person is annoyed about anything?
Do I change what I say, or whether I speak, because of it?
Do other people get the same reaction when they say the same thing?
If someone I trust had watched the same exchange, would they describe the body language the way I do?
Do I feel dismissed, or do I feel afraid?
less_concerning_if: It appears with everyone and in every sort of mood, not just when you disagree.
The person is open when told how a particular look landed, and it changes.
You can still say what you think and be heard after the sigh.
more_concerning_if: The stares and looming come with raised voices, blocked doorways or damage to objects.
It travels with spoken put-downs, monitoring or control of money, so the silence is one part of a larger pattern.
You have stopped raising some subjects altogether because of the reaction you expect.
pattern_over_time_signs: You start sentences with 'sorry' or shrink them before they react.
The subjects that draw the reaction slowly drop off the list of things you bring up.
You read their face and posture as you walk in to work out what kind of evening it will be.
Described aloud to friends, the sigh sounds trivial, which leaves you doubting yourself.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair shows up in the body, not only in a sentence. Look for whether the sighs and looming ease when you disagree, and whether the person can say what the look meant and why it was unfair. An apology followed by the same stare next week has changed nothing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: After you say you would rather hear what they think than guess from a look, what do you see over the next days: words, a quieter version of the same look, or a silence that seems to punish you for asking?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People read faces and posture quickly and below conscious thought, and many learn early to treat a frown or a looming figure as a cue to back down. A wordless signal gives you no statement to argue with, so the response happens in the body first. Over repeated moments, a person can start editing themselves before anything is said.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe going quiet in the room, rehearsing sentences, shrinking in their chair, and feeling tense before they have said anything. Some say they cannot explain to others why a sigh frightens them, and begin to wonder if they are oversensitive. Others describe losing the habit of disagreeing at all.

response_options.soft_clarification: Pick a calm moment and ask for words: 'I can't always tell what that look means. Can you tell me what you think?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Describe the effect on you once, without asking for a promise: 'When I get a stare after I speak, I stop saying what I think. I would like to hear it in words.'
response_options.disengagement: Choose where you sit and stand so you are level with the person, near a door and, where you can, in view of others. Keep harder subjects for times when someone else is around.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe what you see and how your body reacts to a trusted person or a domestic violence advocate, and ask if it sounds like part of something larger, especially if you feel afraid.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Write down dates, who was present and what you saw in plain description ('stood over my desk while I spoke, arms folded'), and ask for meetings to run with an agenda or a third person present.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I can't always tell what a look means, and I would like to hear what you think in words. Could we sit down and each say our piece?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Stares, looming and slow exhales weigh more when they sit beside shouting, broken objects, blocked doorways or being followed from room to room, because the body language can then be a reminder of what has happened before. If you fear the person's reaction, avoid confronting the signals directly. Write down each incident with the date and bring the list to a domestic violence advocate before changing how you respond.
misuse_warning: Reading contempt into every sigh turns ordinary tiredness into an attack. A look is ambiguous; the label needs a repeated link to your disagreement, not one frown.
Accusing someone of dominating a room because of their height or build turns a body into a charge. The pattern is the timing around disagreement, not the body itself.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Spatial Invasion uses closeness itself, such as cornering, blocking an exit or removing personal space, so the body is the barrier. Nonverbal dominance can work from across a room, through a sigh or a stare. Emotion Control governs which feelings you are allowed to show, using shame, reward and punishment, and is often spoken; the silent signal here is aimed at your disagreement, not at your feelings.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Spatial Invasion
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Standing too close, blocking a doorway or cornering someone during tension, so they feel physically hemmed in though nothing is threatened aloud.
codex_completed.short_definition: Standing too close, blocking a doorway or cornering someone during tension, so they feel physically hemmed in though nothing is threatened aloud.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Spatial invasion is the use of body position in a conflict: standing within arm's reach, stepping into a doorway, backing someone toward a wall, following from room to room. No spoken word needs to be threatening, which makes it hard to describe afterward. A crowded lift or a cramped kitchen forces closeness on everyone. What marks the pattern is that the closeness or blocking appears when things get tense, narrows your way out, and returns each time. The body often reacts before the mind has a name for it.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: During an argument someone stands so close, or so squarely in your way, that you feel trapped, though they never say anything threatening.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The body reacts to a blocked exit well before there are words for it, so fear arrives in a conversation where nothing was ever threatened out loud.
what_it_is: Closing the distance during a disagreement until you are within arm's reach, or backed against furniture or a wall.
Standing in a doorway, hallway or beside a car door so the quickest way out is blocked.
Following you from room to room while the argument carries on.
Taking up the only path, step or seat so you cannot pass without touching or asking.
Leaving nothing quotable: the message sits in where a body is placed, which is why people doubt themselves afterward.
what_it_sounds_like: They step in as you stand to leave the room, and stay there while they keep talking.
You reach the hallway and find them already standing in it.
Their face is inches from yours while they speak quietly.
Where do you think you're going? We're not done.
You back up one step at a time until the wall is behind you.
They stand against the closed door of the room you are in.
Sit down. I'm talking to you.
what_it_is_not: Personal-space norms vary widely between cultures and individuals, and small rooms, lifts and crowded venues force closeness on everyone. A closeness noticed and corrected once is not this.
Leaning in to hear someone in a loud room.
A parent standing in a doorway to stop a toddler running toward the road.
Someone upset who stands near you and moves back as soon as you say it is too close.
Sharing a narrow hallway or kitchen where both of you shuffle past each other.
A person who steps nearer because they are hard of hearing or have low vision.
this_may_be_it_when: The closeness appears mainly in arguments and not in calm moments.
When you step away, they move with you to keep the gap closed or the exit covered.
You find yourself planning where to stand before a difficult talk, so as to stay near a door.
They stay close after you have said it feels too near.
Your body reacts (racing heart, shaking, going quiet) before anything has been said.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They step back when you ask for room.
The space is cramped and they are as squeezed as you are.
The same closeness shows up in warm moments, such as hugs.
You can walk out of the room freely and nobody follows.
They have asked whether this distance is okay.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Crowded buses, lifts and small flats put people closer than anyone would choose.
People raised with closer conversational distance may stand nearer with no wish to unsettle you.
Someone hard of hearing or short-sighted may step in simply to follow what is said.
common_false_positives: A friend leaning in over the noise in a bar.
A relative who blocks a doorway while chatting and steps aside the moment you ask.
Someone standing in a hallway because a child, a pet or a hot pan is in the way.
discernment_questions: Does the closeness show up in tense moments and not in easy ones?
When I move, do they move with me?
Can I leave the room whenever I want and be let past without comment?
Does my body react before any words have been said?
When I say it is too close, does the distance change?
less_concerning_if: They step back as soon as you say you need room.
The same person stands equally near in relaxed moments.
The setting is cramped and the closeness is shared.
more_concerning_if: Blocking or following goes together with raised voices, slammed doors, or things thrown or broken nearby.
It moves on to holding, grabbing, or taking your keys or phone.
You have started avoiding rooms where you would be alone with them, or arranging your day around exits.
pattern_over_time_signs: You choose where to sit so you are never farthest from the door.
You avoid starting conversations in small rooms.
Your shoulders tighten when you hear them approach.
You stop raising issues at home, because raising them has meant being cornered.
codex_completed.repair_check: Watch the physical record, not the words. After an apology, do they leave you the doorway, keep an arm's length and let you walk out of a room mid-sentence? Sorrow said while the same positioning returns in the next argument has changed nothing you can feel.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice whether a quiet request for more room changes where their body goes, not just what they say. Distance that opens and stays open is a request respected. Distance that closes again within the minute, or a response that mocks the request, is not.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Humans react to people very close to them and to blocked ways out without needing to think. Being cornered can set off a fight-or-flight response before any words register, which can leave the person afraid and then doubting the fear, because nothing was said. With no sentence to quote, the person may also struggle to explain it to others, which can add to the doubt.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Accounts include a pounding heart, shaking, a dry mouth, and going quiet or freezing in the moment. Afterward there may be self-doubt, since nothing was said that could be repeated. Some start steering conversations toward open rooms, sitting near exits or avoiding being alone with the person, and the habit can stay in other settings long after.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for a small change in the setting: 'Can we both sit down for this? I find it easier to talk with a little room.'
response_options.firm_boundary: If it feels safe, say once and quietly: 'I need a bit more room to think.' If it does not feel safe, skip the words and focus on staying near a way out.
response_options.disengagement: If a talk starts to close in, move toward a shared space where others are present, or step out for water or the bathroom. The aim is distance without a confrontation.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone you trust what happens in your body in these moments, and ask a domestic abuse advocate how to plan for them. An advocate can talk through safety planning without you having to say anything to the other person.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, note dates, places and who was present, and report to a manager, HR or a union representative. Ask for meetings in open spaces or with a third person there.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'd like us to sit down for this. I think better with a bit of space between us, and I want to hear what you're saying."
codex_completed.safety_note: Blocked doors and cornering can come before, or sit beside, grabbing, threats, or taking keys and phones. Watch for blocking that grows more frequent, any holding or pushing, fear of being alone with them, or being unable to leave a room. A domestic abuse advocate can help you plan exits and what to keep within reach, and emergency services are for when you are being held or hurt right now.
misuse_warning: Reading any close or crowded moment as invasion can turn a cramped kitchen or a loud bar into an accusation. The label fits closeness that tightens in conflict and blocks your way.
Using the label for a person who stood in a doorway once while upset turns a worry about safety into a verdict. Look at repetition, and at what happens when you ask for room.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Nonverbal Dominance unsettles through looks, sighs and eye rolls and can work from across a room. Spatial invasion works through where a body stands, closing distance or covering the way out. Emotion Control penalizes the feelings you show and does not depend on where anyone stands. Resource Sabotage removes tools and support over weeks, while this plays out inside one tense moment.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Resource Sabotage
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Withdrawing the tools, information, money or help a person needs to do something, then treating the resulting failure as proof they are not up to it.
codex_completed.short_definition: Withdrawing the tools, information, money or help a person needs to do something, then treating the resulting failure as proof they are not up to it.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Resource sabotage is a pattern in which what someone needs to succeed goes missing: the budget is cut, the login stops working, the car is unavailable, the instructions never get passed on. The shortfall is then treated as the person's own failing. It can occur in a job, a household, a study program or a caring role. Shortages happen to everyone. Look at whether the gap lands on one person, tends to arrive just before something important, and goes unmentioned when the work then falls short.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: The things you need to succeed keep going missing, and then the failure is blamed on you.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Failing without the tools needed to succeed reads to everyone watching, and often to the person themselves, as plain incompetence.
what_it_is: Information that never reaches you, such as a changed deadline, a moved meeting or a form you were meant to see.
Access cut off at the point it matters: a shared login, a car, a key, a bank card, a budget line.
Help promised and then withdrawn at the last minute, such as childcare or a handover.
Followed by blame: the missed target is described as your lack of drive or skill, with no mention of what was missing.
Shows up in workplaces, households with shared money or transport, studies and creative projects.
what_it_sounds_like: Oh, I thought I told you the venue had changed.
The budget got reallocated. Surely you can still make it work.
I can't drive you, I have my own things. But you knew the exam was today.
If you were more organized you'd have found the file yourself.
Funny, everyone else got the memo.
You should have asked for the login sooner. (It was changed without notice.)
The one piece of equipment you need goes to someone else the week before your presentation.
what_it_is_not: Budgets get cut, colleagues forget things, and money and attention are legitimately redirected for real, stated reasons. The question is whether the shortfall lands on everyone or only ever on one person, and whether the missing support is acknowledged when the work then fails.
A team-wide shortage that everyone is working around together.
An honest mistake, such as an email sent to the wrong list, put right quickly once pointed out.
A partner who truly cannot help this week because of their own crisis, and says so.
A manager who turns down a request for a reason given openly and suggests an alternative.
A spending limit agreed jointly in a family budget.
this_may_be_it_when: The missing item is missing for you and not for people in similar positions.
Support disappears close to a deadline, exam, interview or launch.
Requests for the missing item meet delays or a shifting set of reasons.
When the work falls short, nobody mentions the missing support.
The thing withdrawn was previously available to you.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Everyone in your position faces the same shortfall.
The reason was given before the gap mattered.
Once you raise it, the item or an alternative arrives.
The person who withdrew it also bears the cost and says so.
It happened once, and the person took responsibility for the knock-on effect.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Organizations cut budgets and lose staff for reasons that have nothing to do with any one employee.
People forget a message or a lift when overloaded.
Households sometimes pull back money or time when they are under real strain.
common_false_positives: A shared project where everyone received the same late brief.
A teacher or boss who holds back hints so you can learn to solve it yourself, has said so, and checks in.
A funding shortage that halts several programs at once.
discernment_questions: Does the shortfall affect others in my position, or only me?
When I raise a missing item, is it restored, or do new obstacles appear?
Does what is missing keep arriving just before something important?
When the work falls short, is the missing support part of the account?
Could I show a neutral colleague or friend a list of what went missing and when?
less_concerning_if: The shortage is shared and its cause is stated openly.
Missing items are restored quickly once you flag them.
The person acknowledges the knock-on effect when your work suffers.
more_concerning_if: What goes missing is money, transport or documents, or the tools for work or study, and you rely on them.
Your failure is cited in front of others, in reviews or family talk, with the gap left out.
Access is cut right after you did well, sought independence or voiced a disagreement.
pattern_over_time_signs: A growing list of things that used to be yours to use are now held by someone else.
You start double-checking, backing up, and carrying your own copies of everything.
Your record of failures grows, though your skill has not changed.
You ask less often, since asking has produced delay or a new reason.
codex_completed.repair_check: Check whether the missing thing is back in your hands with no strings attached, and whether the next shortfall is named at the time rather than discovered later. A heartfelt apology while access stays withheld has restored nothing you can use.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask in plain terms for the one item you need by a stated day, and see whether it appears on that day. If it arrives with no commentary on how you asked, the request was respected. If new conditions or reasons attach, the shortfall is still operating.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When the tools for a task go missing, the person who fails is usually the only one anyone looks at, and the missing support can be forgotten by everyone, including them. Repeated failures can wear down confidence and lead the person to ask for less, depend more, and accept the story that the problem is them. Control over money, transport or information also raises the cost of objecting.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Common accounts: working harder and getting less, always feeling slightly behind, and shame about failures that cannot be fully explained. Some begin keeping copies, receipts and lists to show what went missing. Others stop applying for things or asking for help, since asking brought delay. Seeing the whole list written out can bring relief.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask what you need and when: 'The file I need for Thursday hasn't arrived. Can you tell me when I'll get it?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Put the request in writing, with a date, and keep a copy: 'I need the login and the budget figures by Wednesday to finish on time.'
response_options.disengagement: Build your own backup: copies of key files, a second route to your work, a little money or a ride you control. That reduces how much one withheld item can stop you.
response_options.support_seeking: Show a list of what went missing, and when, to a friend, mentor or advocate who can compare it with what others had. If money or housing depends on the person, legal aid can look at your options privately.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Keep a dated log of requests and responses, follow up by email, and raise the pattern with a manager, HR or a union representative along with its effect on your results.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I can only do this well if I have the figures and the login. Could you tell me today when I'll have them, so I can plan around it?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Cut-off money, transport, documents or phones can be part of financial or coercive control, especially at home. Watch for needing permission to spend, being kept from your own accounts or papers, or fear of what happens if you ask. A financial abuse advocate or legal aid service can help you plan, and copies of important documents are safest with someone you trust.
misuse_warning: Calling every shortage or forgotten message sabotage turns ordinary mistakes into accusations. The label fits a gap that falls on one person, repeatedly, and is then blamed on them.
Raising it at work without dates or comparisons can sound like blame when what you hold is a timeline worth showing.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Ritualized Exhaustion fills your hours so you have nothing left, while resource sabotage takes away what you need for the task itself. "Managed Out" Through Exhaustion is a slow thinning of purpose and visibility across months, whereas this concerns particular tasks and the tools for them. Nonverbal Dominance unsettles you in a moment with looks, and takes no tools away.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: "Managed Out" Through Exhaustion
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Slowly removing a person's meaningful work, visibility and belonging until their departure looks like a free choice on paper.
codex_completed.short_definition: Slowly removing a person's meaningful work, visibility and belonging until their departure looks like a free choice on paper.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Being managed out is a gradual loss of a place: projects are reassigned, invitations to meetings stop, feedback dries up, and the person is left with little to do and no one asking for their view. Nothing is formally taken away and no complaint is filed, so a resignation reads as their own decision. Restructures and role changes hollow out jobs too. Telling signs are a loss that is quiet, falls on one person, and often starts after a conflict, a complaint or a change of leadership.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Your work, your say and your place at the table slip away bit by bit, until quitting starts to feel like your only choice.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A departure produced by these conditions looks, on paper and in memory, like a free choice, which leaves the person carrying the story that they simply could not cope.
what_it_is: Meaningful projects reassigned one at a time, with no conversation.
Being dropped from meetings, email threads and decisions you used to take part in.
Praise and feedback stop, and reviews turn vague or oddly critical.
No formal step is ever taken, so there is nothing to appeal or complain about.
Mainly seen at work, and also in volunteer groups, congregations and family businesses.
what_it_sounds_like: We're just going in a different direction.
Don't worry about that meeting. It wouldn't be useful for you.
You're welcome to stay, of course. Nobody is pushing you.
We thought you had enough on your plate. (As the project goes to someone else.)
