Your calendar goes from full to nearly empty over a few months.
You hear about a decision in your own team from a colleague, after the fact.
Maybe it's time to think about what you really want.
what_it_is_not: Restructures, shrinking budgets and real role mismatches hollow out jobs, and an employer in decline has less for everyone. A transparent change across a group differs from a quiet removal that falls on one person while no complaint is filed.
A skills mismatch discussed openly, with a plan to move you or train you.
A planned handover to a successor, announced and explained.
A documented performance process with stated expectations and a chance to meet them. It can be painful and still be transparent.
Seasonal quiet in a role where work comes in waves.
this_may_be_it_when: The reduction affects you and not colleagues with similar roles.
It began soon after you raised a complaint, disagreed, or took leave.
Nobody will tell you what has changed or why, and requests for a conversation get put off.
Your responsibilities shrink while your title and pay stay the same.
People are friendly, but nothing you do brings the work back.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The change was announced, explained, and applies to a group.
Someone has offered a path: a new project, training or a move.
Your workload dropped when a project ended, and new work is being planned.
A formal process exists and you have been told what is expected.
Colleagues in your role describe the same thinning.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Teams reorganize and priorities shift without any one person in mind.
A busy manager may stop including someone through habit and oversight.
A person's skills and the role can drift apart, and a quiet period follows.
common_false_positives: A slow season in a project-driven job.
Being moved off a project after a clear change in company strategy.
A new manager taking time to learn who does what.
discernment_questions: Is the change announced and shared, or silent and limited to me?
Has anyone given me a reason, a plan or a date?
Did the change follow a particular event, such as a complaint or a disagreement?
Are colleagues in similar roles going through the same thing?
If I did go, would it look like a free choice on paper?
less_concerning_if: The change is explained and applies across a team.
A conversation about your role is available and leads somewhere.
New work or training appears when you ask.
more_concerning_if: You are told it is up to you whether to stay while the conditions keep worsening.
Your pay, visa, health cover or housing is tied to the job.
Records of the change are missing, so nothing shows what happened.
pattern_over_time_signs: Month by month, your calendar and inbox thin out.
People who used to ask for your view stop asking.
A mention of your performance appears in conversation without any earlier feedback.
You begin to question whether you ever did good work.
codex_completed.repair_check: Look for work and a voice actually restored: a real project with real decisions attached, a seat back at meetings, a straight conversation about what happened. Reassurance that you are valued, while the calendar stays empty, has repaired nothing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask in writing for a conversation about your role and what is expected. Watch whether a date is set and kept, and whether what you hear matches what happens next. Being told nothing has changed, while the empty calendar says otherwise, answers a different question.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Work gives people purpose, status and routine, and losing them gradually can feel more like personal inadequacy than like something happening to them. Because nothing is formally removed, there is no event to point to, which can make the person doubt their own read. As confidence falls, going can start to look like relief, and the departure may be recorded and remembered as a free choice.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Accounts include dread on Sunday evenings, checking whether you have been left off an email, feeling invisible, and doubting your own competence. Some wonder whether they imagined the change. Afterward, some carry the belief that they could not cope even when they did their work well, while others feel relief on seeing it laid out.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask a plain question about the work: 'I've noticed I'm not on the planning meetings anymore. Is that a change in my role?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Request clarity in writing: 'Could we meet this week to talk about my responsibilities and what is expected of me over the next quarter?'
response_options.disengagement: Put quiet energy into skills, contacts and records outside the situation, and decide privately what you want before taking any step.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk to a trusted colleague outside your chain, a mentor or a counselor about what you are seeing. An employment advice service or union can explain your rights before you decide anything.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Keep a dated log of projects removed, meetings dropped and feedback received, and keep your own reviews and praise where company policy allows. Raise the pattern with HR or a union representative.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Help me understand how my role has changed over the last few months. Could we set up a time to talk about what I'm responsible for and what you expect from me?"
codex_completed.safety_note: The risk here is mostly to income and standing, and for some people to a visa or housing tied to the job. Watch for pay or immigration status depending on staying, pressure to sign a separation agreement quickly, or distress affecting your sleep or safety. Before signing anything, get advice from an employment lawyer, union or legal aid service, and keep dated notes of what changed.
misuse_warning: Reading every quiet spell or reassignment as being managed out can turn ordinary reorganizing into a grievance. The label needs a comparison, a timeline and a lack of explanation, not just a bad feeling.
Telling a coworker they are being managed out can add to their distress or push a decision that the evidence does not support.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Resource Sabotage takes away tools and information for a task and cites the failure, while being managed out takes away the role itself, across months, with no task to fail at. Ritualized Exhaustion overloads you until nothing is left, the opposite of the empty calendar here. Emotion Control sets which feelings may show and has nothing to do with the work you are given.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Evidence Traps
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Saving a person's messages, posts or remarks without their context, then bringing them out later at a moment when they do the most damage.
codex_completed.short_definition: Saving a person's messages, posts or remarks without their context, then bringing them out later at a moment when they do the most damage.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Evidence traps are genuine words, screenshots or recordings that are kept rather than answered, then returned later with the surrounding conversation removed. Nothing is faked, which is why it is hard to dispute. A joke becomes a position, and a vent at midnight becomes a confession. Keeping records is ordinary and often wise, and people do bring up old remarks. What stands out is comments stored instead of discussed at the time, context stripped away, and a return that arrives in a moment of conflict, review or dispute.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Things you said casually are saved, then held up later without their context, so that everything you say starts to feel like it could be used against you.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Knowing that anything said may be stored and re-timed makes ordinary candor feel risky, and speech starts being drafted rather than spoken.
what_it_is: Real material, such as texts, posts, voice notes and emails, that is kept and later quoted in part.
The original exchange often had a tone, a joke or an earlier message that has been left out.
It surfaces at a chosen point: an argument, a performance review, a group dispute, a custody or legal exchange.
Different from forgery: the words are yours, and the harm lies in what is cut away and when it appears.
Occurs in relationships, friendships, families, workplaces and online communities.
what_it_sounds_like: Oh, you don't remember saying this? I have it right here.
Here's what you wrote in March. So you did say you hated your job.
I've been keeping this for a while.
A screenshot cropped to show only your angriest line, posted to a group chat.
You said it, so don't tell me you didn't mean it.
A colleague pastes one line of your email into a meeting thread without the lines around it.
I took a screenshot back then, just in case.
what_it_is_not: Keeping records is legitimate and often wise, and raising something someone said because it still matters, in the context it was said in, is just conversation. What is being described is the stripping of that context and the choosing of the moment it returns.
Quoting an email in a work dispute with the full thread attached.
Saving threatening or abusive messages to show an advocate, lawyer or police. That is documentation for safety, a different use altogether.
A friend who remembers what you said and says 'but you told me last week' in good faith.
Receipts kept for an HR or legal process and shared in full with the people entitled to see them.
this_may_be_it_when: Something said weeks ago, which got no reply then, comes back in the middle of an unrelated argument.
Only the sharpest line returns, without the lines before or after it.
Other people are shown the quote before you are told it is being raised.
A casual remark is treated as a formal commitment or confession.
You find out items were saved at the time and not simply remembered.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The quote comes with the surrounding exchange and you are free to explain it.
It is raised promptly and plainly, as in 'this bothered me when you said it'.
The record is being kept to document threats or abuse.
They are equally open about their own messages being shared back.
You asked for the thing to be kept, such as a promise put in writing.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People often keep chats and emails for practical reasons, and referring back is a normal way to settle a factual question.
Memory itself can bring up an old remark in a heated moment, with nothing stored.
Cloud backups and message history keep things automatically, with no plan behind it.
common_false_positives: A boss who keeps an email thread confirming what was agreed.
A partner who quotes your promise of a deadline in full, since it was a plan you both made.
An app's 'on this day' memory resurfacing an old post.
discernment_questions: Does the quote still mean the same thing once the surrounding messages are put back?
Was it ever raised at the time, or only now?
Is it being used to settle a question, or to quiet me?
Do I now draft my words with an audience in mind?
Would they be willing to show the full thread to a third person we both respect?
less_concerning_if: Old messages are quoted in full and with context, and you are free to explain.
Records are kept in the open and you can keep copies too.
Concerns are raised promptly rather than banked.
more_concerning_if: Stored material comes with threats to share it with family, an employer or a court.
Recordings are made without your knowledge during emotional moments.
Material is shared with others to shape their view of you before you can reply.
pattern_over_time_signs: You edit what you write, or stop confiding in writing at all.
More of your talk moves to calls or in person, where nothing is kept.
You are surprised by what has been kept: dates, screenshots, details.
Old remarks come back at each new dispute, whatever the subject.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair would mean saying openly what was kept, showing the whole exchange, and raising concerns on the day they arise from now on. An apology that arrives while the folder of screenshots stays and keeps being used has changed nothing about how safe it is to speak.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask that concerns be raised when they happen, not stored. Then see whether next month brings 'this bothered me', said that day, or another old quote out of nowhere. Also watch whether your own words are given the same openness.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People relax their guard when they believe words fade, and talk more honestly as a result. Learning that remarks may be saved and replayed can make speech feel risky, so the person edits themselves, guards what they write, and may start to doubt their own earlier words when shown a fragment. Because the material is real, it is also hard to contest, which can add to the sense of being trapped.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Accounts include going quiet in writing, rereading messages before sending, feeling watched in your own home or friend group, and wariness about telling anyone anything. Doubt about what you really meant can set in when you are shown a fragment. Others feel anger that something said in trust was held back for later.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the whole picture: 'Can you show me the messages around that one? I remember the conversation going differently.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask for concerns in real time: 'If something I say bothers you, tell me then. I don't want old messages used in new arguments.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop sharing delicate things with someone who keeps them for later, and move sensitive talk to a call or an in-person conversation.
response_options.support_seeking: Show the full thread to someone neutral and ask how it reads. If material is being shared, or threatened to be, keep your own copies of what was sent and talk to an advocate or lawyer.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, keep your own copy of the full email thread, reply with the missing context in writing, and ask a manager or HR to review the whole exchange and not the fragment.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'm happy to talk about anything I've said, if we look at the whole conversation and talk about it when it comes up. I'd rather not have old messages brought out in the middle of something else."
codex_completed.safety_note: Someone quietly saving your words is pressure on trust, not a physical danger. The picture changes if saved material is paired with threats to release it, intimate images or recordings, a custody or legal case, or demands that you do something or stay. Keep your own copies of what has been sent, and take them to a lawyer or a domestic abuse or cyber-abuse advocate before replying to any threat.
misuse_warning: Calling any reminder of an earlier statement an evidence trap can make accountability look like an attack. People are entitled to say 'you told me this'.
Using the label to avoid being quoted accurately confuses stripped context with unwelcome content.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Emotion Control penalizes a feeling as soon as it is shown, whereas evidence traps bank the remark and bring it out weeks later. Resource Sabotage takes away something you need in the present, and here the material is something you already gave. Unlike a faked screenshot, nothing in an evidence trap is invented; the words are yours.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Moral Framing
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Answering someone's boundary, objection or criticism with a judgment of their character, such as selfish or disloyal, instead of with the thing they raised.
codex_completed.short_definition: Answering someone's boundary, objection or criticism with a judgment of their character, such as selfish or disloyal, instead of with the thing they raised.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: In moral framing, a boundary or complaint is met with a verdict on the kind of person who made it. A no becomes selfish, a fair criticism becomes disloyalty, a request for change becomes cruelty. The original issue drops out of sight, because the conversation is now about the person's worth. A hurt remark in a heated moment is common. The tell is character judgments replacing the subject every time, so a request has to be defended as virtue before it can be discussed.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You say what you need or what bothered you, and the reply is about what kind of person you are, so the issue never gets discussed.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Once the subject has become what kind of person you are, the original issue is no longer on the table and cannot be settled.
what_it_is: Naming a moral failing, such as selfish, cold, ungrateful, disloyal or a bad mother, in reply to a specific request.
A reply that moves from the event to the person, so the question 'can we change this?' is never reached.
Often borrows values the person holds dear, such as family loyalty, generosity or faith, and turns them into a test.
Makes saying no feel like a character flaw instead of a choice.
Occurs in families, couples, friendships, congregations and workplaces.
what_it_sounds_like: A good daughter would come.
That's a really selfish way to think about this.
I never thought you'd be so cold.
After all we've done for you, this is how you repay us?
Decent people don't keep score.
If you cared about this family, you wouldn't be asking.
I'm disappointed in the person you've become.
what_it_is_not: Sometimes an observation about character is accurate, specific and offered as real feedback, and sometimes two people hold different values and read the same event through them. A hurt remark later walked back and replaced with substance is not this.
A specific, honest observation about a behavior, given along with a discussion of the issue itself.
A disagreement rooted in different values, such as how much to give to family, where each side explains their own.
Someone telling you honestly that your action conflicted with a promise you made.
A friend saying 'that wasn't like you' about something out of character, and asking what was going on.
this_may_be_it_when: Every boundary you set is answered with a character label.
The label is about you as a whole, such as 'selfish', and not about the single act.
You end up justifying your goodness instead of your request.
Your original point gets lost and is not addressed later.
Other people hear what kind of person you are, in terms like these, before you have spoken.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They address your request and add how they feel about it.
They describe the effect on them without labeling you.
They apologize for a harsh word and return to the topic.
Their values clearly differ and they say so without condemning yours.
The comment is specific to one act and accurate, and you would agree on reflection.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People often reach for moral language when hurt, because it is the language they learned for strong feeling.
Two people with different upbringings can read the same act as generosity or as a failure of duty.
Family or community expectations may be voiced as duty by someone repeating what was said to them.
common_false_positives: A friend saying 'that wasn't kind' about a comment you made, and explaining why.
A mentor giving accurate, difficult feedback about honesty in your work.
A family member expressing disappointment in a decision while still accepting it.
discernment_questions: After I state my need, is the next thing said about my request or about me?
Can the original issue be discussed once the label is set aside?
Do I find myself proving I am a good person instead of explaining what I need?
Does the person apply the same standards to themselves?
Is the character comment specific and accurate, or global and sweeping?
less_concerning_if: The sharp word is taken back and the topic resumes.
The label describes one act, not who you are.
Different values are stated as differences rather than as failings.
more_concerning_if: Other people are recruited to repeat the verdict.
Support, affection or belonging is offered only if you drop the boundary.
You begin to hold the label yourself and apologize for having needs.
pattern_over_time_signs: You say 'sorry, I know I'm being selfish' before asking for anything.
You stop making requests you would once have thought ordinary.
You weigh each choice by what it will say about you instead of by what you need.
Your sense of being a good person starts to depend on going along.
codex_completed.repair_check: Watch whether the original topic gets its turn. If, after the character remark is withdrawn, the conversation returns to your request and the answer can be no without a new verdict, something has shifted. A kind apology that leaves the request unheard, and reappears next time, has not.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: State the boundary once without defending your character, and see what is said next. If the reply is about the boundary, even in disagreement, it was heard. If the next thing you hear is a statement about who you are, the boundary became a test of your character.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Most people want to see themselves as good, and moral labels reach that wish directly. When a request is recast as a flaw, the person may drop the request to protect their self-image, because defending their character feels more urgent than the original point. If the language borrows values they hold, such as loyalty or generosity, giving in may seem consistent with who they believe they are.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe guilt out of proportion to what they asked for, rehearsing justifications, and apologizing for ordinary needs. Some say they started to doubt whether they were selfish, and gave in to prove otherwise. Others describe a mix of relief and anger on realizing that the question they raised was never answered.

response_options.soft_clarification: Bring the conversation back to the request: 'I hear that you think I'm being selfish. Can we go back to what I asked?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to argue character: 'I'm not going to debate whether I'm a good person. I've told you what I can do, and that is my answer.'
response_options.disengagement: If the labels keep coming, close the talk on the original topic: 'Let's leave this for now.' You do not need to win the point about who you are.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe the exact words used and your request to someone outside the situation, and ask whether the request seems reasonable. A counselor or a leader you trust can help separate your values from the pressure.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, restate the issue in neutral terms and in writing: 'To be clear, my request is about the schedule.' If personal remarks continue, note them and raise them with a manager or HR.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "You may be right that we see this differently, but I'm asking about one specific thing. Can we talk about that request, and leave out what kind of person either of us is?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Moral labels on their own press on your self-image, not on your physical safety. That can change when a judgment comes with threats of exposure to a community, loss of housing, money or contact with children or family, or being told you deserve harm. If a verdict carries that weight, speak to someone outside the group, such as an advocate, a counselor or legal aid, before deciding anything.
misuse_warning: Calling every disapproving remark moral framing can wave away honest feedback. Sometimes a hard thing is true and said kindly.
Using the label to dismiss a family's real worries about a decision you have made turns a pattern into a way to avoid a conversation.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Emotion Control penalizes certain feelings as they appear, while moral framing answers a boundary or complaint with a verdict on the person's goodness. Nonverbal Dominance conveys disapproval through sighs and stares without words, and this one is put into words. Resource Sabotage takes things away; here nothing is removed, and the request is simply turned into a test of your character.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Reproductive Coercion
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Pressuring or penalizing someone over whether, when or how to have children, through money, work, family standing or withdrawal of support.
codex_completed.short_definition: Pressuring or penalizing someone over whether, when or how to have children, through money, work, family standing or withdrawal of support.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Reproductive coercion is pressure over another person's decisions about pregnancy and children: whether to have a child, when, how many, whether to continue a pregnancy, or whether to use contraception. The pressure can come from a partner, relatives, an employer or an institution, and works through consequences: money, a job, housing, belonging or support made to depend on the answer. Stating hopes is normal. The line is crossed when a cost is attached to the answer and the pressure continues after it has been given.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone ties your job, money, home or place in the family to what you decide about having children, and keeps pressing after you have answered.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A decision that belongs to one person's body and life ends up made under the weight of what refusal would cost them: job, money, support, standing in the family.
what_it_is: Consequences attached to a decision: pay, promotion, housing, money or support depend on having or not having a child.
Pressure repeated after you have given your answer, passed from partner to parents to in-laws to a community leader in turn.
Can include interference with contraception or with access to health care, which takes the decision out of your hands.
Can come from a partner, a family, an employer or an institution, and each works differently.
Runs in both directions: pressure to have a child, and pressure not to, or to end a pregnancy.
what_it_sounds_like: If you really loved me, you'd give me a baby.
People in this role who start families don't last here.
My parents will cut us off if there isn't a grandchild by next year.
We'll see how long your position lasts if you're expecting.
I'll support you only if you keep it. (Or: only if you end it.)
You don't get to decide that on your own.
You've said no three times, and we're not done talking.
what_it_is_not: People may want things and say so: a parent hoping for grandchildren, a partner describing the family they imagined. A neutral, lawful employment policy can touch a reproductive decision without targeting it. What changes the picture is a consequence attached to the answer.
A partner who says they want children, talks about timing, and accepts a 'no' or a 'not yet' while the relationship stays on the same terms.
Grandparents' hopes shared once or twice, with no money or standing attached.
A doctor or counselor explaining the medical risks of a pregnancy or a treatment, then leaving the decision to you.
Parental leave rules applied the same way to everyone at a workplace.
this_may_be_it_when: Money, housing or work is mentioned in the same breath as your decision.
The question is raised again right after you have answered it.
Other people are lined up to press you.
You have been told that your place in the family depends on it.
Your access to contraception, appointments or your own records has become something you must account for.
this_may_not_be_it_when: A wish is stated and then your answer is accepted.
Your income, home and standing do not change with your answer.
The pressure is one conversation and both sides are open.
Medical advice is given in full and the decision is left to you.
Everyone at the workplace is under the same stated policy.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People hope for grandchildren or a larger family, and say so without realizing how it weighs on you.
Couples often change their minds and need several conversations over years.
Employers have leave and scheduling rules that touch on parenthood without targeting any person.
common_false_positives: A relative asking 'any news?' at every holiday, who stops when told it is private.
A partner who is sad about a difference over children and grieves openly, with no leverage attached.
A clinic asking routine questions about pregnancy plans before prescribing.
discernment_questions: Is there a cost to me, in money, work, home or standing, tied to my answer?
Does the pressure stop when I answer, or does it come back?
Is anyone interfering with my contraception or appointments?
Can I say no, or not yet, and keep the same life?
Can I see a doctor on my own?
less_concerning_if: Hopes are voiced but your answer is accepted.
Support continues whichever way you decide.
Medical and practical information is shared openly, with the choice left to you.
more_concerning_if: Contraception, medication or appointments are controlled, hidden or monitored.
The pressure comes with threats about money, housing, children or immigration status.
Others in the family or workplace are being used to repeat the pressure.
pattern_over_time_signs: The question returns after each 'no', with higher stakes each time.
Your access to your own money, papers or health care has been shrinking.
You have started saying what is wanted to keep the peace.
Conversations about the future always lead back to children.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair would mean the decision stays yours and the cost attached to it disappears: the support, the job conditions and the family welcome continue as before, whatever you decided. Regret expressed while the pressure or the conditions remain is not repair.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: After you have given an answer, notice whether the subject is closed or reopened. A respected answer is followed by an unchanged life and a different topic. If it is followed by a quiet drop in help, warmth or hours, or by a new person raising it, the answer is still being negotiated.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When the price of a choice is housing, income or family belonging, the choice gets weighed against security instead of against one's own wishes. Pressure repeated through several people can make a 'no' feel selfish or impossible to hold, and reduced access to money or care can make going along seem the only workable route. Over time a person may report agreeing without feeling the decision was theirs.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Accounts include a sense that your body and future are being decided by others, dread around conversations about family, and anxiety about money or work. Some feel grief over a decision made under pressure, or anger years afterward. Others fear that questions about their health care would be followed by consequences.

response_options.soft_clarification: If it feels safe, answer briefly and without arguing: 'That's something I'm still thinking about. I'll let you know.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask for the topic to be set aside: 'I'd like to leave this for now, and I'd like to talk about something else.'
response_options.disengagement: Without announcing anything, keep your own medical appointments, records and money where you can reach them, and let a clinic know if you need to speak to a clinician alone.
response_options.support_seeking: A sexual and reproductive health clinic, a doctor or a domestic abuse advocate can talk with you privately. They can explain your options and how to keep care confidential where you live.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a work decision seems tied to pregnancy or plans for children, write down what was said and when, and take it to HR, a union representative or an employment-rights service before replying to anything.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I understand this matters a lot to you. It's a decision about my own body and life, and I need to think it through at my own pace. Can we talk about something else for now?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Pressure about pregnancy can sit alongside coercive control, violence, and threats to money, housing, children or immigration status. Pregnancy can also be a time when abuse begins or worsens. Warning signs include controlled contraception or appointments, being watched at clinics, and threats tied to your answer. A domestic abuse hotline or clinic can talk privately; ask about safe ways to reach them from a phone or device the other person cannot see.
misuse_warning: Treating any wish for a child, or any employer's parental-leave policy, as coercion can silence honest wishes. The label fits consequences attached to the answer, not the wish.
Calling a partner's grief over a difference about children coercion can turn a painful, honest disagreement into an accusation.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Resource Sabotage removes tools or support so that a task fails, while reproductive coercion ties the loss of money, work or support to a decision about children. "Managed Out" Through Exhaustion strips a person's place at work gradually, whereas here the consequence is tied to one decision and follows the answer. Emotion Control penalizes feelings generally, not a specific choice about family.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Negative Reinforcement Traps
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A cycle in which coldness, criticism or withdrawal stays in place until someone gives in, then lifts at once, so giving in comes to feel like relief.
codex_completed.short_definition: A cycle in which coldness, criticism or withdrawal stays in place until someone gives in, then lifts at once, so giving in comes to feel like relief.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: In psychology, negative reinforcement means a behavior becomes more likely because it makes something unpleasant stop. In a relationship or team, the unpleasant thing might be a cold shoulder, sharp remarks or a sulk that fills the house, and it ends the moment you agree, apologize or drop the request. One tense stretch that eases after a talk is ordinary life. What sets this apart is easing that is tied to your compliance and not to anything being settled, and giving in that starts before the chill has even arrived.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: The atmosphere stays tense until you do what is wanted, and then it turns warm at once, so giving in starts to feel like the only way to get peace.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Relief becomes the reward for giving in, and in time the giving-in starts arriving early, before the pressure does. The disagreement underneath never gets discussed, so it never gets settled either.
what_it_is: A tense stretch (silence, clipped answers, pointed criticism) that stays in the room until a particular outcome happens.
A sudden return to warmth the moment you agree, which can feel like being forgiven for something you never found out you had done.
A learned link in your own body: you tighten when a certain tone appears and loosen only after you yield.
Found in couples, families, friendships and workplaces where a manager's mood tracks whether you did as asked.
Different from a single sulk because the sequence of pressure, yielding and relief repeats and the yielding gets quicker.
what_it_sounds_like: (Three days of one-word answers, then, the minute you say yes:) There you go, was that so hard? Let's get dinner.
I'm fine. (Said flatly, while the whole house feels tense.)
You go ahead and do what you want. I'll just be here.
(After you drop your request:) Oh good, now I can actually breathe around you.
I only get like this when you push me. Just do it and we can all relax.
(Your own thought:) It is easier to say yes now than to sit through the next two days.
Why can't things be this nice all the time? They would be, if you'd just listen.
what_it_is_not: Moods that rise and fall for reasons that have nothing to do with what you decided. Some people are simply changeable, and their weather does not track your answers.
Tension that eases because something got resolved. Calm after a real conversation is different from calm that only ever arrives at the moment of compliance.
A person who needs quiet to cool down after an argument, says so, and comes back to talk it through whatever you decided.
Warmth returning because you made up and both of you changed something, not because only one of you did.
A natural consequence you chose, such as a friend being disappointed when you cancel. Disappointment that fades on its own is not a lever.
A routine at work where a deadline stress lifts when the project ships, whoever delivered it.
this_may_be_it_when: The chill ends within minutes of you agreeing, even though nothing about the original disagreement was talked through.
The same sequence plays out over many different topics, from where to spend a holiday to what you wear.
You notice yourself saying yes before the cold has fully set in.
Your relief at the thaw is bigger than your pleasure in the outcome you agreed to.
If you hold your position, the pressure deepens or lasts longer, and it ends only when you give way.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The tension lifts after you both talk, whichever way the decision went.
The other person's moods are just as stormy when you are not in the picture, with no link to your choices.
You can say no and the atmosphere stays steady, perhaps with some honest disappointment.
They name what is bothering them and ask for a conversation instead of waiting for you to guess.
You went along with something because you were persuaded, and you would do it again.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people withdraw when upset because they were raised to cool off alone, and the return of warmth is relief at the quiet ending, not a reward.
Both of you may be stressed by the same thing, such as a move or a sick relative, and the mood in the house lifts for everyone when it passes.
A person who struggles to say what they feel may go silent and then ease up once they feel heard, with no link to who gave way.
common_false_positives: A couple who go quiet after a fight and warm up after a real apology from the person who was wrong, whichever of them that was.
A parent who is genuinely upset about a teenager's lie and is friendly again once the truth is out.
A colleague who is curt during a crunch and cheerful when the launch is over.
discernment_questions: Does the warmth come back because we settled something, or only because I stopped asking?
Have I started agreeing earlier, before the cold even begins?
When I hold my position, does the chill grow instead of staying level?
Can I name a recent disagreement that was actually talked through to an end, with neither of us giving way in silence?
Do I feel more relieved than glad when I say yes?
less_concerning_if: The quiet period is short, is described out loud ('I need an hour'), and ends in a conversation.
Your answer does not decide how warm the next day is.
Both people sometimes yield and both sometimes hold their ground, and the mood stays about the same.
more_concerning_if: Your giving-in is the only thing that has ever ended a cold spell.
The areas where you yield keep growing: friends, money, time alone, work.
Holding your position brings escalation such as harsher remarks, threats to withdraw support, or longer silence.
pattern_over_time_signs: The stretch of coldness before you give in gets shorter, because you give in sooner.
You stop bringing up topics that you know will be followed by a chill.
You find yourself planning around moods, picking days and words to avoid setting one off.
Warm patches feel fragile, like a lull you can lose by saying the wrong thing.
codex_completed.repair_check: A real change would show up as a disagreement getting talked through while the mood stayed steady, even when you did not come round. A kind week after you yield tells you only that the cycle finished.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Hold a position on something small and watch what the next two days feel like. Does the atmosphere stay level, or does the cold appear and linger until you reverse? Your answer to that question tells you more than anything either of you says.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When an unpleasant state reliably ends the moment a person complies, the body can learn the link without any words being said. The relief feels good, and the next time tension appears, giving in comes sooner. Over many rounds, the anticipation alone can be enough to produce the yielding, and the original disagreement never gets examined.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A low hum of dread when a certain tone appears is common, along with quick agreement that is hard to explain afterwards and a habit of stepping carefully around the house. Some can no longer tell which of their choices they really wanted. Seeing the sequence written down at last brings a flood of relief to some.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask once, in a calm moment: 'I notice things get tense until I say yes, and then they lift. Can we talk about the actual disagreement while it is still calm?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold your position without arguing it, and let the quiet be quiet: 'I've decided, and I'm happy to talk about why. I'm not going to change my mind to make the mood better.'
response_options.disengagement: When the chill sets in, put your attention on something that is yours, such as a walk, a call with a friend or a task, and do not negotiate with the silence.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone outside the relationship about two or three rounds of the cycle, including how fast you gave in. Hearing yourself say it often shows the sequence.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager's mood tracks whether you comply, move requests and decisions into email or a shared tracker so the outcome rests on what is written, not on how the day felt.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Saying yes just to make things easier is not something I'm going to do, and I want to think this through properly. I'm glad to talk about it whenever you are ready."
codex_completed.safety_note: A cycle of pressure and relief is a strain on a relationship, not a sign of physical danger. Take it more seriously if the pressure expands to include threats, cutting you off from friends or money, monitoring, or if you start to fear what happens when you hold your position. Those are the changes that call for a domestic abuse advocate or a counselor you trust.
misuse_warning: Calling every mood after an argument a 'trap' can make normal cooling-off look sinister. A person who needs time and returns to talk is not applying pressure.
Using the label to prove that someone is manipulating you, based on how your own body responded, skips the question of what they actually said and did.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Emotion Control sets which feelings are allowed and punishes the rest, whatever the topic, while this cycle ties the pressure to one outcome: your yes. Nonverbal Dominance is the sigh, stare or eye roll itself; here the point is how long the chill lasts and what ends it. Ritualized Exhaustion wears down a person through demands and lost sleep, whereas this pattern leaves your rest alone and works through the timing of relief.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Moving-in-Silence
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Making major decisions that change another person's life without telling or asking them, so they learn of it only once it is done.
codex_completed.short_definition: Making major decisions that change another person's life without telling or asking them, so they learn of it only once it is done.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Moving in silence means settling something large, such as a lease, a loan, a job offer, a school for the children or a sale, and keeping it from the person it will change until it cannot be undone. The decision-maker may have had reasons, and keeping quiet once does not make a pattern. What marks it is weighty choices made alone again and again while small ones are put to a vote, and news that arrives as a finished fact rather than a question.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Big choices that change your life get made without you, and you find out afterwards, when there is nothing left to say except 'okay'.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Finding out after the fact that your life has been rearranged leaves nothing to discuss, only something to absorb. Over time it can teach you that your say does not reach the decisions that count.
what_it_is: A large decision about money, housing, children, work or family that is finished before the affected person hears about it.
A split in who gets asked: your opinion is welcome on the paint color, not on the move across the country.
News delivered as a done deal, so the only available reactions are acceptance or an argument that cannot change anything.
A pattern that can show up between partners, in a family business, among adult siblings sharing a parent's care, and in a workplace that reorganizes your job.
Different from a private choice about your own life: what matters is that the decision lands on someone else and was kept from them.
what_it_sounds_like: Oh, I signed the lease on Friday. We move in six weeks.
I didn't want to stress you out, so I just took care of it.
It's already done, so there's no point getting upset now.
You would have only said no, so I saved us the argument.
(Found in the post:) A letter confirming a loan in both names that nobody discussed.
I told your mother we're hosting. I assumed you wouldn't mind.
The new schedule starts Monday. HR sent it to everyone except you.
what_it_is_not: An emergency that forced a fast choice, followed by an honest explanation and an apology for the lack of consultation.
A part of life that you both agreed is one person's call, such as who manages the car insurance or the grocery list.
A surprise party, a gift or a planned trip kept quiet for a kind reason, where the surprise is revealed and welcomed.
A manager changing a rota inside their normal authority, and giving as much notice as they can.

Poor communication from someone who is disorganized or forgetful about everyone, including themselves. What distinguishes this is whether the exclusion is explained afterwards, and whether it falls only on the decisions that carry weight.
Someone making a choice about their own money, health or career that does not rest on you.
this_may_be_it_when: The decisions kept from you are the heavy ones: housing, debt, children, jobs, large purchases.
You find out from a third party, a document or a bill, and not from the person who decided.
When you object, you hear that it is too late, as though the lateness were your doing.
Your say is asked for on small matters and not on matters that change how you live.
The explanation offered is that you would have reacted badly, not that there was no time.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They told you as soon as they could and acknowledged you should have been asked.
You had agreed ahead of time that this kind of decision could be made alone.
The decision could still be changed, and they were willing to undo it when you objected.
It was a one-time event, and since then they have asked about big things before acting.
The secret was a pleasant surprise that was soon revealed.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A fast-moving offer, such as a flat that would be gone within hours, can force a decision before everyone can be reached.
Some people avoid hard conversations out of dread and make a decision first, then confess, which is poor communication more than exclusion.
In some families or cultures one adult is traditionally the decision-maker for certain matters, and both people may have accepted that.
common_false_positives: A partner who took a job offer on the spot after talking with you for weeks about whether to take it.
A sibling who paid for a parent's care without asking, and who was asked by that parent to keep it quiet.
A team lead who restructured responsibilities over a weekend because the client demanded it, and who sent an apology on Monday morning.
discernment_questions: Was there time to ask me, or was silence a choice?
Do I get a real voice in the decisions that change my daily life, or only in the minor ones?
When I object after the fact, is the decision open to change, or is it presented as closed?
Is there a pattern of finding out from documents, bills or other people?
If this person had expected me to agree, would they have told me first?
less_concerning_if: The decision was sudden, outside anyone's control, and explained with regret.
You can reverse or reshape what happened, and your objection changes what follows.
Both of you have at times acted first and told the other later, and both treat it as a lapse.
more_concerning_if: The silent decisions involve your money, your home, your children or your documents.
You are blamed for being upset about what you were not told.
Your access to information, accounts or paperwork is shrinking, so surprises become harder to catch.
pattern_over_time_signs: You start checking mail, accounts and calendars in case something has been decided.
Over months, more of your life is arranged by someone else, and fewer questions reach you.
You stop objecting because earlier objections changed nothing, and that silence gets counted as agreement.
Friends and relatives learn about plans before you do.
codex_completed.repair_check: Look at the next large decision. Do they bring it to you while it can still change, even if that makes it slower and harder? Apologizing for the last surprise while making the next one in private is not repair.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask to be consulted before anything over a certain size, and notice what happens then. Does the next big choice reach you as a question? An answer that tells you the rule is unreasonable, or that you are making it hard, is a different signal.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A decision that is finished when you learn of it leaves little room for influence, and objecting can look like being unreasonable about something already settled. Repeated over time, this can teach a person that their input is pointless, so they stop offering it and the decision-maker's authority grows without ever being claimed out loud.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Feeling like a guest in your own life is a common description, as is going quiet at home or in meetings because nothing said has changed anything, and checking letters and statements for news. Some feel foolish for not having known. Others carry an anger with nowhere to go, because the thing is already done.

response_options.soft_clarification: Say what you noticed and ask for a different order: 'I found out about the loan after it was signed. Can we agree to talk about big things before they happen?'
response_options.firm_boundary: If it feels safe, ask for early notice of big decisions: 'Anything involving our home, our money or the children, I'd like to hear about before it is final.'
response_options.disengagement: When news arrives as a done deal, you can decline to respond in the moment: 'I need a day to take this in before we talk about it.'
response_options.support_seeking: Make a private list of the large decisions you learned about afterwards, with dates, and go through it with a trusted friend, a counselor or a legal adviser if money or housing is involved.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask that changes affecting your role be sent to you in writing before they take effect, and keep copies of the notices you did and did not receive.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Big decisions that change my life matter to me, and I want to hear about them while they can still change. Could we agree that large things get talked through first?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Silent decisions become more serious when they take away your money, your home, your documents or your ability to reach other people. If you find accounts you cannot see, a lease you did not agree to or paperwork that is hidden from you, quietly photograph or note what you can, and speak to a legal aid service or a domestic abuse advocate before raising it with anyone.
misuse_warning: Treating every unilateral choice as a controlling act can punish ordinary mistakes, forgetfulness or a household where one person handles most logistics by agreement.
Using the label to demand a veto over every decision can create the same one-sidedness you are trying to name.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Resource Sabotage removes the tools, money or access you need and then blames you for the result; moving in silence is the decision itself being made out of your sight, whether or not your resources are touched. Emotion Control comes in after the news, when your reaction is called an overreaction. The difference is the timing: here the harm is in what happened before you knew.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Smart-Home Coercion
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Using internet-connected household devices such as locks, cameras, thermostats and speakers to watch, unsettle or control another person at home.
codex_completed.short_definition: Using internet-connected household devices such as locks, cameras, thermostats and speakers to watch, unsettle or control another person at home.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Smart-home coercion is the use of connected devices, which were sold for convenience, to monitor or pressure someone who lives in or visits the home. It can look like a thermostat that changes by itself, lights that flicker, a lock that stops working, a camera feed someone else can see, or a speaker that records. Each device usually works normally most of the time, so it is hard to point to. One glitch means little. The picture changes when odd events cluster around conflict or independence, and when one person holds the accounts and the other does not.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Devices in the home, such as locks, cameras and heating, are used to watch you or make you feel on edge, and they are hard to prove because they mostly work as normal.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: When the house itself becomes unpredictable, there is nowhere to be unobserved and nothing that can be shown to anyone else afterwards. A person can start doubting their own senses or feeling that even a private phone call is not private.
what_it_is: A device account (the app, the hub, the router login) held by one person, who can see or change what the others cannot.
Changes that serve no practical purpose: temperature swings, lights or music at night, doors that will not unlock, a doorbell camera that is suddenly offline.
Remarks that show knowledge of things only a device would have recorded, such as when you came home or what was said in a room.
A form of environmental control that borrows technology, and one that often outlasts a separation if the accounts are never changed.
Different from ordinary smart-home annoyance because the events line up with moments of conflict, and the person controlling the system will not share it.
what_it_sounds_like: The heating drops by six degrees the evening after an argument and comes back up when it is over.
Your phone shows a camera in the hallway that you did not install, and the app belongs to another account.
You hear: You got in at 11:40 last night, didn't you? (You did not say.)
The front door code stops working on days you have plans.
A speaker lights up or plays a voice message nobody sent from the room.
Why would you need to know the thermostat password? I handle all that.
Lights switching on and off in a room only you are using, with no schedule you set.
what_it_is_not: A genuine malfunction or a software update that resets a schedule or drops a device offline. Connected devices misfire, and updates change settings without asking.
A household that shares a system by agreement, with one person handling the technical setup and everyone knowing what is connected.
Someone adjusting the heating to their own preference. Wanting a warmer room is not surveillance.
A security camera on the porch that everyone in the home knows about and can view.
A poor wifi signal, a weak battery or a failing hub that causes devices to behave oddly in one corner of the house.
A child or visitor playing with the voice assistant. Unexplained changes that cluster around moments of conflict are a different picture.
this_may_be_it_when: Odd device events follow arguments, plans of your own or time spent with certain people.
You do not have equal access to the accounts, or you are told you do not need it.
The other person refers to things the devices could have captured, though you did not tell them.
A device you did not buy or agree to turns up, or one you own is linked to someone else's account.
Resetting a device or changing a password is met with anger or followed by new problems.
this_may_not_be_it_when: A technician or manufacturer explains the fault and fixing it stops the behavior.
Everyone in the home has the same access and knows what each device does.
The odd events happen at random times, unrelated to anything you or anyone else did.
The other person has no account access at all, and you have checked.
A shared system's settings changed after a recent firmware update, and other households report the same fault.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Smart devices genuinely misbehave, losing their schedule after a power cut or an update.
One person may have set up everything because they are the one who understands technology, and may not have thought to share the login.
Old accounts from a previous tenant, an ex-partner or a family member who helped with setup may still be linked without anyone meaning to watch you.
common_false_positives: Hearing a voice assistant respond because it misheard a word on the television.
A thermostat that follows a weekday schedule you forgot you had agreed to.
A parent checking a doorbell camera to see when children arrive from school, with the family's knowledge.
discernment_questions: Who holds the accounts for each device, and can I see them?
Do the strange events line up with moments of conflict or with my plans?
Does anyone refer to things they could only have learned from a device?
When I ask about a device, do I get a clear answer or irritation?
Would the behavior stop if the accounts were reset by someone I trust, such as an electrician or the landlord?
less_concerning_if: Everybody in the home can see the settings and the accounts, and the events have a technical explanation.
Fixing or resetting a device ends the behavior and nothing else follows.
The person who manages the system has shown you the app and welcomes questions.
more_concerning_if: Events cluster around conflict, independence or time with other people.
You cannot get into the accounts, or you are told you must not.
Someone knows things about your movements or conversations that you did not share.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find yourself lowering your voice, dressing in the bathroom or whispering on calls in your own home.
New devices appear in the house, and each time the setup is done by one person.
You change how you speak and where you go because you cannot rule out being observed.
The strange events return after each reset, and linger after the relationship has changed.
codex_completed.repair_check: Access over time tells the story. Do the accounts become visible and shared equally, or does it stay a promise that it will stop? A promise with the same logins still in place leaves the situation unchanged.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: If it feels safe, ask who can see or control a particular device and note the answer. Does a clear list come back, with a willingness to change it? Defensiveness, vagueness or a change in the device's behavior afterwards tells you the question itself is not welcome.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Knowing you might be watched can change behavior even when nobody is watching at that moment, because the possibility is enough. Devices that work most days make each odd event easy to explain away, which can lead a person to doubt their senses and to say nothing, since there is little to show anyone.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe never feeling private at home, speaking in lowered voices, testing devices to see if something responds, and wondering whether they are imagining it. Some stop using their own rooms comfortably. Others describe relief when a technician or advocate confirms that the devices really were connected to another account.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask out of curiosity, not accusation: 'How does the new system work? Which of the devices record anything?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decide privately which rooms and conversations you will treat as unprotected, and keep sensitive talk and plans elsewhere. You do not need to explain why.
response_options.disengagement: For private calls and plans, use a phone on mobile data, a friend's home or another place that sits outside the household network.
response_options.support_seeking: A domestic abuse advocate or a technology-safety service can help you check devices safely. Contact them from a phone or computer the other person has never had access to.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If the home is rented, a landlord or letting agent may be able to reset devices they supplied. Keep any messages with them as a record.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'm still getting my head around how the system works. Could you walk me through which devices record or listen, so I know what's in each room?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Watch for signs that someone knows where you have been, tracks your phone or controls who can enter. If you suspect it, do not search for or disable devices at once, because that can be noticed. Use a safe device to contact a domestic abuse or tech-safety service, and plan any changes with them first.
misuse_warning: Treating every glitch or update as proof of surveillance can create fear where the cause is a faulty hub or a software update. Check for a technical explanation before concluding anything.
Accusing a housemate or partner of watching you, without checking the accounts, can damage trust over a fault that nobody caused.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Spatial Invasion uses a person's body, standing too close or blocking a doorway, while this is done through devices, often when nobody is in the room. Resource Sabotage takes away money, tools or information you need; here the devices stay in place and work as a form of watching or unsettling. The telltale sign is access that only one person holds.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Health Sabotage
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Interfering with another person's medication, sleep, food, exercise or medical care in ways that leave them weaker and more dependent.
codex_completed.short_definition: Interfering with another person's medication, sleep, food, exercise or medical care in ways that leave them weaker and more dependent.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Health sabotage is interference with the things a body and mind depend on: medication, sleep, regular meals, movement and doctor visits. It can be direct, such as hiding pills, or indirect, such as picking a fight at midnight before an early appointment or never having the car free on clinic days. Illness, newborns and money worries disrupt everyone's routines without anyone doing anything. The pattern is different when the disruption falls on one person, has no ordinary explanation, and lands when that person is trying to act on their own.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone interferes with your pills, your sleep, your food or your appointments in ways that wear you down and make you rely on them more.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Sleep, medication and medical care are the ground a person stands on to think and act. When those go, so does the capacity to notice what is happening, or to make a plan to get somewhere safer.
what_it_is: Disrupting medicine: pills misplaced, doses discouraged, prescriptions not picked up, or scorn for treatment.
Breaking sleep with late-night arguments, noise or demands, especially before something important.
Making appointments hard to attend by withholding transport, money or childcare, or by creating a crisis on the day.
Controlling food and rest, for example mocking a diet a doctor prescribed or pushing exercise or fasting beyond what the person wants.
Different from neglect caused by exhaustion: the interference tends to track moments when the person is asserting independence.
what_it_sounds_like: You don't need those tablets. You were fine before them.
(At 1am:) We need to talk about this now. It can't wait until morning.
I can't take you to the clinic today, something's come up. Again.
Doctors just want your money. Skip it.
(The pill organizer is empty and nobody knows why.)
Sleep is for people who aren't serious about this family.
You're being dramatic about your health, as always.
what_it_is_not: New babies, illness and crises wreck everyone's sleep and routines at once. When the whole household is affected, nobody is being singled out.
Transport, money and shift patterns genuinely get in the way of appointments, and the other person may be doing their best.
Someone struggling with their own health may be unable to help, without doing anything to harm.
A sincere worry that a medication is making you unwell, voiced once and followed by support for you to ask your doctor.
Different medical opinions, such as a relative who prefers a diet change to a particular pill, while still respecting your decision.
A caregiver who is run ragged and forgets a task. Interference that specifically tracks moments you are acting on your own, with no ordinary explanation, is what stands apart.
this_may_be_it_when: Your pills, appointments or rest are disrupted most when you are making your own plans.
The disruption falls on you and not on other people in the home.
You lose track of a medicine that was always in the same place, and it turns up later.
Someone is angry or mocking when you mention a doctor, therapist or treatment.
Your health has worsened in a way that suits the other person, who seems more at ease when you are unwell.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Everyone in the household is run down by the same event, such as a baby, a move or an illness.
The appointments you missed were hard to attend for reasons you can both name, and you worked out another way.
Concerns about a treatment are raised once and you are supported to talk to your doctor.
The person cannot help because of their own illness, but would if they could.
Missed doses are explained by your own forgetfulness, and a pill organizer or alarm fixes it.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Shift work, a long commute or lack of money can make clinic visits hard without anyone intending to block them.
A caregiver who is exhausted may forget a task or let routines slide, which is neglect from overload, not interference.
Some people hold strong beliefs about medicine or diet and voice them clumsily without wishing to limit your choices.
common_false_positives: A flatmate who is noisy at night because of a different work schedule, and who apologizes and adjusts.
A relative who is anxious about side effects and who encourages you to ask your doctor.
A partner who can't drive you because they work the same hours, and who helps you book a taxi instead.
discernment_questions: Does the disruption to my sleep, medication or appointments fall on me and not on everyone?
Does it get worse when I make plans of my own or seek help?
Is there an ordinary explanation, such as money, transport or a new baby, that both of us would accept?
Do I feel physically or mentally worse in ways that match the other person's preferences?
When I ask for help getting to a doctor, do I get support or obstacles?
less_concerning_if: The disruption has a clear shared cause, and the other person is working with you to fix it.
You can still reach your doctor, medicine and rest when you need to, with some effort.
When you raise a concern about your health, you are helped and not mocked.
more_concerning_if: Medication, sleep or care is interfered with right before an appointment, a decision or a move to get help.
Your health is declining and the other person minimizes it or seems satisfied that you rely on them.
You are cut off from doctors, pharmacies or insurance papers.
pattern_over_time_signs: Appointments you used to keep slip away one by one, always for a reason that sounds reasonable.
You are more tired, foggier or less well than you were, and increasingly dependent on one person for care.
Medicines or health information are kept in places only the other person controls.
Your own ability to plan a day, a trip or a job shrinks as your health becomes less certain.
codex_completed.repair_check: Watch what changes in practice: are your medicines, sleep and appointments left alone, and does the other person help them happen? Regret that comes with the same obstacles on clinic days has not repaired anything, while quiet practical support over months has.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Consider who now decides about your pills, bedtime and clinic visits. When you take a dose, go to bed or book a visit, does it pass without a fuss, or is there a cost? A request treated as an attack, or followed by a new crisis, is worth noticing.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Poor sleep, missed medication and poor nutrition can reduce concentration, mood and energy, and a person who feels unwell often has less capacity to question what is happening or to make plans. When a caregiver or partner is also the person who controls the interference, dependence can grow without anyone naming it.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Constant tiredness, symptoms that keep returning and confusion about whether the illness is really worse than it seems are all described, along with shame about needing help. Some stop trusting their own sense of how they feel. A few notice slowly that they felt better after a few days away from home.

response_options.soft_clarification: Say what you need in practical terms: 'I need to take my medication at the same time each day, and I'd like your help making that easy.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep your care in your own hands without making it an event: book appointments yourself, put them in your own phone, and mention them only when you need practical help.
response_options.disengagement: Keep a second supply of medication, a copy of prescriptions and appointment details somewhere safe outside the home, such as with a friend or at work.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell your doctor, a nurse or a pharmacist what is happening, including that doses or appointments have been disrupted. They see this often and can help you plan care quietly.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If sleep or time off is being disrupted by an employer or manager, document dates and hours and raise it with HR, a union or an occupational health service.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "My health care matters to me, and I'm going to keep my appointments and take my medicine as my doctor advised. I would really appreciate your help with that."
codex_completed.safety_note: Take extra care if medicines go missing, if you are kept awake or cut off from care around the time you try to make a change, or if you feel physically unwell for no clear reason. A doctor, pharmacist or domestic abuse advocate can help you privately. If you feel seriously ill or think you have been given something you did not take knowingly, get medical help straight away.
misuse_warning: Assuming that every missed dose or exhausted caregiver is sabotage can hurt a person who is stretched thin and doing their best.
Using the label to dismiss a family member's real concern about a treatment can cut off conversations that a doctor could help with.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Ritualized Exhaustion uses forced schedules and relentless demands inside a group or program to lower resistance; health sabotage may include broken sleep but also reaches medicines, food and care. Resource Sabotage removes tools, money or support so you fail at a task; here the thing being worn down is your body and your access to treatment.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Blackmail / Leverage Exploitation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Using private or damaging information, true or not, as a hold over someone to force compliance or silence under a stated or implied threat of exposure.
codex_completed.short_definition: Using private or damaging information, true or not, as a hold over someone to force compliance or silence under a stated or implied threat of exposure.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: The two names in the title describe closely related behavior. Blackmail is the plain form: a demand with a threat of exposure attached. Leverage exploitation is the wider description, including cases where no demand is spoken and a pointed reference to something private does the work. The information might be a secret shared in trust, an old mistake, images, immigration status, or something invented. One furious remark in a fight, retracted, is different. The pattern is a specific demand tied to the possibility of exposure, and fear that keeps working long after any one demand has passed.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone holds something private or damaging over you and makes it clear it could come out if you do not do what they want.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Something shared in trust becomes the reason compliance is no longer optional, and the fear of exposure keeps working long after any particular demand has passed. It can make asking for help feel impossible, because asking means risking the thing you were told would come out.
what_it_is: A demand (money, silence, staying, sex, a signature) joined to a threat to tell, show or post something.
A quieter form in which no demand is spoken: a pointed mention of a private matter that makes the point.
Information that may be real, exaggerated or invented. Fear of exposure works the same either way.
Material taken from trust: a confession, a private photo, a past mistake, a debt, a visa or health detail.
Possible between partners, ex-partners, relatives, colleagues, strangers online, and in workplaces where someone holds a record over another person.
what_it_sounds_like: Do this for me, or everyone at your work will see those messages.
I wonder what your family would say if they knew about what you told me last year.
I'd hate for that photo to end up somewhere. You know I wouldn't want to. Just be sensible.
(After you refuse:) Fine. But remember I'm the only one who knows about the thing in 2019.
Pay me and it goes away. Otherwise you're done.
You owe me. Don't forget what I've got on you.
(A message from an unknown account, with a screenshot of a private conversation, and a deadline.)
what_it_is_not: Real hurt about something you once shared or did, said out loud with no demand attached. Hurt and leverage are different things.
Pursuing genuine wrongdoing through proper channels, such as reporting a crime or a policy breach to the police, a regulator or a manager. That is not holding a secret over someone.
A furious remark made in a single heated moment and retracted afterwards, which may be anger and not a lever.
Someone warning you honestly about a consequence they do not control, such as 'if the landlord finds out, you may lose the flat'.
A friend who says they must tell a safeguarding lead about something you told them, because they are bound to.
Asking for a debt to be repaid and mentioning that legal steps exist, which is different from threatening to expose private matters.
this_may_be_it_when: A specific demand is tied to a threat of exposure, spoken or heavily implied.
The information is something you shared in trust or something private that could cost you your job, home, standing or safety.
