codex_completed.name: Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation)
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Repeated watching, tracking or following of a former partner after a breakup, in person or through phones and accounts, leaving them unable to live unobserved.
codex_completed.short_definition: Repeated watching, tracking or following of a former partner after a breakup, in person or through phones and accounts, leaving them unable to live unobserved.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Two words are joined here, for two related behaviors that overlap. Stalking is repeated unwanted following, contact or appearing where you are. Surveillance is the monitoring: location tracking, access to accounts, questions put to friends or relatives. Either can appear without the other. Because shared custody and mutual friends make some contact normal, a single run-in or piece of news says almost nothing. What stands out is knowledge or presence that fits no channel you chose to open.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: After a relationship ends, the other person keeps showing up, tracking you, or knowing things about your life that you never told them.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Separation is supposed to end the other person's access. When it does not, ordinary life, including where you live, who you see and what you do next, goes on under observation, and nowhere feels fully private.
what_it_is: Following or turning up: waiting outside a home or workplace, appearing at places you go regularly, driving past.
Digital watching: location sharing left on, an unfamiliar app or tracker on a device, shared cloud or family-plan logins that were never switched off.
Indirect watching: questions to friends, coworkers, children or relatives about where you are and who you are with.
Contact that goes on after it has been declined, including messages from new numbers or accounts.
Knowledge of your plans or whereabouts that cannot be traced to anything you shared.
Two behaviors that often travel together after a breakup, watching and approaching, though either can happen alone.
what_it_sounds_like: I saw you at the grocery store on Saturday. Nice jacket. (You told them nothing about your weekend.)
How was dinner with your sister? (You never mentioned it.)
The same car parked across from your building more than once.
Messages arriving from a new number minutes after you blocked the old one.
A friend says: they keep asking me where you are and who you're seeing.
A device you never set up shows in your list of signed-in devices.
I just happened to be in the area.
what_it_is_not: Shared custody and shared property need real, continuing contact: handoffs, schedules, a lease, a car loan.
News traveling through mutual friends, with nobody asking or monitoring anyone.
A former partner who sees you at the same gym or town event, says hello and moves on, in a small community.
Public posts that anyone could read. Seeing what you chose to post openly is not tracking.
A co-parenting arrangement in which both parents agreed to share a child's location.
Lingering fear of being watched after real contact has ended. It is common and deserves support, and it is not always evidence of present monitoring.
this_may_be_it_when: They know details you never told them, and your mutual friends deny passing them on.
They appear at your home, work, gym or a child's school with no logistical reason.
Contact continues after you asked for it to stop, shifting to new numbers, accounts or messengers.
A device, account or location setting turns out to be shared or accessed without your say.
The attention rises when something in your life changes, such as a move, a new job or a new relationship.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Their contact stays inside shared logistics, such as exchange times and bills, and ends once those are settled.
What they know came from something you posted openly or from a friend who passed it on openly.
Run-ins happen in a place you both have an ordinary reason to be.
They have respected the end of contact, and any request to stop, for months.
A neutral technician checked your devices and accounts and found nothing unfamiliar.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: In a small town or shared social circle, former partners meet often by chance.
Mutual friends talk, and news about your life can reach your ex without anyone being asked.
Shared accounts, family phone plans or old logins can leave access open simply because nobody closed them.
Co-parents may need to know pickup times and school events.
common_false_positives: A former partner who messages about the children's schedule and nothing else.
A shared streaming or cloud account that shows old photos or viewing history because nobody closed it.
A mutual friend who repeats what they saw on your public page without being asked to.
discernment_questions: Does this person know things I never told them, and can I trace how?
Does contact about shared children or property stay on those subjects?
Has the attention grown since we separated, instead of fading?
Do I know which devices and accounts are signed in to my life, and who shares them?
Do I change where I go, or when, because I expect to be seen?
Has anyone else noticed the car, the messages or the questions?
less_concerning_if: Contact is limited to scheduled exchanges and stops when each exchange is over.
Whatever they know can be traced to something public or something a friend said openly.
Time has reduced the contact rather than raised it.
more_concerning_if: They appear at places you did not announce, or know your plans in advance.
Contact has increased since you ended things, or since a new relationship, move or job.
There have been threats, damage to property, or messages that hint at what they know about your movements.
pattern_over_time_signs: You change your route, your hours or your gym without a practical reason.
You check mirrors, windows and parking lots more than you used to, and dread opening a new message.
Friends and relatives report being questioned about you, in small amounts, over many months.
Moments when your life changes, such as a new apartment or partner, are followed by a rise in the signs.
codex_completed.repair_check: Distance that holds over months is the sign to look for: contact narrows to logistics, the questions to friends stop, and nothing surfaces that they should not know. A promise to stop followed by a message from a new number is not it.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Treat the hours and days after any limit you set as the data. A gradual silence that holds is one kind of answer. New numbers, messages through friends, anger, or more precise knowledge of your movements is another, and a reason to involve an advocate before anything else.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Knowing you may be watched can change behavior even when nothing visible happens, because a person begins to plan around where the other might be. Uncertainty about what is known, and how, tends to wear down the sense of private space. Surprises, such as being quoted something you never shared, can make the watching feel larger than any single incident.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe checking locks and parking lots, changing routes or phones, sleeping badly and flinching at new notifications. Some stop going to places they love. Others describe being told they are imagining it, and feeling more alone for it. Many describe relief when someone helps them document what is happening.

response_options.soft_clarification: Notice and note first. Write down what they knew, when, and how it could have reached them. Hold off on asking them how they know; an advocate can help you decide whether asking is safe.
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep necessary contact to one written channel and to the shared subject only, answering what is asked and nothing more. This is a quiet limit that you do not need to announce.
response_options.disengagement: Decide privately, with an advocate, how and when to change routines, numbers or devices. A sudden change can be noticed, so the order of steps is worth planning.
response_options.support_seeking: Call a domestic violence or stalking helpline and describe what you have noticed. Advocates can help you assess risk, plan, and decide what to document, without you having to decide anything on the call.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Let one trusted person at work, such as security or a manager, know that someone may come to the workplace uninvited, and give them a photo and the key facts. Keep a dated log of any visit or message there.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "For the schedule and the bills, can we keep everything in writing in one place, like email or a co-parenting app? That way neither of us has to guess what was agreed."
codex_completed.safety_note: Danger signals include showing up where you never said you would be, threats, damaged property, knowledge of private conversations, tracking devices, and contact that rises after you set a limit or begin a new relationship. Risk can rise around a separation. Before you change numbers, devices or routes, ask a stalking or domestic violence advocate to help you plan the order, since sudden changes can be noticed.
misuse_warning: Reading every run-in, friend's remark or unanswered question as stalking can frighten you more than the facts support. Check how the information could have arrived before deciding.
These words carry legal weight in many places. Using them against a co-parent who is only handling logistics can harm someone who has done nothing wrong.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Ghosting as Control is absence, a silence that ends when you move on, and what is described here is presence or awareness that continues after you ask it to stop. Legal Abuse reaches you through courts and filings with a paper record, where this reaches you through your movements and devices. A Smear Campaign talks about you to others; here the others are mostly being asked about you.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Legal Abuse (Post-Separation)
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Using court filings, motions and hearings after a separation, over and over, in ways that drain the other person's money, time and stability.
codex_completed.short_definition: Using court filings, motions and hearings after a separation, over and over, in ways that drain the other person's money, time and stability.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Legal abuse is the repeated use of legitimate court processes, such as custody petitions, motions, contempt filings and requests for hearings, so that responding becomes a heavy burden in itself. Each filing may look ordinary, and a judge may see nothing wrong in any single one. Complicated separations do need several legal steps, so volume alone is weak evidence. The concern arises when settled issues return without new grounds and the cost to one side far outweighs what is being disputed.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: After a split, someone keeps taking the other person back to court, with filings that look normal one by one, until the cost in money and nerves is the harm.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Each filing looks procedurally normal on its own, so the cost builds in money, time and nerves without producing one moment anyone would call abuse. Meanwhile the person responding may risk their home, income or time with their children if a deadline is missed.
what_it_is: Court filings, motions, requests for hearings and appeals that return to matters already decided, without new facts or changed circumstances.
Use of timing: papers served close to holidays, exams, a new job or a move, so the response window is short.
Costs that fall unevenly: the person with fewer resources must still answer each document or risk losing by default.
Complaints to agencies or professional bodies that each have to be answered separately.
Found in custody, child support, property and protective-order disputes.
Different from litigation that is merely hard-fought: each side may fight hard and still be using the court for a real question.
what_it_sounds_like: A fourth motion to change the parenting schedule in a year, citing no new events.
Papers delivered the week of your move, with a hearing set two weeks out.
You'll be hearing from my lawyer, again.
A request to re-hear the finances already settled in the agreement.
A filing that accuses you of contempt over a minor, late exchange time.
Another subpoena for records you already provided.
I'm only doing what's best for the kids, said with each new filing.
what_it_is_not: Complicated separations legitimately need many legal steps, such as valuing a business, settling property or setting a parenting plan across several courts.
Courts are slow and expensive by themselves. Delay and cost may come from the system and not from either person.
Someone protecting a real interest, like a child's safety or a financial right, will feel adversarial to the other side.
A genuine request to change an order after circumstances shifted, such as a relocation, a job change or a child's new needs.
Enforcement of an agreement the other person truly has not followed.
this_may_be_it_when: The same issues come back in new papers with nothing that has changed.
Filing dates cluster around events in your life.
You spend more responding than the disputed amount or issue is worth.
Several filings have been declined or dismissed, and new ones follow.
Offers to settle are refused, then the matter returns later in another form.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Each filing cites a new fact, such as a new job, a move or a school change.
Courts have granted at least some of the requests.
Your own lawyer says the volume is routine for cases like yours.
The timeline follows deadlines the court itself set.
The matters in dispute are real, large and unresolved, like a pension or a relocation.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Property, business or support questions can take several rounds because the numbers are truly hard to pin down.
A new lawyer may file procedural papers to bring a file up to date.
Court calendars set dates in bursts, so papers can arrive close together without anyone timing them.
People who feel unheard sometimes file again in the hope that a different judge will listen.
common_false_positives: A long custody case with real disagreements on both sides, run by two lawyers who file regularly.
An appeal of a decision, which is a lawful and routine step.
Notices from the court's own system, such as reminders and scheduling letters, which can feel like attacks.
discernment_questions: Does each filing cite something new, or return to something already decided?
Has a lawyer or legal aid worker looked at the pattern and said whether it is ordinary?
Would the cost of responding make sense if the stakes were as large as the filings say?
Do the dates line up with events in my life more than with any court deadline?
Have any judges commented on the repeated filings?
Can I keep a clean timeline of every filing, date and cost?
less_concerning_if: The court has treated each request as serious and mostly granted it.
The filings are spread out and tied to real changes.
Both sides are filing, and both sides have lawyers.
more_concerning_if: You are missing work, falling behind on rent or borrowing money to respond.
Filings reach into custody time or housing, and a missed deadline could lose either.
A judge has commented on the repeated filings, and they continue.
pattern_over_time_signs: You dread the mailbox, the process server and the email from the court portal.
Each time something settles, new papers arrive within weeks.
Savings or credit are drawn down by legal costs far beyond what you planned.
You agree to terms you dislike to end the filings, not because you think they are fair.
codex_completed.repair_check: Change would show in withdrawn or narrowed filings, a settlement that is honored without return trips to court, and proposals made through lawyers or mediation instead of fresh papers. A friendly message arriving alongside a new motion has changed nothing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Look at what follows a request to settle a matter through mediation or between lawyers. Agreement and a real drop in filings is one kind of answer. A fresh filing within weeks, or word that the request itself will be raised in court, is the other.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A long process can wear down money, sleep and concentration, and people sometimes begin to accept terms to make the process stop, not because the terms feel fair. Uncertainty about the next filing keeps the body on alert, and every envelope can bring the dread back. The official look of the papers can also make a person feel it must be their fault.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe dread over the mail, financial strain, trouble working, and a sense that the case never ends. Some give in on money or parenting time just to stop. Others describe shame about being 'in court again', and anger that every step looked lawful and so nobody saw it as harm.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask your lawyer or a legal aid clinic one question: 'Is this volume of filings ordinary for a case like mine?' An outside professional read helps you tell heavy litigation from a pattern.
response_options.firm_boundary: Respond on time through your lawyer, in writing, keeping replies to the facts. Deadlines are where a stretched person loses the most.
response_options.disengagement: Move all talk about the case to counsel and let lawyers carry the correspondence, so you are not answering personal messages about the filings.
response_options.support_seeking: Seek a legal aid office, a court self-help center or a domestic violence legal advocate. Ask them to read the filings and say what they see.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Tell one trusted manager only what you need to, such as that you have court dates, and arrange leave in advance, so a hearing does not put your job at risk.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Anything about the schedule or what has changed, we can talk about directly. For the court matters, could we go through our lawyers, or a mediator, so that everything is in writing and nothing is missed?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Concern grows when filings sit alongside threats, danger to a child, or the chance of losing your home, income or custody time at the next hearing. Courts also hear true accounts of danger, so a filing is not proof of abuse. Bring the full file to a family law attorney or legal aid advocate and ask what limits or protections your court offers.
misuse_warning: Calling a hard-fought custody case legal abuse can dismiss a parent with a real concern about a child's safety. Courts need to hear those.
Reading a hostile lawyer's letter, or a motion you disagree with, as proof of a campaign can harden a case that might have settled.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Forced Submission presses a person directly for words, while Legal Abuse works through an official channel, where the pressure arrives as paperwork. A Smear Campaign damages reputation among people, whereas filings damage mostly through cost and time, and may become public record. Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation) follows a person's movements, but legal filings can arrive without any physical contact.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Edited Recordings
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Presenting a cut, trimmed or out-of-context recording as if it were the whole, so that it seems to prove more than the full version supports.
codex_completed.short_definition: Presenting a cut, trimmed or out-of-context recording as if it were the whole, so that it seems to prove more than the full version supports.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Edited recordings are real audio or video, cut, rearranged or clipped so that they seem to show something the full version does not. The recording is usually genuine, unlike a deepfake that fabricates speech or faces, but the cut changes what it seems to prove. Trimming for length is normal, and a short clip labeled as a clip is honest. The concern is an excerpt offered as the whole, or a splice that joins words that were never said together.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A real recording that has been trimmed or stitched so it seems to show something the whole thing does not.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A recording carries the authority of evidence, so the burden falls on the person in it to talk their way out of something that appears to show itself. An explanation of the missing context rarely travels as far as the clip did.
what_it_is: A genuine recording that has been cropped, trimmed, spliced or re-ordered, so the meaning shifts.
A clip that starts after the provocation or ends before the reply, so the response seems to come from nowhere.
Words from different moments joined into one sentence, or pauses removed so a hesitation looks like an admission.
Shared in disputes, workplace complaints, custody conflicts, group chats, social media posts and news clips.
Different from a deepfake: nothing is invented, so checking the original is the best test.
what_it_sounds_like: A call recording that begins mid-argument, with no sign of who raised their voice first.
A video that jumps at the exact second before an explanation.
A transcript whose line numbers skip, or timestamps with gaps.
A voice memo played aloud with 'listen, he admits it', stopping one second before the next sentence.
A clip said to be 'the full conversation' that runs two minutes when the call lasted forty.
Background sound that changes in tone or volume mid-sentence.
You remember the moment, and the clip does not sound like what happened.
what_it_is_not: Clips shortened for length and clarity. An excerpt honestly labeled as partial makes no claim to be the whole picture.
Poor recording quality and natural gaps in a device's capture, such as a phone that stopped when its storage ran out.
A highlight reel or summary that says it is a summary.
Two honest recordings of the same event from different angles that show different parts of it.
A genuine, complete recording of something you wish you had not said. Being quoted accurately is uncomfortable, but it is not editing.
this_may_be_it_when: The clip begins or ends exactly where context would change the meaning.
There is an unexplained jump in sound, lighting or background at a key moment.
The person presenting it will not share the original file, or says they do not have it.
It is described as complete but is much shorter than the event it comes from.
Other people who were present remember a different order or tone than the clip shows.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The clip is labeled as an excerpt, with a source and a link to the full version.
The full recording is available and says the same thing.
The jumps are explained by how the app or device works, such as pausing for silence.
Others who were there recall it the way the clip shows it.
The only thing you can find wrong is that you dislike what it shows.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Phones and meeting apps trim silence or stop recording on their own, which can leave gaps.
People cut clips to fit a platform's time limit without thinking about context.
Someone with a long recording may share only the part they found relevant, assuming the rest was not needed.
Compression and noise reduction can make audio sound spliced when it is not.
common_false_positives: A news report using a ten-second quote that is faithful to the longer speech.
A meeting recording that cut off when the call dropped.
A recording of a heated moment that sounds worse on its own than it felt in the room, but contains everything that was said.
discernment_questions: Is there a complete version, and who holds it?
Where does the clip begin and end, and what was said just before and just after?
Is the clip labeled as an excerpt, or presented as the full record?
Do the jumps in sound or picture land on the most important sentence?
Would the people who were there describe it the way the clip does?
Could someone neutral check the file's original?
less_concerning_if: The excerpt is clearly marked, and the full version is easy to get.
The person sharing it provides the full recording once asked.
People who were there confirm the clip's gist.
more_concerning_if: The clip is being used against you in a complaint, a legal matter or a public post, and the original is withheld.
It is circulating widely before anyone can check it.
Your recollection, and that of several others, differs sharply from what the clip implies.
pattern_over_time_signs: Short clips of you keep appearing and the full versions never do.
You have started recording your own conversations out of worry about what might be cut.
People quote a line back to you that you say you never said that way.
Each time you ask for the original, it is described as lost, deleted or unavailable.
codex_completed.repair_check: Fixing it means the full recording is produced, the clip is corrected or taken down wherever it was posted, and the people who saw it are told. A comment saying 'sorry if that was unclear' while the clip stays up leaves the effect in place.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask for the full file, or the timestamps on either side of the clip. Watch whether it arrives with an explanation, or whether the question is met with 'why do you need it?' and the clip travels further.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Audio and video are often treated as direct evidence, so a clip can persuade before anyone asks what was left out. A first impression of a clip can also stick after a longer version is seen. Missing context leaves viewers to fill the gap with their own assumptions, often the least generous ones.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Seeing themselves quoted brings a drop in the stomach, then a scramble to explain, and tiredness from explaining to each new audience. Some start to doubt their own memory of the event. Others pull out of group chats, workplaces or platforms where the clip has circulated.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the person sharing it for the full recording and the times where the clip begins and ends: 'Can I hear the whole thing, starting from a few minutes earlier?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to argue about the clip's meaning until the full recording is on the table: 'I'm happy to discuss what was said once we've both heard all of it.'
response_options.disengagement: Do not reshare or reply to the clip in public threads, which gives it more reach. Save a copy and a link for later use.
response_options.support_seeking: Play the clip and the full version for a friend who was not there, without telling them what you think, and ask what each leaves them believing.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In a complaint process, ask the investigator in writing to obtain the original, complete, unedited file and its metadata, and attach your own written account of the missing part.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Could we hear the whole recording, from before this starts to after it ends? Once we've both listened to all of it, we can talk about what was said."
codex_completed.safety_note: A doctored clip is not a danger by itself. What changes that is its use as leverage: a threat to send it to your employer, family or a court unless you comply, or a clip tied to intimate content. In that case, keep the evidence, hold off on replying, and take it to a lawyer or advocate who can advise on the next step.
misuse_warning: Calling any unflattering clip edited lets you dismiss what you actually said. Check whether something you can point to is missing before accusing anyone.
Insisting that someone produce a recording they never made, or that no longer exists, treats a missing file as proof of bad faith.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: A Smear Campaign spreads claims, true or false, about a person and may use no recording at all, while an edited recording gives a claim a piece of apparent proof. Legal Abuse can bring such a clip into a court filing, whereas this entry names only how the clip was cut. Forced Submission demands words from you, but an edited clip can put words in your mouth without your input.

codex_completed.name: Account Takeover
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Taking over someone's email, social media, banking or cloud accounts so they are watched, spoken for, cut off or locked out of their own online life.
codex_completed.short_definition: Taking over someone's email, social media, banking or cloud accounts so they are watched, spoken for, cut off or locked out of their own online life.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Account takeover is control of another person's digital accounts that the account holder did not agree to: changed passwords, redirected recovery details, messages read or sent in their name, access handed back only on conditions. Account Control is just another label for this, not a separate thing. It can start as casual shared access and harden into sole control. One reset after a forgotten password means little. It becomes a pattern when access changes without your knowledge and your ways back in are blocked.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone gets control of your email, social media or bank logins, so they can read your messages, write as you, or keep you out, and getting back in depends on them.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Being pushed out of your own accounts costs more than access. Messages can go out under your name to people who have every reason to believe them, and everyday tasks like paying a bill or reaching a doctor start to need permission.
what_it_is: Passwords, recovery email addresses or phone numbers changed by someone else, so the account holder cannot get back in.
Reading, deleting or sending messages from an account while the owner is unaware, or aware and unable to stop it.
A step beyond ordinary shared access: the person once had independent use of the account and now needs someone's help to open it.
Access used as leverage, handed back only after an apology, an agreement or a favor.
Covers email, banking, social media, phone accounts and cloud storage where photos, documents and contacts are kept.
what_it_sounds_like: Your usual password stops working and the reset code goes to a phone number you do not recognize.
Friends ask about a post or message you never wrote, and it reads as cruel or out of character.
You are told: 'I changed it because you can't be trusted with it. I'll give it back when we've sorted this out.'
Your bank statements stop arriving, and the contact address on the account has been changed.
Sent mail you did not send, or messages marked as read before you open them.
'Why do you need your email? Ask me and I'll check it for you.'
A recovery attempt is canceled within minutes by someone else approving a new device.
what_it_is_not: Forgotten passwords, expired codes and lost phones. A locked account on its own is a common technical problem.
Platform outages, bugs and automatic security locks that follow an unusual login, which affect many users at once.
A parent managing a young child's accounts openly, with access that eases as the child grows.
An authorized family member resetting a shared account, saying so, and handing it back.
A hacker or scammer with no personal link to you, which is a crime of a different kind from control inside a relationship.
Mutual agreement to share a streaming login or family calendar that either person can leave.
this_may_be_it_when: You lost access without changing anything yourself, and recovery options point to details that are not yours.
Content appears in your accounts that you did not create.
The other person knows things only your private messages would have shown them.
Access comes back only after you concede something unrelated to the account.
You can no longer pay, apply or contact anyone without going through them.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Many people report the same lockout at the same time, and the provider confirms a fault.
The change was announced beforehand, you agreed to it, and you can reverse it.
A recovery code or reset email arrives at an address you set up yourself.
Your own old password was reused and leaked, and the provider's alert shows an unknown login from abroad.
Access is returned straight away, with an explanation you can check, and nothing is held back.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A forgotten password, a new phone or a failed two-step code can lock anyone out.
A relative who sets up a shared account may reset it without realizing you wanted to be told.
Companies sometimes freeze accounts after suspicious activity, which looks like a takeover but comes from the provider.
common_false_positives: A genuinely forgotten password fixed through the provider's recovery steps.
A shared household account reset by another authorized user who tells you.
A provider-side security problem that hits many users, unconnected to anyone you know.
discernment_questions: Did you lose access suddenly, without starting any change yourself?
Do the recovery email and phone number on the account still belong to you?
Does anyone close to you gain from you not having this account?
Does anything appear from your account that you did not write or send?
Is getting back in described as something you must earn?
Could you reach this account independently on a device nobody else touches?
less_concerning_if: The lockout has an explanation from the provider that you can verify.
Anyone who held your login before gives it back without conditions.
You can open every account yourself, on your own device, whenever you choose.
more_concerning_if: Recovery attempts keep being blocked or intercepted by someone with your details.
Messages are sent in your name to people close to you, damaging a friendship, a job or a family tie.
Control of these accounts comes with checking where you are, who you speak to, or how you spend money.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your list of accounts that only the other person can open grows, from one streaming login to email, then bank.
You copy important documents to a place nobody else can reach, because anything stored in one account may vanish.
People you used to message say they have not heard from you, or heard strange things.
Each time access comes back, it arrives with a new term attached.
codex_completed.repair_check: What happens to the logins themselves is the clearest sign. Repair means every password and recovery detail returned to you with nothing attached, an account history you can read, and no new lockout later. An apology while they still hold the keys has fixed nothing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself whether you can now open each account yourself, today, on a device you control. If the only route is still through them, or a request to be left alone is followed by new changes, the request has not been respected.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Accounts hold a person's contacts, money, history and voice, so losing them tends to feel like losing the ability to act. Control through logins works quietly because each step looks small and administrative, and because getting access back turns into a favor to be asked for, which can shift who seems to be in charge of ordinary life.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe panic at being unable to reach their own contacts or money, shame about messages sent in their name, and a constant sense of being watched. Some stop trusting every device or app. Some say the practical problems, such as missing a work email or a bill, hurt as much as the intrusion.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask a plain question about the change: 'My login doesn't work and the recovery number isn't mine. Do you know why?' Then see whether the answer is specific and whether it is fixed.
response_options.firm_boundary: If it feels safe, ask once for your logins and recovery details back with nothing attached. If you are unsure how they would react, skip this step and use the private options below.
response_options.disengagement: Do not argue over each message. Use a trusted device, such as a library computer or a friend's phone, to check what you can still reach and begin setting up new accounts.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a trusted person or a domestic abuse or tech safety advocate what you have seen, and write down dates, screenshots of login alerts and unfamiliar devices before anything changes.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a work account is involved, report it to your IT or security team at once, and ask your bank or phone company to put a block on changes without extra verification.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'm having trouble getting into my own accounts, and I want to sort it out with you. Can we go through what changed and when, and what I need to do to have the logins back the way they were?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Losing control of accounts can go with monitoring, isolation, threats or control of money. Changing passwords or removing a device can alert the person to what you are doing. Work out your next step on a device they cannot see, with a domestic abuse advocate or a tech safety service, before you change anything on the compromised account.
misuse_warning: A locked or hacked account does not show that someone close to you did it. Look at the provider's login history and recovery details before suspecting a person.
Accusing a partner or relative of taking over your accounts because of one failed login can damage trust over a fault that belongs to the platform.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation) tracks your movements and contacts after a break-up and need not touch your accounts at all, while account takeover works through your own logins, recovery details and the messages stored there. Resource Sabotage removes things you need to succeed, such as tools or funding, and blames you for the failure. Here the thing removed is your access and your own voice.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: SIM Swap / 2FA Interception
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Taking over a person's phone number, or the text codes sent to it, to get into their accounts, lock them out or read their messages.
codex_completed.short_definition: Taking over a person's phone number, or the text codes sent to it, to get into their accounts, lock them out or read their messages.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Two names are joined here, for two related things. A SIM swap is when a phone number is moved onto a different SIM card than the owner's, so calls and texts go to someone else. 2FA interception is the wider outcome: the one-time codes that prove who you are reach another person, by a swap or by other routes. Carrier outages and glitches happen, so one odd code means little. The telltale run is a lost signal, followed by lockouts and by account changes that someone else made.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone gets control of your phone number or the codes sent to it, then uses them to get into your accounts while you are locked out.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The phone number that secures everything else becomes the way in, and the lockout usually arrives before there is any way to understand what has happened. Email, banking and messaging can all be reached from a single number, so a loss can spread quickly.
what_it_is: A phone number moved to a SIM or device the owner does not hold, which takes over their calls and texts.
Text-message codes that arrive with someone else, so they can pass the checks for logins and password resets.
Often arranged through a carrier's account processes and not by breaking into your device.
Used for theft, impersonation, reading private messages, or cutting a person off from their own accounts, and sometimes by someone the person knows.
Two overlapping behaviors: swapping is one method, interception of codes is the broader result, and interception can also happen without a swap.
what_it_sounds_like: Your phone suddenly shows 'No service' or 'SOS only' in a place where you normally have full bars.
Texts with verification codes you did not ask for, arriving in a bunch.
An email from your carrier saying your SIM or number was changed, which you did not do.
A bank alert about a password reset, a new payee or a login from a device you do not own.
Friends telling you they received odd messages from your number or account.
Being signed out of email and social accounts at once, with the recovery address changed.
A call or text from 'your carrier' asking you to read out a code.
what_it_is_not: Carriers have outages, tower maintenance and billing errors that drop service for hours.
A single odd authentication code on one platform, which often means someone mistyped their own address.
A SIM replacement you asked for yourself, after a lost or broken phone or an upgrade, that you forgot in a stressful week.
A line moved to a new plan or eSIM by a family-plan owner who legitimately manages the account.
Travel or roaming problems that cut service when you cross a border.
this_may_be_it_when: Service drops without explanation and the carrier later confirms a SIM or number change you did not request.
Several unrelated accounts show resets or sign-ins from new devices within the same day.
The recovery phone number or email on an account has been changed without you.
Texts or calls meant for you stop arriving at your phone.
The timing matches a falling-out with someone who had access to your carrier account or devices, which shows only access and not who acted.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The carrier confirms an outage or maintenance in your area, and service returns on its own.
Your carrier's account history shows only changes you or the account owner made.
Only one platform is affected, and everything else works.
Codes arrive when you are actually trying to sign in.
The lockout comes from too many password attempts and clears after a wait or a verification.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Mobile networks drop service for outages and repairs, often without notice.
People forget their own SIM or eSIM changes when moving to a new phone.
Family-plan owners can legitimately change numbers and lines on the account.
Apps send codes automatically whenever anyone, including a stranger mistyping an address, enters yours.
common_false_positives: Service cut after a missed bill payment.
Verification codes sent because a bot or stranger entered your number in a sign-up form.
A new phone that took a few hours to register your number properly.
discernment_questions: Has my carrier confirmed an account change that someone other than me requested?
Did my signal vanish around the same time that accounts began to lock?
Are the changes to recovery emails and numbers ones I made?
Who else has ever had access to my carrier account, number or devices?
Is it one account or many, and did it begin all at once?
Do bank alerts or messages from friends show activity I did not do?
less_concerning_if: The carrier shows an outage, a billing hold or a change you made.
Only one service is affected and the others work normally.
Service returns within hours and your accounts show nothing unfamiliar.
more_concerning_if: Money has moved, or new payees, cards or limits have appeared at your bank or card account.
Your recovery email or number on accounts has changed, or messages are being forwarded.
Someone from your past with access to your plan or devices has already shown knowledge of your private messages.
pattern_over_time_signs: Accounts keep being re-accessed after you reset passwords.
Your messages seem known to someone outside the conversation.
Verification codes arrive repeatedly for logins you did not attempt.
Friends report unusual messages that look as if they came from you, more than once.
codex_completed.repair_check: Resolution looks like the carrier confirming it has reversed the change and added extra protection to the line, each account recovering with a clean sign-in history, and no new unexplained codes over the following weeks. Regaining one login while the number stays exposed is only a partial fix.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Treat the weeks after you tighten security as the test. If codes stop arriving and sign-in histories stay clean, the change held. If lockouts return, new-device alerts reappear, or someone seems to know about changes you only made privately, treat access as still open and contact your carrier's fraud team.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Losing the number that proves who you are can resemble losing your identity at once, since email, money and friends all hang from it. Rapid, unexplained lockouts tend to push people to act fast, and urgency makes it harder to sort real alerts from fake ones. Messages posing as 'your bank' or 'your carrier' can take advantage of that urgency.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe panic when the signal vanishes, then dread as accounts lock one by one. Some lose money or access to years of photos and messages. Others feel exposed in the days afterward, afraid of what was read, and distrust their own phone. When someone known to them is involved, they describe an added sense of betrayal.

response_options.soft_clarification: Check first from a different, trusted device or a friend's phone: look at your carrier account's recent changes and at the sign-in history on your email. Write down what you find, with times.
response_options.firm_boundary: Do not read out codes or PINs to anyone who calls or texts, even if they seem to be your carrier or bank. Hang up and contact them through the number on your card or their official app.
response_options.disengagement: Once you are back in control, move key accounts such as email and banking off text-message codes, where the service allows, onto an authenticator app or a physical security key.
response_options.support_seeking: Contact your carrier's fraud team, your bank and, where one exists, your country's fraud reporting service. If an ex-partner may be involved, also speak to a domestic abuse or stalking advocate.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a work account is affected, tell the IT or security team right away, and treat any message sent from your number or email during that window as suspect.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I did not request a change to my SIM or my number. Please note that on the account, require extra verification for any future change, and send me a written record of what changed and when."
codex_completed.safety_note: Danger signals include money moving, access to your private messages, or messages that show someone knows your movements, especially a former partner who once held your carrier details. A SIM problem in that setting may be one piece of wider monitoring. Contact your carrier and bank from a device that person has never touched, and reach a stalking or domestic abuse advocate before changing anything they might notice.
misuse_warning: Reading a one-off dropped signal or a stray verification code as a SIM swap can cause alarm that the facts do not support. The first check is your carrier's account history.
Pointing at a particular person from nothing but timing can turn a technical fraud into a family or workplace accusation.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation) is the watching of a former partner's life, and a SIM swap can be a route to it by sending that person's messages and codes elsewhere, but strangers also do it for money with no personal link. Legal Abuse works through courts and paper, in the open, while a swap works quietly through accounts and is found by what stops working. Forced Submission needs the person's own words, where a swap takes control with no input from them.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Intimate Image Abuse
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Sharing or threatening to share private sexual images of someone without consent, including fake ones, often tied to a demand for money, contact or compliance.
codex_completed.short_definition: Sharing or threatening to share private sexual images of someone without consent, including fake ones, often tied to a demand for money, contact or compliance.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Intimate image abuse covers real or fabricated sexual images used against the person shown: posted, sent on, or threatened with exposure. The threat can be attached to a demand for money, more images, contact or silence, or can follow a breakup. Images shared willingly within trust do not become abuse by existing; the line is passed when they are spread or held over the person without consent. Fear of exposure can steer behavior whether or not anything is shared, and a bluff has the same effect.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone shares, or says they will share, private sexual pictures or videos of you without your agreement, sometimes real and sometimes faked.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Control over the most private material about a person passes to somebody else, and the fear of exposure keeps working whether or not anything is ever actually shared. The shame it brings often leads people to hide it, which is when help is hardest to reach.
what_it_is: Real images shared, posted or sent onward without the consent of the person shown.
Threats to share, with or without a stated demand, that keep the person afraid even if nothing is ever sent.
Fabricated or altered images, such as a face placed on another body, used in the same way.
A claim to hold images that may not exist; the fear and pressure still land, though the response steps differ.
Seen after breakups, in sextortion scams run by strangers, and sometimes inside ongoing relationships.
Often tied to a demand: money, more images, contact, silence or compliance with something else.
what_it_sounds_like: Send me what I ask, or everyone in your contacts sees these.
I still have the pictures, you know.
A message with a screenshot of the picture, your contacts list and a countdown.
Nice to see you've moved on. Maybe your new boyfriend should see what I have.
A fake explicit image of you, with your name on it, posted in a group chat.
Pay now and I'll delete everything. I swear.
An unknown account posting your pictures beside a link to your workplace page.
what_it_is_not: Images shared consensually inside a relationship, with no threat and no sharing beyond it.
Adults who agreed to publish or sell their own content, such as a creator or a couple who chose to post together.
An accidental send to the wrong chat that the recipient deletes at once and tells you about.
A claim to hold images when none exist. It is not exposure, but it is still coercion; the difference matters because there may be nothing to remove, while the threat can still be reported.
A vague line like 'I have stuff on you' with no mention of images, which is a different kind of threat.
this_may_be_it_when: A specific threat names the images, who would see them and what you must do to stop it.
Images appear, or are shown to others, that you did not agree to share.
The threat starts, or returns, after you end contact or begin a new relationship.
An unknown account contacts you after a private chat and shows part of your image or your contact list.
A fake explicit image of you circulates, whether or not you ever took a photo.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Nothing has been shared or threatened, and the images were given in a relationship that remains on good terms.
The message is a vague boast with no mention of images, who would see them or what you must do.
The only images are ones a couple openly agreed to keep, with a shared understanding of what they are for.
Everyone shown agreed to the use, with no pressure.
The message went to hundreds of people as a template and no real image of you was ever included, though it is still worth reporting.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A partner may keep photos you willingly shared, with no plan to do anything with them.
Pictures sent to the wrong chat by accident can spread because someone forgot to delete them.
A hacked cloud account can expose images even though nobody you know chose to share them.
Two people in a loving relationship may exchange images that stay private for years.
common_false_positives: A friend joking 'I have embarrassing pictures of you' about a clothed holiday photo.
A scam message sent to thousands of strangers saying 'I recorded you', with no real image of you. It is still a threat to report, but it is not a leak.
A relative posting a swimsuit photo from a family holiday, which may be tactless but is not sexual exposure.
discernment_questions: Has anything actually been posted or sent, or is it a threat so far?
Is a demand attached, such as money, more images or contact, and does it keep changing?
Do I know the images exist, or only that someone says they do?
Who could have copies, and could one of my accounts have been breached?
Is the threat tied to something I am doing, such as ending contact?
Do I have a safe place to save screenshots and links?
less_concerning_if: No image exists or has been shown, and the message is generic and sent to many people.
The images stayed private after an amicable end.
A copy was removed from the platform where it appeared, and you can see the link no longer works.
more_concerning_if: Images have been shared or shown to people who matter to you, such as family, an employer or a school.
The demands escalate, a deadline is set, or contact arrives from several accounts.
You feel unsafe in person, or the threat comes with other controlling behavior, such as monitoring, stalking or control of money.
pattern_over_time_signs: The reference returns whenever you pull away: 'remember what I have.'
You change what you post, who you see or your job search out of fear of what could appear.
Demands shift from one thing to another, and each payment or image buys only a pause.
You have started to check search results, group chats and tagged posts for your own pictures.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair shows in things you can see for yourself: posts taken down, links that now fail, and threats that stop and do not come back. A promise to delete with nothing visible behind it leaves the option open, and so does an apology that arrives alongside a new demand.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: A limit on this subject is judged by the next message. A reply that ends the threat, followed by a gap that holds, is one kind. A larger demand, a deadline, or a copy sent to someone close to you is the other, and that is the point to stop replying and reach a helpline or advocate.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Fear of exposure works through shame and the picture of everyone you know seeing it. The threat does not need to be carried out to work, because imagining it can be enough. Secrecy tends to deepen the hold: the longer a person handles it alone, the more the other party's control can feel total, and each demand can feel smaller than the feared exposure.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe panic, nausea, shame, trouble sleeping and a feeling of being watched wherever they go. Some stop using social media or avoid work and school for fear of being recognized. Many describe relief once they told one person, and some describe anger at being blamed for taking the picture in the first place.

response_options.soft_clarification: Before replying, save everything: screenshots of messages, usernames, links and dates, stored somewhere private. Questions and arguments with the sender can wait until you have advice.
response_options.firm_boundary: Do not pay, send more images or negotiate. Payment or new images tend to bring further demands, not an end. Further contact can be limited to the one line in the script, or none at all.
response_options.disengagement: If the sender is someone you know, ask an advocate before blocking or going silent, since a sudden change can raise the pressure. With a stranger, blocking after saving evidence is usually fine.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone you trust and contact an image-abuse helpline or advocate. StopNCII.org (adults) and Take It Down (images of under-18s) let you flag an image so participating platforms can block it, without sharing the image itself.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If images or threats reach your job or school, tell one trusted person in HR, student services or security early, so it does not arrive as a surprise. Give them the links, not the images.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I did not agree for any of these to be shared with anyone, and I'm not going to negotiate about them. Please send anything further to someone I trust, who can answer for me."
codex_completed.safety_note: Take seriously a deadline, a demand that keeps growing, contact from several accounts, messages to your family or workplace, or threats of self-harm used to keep you quiet. If shame feels unbearable, a crisis line can help tonight. If the person shown is under 18, treat it as urgent and contact your country's child-safety or police service. Save links and screenshots, then ask an advocate about takedown options before replying.
misuse_warning: Using the label for any private picture someone still has can accuse a former partner of abuse when nothing has been threatened or shared. The line is consent and use, not possession.
Treating the person shown as responsible because they once took or sent the picture adds blame to someone who needs help. The picture existing is not the wrongdoing.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Public Humiliation exposes someone in front of others, though not necessarily with sexual material or an attached demand. Forced Submission presses a person to say words, while intimate image abuse presses with a threat of exposure and may ask for money or more images instead. Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation) may sit alongside it, but concerns following and watching, not the exposure of private images.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Algorithmic Manipulation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Using feed ranking and recommendation systems to steer what a person sees and how they feel, in ways the person cannot inspect or switch off.
codex_completed.short_definition: Using feed ranking and recommendation systems to steer what a person sees and how they feel, in ways the person cannot inspect or switch off.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Feeds, autoplay queues and recommendation lists decide what appears first, what repeats and what never shows up. Ranking alone is ordinary product design. The concern is when that ordering is used to push someone's mood, beliefs or habits somewhere they did not choose, and they cannot see it happening. One odd recommendation proves nothing. Only researchers with access to the systems can show deliberate steering, so a reader can notice effects but rarely confirm cause.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A hidden process decides what shows up in your feed and in what order, and it may be tuned to move your mood or opinions without telling you.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: What a person sees shapes what they take the world to be like. When the selection is made by a process they cannot inspect, the resulting beliefs and moods feel entirely their own, which makes them hard to question.
what_it_is: Ranking, recommendation and autoplay systems used to shape what someone is exposed to, and in what order.
Tuning for attention or reaction, so that upsetting or outrage-heavy items can rise because people respond to them.
Personalization that narrows a feed toward one theme, so the person sees a smaller world over time.
Almost entirely invisible from the user's side: the ranking rules and the reasons for any one item are not shown.
Different from a person pressuring you, because no individual message needs to be false for the overall picture to be skewed.
what_it_sounds_like: A feed that is mostly one emotion, such as anger or dread, on topics you only looked at once.
A recommendation queue that keeps drifting toward more extreme versions of what you watched.
The same story or claim appearing again and again in different packaging.
Posts from friends you care about seldom appearing, while strangers' posts about a single issue fill the top.
A sudden run of content on a sensitive subject right after you searched for it once.
Autoplay carrying you well past where you meant to stop, with no natural endpoint.
A sense that everyone online holds one opinion, when people around you hold several.
what_it_is_not: Ranked feeds are the default almost everywhere, and sorting content by what you tend to engage with is ordinary product design.
Personalization that shows more of what you already read, because you read it, is not a campaign against you.
A bad stretch of content after a major news event, when real people are all posting about the same thing.
Your own habits: you may be clicking more of one kind of item than you realize, which then gets you more of it.
A one-time odd recommendation. Systems get things wrong all the time without anyone aiming at you.
Nothing in a conversation or a single screenshot can settle deliberate steering either way.
this_may_be_it_when: Independent researchers or regulators with access to the system have documented the specific effect.
A platform's own published findings or leaked internal documents describe tuning content to move users' mood or behavior.
Your feed's tone shifts sharply and persistently after a change in the platform's settings, with no change in what you do.
Several unrelated users report the same pattern at the same time.
The content on offer rewards staying and reacting more than it informs, and that is consistent across weeks.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The content matches what you have been searching, liking and following lately.
The mood of your feed tracks a real event that everyone is talking about.
You see mixed viewpoints and friends' posts alongside the repetitive items.
Your own screen time and clicking are the only thing you can point to as evidence.
You are inferring a plan from a single recommendation that felt eerily well timed.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Interest-based sorting working as designed, showing more of what you stopped to look at.
Coincidence: a recommendation that seems to read your mind may simply match what millions of similar viewers watched.
A news cycle in which one topic really does dominate what people are posting.
common_false_positives: Noticing an ad for something you only talked about, when you had also searched for it, or friends nearby had.
Assuming a feed that leans one way proves the platform holds that view.
Feeling manipulated by content that is simply upsetting because the real news is upsetting.
discernment_questions: Does my feed differ from what friends who follow the same accounts see, or only from what I expected?
Has my mood after using this app changed over months, and does that track what I'm shown?
Is there a natural place to stop, or does the app keep supplying one more item?
Would I hold this view if I had also been shown the strongest case against it?
What evidence do I have beyond the feeling that the feed is aimed at me?
less_concerning_if: You can switch the feed to a plain chronological or followed-accounts-only view and the content looks much the same.
The platform publishes how its ranking works and lets you adjust it.
Your views and moods stay steady when you take a week away from the app.
more_concerning_if: The system keeps serving content on a vulnerable subject, such as self-harm, to someone who has shown distress.
The person using it is a child or a teen who cannot easily step away.
The platform denies there is any ranking at all, or cannot say why a given item was shown.
pattern_over_time_signs: You feel more anxious or angry about topics you used to feel neutral about, after months of scrolling.
Your sense of what most people think moves toward whatever your feed repeats.
Sessions run longer than planned, and leaving takes effort even when you are not enjoying it.
People who use a different platform describe a quite different world on the same topics.
codex_completed.repair_check: Platforms that take this seriously let outside researchers study the effects, explain why items are shown, give you controls that really change the feed, and change the system when harm is found. A blog post promising to care, with no access and no change, does not do those things.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice whether your controls do what they say. When you mute a subject, reset recommendations or switch to a followed-only view, does the feed actually change? Controls that quietly revert or do nothing suggest your choices are not the ones steering.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Whatever shows up often or first is easily taken as common or important. A feed ordered by how strongly viewers react can tilt a person's sense of what is normal, urgent or frightening. Each item looks like a free choice to click, so the shaping goes unnoticed, and the resulting mood is easily read as one's own.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Some report feeling irritable or fearful after long sessions, a narrower sense of who agrees with them, and surprise when a week away lifts the mood. Others recall embarrassment on realizing a strong opinion came mostly from repetition, or simply notice that hours disappeared.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask yourself or a friend to compare feeds side by side for a few minutes, and see how much of what looks like 'everyone thinks this' is only your feed.
response_options.firm_boundary: Turn off autoplay and personalized suggestions where the settings allow it, and decide ahead of time how long a session will last.
response_options.disengagement: Take a break from the app for a week and notice how your mood and views feel without it. Use the plain followed-accounts view if one exists.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk with a friend, parent or counselor if a feed seems tied to low mood, self-harm content or a teenager's distress. Report harmful recommendations to the platform.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If your role touches platform design, moderation or policy, document specific harm examples with dates and raise them through your organization's review or ethics channel.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "This feels true because I keep seeing it, and that is not the same as it being true. What would I think if I looked at three sources I chose myself, not the ones that were handed to me?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Feed steering is a personal safety issue when it serves harmful content to someone in distress, such as material about self-harm or eating disorders, or when a child cannot step away. Then the step is to involve a trusted adult or counselor, report the content, and reach emergency services if there is immediate danger.
misuse_warning: Treating any unwelcome feed as proof of a hidden plot can feed paranoia and ignores that most ranking is blunt commercial sorting.
Telling someone their opinions are 'just the algorithm' dismisses views they may have reached through their own thinking.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Dark Patterns work on a single screen or decision, such as a button or a checkout, while this works across a whole feed over time. Context Poisoning corrupts the underlying material that is stored or trained on, whereas here the material may be real and only its selection and order are skewed. Synthetic Persona Networks supply fake voices; algorithmic steering can run entirely on real posts by real people.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Dark Patterns (AI-Adaptive)
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Interface designs that push people toward purchases, data sharing or consent they did not intend, and that adjust to each user's apparent weaknesses.
codex_completed.short_definition: Interface designs that push people toward purchases, data sharing or consent they did not intend, and that adjust to each user's apparent weaknesses.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Dark patterns are screens built so the quickest path is not the one a person would pick with time to read: a hidden decline button, a pre-ticked box, a countdown timer, a cancel flow that takes ten steps. The AI-adaptive version changes the screen for each user, based on what the system has learned about them. Good design nudges too, and a confusing checkout is usually just badly built. The concern is design that gets harder to escape the more it learns.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Apps and websites sometimes set up screens so you agree, buy or share more than you meant to, and some now adjust the screen to what works on you in particular.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Money, personal data and consent leave a person's hands through interfaces built so the default path is not what they would have chosen. People often blame themselves for clicking, when the screen was arranged to produce the click.
what_it_is: Screens that make one choice easy and bright and the other small, hidden or phrased as a loss.
Subscription traps: signing up takes one tap and canceling takes a maze of pages or a phone call.
Consent boxes that are pre-ticked, or whose decline option is worded to make you feel foolish.
Pressure cues such as countdown clocks or 'only 2 left' notices that may or may not be true.
In the AI-adaptive form, the layout, timing or message changes between users based on what the system predicts will work on each of them.
what_it_sounds_like: A 'No thanks, I don't like saving money' button beside a bright 'Yes' button.
A cancel link buried under several menus, or replaced with 'call us during business hours'.
A countdown timer that resets when you reload the page.
A price that rises by small fees on the last screen of checkout.
A pop-up asking for your contacts or location with only 'Allow' or 'Maybe later' as options.
A page that shows you different urgency messages from what a friend sees for the same item.
A chatbot that answers a cancel request by offering another discount, repeatedly.
what_it_is_not: A prominent save button or a sensible default is ordinary design and helps people finish what they came to do.
A confusing checkout is much more often badly built or hurried than built to work against you.
A real limited-time sale or truly low stock. Scarcity messages can be accurate.
A retention offer that appears once and then lets you cancel without further obstacle.
A business making its preferred option more prominent while keeping the other one clear and easy.
An interface that gets harder to escape the more it learns about one user is what separates this from ordinary clutter.
this_may_be_it_when: Leaving, declining or canceling is much harder than signing up, with no practical reason.
The wording of the decline option is built to shame or confuse you.
Urgency notices change or vanish when you wait or reload.
Two people see noticeably different prices, offers or pressure for the same product.
Settings that protect your data are hidden several screens deep or switch back on after updates.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Everyone sees the same screen, and canceling takes about as many steps as signing up.
The extra step is a real safeguard, such as confirming a deletion that cannot be undone.
The timer or stock count is accurate and shown to everyone.
The page is simply cluttered, old or poorly translated.
You skipped reading the options on a screen that was fairly laid out.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A rushed or outdated site where design shortcuts pile up without anyone planning them.
A company testing which layout converts best, which is common and not always aimed at undermining choice.
A cancellation step that exists to prevent accidental loss of an account.
common_false_positives: Prices that differ because of region, tax, shipping or sign-in status.
A real stock shortage presented as 'only 2 left'.
A privacy prompt that is clear but repeated on each new device.
discernment_questions: Are the accept and decline options equally easy to see and equally easy to tap?
Could I leave this service as quickly as I joined it?
Would a different person with the same screen see the same offers and warnings?
Is the urgency real, or does it reset when I come back?
Did the screen tell me plainly what I was agreeing to, or did I have to hunt for it?
less_concerning_if: Both choices are shown clearly, in the same style, with honest wording.
You can cancel in the same place and with about the same effort as signing up.
Terms and total price are stated before you commit.
more_concerning_if: The service targets people the system has flagged as stressed, lonely, in debt or young.
Charges continue after you believe you canceled.
Data or permissions are taken that the service does not need to work.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find charges for services you never meant to keep.
Privacy settings you turned off are back on after an update.
Each time you try to leave, a new obstacle or offer appears.
You spend more on the app during low moments, and the app's prompts seem to arrive at those moments.
codex_completed.repair_check: When a company fixes this properly, the refund arrives without a fight, the cancel path becomes short and plain, and the screen changes for everyone. A new apology banner over the same maze, or a refund only for those who complain loudly, is not a fix.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: A fair test is whether your 'no' holds. After you decline an option, does it stay declined, or does the same request return next session in new wording? A choice that keeps being re-asked was never being treated as a choice.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People under time pressure, tired or distracted tend to take the path that looks default or bright, and to avoid effort that feels like it will be a fight. Screens that put friction on one choice and not the other can use this. When the system also adjusts to a person's habits or low moments, the pressure can land more precisely than a fixed design would.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe surprise charges, finding subscriptions they forgot, feeling foolish for clicking, and tiredness from fighting cancellation flows. Some describe giving up on privacy settings because they keep resetting. Others say they trust no checkout screen afterward, and read every box with suspicion.

response_options.soft_clarification: Contact the company in writing and say exactly what you believed you agreed to and what you were charged, and ask for a correction.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline the optional add-ons and data permissions on each screen, and keep a screenshot of the final confirmation before you pay.
response_options.disengagement: Close the page when the pressure cue appears and come back later. Check the same offer on another device before committing.
response_options.support_seeking: If a charge will not reverse, contact your card issuer or bank, and consider a consumer protection office or a local consumer advocate.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you work in product or design, flag screens where the decline path is harder than the accept path, using your organization's review or ethics process.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I did not set out to buy this or share that. Before I tap anything, is the 'no' option as easy to find as the 'yes', and would I choose this if there were no clock on it?"
codex_completed.safety_note: This is mainly a consumer harm, but it becomes more serious when it takes money from someone who cannot afford it, targets children, or collects location or contact data that could be used against them. Gather statements and screenshots, contact your bank or card issuer, and ask a consumer advocate or legal aid for help.
misuse_warning: Calling every upsell a dark pattern ignores honest businesses that simply want to sell something and show the options clearly.
Blaming people who clicked can hide the fact that a screen was arranged to produce that click.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Algorithmic Manipulation works through what a feed shows over weeks, while a dark pattern works at the point of a specific decision, such as a button or a form.
