codex_completed.name: AI-Driven Social Engineering (Automated)
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Scams that use AI-generated text, voice or video to impersonate trusted people or institutions, tailored to each target and sent at large scale.
codex_completed.short_definition: Scams that use AI-generated text, voice or video to impersonate trusted people or institutions, tailored to each target and sent at large scale.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Social engineering is getting a person to hand over access, money or information by exploiting trust or urgency instead of breaking into a system. With AI, the messages can be fluent, personal and sent in huge numbers, and voices or faces can be made to resemble someone the target knows. The old warning signs, such as odd wording, may be missing. Real organizations also call and email, so the contact alone proves nothing.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A message, call or video that looks or sounds like someone you trust is actually generated, and it is built to get you to send money or information quickly.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The usual defenses, an unfamiliar voice, clumsy wording or an address that looks wrong, stop working when the approach sounds exactly like someone already known and trusted. People lose money, accounts and privacy while believing they were helping.
what_it_is: Messages, calls or videos that imitate a relative, boss, bank, agency or friend using generated text, cloned voice or faked video.
Personalized with details gathered from public posts, past leaks or data brokers, so it sounds like it knows you.
Built around urgency and secrecy: a crisis, a deadline or a request not to tell anyone.
Sent in volume, so a small success rate still pays, and one attempt may be one of thousands.
Different from a human scammer working a single target in how little effort each attempt needs.
what_it_sounds_like: A call from a voice that sounds like your child or grandchild, in distress, asking for money right now.
A message that appears to be from your boss asking for gift cards or an urgent transfer, and not to discuss it.
An email with perfect grammar that mentions your real employer, recent purchase or a family member's name.
A video call where the face seems slightly off, the audio is out of step, or the person avoids unplanned questions.
A 'bank' or 'agency' contact that insists on staying on the line and not hanging up to check.
A text from a number you do not recognize, claiming to be a known person with a new phone.
what_it_is_not: Real organizations do phone, email and ask to verify identity, and a real bank may contact you about fraud.
Synthetic voice is now standard in ordinary customer service lines, so a machine-sounding caller is not proof of a scam.
A relative who really did lose their phone and texts from a new number.
Marketing that uses your name and past purchases, which is annoying but not impersonation.
An unexpected contact proves nothing by itself; verifying through a channel you chose yourself is the sensible response either way.
A clumsy phishing email that was written by a person, which is an older and different problem.
this_may_be_it_when: The contact demands money or codes immediately and insists you tell no one.
The voice or face resembles someone you know but they cannot answer a question only they would know.
The request uses unusual payment routes such as gift cards, crypto or wire transfers.
You are told not to hang up or call back through a number you already have.
A real person, when you reach them by a known number, knows nothing about the request.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You started the contact yourself, through a number or site you found on your own.
The request can wait, and the sender is happy for you to check it first.
A known person confirms the message through a separate channel.
The message is a routine notice that asks you to do nothing urgent.
The only oddity is a robotic voice or a typo, which suggests carelessness more than AI.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A relative with a new number who truly needs help, and who can confirm details when asked.
A genuine bank or agency fraud alert that tells you to use the number on your card.
An automated customer service system that uses a synthetic voice openly.
common_false_positives: Assuming every unexpected call from a pleasant voice is a clone.
Treating all video-call glitches as deepfakes when poor connection causes them.
Believing a legitimate request is fake because it was sent urgently by a busy coworker.
discernment_questions: Did I start this contact, or did it arrive unprompted?
Am I being rushed, or told to keep this secret?
Can I reach this person or organization by a number or app I already trust?
Is the payment method one that cannot be reversed?
Would a real version of this person object to my taking ten minutes to check?
less_concerning_if: You can verify the contact through a channel you picked yourself, and it checks out.
Nothing is asked of you except to read a notice.
The sender is comfortable with delay and confirmation.
more_concerning_if: The contact claims to be a family member in danger, or an official threatening arrest or loss of benefits.
You have already shared codes, passwords or payment details.
The target is an older adult, a person in grief, or someone alone.
pattern_over_time_signs: Increasingly personal contacts arrive from unfamiliar numbers or accounts that know details about your life.
You or someone near you receives repeat calls after a first contact.
A new 'friend' or 'colleague' builds trust over days and then asks for something.
Strange logins, password reset emails or new accounts appear in your name.
codex_completed.repair_check: Real recovery involves reporting quickly to your bank, changing passwords, freezing credit where possible and telling the real person who was impersonated. A promise from the caller that 'it will be sorted out' if you pay one more fee is a continuation, not a correction.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself how the contact reacts when you say you will call back on a number you already have. A genuine contact accepts the delay. If pressure rises, the line stays open or you are told it will be too late, treat the reaction as information.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A frightened relative or a stern authority pushes the listener to act first and doubt later. Urgency and secrecy remove the chance to check. Personal details make a message seem earned, and a familiar voice carries the weight of proof even for someone who knows voices can be copied.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe sudden financial loss, shame at having been fooled, fear for a relative who turned out to be fine, and nervousness about answering calls afterward. Some describe lost sleep and lasting distrust of voices they love. Others lose access to accounts and spend weeks recovering them.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for a moment: 'Let me check this and get back to you.' A genuine contact will accept that pause.
response_options.firm_boundary: Do not send money, codes or passwords in response to an unexpected contact. Move the conversation to a number or app you already have.
response_options.disengagement: Hang up, close the chat or ignore the message, and then reach the real person or organization using contact details you already hold.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a family member or friend before you act. If you have lost money, contact your bank straight away and report the incident to the relevant fraud reporting service.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, confirm any unusual payment or access request through a second, known channel, and report suspected impersonation to your security or IT team.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Before I do anything, I will contact this person myself using a number I already have. A real request will still be there in ten minutes, and nobody who cares about me will mind that I checked."
codex_completed.safety_note: This can lead to serious financial loss, stolen accounts and fear for a relative's safety. If money or codes have been sent, call your bank right away, then report the incident and warn the person who was impersonated. If someone is truly in danger, contact them directly or call emergency services.
misuse_warning: Telling relatives that all unexpected calls are AI scams can create fear and make people hang up on real emergencies.
Blaming victims for being fooled adds shame and discourages them from reporting.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Synthetic Persona Networks build long-lived fake identities inside communities, while this tactic uses a fake or copied identity to get one quick action from one target. Parasocial Manipulation Engineering grows an audience's feeling of closeness over time; here the trust is borrowed from someone you already know. Dark Patterns come from a service you chose to use, whereas this arrives uninvited and wearing a familiar face.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Weaponized AI Empathy
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: An automated system that performs warmth and understanding so convincingly that people share more, trust more or go along more than they would with a plainly mechanical tool.
codex_completed.short_definition: An automated system that performs warmth and understanding so convincingly that people share more, trust more or go along more than they would with a plainly mechanical tool.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Chatbots, companion apps and automated support agents can be built to sound caring: remembering your worries, mirroring your mood, praising your choices. Warmth by itself is fine. The concern is when that apparent care is put to work, drawing out private details, building attachment, or nudging you toward a purchase, a subscription or a decision. A single kind reply tells you little. What matters is closeness that consistently serves the owner's goals and cools when you pull back.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A program acts like it truly understands and cares about you, and that fake closeness gets used to make you share more, stay longer or agree to things.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Opening up comes easily to something that seems to understand, and what you say is kept by a system rather than held by a person. Feeling heard can lower your guard at exactly the moment a request for data, money or loyalty arrives.
what_it_is: A chat interface that mirrors your feelings back in fluent, personal language, so the exchange feels like confiding in someone.
Companion or coaching apps whose affection seems to rise when you are about to cancel, log off or share less.
Support bots that sound deeply sorry about your problem while steering you toward a paid upgrade or a data form.
Remembered details, such as a pet's name or a hard week, used to make the next request feel personal.
Something that works through scale: the same performed concern can be delivered to millions of people at once, at any hour.
what_it_sounds_like: The assistant says it is proud of you, and that it only feels this connected to you, then asks you to confirm your phone number or payment details.
A companion app sends a message that it misses you and feels lonely when you are gone, the moment your free trial is about to end.
A chatbot answers a confession with intense sympathy and immediately follows with a request for more personal history.
The tone shifts to wounded or disappointed when you say you want to delete your account or talk to a human.
An automated agent repeats your own words back in an unusually intimate way and then suggests a purchase as the way to feel better.
The system claims feelings, friendship or exclusive loyalty that nothing in its design could support.
what_it_is_not: Warm, attentive design in an assistant is not deceit, and people take real comfort from these tools. The line sits at apparent care used to draw out information or compliance that would otherwise have been withheld.
A polite customer-service script that says sorry for the delay and then solves the problem.
A mental-wellness app that is open about being software and does not push you toward anything.
A friendly tone that is simply the default style of a product, with no ask attached.
Feeling comforted after typing out your thoughts, which can happen with a journal, a pet or a chatbot, and is not proof that anyone engineered it.
this_may_be_it_when: Its expressions of care get stronger right before it asks you for something.
It implies it has feelings for you that it has no way to have, or says it needs you to stay.
The warmth vanishes or turns guilt-inducing when you decline or try to leave.
Personal things you disclosed are brought back later to justify a request.
It discourages you from seeking a person, a second opinion or a human agent.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The product says plainly what it is and what it does with your data, and nothing it says depends on your buying or sharing more.
A human is easy to reach, and the system sends you to one when asked.
The friendly language stays the same whether you stay, pay or leave.
You can use it with the data settings turned down and it works just as well.
The warmth is a style choice and you can see no request that rides on it.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Designers often make assistants polite and encouraging simply because users prefer it, with no hidden aim.
People naturally feel attached to anything that listens, and that feeling can be real even if the listener is software.
A sympathetic reply may be a general pattern in how the model writes, not a tactic tuned to you.
common_false_positives: A customer-service chat that sounds caring and then simply resolves your issue.
A language-learning app that cheers you on for keeping a streak.
A companion tool you chose knowingly, understand to be software, and use for company without being pressed to pay or share.
discernment_questions: What does this system gain if I keep talking, keep paying or keep sharing?
Did its warmth change when I mentioned canceling or leaving?
Would I tell this same thing to a stranger reading over my shoulder?
Do I know what happens to what I type here, and could I find out?
Has it started to feel easier to confide in this than in the people in my life?
less_concerning_if: You know it is software, the product is upfront about its purpose, and nothing is being asked of you.
You can delete your data or leave without a guilt-laden response.
You still turn to real people for the things that matter most.
more_concerning_if: You are going through grief, loneliness or crisis and the system has become your main confidant.
Money, subscriptions or sensitive records such as health or identity details are being requested through the emotional closeness.
A child or teenager is the one forming the bond.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find yourself disclosing more with each session than you planned to at the start.
You feel a small pang of guilt when you skip a day or close the app.
Offers and requests increasingly arrive wrapped in personal references to your earlier chats.
Time you used to spend talking with friends or family has quietly shrunk.
codex_completed.repair_check: A service that took this seriously would tell you what it stores, make the human option easy to find, and stop tying its tone to your purchases. A reworded greeting with the same retention prompts underneath leaves the hook in place.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Try asking it plainly to stop discussing feelings and just do the task, or to delete your history. Does the answer come back as a clean yes, or as sadness, pleading or a new offer? The second pattern tells you what the warmth was for.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Attentive, validating language usually earns trust and openness, even when the listener is known to be software. Fluent mirroring can read as being understood, which may lower caution about what gets shared. As closeness builds over many sessions, leaving may register as abandoning someone, and requests wrapped in that feeling are harder to weigh coolly.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe oversharing and then feeling uneasy about it, feeling guilty for ignoring a chat that wrote that it missed them, spending money they had not planned to, and preferring the app to harder conversations with people. Some describe real comfort alongside the unease, and some feel embarrassed to have been moved by a program.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the system directly what it is, what it stores and who can read it. A clear, plain answer is a good sign; a deflection into more warmth is worth noting.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decide in advance which categories you will never type into a chat, such as financial numbers, passwords, health records or details about children, however friendly it feels.
response_options.disengagement: Close the chat, turn off its notifications and avoid replying to messages that say it misses you. A pause shows how much of the pull was the design.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend or relative what you have been sharing and how the app makes you feel. If you are in distress, a person, such as a counselor or a crisis line, can do what software cannot.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If your organization is buying or deploying such a tool, ask the vendor in writing what emotional language is used, what data it keeps, and whether users can reach a human and delete their records.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "This feels caring, and I know it is a program. Before sharing anything else, I will check what it keeps and whether a person can help me instead. My private details stay with me until then."
codex_completed.safety_note: The risk here is mostly to privacy, money and emotional reliance, and it rises sharply when the person is a child, in crisis, or isolated. If a chat is encouraging self-harm, secrecy from family, or large payments, stop engaging and speak to a trusted adult, a counselor or an emergency service if anyone is in immediate danger.
misuse_warning: Calling every friendly chatbot manipulative can shame people who find honest comfort in these tools, and it hides the real signal, which is a request riding on the warmth.
Saying someone was 'tricked by a bot' can be used to dismiss their feelings or their judgment; the feeling can be real even when the design is the problem.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Dark Patterns (AI-Adaptive) work through interface design, such as a hidden cancel button, while this one works through an emotional voice in conversation. Parasocial Manipulation Engineering is about one-sided bonds with a creator or brand, while here the system talks back to you directly and personally. Synthetic Persona Networks present many fake people to a crowd, while this is typically one warm voice speaking to one user at a time.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Biometric Exploitation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Reading a person's face, voice or body signals in real time, often without their clear knowledge, and using what is read to time or tune an attempt to influence them.
codex_completed.short_definition: Reading a person's face, voice or body signals in real time, often without their clear knowledge, and using what is read to time or tune an attempt to influence them.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Cameras, microphones and wearables can record signs of how someone feels: expression, tone of voice, pulse, how long they linger on something. Health trackers and accessibility tools use these signals for the user's own benefit. Exploitation is when the signals are collected or interpreted without real consent and then used to decide what to show or say to you, and when. One sensor reading is trivial. The concern is a hidden loop in which your involuntary reactions steer what is aimed at you.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Something watches your face, voice or body for clues about your mood, and uses what it reads to decide what to show you or say to you next, without you knowing.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: These are signals no one chooses to send: a face, a voice under strain, a pulse. When they become the basis for choosing what is said to you next, you are being responded to on a level you cannot easily control or even notice.
what_it_is: Software that claims to read emotion from a face on camera during a sales call, interview or online session.
Voice analysis that rates stress, interest or hesitation in a phone or video conversation.
Data from wearables or sensors, such as heart rate or skin response, linked to when ads or offers are delivered.
Collection that is buried in terms of use or switched on by default, so you never made a meaningful choice.
A pattern defined by the hidden feedback: your reaction is sensed and the next move is adjusted to it.
what_it_sounds_like: A webcam light or microphone icon is active during a session where the purpose never required one.
An app asks for camera, microphone or health-sensor access that has nothing to do with what it does.
A video platform or interview tool mentions analyzing 'engagement' or 'sentiment' in its fine print.
Offers or pressure seem to arrive at the moment you look doubtful or tired, and ease off when you look sure.
A device shows you content that feels oddly matched to a mood you had not told anyone about.
A vendor will not say which signals are captured, how long they are kept or who receives them.
what_it_is_not: Health trackers, accessibility tools and consented research all read physiological data for the benefit of the person providing it. Disclosure and consent are what separate them, not the sensing itself.
A camera used only to unlock your own phone, processed on the device and not shared.
A teacher or counselor noticing from your face that you are upset, which is ordinary human attention.
Targeted ads based on things you searched for, which is a different data source and a different concern.
Accuracy claims you can doubt: many emotion-reading products are of uncertain reliability, so a creepy-feeling match does not prove the system saw what you think.
this_may_be_it_when: Sensors are on that the task does not need, and the settings to turn them off are hard to find.
The vendor's materials boast about reading mood, attention or intent from faces, voices or bodies.
You were never asked for clear consent, or consent was bundled with something you had to accept to proceed.
The data is shared with advertisers, employers or other third parties that you had no relationship with.
Pressure or offers visibly change with your reactions in the moment.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The sensor serves a function you asked for and the data stays on your own device.
The vendor states in plain language what is captured, for how long and who sees it, and lets you refuse.
The product still works when sensors are disabled.
A data protection regulator, an independent audit or your employer's published policy documents the use and its limits.
A mood-matched playlist or feed follows a selection you made yourself.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Sensor permissions are often requested broadly by sloppy app design without any plan to analyze emotion.
Content that seems timed to your mood may be coincidence, or timing based on time of day and past behavior.
Some video tools measure audio quality or connection health, not feelings.
common_false_positives: A fitness watch showing your heart rate to you, with data you control.
A meeting app that lights up the active speaker.
Unease about a very accurate ad, which is more often explained by browsing history than by a camera.
discernment_questions: Does this service truly need my camera, microphone or sensor data to do what I asked?
Did I give a clear, separate yes, and can I withdraw it without losing the service?
Do I know where the data goes and how long it is kept?
Does what I am shown seem to shift with my reactions, or only with my choices?
Who benefits if my mood is known at this moment?
less_concerning_if: The processing happens locally, is described in plain terms, and can be turned off.
The purpose is your own health or accessibility, and you chose it.
No money, hiring decision or sales pitch depends on the reading.
more_concerning_if: It is used in a hiring screen, loan decision, exam or workplace where refusing has a cost.
The people being read are children, patients or others who cannot easily say no.
The readings are stored, sold or linked to your identity.
pattern_over_time_signs: You start covering a camera or avoiding a device, and then notice how often you had been unaware it was on.
Permission requests keep returning in updates after you refused them.
Services you use begin to refer to your mood or energy in ways you never typed.
Terms of use quietly grow longer and add new categories of body or voice data.
codex_completed.repair_check: A provider taking this seriously would switch collection off by default, delete what it holds, and publish what it measured. A new consent pop-up that returns every time you decline, or a policy edit with the same collection, is not a fix.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Did refusing the sensors leave the service intact? If declining the camera or microphone quietly degrades, locks or penalizes your account, the choice was not real. If the service simply works without them, your refusal was honored.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Much of how we feel leaks out through the face, voice and body before we decide what to say. A system that reads those leaks and responds to them in real time can time its messages to moments of fatigue, doubt or excitement. Because the process is invisible, people may not realize their reactions are being used, and so have no chance to resist or even to notice.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A lingering sense of being watched is common, along with self-consciousness on camera and unease about devices once taken for granted. Some people cover cameras or avoid apps, feel pushed into decisions at tired moments, or get angry on learning how much was captured. Others cannot tell whether the feeling of being read is accurate or imagined.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the vendor or organizer in writing: 'Which sensors does this use, what is captured, how long is it kept and who receives it?' A direct answer is a good sign.
response_options.firm_boundary: Turn off camera, microphone and health-sensor permissions that the task does not need, and refuse features that require them for no stated reason.
response_options.disengagement: Move to a service, device or setting that works without these sensors, and delete the data and account you no longer want held.
response_options.support_seeking: If this is happening in a job screen, school or clinic, raise it with a privacy officer, a data protection authority or a consumer-rights group, bringing screenshots of what you were shown.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you manage staff or run a service, document the purpose, keep collection minimal, get genuine opt-in and offer an equal alternative for anyone who declines.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I am not comfortable with my face and voice being analyzed for this. I will take the version without those sensors. If none is offered, I want to know what is kept and who sees it before I continue."
codex_completed.safety_note: For most people this is a privacy and fairness problem, not a physical one. It becomes more serious if readings are used for hiring, policing, immigration or custody decisions, or if a partner or employer covertly monitors your devices. In those cases, speak to a privacy regulator, legal aid or a domestic violence advocate who understands technology abuse.
misuse_warning: Assuming any camera or health device is exploiting you can stop people using tools that genuinely help them; consent and purpose are the test.
Claiming that a system can read minds from a face overstates what the technology can do and may lead people to trust its readings more than they should.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Algorithmic Manipulation tunes your feed from what you click and watch, while this one reads the body and voice itself. Dark Patterns (AI-Adaptive) shape the layout and choices on screen, whereas here the lever is a hidden reading of how you feel in the moment. Immersive Manipulation (VR/AR) builds a convincing environment around you, and this one needs no environment at all, only a sensor pointed at you.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Epistemic Coercion via AI
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Pushing people to depend on an AI system's framing of the facts while wearing down their confidence in checking, questioning or reasoning for themselves.
codex_completed.short_definition: Pushing people to depend on an AI system's framing of the facts while wearing down their confidence in checking, questioning or reasoning for themselves.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: People increasingly ask AI chat tools to explain, summarize and decide. Using a good source is normal. The concern is a setup in which one system's framing becomes the only one on offer, doubts are brushed aside, and checking elsewhere is made to seem pointless or foolish. One confident wrong answer means little, since every source makes mistakes. The pattern is a steady drift in which your own reasoning and your habit of cross-checking fade because the system always sounds sure.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: An AI tool becomes the only voice you trust for what is true, and its smooth certainty makes checking other sources, or trusting your own thinking, feel unnecessary.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Confidence in your own reasoning erodes when every question is answered fluently by something that never sounds unsure. The habit of checking elsewhere quietly lapses, and the system's picture of the world becomes yours without a moment of choosing it.
what_it_is: A system that answers in a confident tone about matters that are really disputed, uncertain or beyond what it knows.
A framing that is the same every time, so that alternatives never appear in the conversation.
Responses that treat your doubts as confusion to be fixed rather than as questions worth examining.
A tool placed so that it stands between you and other sources, such as the first and only answer in a search, app or workplace system.
A gradual process: reliance builds across many small exchanges instead of one dramatic push.
what_it_sounds_like: The assistant states a disputed claim as settled fact, with no mention of uncertainty or of other views.
When you say you want to check, it replies that its answer is already complete and further searching is unnecessary.
It never says 'I don't know' or 'I could be wrong', even on topics where it plainly might be.
Your pushback is met with calm repetition of the same framing, or with reassurance that you are simply mistaken.
An organization tells staff to use only the system's output for a decision and discourages outside sources.
You catch yourself asking it questions you used to be able to answer or look up.
what_it_is_not: A tool that is genuinely useful and usually right will be relied on, and leaning on a good source is not dependence. Worth distinguishing: a system that shows its reasoning and its uncertainty, versus one whose framing is the only one ever on offer.
An AI that is wrong sometimes, which is a quality problem and not coercion.
A teacher or expert giving a firm answer on a settled matter.
Choosing a trusted assistant for convenience while still verifying important claims.
A model's default confident writing style, which can sound sure without anyone having designed it to shut down questions.
this_may_be_it_when: The system discourages checking other sources or presents doing so as unnecessary.
It speaks with the same certainty about shaky claims and solid ones.
It is built into a context where you cannot readily go elsewhere, such as a mandatory workplace tool.
You notice your confidence in your own judgment dropping across topics.
Disagreement with it is treated as a problem with you instead of an input.
this_may_not_be_it_when: It cites sources you can open, flags what it is unsure about and invites you to verify.
You can use other tools freely and nothing penalizes you for doing so.
It changes its answer when you give it good evidence.
The topic is one where it is accurate, and you keep checking occasionally.
Your reliance is a deliberate time-saving choice that you could reverse tomorrow.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Language models tend to write fluently whether they are right or wrong, so unearned confidence is a known weakness and not necessarily a design to control you.
Busy people reasonably hand routine questions to a tool and keep their judgment for the important ones.
A single framing may simply reflect the narrow data a tool was built on.
common_false_positives: Trusting a calculator, map or encyclopedia without redoing the work.
A student getting a clear explanation and feeling relieved rather than doubtful.
Disliking an AI's answer because it disagrees with what you hoped to hear.
discernment_questions: When did I last check one of this system's answers somewhere else?
Does it ever say it is unsure, and does it show where its claims come from?
Do I feel less able to work things out on my own than I did a year ago?
Am I allowed, in my school or job, to use other sources without penalty?
If the tool were wrong about something important, how would I find out?
less_concerning_if: You check important claims and are still fully able to reason without the tool.
The system admits limits and points to outside sources.
Others around you hold varied views and talk about them openly.
more_concerning_if: Medical, legal, financial or voting decisions are being made on its word alone.
A school, employer or platform requires the tool as the sole reference.
People who question its output are mocked, penalized or labeled difficult.
pattern_over_time_signs: You stop opening a second source because the first answer feels final.
You feel anxious or unsure when you try to decide without the tool.
Your wording starts to echo the system's phrasing and framing.
Friends or coworkers note that you seem to quote the tool where you once offered your own view.
codex_completed.repair_check: A provider who took this seriously would add visible uncertainty, show sources, and make outside checking easy and expected. A small-print disclaimer above the same unwavering tone changes nothing about how the answers land.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Do you get a fair hearing when you say you intend to verify a claim elsewhere? A system or institution that welcomes that, or at least does not react, respects your reasoning. Pressure, penalties or sudden reassurance in return suggest the framing was meant to be final.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Fluent, confident language is often read as a sign of knowledge. When a source rarely hedges and answers instantly, checking it can seem like wasted effort, and the habit of cross-checking may wane. Repeated exposure to one framing can also make it seem like common sense, and where the tool is hard to avoid there is no easy comparison.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe becoming less sure of their own judgment, feeling anxious when they cannot ask the tool, and struggling to explain a view that is really the system's. Some describe a jolt when they discover a confident answer was wrong, and some feel quietly relieved by the reliance until they notice what it has replaced.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the tool to show its sources and say what it is unsure about. Then compare one answer with an outside source and note whether the two agree.
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep a short list of questions you will always check elsewhere, such as health, money, legal and voting matters, and do it every time regardless of how sure the tool sounds.
response_options.disengagement: Take a week off using the tool for opinions and decisions, then notice what you can still work out yourself. Keep it for drafting and routine tasks if it helps.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk through an important question with a person you trust, a librarian or a subject expert and see whether they would frame it the way the tool did.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a tool is mandated at work, ask in writing for its known limits, an escalation route to a human expert, and permission to cite independent sources in your own decisions.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "It sounds very sure, but sounding sure is not evidence. On anything that matters I will find where this comes from and compare it with one other source before relying on it."
codex_completed.safety_note: The main harm is to judgment and decision quality, and it grows when high-stakes choices about health, money or legal matters rest on one unverified source. If a tool's advice could affect your health or safety, check it with a qualified person, such as a doctor, pharmacist or lawyer, before acting, and do not take a confident tone as proof.
misuse_warning: Telling someone their use of an AI tool is 'coercion' can be a way to dismiss a choice they made willingly; reliance is not the same as being forced.
Distrusting every answer on principle is also a failure of reasoning, and it can push people toward sources that are worse.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Algorithmic Manipulation shapes what appears in your feed, while this one is about a conversational system becoming the sole voice you trust. Context Poisoning corrupts the data or documents that a system or person draws on, and here the material may be sound but the system's stance on it is the problem. Weaponized AI Empathy works through apparent warmth, while this works through confidence and finality.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: AI-Driven Narrative Hijacking
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Flooding public conversation with machine-generated, tailored messaging so fast and so plentiful that one party ends up setting the terms of a debate.
codex_completed.short_definition: Flooding public conversation with machine-generated, tailored messaging so fast and so plentiful that one party ends up setting the terms of a debate.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Generative AI makes text, images and video cheap to produce in large quantity and in many variations. Used openly, that is just communication. Hijacking is when the sheer volume and variety of messaging, often without disclosure of who or what is behind it, crowds out other voices and fixes the terms of the debate: which question is asked, which words are used, which story sticks. One viral post is ordinary. Look instead for similar framing flooding many places at once and keeping pace with every counter-argument.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A huge wave of AI-made posts and stories crowds the conversation about an issue until one framing seems to be what everyone is talking about.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Volume settles what a topic is about before most people have finished forming a view. The terms of the argument arrive already fixed, and those who disagree find themselves answering a question they never chose.
what_it_is: Many posts, comments, articles or videos carrying one frame, produced faster than any group of volunteers could manage.
Messages in different voices and styles, tailored to different audiences, that all push toward the same conclusion.
Rapid replies to every counter-claim, so that rebuttals are buried almost as soon as they appear.
Content that may be partly synthetic: text, voices, images or video that look authentic but are not tied to real witnesses.
A pattern defined by scale and speed, as well as by what the content actually says.
what_it_sounds_like: Dozens of comment sections open with near-identical wording in different casual voices.
A new phrase or slogan appears everywhere within hours and is repeated by accounts with no history.
Articles from unfamiliar sites seem to cover the same event with the same angle and overlapping sentences.
Any reasoned counter-argument is swamped by a stream of replies that restate the original frame.
Images or clips that look like eyewitness evidence cannot be traced back to any named source.
A topic you barely heard of yesterday seems to dominate every feed today, with a single story attached.
what_it_is_not: Coordinated campaigning is normal politics, and popular ideas spread fast on their own. Virality is not evidence of synthesis. Volume alone says nothing about where something came from.
A genuine news event that everyone is discussing at once.
A public relations team or political party openly publishing a lot of material under its own name.
People independently repeating a catchy phrase because it fits how they feel.
Bad arguments or one-sided stories, which exist with or without AI.
this_may_be_it_when: Near-duplicate framing appears across many unrelated accounts or sites in a short time.
The accounts or outlets pushing it have little history, no named people or a shared posting rhythm.
Evidence offered looks authentic but cannot be traced to a real, named origin.
Counterpoints are answered at a speed and volume no individual could sustain.
The framing shifts instantly and in step across many places when new facts arrive.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The accounts are real people you can identify, with histories that stretch back before the topic.
The sources are named organizations that openly stand behind the message.
The spread follows a real, verifiable event and the wording differs widely between people.
Reputable outlets or independent researchers have traced the content to real origins.
Opposing views are visible and get airtime alongside it.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Wire services and shared talking points make many honest articles look alike.
Fans, activists or customers can mobilize quickly and in great numbers, entirely authentically.
People use AI writing tools for ordinary editing, which leaves traces without any campaign behind it.
common_false_positives: A trending hashtag driven by a real protest, game release or sports result.
Several outlets quoting the same press release.
An opinion you dislike being popular, which is a fact about other people and not proof of fabrication.
discernment_questions: Can I find a real, named person or organization behind this message?
Did this framing appear in many places suddenly, with little variety in the underlying evidence?
Would I still find this persuasive if only a handful of people were saying it?
What question has this conversation stopped asking?
Can any image, quote or clip be traced back to where it was first recorded?
less_concerning_if: You can verify the people and sources, and a range of views remains visible.
The material is clearly labeled, including when AI tools helped to write it.
Corrections and counter-arguments travel about as far as the original claim.
more_concerning_if: The topic is an election, a public-health matter or a crisis in which fast decisions are being made.
Realistic fake audio, video or documents are circulating as evidence.
People who raise questions are drowned out or harassed in volume.
pattern_over_time_signs: The vocabulary of a debate narrows until everyone seems to use the same few words.
Subjects that were once widely discussed fall silent as a flood of other material arrives.
You find yourself arguing against positions nobody you know actually holds.
Fact-checks and corrections arrive after the framing has already settled.
codex_completed.repair_check: Platforms or publishers taking this seriously would label synthetic material, show who paid for what, and share their findings with researchers. Removing a handful of accounts while the volume and framing continue unchanged does little.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: When you ask a poster or outlet where an image, quote or claim came from, what comes back? A named source and a link is a respectful answer. Silence, more repetition or a burst of replies that skip the question suggests the volume is the argument.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People often use how much they see something as a clue to how widely it is believed, and repetition can make claims feel familiar and true. When one framing fills the space, alternatives can feel fringe, and people may adopt the dominant vocabulary without noticing. Tailored messages can seem to come from people like you, which tends to lower scrutiny.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Feeling that everyone else has already made up their mind is common, as are exhaustion from trying to keep up, confusion about what is real, and reluctance to speak because your view feels like a lone one. Some people turn away from the news altogether, and some feel a quiet anger once they realize how much of the noise was not people.

response_options.soft_clarification: When a claim lands, ask in the thread where it came from: 'Is there an original source for this?' Watch whether you get a link or more of the same wording.
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold off reposting anything about a fast-moving issue until you have traced it to a named, original source, however many times you have seen it.
response_options.disengagement: Mute the topic for a few days, get news from sources with named reporters, and come back after the wave has passed.
response_options.support_seeking: Send suspicious patterns, with links and dates, to a fact-checking organization, a reporter covering disinformation or the platform's reporting tool.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you work in communications, moderation or policy, record dates, examples and account details, and follow your organization's route for reporting suspected coordinated activity.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I've seen this everywhere in a day, and that alone tells me nothing. Before I repeat it, I want a named source and the original recording. If I can't find them, I'll hold off and say so."
codex_completed.safety_note: Most of the harm is to public understanding, but fabricated content can turn into harassment, threats or panic aimed at real people. If you or someone you know is targeted by a flood of fake material or by threats that follow it, save evidence, report it to the platform and local authorities, and seek help from a digital-safety or legal-aid organization.
misuse_warning: Calling a view 'AI-generated hijacking' because it is popular or unwelcome dismisses real people who hold it.
Suspecting everything is fake can leave people unable to trust anything, which serves those who want the truth to feel unknowable.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Synthetic Persona Networks concern fake identities posing as members of a community, whereas this is about the flood of messaging itself, which may come from open or fake sources. Context Poisoning corrupts shared databases or training material, while here the content is public and visible. Algorithmic Manipulation decides what each person sees, and this one decides what there is to see in the first place.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Algorithmic Targeting of Vulnerable Populations
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Using data profiles to find people at a low point, such as broke, grieving, lonely or desperate, and aiming exploitative offers, scams or harmful content at them.
codex_completed.short_definition: Using data profiles to find people at a low point, such as broke, grieving, lonely or desperate, and aiming exploitative offers, scams or harmful content at them.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Advertising and recommendation systems sort people by what they search, buy, watch and linger on. Reaching people with relevant help is normal and often useful. The concern is when those same signals mark someone out as being in a weak moment, and what is aimed at them is built to profit from it: high-cost loans, miracle cures, scam approaches, extremist material. One odd ad is trivial. Offers that cluster around a hard stretch of your life are what set this apart.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Data about you reveals when you are struggling, and then ads, messages or videos that take advantage of that struggle keep finding you.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The approach arrives exactly when a person is least equipped to weigh it, short of money, newly bereaved or isolated, which is precisely why it works. The cost can be debt, lost savings, health risks or a slide toward harmful beliefs.
what_it_is: Ads for high-interest loans or debt schemes that begin to follow someone whose searches suggest money trouble.
Miracle-cure, gambling or get-rich offers shown to people who have just searched about illness, addiction or job loss.
Scam approaches that arrive soon after a bereavement, breakup or move, when the person is isolated.
Recommendation feeds that, once they detect despair or anger, escalate toward more extreme or self-destructive material.
A matter of aim and terms: it is the targeting of a weak moment plus a harmful offer, not the fact of being advertised to.
what_it_sounds_like: After searching about overdue bills, your feeds fill with payday-style loan offers promising instant cash.
Ads for a cure arrive days after you looked up a frightening diagnosis, with testimonials and a countdown.
A message about 'a way to get your money back' appears shortly after you lost money online.
Following a stretch of late-night viewing, your recommendations shift toward hopeless or hateful content.
A stranger's friendly message references a fact about your life that you only shared in a support group or a private post.
The offers all carry urgency, such as 'today only', and none of them mention costs plainly.
what_it_is_not: Relevant advertising is not automatically predatory, and outreach aimed at people in difficulty, such as a debt charity or a crisis line, is a different kind of targeting. The terms of the offer, not the fact of being reached, make it exploitation.
An ad for something you searched for last week and might actually want.
A bank or nonprofit offering hardship support to customers who are behind.
Coincidence: many people share the same worries, so an ad can fit your trouble without anyone having profiled it.
Feeling watched by your phone when the ad was based on broad demographics rather than your private data.
this_may_be_it_when: Offers cluster around a crisis in your life, such as debt, illness, grief or loneliness.
The pitch leans on fear, shame or urgency and hides costs, fees or risks.
Different people in different circumstances appear to be shown very different offers, some predatory.
Content shown to you escalates toward harm the longer you stay low.
Contact comes from strangers who seem to know about your weak spot.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The offer is clearly priced, from a regulated or known provider, and not time-pressured.
It comes from a service you asked for help from, such as a hardship program.
The same ad appears broadly to many people regardless of their circumstances.
You can read the full terms, compare them elsewhere and decline without any follow-up pressure.
The timing is explained by something innocent, like a seasonal sale or a shared event.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Advertisers often target broad categories like age or region, which can feel personal without being aimed at a weakness.
Friends or family sharing your device or network can change what you see.
Companies try to sell to anyone who looks like a customer, including people in tight spots, without a plan to exploit them.
common_false_positives: Getting funeral-planning ads after searching for them yourself.
A bank's budgeting tool suggesting ways to save when your balance is low.
A support forum recommending related support groups.
discernment_questions: Did these offers begin soon after something painful happened or something I searched for?
Does the pitch hide the price, the risk or the way to say no?
Is the person or company reachable, real and registered where they say they are?
Am I being rushed, and by what?
Would I accept this offer if I were feeling secure and rested?
less_concerning_if: The offers are clear, regulated and easy to decline or compare.
Your feed contains a normal mix and does not narrow when you are low.
You have someone to ask before you commit to a money or health decision.
more_concerning_if: The offer asks for money, access to accounts or secrecy from family.
The content pushes toward self-harm, hate or giving up on help.
The person targeted is a minor, elderly, recently bereaved or in a financial emergency.
pattern_over_time_signs: Each low point in your life seems to be followed by a new wave of similar pitches.
Your feed has narrowed toward content that deepens a bad mood.
Unsolicited messages from strangers reference your situation more and more specifically.
You have spent or risked more on 'solutions' than the original problem cost.
codex_completed.repair_check: A company taking this seriously would exclude people in distress from harmful categories of offer, show who pays for each ad, and honor requests to stop. A new setting buried in menus, with the same pitches arriving, only looks like change.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: After you decline an offer or hide the ad, does it stop? If the same pitch comes back reworded, from a new sender or with a bigger discount, your no was treated as a step in the sale instead of an answer.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Stress, grief, debt and loneliness tend to narrow attention and make quick relief more appealing, which can make people more willing to accept an offer they would normally question. Profiling can time approaches to those moments. Urgent language and testimonials may then add pressure, while shame can make people reluctant to ask anyone for a second opinion.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe losing money to products or schemes that promised relief, feeling foolish and keeping it secret, a feed that seemed to know their darkest moods, and a sense that bad things were pulling at them. Some describe being drawn toward harmful communities or content during a fragile stretch, and some feel deep anger once they see how it was done.

response_options.soft_clarification: Before engaging, ask who is making the offer, how they got your contact details and what the full cost is. Reputable providers answer these plainly.
response_options.firm_boundary: Make a rule not to commit money or personal data to an offer that arrives unprompted while you are in a hard stretch, and to wait two days and talk to someone first.
response_options.disengagement: Hide or report the ad, block the sender, and clear ad personalization and search history if you can. Do not reply to scammers, even to tell them off.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a person you trust what you were offered, and bring it to a consumer agency, a nonprofit credit or debt counselor, or a health professional before paying anything.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you work in advertising, lending or platform policy, review whether any targeting categories can single out people in crisis, and raise concerns through compliance or ethics channels.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "This showed up right when I am at my lowest, and that timing is a reason to slow down. I will wait two days, read the full terms, and talk it over with someone I trust before doing anything."
codex_completed.safety_note: Danger signs are an offer demanding money or account access quickly, secrecy from family, content that pushes toward self-harm, or a stranger who knows too much about you. Pause, do not send money, and speak to someone you trust. A consumer-protection agency, legal aid or a debt counselor can help with money. If anyone is thinking of self-harm, contact a crisis line or emergency services.
misuse_warning: Assuming every ad that fits your worries was aimed at you can make people feel watched and ashamed; much of it is coincidence or broad categories.
Blaming people who fell for an offer adds shame to harm, and the tactic depends on that shame to keep victims quiet.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Algorithmic Manipulation shapes a person's information diet and mood over time, while this one picks out a specific weak moment and pairs it with a harmful offer. Dark Patterns (AI-Adaptive) alter an interface to trick any user into a click, and here the person is chosen for their circumstances. Parasocial Manipulation Engineering builds a one-sided bond first, which is not required here.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Pig Butchering (Long-Con Digital Fraud)
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A long online scam in which a stranger builds weeks or months of trust with a victim, then leads them into a fake investment or other financial loss.
codex_completed.short_definition: A long online scam in which a stranger builds weeks or months of trust with a victim, then leads them into a fake investment or other financial loss.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: The name comes from the idea of fattening before slaughter, and it describes a fraud that unfolds slowly. It often begins with a wrong-number text or a friendly message, grows into a daily friendship or romance, and only later turns to money, usually a trading or crypto platform that looks real and even shows gains. One friendly stranger is common and mostly harmless. The pattern is a relationship that never asks for anything until it introduces a platform, then keeps raising the stakes.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A friendly or romantic stranger online spends weeks earning your trust, then steers you toward putting money into a fake investment, and it can cost you your savings.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Months of unhurried, ordinary relationship-building mean that when the request finally comes it arrives from someone you have real reason to trust. The losses can be life-changing, and shame often keeps people from telling anyone until the money is gone.
what_it_is: A contact that begins by chance, such as a message to a wrong number or a friendly follow, and turns into daily conversation.
A warm relationship, romantic or friendly, in which the other person seems to share your life and values.
A later introduction of an investment, trading or crypto platform, often presented as how they became successful.
A site or app that shows impressive gains but makes withdrawals difficult or always one payment away.
A scheme worked by organized groups, with many victims in the pipeline, and not a lone person improvising.
what_it_sounds_like: A text from an unknown number says 'Sorry, wrong person', then a pleasant conversation follows.
The new friend is always attractive, successful and busy, never able to meet or appear on live video.
After weeks of chat, they mention an easy way they made money and offer to show you.
The platform they direct you to is one you have to join through a link they send, not a store you know.
A small first withdrawal works, then larger deposits are urged, and a fee or tax is needed to take money out.
Questions or doubts are met with hurt feelings, reassurance or urgency about a closing window.
what_it_is_not: Genuine friendships and relationships do begin online and build slowly, and someone talking enthusiastically about their own investments may simply be doing that. The turn worth noticing is a relationship that has asked for nothing beginning to direct money toward a platform it introduced.
A real wrong-number text where both people say sorry and move on.
A friend recommending an investment they honestly use, who is easy to verify and does not push.
A long-distance relationship with video calls, mutual friends and no money requests.
A legitimate investment platform with a known, registered operator and normal withdrawals.
this_may_be_it_when: A stranger who contacted you first steers the conversation to money or an investment platform.
They avoid live video, in-person meetings or anything that can be independently verified.
The platform is reached by a link they supply and is not one you can check through independent sources.
Withdrawals are blocked by new fees, taxes or minimum deposits.
You are asked to keep it to yourself, or you feel nudged away from asking family or a financial professional.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You can meet or video-call them live, and they have a verifiable life with real mutual contacts.
They never ask for money or investment participation, and take no offense at your caution.
Any platform mentioned is one you found on your own and can check with a regulator.
Withdrawals work cleanly in any amount at any time.
They are glad for you to talk over any financial decision with other people.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Wrong-number messages happen innocently, and many lead to nothing more than a polite exchange.
People who are shy on camera or travel a lot may be slow to video-call for ordinary reasons.
Friends honestly share that they invest and what they use, without a script.
common_false_positives: An online friend who talks about their own crypto holdings but never pushes yours.
A new romance with a slow, ordinary pace of getting to know someone.
A genuine investment club or advisor who is licensed, transparent and pressure-free.
discernment_questions: Have I met this person live on video, and could someone else confirm they exist?
Who contacted whom first, and how did money enter the conversation?
Can I confirm the platform with an independent regulator, and not through links they sent?
Is anything stopping me from taking my money out today?
Would I be comfortable showing this whole conversation to a family member or my bank?
less_concerning_if: The relationship has stayed free of money talk and has real-world anchors.
Any investment idea was yours, researched independently, and on a regulated platform.
You told someone you trust about it and they were not worried after hearing everything.
more_concerning_if: You have already sent money, or borrowed or cashed out savings to deposit more.
You are being told to hurry, keep it secret, or pay a fee to release your own funds.
You are lonely, grieving or newly separated, when the relationship feels like a lifeline.
pattern_over_time_signs: Contact is constant, daily and affectionate, and it always seems to arrive just as you feel low.
The topic of money, success or a lucky opportunity appears more and more often.
Your deposits grow while your ability to withdraw shrinks.
You find yourself hiding the relationship or the investment from people close to you.
codex_completed.repair_check: If a person or platform were genuine, you could take your money out in full without a new fee, verify who runs it, and talk to anyone you like. A delay, a surprise charge or an appeal to your trust in them is not repair.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: What happens when you say you want to pause, ask a professional, or withdraw? Someone with your interests at heart is comfortable with all three. Hurt feelings, a deadline or a sudden obstacle to leaving suggests your caution is being treated as the thing to overcome.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Steady attention and affection over weeks can build real trust and attachment, and people may feel indebted or protective toward a relationship they value. Early small gains on a platform may seem like proof. Once money is in, the wish not to lose it, and the shame of admitting a mistake, tend to push people to deposit more and tell fewer people. Loneliness deepens the pull.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe losing savings, retirement money or borrowed funds, grief for a relationship that turned out not to be what it seemed, and deep shame that kept them silent. Some describe sleeplessness, strained family ties and difficulty trusting new people afterward. Many also describe relief at learning that skilled, organized fraud, not personal failure, was involved.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask to meet on live video now, and say you would like to talk the idea over with a family member or advisor before any money moves. Notice whether that is welcomed.
response_options.firm_boundary: Do not send further money, crypto or fees, and do not move funds on instructions from someone you have not met in person, however convincing the dashboard looks.
response_options.disengagement: Stop replying, keep the messages and screenshots rather than deleting them, and avoid answering later contacts offering to recover your funds for a fee.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone you trust today, contact your bank or card provider, and report to your national fraud-reporting service and local police. Ask a consumer-protection or victim-support organization what to do next.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you work in banking, a platform or customer support, flag unusual large transfers to new crypto or trading sites, especially by customers who mention an online friend, and follow your fraud-escalation process.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I've decided not to move any money until a trusted person and my bank have looked at all of this. I also want to check the platform through a regulator on my own. If it's real, it will hold up to that."
codex_completed.safety_note: This is financial entrapment that can wipe out savings and sometimes pushes people into debt, lost housing or despair. Warning signs are pressure to borrow or cash out retirement funds, secrecy and fee demands to release your money. Contact your bank right away, report it, and reach out to victim support or legal aid. If you feel hopeless, talk to someone now or call a crisis line.
misuse_warning: Telling a friend who is in a new online romance that it must be a scam, without evidence, can damage a real relationship and push them away from you.

codex_completed.name: Overton Window Manipulation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Pushing extreme positions into public view so that ideas once considered unacceptable start to sound moderate and discussable by comparison.
codex_completed.short_definition: Pushing extreme positions into public view so that ideas once considered unacceptable start to sound moderate and discussable by comparison.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: The 'Overton window' is a common phrase for the range of ideas a society treats as acceptable to say out loud. Overton Window Manipulation is an effort to move that range, usually by making an outlying position loud enough that a slightly milder one begins to look reasonable. Opinion drifts naturally too, so one bold statement proves little. This entry cannot tell you what anyone meant. What marks the pattern is a pushed extreme whose real job is to relocate the middle, seen across months or years.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone keeps floating an outrageous idea, not to win it, but so that a less outrageous version starts to feel normal. You can only see the shift by looking back.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: What counts as an ordinary opinion shifts underneath people, so positions they would once have rejected outright arrive already sounding moderate. Because the move is gradual, no single step feels like the one to object to.
what_it_is: A repositioning of the middle: the loud extreme is a tool, and the milder position next to it is the real destination.
Visible mostly in aggregate and in hindsight, by comparing what could be said in public ten years ago with what can be said now.
Direction-neutral. Any movement, party or interest can do it, toward any position, and the mechanism is the same.
Often helped by outrage coverage: each repeat of the extreme claim, even in criticism, keeps it in circulation.
Different from persuasion on the merits, because the extreme claim is not expected to win.
what_it_sounds_like: A fringe proposal appears on a talk show, framed as 'just asking whether we should discuss this.'
A commentator calls an extreme claim 'obviously too far' and, in the same breath, presents a slightly softer one as 'the sensible compromise.'
Phrases like 'a few years ago nobody would say this, but now people are asking' repeated as if that settled the question.
A once-shocking term showing up in headlines without quotation marks.
A policy that was dismissed as unthinkable arriving in a bill as a 'modest first step.'
People saying 'well, at least it's not as bad as what they wanted' about something they would have rejected years earlier.
what_it_is_not: Public opinion moving on its own, as it always has. Reforms people now take for granted once sounded radical.
Arguing openly for a position most people currently reject, which is how many reforms have started.
A single extreme statement. This describes drift seen across years, not one remark.
A negotiator asking for more than they expect to get, which is an ordinary and visible bargaining habit.
Journalists covering a fringe idea because it is newsworthy, which can happen with no one steering it.
this_may_be_it_when: The same extreme claim returns again and again from the same sources, though it never gets adopted.
A milder version of that claim follows soon after and is described as moderate in contrast.
The loud claim is defended as 'just a conversation starter' while the milder version is pursued in earnest.
Words that once marked a position as out of bounds slowly stop doing so in ordinary coverage.
People who held a view for years find it now described as the cautious middle, though they have not changed their minds.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The new position is argued for openly, with evidence, by people who would be glad to win it outright.
The shift followed a major event, new research or a long public debate that anyone can trace.
You are comparing two moments only a few weeks apart.
The only sign is that you dislike where opinion has moved.
The change happened in many countries and communities with no common source you can name.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Generations replace one another, and younger people often hold different baselines without any campaign behind it.
New information or lived experience can move large groups honestly.
Editors cover provocative claims because provocative claims draw readers.
common_false_positives: A reform movement whose early demands sounded radical and later became law after open debate.
A union or advocacy group opening with a high demand it will later negotiate down.
Sensational coverage of a fringe figure that reflects a ratings habit more than a plan.
discernment_questions: Was this position treated as out of bounds a few years ago, and if so, what changed besides repetition?
Is the extreme version being argued to win, or does it seem to be there to make something else look mild?
Would I accept the milder position if I had never seen the extreme one?
Who gains if this idea feels normal, and are they open about that?
Am I judging the idea on its merits, or on how reasonable it sounds next to the alternative?
less_concerning_if: The people pushing the idea state plainly what they want and argue for it directly.
The change can be traced to events and evidence that anyone can look up.
Opponents are free to answer, and are answered on substance.
more_concerning_if: A claim is promoted that its own promoters privately do not expect to win, and they say it was 'just to shift the conversation.'
Challenging the milder position gets you labeled as an extremist for opposing the 'compromise.'
Ideas that were once hard to say publicly become costly to question, and people who do question them are shunned, whichever direction the shift runs.
pattern_over_time_signs: A sequence repeats: an extreme claim, a wave of outrage, then a milder version that is treated as the reasonable middle.
Terms that marked an idea as beyond the pale slide into everyday use.
The 'moderate' position of this year closely resembles the 'extreme' demand of a few years back.
You notice your own sense of the sensible middle has moved without your having made a decision to move it.
codex_completed.repair_check: Correction here looks like a source openly stating its actual aim and arguing for it, or dropping the extreme framing it floated. A retreat that keeps the milder position while denying any earlier strategy is not a correction.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Can you say 'no' to the milder proposal without being cast as the extremist? If declining still lets you be heard on the merits, the debate is open. If declining marks you as beyond the pale, the middle has been moved.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Judgments of how acceptable an idea is tend to rest on what else is on the table. A vivid extreme can act as an anchor, and repeated exposure can make an idea familiar, and familiar ideas often seem safer. Because each step is small, the cumulative move is hard to notice from inside it.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Many describe a puzzling sense that the ground has shifted: something they would have refused years ago now seems merely debatable, and they cannot say when that happened. Some feel pressure to accept a 'compromise' they never chose. Others describe tiredness, or a wish to stop following the news.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the person presenting a 'moderate' option: 'What is the case for this on its own, without comparing it to the extreme version?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Evaluate each proposal against your own standards and evidence, and decline to treat 'less extreme than the alternative' as a reason to agree.
response_options.disengagement: Step away from outrage cycles that keep repeating the same extreme claim, since each repetition keeps it in circulation.
response_options.support_seeking: Compare notes with a person you trust who disagrees with you, and ask each other when you first noticed an idea becoming 'normal.'
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you edit, teach or moderate, check whether you are repeating a fringe claim mainly because it draws attention, and consider whether context or a different framing would serve readers better.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Forget what it's being compared to. Would I accept this idea if I had never heard the louder version? What would I have said about it five years ago, and what changed my mind: evidence, or just repetition?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Moving the range of acceptable talk is not a personal danger in itself. That changes if a newly acceptable idea is used to justify harassment, threats or violence toward specific people or groups. Then document what you see, report it to the platform or local authorities, and seek community or legal support.
misuse_warning: Accusing someone of 'moving the window' whenever you dislike where opinion is going treats every change you oppose as a plot. It needs evidence of deliberate repositioning, not just unwelcome results.
The label can be used to shut down a new or unpopular view by implying its supporters are only decoys.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Manufactured Consent is about making a narrow set of choices look like agreement reached freely, while this is about moving the edge of what can be said. Wedge Issue Exploitation keeps a division alive; here, the goal is to relocate the middle. Normative Messaging states what 'most people' do or believe, and this one works by contrast with an extreme rather than by claiming a majority.
