codex_completed.name: Manufactured Consent
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Shaping which facts, voices and choices the public sees so that agreement with a policy or decision feels freely reached but was steered.
codex_completed.short_definition: Shaping which facts, voices and choices the public sees so that agreement with a policy or decision feels freely reached but was steered.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Manufactured Consent describes agreement that looks like free choice but rests on a narrowed picture. The range of voices is kept small, some facts get little airtime, and the framing of the question limits which answers seem sensible. The phrase echoes the title of a 1988 book by Herman and Chomsky, 'Manufacturing Consent'. Editors must choose and every account frames, so the pattern shows only through analysis of coverage over time, never from one disliked story.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: People agree with a decision believing they reached that view themselves, but the information and choices they were given were arranged beforehand to point one way.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Agreement reached from a curated picture is still experienced as one's own conclusion, which leaves nothing obvious to object to. People may defend a position fiercely without realizing which options and facts were never put in front of them.
what_it_is: A narrowing of what the public sees: which experts are quoted, which questions get asked, and which options are treated as realistic.
Something that works on framing and omission more than on false statements, so a story can be accurate and still leave a distorted whole.
Visible only through analysis over time, such as counting whose voices appear on a topic across many months of coverage.
Possible across the political spectrum and in any system where a few channels control what most people read, hear or see.
Different from persuasion, because the audience does not know a choice was shaped for it.
what_it_sounds_like: A debate where every guest, from either side, accepts the same starting assumption, so the real alternatives never come up.
Coverage of a decision that quotes only officials and industry spokespeople, with no one affected by it.
A question framed as 'how should we do this?' when whether to do it at all was never put to anyone.
A major topic receiving a day of coverage while a decision about it is quietly made.
Phrases like 'there is no alternative' or 'the debate is over' used before most people have heard the debate.
Many outlets using near-identical wording for the same event.
what_it_is_not: Governments and institutions explaining their decisions, which is their job and is not hidden.
Editors choosing what to cover. Space is limited, and choice is unavoidable.
Framing in general, because every account of anything frames it.
Disagreeing with a particular story, which shows nothing without a look at coverage across time.
Public agreement that comes from shared experience, such as a widely felt crisis, with no steering needed.
this_may_be_it_when: A count of sources across many stories shows the same few kinds of voices and almost no others.
The options presented all lead to the same outcome.
Facts that are easy to find in specialist sources barely appear in the places most people get their news.
People who raise the missing option are treated as unserious rather than answered.
Surveys show people hold a view yet cannot name a single argument for the other side.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The disagreement is with one headline or one outlet, and other outlets cover the topic differently.
The viewpoint you miss has been covered fully and simply did not persuade many people.
A topic is quiet because nothing happened, not because something was withheld.
You are comparing a wire report with a long-form analysis and expecting the same depth.
The evidence is a feeling that 'the media is biased' without any examination of what was and was not covered.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Newsrooms are small, deadlines are short, and reporters lean on the sources they already know.
Audience taste, advertising and habit shape coverage with no one directing it.
Some positions really are held by few people, so they get less space.
common_false_positives: Several outlets reporting the same event in similar words because they used the same wire service.
A government press conference, which openly tells you who is speaking and why.
A broad consensus among experts that critics call suppression, when the dissenting claims have in fact been examined.
discernment_questions: Whose voices are missing from this story, and where could I find them?
Was I ever shown more than one real option, or only versions of the same one?
Can I state the best argument for the other side, in words its supporters would accept?
Who owns or funds the outlets where I mostly hear about this issue?
Over several months, has coverage of this topic changed when events did, or only when interests did?
less_concerning_if: A wide range of sources, including critics, appear on the topic, and they are answered on substance.
Outlets correct errors and publish their funding and ownership.
You can easily find strong arguments against the dominant view.
more_concerning_if: Dissenting voices are consistently left out or labeled unserious before they are heard.
Those who control the channels also benefit from the decision they are covering, and do not say so.
People hold the same view in nearly identical words without having heard any alternative.
pattern_over_time_signs: The same few framings and the same few experts recur on one topic for months.
Contrary evidence, when it appears, is covered briefly and then dropped.
The range of 'reasonable' answers gets narrower rather than wider as a decision approaches.
You find that people you know defend a view with the same phrases yet struggle to explain why.
codex_completed.repair_check: Meaningful repair would show up as visibly wider coverage after the narrowing is pointed out: new voices, corrections that run as prominently as the original, and disclosure of interests. A small note on an inside page does not change the picture most people received.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Does the source welcome a request to see the evidence and the opposing case? Openness to a hard question about its sourcing is a good sign. Defensiveness, or attacks on the person asking, suggests the picture was meant to go unquestioned.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People usually reason from what they have been shown, and rarely notice what was left out. When every channel offers a similar set of options, agreement may seem like one's own independent conclusion. Repetition across many sources tends to add credibility, even when the sources draw on the same origin.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe confident opinions they later found were built on a partial picture, a feeling of being surprised by how differently others saw an issue, and a loss of trust in everything once the gap is noticed. Some swing toward distrusting all information, which carries its own costs.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the person sharing a claim: 'Where did you first read this, and have you seen how people who disagree describe it?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to treat a topic as settled until you have read at least one serious account from outside your usual sources.
response_options.disengagement: Take a break from the channels that cover an issue in the same way and see what you notice when you return.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk to a librarian, a media-literacy teacher or a journalist about how to compare coverage across outlets with different owners and viewpoints.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you edit or commission content, keep a simple record of whose voices you rely on, and ask whether the range matches the people affected.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "What choices was I actually shown, and who picked them? If I read the strongest case from the other side, in its own words, would my view hold up, or have I only ever heard one version?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Narrowed coverage is a concern for public life, not a personal danger. That changes if dissent is met with threats, doxxing or harassment of named people. Then save the evidence, report it to the platform, and contact a press-freedom group or a lawyer.
misuse_warning: Declaring any widely held view 'manufactured' dismisses the many people who reached it honestly. The claim needs evidence of narrowed coverage, not just a disliked majority.
The label can become a way to wave off all journalism, which leaves you with nothing to check claims against.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Astroturfing fakes grassroots voices, while Manufactured Consent needs no fake voices, only a narrowed set of real ones. Reflexive Control feeds chosen inputs to a particular opponent to steer a specific decision; here the audience is a whole public. Normative Messaging announces what most people do, whereas this works through which facts and options never appear.

codex_completed.name: Astroturfing
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Making a campaign look like spontaneous public support when it is staged, funded or run by a hidden sponsor.
codex_completed.short_definition: Making a campaign look like spontaneous public support when it is staged, funded or run by a hidden sponsor.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Astroturfing is the staging of apparent grassroots support: letters, reviews, comments, rallies or accounts that look like independent members of the public but are organized by a concealed party. The name plays on AstroTurf, the artificial grass. What marks it is concealment of who stands behind the voices, not the use of organization or money, which real movements also use. It matters because people read the size of a crowd as evidence of what others believe.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A campaign that looks like ordinary people spontaneously agreeing, but is actually being run by someone who isn't telling you.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A view carries more weight when it looks like many ordinary people hold it, so a manufactured chorus crowds out the real one, and genuine grassroots voices then get doubted too.
what_it_is: Support presented as coming from unaffiliated people when a hidden sponsor, such as a company, agency or political group, is behind it.
Volume used in place of an argument: many apparent voices standing in for a case made on the merits.
Found in many settings, including public comment periods, product reviews, social media replies, letters to editors and petition drives.
Often a mix of real participants and staged ones, which makes the whole effort look more credible than it is.
what_it_sounds_like: Dozens of letters to a local paper that share the same unusual phrases.
A wave of five-star reviews posted within a few days, worded alike.
New social media accounts with few connections and a feed that pushes a single issue.
A 'concerned residents' group whose funding and staff are hard to find.
Public comment submissions bearing names of people who say they never wrote them.
Rally attendees who later say they were paid or bused in without being told who organized it.
what_it_is_not: A real movement that uses professional organisers, paid staff or a national network. Organization is not fakery.
A group that openly states who funds it and why.
People who independently hold the same view and use similar words because they read the same news story.
Supporters who were handed a sample letter and chose to sign and send it under their own names.
A business asking satisfied customers to leave honest reviews and saying so.
this_may_be_it_when: The people supposedly speaking cannot be found, or turn out not to exist.
The sponsor's role is hidden and surfaces only through leaks, filings or reporting.
Many messages match in wording, timing and structure across supposedly unconnected accounts.
Participants say they did not know what they were taking part in.
Independent investigators or regulators have documented the link between the sponsor and the voices.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The only evidence is that messages sound alike, which also happens when people share a news story.
The group is organized but openly says who runs it.
You have found one odd account, which is not a campaign.
The suspicion rests on disliking the cause rather than on anything shown about who is behind it.
You have seen only a screenshot and have not looked at the original source.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Neighbors who talk to one another often end up using the same phrases.
A popular cause can draw a large and genuinely spontaneous response, and size alone proves nothing.
Template letters supplied by an advocacy group are an openly used and long-standing practice.
common_false_positives: A hashtag that spreads fast because many real people care about the same event.
A well-funded charity campaign that names its funders on the front page.
Customers praising a shop in similar words because the shop is known for the same thing.
discernment_questions: Can you identify who is behind the campaign, and is that information easy to find?
Do the supposed individuals exist outside this campaign, with a history that predates it?
Would the message still persuade you if only five people were saying it instead of five hundred?
Is the wording suspiciously uniform, or only similar in the way a shared news story would produce?
Has a journalist, regulator or court looked into who organized it?
less_concerning_if: The sponsors are named openly and their interest is stated.
Participants can be reached and describe their own reasons in their own words.
Coverage by independent outlets confirms that real people showed up.
more_concerning_if: The sponsor stands to gain directly from the outcome and does not disclose that.
Voices appear in large numbers just before a decision date and vanish afterwards.
People who question the campaign are attacked or dismissed as outsiders instead of answered.
pattern_over_time_signs: The same messages reappear under different names after one set of accounts is removed.
Support swells ahead of votes or hearings and drops off immediately after.
Later reporting or filings reveal a funder or agency that was not mentioned at the start.
The apparent crowd mirrors the sponsor's talking points more closely than real local concerns.
codex_completed.repair_check: Once the sponsor is exposed, watch whether they name themselves and take the staged material down, or rename the group and carry on. An organization that corrects the record says who paid for what.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Put one plain question to the campaign: who funds it? An open answer separates organizing from disguise. A reply that praises the cause and accuses you of attacking it is the opposite signal.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People use what others appear to think as a guide to what is safe and sensible to think themselves. A staged crowd borrows that habit, and it works better when the apparent supporters look like us. Asking who is behind a message weakens the effect.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe feeling out of step with a majority that turns out not to exist, dropping a view because it seems unpopular, or growing suspicious of every campaign afterwards, including honest ones. Cynicism can cost as much as being fooled.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the group a direct question in public: 'Who is funding this campaign?' Their answer, or the lack of one, tells you something.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to share or sign until you have found out who is behind it and confirmed that the people involved are real.
response_options.disengagement: Mute or step back from a thread that is flooded with near-identical posts, rather than arguing with accounts that may not be people.
response_options.support_seeking: Take a suspicious pattern to a reporter, a fact-checking service or the platform's reporting tool, with the examples you collected.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you work in communications, policy or moderation, record what you saw, with dates and examples, and follow your organization's process for reporting suspected coordinated activity.

codex_completed.boundary_script: Verification script (to yourself, before sharing): "Who is actually behind this, can I find them, and would I still be persuaded if only five people were saying it instead of five hundred?"

misuse_warning: Calling every large or noisy campaign astroturf is a way of dismissing real people who disagree with you. The claim needs evidence about who is behind it.

codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Manufactured Consent shapes what a whole society treats as normal through media and institutions, and it needs no fake voices. Computational Propaganda leans on bots and algorithms at scale, while astroturfing can be done with a few dozen paid or fake accounts. Normative Messaging uses real people's norms to nudge behavior openly. Astroturfing is the one built on voices that conceal who is behind them.

codex_completed.name: Wedge Issue Exploitation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Keeping a divisive social issue inflamed, not to resolve it, but to split a group, distract attention or rally a base.
codex_completed.short_definition: Keeping a divisive social issue inflamed, not to resolve it, but to split a group, distract attention or rally a base.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A wedge issue is one on which a group that mostly agrees is sharply divided. Wedge Issue Exploitation is the deliberate use of such an issue to break up an alliance, pull focus from something else, or fire up supporters. Many divisive issues are important and deserve real argument, so raising one proves nothing. The sign is an issue that is kept warm because the division is useful, while the underlying problem stays unaddressed.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A hot-button issue is pushed hard not to solve it, but because fighting about it splits people who would otherwise agree on other things.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: People end up divided along a line drawn for someone else's benefit, arguing about who they are while the things they actually share go unaddressed. Friendships and coalitions can break over a fight neither side chose.
what_it_is: A deliberate focus on an issue that cuts across a rival's supporters, so they argue with each other instead of with the people who raised it.
Used to change the subject: a loud fight on one topic can crowd out a quieter story about another.
Often aimed at identity and emotion, such as a sense of respect, belonging or fear, more than at the details of the policy.
Possible from any side and about any issue. The mechanism is the same whichever cause is at stake.
Different from honest advocacy in that the pushing continues even when there is a chance to settle the matter.
what_it_sounds_like: A story about one contested issue suddenly leading every feed just before a vote on something unrelated.
A question phrased so that any answer offends part of the audience: 'Whose side are you on?'
A leader asking supporters to 'defend' their identity against a threat that has no actual bill attached.
Posts that are written to provoke the strongest reaction from the other camp and are then reshared by that camp.
A coalition meeting that falls apart over a side topic that was not on the agenda.
Offers of a practical compromise rejected because 'it would end the fight.'
what_it_is_not: Divisive issues are frequently important and deserve real argument, and raising one is not evidence of strategy.
A group sincerely pressing on a cause it cares about, even when it splits its own allies.
A politician taking a clear stand on a contested question when asked, which is part of the job.
Real disagreement inside a movement, which is normal and often healthy.
Media covering a controversy because it is big news.
this_may_be_it_when: The issue is raised loudest when other news is unfavorable to the people raising it.
The same actors who stoke the fight turn down chances to settle it.
A group whose members agreed on many practical matters now treats the one divisive issue as a loyalty test.
Messages are built to make the opposing camp look like a caricature.
The fight gets far more attention than the thing at stake would warrant.
this_may_not_be_it_when: People are trying to settle the issue and propose a concrete outcome.
The topic has been contested for years and no single actor controls the attention it gets.
The conflict follows a real event that touches people's lives.
You are suspicious only because the issue is uncomfortable.
Both sides are speaking in their own voices and no hidden party is in view.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People hold deep convictions on moral questions, and passionate disagreement is not staged.
News cycles naturally cluster around the most emotional story of the week.
A group may sincerely decide a principle matters more than keeping the peace.
common_false_positives: A vote on a rights question that divides a party because members truly differ.
A heated town hall about school policy where the anger is genuine.
A campaign that openly states a stance on a hot topic and asks for support.
discernment_questions: Does anyone involved seem to want the issue settled, or does the fight seem to be the point?
What else is happening right now that this issue is keeping me from looking at?
On which practical matters do I agree with the people I am being told to oppose?
Is the question phrased so that no honest answer feels safe?
Who benefits if my group splits over this?
less_concerning_if: The people raising the issue also offer a concrete way to resolve it.
Disagreement stays on the substance of the policy and does not turn into questions about who people are.
Coalitions survive the argument and continue to work on shared goals.
more_concerning_if: The issue is escalated precisely when a related decision needs a united response.
Members who want compromise are attacked as traitors by their own side.
The same disputes are reopened each time a settlement comes near.
pattern_over_time_signs: The same hot topic returns before each election or major decision, with little change in what is actually proposed.
Groups that once worked together begin to treat each other as enemies over this one point.
Calls to compromise are repeatedly framed as betrayal.
You notice you feel anger at neighbors or relatives over a topic that has not touched your life directly.
codex_completed.repair_check: Real movement looks like the issue being taken up in a way that could end it, with a concrete proposal and a hearing for the other side. A temporary calm that returns with new heat before the next vote is not progress.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Can you say 'I disagree on this one but agree on that' and still be welcomed? If shared ground is acknowledged, the dispute is probably honest. If any partial agreement is treated as disloyalty, the division itself may be doing the work.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Strong emotions around identity and belonging tend to make people watch for threats and pull toward their own side. codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe strained family dinners, friendships that cooled, a feeling of being forced to pick a side on a topic they have mixed views about, and a sense that real problems at home get less attention than the latest fight. Some describe exhaustion and a wish to stop discussing politics at all.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the other person: 'Is there a part of this we both want fixed, even if we disagree about the rest?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Refuse to treat one issue as the test of a person's worth, and say you will talk about the specifics of the policy but not about who is good or bad.
response_options.disengagement: Leave the thread or conversation when it becomes a contest of insults, and return to the practical question another day.
response_options.support_seeking: Seek out a trusted friend or a community group that works across the divide, and ask how they manage disagreement.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you run a team or a community space, set a rule to keep discussion on the task or the specific proposal, and apply it equally to every side.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Is this fight about solving something, or about keeping us apart? What are we not talking about while we argue over this, and what do I actually agree on with the people I'm being told to oppose?"
codex_completed.safety_note: A heated public fight over an issue is rarely a personal danger by itself. Then save the evidence, report it to the platform, and contact local authorities or a community group that supports those targeted.
misuse_warning: Calling a sincere opponent's deeply held cause a 'wedge issue' dismisses their conviction. The label needs evidence that the division is being used, not just that the topic is heated.

codex_completed.name: Computational Propaganda
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Using bots, fake accounts and automated tools to flood public conversation with political messages so they look like organic opinion at a scale no crowd could match.
codex_completed.short_definition: Using bots, fake accounts and automated tools to flood public conversation with political messages so they look like organic opinion at a scale no crowd could match.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Computational Propaganda is political persuasion carried out with software: automated accounts, networks of fake profiles and algorithm-boosted content that pass as ordinary people talking. It differs from a single troll or a loud real user because it relies on volume and coordination that no group of individuals could produce by hand. Parties and campaigns openly coordinate messaging and use scheduling tools, so automation alone is not the sign. Attribution is technical work, and a hard-arguing account is not evidence of a network.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Software and fake accounts pretend to be many ordinary people so a political message looks far more popular and spontaneous than it really is.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The sense of what most people believe, which shapes what any individual feels able to say aloud, gets set by accounts that are not people. Real voices can feel outnumbered, and honest users get wrongly accused of being bots.
what_it_is: Political messages pushed through automated or fake accounts that imitate real, independent users.
A matter of scale and speed: the same message can appear thousands of times in minutes, which a crowd of real people rarely does.
Sometimes mixed with real users who are drawn in and share the content, which then spreads it further.
Seen on screens as patterns in accounts and timing, rather than in what any single post says.
Different from a hired commentator who writes under their own name, because the hallmark is simulated people.
what_it_sounds_like: Dozens of accounts posting the same sentence within seconds of each other.
Profiles created recently, with stock-photo faces, few friends and a feed devoted to a single political topic.
A hashtag that trends overnight with most activity coming from accounts with no earlier history.
Replies under a post that arrive almost instantly and repeat the same talking points whatever the post said.
Accounts that post around the clock without any break for sleep.
A burst of identical comments on a news article, all from profiles with no personal content.
what_it_is_not: Parties, campaigns and advocacy groups legitimately coordinating their messaging, which is ordinary politics.
Scheduling tools and staff-run accounts, which are not bots.
An account that argues aggressively or repeats a view often. Intensity is not proof of a network.
Many real people sharing a viral post for their own reasons.
A news organization's automated feed that is clearly labeled as automated.
this_may_be_it_when: Large numbers of accounts share very similar wording, timing and links, yet have no visible connection.
Account histories are short, blank or inconsistent with the persona they present.
Researchers or the platform itself have documented the network and removed it.
The activity spikes around a political event and disappears afterwards.
Accounts respond to criticism with the same stock replies rather than the content of your reply.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The only evidence is that someone disagrees with you strongly and often.
The accounts are real people who found the same post and shared it.
You have judged by a single profile feature, such as a missing photo.
Similar wording comes from a widely circulated news line.
You cannot see the account's history and are guessing from one post.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people copy a funny or striking phrase and spread it quickly without any coordination.
Shy or privacy-minded users keep sparse profiles and no photo.
Fans or supporters may organize openly in a group chat to post together, which is visible coordination, not a hidden one.
common_false_positives: A hashtag that trends because a real event drew millions of genuine reactions.
A brand or party running its own clearly labeled, scheduled posts.
An elderly relative who reposts the same chain message to everyone.
discernment_questions: Does this account have a history that predates the topic, with signs of a real life?
Is the pile-on built of accounts with nothing in common except the message?
Would I judge the claim differently if I knew only a few people were behind it?
Has a platform, researcher or journalist reported on this particular activity?
Am I calling this fake because the evidence shows it, or because I cannot believe so many people disagree?
less_concerning_if: The accounts are identifiable people or organizations who are open about their affiliations.
Spread of the message tracks real events and real conversations.
Independent researchers have looked and found ordinary activity.
more_concerning_if: Accounts posing as local citizens turn out to be run from elsewhere or by one operator.
Messaging targets real individuals with harassment or the spread of their personal details.
Platform or independent reports connect the activity to a concealed sponsor.
pattern_over_time_signs: Clusters of near-identical accounts reappear under new names after earlier ones are removed.
The same talking points rise and fall in step across unrelated topics.
Activity surges around elections or debates and falls sharply after.
You find your own feed shows one view as dominant while people you know offline hold a wider range.
codex_completed.repair_check: Meaningful correction means the operator is identified, the accounts are taken down, and a public explanation says what was automated and by whom. Quiet deletion followed by the same messages from new profiles leaves the network intact.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: When you ask a suspicious account a genuine question about itself, does it engage with what you said, or fall back on stock lines? A real person can answer in their own words. Canned repetition, or silence followed by more of the same, is informative.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People often read the number of voices saying something as a sign of what is common and safe to think. A large, steady stream of apparently independent posts can make a view feel mainstream and can make dissenters feel isolated. Seeing the same claim many times also tends to make it feel more familiar and so more plausible.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe doubt about their own views after seeing an apparently overwhelming majority, reluctance to post, anger at accounts that later turn out to be fake, and suspicion of strangers online, including honest ones. Some start calling every opponent a bot, which damages real conversation.

response_options.soft_clarification: Before replying to a surprising account, check its profile and history. A single honest question such as 'Can you tell me more about how you came to this view?' shows whether anyone is there.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decide not to share or amplify content from accounts you cannot verify as real people, however well it fits your opinions.
response_options.disengagement: Mute, block or leave a thread filled with identical replies, and avoid arguing with accounts that may not be people.
response_options.support_seeking: Send suspicious patterns, with links and dates, to the platform's reporting tool, a fact-checking group or a reporter who covers online influence.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you work in communications, moderation or research, keep dated records of what you observed and follow your organization's process for reporting suspected coordinated activity.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Is there a real person behind this? Does the account have a life that predates this topic? If only a handful of people were posting this, would I still believe so many agree, or am I counting accounts instead of people?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Reading or being outnumbered by suspect accounts is not a physical danger. It would change if networks target a named person with harassment, threats or the spread of their address or workplace. If that happens, document everything, report it to the platform, and contact a lawyer, a support service or the police if you feel unsafe.
misuse_warning: Calling anyone who disagrees with you a 'bot' dismisses real people and ends conversations. The claim needs evidence about the account, not just its opinions.
Public accusations against a named account can wrongly expose an ordinary person to harassment.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Astroturfing stages grassroots support by many means, including paid people and letters, while Computational Propaganda depends on software and fake accounts. Manufactured Consent shapes which real voices get coverage and needs no fake accounts. Wedge Issue Exploitation is about which divisive topic gets pushed, and bots are only one possible amplifier.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Reflexive Control
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Shaping the information another party receives so that their own reasoning leads them to a decision that benefits the sender, without their noticing.
codex_completed.short_definition: Shaping the information another party receives so that their own reasoning leads them to a decision that benefits the sender, without their noticing.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Reflexive control is a concept associated with Soviet and Russian military and influence theory. The idea is that a choice can be steered by shaping the picture a rival reasons from, so the rival feels it decided freely. From the receiving end, the decision looks like your own. One slanted briefing or selective news item proves little, since everyone argues from chosen facts. What marks the pattern is sustained shaping of the whole picture, plus a decision that lands conveniently for someone else. Observers can rarely prove it as it happens.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone arranges what you get to see so that your own careful thinking walks you to the choice they wanted. You feel you decided freely, which is why it is hard to spot.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A choice we reach by our own reasoning feels like ours, so we defend it and rarely revisit it. If the inputs were selected for us, we can end up protecting a decision we never truly weighed, and finding that out later is costly.
what_it_is: A way of influencing a decision by working on what goes into the decision, not by pressuring the person who makes it.
A concept associated with Soviet and Russian military and influence theory, often described as aimed at rivals such as commanders, governments or institutions.
Open pressure and visible threats are the opposite of it, because it depends on the target believing the conclusion is self-made.
Can touch ordinary audiences when a whole information environment is tilted, though it is hard to show that any single audience was the target.
Rarely provable in the moment. Claims about it usually rest on documents or testimony that surface later.
what_it_sounds_like: A sudden run of reports, from several outlets, all pointing toward one 'obvious' course of action.
A leaked document or 'insider' tip that arrives just as a decision is due and happens to settle it.
Two options presented as the only ones, with every other path described as already ruled out.
A deadline framed as the result of events and not of anyone's choice, so the decision feels forced by facts.
Cautious voices on your own side drowned out by an alarming story that later turns out to have been thin.
Afterward, a feeling that 'everyone saw it coming' about a choice that looked surprising beforehand.
A decision-maker quoted as saying they simply followed the evidence in front of them.
what_it_is_not: Everyone decides on incomplete information, and negotiators, advertisers and friends all present the facts that favor their case. Ordinary selectivity in an argument is not a sustained effort to shape someone's whole picture.
A one-sided briefing that is labeled as advocacy, so you know whose case you are hearing.
A genuine news or intelligence failure, where sources were simply wrong or slow.
A rival's public bluff or signal, which is meant to be seen and weighed as a signal.
Hindsight, where a decision looks engineered only because you now know how it turned out.
Persuasion by open argument, where the case is stated and you can answer it.
this_may_be_it_when: Your information on a topic comes through a narrow set of channels that all trace back to one origin.
Alternatives drop out of view one by one until only one choice looks reasonable.
Documents, testimony or an investigation later show who shaped the inputs and how that fit the outcome.
Warnings that did not fit the story were hard to find or were set aside as unreliable with no explanation.
The decision benefits a party that also supplied much of the information behind it.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The inputs came from many independent sources that disagree with each other in ways you can see.
The sender states its interest openly and you weigh the claims knowing that.
The only evidence is that the outcome helped someone, which many honest outcomes do.
The surprise is explained by ordinary error, delay or confusion with no common source.
Your suspicion rests on disliking the decision, not on anything shown about where the inputs came from.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Experts and officials lean on the same few trusted sources, so their information overlaps without any plan.
Early reporting in a fast crisis is thin and often wrong, and gets fixed later.
Parties in a dispute each present their best case, as in any negotiation.
A decision can favor someone simply because interests happen to line up.
common_false_positives: A well-sourced newspaper campaign that shifts public opinion by open argument.
A government information drive that says plainly what it wants people to do.
A salesperson who highlights the features that favor a sale.
A news cycle in which every outlet covers the same story because it is big.
discernment_questions: Where did each key fact I am relying on first come from, and can I trace it past the first repeater?
How many truly independent sources agree with one another here?
Which options did I stop considering, and who told me they were off the table?
Would I make the same choice if the most dramatic piece of information turned out to be wrong?
Who gains if I choose this, and have they been open about wanting it?
less_concerning_if: You can name each source, and the sources openly disagree.
The decision is easy to reverse, so a mistake is cheap.
Corrections to earlier reports are published and the decision is revisited.
more_concerning_if: The decision is costly or hard to undo, such as a war, a major vote or a large payment.
Contrary evidence is waved away as unreliable without being addressed.
Later records show that the information was gathered or shaped by the party that gained.
pattern_over_time_signs: A single storyline keeps returning in new forms, from sources that seem unrelated.
Your list of reasonable options shrinks over weeks until one remains.
Claims that proved wrong are quietly dropped while the conclusion they supported stays.
After the decision, the evidence that favored it becomes hard to find again, or has changed.
codex_completed.repair_check: Correction here means the shaped inputs are named and the choice is reopened with a fuller picture. A quiet retraction of one detail, while the decision it justified stays untouched, corrects very little.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask a source for the original document behind a claim and note what comes back. Handing over the primary material, and saying what it does not show, points away from steering. Vague reassurance or irritation at the question points toward it.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A conclusion we reached ourselves feels earned, and few of us go back to audit the inputs once it does. Reasoning can only work with the facts in front of it, so a tilted set of facts can produce a sincere, confident and tilted choice. Time pressure and a shortage of independent sources can strengthen this.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A jolt of embarrassment is common on learning that facts once trusted were selected for you, along with anger and a reluctance to trust your own judgment afterward. Some become suspicious of all information, which carries its own cost. Others dig in to defend the earlier choice, because it felt like their own.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask where a key claim started: 'What is the original source for this, and has anyone independent confirmed it?' Ask it of sources you like as well as those you doubt.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to decide under a deadline nobody can explain. Take extra time to find sources that do not trace back to the same origin before you commit.
response_options.disengagement: Step away from a flood of one-direction news about a pending decision, and come back after a day to compare it with older, slower reporting.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk the situation through with a friend who holds a different view and ask which sources they would trust. A librarian or fact-checking service can help trace where claims began.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In an organization, ask for a written list of the sources behind a recommendation, and invite someone to argue the opposite case before a major decision is signed off.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Before I act on this, where did it first come from? Who else, with no stake in it, has confirmed it? And which options have I stopped considering, and who told me to stop?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Reflexive control works on judgment and is not usually a direct threat to your body. That changes when a decision pushed on you involves money you cannot lose, your home, your legal status or a dangerous confrontation. Then slow down, ask a lawyer, financial counselor or trusted outside person for advice, and ask for the decision to wait.
misuse_warning: Blaming any decision you dislike on reflexive control dismisses the people who made it, and requires a hidden planner for what may be ordinary error.
Used about political opponents, it becomes a way of saying anyone who disagrees was tricked, which ends the conversation.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Manufactured Consent works on what a whole population seems to agree with, while reflexive control concerns one party's specific decision and the facts that party was given. Computational Propaganda is a delivery method, bots and networks, which could supply inputs but says nothing about a decision. Normative Messaging leans on what others supposedly do; reflexive control leans on which facts you were shown.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Normative Messaging
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Telling people what 'most others' believe or do, so that they drift toward that apparent norm whatever they privately prefer.
codex_completed.short_definition: Telling people what 'most others' believe or do, so that they drift toward that apparent norm whatever they privately prefer.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Normative messaging is any communication about what is normal, common or expected in a group, from a poster saying most neighbors recycle to a headline saying everyone has moved on. People tend to adjust toward what they think others do. When the stated norm is accurate and the aim is disclosed, it is a mainstream public-health and civic tool. The concern begins when the claim is false, unverifiable or invented, or the sender hides a stake. One poster means little; the pattern is a steady drumbeat of 'everyone' claims you cannot check.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Being told that 'everybody' thinks or does something, so you go along. It is fine when the claim is true and the reason is stated, and a problem when you cannot check it.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Behavior shifts to match what everyone else is said to be doing, even where private preference points elsewhere. Because the claim about what everyone does is rarely checked, a person can be moved by a majority that is smaller than described, or does not exist.
what_it_is: Messages about the typical person: 'most people in your area', 'nine in ten', 'nobody still believes that'.
Works through a wish to belong and a fear of standing out, not through argument about the merits.
Can describe what people do, or what they approve of; the second is harder to check.
Appears on posters, bills, utility letters, ads, news framing, and social feeds with visible counts.
Can be honest and helpful when the figure is accurate and the purpose is stated.
what_it_sounds_like: Most of your neighbors have already signed up.
Everyone knows that view is finished.
Join the millions who have switched.
Nobody serious still thinks that.
A letter comparing your energy use with 'similar households' nearby.
A feed counter showing a huge number of people agree, with no way to see who.
People like you are choosing this option.
An announcer saying 'the country has decided' before the vote.
what_it_is_not: Accurate social-norms messaging is a mainstream and often benign public-health tool. It is not manipulation when the norm stated is true and the purpose is disclosed. An unverifiable or false claim about what everyone else does is the part to notice.
A health notice that gives a correct figure from a named survey.
A friend telling you that most of your team brings lunch, so you know what to expect.
Describing a real custom to a newcomer, such as how people queue or tip.
Reporting that a view really is held by a majority, when it is.
Open advocacy with a stated purpose, such as 'join us, there are many of us'.
this_may_be_it_when: The figure has no named source, date or sample behind it.
The group called 'most people' is left vague or shifts between messages.
The claim is repeated far more than it is explained.
Dissent is described as rare or fringe without any evidence.
The pitch spends more words on belonging than on what the thing actually does.
this_may_not_be_it_when: A named survey with its method and date is linked, and you can read it.
The message states who sent it and what they want from you.
The numbers are modest and come with caveats.
Outlets with different interests report similar figures independently.
The point is a custom you are new to, offered so you can find your feet.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People say 'everyone' loosely when they mean a lot of people.
A group's custom may truly be strong where you have newly arrived.
Public agencies often use real data about behavior to encourage useful habits.
Friends mention their own choices without wanting you to copy them.
common_false_positives: A bestseller list that reports actual sales.
A poll result in a news story from a pollster that publishes its method.
A neighbor explaining how the street handles trash day.
A teacher noting that most of the class has handed the work in.
discernment_questions: Who says that most people think or do this, and how would they know?
Can I find the number itself, with a date and a sample?
Would I want this if no one else did?
Is the message describing what people do, or telling me what I ought to approve?
Does anything in it tell me what the sender gains?
less_concerning_if: The claim comes with a source you can open.
You can say no without social cost, and the message does not shame you.
The sender discloses the purpose, as an open health campaign would.
more_concerning_if: The 'majority' claim is aimed at a vote, a purchase or a heated dispute and cannot be checked.
People who doubt it are pictured as isolated, strange or disloyal.
The same 'everyone agrees' line shows up across channels with no source behind it.
pattern_over_time_signs: You catch yourself repeating 'everyone says' without remembering where you heard it.
You hesitate to state a view you hold because it feels like a minority one, though you never saw evidence that it is.
Counts and percentages shown to you keep rising while nobody can say who was counted.
When you talk to people in person, their views turn out to be more varied than the feeds suggested.
codex_completed.repair_check: A sender who is fixing this names the source of the figure, corrects it once it is shown to be inflated, and stops using it. A message that swaps the claim for a different 'everyone' statement has not corrected anything.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Does asking for the source change how you are treated? Calm sharing of the survey is a good sign. Being called out of step, or told that asking is itself odd, suggests the claim leaned on pressure and not on evidence.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Others' behavior serves as a quick guide to what is safe, correct and approved, especially in unfamiliar settings, and a norm claim borrows that shortcut. It can work even when we privately disagree, because standing out can feel costly. The effect tends to weaken when we can see the data or meet real members of the group.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe quietly dropping a view because it seemed unpopular, feeling alone in a disagreement that was widely shared, or feeling embarrassed on finding that the majority was a fraction of what had been described. Some become wary of every statistic, including honest ones.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask politely where the figure comes from: 'Which survey is that, and when was it taken?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to change your mind or sign up on the strength of a claim about what others think until you have seen the number for yourself.
response_options.disengagement: Turn off visible counters, trending panels and 'people also' prompts for a while, and decide from what you value instead.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask two or three people you know, in person, what they actually think. Real answers are often more varied than a headline suggests.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a colleague says everyone has already agreed, ask who, and ask to hear it from them. Request that any poll be run with the question and result shared openly.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Who counted these people, and when? Would I want this if I were the only one? Am I going along because it is true, or because I fear being the odd one out?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Norm claims are usually low-risk to your safety. The risk grows when a claim about what 'everyone' will do is used to rally a crowd against named people or to build pressure for harassment. If that appears, save the examples, report them to the platform, and contact a local support service or lawyer if you are targeted.
misuse_warning: Calling every statement about what most people think 'normative messaging' makes ordinary reporting of a true majority look sinister.
Treating a person who changed their view as sheep-like ignores that they may have been persuaded by good reasons.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Astroturfing fakes the crowd itself, with voices that hide their sponsor; normative messaging only describes a crowd, real or not. Manufactured Consent shapes a society's agreement through media and institutions over time. Overton Window Manipulation shifts which ideas feel thinkable by pushing extremes, not by claims about what most people already think. Here, the work is done by a statement about the majority.
