codex_completed.name: False Flag Operations
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Staging an attack or incident so that another group appears to be responsible, in order to justify a response or damage the blamed party.
codex_completed.short_definition: Staging an attack or incident so that another group appears to be responsible, in order to justify a response or damage the blamed party.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A false flag operation is an event arranged so that it looks like the work of someone else. Historians have documented some cases, usually through archives and investigations years later. In real time the label is claimed far more often than shown, because early facts about any incident are confused. A gap in the official story, an odd coincidence or a convenient result does not establish staging. What it would take is evidence about who arranged the event, which ordinary readers rarely hold.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: An attack or incident is arranged to look like someone else did it, so blame, anger and action land on the wrong party. It is also a label people often apply far too fast.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Retaliation, suspicion and public anger land on a group that did not do the thing, and the record that would correct it is the very thing that was arranged. The opposite harm exists too: calling real tragedies staged wounds the people who lived them.
what_it_is: A deception about who is responsible for an event, not only about what happened.
The phrase comes from old naval ruses that involved flying another side's flag.
Cases accepted as real have been established by archives, documents, testimony and investigation, usually long after the event.
The idea can apply to a state, a group or a company, so scale does not define it.
The claim 'it was a false flag' is itself widely used to explain events people dislike, so it needs strong evidence.
what_it_sounds_like: Within hours of an incident, a confident claim that it was obviously staged by the other side.
A list of 'coincidences' offered as proof, with no document or witness behind them.
Blame assigned to a group before investigators have said anything.
Demands for a sweeping response that leans on the identity of the supposed culprit.
Posts claiming victims never existed, a common over-claim that is not evidence of staging.
Later findings that the party first named was not involved.
what_it_is_not: Most disputed events are confusing in their first days, and unanswered questions after an incident are normal, not proof of staging. Documented cases were established through archives and investigation years afterward, never through pattern-spotting in real time.
A real attack that was carried out by the group blamed for it.
Early reporting mistakes, which are common in the first days of any incident.
An accidental event whose cause stays unclear for a while, such as an industrial failure.
A group falsely claiming credit for something it did not do, which deceives about credit and not about a staged event.
Official secrecy or slow release of files, which can be poor transparency without hiding a staged event.
this_may_be_it_when: Archives, leaked documents or sworn testimony from people involved describe the arrangement.
Independent investigators with different interests reach the same conclusion about who arranged it.
Physical or digital evidence at the scene points to a source that contradicts the story given.
The blamed party's own records or witnesses credibly rule it out.
A party that gained from the blame is shown, with evidence, to have had the means and access.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The case rests on who benefited, since many events benefit someone.
The evidence is a photo or video clip whose origin you cannot trace.
Unanswered questions are being treated as proof.
Several independent bodies agree on a different explanation.
The claim says an event was staged but cannot say who, how, or what record would show it.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Casualty counts, names and timelines change as facts come in, which looks like cover-up when it is correction.
Eyewitnesses disagree honestly, because stress affects memory.
A convenient outcome can follow from honest events when unrelated interests happen to align.
Officials delay releases for legal or safety reasons.
common_false_positives: A group that carried out a real attack, denies it, and says someone else staged it.
A viral clip from a different year or place presented as proof.
An emergency drill or a film set mistaken for a real event.
A coincidence of dates between an incident and a political debate.
discernment_questions: What kind of evidence, not rumor, would show who arranged this, and has anyone with access to it said what it shows?
Is my conclusion based on a document or testimony, or only on who seems to benefit?
Would I find this convincing if the supposed culprit were a side I support instead of one I dislike?
What evidence, if it appeared, would change my mind about this?
Am I judging in the first days, before investigations have reported?
less_concerning_if: The event is recent and you hold your view loosely, waiting for investigators.
Your doubt is about one detail, not a claim that the whole event was arranged.
Multiple independent sources describe it consistently.
more_concerning_if: A claim of staging is used to justify harassing survivors or relatives.
The same claim is made across many unrelated events in the same shape.
The claim is pushed with certainty before any evidence exists.
pattern_over_time_signs: Each new incident brings the same 'it was staged' claim within hours, whatever the facts.
A theory is adjusted whenever a detail is disproved, and never dropped.
Blame follows group identity more than evidence, a pattern you may notice in your own reactions too.
Survivors or neighbors report being contacted or accused by strangers who are sure it was staged.
codex_completed.repair_check: When a blamed party is later shown to be innocent, correction looks like a public record that names the error, a retraction from those who spread the blame, and a plain acknowledgment to the group wrongly accused. Silence or a changed subject is not correction.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice whether doubting the claim is allowed. A person confident in their evidence will show you the document and accept your questions. Anger at the question, or an accusation that you are part of the plot, suggests the claim is held on faith.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: After a shocking event, people seek a cause and a culprit, and an explanation that feels satisfying can be accepted before it is checked. Anger can narrow attention toward a group already disliked. Where trust in institutions is low, a claim that officials lied can seem plausible whether or not any evidence supports it.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe fury at a group that may be innocent, fear of retaliation, and later shame at having shared an unverified claim. Survivors of real events describe hurt when told their loss was staged. Some people grow so wary that they cannot believe any report of an attack.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask what evidence is cited: 'Is that from a document or testimony, or is it an inference from who benefits?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to repeat a claim of staging, or of blame, until investigators or independent reporting support it, and say that you are waiting.
response_options.disengagement: Step away from fast-moving threads in the first days after an incident, when claims are least reliable, and return when fuller reporting exists.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk with someone who reads the incident differently and ask what evidence they would accept. If you are a survivor accused of faking, reach out to friends, a local support group or a lawyer.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you edit or report news, label unverified claims of staging as unverified, and cite what investigators have actually said, with dates.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I do not know who did this yet. What document, record or witness shows it, not just who benefits? Would I accept the same quality of proof if the blamed group were one I support?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Reading about this carries no danger. What changes that is the aftermath: a wrongly blamed group can face harassment or violence, and survivors falsely called actors can be stalked. If you or someone you know is targeted, save the messages, report them, and contact local authorities or legal aid. If danger is immediate, call emergency services.
misuse_warning: Shouting 'false flag' at any event you dislike turns a rare, evidence-based finding into a reflex, and can harm survivors and the groups blamed.
Dismissing every question about an official account as conspiracy thinking is also a misuse, since documented cases exist and asking for evidence is fair.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Astroturfing fakes ordinary supporters; a false flag fakes an event and its author. Reflexive Control steers a rival's decision through selected information and need not stage anything. Wedge Issue Exploitation uses real divisions to fracture a coalition, with no deceit about who did what. A false flag is the one where the deception is about who stands behind a staged act.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Post-Truth Epistemic Manipulation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Wearing down belief that facts can be established at all, until people stop trusting any source and claims cannot be held to account.
codex_completed.short_definition: Wearing down belief that facts can be established at all, until people stop trusting any source and claims cannot be held to account.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: 'Post-truth' is a term for public life in which appeals to emotion and identity count for more than checkable facts. As a manipulation pattern, it means a sustained flood of contradictions, denials and 'who can really know' messages that leaves people unsure whether anything can be verified. Doubting a specific claim is healthy. This pattern pushes doubt about whether claims can be tested at all. One dishonest statement, or one sincere moment of cynicism, does not show it. What marks it is the scale and the effect: fatigue and giving up.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: People are pushed to feel that no one can know what is true, so they stop checking and stop objecting. Honest doubt about one claim is different; this is giving up on checking.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: When nothing can be known, nothing can be checked, and someone left doubting everything has no ground from which to object to anything. They may also fall back on whoever sounds most certain, or on their own group.
what_it_is: A climate of doubt about whether facts can be established, not a single false claim.
Works through volume and contradiction: many stories, denials and counter-stories, so that sorting them takes more effort than most people have.
Can come from governments, parties, companies or influencers, or from ordinary audiences repeating the mood themselves, so its source is rarely clear.
Often voiced as 'both sides are the same' or 'no one can really know'.
Different from honest skepticism, which still holds that claims can be tested and wants better tests.
what_it_sounds_like: Nobody can really know what happened, so why bother?
The media lies, the experts lie, the other side lies; it is all just spin.
That's your truth; here's mine.
A dozen conflicting explanations of one event pushed at once, none withdrawn when disproved.
Accused of a lie, a speaker answers that everybody lies.
Checking a claim is mocked as naive.
A real document dismissed as 'fake' with no reason given beyond who published it.
what_it_is_not: Distrust of institutions is often earned, and saying that reporting has bias or uncertainty is honesty. The difference lies between doubting a particular claim and abandoning the idea that claims can be tested at all.
A scientist saying results are uncertain and giving the margin of error.
Reporters who correct their own mistakes in public.
Philosophical debate about knowledge, which is a serious subject and not a campaign.
Fatigue after a hard news cycle, when anyone may say 'I can't keep up'.
Healthy disagreement over what the evidence shows, with both sides citing evidence.
this_may_be_it_when: Disproved claims are replaced by new ones instead of being withdrawn, and the supply never stops.
Checking is treated as pointless or naive, regardless of what the check shows.
The message targets the idea of verification itself, not only one fact.
Contradictory stories about a single event flood in at once, and the confusion itself becomes the main result.
Real records and fake ones are treated by the speaker as equally untrustworthy.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The doubt is aimed at a specific claim and the speaker explains what evidence would settle it.
The skeptic accepts a result when the evidence is shown.
Sources disagree because the event is complex and new.
You feel worn out after heavy news, and the doubt fades with rest.
The criticism of a source gives concrete, checkable examples of past errors.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Past institutional failures give people real reasons to question official statements.
Fast news creates contradictory early reports, which is normal.
Many people say 'no one knows' as a way of staying humble about complex topics.
Algorithm-driven feeds serve conflicting content with no plan by anyone.
common_false_positives: A teacher who tells students to question every source and then shows how to check.
A friend venting 'I trust nothing now' after a scandal.
Researchers who disagree in print on a hard question.
A satirical show that mocks all sides.
discernment_questions: Am I doubting this particular claim, or have I begun to doubt that anything can be checked?
What would count as good evidence on this, and have I looked for it?
Is there anyone I trust to be right about something? Who, and why?
Who benefits when I stop checking?
Has the volume of conflicting stories left me too tired to sort them?
less_concerning_if: You can still name a few sources that have earned your trust, and say why.
Doubt leads you to look further rather than to stop.
The speaker shares how to test a claim.
more_concerning_if: You catch yourself saying nothing can be known and have stopped reading, voting or checking.
People around you treat the same record as proof or forgery depending on whose side it favors.
Pressure to give up on facts comes with encouragement to rely on one personality or group for the answers.
pattern_over_time_signs: Conflicting claims keep arriving, and few are settled before the next wave.
A growing share of conversations ends in 'you can't trust anything'.
People you know shift from 'I disagree' to 'it doesn't matter what's true'.
You notice yourself or others sharing without checking, because checking stopped seeming worth it.
codex_completed.repair_check: Where trust is restored, sources publish their evidence, admit errors and let others check. A promise to be more honest next time, with no method others could test, restores very little.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask what evidence would change their mind, and listen to the answer. A concrete answer shows that claims can still be tested. 'Nothing would, they all lie' shows that the idea that testing is impossible is holding steady.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Faced with more contradictory claims than they can sort, many of us conserve effort by disengaging, or by retreating to the group we feel loyal to. Repeated falsehoods that carry no cost can teach that truth does not matter. Doubt can then spread from the false claim to the whole idea of checking.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe exhaustion, cynicism, a sense that the effort to find out is wasted, and withdrawal from news or civic life. Others describe leaning harder on one trusted voice or group because everything else feels unreliable. Some feel shame at having been fooled and stop trusting even honest sources.

response_options.soft_clarification: Separate the two doubts out loud: 'I doubt that claim, and here is what would settle it. I do not doubt that things can be checked.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to accept 'everyone lies' as an answer. Ask for the specific claim and the specific evidence, and stay on that.
response_options.disengagement: Limit how much conflicting commentary you take in. Follow a few sources with a record of corrections, and check them less often but more carefully.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk to a librarian, a teacher or a friend who enjoys checking things, and practice tracing one claim from start to finish together.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In a team, agree on how disputed facts will be settled: which records count, who can check them, and where corrections are posted.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I can doubt this one claim without doubting everything. What would settle it, who has checked it, and have I read the original? If I cannot tell, I will say I do not know instead of pretending I do."
codex_completed.safety_note: Post-truth pressure is usually not a physical danger. It matters for safety when doubt about everything leads people to ignore real warnings, such as medical, weather or financial ones. If a decision touches your health, money or home, check with a doctor, an official emergency channel or a trusted professional, not only your feed.
misuse_warning: Calling a person's honest doubt 'post-truth' can be used to shut down legitimate criticism of institutions.
Using the label for views you simply disagree with turns a description of a method into a way of saying your opponents do not care about facts.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Manufactured Consent tries to install an agreement; this pattern tries to dissolve the ground on which agreement or disagreement is judged. Computational Propaganda names the automated machinery that can flood a feed, while this entry names the climate of doubt that results. Overton Window Manipulation moves what is acceptable to say, not what can be known. The difference is the target: the possibility of knowing at all.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Honey Trapping
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A romantic or sexual relationship used as a cover for an intelligence aim, such as gaining access to secrets, recruiting someone, or gathering material to pressure them later.
codex_completed.short_definition: A romantic or sexual relationship used as a cover for an intelligence aim, such as gaining access to secrets, recruiting someone, or gathering material to pressure them later.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Honey trapping is the use of an apparent romance or sexual relationship as the means of an intelligence operation. The affection is the delivery method, and the goal sits behind it. It is discussed in espionage history and counterintelligence training, and it is rare compared with ordinary dating. From the inside it feels like a normal relationship, which is why one odd detail proves nothing. What matters is a combination: sensitive access, a relationship that outpaces the facts, and later pressure.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A relationship that looks real to one person but is being used by the other, or by someone behind them, to reach secrets, win cooperation, or get leverage.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The relationship itself was the mechanism, so finding out means losing the connection and facing the consequences of everything disclosed inside it at the same moment. Shame and fear of exposure can keep people silent when telling a security officer early would limit the damage.
what_it_is: A relationship that is real in feeling for the person targeted but staged in purpose for the other side.
Mostly discussed in connection with people who hold sensitive jobs, clearances, or access to information others want.
Often described as having two phases: closeness first, and only later a request, a favor, or a pressure point.
A romance scam is a separate pattern: a stranger online builds affection to ask an ordinary person for money, with no access or secrets involved.
Usually visible only in hindsight, once the pieces are laid side by side.
what_it_sounds_like: A new partner who asks more about your workplace, travel schedule, or projects than about your friends.
A sudden, intense romance that begins soon after you took on sensitive responsibilities.
Someone who always seems to be at the same conference, hotel, or event as you, and finds the coincidence charming.
A partner who is hard to verify: no mutual friends, vague employer, photos that never include other people.
A warm message followed weeks later by 'I have copies of what we shared, and I would hate for anyone to see them.'
A partner who is gentle about your confidential work at first, and then starts to frame small favors as proof of love.
what_it_is_not: Relationships involving people in sensitive positions are overwhelmingly just relationships, and suspicion about a partner's motives is not evidence of an operation.
Attraction between colleagues, conference-goers, or neighbors, which happens constantly without anything being arranged.
A partner who is curious about your day, including your job, because they care about you.
A romance scam, where a stranger online builds affection to ask for money. It hurts, but it is a different pattern.
A partner who is private about their past or family for reasons of shame, grief, or safety.
Ordinary jealousy or secrecy in a relationship, which says nothing about espionage.
this_may_be_it_when: You hold a role with real access, and a close relationship formed unusually fast around the time you gained it.
The partner's questions keep steering toward specifics that matter to outsiders, such as names, systems, or schedules.
Basic facts about them do not hold up when you gently check, such as where they work or who they know.
Intimate photos, recordings, or messages are mentioned as something that could be shared, even as a joke.
A friend, security officer, or employer's guidance has told you to report contacts of this kind, and the new partner fits.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They know your friends and family, and your circle has met them over time.
Their questions about work are general and fade when you say you cannot discuss it.
The relationship's speed matches how you both usually date.
Their life checks out through ordinary means, such as a known employer and shared acquaintances.
Nothing has ever been requested, hinted at, or held over you.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Two people in the same field meet often because their jobs overlap.
Intense early romance is common and is driven by novelty and hope.
A new partner may ask about work because it is simply a large part of your life.
common_false_positives: A partner who works for a competitor or a rival organization and met you openly through the industry.
A partner who stays vague about money or family because of an unrelated private difficulty.
The anxiety of a person with a clearance who begins to wonder about every new date.
discernment_questions: Can people in my own life confirm that this person is who they say they are?
Did their interest in my work come before or after I mentioned what I do?
Has any sexual or private material been referred to as something that could be used?
Does my workplace have a duty or a person to whom contacts like this can be reported without penalty?
Am I asking these questions because of something I saw, or only because I am anxious?
less_concerning_if: Friends and family have met the person and know them independently of you.
Questions about your work are rare and general.
You feel free to talk to others about the relationship.
more_concerning_if: Intimate material is mentioned as leverage, even indirectly.
The person begins to ask for favors tied to your access, framed as proof of caring.
They discourage you from telling colleagues or friends about the relationship.
pattern_over_time_signs: The balance of questions shifts from you to your job.
People who might check on the relationship are kept away from it.
Warmth rises and falls with how much you share or provide.
You start hiding things from your own workplace to protect the relationship.
codex_completed.repair_check: If you raise concerns, a genuine partner can tolerate being checked: they introduce friends, answer plain questions, and do not bristle at your employer's rules. What only looks like repair is more intensity, new promises, or a tearful appeal that you trust them.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Watch how they react when you say you will not discuss work. Do they let it go and ask about something else? Or does affection cool, or pressure rise? The reaction to a closed door is more telling than any single question.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Closeness can lower a person's guard, and sexual or romantic attachment can make someone want to please a partner and hide anything that might spoil it. Shared secrets can create a sense of obligation. Later, embarrassment and fear of exposure can make a person comply or stay quiet rather than report, which keeps the situation going.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: The loss lands twice: the relationship they believed in turns out to have been something else, and there may be professional consequences for what was shared. Many report shame, anger at themselves, and a fear of telling anyone. Some pull away from friends because of the embarrassment.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask a plain, calm question about something checkable, such as 'Can I meet your coworkers or friends sometime?' and notice how it is received.
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep work details out of the relationship altogether: 'I do not discuss work with anyone, including people I love.' Say it the same way every time.
response_options.disengagement: Pause sharing anything sensitive while you check things out, and keep your conversations about everyday life.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a trusted friend what has been happening, and consider a lawyer or counselor, so you are not holding it alone.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If your job has a security office or a reporting process for unusual contacts, going early is usually better than waiting. Early disclosure is usually treated more gently than late.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I keep my work separate from my relationships, with everyone. I am happy to talk about anything else. Can we talk about something else, or can I meet some of your friends this weekend?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Watch for any mention of private photos, recordings or messages being shared, and for pressure that grows once you have shared something. Do not handle it alone: a lawyer, the security or legal contact at your workplace, or a trusted person can help you plan the next step before anything is disclosed.
misuse_warning: Accusing a partner of being an operative on thin evidence can wreck a real relationship and invite harassment of an innocent person.
Using the label to explain away any breakup or betrayal turns a rare category into a catch-all.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Agent of Influence Operations works through public figures who speak to an audience, while honey trapping works in private through one person's intimate trust. MICE Framework Exploitation is the analyst's checklist of levers such as money or compromise, and honey trapping is one route to the compromise lever. Strategic Deception misleads whole adversaries; here, one person is deceived about a single relationship.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Agent of Influence Operations
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A public figure, such as a journalist, academic, politician, or executive, who is secretly guided by an outside party while appearing to speak independently.
codex_completed.short_definition: A public figure, such as a journalist, academic, politician, or executive, who is secretly guided by an outside party while appearing to speak independently.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: An agent of influence is someone with a credible public voice who, without disclosing it, promotes another party's interests. The key word is undisclosed. Taking funding, access, or advice openly is common and often legitimate. The concern arises when the direction is hidden and the audience believes they are hearing an independent view. From the outside it looks like a persuasive voice. Proof usually takes documents or testimony, not a hunch about whose side someone is on.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone people trust to speak for themselves is quietly being steered by someone else, so the audience thinks they are hearing a free opinion when they are not.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Audiences weigh an argument partly by how independent its source appears; where that independence is not real, their judgment is being borrowed rather than informed. Trust in real experts and reporters also erodes when a hidden arrangement comes out.
what_it_is: A public voice with credibility, such as a columnist, professor, official, or business leader, whose positions are shaped from outside and not disclosed.
Distinct from open lobbying, sponsorship, or advocacy, where the relationship is stated.
A concern that usually emerges from leaked records, court filings, or later testimony and not from reading the person's output alone.
A long-running relationship, more than a single favor or one article.
A label that describes an arrangement, not a view: the same opinion held sincerely is not an operation.
what_it_sounds_like: A commentator whose opinions line up closely with one foreign government or company, with no disclosed tie.
Several 'independent experts' who all cite the same think tank, but the funding of that think tank is hard to find.
A reporter's pieces that repeatedly quote the same unnamed source and favor the same side.
A study or op-ed that appeared just before a policy vote, with no mention of who commissioned it.
A public figure who changes position abruptly on one topic after a trip or a new business partnership.
A guest who is introduced as a neutral analyst and turns out later to have been paid by an interested party.
what_it_is_not: Journalists, academics and executives take funding, briefings, access and hospitality openly, and holding a view that happens to suit a government or a company is not proof of recruitment.
Sincere conviction that happens to match a powerful party's interests.
Open advocacy, where the speaker states who they work for or who pays them.
A source who gives a reporter information with their own agenda, which reporters weigh as a matter of routine.
Ordinary changes of mind after new evidence or experience.
Being friendly with officials or businesses, which is part of many public jobs.
this_may_be_it_when: A relationship with an outside party exists and has been hidden from the audience, not just left unmentioned.
Documents or credible testimony, not impressions, show direction or payment that was not disclosed.
The speaker presents themselves as unaffiliated while holding ties that would change how listeners weigh their words.
Their positions track one outside party's interests across many topics over time.
Questions about funding or ties are met with deflection or attack, not a plain answer.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Funding, affiliations, and conflicts are stated openly when the person speaks.
Their views existed before any link to the interested party.
They criticize the party's interests as well as support them.
The only evidence is that they agree with someone you dislike.
They correct the record when shown errors.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A person may honestly hold a view that overlaps with a government's or company's.
Think tanks and universities take funding, and disclose it, as a normal part of research.
Public figures follow their audience, their editors, or their donors without any outside direction.
common_false_positives: A columnist who consistently backs one party, and says so.
An academic whose research is funded by a company and who lists that on every paper.
Someone who spent time in a foreign country, absorbed its perspective, and argues it in good faith.
discernment_questions: Who pays this person, and is that stated where they speak?
Would I weigh their argument differently if I knew about a particular tie?
Is the claim of hidden direction backed by documents, or only by the fact that I disagree?
Does this person ever say things that cut against the supposed interested party?
Have independent reporters or institutions checked the claim?
less_concerning_if: Ties and funding are disclosed in the places the person speaks or publishes.
Positions have changed in both directions over time, as evidence changed.
Others who know the field find the person's arguments sound on their merits.
more_concerning_if: Credible records show payment or direction that the person denied.
They conceal ties when asked directly.
The same message reaches several apparently unconnected voices at once.
pattern_over_time_signs: Their output follows one outside party's calendar and priorities more than their own field's.
Stated independence persists while the actual ties do not appear anywhere.
Disclosures arrive only after outside reporting forces them.
Criticism of the outside party is consistently absent, even when events would normally call for it.
codex_completed.repair_check: If the tie is raised, genuine repair is a plain disclosure of who funded or advised what, a correction notice on past work, and a willingness to be questioned. What only looks like repair is a vague statement about independence with no names, or an attack on whoever asked.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself: if I could see every tie this speaker has, would my trust change? Then notice whether they offer that information or resist it. Openness to the question is a stronger signal than any one opinion they hold.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: An argument often carries more weight when its source seems to have no stake in it. A familiar, respected voice can make a position sound like common sense, and repetition adds to that. When the sponsorship is hidden, listeners cannot apply the discount they would give an advertisement, so the message may land harder than it has earned.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Once a hidden tie comes out, earlier articles or talks look different, and some readers wonder what else they believed because of that voice. Others turn suspicious of every expert, including honest ones. Many say the hardest part was that they had no way of knowing at the time.

response_options.soft_clarification: When you hear a strong claim, ask in a comment or question: 'Do you have any financial or professional ties to the people who gain from this?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to share or rely on a piece until you know who funded it and whether the author disclosed their ties.
response_options.disengagement: Step back from sources that will not say who supports them, and rely on those that publish funding and corrections.
response_options.support_seeking: Take specific, documented concerns to a reporter, a press-standards body, or a research-integrity office, not to a social media pile-on.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you edit, teach, or commission work, ask contributors to state funding and affiliations in writing, and keep a record of the answers.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Before I share this: who pays this person, and is that stated anywhere? Would I find the argument as convincing if I knew every tie they have, and has anyone independent checked the claim?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Learning that a trusted voice was steered is upsetting but not usually dangerous in itself. The risk changes if you are asked to pass on information, or if you are a journalist or researcher who is approached with offers or pressure. In that case, tell your editor or institution and get legal advice.
misuse_warning: Calling a critic an 'agent' with no evidence is a standard way to dismiss a person without answering what they said.
Naming a real person as a hidden agent without documents can be a damaging smear, and it often falls on those who simply disagree.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Honey Trapping works privately on one person through intimacy, while an agent of influence works publicly through an audience. MICE Framework Exploitation names the levers (money, ideology, compromise, ego) that may be used to bring such a person into an arrangement, whereas this entry describes the finished result. PSYOP Message Framing is about the shape of the message; an agent of influence is about who carries it and whether their independence is real.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Strategic Deception (Denial & Deception / D&D)
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Organized efforts by a state or institution to hide what is real and to show something false, so that an opponent plans against a mistaken picture.
codex_completed.short_definition: Organized efforts by a state or institution to hide what is real and to show something false, so that an opponent plans against a mistaken picture.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: The title joins two related behaviors that are usually discussed together. Denial means keeping the real thing out of view: concealing a capability, a plan, or a site. Deception means putting a false picture in its place so others believe it. They are two sides of one effort, and the pairing is used in security studies. It happens at the scale of states, armies and large organizations. Ordinary secrecy is not the same: not being told something differs from being pointed the wrong way.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Powerful groups sometimes hide what is real and show something false at the same time, so that others make decisions based on a picture that was arranged for them.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Plans get laid against a picture of the world that was arranged to be believed, and the error usually becomes visible only once acting on it can no longer be undone. For the public, it also means official accounts and leaked ones both deserve a second look.
what_it_is: Two linked parts: denial hides the real thing, and deception supplies a false substitute. Describing either alone misses the combination.
Done by states, militaries, and large institutions across several channels at once, not by individuals.
Aimed at what an opponent believes about intentions, capabilities, plans or timing.
Judged in hindsight by historians and analysts, usually from released records, because it is meant to be invisible while it works.
Different from simple secrecy, which keeps something quiet without installing a false belief.
what_it_sounds_like: Official statements that are accurate in every detail yet leave out the part that matters.
Several independent-looking sources supporting the same story that later turn out to share an origin.
Visible activity at one site that draws attention while the real activity is elsewhere and hidden.
A 'leaked' document that arrives conveniently and confirms exactly what a rival already feared.
A denial issued confidently and repeated across outlets, then reversed once records emerge.
Analysts later saying that signs which looked like evidence had been put there to be found.
what_it_is_not: Ordinary secrecy is legitimate; institutions and states keep capabilities and intentions confidential without staging a coordinated illusion.
Not being told something is not the same as being actively pointed the wrong way.
An honest mistake or a failure of intelligence analysis, which can look the same from outside.
Ordinary public relations, spin, or a company's carefully worded statement.
A rumor that turns out false, without a coordinating hand behind it.
Bluffing in a negotiation or game, which is limited and understood by the players.
this_may_be_it_when: Records released later show a deliberate effort to mislead, not just a gap in knowledge.
Multiple channels told the same false story, and independent checking shows they traced back to one source.
Something that should have been visible was missing, and something visible was staged.
The people most eager to confirm the story were the ones who gained when you believed it.
Credible historians or investigators have documented the effort with sources, not just inference.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The gap is explained by incomplete information that everyone had.
Independent sources, with different origins, agree on the facts.
The error looks like ordinary analytic bias or wishful thinking.
The party involved has corrected the record when new facts arrived.
The only evidence is that events turned out differently than expected.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Institutions often keep details secret for legitimate security or privacy reasons.
Initial reports in a fast-moving event are often wrong without anyone intending it.
Wrong forecasts usually come from limited information and human error.
common_false_positives: A surprise attack or event that analysts failed to predict, which does not itself show anyone planned the misdirection.
A company's secret product launch kept under wraps for competitive reasons.
A government that said 'no comment' on an operation.
discernment_questions: Is there documentary evidence that the misleading picture was arranged, or only that I was surprised?
Do my sources really have separate origins, or do they trace back to one?
Who benefits if I believe this account right now?
Would a plain mistake or ordinary secrecy explain this just as well?
What would change my mind, and have I looked for it?
less_concerning_if: The silence has an obvious, stated reason, such as a safety or privacy concern.
Independent reports from different directions line up.
The institution later explains and corrects what it got wrong.
more_concerning_if: Released records show a deliberate plan to mislead.
A suspiciously tidy trail of evidence appears, matching what someone wanted you to conclude.
Those who questioned the story were punished or smeared, not answered.
pattern_over_time_signs: Several stories, from several channels, that all point the same way and prove false together.
A mismatch between official accounts and independent physical or documentary evidence.
Revisions that come only after outside pressure.
Later declassified or leaked records that describe the effort in the institution's own words.
codex_completed.repair_check: Once the misleading effort is exposed, accountability looks like release of the underlying records, an open correction, and a named account of who decided what. It does not look like a new statement that is again careful, partial and impossible to check.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: When you press for sources, does the account become more checkable, with named documents and independent confirmation? Or does it become more guarded, and are you told that doubt itself is unpatriotic or irresponsible?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: New information is usually read in line with what a person already expects, so a picture that matches expectations may be accepted with little checking. Several matching reports look like proof even when they share one origin. Attention is limited too, so what is shown prominently can crowd out what is missing, and the absence goes unnoticed.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Readers talk about a gap between the world they thought they understood and what records later showed. Some feel anger or embarrassment at having believed it. After repeated cases, others drift into believing nothing, which leaves them no better equipped. Those who made decisions on the false picture may face real losses.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the basis: 'What is the source for this, and has anyone independent confirmed it?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold your conclusion open until separate, independent sources agree, and say so if you are asked to take a side.
response_options.disengagement: Step away from fast-moving, unverified claims that ask for an immediate judgment, and return when records or reporting have caught up.
response_options.support_seeking: Discuss what you are seeing with a librarian, a teacher, or an experienced reporter who tracks the topic.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you analyze, report or decide on such matters, document your sources and their independence, and flag the points where one origin sits behind many reports.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Do I know where this actually came from? Are these sources truly separate from each other? Who gains if I believe it, and can I wait for records or independent confirmation before I act?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Learning of this kind of effort is rarely a personal danger. It changes if you hold a role where a false picture puts people at risk, such as in emergency, security or journalism work. Raise the concern with a supervisor, an editor or a legal adviser, and keep a record of what you saw.
misuse_warning: Calling every unwelcome fact 'disinformation by design' lets people dismiss inconvenient true information.
Assuming everything official is a staged deception becomes a conspiracy habit that is as unreliable as blind trust.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Honey Trapping targets one person through a staged romance, while strategic deception targets what a whole adversary believes. Agent of Influence Operations uses a credible voice to carry a message; deception concerns the falseness of the picture itself, whoever delivers it. PSYOP Message Framing shapes how people feel about a message, whereas this entry is about hiding the real and showing a false.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: MICE Framework Exploitation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Being pulled into helping an outside party by pressure on one of four common motives: money, ideology, coercion or compromise, and ego.
codex_completed.short_definition: Being pulled into helping an outside party by pressure on one of four common motives: money, ideology, coercion or compromise, and ego.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: MICE is a mnemonic from counterintelligence, usually given as Money, Ideology, Coercion (sometimes Compromise), and Ego. It sorts the reasons people have been drawn into betraying a trust. It is a way of describing cases afterward and of teaching people about risk, not a test that predicts who will do so. Everyone has money worries, beliefs, secrets and pride. Pressure on those is what matters, and that is something only visible in the circumstances, not in the person.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Four ordinary human needs, money, belief, fear of exposure, and pride, can be leaned on by someone else. Knowing the list helps you notice when your own needs are being leaned on.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: What gets used is whatever a person most needs or most fears losing, so the approach can feel less like pressure and more like finally being understood. Because the levers are ordinary, people often feel shame and do not tell anyone, and that silence is what makes the situation worse.
what_it_is: A teaching mnemonic from counterintelligence: Money, Ideology, Coercion or Compromise, Ego.
Used mainly to explain, after the fact, why someone with access cooperated with an outside party, and to train people to notice risk.
A description of motives, not a profile: all four are present in most lives.
Typically combined and changing: one motive can open a door and another keep it open.
Relevant to anyone with sensitive access, and, in a looser sense, to anyone being steered through a need or fear.
what_it_sounds_like: A friendly stranger who takes unusual interest in your debts, your mortgage, or your promotion prospects.
An offer of paid consulting, speaking fees, or gifts that is out of proportion to what you do.
A new contact who shares your frustration with your employer or your country and makes you feel seen.
Flattery about how brilliant you are and how undervalued, from someone you barely know.
A hint that something embarrassing in your past is known, delivered lightly.
A request that begins small and harmless and grows once you have said yes.
what_it_is_not: This is a framework analysts use to describe recruitment after the fact, not a checklist of warning signs.
Everyone has financial pressures, convictions, embarrassments and vanity; having them is the human condition, not an indication that anyone is working on you.
A friendly colleague who offers a compliment, or a generous gift that is part of a normal friendship.
Real disillusionment with an employer or government, which is common and legitimate.
Money trouble that comes from ordinary events like illness or layoffs.
A fraud or scam that targets money only, without any intelligence aim.
this_may_be_it_when: Interest in your finances, beliefs, or private life comes from someone who has no ordinary reason to ask.
Generous attention arrives just as you are under strain, and is tied to something they want from you.
You are asked to keep the contact or the favors secret from your employer or family.
Small requests increase in size, and refusing makes the warmth turn cold.
A private matter you have not told them about appears in conversation.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The person asking about your life is a known friend, relative, or colleague with ordinary reasons.
Gifts and compliments come with nothing asked in return and nothing hidden.
You can talk about the contact openly with others and nothing changes.
Your financial or emotional stress existed long before this person and is unrelated.
No one has ever suggested you share, provide, or conceal anything.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Friendly people ask about money, work, and feelings out of curiosity and care.
Paid speaking or consulting is a normal part of many careers.
Shared political frustration is a common basis for new friendships.
common_false_positives: A mentor who praises your work to help your career.
A lender or advisor discussing your finances for ordinary business reasons.
A coworker who vents about the company and wants to find out whether you feel the same.
discernment_questions: Does this person's attention to my money, beliefs, secrets or pride match any ordinary reason to ask?
Am I being asked to keep this contact quiet, and why?
Would I be comfortable telling my employer or a trusted friend all of it?
Did the closeness grow faster than the facts about this person?
If I stepped back, would the warmth continue?
less_concerning_if: You can describe the contact openly to people you trust, and they are not worried.
Nothing is requested that relates to your access or your duties.
The relationship has history that others can vouch for.
more_concerning_if: You are asked to hide the relationship, payment, or favor from your employer.
Something embarrassing or damaging about you is mentioned, however lightly.
The requests keep growing and are tied to what you can reach.
pattern_over_time_signs: Help with a need, such as cash or a career break, shows up just when you needed it and then comes with expectations.
The contact learns more about your weak points than your strengths.
Your circle of people who know about the relationship narrows.
You begin to feel obliged and ashamed, not free.
codex_completed.repair_check: If you raise the concern, a trustworthy contact accepts that you will report the contact or decline gifts, and does not try to talk you out of it. What only looks like repair is a larger apology gift, a tearful appeal, or an explanation of why telling anyone is unnecessary.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: After you decline a gift, a favor or a private conversation, does the person keep treating you the same? Or does warmth drop, or does a hint about what they know appear? The change in manner is more informative than any one request.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Need and fear can narrow attention and make a way out look attractive. Money pressure can make an offer feel like relief, belief can make a request feel like loyalty, and pride can make recognition feel earned. Embarrassment tends to push people to keep a secret, which can make a hold on them grow because the thing hidden gains weight with time.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Many describe a slow slide in which each step felt small and reasonable at the time. Looking back, they feel shame and a sense they should have known better, which often keeps them from asking for help. Some describe fear about their job, legal standing or reputation once they see the whole picture.

response_options.soft_clarification: Say the plain question out loud: 'Why are you interested in this about me?' A friend can answer; someone with an agenda tends to avoid it.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline gifts, payments and favors that are out of proportion, and keep your answer short and the same each time.
response_options.disengagement: Let the contact lapse without a debate, and avoid being alone or on private channels with them while you decide.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone you trust early, even if it is embarrassing. Where legal exposure is possible, a lawyer can advise confidentially.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you hold access, report approaches that feel odd to your security or compliance contact. Reporting early is generally treated far better than reporting late.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I keep my work and my personal finances separate, so I will pass on the gift. I am happy to keep talking about anything else, and I would like to think about this for a few days."
codex_completed.safety_note: Watch for any hint that private information, images or a past mistake could be exposed unless you cooperate, for requests that keep growing, and for demands for secrecy. Do not deal with it alone: a lawyer, your workplace's security contact, or a trusted person can help you decide what to disclose and when.
misuse_warning: Using the four letters as a checklist to suspect a coworker, partner, or friend turns a teaching tool into a way of accusing people who simply have worries and beliefs.
Applying the label to every case of someone cooperating with a competitor or foreign party hides the many other reasons people do so.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Honey Trapping is one route to the compromise lever, using a staged relationship. Agent of Influence Operations is the end state where a public figure carries another party's message, while MICE names the motives that may have led there. PSYOP Message Framing and Strategic Deception work on audiences and adversaries at scale. MICE is about one person's needs and how they were used.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: PSYOP Message Framing
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Messages shaped on psychological principles to steer how a population sees legitimacy, inevitability, loyalty, or hopelessness, and so what it does.
codex_completed.short_definition: Messages shaped on psychological principles to steer how a population sees legitimacy, inevitability, loyalty, or hopelessness, and so what it does.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: PSYOP, short for psychological operations, is the military term for communication aimed at changing how groups think and act. Framing means the choice of angle that makes a message feel natural: who is legitimate, what is coming anyway, who is us and who is them, and whether resisting is pointless. The techniques overlap heavily with ordinary advertising and campaigns, so a particular frame tells you very little about who sent it or why.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Some messages are built to make you feel that something is already decided, that resistance is pointless, or that a group is on your side or against you. Recognizing the angle helps you decide for yourself.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Messages built around futility or inevitability leave people experiencing their own resignation as simple realism. When a frame feels like your own conclusion, you are less likely to question where it came from or whether other options exist.
what_it_is: A set of message angles used in military and political communication, such as legitimacy, inevitability, futility, group belonging, and authority.
Aimed at populations, not individuals, and measured by what groups do, not by whether they agree.
Overlaps with advertising, public health campaigns and political persuasion, so the frame alone is not evidence of an operation.
Often carried by repetition across many channels so it feels like background fact.
Not the same as lying: many framed messages are true in every detail and persuasive for their emphasis.
what_it_sounds_like: 'The outcome is already decided; there is no point in resisting.'
'Everyone around you has already moved on. You are the last to see it.'
'They are not like us, and they never will be.'
'Only the authorities can be trusted; anything else is a rumor.'
'Your leaders have abandoned you, and no one is coming.'
A flyer, broadcast, or message that arrives in the same wording from sources that claim to be unrelated.
what_it_is_not: The techniques described overlap heavily with ordinary advertising, campaigning and public communication, so spotting the shape of a frame tells you nothing about who wrote it or why.
A rousing or a fatalistic message is not by itself an operation.
An honest statement of bad news, such as a forecast that a project will fail.
A speech designed to rally a team or a community around a shared goal.
A public health campaign that uses fear or belonging to get people to protect themselves.
An opinion piece written with force by someone who sincerely holds the view.
this_may_be_it_when: The same angle appears across many channels with matching wording, and the sources do not seem independent.
The message asks for a feeling (hopelessness, shame, anger at one group) more than for an examination of facts.
It leaves no room for a middle option: you are either with them or already lost.
The source, its funding, and its purpose are hard to identify.
Documented investigations by credible researchers have traced the messages to an organized source.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The sender is identified, openly persuades, and gives you the evidence.
The message is one of many competing views you can easily see and compare.
Its tone is strong, but the claims check out against independent sources.
It appeals to values you hold without telling you that disagreement is hopeless.
It comes from a person who is plainly speaking for themselves.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People naturally describe events with emotion and emphasis.
Campaigners, teachers and advertisers use framing all the time and often do so openly.
Many people repeat the same slogan because they heard it and liked it, not because a coordinated plan exists.
common_false_positives: A strongly worded editorial that you disagree with.
A political ad that is emotional but clearly labeled and attributed.
A friend who is honestly pessimistic about the same event.
discernment_questions: Who is the sender, and what do they want me to do after reading this?
Is it asking me to feel something before I have seen the evidence?
Is it telling me no other option exists, and is that actually true?
Does it pit people against each other in a way that makes me stop listening to them?
Would I react differently if the same facts were presented in a calmer way?
less_concerning_if: The sender is named and their stake is clear.
The message sits alongside other views that you can compare.
The facts hold up when you check them elsewhere.
more_concerning_if: Matching wording arrives from sources that claim to be unconnected.
The message insists doubting it is disloyal or foolish.
It targets a group's fears or grievances and urges immediate action or withdrawal.
pattern_over_time_signs: A phrase or frame spreads and people begin repeating it as if they thought of it.
Your own mood about a topic shifts toward hopelessness or anger after steady exposure.
Options that were once discussed vanish from conversation.
The same sources keep supplying the same angle, whatever happens in the news.
codex_completed.repair_check: When a frame is challenged, a straightforward sender names themselves, supplies the evidence, and revises the claim if it was overstated. What only looks like response is a louder repeat of the message, a change of name, or a claim that questioning proves you are a target.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Try putting the message aside for a day and talking with someone with a different view. Does the message still seem like your own conclusion? And does the source tolerate your distance, or press harder? The answer shows how much you were choosing.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A conclusion is accepted more readily when it arrives with a feeling, is repeated often, and seems widely shared. Messages of inevitability make effort look pointless, and messages of belonging make doubt look like betrayal. When they turn up in many places, they start to read as background fact and not as a claim.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Listeners report feeling worn down, resigned, or unusually angry at one group without knowing why. Some notice later that they had stopped voting, organizing or talking to neighbors who disagreed. Others grow distrustful of all information once they see how they were pulled, which can be as disabling as the original frame.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the person sharing it: 'Where did this come from, and what is it asking us to do?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to pass along a message that tells you to feel hopeless or hostile until you can name its source.
response_options.disengagement: Limit exposure: mute accounts and channels that repeat the same angle, and notice whether your mood changes.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk it through with someone who holds a different view, or with a media-literacy teacher or librarian.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you work in communications, moderation, or public information, log the examples with dates and sources, and use your organization's process to report coordinated patterns.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "What is this message asking me to feel, and who benefits if I feel it? Can I name the sender? Do independent sources back the facts, and is it actually true that nothing can be done?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Exposure to such messages is not usually a personal danger. It changes when a campaign targets named people with harassment or pushes a group toward violence. In that case, save examples, report them to the platform, and contact local authorities or a legal adviser if threats are involved.
misuse_warning: Dismissing any persuasive or emotional message as 'psyops' is a way to avoid engaging with an argument you cannot answer.
Telling someone their views are the product of an operation, without evidence, is insulting and ends the conversation.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Strategic Deception is about hiding what is real and showing something false, while PSYOP Message Framing may use entirely true statements chosen for effect. Agent of Influence Operations concerns who carries a message and whether their independence is genuine; framing concerns the shape of the message whoever carries it. Honey Trapping and MICE Framework Exploitation work on a single person, not a population.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Strategic Leaking
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Releasing sensitive information through channels that look unauthorized, so that a planned disclosure reads as a secret that escaped.
codex_completed.short_definition: Releasing sensitive information through channels that look unauthorized, so that a planned disclosure reads as a secret that escaped.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Strategic leaking is a disclosure that is presented as an accident or a breach but serves the interests of whoever released it. The aim can be to shape opinion, send a signal, test a reaction, or pull attention from something else. A story built on anonymous sources is not suspect by that fact alone. The question for a reader is who gains if this version of events is believed, and whether anyone has checked it independently.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A story arrives as if someone slipped out a secret, but the release may have been planned and may serve the people who let it out.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Information that seems to have escaped carries extra credibility, because people assume nobody would choose to reveal it. A placed story can be read as an exposed one, and readers may never learn who benefited from the timing.
what_it_is: A disclosure framed as unauthorized that actually serves the interests of someone connected to the source.
Used to shape opinion, signal intentions, test how people react, or move attention away from another story.
Passed on through anonymous sources, unnamed officials, documents with no clear chain of custody, or sudden 'insider' accounts.
Hard to spot from outside because real leaks and planned ones can look the same on the page.
Often partial: true details arranged so that the overall picture leans one way.
what_it_sounds_like: A headline citing 'a person familiar with the matter' just before a major vote.
A document appears online with no explanation of where it came from, and is quoted everywhere within hours.
Several outlets report the same insider detail on the same morning, with matching wording.
A damaging story about a rival lands on the day a different embarrassing story is breaking.
An official publicly 'declines to comment' while the account keeps circulating, unchallenged.
A leaked memo that conveniently makes the sources' own side look reasonable and decisive.
what_it_is_not: Genuine whistleblowing, where someone discloses wrongdoing at personal risk. From outside it can look the same, so the label should never be used to wave it away.
An open press briefing, where an official gives reporters information on the record or with the source's role stated.
A reporter's own investigation, built from several independent sources and records.
An honest mistake in which a document was shared with the wrong people.
Any anonymous sourcing at all. Reporters promise anonymity for sound reasons, and it is not evidence of a planted story.
this_may_be_it_when: The timing fits one party's needs unusually well, such as just before a negotiation or a hearing.
The only people who gain from the story being believed are close to the source.
Details that would hurt the source's side are missing, while those that help it are rich.
No independent party has confirmed the material, yet it is treated as settled.
The people involved later acknowledge, or reporting establishes, that the release was authorized.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The material is confirmed by records, other sources or people with no shared interest.
The story harms the party who is assumed to have released it.
The only reason for suspicion is that the story is surprising or unwelcome.
The outlet explains how it checked the material and what it could not verify.
The disclosure was on the record and the source is named.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People talk to reporters for many reasons, including conscience, frustration, or a wish to be heard.
Several outlets can run the same detail at once because they all received the same public filing or announcement.
Timing can be coincidence: news clusters around scheduled events such as budgets, hearings and anniversaries.
common_false_positives: A real whistleblower's disclosure that happens to help one side in a political fight.
A routine, openly attributed statement from an official's office.
A rumor spreading on social media with no source at all, which is a different problem from a placed disclosure.
discernment_questions: Who gains if this account is believed, and does that person have any link to the source?
Has anyone with no stake in the matter confirmed the main claim?
What would a different version of the same events look like, and has it been told?
Why is this coming out now rather than a month ago?
Does the story contain anything that hurts its likely source, or only things that help?
less_concerning_if: Independent records or several unconnected sources back up the central claim.
The outlet is open about what it verified and what it did not.
The release exposes something that its source would clearly prefer to keep hidden.
more_concerning_if: The story arrives with strong claims, no chain of custody, and heavy pressure to react at once.
Corrections or contrary evidence get far less attention than the original release.
The same kind of well-timed disclosure keeps favoring one party over a long stretch.
pattern_over_time_signs: Anonymous stories repeatedly appear just before decisions that matter to one particular side.
Disclosures tend to flatter or protect the same group while damaging its rivals.
Earlier leaked claims quietly turn out to have been partial or wrong, and no one is held to account.
Coverage across outlets follows the same framing, down to the same phrases, within hours.
codex_completed.repair_check: Accountability here looks like a source or outlet later explaining what was released, why, and what was left out, then correcting the record when details prove wrong. Silence, or a fresh unattributed story that shifts attention, is not a correction.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Can you wait a day? A claim that holds up will still hold up after checking. If the surrounding noise pushes you to react before anyone has confirmed anything, that pressure is worth examining before you share.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A secret that seems to have slipped out feels more honest than a statement, because a deliberate lie would seem pointless to hide. That assumption can make a placed account more convincing than an official one. Urgency and an air of forbidden knowledge can also make a claim feel important before anyone has examined it.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe whiplash when a dramatic story is later revised, and a lingering sense of having been used to carry someone else's message. Some start to distrust all anonymous reporting, including the honest kind. Others feel the pull to share an exciting revelation and regret it afterward.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the person sharing the story where it first appeared and whether anyone else confirmed it, in a tone of curiosity rather than accusation.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decide for yourself that you will not pass along a leaked claim until you have seen the original and at least one independent confirmation.
response_options.disengagement: Step away from fast-moving threads about a supposed leak for a day. Real confirmations and corrections tend to arrive after the first wave of reaction.
response_options.support_seeking: Take a doubtful story to a fact-checking service, a librarian, or a reporter who covers the topic, and ask how they would verify it.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you work in media, public affairs or an organization that handles sensitive material, follow its sourcing and disclosure policies and record who decided to release what.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Before I pass this on: who is the original source, who gains if I believe it, and has anyone with nothing to gain confirmed it? If I can't answer those, I'll wait."

In that case do not share it further, report it to the platform, and tell the people named so they can protect themselves.

Accusing a named reporter or source of planting a story without evidence is itself a smear.

Agent of Influence works through a person with a credible public platform, whereas a leak needs no such person. PSYOP Message Framing is about how a message is built to land, and a leak is about how it is delivered.
