Members may also hold their own worth as conditional on obedience, which can make questioning risky and keep them close.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People who have been inside describe guilt over what they once said or did to others, grief for family who now treat them as gone, and a nagging fear that they are worthless outside the group. Some find it hard to trust their own sense of right and wrong afterward. Members still inside may describe a constant effort to stay on the right side of the line.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask a plain question about one specific person: 'What did he actually do, and is he still a person we owe kindness?' Keep it curious and brief.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to join the name-calling: 'I'm not going to talk about anyone that way.' You do not need to argue the doctrine to refuse to repeat contempt.
response_options.disengagement: Change the subject or step out of the room when someone is being written off. Keep your private views private until you have support around you.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk with a counselor experienced in high-control groups or a former-member support organization. Decisions about your place in the group are best made privately with them, never announced.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If this is in a workplace, school or care setting, keep dated notes of people being demeaned for their beliefs or membership and take them to HR, a licensed professional or counsel.

codex_completed.boundary_script: Before repeating this, I ask myself: "Would I say this about someone I loved? Is this person described by what they did, or by what the group says they are? Who outside the group could tell me about them?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Watch for talk that treats named people as deserving harm, threats toward leavers or critics, anyone kept from medical care, money, a home or their children, and pressure to take part in mistreating someone. Reach a cult-recovery or domestic violence advocate or a lawyer, or emergency services if someone is in immediate danger. Plan any exit privately with that support.
misuse_warning: Calling a community's boundaries, or its religious language about being 'lost', this pattern can unfairly condemn a faith many people live in peacefully. The test is withdrawn worth, not strict rules.
Pinning the label on any group whose politics you dislike turns a description into an insult.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Milieu Control manages what members can read, hear and discuss, while this pattern ranks who counts as a person at all. Demand for Purity sets an impossible standard for members; Dispensing of Existence is about how those outside, or those judged impure, are valued. Doctrine Over Person overrules a member's own experience; this one removes someone else's worth. Only here is a person's right to be counted as human the thing at stake.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Bounded Choice
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Shaping a member's world so every remaining option looks like a free personal pick, while the only options left are ones that serve the group.
codex_completed.short_definition: Shaping a member's world so every remaining option looks like a free personal pick, while the only options left are ones that serve the group.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Bounded Choice describes a setting where people feel they decide freely, yet the options have been quietly narrowed to ones that keep them in the group. Other paths may be technically allowed but cost a home, family or standing. Every environment narrows choices; jobs and mortgages do. The concern is when options that would serve the person instead of the group exist only on paper, and any outcome is called the person's own doing.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: The real alternatives were closed off or made so costly that only one answer was left, yet everyone keeps saying you chose it freely.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Choices feel entirely your own while the range they were drawn from has closed, so you carry full responsibility for outcomes you were never given room to avoid. It also makes asking for help harder, since nothing seems to have been forced.
what_it_is: A narrowing of real options, through cost, shame, timing or lost belonging, that leaves one answer looking natural.
Decisions framed as 'your own call' after the group has set the terms, so the member owns the result.
Alternatives that exist in theory, such as seeing a doctor, visiting family or taking a job elsewhere, but carry a penalty so steep nobody tries.
Language of freedom and commitment used to describe what are in effect required choices.
A shared belief among members that they chose this life, which makes complaints seem inconsistent.
what_it_sounds_like: Nobody forced you. You said yes of your own free will.
Of course you can go to the family wedding. You just have to decide where your loyalty lies.
We never tell anyone what to do. We just ask you to pray about the right answer.
You wanted this. Why are you acting like you had no choice?
Sure, take the outside job. Just know what it says about your commitment.
It's your decision, and we'll support whatever you choose, as long as it's the one already shown to you.
what_it_is_not: Every environment shapes what feels choosable. A job, a mortgage or a close family all narrow options, and feeling free within limits is ordinary.
A person freely committing to a demanding path, such as a monastery, a medical residency or a military term, with the costs known ahead of time.
A group whose terms were explained before joining and that does not punish leaving beyond ending the membership.
Honest advice from friends who say a choice will disappoint them without removing the choice.
Limited options caused by money, geography or the job market, which is hardship but not something a group designed to keep you.
Regret about a choice you made, which is common and does not show the choice was rigged.
this_may_be_it_when: Every option other than the preferred one carries a heavy loss, such as shunning, housing or work.
You are told to decide freely, then shown only one answer that will be treated as acceptable.
Information about alternatives, such as what outside life costs, comes only from the group.
Past decisions you now doubt are repeatedly described to you as things you wanted.
Members who picked another option are described as having failed rather than as having chosen differently.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You can name and take several different options without a loss of belonging.
Others have chosen differently and are still treated warmly.
You can get information about alternatives from outsiders and discuss it openly.
The costs of a choice are explained ahead of time and follow naturally from it, not added afterward.
No one reminds you of earlier choices when you question the group.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Every community, workplace and family limits what feels realistic, and people often feel free inside those limits.
The cost of a commitment, such as a long training, can be the honest price of something chosen.
Someone may describe their path as freely chosen because, to them, it truly was.
common_false_positives: A new parent who cannot take a risky career move because of childcare costs.
A menu or default setting that nudges choices while leaving every option available.
A tight-knit religious school that families picked knowing the rules and can switch away from.
discernment_questions: If I picked a different option, what would it actually cost me, and who would still talk to me?
Which alternatives do I know about only because someone in the group described them?
Could I have said no at the start, and would that have been treated as an honest answer?
When members choose differently, are they treated the same afterward?
Do I call my decisions free because I believe it, or because questioning that feels disloyal?
less_concerning_if: People can pick other paths and remain in touch with the group.
The costs of each option are stated truthfully beforehand.
Outside advice is welcomed and sometimes followed.
more_concerning_if: Housing, income, a spouse or children depend on choosing the group's preferred answer.
Questioning a decision is met with reminders that you made it.
Information, money or travel needed to act on another option is held by the group.
pattern_over_time_signs: The list of choices that feel acceptable shrinks year by year.
You start predicting the answer the group wants before you are asked.
Past decisions you later regret are retold as your own preference, even when they were not.
You realize you have not made a major decision without consulting the leaders for a long time.
codex_completed.repair_check: Correction opens options in practice: members can take another path and keep their housing, friends and standing, and past decisions are acknowledged as pressured. Words about freedom that leave every cost in place only repeat the pattern.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Can an alternative be named out loud without a penalty? If it is raised and discussed on its merits, the choice is open. If raising it brings reminders of loyalty or a cooling of warmth, the choice was bounded.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A decision believed to be freely made tends to earn extra loyalty and defense. When alternatives have been made costly or invisible, that loyalty can attach to an outcome that mainly serves the group. Owning the result can make it harder to say that anything was done to you.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Afterward, a confusing mix of guilt and anger is common: they remember saying yes, but also that no other answer felt available. Some find it hard to trust their own decisions or to say whether they ever wanted something. Others report relief when someone names the narrowing.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask what each option would cost: 'If I decided otherwise, what would happen to my place here?' The answer shows how open the choice really is.
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask for time and outside input before deciding: 'I'd like a week to think, and to talk with my sister first.' A real choice can wait.
response_options.disengagement: Postpone big decisions that are presented as now-or-never, and note who benefits from the speed.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk to someone outside the group, such as a former member, therapist or counselor who knows high-control environments, and lay out the options as you see them.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In a workplace or program that frames costly terms as voluntary, ask for the terms in writing and consult a lawyer or union representative before signing or committing.

codex_completed.boundary_script: Before I accept that I chose this freely, I ask myself: "Could I say no and keep my home, my friends and my standing? Who told me the other options are not real, and have I heard it from anyone outside?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Bounded choice alone is a pattern of pressure, not necessarily danger. It becomes safety-relevant when the narrowed options involve housing, money, immigration status, medical care or children, or when anyone is threatened for taking another path. Then consult a lawyer or legal aid, or a cult-recovery advocate, before acting, and plan any big change privately.
misuse_warning: Cost, family duty and a demanding career are ordinary constraints. Treating each of them as coercion erases the real decisions behind a person's life.
Telling someone they never really chose their life can take away their agency. The label is for understanding pressure, not for overriding what a person says they wanted.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Milieu Control restricts what you can read, hear and discuss; Bounded Choice may leave the information in principle but shrinks what you can safely do with it. Doctrine Over Person tells you your experience is wrong, while this tells you your decisions were free. Demand for Purity sets an impossible standard; Bounded Choice leaves a doorway that exists but costs too much to use.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Charismatic Authority Dependence
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Making one leader the only trusted source of truth, meaning and safety, so that the leader's approval becomes a member's deepest need.
codex_completed.short_definition: Making one leader the only trusted source of truth, meaning and safety, so that the leader's approval becomes a member's deepest need.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Charismatic Authority Dependence is a bond in which a member comes to rely on one leader for answers about what is true, what life means, and whether they are safe or good. Admiring a gifted teacher is common and often helpful. The pattern appears when no second source of judgment counts, when the leader's reading of events replaces the member's own, and when losing approval feels like losing everything at once.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: One person becomes the only one whose word counts, so their approval feels like air, and disagreeing with them feels like falling apart.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: When one person holds truth, meaning and safety, losing their approval means losing all three at once, which makes ordinary disagreement feel like self-destruction. It can also leave a member with nobody else to check reality with.
what_it_is: A relationship in which the leader's view of events outranks what the member saw, felt or remembers.
Approval and attention from the leader used as the main measure of whether a member is doing well.
A shrinking circle of other advisers: friends, family, clergy or professionals matter less over time.
Language that links the leader to special insight or divine purpose, so doubting them feels like doubting everything.
Shows up in religious groups, therapy-like programs, wellness communities, political movements and some workplaces.
what_it_sounds_like: Only he really sees what's going on. The rest of us are guessing.
If I lose her approval, I don't know who I am.
Don't ask anyone else. Ask him.
She said it, so it must be right, even if I can't see why.
I was so afraid when he stopped looking at me in meetings.
Everything good in my life came through her.
what_it_is_not: Admiring a teacher, mentor or leader and being genuinely changed by them is common and often good. The pattern differs where no second source of meaning remains.
Deep respect for a teacher, coach or spiritual guide who welcomes questions and encourages you to have other mentors.
Following a doctor or pilot on their specialty while keeping your own judgment about your life.
Shared admiration for a founder or artist in a community where members still disagree openly.
A grieving or struggling person leaning hard on a counselor for a season, with their own strength returning.
this_may_be_it_when: Disagreeing with the leader feels frightening, or like a moral failure, not just awkward.
Members with doubts keep them quiet because the leader's view is final.
Decisions about work, partners, money or children are run past the leader first.
The leader's mood sets the mood of the group, and approval is handed out or withheld unpredictably.
Outside relationships and sources are described as lesser or dangerous.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The leader publicly says they could be wrong and has changed their mind when shown evidence.
Members have other mentors, friends and sources they consult without penalty.
Disagreement with the leader is voiced in meetings and handled without punishment.
You can picture your life going on well if you lost the leader's approval.
The leader refuses special deference and sends people to outside professionals for outside problems.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Strong admiration is normal when someone has helped you through a hard stretch.
New members of any group often defer to experienced people while they learn.
A charismatic speaker can leave a strong impression without any lasting dependence.
common_false_positives: A student devoted to a professor in their field who still argues with them.
A devoted fan of a musician or public figure with no personal relationship.
A patient who trusts a surgeon's judgment about the surgery.
discernment_questions: If this person disapproved of me tomorrow, what else would I lose besides their opinion?
Whose judgment do I trust about my life besides theirs, and when did I last act on it?
Could I tell the leader they were wrong about something and be answered with curiosity?
Have my other relationships and advisers been shrinking while this one grows?
Do I trust the leader's account of events more than my own memory of them?
less_concerning_if: You keep close friends and advisers outside the leader's circle.
The leader's authority covers a defined area such as teaching, not your whole life.
You can disagree and still be welcomed.
more_concerning_if: The leader controls housing, income, immigration status or access to your children.
Members who question the leader are removed, shunned or described as unwell.
Your sense of safety depends on the leader's mood on a given day.
pattern_over_time_signs: Outside friendships and advisers drop away without any clear decision to end them.
You begin reading the leader's expression or mood to decide how you are doing.
Your preferences begin to sound like the leader's, down to their phrases.
Doubts that once seemed normal are now frightening to think, let alone say.
codex_completed.repair_check: Change shows in a leader who takes questions and shares authority: other sources of judgment are encouraged, criticism is answered without punishment, and members' outside ties are welcomed. A moving apology that leaves final say with one person is not that.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: When you disagree out loud, notice whether the response is curiosity or a drop in warmth. A leader who respects limits can hear no without cooling toward you; a chill that follows a no is itself information.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People often look to a confident figure for certainty when they are lonely, grieving or seeking meaning. Warm attention that rises and falls with compliance can build strong attachment, and approval from a single source tends to crowd out other sources of reassurance. Over time, checking everything against the leader's view can become automatic.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe an intense need for the leader's approval, dread at their displeasure, and difficulty making even small decisions alone. After leaving, many describe grief like a bereavement, along with shame about having believed. Some feel lost about what they value without the leader's voice.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask how a question would be received: 'Is it okay if I talk this over with my sister too?' Notice whether the reply is warm or tense.
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep one decision for your own judgment, such as a medical, money or family matter: 'I've decided to handle that one myself.'
response_options.disengagement: Spend more time with people outside the leader's orbit, and let that grow slowly. Avoid dramatic statements about your doubts or plans.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk to a therapist, former member or cult-recovery counselor who knows high-control groups, and bring one specific example.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In a workplace or training program built around a single boss or guru, keep outside mentors, write down instructions you are given, and bring concerns about pressure to HR or an ombuds.

codex_completed.boundary_script: Before I act on this, I ask myself: "Is it true because I can check it, or only because this person said it? What would I decide if I asked two people outside this group? What would I lose if their approval went away?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Watch for a leader who controls housing, money, documents or contact with children, for punishments aimed at doubters, and for pressure toward self-harm or giving up medical care. A lawyer, legal aid, a cult-recovery counselor or a trusted outsider can help. Call emergency services if anyone is in immediate danger. Plan any change privately with that support.
misuse_warning: Devotion to a teacher is not automatically unhealthy. Calling a friend's admiration for a mentor 'dependence' can shame a good relationship.
Using the label to mock a group's believers hides what matters: whether members can question and exit.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Sacred Science puts the doctrine beyond question, while this entry puts a person there. Doctrine Over Person overrides the member's experience in favor of the teaching; here the member's experience yields to the leader's reading. Mystical Manipulation stages events to prove special status, whereas dependence is the bond that shows itself in a member's fear of losing approval.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Forced Confession / Self-Criticism Rituals
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Required, repeated disclosure of faults, doubts or past wrongs to the group, which produces shame and hands the group material it can hold over people.
codex_completed.short_definition: Required, repeated disclosure of faults, doubts or past wrongs to the group, which produces shame and hands the group material it can hold over people.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Forced confession and self-criticism rituals are two forms of one practice: members must disclose faults, doubts or past wrongdoing before the group, either by confessing or by criticizing themselves in set sessions. One leans toward what you did or hid, the other toward what is wrong with you. Healthy settings use disclosure too, but there it is voluntary and bounded. Here it is required, open-ended, and may be recalled later. Lifton's list of thought-reform themes includes a 'cult of confession'.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You are required to tell the group your faults and secrets, again and again, and what you say can be brought back up later to keep you in line.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Material given up under group pressure does not go away. It stays available as leverage, and the habit of confessing on demand can leave a person with no private ground to stand on.
what_it_is: Scheduled sessions in which members must state wrongs, doubts or 'insufficiencies' in front of others.
Self-criticism turned inward: members list their own failings as proof of loyalty, aloud or in writing.
Confessions that are recorded, remembered or passed to leaders, so what was said stays attached to the person.
Disclosure that is never complete, since each session asks for more, including private thoughts and doubts.
Found in religious groups, political movements, some residential programs and high-pressure workplaces.
what_it_sounds_like: Tonight everyone shares one thing they've been hiding from the group.
You haven't told us everything. We can feel that there's more.
Write out every doubt you've had this year and read it aloud.
Remember what you admitted last spring? That's why we're concerned now.
A truly committed person has nothing to hide from the family.
Stand up and tell us how you failed the group this week.
what_it_is_not: Accountability practices exist in healthy settings, such as step work, clinical supervision and restorative circles. Saying something difficult before a group is not itself harmful.
Voluntary sharing in a peer support meeting, where what is said stays in the room and nobody is pressed for more.
A team retrospective that asks what went wrong with a project, not what is wrong with the people.
Confession in a faith tradition that is private, freely chosen and covered by confidentiality.
Apologizing to someone you harmed, which is aimed at repairing that one relationship and ends when it is done.
this_may_be_it_when: Attendance and participation are required, and declining is treated as a sign of guilt or disloyalty.
What one person confessed is referred to later by others or by leaders when that person disagrees.
The depth of a confession is judged, and 'not enough' sends the person back for more.
Public shame or reprimand follows disclosure.
Members are expected to report on each other's faults or doubts.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Sharing is optional, and people can pass without comment.
What is said stays in the room and is never used later.
Disclosures end in comfort or practical support, not in shame or punishment.
The practice is explained before anyone joins, and a person can step out with no penalty.
Leaders disclose their own faults in the same way as everyone else.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People in recovery programs often find that telling the truth in a group feels hard at first.
Some people confess to a friend because they trust them, and feel relief.
Teams or families sometimes hold structured 'what went wrong' talks that feel uncomfortable.
common_false_positives: A twelve-step meeting where you may simply listen and say nothing.
A sports team's film review that points out mistakes.
A public apology by someone who actually hurt others, offered by their own choice.
discernment_questions: Can I decline to share, or pass, without being questioned about why?
Who hears what I say, and has anything I admitted ever come back to me later?
Does a confession ever finish, or is there always more expected?
Do the leaders open up the same way, or only members?
After I disclosed, did I feel supported, or more afraid of the group?
less_concerning_if: Sharing is optional and kept confidential.
The facilitator discloses too, under the same rules.
Nothing said is brought back later.
more_concerning_if: What someone confessed is used to shame them, steer their choices or deter them from questioning.
Members are expected to confess about, or inform on, other members.
Confession is paired with punishment, such as loss of housing, work, status or contact with family.
pattern_over_time_signs: The sessions get more intimate and more frequent over months.
You begin rehearsing confessions in advance, hunting for faults to offer.
You edit what you say in ordinary conversation, sensing it could be recorded or repeated.
Old admissions are mentioned at moments when you are asking questions.
codex_completed.repair_check: A genuine fix ends the requirement itself: disclosure becomes optional, past confessions are not referred to again, and any records are destroyed or returned. An apology for how the sessions felt that leaves them on the schedule has fixed nothing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Pay attention to what follows a plain 'I'll pass.' If the session moves on and you are treated as before, the practice is optional. If you are pressed, watched, or reminded of something you said earlier, it was not.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Public disclosure tends to create shame and a sense of exposure, and shared secrets can make people feel bound to the group that holds them. When confessions are required again and again, a person can learn to see their own thoughts as suspect, and to hand over private material in exchange for belonging.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Sessions bring dread, a habit of searching oneself for faults, and fear that old admissions might be used later. After leaving, some report lingering shame, trouble keeping anything private, or distrust of any setting where people share openly. Some feel relief at finding it was a practice, not a personal failing.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask about the rules for sharing: 'Who hears this, and is it kept private?' You are asking for information, not accusing anyone.
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold some things back: 'I'll share what I'm comfortable with and pass on the rest.' You are allowed to keep your inner life to yourself.
response_options.disengagement: Give brief, general answers that reveal little of your inner life, and avoid writing doubts down where the group can read them. Plan any bigger change privately.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk with a counselor, former member or cult-recovery organization about what you have disclosed and what worries you. Keep your own notes somewhere private and safe.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a workplace or training program requires staff to disclose personal faults or confess to colleagues, ask for the policy in writing and consult HR, an ombuds, a union representative or an employment lawyer.

codex_completed.boundary_script: Before I disclose anything, I ask myself: "Who will hear what I say, what could it be used for later, and could I decline without anything changing? Would I share it if no one could repeat it?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Watch for confessions being recorded, threats to reveal them, pressure to admit wrongdoing that could cause legal trouble or to inform on others, and punishments such as loss of housing or family contact. Legal aid, a cult-recovery counselor or a trusted outsider can help. Call emergency services if there is immediate danger. Make any decision to step away privately, with support.
misuse_warning: Not every group that asks for disclosure is coercive. Calling a recovery meeting or a faith practice a 'confession ritual' can push people away from help they chose.
Using the label to demand that someone reveal what they confessed is itself a privacy violation.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Demand for Purity creates the standard members can never meet, and confession is one way failures against it are paraded and recorded. Milieu Control manages what members can see and say; confession extracts what they think and have done. Doctrine Over Person tells members their experience is wrong, while confession asks them to testify against themselves.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Institutional Betrayal
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: An institution that people depend on fails to prevent harm or to respond fairly when it happens, adding a second injury to the first.
codex_completed.short_definition: An institution that people depend on fails to prevent harm or to respond fairly when it happens, adding a second injury to the first.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Institutional betrayal is the term psychologist Jennifer Freyd introduced for the harm an institution does by failing the people who depend on it, such as a school, employer, hospital, congregation or agency. The first harm may come from anyone. The second comes from how the institution handles it: ignoring it, doubting the person, or protecting its own standing. One slow answer proves little. What makes it a pattern is how the whole process treats the person reporting, from first contact to the last letter.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You were hurt, you turned to the place that was supposed to help, and that place made things worse by ignoring you, doubting you, or protecting itself.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Being harmed and then failed by the body meant to prevent it produces a second injury that often outlasts the first. It can teach a person that reporting brings exposure without remedy, and it can make them doubt their own account of what happened.
what_it_is: A failure at two points: before the harm, when warning signs go unaddressed, and after it, when the response is poor or hostile.
Something the people depending on the institution experience, such as students, patients, employees, members or service users.
Visible in how a report is handled: who is believed, who is questioned, and whose risk is being managed.
Sometimes active, like discouraging a report, and sometimes passive, like letting it sit without any answer.
A second injury that can feel worse than the first because the institution was the place the person trusted most.
what_it_sounds_like: A letter thanks you for coming forward and says the matter is now closed, with no findings stated.
A staff member suggests that a formal report could hurt your own record or your future there.
You are asked to retell the whole event to several different people, and each of them seems to start over.
Weeks pass after a report with no one telling you who is handling it or what happens next.
The person you reported is moved quietly, or promoted, and nobody explains the decision to you.
You are told the institution takes this seriously, while the process described seems to protect the institution first.
Others who spoke up before you were reassigned, ignored or described as difficult.
what_it_is_not: An institution that responds slowly or clumsily, or within genuine legal limits, is not thereby betraying anyone. Formal processes are often bad at speed.
A fair investigation that does not reach the outcome you hoped for. A finding can go against you and still be reached honestly.
Confidentiality rules that stop the institution from telling you what happened to another person.
A single unhelpful employee in an otherwise responsive system, especially when someone above them corrects it.
An institution that was unaware of the harm and acted once it learned of it.
Disappointment that a body lacked power to do what you needed, which is a limit and not a betrayal.
this_may_be_it_when: The institution seems more concerned with its reputation or exposure than with what happened to you.
Your report is met with doubt aimed at you, your motives or your timing, instead of at the facts.
Earlier reports about the same problem were handled the same way and nothing changed.
You are discouraged from using the formal route, or find it hard to learn that one exists.
The harm is never acknowledged in any form, even a private one, by anyone with authority.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The institution explains its steps, gives you a contact person and keeps to the timeline it stated.
The outcome was not what you wanted, but the reasoning was shared and the process was applied evenly.
The delay has a clear cause, such as a required outside review, and you are kept informed.
Someone with authority acknowledged the harm, even if the remedy was limited.
The people you are angry at were not the ones with any power over the response.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Staff may be bound by privacy rules and unable to say what was done, which can feel like silence from the outside.
A small or under-resourced office may be slow because it is overloaded, not because it is protecting anyone.
A process can seem cold because it is built to be neutral toward both sides, including the person you reported.
common_false_positives: An investigation that finds insufficient evidence, which is a different thing from a finding that you were not believed.
A busy office that takes weeks to reply to everyone, not only to you.
A policy that is rigid and unfair but applied to every case the same way, with no sign of shielding anyone.
discernment_questions: Has anyone with authority acknowledged, in any form, that what happened to you was wrong?
Are you being told the steps and timeline, or left to guess what is going on?
Do you know of others who reported similar things, and how were they treated?
Does the response speak to the harm you described, or mostly to the institution's own risk?
Have you felt pressure, even gentle, to drop it or keep it quiet?
less_concerning_if: You were told what the process is, and the institution has followed it.
Your account was taken seriously even though the outcome was limited.
Someone outside the immediate chain, such as an ombuds office, can review how the matter was handled.
more_concerning_if: Other people with similar reports describe the same kind of response from the same place.
Your standing, grades, schedule or job quietly changed after you reported.
No one outside the institution has any way to review what it did.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find yourself dreading contact with the institution more than you dread thinking about the original harm.
You start to doubt whether the event was serious enough to report, a doubt you did not have at first.
You stop telling the institution things, and may stop relying on other institutions too.
Years later, the way you were treated still comes up as often as the original event does.
codex_completed.repair_check: Real accountability from an institution is concrete: someone with authority names what went wrong, explains what will change, and the change can be checked later. A warm statement of regret with no named failure and no follow-up is the part that tends to look like repair without being it.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask whether you can have the process, timeline and outcome in writing, and notice what comes back. A clear written answer, or an honest account of why it cannot be given, suggests respect. Vague reassurance that changes nothing on paper suggests the question was managed, not heard.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Trust placed in a school, employer or agency can make its failure land harder than the original harm, since there may be nowhere else to turn. A person in that spot may start blaming themselves, wonder if they overreacted, or quietly accept the institution's framing just to end the uncertainty.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe distrust of the institution and sometimes of all institutions, a reluctance to report anything again, shame about having spoken, and a sense of having been harmed twice. Some describe losing the place they belonged to, such as a school or workplace, as well as losing trust in it. Some say being believed later by an outsider mattered a great deal.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the office for the process in writing: who is handling your report, what the steps are, and when you can expect an update.
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep your own dated record of every contact, and ask that any decision about your case be put in writing before you agree to anything.
response_options.disengagement: If dealing with the institution directly is wearing you down, ask a trusted person or advocate to handle the contact, or pause and take it up when you have more support.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk with an advocate for the type of harm involved, a counselor, or a lawyer who can explain what routes outside the institution exist. Being believed by someone outside can matter.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask whether an ombuds office, a union representative or an outside regulator can review how your report was handled, and consider a consult with an employment or education attorney.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I would like the steps of this process, who is handling my report, and the timeline in writing. I would also like to bring a support person to any meeting about it."
codex_completed.safety_note: Watch for quiet changes after you report: loss of hours, grades, housing, a role or a reference, or being treated as the problem. Those can be retaliation and are worth documenting with dates. Keep copies somewhere the institution does not control, and talk with an advocate or an attorney before taking any step. If you feel unsafe or have thoughts of harming yourself, contact emergency services or a crisis line right away.
misuse_warning: Labeling any slow or disappointing response as betrayal can overlook genuine legal limits and honest processes. The term fits a pattern of protecting the institution at the person's expense, not every unwelcome outcome.
Using the word to condemn a whole organization, including people who worked hard on your behalf, can leave out the individuals who did try to help.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Silence Engineering is a culture that teaches people not to speak up before anything is reported, while betrayal concerns how the institution responds to a specific report of harm. HR Shielding is one mechanism, the complaint machinery working for the institution, whereas betrayal can also be plain neglect with no one shielded. Performance Framework Manipulation works through scores and reviews, not through a response to a report.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Organizational Silence Engineering
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Building a workplace culture in which people learn that speaking up brings punishment and staying quiet brings safety.
codex_completed.short_definition: Building a workplace culture in which people learn that speaking up brings punishment and staying quiet brings safety.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Organizational silence engineering is a pattern in which a workplace teaches its people, through what happens to others, that raising problems costs more than it gains. Nobody has to forbid anything. People watch who gets sidelined after a complaint, whose concern disappears into a form, and who is praised for going along. Soon they stop sharing bad news. One quiet meeting means little. A habit of silence across a whole team, about things everyone can see, is the signal.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: People at a workplace see what happens to those who raise problems, so they stop raising them, and everyone knows about issues that no one will say out loud.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Problems that people can plainly see go unreported, and the cost lands first on whoever the warning would have protected, then on the person who stayed quiet and knew. Over time, people can lose their sense that anything they say matters.
what_it_is: A culture, not a rule: the lesson is taught by watching what happens to coworkers who spoke up.
Often built from small signals, such as a raised eyebrow in a meeting, a joke about troublemakers or a pointed absence from a later invitation.
Marked by a gap between what is said in private hallway talk and what is said in official meetings.
Reinforced when feedback channels exist on paper but produce nothing visible, so people conclude there is no point.
Costly for the organization too, because safety problems, errors and ethical concerns stay hidden until they get large.
what_it_sounds_like: Everyone nods in the meeting, then the real talk happens in the parking lot.
"Remember what happened to the last person who brought that up."
A manager says the door is always open, and nobody has walked through it in a year.
An anonymous survey is run every year, and no one ever sees what it found or what changed.
A coworker whispers, "I'd keep that to myself if I were you."
Bad news is passed up in softened wording until it no longer sounds like bad news.
A concern is called negativity, and the person who raised it is described as not a team player.
what_it_is_not: A calm, well-run team in which people simply have little to complain about.
A workplace where people prefer to raise things one-to-one, not in meetings, and are heard when they do.
A confidentiality rule that limits what can be shared outside the company for a legitimate reason, such as client privacy.
A culture of politeness or reserve that comes from the industry or a region's norms, with no cost attached to speaking.
A single manager who dislikes criticism, in a company that has other routes and where concerns do get acted on.
A quiet period after a reorganization, while people wait to see how things settle.
this_may_be_it_when: People who raised concerns were reassigned, passed over or pushed out soon after.
Staff share worries privately but nobody will say them in front of leadership.
Nobody can name a concern that was raised and then led to a real change.
New hires are warned informally about what not to say.
Leaders react to bad news by asking who told you, not what is wrong.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Someone can point to a recent case where a raised concern was fixed and the person was thanked.
People disagree openly with leadership and keep their standing.
The silence is limited to one topic that is truly confidential, such as an unannounced deal.
The team is new, and people have not yet learned each other's styles.
Feedback channels report back what they found and what was done about it.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A team may be quiet because people are heads-down on a deadline and will talk later.
Some people are introverts or newer, and hold back until they know the group.
Workplaces in some fields keep a formal tone in meetings and do the real discussion in writing.
common_false_positives: A meeting where nobody speaks because the agenda was dull and the issue was already settled.
A person who was let go for documented performance reasons after raising a concern separately, where the two are unrelated.
A company that keeps a firm line on sharing client information, which can feel like secrecy to staff.
discernment_questions: Can you name a concern someone raised here that changed something, and what happened to the person who raised it?
Do people say different things in private than they will say in meetings?
If you saw a serious problem tomorrow, would you know who to tell and feel safe doing it?
Are feedback surveys followed by visible action, or do they vanish?
How did the last few people who spoke up fare a year later?
less_concerning_if: Concerns raised by staff are acknowledged and followed up in the open.
People in different roles report feeling able to disagree with leadership.
There is a route outside the chain of command, and it is used without anyone being penalized.
more_concerning_if: The silence covers safety, legal or ethical issues, not only matters of taste or preference.
People who spoke up report retaliation such as lost hours, shifts or reviews.
Employees are told, directly or by hint, not to talk to outside parties about concerns.
pattern_over_time_signs: You notice yourself editing what you say in meetings to keep it safe.
People you work with stop volunteering ideas, and meetings get shorter and flatter.
Errors that many people noticed early only come out once they are large.
Turnover rises among those who used to speak most, and the ones who remain say less.
codex_completed.repair_check: Leaders who want to undo a culture of silence show it in what they do with the next bad news: they thank the messenger, fix the problem visibly, and protect the person who raised it. A new open-door announcement with no change in how past speakers were treated leaves the lesson standing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: When you raise a concern, ask yourself what happens next. Does anyone report back, and does your standing stay the same weeks later? Respect shows in follow-through and in how you are treated afterward, not in what is said during the meeting itself.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Watching one coworker get sidelined can teach a whole team what is safe. When speaking up seems to change nothing, effort starts to feel pointless and self-protection takes over. Silence then feels like a personal choice, though it was shaped by what the workplace showed.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe holding back things they know are wrong, feeling complicit, tension between their conscience and their paycheck, and a flattening of enthusiasm for the work. Some describe guilt about not saying anything earlier, and some describe relief at finding that coworkers had seen the same thing. Others describe leaving a job over it.

response_options.soft_clarification: Check your read with one trusted coworker: ask whether they have noticed the same hesitation to raise problems, and whether they know of any concern that led to a fix.
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep a private, dated record of what you raised, to whom and what came back. Keep it somewhere your employer does not control.
response_options.disengagement: You do not have to carry every concern alone. Decide what you can safely raise, and think privately about what you would need before deciding how much to risk.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk to a trusted mentor outside the company, or a lawyer or advocate who works with employees, about what protections may apply where you work.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If your workplace has an ombuds office, a union, or an outside reporting line, learn how each works and what it protects before using one. An employment attorney can explain your options.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Can you walk me through how concerns get handled here? Who reviews them, and how would I hear what came of mine?"
codex_completed.safety_note: The danger signal is retaliation after speaking: lost hours, a sudden bad review, a changed role, or hints that your job is at risk. Treat these as worth documenting with dates, outside the employer's systems. Before any formal step, talk with an employment attorney, a union representative, or a legal aid clinic, since protections differ by place. If a concern involves immediate danger to people, contact emergency services.
misuse_warning: Calling a quiet or reserved workplace silenced can ignore people's real reasons for holding back. The label needs evidence of what happened to those who spoke.
Using it to describe any manager who disagreed with you may turn an ordinary conflict into an accusation about the whole organization.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Whether anyone reports at all is the question here, while Institutional Betrayal concerns the response to a specific report of harm. HR Shielding is complaint machinery that serves the institution once a complaint exists, whereas in a silenced workplace complaints stop arriving. Algorithmic Management controls people through automated decisions, not through the lesson that colleagues learn from watching each other.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Performance Framework Manipulation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Setting up evaluations, targets and reviews so that they reward agreement and loyalty while penalizing skill, dissent and ethical objection.
codex_completed.short_definition: Setting up evaluations, targets and reviews so that they reward agreement and loyalty while penalizing skill, dissent and ethical objection.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Performance framework manipulation is a pattern in which the measures used to judge workers, such as ratings, targets and review steps, end up tracking deference instead of the work. People who go along score well, and those who raise problems or refuse questionable instructions accumulate a record that looks objective. Every scoring system favors some things over others, so one odd rubric proves little. It becomes a pattern when the measures shift whenever the wrong people begin scoring well.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: The way you are scored at work seems to reward agreeing and going along, and to mark down people who are good at the job but raise problems or say no.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Effort shifts from doing the work well to being agreeable about it, and anyone who raises problems accumulates a documented record of underperformance that looks objective to whoever reads it later. That record can follow a person into pay, promotion and job security.
what_it_is: A mismatch between what the job actually requires and what the scoring system measures.
Targets, rating scales or review criteria that are vague enough to be applied differently to different people.
A paper trail that builds up around certain employees, often after they raised a concern or declined something.
Criteria or targets that change without explanation once someone starts meeting them.
Visible in who gets high ratings, and whether it correlates with agreement more than with results.
what_it_sounds_like: You hit every number last quarter, but your rating says needs improvement in collaboration.
A rating criterion called attitude or fit is new this year and has no definition.
Targets are raised the week after you reach them, with no change in the resources you get.
A written warning cites vague concerns that were never mentioned to you before.
Feedback arrives only in the formal review and never in the months before it.
A colleague with weaker results is rated higher and is known to agree with management on everything.
A performance improvement plan lists goals that conflict with each other or cannot be met within the time given.
what_it_is_not: A rubric that undervalues your particular strengths. That is a design flaw, not a control mechanism.
A fair performance plan with clear, achievable goals, regular check-ins and support to meet them.
A stricter review cycle because the company is under financial pressure and is applying new standards to everyone.
Honest critical feedback from a manager who wants you to improve and says so openly.
Ratings forced into a curve that disadvantage some people each year without regard to who they are or what they said.
A bad year for you, in which the results were weak and the review reflected that accurately.
this_may_be_it_when: Ratings move sharply downward soon after you raised a concern or declined an instruction.
Criteria are subjective, undefined or newly introduced right before your review.
Colleagues with similar results get different ratings, and the difference follows who agrees with leadership.
Targets or rules change once you begin meeting them.
You are asked to sign off on documentation that describes problems you were never told about.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The criteria are written down, shared in advance and applied the same way to everyone on the team.
Feedback about the shortfall came early and specifically, with help to address it.
Your numbers were genuinely below the targets everyone else faced.
Others who voice disagreement also receive strong ratings.
The change in criteria came with an explanation and applied across the company.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A manager may be a poor writer of reviews, and vague wording may reflect lack of skill and not a motive.
A new rating system may be clumsy and unfair to many people at first, and get fixed later.
Targets rise in many companies each year as budgets change, and may hit people who did well.
common_false_positives: A tough year that ends with a poor review that was supported by clear data and earlier warnings.
A company-wide switch to new goals that makes everyone's scores drop.
A single unfair rating from a manager who is otherwise consistent, and who corrects it when it is raised.
discernment_questions: Are the criteria written, and were they the same ones in place when the work was done?
Did the problems on your review come up in earlier feedback, or appear for the first time on paper?
Do people who speak up on your team get rated differently from those who do not?
Did the targets change after you met them, and was there a reason given?
Would a neutral colleague reading your results and your review find them consistent?
less_concerning_if: The criteria are clear, shared in advance and checked by someone beyond your direct manager.
Reviews match the feedback you have been getting along the way.
There is a working way to dispute a rating, and it has changed outcomes for others.
more_concerning_if: A negative record is building at the same time as you raised a safety, legal or ethical issue.
A performance plan appears with no earlier feedback and a very short deadline.
You are being asked to resign or sign something while a review is pending.
pattern_over_time_signs: You notice you have started shaping your work around what scores well, not what the job needs.
Colleagues who used to push back have stopped, and the ones who did not have left.
Your good results are no longer mentioned in reviews, while small lapses are recorded.
The documents about you grow in number while the conversations about you shrink.
codex_completed.repair_check: A fair fix is visible in the paperwork: criteria are written and shared, your rating is looked at again by someone outside your reporting line, and past records are corrected where they were wrong. A kind meeting and a promise to do better, with the file left unchanged, only looks like repair.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask for the criteria and examples behind a rating, in writing, and see what comes back. A specific answer you can respond to suggests a genuine measure. Shifting reasons, or a reply that moves to your attitude for asking, suggests the score is not really about the work.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A score that looks neutral can carry more weight than a boss's opinion, so workers adapt to it even when it measures the wrong thing. When the measures reward agreeing, doubting yourself and staying quiet can start to feel sensible. A record that builds slowly can make a person question their own competence before anyone else does.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe anxiety before reviews, losing confidence in work they once did well, a feeling of being set up to fail, and fear for their pay or position. Some describe shifting their effort toward looking agreeable. Some say seeing the pattern laid out on paper helped them stop blaming themselves, and some describe leaving a role they were good at.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask your manager to put the criteria for your rating in writing, with an example of what a stronger result would have looked like.
response_options.firm_boundary: Write down your own account of the facts and add it to your file where your employer allows responses, rather than only signing the review.
response_options.disengagement: You do not need to turn every review into a debate. Keep your copies and your own results records, and take time to decide what, if anything, to dispute.
response_options.support_seeking: Show your records to a trusted mentor outside your reporting line, or to a union representative, to check whether the ratings fit your results.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask whether there is a formal way to dispute a rating or plan, and consider talking with an employment attorney or legal aid before signing anything that you do not understand.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Before I sign, please send me the written criteria for this rating and the earlier feedback it relies on. My own response should go in the file as well."
codex_completed.safety_note: The risk here is to income and standing: a rating or plan that sets up a dismissal, or pressure to resign or sign a release. Keep copies of your results, feedback and reviews outside work systems, with dates. Before signing any plan, agreement or resignation, ask for time and talk with an employment attorney, a union representative, or a legal aid service, since rights vary by place.
misuse_warning: Reading every poor review as manipulation can keep a person from hearing accurate feedback. The label needs evidence that the measures track deference more than work.
Using it to describe any rubric you dislike turns a design flaw into an accusation.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Here the harm is built into scoring and records, with no report involved, unlike Institutional Betrayal, which is a failed response to harm. Silence Engineering teaches people to stay quiet through example, while this works through formal ratings. Algorithmic Management also scores people, but through automated systems with no person to ask, whereas this is usually a human-run process with judgment applied unevenly.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Algorithmic Management
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Using automated systems to assign tasks, track output and make decisions about workers' hours, pay or jobs, with little human review.
codex_completed.short_definition: Using automated systems to assign tasks, track output and make decisions about workers' hours, pay or jobs, with little human review.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Algorithmic management is the use of software to direct and judge work: it hands out tasks, sets schedules, measures speed and flags people for discipline. Software on its own is common and often useful. The concern is when the criteria are hidden, the data cannot be seen or corrected, and no person can be reached to review a decision. Then workers face a boss they cannot question. It shows up in delivery, warehouse, driving, call center and retail work, among others.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Software decides your tasks, your hours or whether you keep the job, and there is no person you can ask why or push back on.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Consequential decisions arrive with no one to ask and nowhere to appeal, so workers adapt to a system they cannot see and blame themselves for outcomes they have no way to examine. Pay, hours and job security can turn on numbers nobody will explain.
what_it_is: Software that assigns work, sets pace, tracks location or output and scores workers continuously.
Decisions about scheduling, pay or discipline that come from the system, sometimes with a manager simply passing them along.
Rules that are hidden or change without notice, so workers cannot tell what they are being judged on.
Data collected about a worker that the worker often cannot see, check or correct.
Found in gig platforms, warehouses, call centers, retail scheduling and delivery, among other places.
what_it_sounds_like: Your account is flagged and the message says only that you violated community standards.
A manager says the system did it and that they cannot change it.
Your hours shift week to week with little notice, and no one can say how they are decided.
A tracker shows a live score for speed, and a drop in the score leads to an automated warning.
Pay for the same task varies from day to day without explanation.
An automatic message says your access has been ended, with no named person to contact.
Appeals go to a form or chatbot that returns the same reply every time.
what_it_is_not: A rota generated by software is not a control apparatus. Automation in scheduling and routing is widespread and often simply efficient.
A tracking tool that workers can see, that is explained in advance and that a person reviews when something looks wrong.
A safety system, such as one that logs hazards or limits driving hours, that protects the worker as well as the company.
Productivity numbers used as a starting point for a conversation with a manager, not as a verdict.
An automated payroll or timekeeping process that is accurate and corrected quickly when it errs.
A one-time glitch that was fixed once reported.
this_may_be_it_when: Decisions about your hours, pay or standing are made by a system and nobody can explain them.
You cannot see the data collected about you or the criteria applied to it.
There is no working path to a human reviewer, or the path ends in an automated reply.
Rules or rates change without notice, and your results shift as a consequence.
Discipline or termination follows an automated flag without a conversation first.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You can reach a person who looks at the data and can change the outcome.
The rules, metrics and rates are shared with you in advance and in plain language.
The system makes suggestions and a person decides, and uses judgment about context.
Errors you reported were checked and corrected, and the record updated.
The tracking covers only things that affect safety or pay accuracy.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A company may use automation mostly to save time on schedules, with managers still free to adjust them.
An odd pay change may come from a bug or a policy update, and be corrected when noticed.
A flag may be a routine check that many workers receive and that a person clears quickly.
common_false_positives: A scheduling app that is clumsy but lets you swap shifts and reach a supervisor.
A speed target applied equally and explained, with a person who adjusts it for conditions.
A warning generated by a system and then reviewed by a human who found it was wrong and removed it.
discernment_questions: When a decision about you looks wrong, is there a person who can look at it and change it?
Can you see what data is collected about you and what rules are applied to it?
Have the rates, rules or targets changed without notice, and did your results change with them?
Does a manager decide, or do they only pass along what the system produced?
Do other workers describe the same unexplained outcomes?
less_concerning_if: There is a clear, working route to a human who reviews decisions and can reverse them.
Workers can see their own data and the rules that apply to it.
Representatives of workers have a say in how the system is set up and changed.
more_concerning_if: Termination or deactivation can happen automatically with no explanation or review.
Data about you is collected beyond working hours or beyond what the job requires.
Workers who dispute the system report having their hours or work quietly reduced.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find yourself guessing at what the system rewards and changing your habits to suit it.
Your hours or pay drift in ways nobody can account for.
Coworkers trade rumors about what the system punishes, since nobody official will say.
You feel watched even during breaks, and start to hurry to keep the numbers up.
codex_completed.repair_check: Meaningful change is practical: a named person who can review decisions, a written explanation of how the system judges workers, and corrected records. An apology that blames the system, with no route for review, leaves the same unanswerable boss in place.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask who can review a specific decision and what data it used. A named contact and a real answer suggest the system is accountable. If every route loops back to the same automated message, the question has not reached anyone.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When a decision comes from a system that cannot be questioned, workers may blame themselves, since the alternative is feeling helpless. Constant measurement can also push a person to work faster and skip breaks without any direct order. Not knowing the rules makes it hard to tell whether a bad outcome was something you did or simply how the system works.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe constant pressure to keep up, anxiety about unseen scores, exhaustion from rushing, a sense of being treated as a number, and frustration at having no one to talk to. Some describe losing income suddenly through a deactivation they could not contest. Some say learning that others were hit by the same system helped them stop blaming themselves.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask a supervisor or the platform's support team in writing what data and rules were used for a specific decision, and who can review it.
response_options.firm_boundary: Save screenshots, messages and records of hours, pay and warnings, with dates, outside the company's own systems.
response_options.disengagement: If the constant tracking is wearing you down, look at where you can safely ease the pace and what your options are for other work, without making sudden changes.
response_options.support_seeking: Compare notes with coworkers or a worker group. Seeing that others had the same unexplained outcomes can show whether it is a system issue and not something you did.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: A union, a worker center or an employment attorney can explain what rights to information and review may apply where you work, and how to raise a dispute.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Which data and rules led to this decision, and who can review it? Could you send me that, along with a way to submit corrections, in writing?"
codex_completed.safety_note: The danger is to income and work: deactivation, cut hours or pay, sometimes with no warning or person to appeal to. Keep your own records of hours, pay and messages, outside the company's systems. Pace pressure can also lead to injury or exhaustion, so protect breaks and safety. A union, worker center or employment attorney can advise on your rights. If you are hurt or unsafe, get medical or emergency help first.
misuse_warning: Calling any software tool at work algorithmic management can overlook systems that help workers and that a person reviews. The concern is hidden criteria and no route to a human.
Blaming an algorithm can also let managers off the hook when they chose the rules; the label should not hide who set them up.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Performance Framework Manipulation is usually human judgment dressed up as measurement, while here a system makes or relays the decision and nobody can explain it. Institutional Betrayal is about a failed response to harm. Silence Engineering teaches people to stay quiet by example, whereas this controls pace, pay and hours through software that sees everything and answers no questions.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored. Pasted personal text cannot establish an institutional- or societal-scale pattern — that requires independent, corroborated, documented evidence at a completely different scale.

codex_completed.name: Revisionist History
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Rewriting the agreed record of past events to fit a preferred present story, even though others clearly remember it differently.
codex_completed.short_definition: Rewriting the agreed record of past events to fit a preferred present story, even though others clearly remember it differently.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Revisionist history, in a personal setting, is retelling a shared past so that it now says something it did not say then. A promise becomes a maybe, an argument becomes a joke, a decision becomes yours alone. Memory blurs for everyone, so a different retelling can be honest. The pattern is a version that changes direction exactly when the original becomes inconvenient, that has no room for the documents or witnesses, and that is repeated until the old account is hard to hold.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: The story of what happened in the past gets rewritten to suit the present, and you are left holding the version that others, and often the paperwork, remember.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Agreements stop being safe to rely on, because the version that counts is whichever suits the present, and the person who remembers accurately spends the conversation arguing about the past instead of the point.
what_it_is: A retelling of a past promise, decision or event that quietly reverses what was understood at the time.
A version that always shifts in the direction that favors the teller, as the facts become inconvenient.
Often aimed at things with outside evidence, such as a signed agreement, a group chat or other people who were there.
Seen in couples, families, workplaces and groups, where the history of who decided what shapes who gets to decide next.
Different from the slow drift of honest memory, which is patchy, runs in no particular direction, and accepts correction.
what_it_sounds_like: "We never actually agreed to that."
"That's not how it went. I was against it from the start."
"I was only joking when I said I'd pay."
"You were the one who wanted to move, not me."
"We've always done it this way."
"That meeting was about something else entirely."
"You're remembering what you wanted to hear."
what_it_is_not: Two people remembering an ambiguous conversation differently is ordinary, and memory blurs for everyone over time.
A person who learns new facts and updates an earlier view openly, saying 'I used to think X, and now I see it differently'.
Different groups telling the history of a shared event from where they stood, each aware that there are other views.
Real historians revising an account in light of new evidence, in public and open to challenge.
A retelling that is warmer or kinder in hindsight, such as smoothing a family story, with no stakes attached.
this_may_be_it_when: A past agreement is described in a way that clearly contradicts what was written or witnessed at the time.
The retelling changes when the original becomes inconvenient, and holds firm after evidence appears.
The new version always turns out to favor the teller, in several unrelated stories.
People who were there say they remember it as you do, and they are called biased or confused.
You are told 'we've always done it this way' about something that began recently.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The record is thin, and neither person can prove their version.
They change their account when shown a message and thank you for the correction.
The retelling changed over years, and no decision or money depends on it.
They say 'I may be remembering this wrong' before you do.
Both versions have been shifting, including yours.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Memory reconstructs the past each time we recall it, so stories shift without any wish to change them.
People often remember their own role as more admirable than it was, without being aware of it.
Time makes small commitments blur into 'we talked about it'.
Two people can walk away from the same conversation with different understandings of what was settled.
common_false_positives: A sibling who tells the childhood vacation story with themselves as the hero, and laughs when others tease.
A colleague who thought 'let's explore it' meant a maybe, while you heard a yes.
A friend who now says they never liked a band they loved years ago.
discernment_questions: Is there something written, dated or witnessed that shows what was said?
Does the retold version change in a way that helps the teller each time?
When shown that record, does the story adapt or does it stay put?
Do I feel that my own memory is solid, or am I starting to second-guess it?
Do other people who were there recall what I do?
less_concerning_if: The retelling shifts a little, but they accept the record when it is produced.
No decision, money or blame depends on which version is true.
They tell the story differently to different people in a way that is plainly just storytelling.
more_concerning_if: The rewritten past is used to decide who owes what, who is at fault or who gets to decide.
People with evidence, such as the group chat or the contract, are told they have misread it.
The retelling is repeated to others, so that the false account becomes the shared one.
pattern_over_time_signs: You have started to save messages and emails because you expect the past to be rewritten.
You find agreements harder to rely on, so you ask for everything in writing.
Conversations about the present are taken over by arguments about what was said before.
You notice that the story of your shared history keeps changing in one direction.
codex_completed.repair_check: What matters is whether the record becomes shared again. A real change is an account that matches the documents, an admission that the earlier retelling was wrong, and agreements that then hold. A smooth 'we both remember it differently' that leaves the rewritten version standing is not that.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Do they agree on a record both of you can point to, such as a shared note or an email? Watch whether the new account then respects it or whether the record itself is suddenly disputed as 'out of context'.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A story told confidently and often can start to feel like memory, both for the teller and the listener. When the retold version is the only one anyone brings up, the original can fade, and a person may begin to wonder if they are the one who has it wrong. Having no shared record to point to tends to make that doubt stronger.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe being unsure whether to trust an agreement, spending conversations defending the past and not discussing the point. Some say they began to take notes or save messages and felt guilty doing so. Others describe a strange loneliness in being the only one who remembered it the way it was.

response_options.soft_clarification: Point to the record in a neutral way: 'That isn't how I have it. Can we look at what we wrote at the time?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold to what was agreed: 'We agreed on this, and it's in writing. I'm not willing to treat it as something else now.'
