response_options.disengagement: If the version keeps changing, stop negotiating from memory and move any further agreements into a written form both of you sign or send.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask someone who was there what they remember, and share the documents with a person you trust to confirm what they say.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Send meeting summaries and decisions by email the same day, and file them where others can see, so that the agreed record exists beyond anyone's recollection.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I have the agreement in writing, and it says what I've told you. If you remember it differently, I'm happy to look at the document together. I won't treat the new version as what we decided."
codex_completed.safety_note: A rewritten past is mostly a trust and fairness problem. It becomes a risk when the rewritten item involves money you rely on, housing, child arrangements, immigration paperwork or legal commitments, or when keeping records brings anger. Keep copies of important documents somewhere private and consult legal aid, a mediator or an advocate before any big decision rests on the disputed account.
misuse_warning: Calling every different recollection 'revisionism' treats ordinary memory drift as bad faith. The label needs evidence of a direction, a record and a refusal to adjust.
Using it to dismiss a person who is genuinely reappraising a painful past, such as a survivor re-reading events, would be a misuse.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Revisionist History rewrites the shared record, usually in the direction of the teller's gain. Selective Memory claims a blank and offers no new story. Countering contradicts a single account on the spot, without needing a new narrative. Gaslighting works on your trust in your own mind, where revisionism works on the record of what was agreed. Moving Goalposts accepts the deal and changes the standard.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Word Salad
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Answering with long, circular, tangled language that never lands on a point, leaving the listener unable to pin anything down.
codex_completed.short_definition: Answering with long, circular, tangled language that never lands on a point, leaving the listener unable to pin anything down.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Word salad is speech that goes on at length, sounds as if it is about your question, and never actually answers it. Phrases loop back, ideas change mid-sentence and clarifying questions bring more of the same. Plenty of people talk this way when they are anxious, tired or thinking aloud, and some conditions affect how thoughts come out, so this does not show what anyone meant. The concern is when the fog reliably appears where a clear answer would be costly, and the listener leaves exhausted.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You ask a simple question and get a long, winding reply that never answers it. Asking again makes it more confusing, and you walk away not knowing what was said.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Hours can pass with nothing established, with no claim to answer and no agreement reached, and the exhaustion left behind is easy to mistake for having been unreasonable.
what_it_is: A long answer to a short, direct question, with no answer in it.
Circular phrasing, where each sentence points back to the previous one and none arrives anywhere.
A reply to a request for clarification that adds new tangled material.
A conversation that runs for a long time, after which neither person can say what was agreed.
Different from a person struggling to explain a hard, half-formed thought, who becomes clearer when given time and simple questions.
what_it_sounds_like: A two-minute reply to 'did you pay the bill?' that mentions the bank, a cousin and how money works, but never says yes or no.
"Well, it depends on what you mean by 'pay', and what you mean by 'bill', and when."
"I'm not saying I did, and I'm not saying I didn't, it's more about the whole picture."
Each time you rephrase, a new set of terms is introduced that has to be defined first.
"You see, it's like a circle: what I said is what I meant, which is why it is as it is."
A reply that ends with 'so, you understand now?' when nothing has been said.
Sentences that start in one direction, turn halfway and finish somewhere else.
what_it_is_not: Plenty of people struggle to say a complicated or half-formed thing clearly, and thinking aloud is naturally circular while the thinking is unfinished.
A communication difference, such as an associative or tangential style, that is part of how someone's mind works and not a tactic.
Speaking in a second language or in a technical field, where precise words are hard to find.
Fatigue, anxiety, a panic response or medication that scrambles speech temporarily.
A person who truly does not know the answer and is talking around the gap, and says so when asked directly.
this_may_be_it_when: The fog arrives on questions where a clear answer would commit them to something.
The same person is clear and direct on topics that do not involve accountability.
A request to simplify produces more complexity, not less.
You come out of the conversation unsure what you asked, as well as what they said.
Direct, closed questions such as 'yes or no?' are met with another loop.
this_may_not_be_it_when: A simpler, slower question gets a clear answer.
They speak this way about everything, including topics that are neutral or happy.
They ask for time to think, and come back with a plain answer.
There is a known health, language or neurological reason for their speech.
They say 'I'm not making sense, let me try again', and do.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Anxious people may over-explain to avoid disappointing anyone.
Someone who has not decided what they think may talk around it while they find out.
Exhaustion can make anyone ramble and lose the thread of their own sentence.
Some conditions affect how thoughts are organized, and the speaker would give a clear answer if they could.
common_false_positives: A colleague describing a technical system in jargon you do not share.
A nervous friend telling a long story to avoid a hard answer, who gives the answer once pressed gently.
A relative with dementia or a mental illness whose speech has become disorganized, which is a health issue and not a tactic.
discernment_questions: Does a simple, closed question get a simple answer at any point?
Is the confusion specific to topics where they would have to commit or admit something?
Do I leave conversations with them feeling foggy in a way that I do not with others?
Could health, language, stress or exhaustion explain what I am hearing?
If I wrote the question down, would I get a written answer?
less_concerning_if: They get clearer when the question is made smaller or you give them time.
The long-winded style shows up with everyone, on every topic.
They notice and name the muddle themselves and try again.
more_concerning_if: The fog appears only around decisions, money, promises or blame, and clears on easy topics.
You are told you are the confused one after hours of conversation.
Decisions are reached while you are exhausted, and those decisions are then described as agreed.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find yourself avoiding raising questions because the talk will take hours and settle nothing.
You leave long conversations unable to summarize what was agreed.
You start writing the question down beforehand, or asking for answers by text.
You feel slower or less intelligent after conversations with this person than with others.
codex_completed.repair_check: Watch what a direct request produces. Something real is a short answer given on a topic where it used to be a loop, or a plain 'I don't know yet, give me a day'. A promise to 'try to be clearer' followed by the same maze the next time has not made a difference.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: When you ask for a one-line answer, what comes back? A single sentence, even an uncomfortable one, is respect for the request. Another long reply that sidesteps the request shows that the maze, not the answer, is still on offer.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Trying to follow a tangled reply uses a lot of attention, and the effort of searching for the point can leave a person tired and doubting their own comprehension. After enough such exchanges, some people may give up asking, or agree just to end the conversation, and then find they have committed to something unclear.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe leaving talks drained, with a headache or a heavy fog, and no clear idea what was said. Some say they began to wonder if they were slow or unable to follow. Others describe agreeing just to escape and feeling frustrated with themselves later.

response_options.soft_clarification: Narrow the question: 'Let me ask just one thing. Yes or no: did you send it?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say that you cannot continue without an answer: 'I can't follow this. I need one sentence on that one point before we go on.'
response_options.disengagement: Pause the talk when you notice you are tired and the point has not appeared, and return only to written questions.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend what was said and ask whether they can find the answer in it. If neither of you can, you have learned something.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Put the question in an email with numbered points and ask for a written reply, so that a clear record exists of what was and was not answered.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I want to understand, but I've lost the thread. Could you answer in one sentence: yes or no? If you need time to think, that's fine, and we can pick it up tomorrow."
codex_completed.safety_note: Confusing speech is usually a communication or health matter, not a danger. If sudden disorganized speech shows up in someone who is normally clear, it can be a medical emergency, so seek help. If long confusing talks are used to wear you down until you agree to money, legal or housing decisions, stop signing or agreeing and get advice from legal aid or an advocate first.
misuse_warning: Calling someone's speech 'word salad' can be an insult to people whose thinking or language works differently. Use it only for a pattern, never for a person's way of speaking.
Applying it to anyone whose argument you find hard can be a way of dismissing the content.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Word Salad overloads you with language and gives no answer. Deflection gives a clear but different answer, changing the subject or posing a counter-question. Thought-Stopping Clichés use a short phrase to close the topic, while this uses a long one to dissolve it. Gaslighting contradicts what you remember, where word salad leaves you unsure what was said at all.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Contradiction Stacking
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Denying that something happened and, in the same conversation, defending it as justified, so no single answer settles anything.
codex_completed.short_definition: Denying that something happened and, in the same conversation, defending it as justified, so no single answer settles anything.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Contradiction stacking puts two incompatible positions on the table at once: it did not happen, and if it did, it was fair. Each one blocks the other, so whichever you answer seems to give up the second. It can start as a muddled defense in a heated moment. It becomes a pattern when the same pair of claims returns after each new complaint and the conversation never reaches which one is true.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Whatever you say back seems to prove the other half right: first the thing never happened, then it was deserved anyway.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Answering one claim feels like accepting the other, so you never get a position to stand on, and what actually happened is never settled. Many people leave these talks more tired than angry, unsure what they were even trying to prove.
what_it_is: Two answers to one complaint that cannot both be true, offered together or minutes apart.
A denial that sits next to a justification, as in 'I never raised my voice, and you would have yelled too.'
A setup where disputing the denial feels like admitting the justification, and the reverse.
A form of conversation that ends without any version of events being agreed, instead of one being argued and lost.
what_it_sounds_like: "I never told you that. And honestly, after the way you acted, I had every right to."
"That didn't happen, but if it did, you made me do it."
"I wasn't even there. Besides, anyone would have left early."
"I don't remember that at all, and it wasn't a big deal anyway."
"Prove it. Not that it would matter, because you started it."
"You're making that up, and I'm not going to apologize for something that was fair."
what_it_is_not: Someone who truly cannot recall an event, trying out explanations aloud while they sort out what happened.
Two statements that sound opposed but concern different days, topics or people.
A person who first denies, then admits it once they remember, and says so plainly.
Defensiveness in the first minutes of a hard talk, which often loosens as the person calms down.
A fair disagreement about whether an action was reasonable, after both sides agree it took place.
this_may_be_it_when: The denial and the justification both concern the exact same moment, and both are kept alive after you point that out.
Each new piece of evidence brings a different reason, but never an acknowledgment of the first answer.
You notice you are arguing against two opposing claims in a single reply.
The same two-part reply shows up around several unrelated complaints over time.
You leave the talk unable to say what the other person actually concluded happened.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They say 'I may be wrong about that' and pick one position to stand behind.
The justification only appears after they have accepted that the event occurred.
The two statements concern different incidents once you lay them side by side.
They notice the mismatch themselves and say it sounds contradictory.
The mixed answers came in one tense moment and have not reappeared.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Embarrassment can push someone to deny a mistake and explain it in one breath before they have had time to think.
A person who recalls part of an event may deny the bit they cannot remember while defending the bit they can.
Tired or rushed people give answers that conflict without any plan behind them.
common_false_positives: A friend who says 'I didn't text you that, oh wait, I did, but I meant something else' and then corrects the record.
A manager who says a deadline was never set, then explains a loose target mentioned in passing.
Two relatives retelling a family argument, each defending their own part and forgetting their own slips.
discernment_questions: Do the denial and the justification truly refer to the same event, or have two events blurred together in my mind?
When I name the mismatch calmly, does the other person engage with it, or does it become a new fight?
Can I say, in one sentence, what they believe happened?
Does this two-part answer show up in many conversations, or only this one?
Is every reply I could give already blocked by one half of their answer?
less_concerning_if: One of the two positions is dropped once the mismatch is pointed out.
The mixed answers came during a heated moment and a calmer later talk produced a single account.
They can tell you which statement they stand behind and why.
more_concerning_if: The denial returns each time the justification is challenged, and the justification returns each time the denial is challenged.
Noticing the contradiction is treated as another offense, such as nitpicking or twisting words.
You have begun to avoid raising problems because you expect to be caught between the two answers.
pattern_over_time_signs: You plan your complaint in advance, trying to leave no gap for either half of the reply.
Past disputes feel unfinished, because no one ever said which version was right.
You catch yourself agreeing with the justification just to end the talk.
A friend notices that you apologize for events you are fairly sure were not your doing.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair here sounds like one account of what happened, said without a justification stapled on, followed by different behavior the next time. A sorry that arrives wrapped in 'but you' is the same pair of claims again in softer clothes.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: One answer or two? State your concern once and count what comes back. A single answer, even an unwelcome one, gives the exchange footing. If the reply splits into denial plus defense again, the boundary is not being heard.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Two answers that block each other can leave a listener working on a puzzle with no solution. The effort of holding both in mind tends to use up the energy needed to press the original complaint. Over repeated rounds, a person may drop the complaint to stop the mental strain, and may begin to wonder whether the confusion is their own fault.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Cornered by their own words, some replay the talk for hours looking for the reply that would have worked. Many end up exhausted without having said what they meant, and some stop raising problems with that person at all. Others describe relief on seeing that the puzzle had no answer built into it.

response_options.soft_clarification: Point at the mismatch gently and ask for one answer: 'Those two things don't fit together for me. Which one is closest to how you see it?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say you will take one answer at a time: 'Let's settle whether it happened first. Whether it was fair is a separate question, and I'll talk about it after.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop when the second claim arrives and say you will pick the topic up later, then put the original concern in a short written note.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend the two replies exactly as you heard them and ask whether they read as contradictory to someone outside the talk.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, send a brief written summary naming the one fact in question, and ask the other person to confirm or correct that single point before discussing reasons.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I heard two things just now: that it did not happen, and that it was fair. I can talk about either one, but not both at once. Which would you like to start with?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Mixed denial and defense is a confusing conversation, not a danger sign in itself. It would call for more care if the justification starts to include blame that leads to punishment, if you are made to feel afraid of the reaction when you disagree, or if money, access to children or housing hang on the outcome. In those cases, talk with a counselor or advocate.
misuse_warning: Spotting two clashing statements in a single argument does not prove a tactic. People under stress contradict themselves all the time, so look for the same pair returning across many incidents.
Pointing out someone's contradiction in a triumphant way can become its own way of winning rather than understanding.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Gaslighting works on your confidence in your own memory, whereas contradiction stacking leaves your memory alone and buries the issue under two clashing replies. Deflection moves to a different subject, while here the subject stays put and two answers pile onto it. Minimization shrinks the harm, but this tactic first denies it happened and then defends it.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Circular Arguments
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Defending a claim by pointing back to the claim itself, so no outside fact is ever allowed to test it.
codex_completed.short_definition: Defending a claim by pointing back to the claim itself, so no outside fact is ever allowed to test it.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A circular argument offers the conclusion as its own reason: it is true because it is true, or because the speaker feels sure. Everyone slips into this in a quarrel. It matters when it is the main way a disagreement gets handled, and when your questions are answered by a looped restatement. Because the loop contains no checkable fact, there is nothing to agree or disagree with, and the talk can run for an hour without moving.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Every reason you are given turns out to be the original claim in new words, so the conversation goes around and never lands on anything you can check.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: When every challenge returns you to the starting point, you cannot win, lose or even learn what the other person actually bases their view on. Long loops can wear a person down until agreeing feels easier than continuing to ask for a reason.
what_it_is: A claim supported by itself, as in 'I'm right because I'm not wrong.'
Reasons that, when examined, only repeat the point in different wording.
A closed loop that gives your questions no checkable fact to land on.
Often paired with a personal reason to dismiss your input, such as 'you are too close to this to judge.'
what_it_sounds_like: "I know I'm right because I've thought about this more than you have."
"You can't judge this fairly because you're too sensitive, and the proof is that you're upset."
"We're not being unreasonable. Reasonable people would agree with us."
"It's the rule because that's how we do things here."
"If you were really listening you would see I'm right."
"I'm telling you the truth, so there's no reason to ask for proof."
what_it_is_not: Someone summarizing their view in a different way because they think you missed it the first time.
A rule that is explained by its purpose after you ask, even if the purpose is one you dislike.
A principle held as a basic value, such as 'I don't lie to my children,' that is not meant to be argued from further evidence.
A tired person repeating themselves because they are worn out and the talk has gone long.
A real disagreement about premises, where each side honestly cannot see what would persuade the other.
this_may_be_it_when: You ask 'why do you think that?' and the answer is the claim again, slightly rearranged.
The reason offered is that the speaker is certain, experienced, or more thoughtful than you.
Your disagreement is treated as proof of your lack of understanding.
The talk keeps returning to the same sentence, with no new fact appearing for many minutes.
A request for a source, example or witness is brushed off as insulting.
this_may_not_be_it_when: A short, independent reason appears when you ask, even if you do not find it convincing.
They say 'we may just see this differently' and leave the point there.
The restating is a clarification, and they invite you to say which part is unclear.
They point to a document, policy or person that you can go and check.
The loop ends once someone takes a break or sleeps on it.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People under strain often repeat their strongest sentence rather than searching for a new one.
Some beliefs rest on values and intuitions that are hard to put into outside evidence on the spot.
Someone may not have thought about why they hold a view until you ask, and can only restate it at first.
common_false_positives: A parent who says 'because I said so' once, in a rushed moment, and explains the reasoning later.
A friend who loves a film and says 'it's just great,' where taste has no further proof to offer.
A debate class exercise where each side is assigned a position to restate and defend.
discernment_questions: If I ask what evidence would change their mind, do I get an answer?
Is the reason given different from the claim, or the claim in new words?
Has any new fact entered this conversation in the last ten minutes?
Does my disagreement itself get used as the proof that I am wrong?
Do they accept this kind of reasoning from me, or only from themselves?
less_concerning_if: An outside fact eventually enters the discussion, even if it arrives late.
The other person is willing to say what would count as evidence against their claim.
The loop is limited to one heated topic and does not shape the rest of your talks.
more_concerning_if: Asking for a reason is treated as disloyalty or disrespect.
The loop covers decisions that matter, such as money, parenting or where you live.
You have noticed that you now avoid asking why, because you know what comes back.
pattern_over_time_signs: Disagreements end with you giving in, though no one has offered a reason you could weigh.
You hold fewer opinions out loud, because defending them has become so tiring.
You can recall arguments that lasted hours and cannot name a single point that was actually made.
You start to quote their circular phrases back to yourself, such as 'I'm too sensitive to judge.'
codex_completed.repair_check: Mending this looks like a reason you can check turning up in the next disagreement, or an honest 'I can't explain why I think so, but I do.' A promise to listen better, followed by the same loop, leaves the loop running.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Try asking once for a single concrete reason, then notice what changes. A person who respects the request will name something, even a weak thing. If the request is treated as proof that you are not listening, the boundary is not landing.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A loop with no fact in it offers no weak point to test, so a listener may keep searching for one and read the failure as their own slowness. The same sentence returning over and over can start to feel like support just because it is familiar, and giving in may become the quickest way out of the discomfort.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Long talks end with a dizzy feeling of having missed something, followed by replaying the argument in search of the point nobody grasped. Some doubt their own reasoning, some stop asking questions, and some feel oddly guilty for wanting a reason at all.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the step between the claim and the reason: 'I'm not following how you got there. What is the evidence underneath it?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Name the loop and decline to continue it: 'We have said the same sentence three times. I'd like one reason that's different from the claim.'
response_options.disengagement: Pause the discussion when a new fact has not appeared for a while, and offer to pick it up after each of you has looked up what you can.
response_options.support_seeking: Write the argument out in a few lines and ask a friend whether the reasoning goes anywhere. Seeing it on paper often makes the loop obvious.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask for the policy, data or decision-maker behind a claim, and note in writing that 'it is how we do things' was the explanation you were given.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I've listened closely, and the reason I keep hearing is the claim itself. I'm happy to continue if you can give me one reason that stands apart from it. If not, let's leave it for today."
codex_completed.safety_note: A loop of this kind is tiring but rarely dangerous on its own. It becomes more serious when the unquestionable claim is used to control your movements, spending or contact with other people, or when asking for a reason is met with anger or threats. Then, speak to someone outside the relationship, such as an advocate or counselor.
misuse_warning: Calling an argument circular can be a way of dodging a point you cannot answer. Check first whether you have really been given a reason.
Accusing someone of circular logic in the middle of a quarrel may simply start a new loop about who is being logical.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Deflection leaves the topic and wanders somewhere else, while a circular argument stays on the topic and goes round it. Moving Goalposts changes what would count as proof after you meet it, but here nothing could ever count, since no proof is allowed in. Countering flatly contradicts your account, whereas this tactic answers your question with the claim itself dressed as a reason.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Loaded Language
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Choosing words that carry a verdict, label or insult so that a judgment is made before the facts are discussed.
codex_completed.short_definition: Choosing words that carry a verdict, label or insult so that a judgment is made before the facts are discussed.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Loaded language uses words that already contain a judgment, such as calling a forgotten errand 'betrayal' or a question 'an attack'. The label does the arguing, so the facts never have to. Everyone reaches for strong words when hurt. The concern is when the biggest available word is applied to ordinary behavior again and again, and when pushing back on the word is treated as further proof it fit.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A heavy label is stuck onto something ordinary, and the label does the arguing, so you end up defending against the word instead of discussing what happened.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Once a word like 'selfish' or 'abusive' is attached, the discussion shifts from what happened to whether you are that kind of person. Defending against the label can take over from addressing the actual issue, and a label repeated often enough can start to shape how you see yourself.
what_it_is: Words picked for their emotional charge, such as 'betrayal,' 'manipulation' or 'crazy,' rather than for describing what took place.
A way of describing one action in two different vocabularies, with the choice depending on who did it.
Labels that name a whole identity ('you are a liar') instead of a single behavior ('that was not true').
Seen in households, workplaces, news headlines and political speech, with different words but the same mechanism.
what_it_sounds_like: "Don't be so dramatic. This isn't a disagreement, it's an attack on me."
"When I stay late it's dedication. When you do, you're avoiding your family."
"I'm just being honest. You're being hysterical."
"You abandoned me," said about a friend who went to bed at ten.
"Normal people would never be upset about this."
"If you were not so controlling, we wouldn't be having this talk."
"Calling it a mistake is a lie. It was sabotage."
what_it_is_not: A person in real pain using strong language for how something felt, then settling on plainer words once the first rush passes.
A fair label for something that really fits, such as calling a repeated, deliberate lie a lie.
Cultural or family styles of speech where dramatic words are normal and not meant literally.
Everyday exaggeration, like 'you always do this,' which is imprecise but not an attempt to pin an identity on you.
Technical or legal terms used precisely, such as 'trespass' or 'overdraft,' which carry meaning without implying a verdict about you.
this_may_be_it_when: A severe label arrives before anyone has described what happened.
The same action gets a gentle word for one person and a harsh word for another.
When you object to the word, the objection is used to show the word was accurate, as in 'only a guilty person would argue.'
The labels name who you are, and not what you did.
You catch yourself using their harsh vocabulary about your own behavior.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They are willing to swap the word for a plain description when you ask what they mean.
The strong word is applied to an act that fits it and backed by specific examples.
The same vocabulary is used for their own conduct as readily as for yours.
Their language is dramatic about everything, including small things that do not involve you.
They take back the label later and say it was heat of the moment.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Hurt and surprise can push anyone into big words that they would not choose on a calmer day.
Some people grew up in homes or communities where intense wording is simply how feelings are shared.
A person may only have a few words for an emotion and reaches for the strongest one available.
common_false_positives: A friend who says 'I was devastated' about a canceled trip, meaning disappointed, and is happy to say so when asked.
A manager who calls a missed deadline 'unacceptable' in a performance review that gives the specifics.
A news headline that uses punchy language, which is a sales choice rather than a personal judgment of you.
discernment_questions: If I replaced the loaded word with a plain description, would the complaint still stand?
Is the label about something I did, or about who I am?
Does the same behavior get the same word when it comes from them or from others?
When I object to the word, does the conversation return to the facts?
Have I begun using their words about myself?
less_concerning_if: The person can restate the complaint in neutral words without losing the point.
Heavy words appear only in rare, intense moments and are followed by an easier talk afterwards.
They use the same strong language about their own behavior as about yours.
more_concerning_if: A particular label sticks to you and is repeated in front of other people.
Disputing the label is described as aggression, denial or an attack.
The harsh vocabulary is applied to ordinary choices like where you sit, who you call or how you dress.
pattern_over_time_signs: You hear a few particular labels about yourself so often that you begin to hear them in your head.
You choose your words with great care to avoid setting off a label.
Other people begin repeating the same word about you without having seen what happened.
You apologize for the label, not the action.
codex_completed.repair_check: A genuine repair names the specific action that bothered them and drops the identity word, even when angry. Someone saying 'I shouldn't have called it that' and then reaching for the same word next week has only paused, not changed.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: You might ask yourself whether asking to keep to plain description is welcomed or mocked. When it is accepted, the conversation tends to name actions. When the request itself gets labeled, as in 'now you're policing my language,' the label is still doing the arguing.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A word that carries a verdict can skip past the facts and land on identity. The listener is pulled into defending against the label, so the original issue goes undiscussed. Hearing the same word often, from someone whose opinion counts, may also lead a person to try it on and half accept it after first rejecting it.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Having to prove you are not the word uses up the energy that should go to the real question. Some begin to censor ordinary behavior, some start applying the label to themselves, and some say they only saw the effect when a friend repeated it back to them.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the plain version: 'That word feels very big to me. Can you tell me what I did, in a sentence, without the label?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep the talk on actions: 'I'll talk about what I did. I won't agree to a word that describes who I am.'
response_options.disengagement: Step out of a conversation once it becomes a back-and-forth about the label, and invite them to return when the action itself is the topic.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask someone who knows you well whether the word fits, and tell them the specific event so they judge it, not just the label.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask for specific examples when a label like 'difficult' or 'unprofessional' is used, and record the dates and facts in your own words.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I understand you are upset, and I want to hear what happened. I'm going to keep to what I did, and not accept a word that describes me as a person. What was the thing that hurt?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Heavy labels are usually a communication problem, not a danger signal. Take more care if the labels are used to isolate you from friends ('they're toxic, they're against us'), to threaten your job or custody of children, or to justify punishment. In those cases, document what is said and speak with an advocate or counselor outside the relationship.
misuse_warning: Accusing someone of 'loaded language' can dismiss a person who is truly hurt and has no gentler words available yet.
Not every strong word is a tactic. A fitting label, backed by examples, is accurate speech and not manipulation.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Gaslighting disputes what happened, whereas loaded language accepts that it happened and wraps it in a verdict. Minimization shrinks the weight of the event, while a loaded word usually inflates the other person's part. Deflection moves the subject. Loaded language stays on the subject but settles the judgment through the vocabulary alone.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Semantic Traps
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Turning a conversation toward the exact wording someone used, so the original concern is lost in a fight about definitions.
codex_completed.short_definition: Turning a conversation toward the exact wording someone used, so the original concern is lost in a fight about definitions.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A semantic trap takes one imprecise word or phrase from your complaint and makes it the whole discussion. You said 'always' and it was twice. You said 'yelled' and the reply is that it was only a raised voice. Wording does matter sometimes, and careful people do correct each other. It becomes a trap when the correction replaces the concern, and you spend the talk defending vocabulary.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: One small slip in how you phrased something becomes the whole argument, so you end up defending your words and the thing you came to say never gets answered.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Your concern can be real and still lose, simply because one word was imperfect. When talks keep turning to your phrasing, you may start choosing words so carefully that you stop raising issues at all, and the actual problem stays where it was.
what_it_is: Seizing on a single word, such as 'always,' 'never' or 'yelled,' and treating its precision as the main matter.
A move from 'what you did' to 'what you called it,' so the behavior drops out of view.
'That's not what I said' used about the exact phrasing and not the meaning.
A form of argument that works best on people who are emotional or short of time, since they are the least able to word things perfectly.
what_it_sounds_like: "I did not 'scream.' I spoke loudly. Those are different things."
"You said 'never.' I did it last March. So that's wrong, and the rest of it is too."
"That's not what I said. I said 'maybe,' and you heard 'yes.'"
"Define 'ignored.' I replied the next morning."
"If you can't even describe it accurately, how can I take it seriously?"
"Don't put words in my mouth."
what_it_is_not: A fair correction of a fact that changes the picture, such as the right date of an event.
Someone who truly has a different understanding of a word, and says so while still addressing the concern.
A contract, a diagnosis or a legal question, where exact wording is the whole point.
A person who feels misquoted and asks to restate their own words, then returns to the topic.
Gentle humor about a phrase that ends with them hearing you out.
this_may_be_it_when: A word you used once is quoted back to you several times while the rest of your sentence is ignored.
Your concern disappears from the talk after the wording is challenged.
Admitting the imprecision is treated as admitting the whole complaint was wrong.
The dispute over a word returns across many different complaints.
You end the talk having defended your vocabulary and not heard a single reply to your point.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Once the word is clarified, they return to the concern and respond to it.
They offer their own fix, such as 'I'd call it loud, but I see that it upset you.'
The exact wording matters here, as in a signed agreement or a medical instruction.
They are equally exacting about their own words, and invite you to correct them.
The wording question comes up once and is not repeated in later talks.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Detail-minded people may honestly care about precise language and correct it out of habit, in every setting.
Defensiveness can lead a person to cling to a small inaccuracy because it is the one part they can answer.
People from different regions or families may mean different things by the same word.
common_false_positives: A coworker who corrects 'we agreed on Tuesday' to Wednesday, because the date really matters for the schedule.
A partner who says 'I wasn't angry, I was frustrated,' and then goes on to discuss what frustrated them.
A friend who teases you over a word and then listens to the actual story.
discernment_questions: After the wording is settled, does the other person return to my actual concern?
Would my point still stand if I swapped in their word?
Do they hold themselves to the same precision?
How many times has the topic shifted from my concern to my phrasing in the past month?
Am I now rehearsing my wording before I speak, to make it unchallengeable?
less_concerning_if: Correcting the wording is quick and the talk then goes back to the concern.
They are open to your corrections of their wording too.
The picky moments cluster around rare topics, not every disagreement.
more_concerning_if: No wording is ever precise enough, so the concern is never reached.
You are told that you are dishonest or unreliable because of one imperfect word.
Your own statements are repeated back to you in altered form and then disputed.
pattern_over_time_signs: You prepare script-like sentences before bringing up a problem.
You qualify everything with 'I might be wrong, but,' so there is less to pick apart.
You have stopped raising smaller worries because the wording fight feels too costly.
You notice that complaints from months ago were never actually answered.
codex_completed.repair_check: Real repair here means they respond to the substance you meant, even when the wording was messy, and they can say 'I got stuck on your word and missed your point.' If they agree about the word and drop the topic anyway, that is not repair.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Offer a swap and watch the result: use their word in place of yours and ask whether the concern still stands. If they do so and answer the point, the boundary works. If the offer is called yet more twisting, it has not been heard.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Because feelings are rarely worded perfectly, a challenge to wording can nearly always find something to hold onto. Defending a phrase takes the person's attention away from the complaint, and each lost round may teach them that raising an issue costs more than it gives. Over time, a careful speaker may start to doubt their own ability to describe events.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A sense of having lost on a technicality, while still believing the original concern, is common. Some become guarded speakers who rehearse and over-qualify. Some stop speaking up, and some say they began to doubt whether they could describe their own life accurately.

response_options.soft_clarification: Accept the word and go back to the point: 'Fair, call it loud if you like. What I'm trying to say is that I felt scared.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline the side-trip kindly: 'I'm happy to use your word. I'd like us to talk about what happened, not which word is best.'
response_options.disengagement: When the wording debate takes over, pause it and say you will write your concern down in plain terms and send it later.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend the complaint and the reply, then ask whether the reply answered the complaint or only its phrasing.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, put your concern in an email with dated facts, so there is less loose wording to seize on, and ask for a reply to the facts.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "You may be right about my word, and I'm fine using yours. It doesn't change what I came to say. Can you tell me what you make of the substance of it?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Quibbling over words is draining, but it is not a danger signal by itself. The picture changes when the wording fights are used to deny things that have real consequences, like threats, injuries or money taken, or when you are punished for how you describe them. Keep your own record of events and talk to an advocate or legal aid if that happens.
misuse_warning: Labeling any request for precision as a 'semantic trap' can dismiss fair corrections, which matter in agreements and facts.
If you use the label to avoid hearing a correction that was right, the label becomes your own way of skipping the point.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Countering flatly contradicts what you said happened, whereas a semantic trap leaves the event alone and attacks the way you described it. Deflection changes the subject to something unrelated, while here the topic is still your complaint but its words get all the attention. Minimization says the harm was small, but this tactic never gets as far as discussing size.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Frame Control
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Deciding what a conversation is about, through loaded labels or topic swaps, so that your actual concern has no place to land.
codex_completed.short_definition: Deciding what a conversation is about, through loaded labels or topic swaps, so that your actual concern has no place to land.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Frame control sets the terms of an exchange: what it is about, what is at stake and who plays which part. It covers more than one move. False Framing is another name for it, when a loaded label or extreme comparison settles the verdict before the facts arrive. Frame Assassination is a third name for it, when your point about an action is answered by turning the talk to your mood or character. One topic change in a tense talk is ordinary. The pattern is a frame that no version of your concern can fit inside.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: The conversation keeps getting redefined as being about something else, often about you, so what you actually wanted to say never gets answered.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: An accurate account can come out sounding irrelevant, because the terms were set to leave it out before you spoke. You arrive with a concern about something that happened and leave defending your mood or motives, with your original point never refused and never answered.
what_it_is: Redefining the topic, the stakes or the roles so that your concern no longer matches the conversation.
Opening with a loaded label or an extreme comparison, so the verdict is settled before the facts are laid out.
Swapping a concern about an action for a remark about your tone, mood, character or history.
Persistent: restating your point sends it back into the same frame.
Can happen in writing, in meetings, in family disputes and in public statements, anywhere one account is allowed to name the subject.
what_it_sounds_like: This isn't about the dishes. This is about how unstable you've been lately.
We're not talking about what I said, we're talking about the way you took it.
Let's be honest, this is basically abandonment.
Do you hear yourself? That's the real issue here.
I think what you need to ask yourself is why this bothers you so much.
So now I'm the kind of person who would cheat. Is that what you think of me?
Your email asks about the missed payment, and the reply is two paragraphs on how hostile your tone was, with nothing on the payment.
what_it_is_not: Disagreeing in good faith about what the real issue is happens constantly, and both readings can have merit.
Steering a drifting talk back on topic together.
Someone raising a real worry about your wellbeing without meaning to displace what you said, who then returns to your point.
Describing a hurt in strong words because that is how it felt.
Choosing emphasis in an open argument, which is part of ordinary persuasion.
Agreeing to pause a heated talk and come back, with a time named and kept.
this_may_be_it_when: Your complaint names an action and the reply names a trait.
You can state your point three times and each time end up back at the new topic.
A label is attached to the situation before anyone has described what happened.
The conversation ends with you apologizing for how you raised it.
Days later, the original issue has no answer and nobody has mentioned it.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Your original point gets an answer, even a disagreeing one, before anything else is raised.
They ask 'can I say how this feels to me first?' and then return to your issue.
The concern about you is specific, such as that you have been sleeping badly, and they stay on your topic too.
The strong label still holds when the facts are listed plainly.
A time to resume is named and kept.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Some people go straight to their feelings when they feel attacked, and hear a complaint as a verdict on them.
In a long, tense talk both people lose the thread, and the topic changes without anyone choosing it.
People describe a hurt in dramatic words because that is how it felt, without meaning to settle the case in advance.
common_false_positives: A friend who says 'let's park this, I'm too tired to do it justice' and brings it back the next day.
A counselor who asks what else is going on for you, as part of an agreed session.
A partner who answers your complaint and also adds their own, so two topics now share the table.
discernment_questions: Can I still find my original point anywhere in this conversation?
When I restate it, does it get answered, or is it sent back to the new topic?
If I list only the facts, without the label, does the same conclusion follow?
Is the new subject one they would also raise on a calm day, with no complaint from me?
Would someone listening in say my concern was ever answered?
less_concerning_if: Your point gets at least a short answer before the talk widens.
The subject changes only when both of you are worn out, and returns when you are rested.
A strong label, once checked against the facts, turns out to hold.
more_concerning_if: The substitute topic is nearly always your character, mood or mental state.
You have stopped raising concerns because you know how they will end.
Other people are told the argument was about your reaction, not about the thing that set it off.
pattern_over_time_signs: You open complaints with long disclaimers about your tone, hoping to prevent the swap.
You find old concerns unanswered, with no memory of them being settled.
You say 'never mind' to end the talk, though the issue is unchanged.
Over months you bring up fewer concerns, and the list you keep in your head gets longer.
codex_completed.repair_check: Once you point out the swap, a changed exchange looks like them stating your original point back to you and answering it, even if the answer is no. An apology about the argument that never touches the original issue leaves that issue where it was.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice whether you can hold your topic. Say once, 'I'd like an answer to my first question,' and see if it gets one. If the reply is more about you, the request was met with the very move it was about.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Conversations follow whichever topic is emotionally louder. A remark about your stability or character is hard to ignore, so your effort moves to defending yourself, which is more tiring than complaining. A loaded label does similar work early, since later facts tend to be read through it. Pushing back on a personal remark can sound like proving it, and the original concern gets quietly dropped.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe leaving a talk unable to say what they had meant to ask, replaying it for hours, and wondering whether they really are as difficult as they were just told. Some begin rehearsing complaints in advance, or stop raising them. A slow sense that nothing they bring up ever gets settled is also common.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name the swap and ask for both topics: 'I'd like to hear how I come across, and I'd also like an answer to what I first asked. Can we do mine first?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold your topic: 'That may be worth talking about, but it's not the subject today. I asked about the canceled plans.'
response_options.disengagement: If the new topic keeps winning, stop the exchange and put the original concern in a short written note you can point back to.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend your original question and ask them to say back what they hear. If they can state it clearly, you know the question was not the problem.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, put the concern in an email naming the action and the date, and ask for a reply on that point. A written thread keeps the topic from drifting.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I notice we've moved from what I asked to how I'm asking. Could you tell me in one sentence what you make of the canceled plans? Then I'll gladly hear what's on your mind."
codex_completed.safety_note: A conversation where someone else sets the terms is a conversation problem, not a danger sign. The picture changes if raising a concern starts to bring threats, punishments, or talk of your mental state to doctors or relatives. If that happens, note what was said and when, and talk to a counselor or advocate you trust before the next conversation about it.
misuse_warning: Calling it frame control whenever a talk changes topic punishes ordinary drift and hides the times you changed the subject yourself.
Used as an accusation, 'you're controlling the frame' can itself replace the other person's concern, which is the move it describes.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Deflection steps away from the issue with a tangent or a counter-question, and often leaves the original frame standing; frame control replaces the frame itself, usually with you at the center. Projection hands your complaint back as an accusation of the same behavior, while this hands it back as a remark about who you are. Priming / Narrative Seeding installs a lens before a talk begins, whereas this works inside the talk, as it unfolds.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Strategic Ambiguity
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool can technically match phrasing linked to this tactic, but text alone cannot reliably establish intent here — the same words are too easily produced by an innocent explanation. It is shown as low-signal information only and is never scored.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Phrasing a promise, an exclusion or an intention so loosely that several readings stay open, and the one that gets used is picked afterwards.
codex_completed.short_definition: Phrasing a promise, an exclusion or an intention so loosely that several readings stay open, and the one that gets used is picked afterwards.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Strategic ambiguity is wording left loose enough that two people can leave the same conversation with different understandings, with nothing firm to show which was meant. It is also called Ambiguity as Weapon, and the two names describe one tactic: one stresses vague promises and terms, the other stresses vague exclusion and tone that leave you unable to confirm what is happening. A single fuzzy sentence proves nothing. What stands out is vagueness that keeps resolving the same way, on matters that carry weight for you.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone's words can be read two ways, so later you cannot prove what was promised or whether you were being left out, and you are the one left unsure.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You can feel that something was agreed, or that you are being left out, yet there is nothing firm to point to. Raising it risks sounding picky or paranoid, and staying quiet means carrying the doubt alone, sometimes while acting on a promise nobody pinned down.
what_it_is: Commitments phrased softly, such as 'we'll see' or 'I'll try', on exactly the matters where a clear yes or no would cost something.
Dates, amounts or reasons left unstated, so each person fills the gap with what they expected.
Exclusion that is never spoken: a plan you hear about late, a cooler tone, a 'maybe next time' with no next time.
An explanation that arrives only after the loose wording is questioned, and that often differs from what you understood.
Found in households, workplaces, friendships, rental dealings and group chats.
what_it_sounds_like: We'll sort the money side out at some point.
I never said I'd do that. I said I'd see what I could do.
It's not that you weren't invited. It just wasn't really a proper thing.
Let's keep it flexible. (said about the one point you need fixed)
Things might change at work, so I can't say any more than that.
Don't read so much into it. (after a pointed silence or a vague message)
We should do something soon. (and no date ever follows)
That's not what I meant. I meant something different.
what_it_is_not: Honest uncertainty about the future, said as uncertain and firmed up when you ask.
A person who is loose with words about everything, their own plans and deadlines included, and not only the ones that matter to you.
A plan that was genuinely still being worked out, where nobody had the details yet.
Tact: a polite 'maybe' used to soften a no, which most people will clarify if asked directly.
A group event that really was informal, where nobody counted heads and others were missed too.
Indirect styles of speech where hints are the usual way of declining, and both sides read them fluently.
this_may_be_it_when: Precise wording appears for the speaker's own tasks and loose wording for what they owe you.
You ask a direct question and get a smoother, vaguer answer instead of a clearer one.
After a dispute, the speaker explains what they 'really' meant, and it differs from what the words allowed.
Different people report hearing different things about the same plan.
You cannot tell whether you are being excluded, and each time you try to check, the evidence slips away.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Asked to name a date or an amount, they do so without fuss.
The vagueness spreads across all topics, including ones that cost them something.
The loose reading goes against them as often as in their favor.
They tell you at the outset that they do not know yet, and say when they will.
Others in the same group got the same loose wording, and nobody had firmer information.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people dislike conflict and say 'maybe' when they mean no.
Real plans shift, and broad words can be an effort not to promise what is out of their hands.
Busy or anxious people speak in shorthand and assume the details are understood.
People from different backgrounds can give the same phrase very different weight.
common_false_positives: A friend who says 'let's catch up soon' as a warm goodbye, with no plan implied.
A manager who truthfully cannot say yet whether roles will change, and says exactly that.
Being left off a guest list by oversight, when others were missed as well.
A contract clause that is vague because neither side foresaw the situation.
discernment_questions: If I ask for the specifics in writing, do I get them?
Is the loose wording used only where being precise would cost them something?
Did we both leave with the same summary, or did I learn we differed only later?
Do other people get the same vague answers, or only me?
When a vague promise goes unmet, which meaning gets used, and who does it favor?
If I feel excluded, can I name one concrete thing that happened, apart from a feeling?
less_concerning_if: A request for specifics is met with specifics, or an honest 'I don't know yet'.
The looseness cuts both ways, and the speaker accepts the reading that costs them.
Others in the same position report the same uncertainty.
more_concerning_if: The vague wording surrounds money, housing, work or a legal matter, where a later reading carries real consequences.
Asking for clarity is treated as distrust, or answered with 'why are you making this so hard?'
You have started acting on promises you are no longer sure were ever made.
pattern_over_time_signs: You begin sending recap messages after every conversation to fix what was agreed, and the replies stay loose.
You find out about plans or decisions only after they are settled.
You argue both possible meanings in your head before asking anything.
You feel unable to call something exclusion or a broken promise, because it was never put in so many words.
codex_completed.repair_check: The wording changes and not only the tone: dates, amounts and names start to appear, and a written recap is welcomed. An apology for 'the confusion' followed by an arrangement just as loose is not a change.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself what happens when you request the arrangement in a text or email. If it comes promptly and says something checkable, the request was respected. If it is delayed, softened again or called overkill, the loose wording is being protected.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Loose wording hands each listener the job of filling in the gaps, and listeners often fill them with what they hope or expect. Afterwards there is nothing quotable to hold anyone to, so the listener may start blaming their own hearing. When the vagueness concerns exclusion, the lack of any concrete event can lead a person to suspect their own reading instead of the situation.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe replaying conversations to work out what was actually said, feeling picky for asking, and hesitating to act on anything that is not in writing. Some describe turning down plans or work because they could not tell whether they were wanted, and others a lingering ache about whether they imagined being left out.

response_options.soft_clarification: Offer a recap that invites correction: 'So we agreed you'd pay half by the first of the month. Have I got that right?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask for the point to be settled before you act: 'I need a yes or a no on this by Friday, in a message I can keep.'
response_options.disengagement: Hold off on anything that depends on the loose promise, and make plans that do not rely on it, without arguing over what was meant.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe the exchange to a friend and ask what they would take it to mean. An outside reading shows whether the gap is as wide as it feels.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Follow meetings with a short email stating the decision, the owner and the date, and ask people to reply if they read it differently.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "We should both be working from the same understanding. Can you tell me, in a message, exactly what you will do and by when? If you're not sure yet, just say that, and we can pick a day to decide."
codex_completed.safety_note: Vague wording is a clarity problem, not a danger signal. It changes when the vague wording covers housing, immigration paperwork, custody arrangements or money you depend on, or when asking for specifics brings anger or threats. In those cases, have the arrangement reviewed by a tenants' group, legal aid or a caseworker before you act on it.
misuse_warning: Not every 'maybe' or 'we'll see' is a trap. Treating ordinary hedging as proof of bad faith can turn a clumsy communicator into a villain.
Being unable to tell whether you are excluded does not show that you are. Asking plainly before concluding is fair to both sides.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Moving Goalposts changes a standard that was stated after you meet it, whereas here the standard was never stated clearly. Selective Memory is failing to recall what was said, while here the words were said but left wide. Deflection answers a question with another topic, and here the question gets an answer that simply stays open. Strategic ambiguity is the one where the wording is the problem: it gives you nothing firm to hold.
codex_completed.detection_notes: A phrasing pattern exists in this tool's library for this tactic, but it is deliberately capped below the scoring threshold: this signal is too context-dependent and too easily produced innocently for text alone to establish intent. It is never scored.

codex_completed.name: Repetition as Truth
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Saying the same claim over and over, with no new evidence, until its familiarity begins to feel like proof.
codex_completed.short_definition: Saying the same claim over and over, with no new evidence, until its familiarity begins to feel like proof.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: People tend to believe what they have heard many times, because familiar statements feel easier and truer. This tactic relies on that effect: a claim returns in nearly the same words, from conversation to conversation, without anything new behind it. Repeating a fact you have good reason for is ordinary. What marks the pattern is that the repetition is the only support, and 'I've told you before' stands in for a reason.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A claim is said so many times, in the same words and with no new proof, that it starts to feel true simply because you have heard it so often.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Familiar claims can come to feel true even when you cannot say what supports them. If you hear the same sentence about yourself or about what happened, you may start repeating it without noticing, and lose track of whether you ever had a reason to believe it.
what_it_is: The same claim, in near-identical words, returning across days, weeks or years.
Repetition used in place of proof, as in 'I've said it a hundred times.'
A cousin of how slogans, rumors and advertisements work, now applied to a personal or workplace claim.
A pattern in which the claim is never reworked or defended, only restated more firmly.
what_it_sounds_like: "You're bad with money. You've always been bad with money."
"I've told you before, that's just how it is."
"Everyone knows you can't be trusted with the car."
The same sentence about your 'attitude' appearing in every meeting, with no examples.
"How many times do I have to say it? It was your fault."
A single accusation heard from three different relatives, all in the same words.
what_it_is_not: A person who repeats a fact because they have good evidence and you keep disputing it.
A reminder of a real agreement, such as 'we said the recycling goes out on Thursday,' repeated for practical reasons.
A worried parent saying the same safety rule many times to a young child, where repetition is how children learn.
Teaching, where an idea is rehearsed for learning and the evidence is shared when asked.
Two people stuck on an honest disagreement who each keep restating their view because they have not found common ground.
this_may_be_it_when: The words of the claim hardly change from one occasion to the next.
Asking for the basis of the claim brings only another repetition, or irritation.
You realize you believe the claim but cannot name a single instance behind it.
The claim is about you and your character, and is repeated even after you give counter-examples.
Other people begin repeating it, and when you trace it back it all comes from one source.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Each time it comes up, they add a new example, date or document.
You can look up the thing being repeated and it holds up.
They are happy to drop it when you show them evidence that it is wrong.
The repetition has a clear practical purpose, such as a deadline, a rule or a safety step.
They say it only once or twice, and not as a way to close a conversation.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People repeat themselves when they feel unheard, hoping that saying it louder will help it land.
Habits of speech, such as family sayings, may be repeated without anyone treating them as proof.
Some people truly hold a belief firmly and have no further explanation than that they were raised with it.
common_false_positives: A coach who says 'keep your eyes on the ball' at every practice, because that is the instruction.
A relative who retells an old family story at every holiday, which is nostalgia and not an argument.
A colleague repeating a deadline in each email because it has not been met.
discernment_questions: Can I say what the claim rests on, other than that I have heard it many times?
Has anyone ever shown me an example, or only told me again?
When I give a counter-example, is it weighed or simply passed over?
Would I believe this claim if I were hearing it for the first time today?
Where else have I heard this exact wording, and who did it come from?
less_concerning_if: Each repetition brings a new detail, example or source that you can check.
The claim gets updated or dropped when you give evidence against it.
The repeated phrase is a harmless family or workplace habit, with nothing riding on it.
more_concerning_if: The repeated claim is about your character, competence or sanity.
It is repeated to other people, who then repeat it to you.
It is used to justify decisions made about you, such as money, schedule or role.
pattern_over_time_signs: You catch yourself saying the claim about yourself, in their words.
You can no longer remember the evidence for or against, only the slogan.
Counter-evidence you once held now feels weaker than the repeated line.
People who barely know you describe you with the same phrase.
codex_completed.repair_check: Fixing this would show up as the claim being put to an actual test: they look at the evidence with you, say what they found, and change what they say afterwards. An apology that is followed by the old sentence the next week has only gone quiet.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: You can ask yourself what happens when you say 'please show me one new example.' Someone willing to look for one is treating the claim as testable. Someone who answers with the same sentence, louder, is repeating the claim again and has not heard the request.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Humans tend to rate familiar statements as more likely to be true, even when they were first heard in doubt. Repetition can also wear down the effort to argue back, because each reply feels like starting again. When the repeated claim comes from someone who matters to you, it can slip from something you hear to something you believe about yourself.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A slow slide from 'that's not true' to 'maybe there's something in it' is what some report. Some notice they have taken the claim on as part of how they describe themselves, and some feel angry on discovering the same sentence has been planted in several people. Others felt relief once they asked for a reason and saw there was none.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the evidence behind the line: 'You've said that a few times. Can you give me one example from this month?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say you will not accept a claim on repetition alone: 'Hearing it again doesn't make it more true for me. I'll respond when there's something I can check.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop responding when the same sentence comes back with nothing new, and keep your own notes of what is actually true.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask someone who has seen you in many settings whether the repeated claim matches what they see, and write down their answer.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask for specific, dated examples whenever a vague criticism returns, and keep your own record of your work and feedback.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I've heard that sentence several times now. I'm not going to treat it as true because it's familiar. If there's a specific example, I'll listen to it. If not, I'd like to move on."
codex_completed.safety_note: A repeated claim is a pressure on your beliefs, not a physical danger in itself. It deserves more care when the repeated line concerns your fitness as a parent, your sanity or your honesty, and is told to schools, courts, employers or relatives. In that case, keep dated records and talk to a lawyer, an advocate or a trusted person.
misuse_warning: Repeating a true thing is not manipulation. If you have not checked whether the claim is accurate, the label may only mean you dislike hearing it.
Accusing someone of 'repeating' can brush off a person whose concern keeps coming back because it has not been addressed.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Gaslighting flatly denies what you saw or remember, whereas this tactic states a claim, usually about you or a past event, and relies on volume. Selective Memory leaves things out as though forgotten, but repetition keeps pressing one thing forward. Countering contradicts your account on the spot, while this works slowly, by wearing a line into familiarity.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Firehose of Falsehood
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Flooding people with a high volume of fast, shifting and often contradictory claims so that checking and answering each one becomes impossible.
codex_completed.short_definition: Flooding people with a high volume of fast, shifting and often contradictory claims so that checking and answering each one becomes impossible.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: The firehose of falsehood is a propaganda style, described by researchers who studied Russian state media, that sends out a large number of claims through many channels, quickly and without worrying about consistency. The aim is not to persuade with one story. It is to leave listeners overloaded, unsure what to believe and tired of checking. The same overload can happen in a family or workplace argument, when accusations arrive faster than anyone can answer them.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: So many claims arrive so quickly, and from so many directions, that you cannot check them all, and you may give up trying to work out what is true.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Fact-checking one claim takes minutes, while a flood can arrive in seconds. People who cannot keep up may stop trusting everything, or fall back on whoever sounds most confident. Either way, the thing they set out to understand stays buried.
what_it_is: A flood of claims at high volume, sent through many outlets or voices at once.
Claims that do not need to agree with each other, since the aim is to overload and not to persuade with one story.
A style that treats speed as more important than accuracy, so corrections come after the damage is done.
Shown at population scale in media and online campaigns, and at small scale in arguments that pile accusation on accusation.
what_it_sounds_like: A stream of posts in one hour offering three different explanations for the same event, none of them agreeing.
A reply to your single question that raises five new accusations.
Many accounts or outlets pushing different versions of an event, all arriving before any has been checked.
A debunked claim returning in new wording a day later, as though it had never been answered.
Official statements that shift from denial to alternative explanations without acknowledging the change.
A heated argument in which each time you answer one charge, two more are added.
Being told 'there are so many reports, something must be true.'
what_it_is_not: A fast-moving real news event, where early reports are confused and are corrected as facts come in.
Many people honestly holding different views and saying so, as happens in any lively public debate.
Someone who is anxious or overwhelmed, listing every worry at once, with no plan to confuse you.
A breaking story in which an organization changes its account as it learns more, and says it has.
