response_options.firm_boundary: Say what you cannot be: 'I can't be the only support you have. I care, and I think you deserve a counselor or friends who can give you more.'
response_options.disengagement: Let messages and meetings settle to the rate that matches how long you have actually known each other, and end calls warmly at the time you said you would.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe the first few weeks to a friend who knows you well and ask whether the speed seems as fast to them as it does in hindsight.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a colleague or client confides heavy pain, point them toward an employee assistance program, a counselor or HR, and keep your own disclosures to a level you would accept a manager reading.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Trusting me with this means something, and I'm sorry you went through it. I'm still getting to know you, so I'd like this to grow over time instead of all at once. That is about my pace, and it isn't a no. Who else could support you too?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Fast closeness alone is not a danger sign. Take it more seriously when it comes with pressure to hide the relationship, to give money or housing, or when you are told you are responsible for someone's life. If someone says they may hurt themselves, do not carry that alone: contact a crisis line or emergency services for them, and tell a trusted person.
misuse_warning: Treating every quick friendship, open-hearted new partner or person sharing grief as manufactured can punish people for being warm. The label needs a mismatch between closeness and evidence, not just speed.
Using the term to avoid ever supporting someone in real crisis turns a pattern name into permission to dismiss.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Love Bombing is marked by praise, gifts and affection; this tactic can run on confiding and pain alone, with hardly a compliment. Exclusive Meaning asserts that only one person truly understands you, a line that may show up after weeks of closeness. Future Faking borrows from tomorrow with promises, while manufactured intimacy borrows from the present by speeding it up.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Manufactured Destiny
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Presenting a relationship as fated or cosmically arranged so that doubting it, slowing it down or leaving it feels like going against destiny.
codex_completed.short_definition: Presenting a relationship as fated or cosmically arranged so that doubting it, slowing it down or leaving it feels like going against destiny.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Manufactured destiny is the use of fate language, such as 'we were meant to meet', 'the universe brought us together' or 'you are my one', to raise the stakes of an ordinary choice. Saying such things once, in love, is common and carries little weight. It becomes a pattern when the fated story arrives very early, grows louder when you hesitate, and turns your doubt into a mistake against something larger than either of you.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone tells you the two of you are meant to be, and each time you hesitate that story is used to make stepping back feel like a mistake you can't undo.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Leaving stops feeling like ending a relationship and starts feeling like defying something larger, which raises the cost of an otherwise ordinary decision to go. Doubt gets treated as a flaw in you rather than as information.
what_it_is: The relationship described as arranged by fate, the universe, God or a past life, so it is more than a choice two people made.
A story told early, when there has not been time to learn whether the match is as rare as claimed.
Hesitation recast as fear, resistance or a failure to see what is plainly written.
The grand language can be sincere, so the sign is in how it is used when you are unsure, not in the words alone.
A cost placed on exit: the idea that no one else will ever fit, so walking away would be wasting something irreplaceable.
what_it_sounds_like: We were meant to find each other. This isn't a coincidence.
The universe doesn't hand out connections like this twice.
If you walk away from this, you'll regret it your whole life.
I knew the moment I saw you. You can't fight something like this.
Everything lined up for a reason. Why are you resisting it?
You'll never find anyone who gets you like I do.
We have been through too many signs for this to be an accident.
what_it_is_not: Two people who sincerely feel something remarkable has happened between them, and both say so in their own words.
Romantic or spiritual language that is part of someone's culture, faith or personality, used in the same way with everyone they love.
A person who truly believes in fate, who talks about meaning and timing in many parts of life and is not threatened by your doubts.
Looking back on a good relationship and calling it lucky or meant to be, after the fact.
A grand gesture or sentimental line in the first flush of romance that is not repeated when you hesitate.
Hope for a future together, expressed without making your doubts a problem to be fixed.
this_may_be_it_when: The fate story gets louder specifically when you say you are unsure or want more time.
Your hesitation is answered with a sign, a coincidence or a prophecy instead of a conversation.
You are told that leaving would defy something larger, and you notice you feel afraid of the idea.
The 'meant to be' claim arrived within days or weeks, before there was evidence either way.
Practical concerns, such as differences in values or past hurts, are waved away as small in light of destiny.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They use the language only when things feel good, and drop it, calmly, when you want to talk through problems.
They say it of other relationships in their life and apply it to friends and family too.
When you say you want to slow down, they say 'okay' and the connection is unchanged.
They treat the belief as theirs, and do not require you to share it.
The sentiment is mutual and you use it yourself without feeling pressed.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people truly feel, in the early rush of romance, that it was meant to be.
Fate and soulmate language is a widely shared way of expressing how big a feeling is.
Faith traditions often frame relationships as arranged or blessed, and the speaker may mean exactly that.
Someone who has been through loss or loneliness may reach for large words to describe relief.
common_false_positives: A partner of many years who says they were lucky to meet you, in a moment of gratitude.
A new partner saying 'it feels like fate' on a good date, with no pressure on what you say back.
A shared religious background where talk of providence is simply how both of you speak.
A wedding speech or anniversary card that uses destiny language for the occasion.
discernment_questions: When did the destiny talk begin, and how much did you actually know each other by then?
What happens to the fated language the moment you voice a doubt?
Do you feel allowed to make an ordinary, reversible decision about this relationship?
Would you still want this relationship if no one had ever described it as meant to be?
Do you have a sense of what you value in this person apart from the idea that it was always going to happen?
less_concerning_if: The language is warm and occasional, and it comes without any request that you stay.
They are as comfortable with your doubts as with your certainty.
Other people in their life describe them as sentimental or spiritual in general.
more_concerning_if: Threats of loss, regret or bad luck are attached to the idea of leaving.
Signs, readings or dreams are used to decide things for you, such as where you live or who you see.
Anyone who questions the relationship, whether friends or family, is described as blocking what was meant to be.
pattern_over_time_signs: You notice the fate story comes back every time the two of you hit a hard stretch.
Disagreements get settled by 'we are meant to be together, so this will pass' rather than by talking.
You begin to defend the relationship to others in destiny terms, because ordinary reasons no longer seem to be enough.
Your own wishes for your life shrink as the shared story becomes bigger.
codex_completed.repair_check: Listen for ordinary language to take over: 'you're allowed to be unsure, and I'll stop using fate to answer your questions.' If a new sign, dream or omen turns up a week later, the pressure has only changed costume.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself if you could say 'I don't believe it's fate, and I'd like to decide this as an ordinary choice' and still be safe, liked and listened to. If that sentence is welcomed or argued with kindly, the belief is theirs to hold. If it starts a fight about your faith in the relationship, it was functioning as leverage.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A choice that feels like fate can seem to carry no personal responsibility and an impossible price for reversal. People also tend to resist actions that might waste something they have been told is rare. Framing a relationship as destined can make the ordinary tools of weighing, comparing and slowing down feel disloyal rather than sensible.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Reported experiences include feeling trapped by something beautiful, guilty for doubting, and unable to explain to friends why leaving felt so large. Some stayed longer than they wanted because the story made the choice seem not theirs to make, and some grieved the idea itself once the relationship ended.

response_options.soft_clarification: Separate the feeling from the decision: 'I can feel this is special to you. I still need to make my choices by what I see, not by what was written for us.'
response_options.firm_boundary: State that the decision is yours and ordinary: 'I'm not going to treat leaving as defying fate. If I need time, I'm taking it.'
response_options.disengagement: When the conversation shifts to signs and destiny, move it to practical terms or end it for the day, and come back to the facts later.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask someone who has known you a long time to hear the story as you tell it and say what they would have advised a friend in the same position.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If this appears in a mentoring or coaching setting, such as a leader saying you were 'meant' to join, ask for the role, the pay and the exit terms in writing.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Fated is how it feels to you. I'm treating it as a regular decision that I'm allowed to think about, and slow down, and change my mind on. Please don't use destiny to answer when I say I'm not sure."
codex_completed.safety_note: Fate talk by itself is not a danger signal. Be more careful if leaving is met with threats, if you are told you or others will be harmed or cursed for going, or if decisions about money, housing or contact are taken out of your hands. Then speak to a domestic abuse advocate or someone you trust before you make any announcement.
misuse_warning: Calling every romantic or spiritual declaration manipulative can shame people for sincere feeling. The pattern is in how the story is used against hesitation.
Using the label about someone's religious belief in providence confuses their faith with a tactic.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Attention, gifts and praise are the flood of Love Bombing, which needs no talk of fate. Exclusive Meaning is a claim about your bond with one person, uniquely understood, while destiny is a claim about the relationship's cosmic standing. Future Faking promises particular events to come; this tactic says the future is already settled and your hesitation cannot alter it.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Mirroring-on-Demand
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Quickly taking on your interests, opinions and way of speaking so that you feel unusually understood and matched, whether or not the match is real.
codex_completed.short_definition: Quickly taking on your interests, opinions and way of speaking so that you feel unusually understood and matched, whether or not the match is real.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Mirroring-on-demand is the habit of reflecting back what you have just revealed: your taste in music, your politics, your childhood wound, your phrases. Everyone mirrors a little, and rapport usually involves it. The pattern is different in scale and speed. Every interest you mention turns out to be theirs, nothing they say disagrees with you, and the match seems to move when your account of yourself moves. The feeling of rare compatibility rests on a reflection.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A person seems to share everything you like and believe, and it feels like a perfect match, but the sameness changes shape depending on what you tell them.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A sense of rare alignment forms with a reflection rather than a person. What is later found to be missing was never actually there to lose, and you may come to doubt your own judgment about who you fell for.
what_it_is: Echoing your tastes, values and stories back so closely that you feel you have found a twin.
Adjusting to whatever you say next: if you shift your view, theirs shifts with you.
Sameness that has no history behind it, such as a favorite band they cannot describe or a hobby with no past.
A fast way to produce trust, because people tend to like those who seem similar to them.
Often visible only from outside: friends notice that the person behaves differently around different people.
what_it_sounds_like: No way, that's my favorite too! I can't believe it.
I've always felt exactly like that about my family.
Same here. I hate that too. I really never liked those people either.
We think so alike it's almost spooky.
I used to think the opposite, but you've completely changed my mind.
Your politics are my politics. You put it better than I ever could.
I've never met anyone I agree with on everything until now.
what_it_is_not: Real compatibility, especially between people who met through a shared interest, produces genuine excitement at how much overlaps.
An agreeable, accommodating style is not strategic reflection. Some people avoid conflict with everyone.
Normal rapport, where people unconsciously pick up each other's gestures and speech rhythms in a good conversation.
Being nervous and wanting to be liked on a first date, so you both agree more than you will later.
A person who really is changing their mind because of what you said, openly, and can tell you why.
The distinction lies in whether the shared enthusiasms have any independent history behind them, or appear complete the moment they are mentioned.
this_may_be_it_when: Their stated interests have no earlier trace: no old posts, belongings, stories or friends who recognize them.
Their opinions line up with yours on topics where most people disagree with each other.
When you change a view, their view moves to match within days.
They never disagree with you, even about small things, and bristle or sulk if you disagree with them.
Friends who have seen them with other people say they seem like a different person.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They can say where an interest came from and show something done about it before you met.
They disagree with you now and then, mildly, about things that matter to them.
Their shared tastes were obvious from the start, such as a club you both joined for the same reason.
Their way of speaking stays the same around other people.
Their agreement is general warmth toward everybody, not tuned to you.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Insecurity can make a person agree with whoever they are speaking to, without any plan.
People who grew up having to keep the peace sometimes become expert at fitting in.
Early dates are performances, and both people tend to show their most compatible side.
Real overlap is common when two people meet through the same community, school or hobby.
common_false_positives: Meeting at a book club and finding you both love the same authors.
A new colleague who is friendly and agrees easily because they are anxious to fit in.
A friend who adopts your slang after spending a lot of time with you.
A date who is open to your views because they are curious, and then later reveals disagreements.
discernment_questions: Can you point to a time they disagreed with you, or held an opinion you did not share?
Do their interests have a history you can see, apart from what they told you?
Does the way they talk or the views they hold change when they are with other people?
If you changed your mind about something, would theirs follow?
Is the connection built on what they did, or on how closely they reflected what you said?
less_concerning_if: Differences between you appear over time and are handled with interest rather than hurt.
Their interests can be traced to something they did before they knew you.
People who know them in other settings describe the same person you know.
more_concerning_if: Their agreement disappears the moment you disagree, and warmth is replaced by coldness or sulking.
They tell different people incompatible things, each time presenting a perfect match.
You find that you have started altering your own views to keep the match going.
pattern_over_time_signs: The shared passions fade once the early stage is over, leaving little actual common ground.
You discover pieces of their real preferences that contradict what they had agreed on earlier.
Their opinions keep tracking the opinions of the most important person in the room.
You begin to feel you do not know who they are, even though you feel you have told them everything.
codex_completed.repair_check: After you name it, listen for a first disagreement, offered calmly and early. Someone willing to be known will tell you something you did not expect to hear about what they like. A fresh round of 'we're so alike' with new details adapted to what you just said is the pattern continuing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Try offering a mild, honest disagreement and see what follows. Can they hold a different view and still be warm? Or does the closeness drop off, or do they swing back to agreeing? Your own comfort in disagreeing is as much of an answer as their reaction.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: We lean toward those who seem similar to us, and similarity is easily mistaken for being understood. A person who reflects you efficiently supplies that impression without any of the shared history behind it. Because the reflection follows what you reveal, it seems to confirm that you are special, when it may only confirm that you were heard and echoed.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: An early rush of being understood is common in accounts, followed by confusion once the person's own tastes appear or contradict the match. Some felt foolish, some mourned someone partly invented, and others doubted their instincts because the similarity had been so convincing. A few found they had been quietly editing their own views to protect the match.

response_options.soft_clarification: Invite a real difference: 'We seem to agree on a lot. Tell me something you like that I probably wouldn't.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold your own opinion without softening it: 'I actually don't see it that way, and I'd like to be able to disagree without it being a problem.'
response_options.disengagement: Slow your sharing. Keep conversations to things you can verify, and step back until their own preferences show up on their own.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask a friend who has met them in a different setting whether the person you describe sounds like the person they saw.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In professional settings, notice colleagues who agree with everyone, and weigh decisions on documented work rather than on rapport.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I like how much we seem to have in common. I also want to know the parts we don't, and I'd rather hear a real disagreement than a perfect match. Can you tell me something you think I'd disagree with?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Being mirrored is rarely dangerous in itself. It deserves more care when the match is built to gain access to money, your home, your children or private information, or when you learn that the person has been presenting different identities. In that case, stop sharing sensitive details and check their identity with a trusted friend or, for online contacts, the platform's reporting tools.
misuse_warning: Calling every agreeable person a mirror can mislabel shyness or politeness as strategy. Many people agree easily without any plan.
Using the label to dismiss genuine shared interests can punish someone for a real connection.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Praise and affection are what Love Bombing delivers, whereas a mirror may flatter you not at all and simply seem to be you. Exclusive Meaning states outright that you are understood like no one else; mirroring lets you draw that conclusion yourself. Negging lowers your confidence with backhanded compliments, and mirroring does the opposite, by making you feel perfectly matched.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: The Rescue Hook
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Showing need that seems helpless, so that you step in, take over tasks or feelings without being asked, and your effort is treated as devotion.
codex_completed.short_definition: Showing need that seems helpless, so that you step in, take over tasks or feelings without being asked, and your effort is treated as devotion.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: The rescue hook is a pattern where need is shown rather than stated. The person sighs over the bill, the broken appliance or the hard day, and you step in because they obviously cannot cope. No request is made, so there is nothing to decline. Over time you become the one who manages logistics or feelings, and it is called love. A single bad week proves nothing. What marks the pattern is need that appears reliably around you, with help expected and never asked for.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone seems unable to cope, you step in without being asked, and over time you are doing a large share of their life while it is called caring.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Substantial labor is given without ever having been asked for, so there is nothing to point at as an imposition and no clear moment at which it could have been declined. You can end up exhausted, with no way to name how it began.
what_it_is: Need that is shown through sighs, hints and visible struggle rather than requested outright.
Help that arrives because you volunteer, so it feels like your own choice and not something drawn out of you.
Tasks, decisions or emotional steadiness gradually shifting onto you until you are managing their life as well as yours.
Gratitude that carries a weight: the relationship is described as depending on your continuing to help.
Struggle that appears in front of you and eases when you are not there or when someone else is.
what_it_sounds_like: I just don't know how I'm going to manage this. (sighing, and looking at you)
I'd ask you, but I know you're busy. I'll figure it out somehow.
I don't know what I'd do without you. I really can't do this by myself.
You're so good at this. I always get it wrong. Never mind, forget it.
Everything falls apart when you're not around.
I tried, but I couldn't. It was too much. I'm sorry to be like this.
Don't worry about me. I'll just have a bad week.
what_it_is_not: People genuinely struggle with specific skills, and someone raised without a task ever modeled to them has real rather than performed difficulty.
An uneven division of tasks along the lines of who is better at what is normal in most households.
A person going through illness, grief, a new baby or job loss who truly needs help for a while and says so plainly.
A direct request such as 'Could you help me with this on Saturday?', which you can accept or decline.
Someone who is slow to ask for help because they find it hard, and thanks you without expecting it again.
The pattern is need that appears reliably rather than help that is asked for plainly.
this_may_be_it_when: They struggle with tasks around you that they handle well at work or with other people.
Offers to step back are met with distress, guilt or a drop in warmth.
You feel you are doing things because you cannot bear to watch, not because anyone asked.
There is little sign of learning the skill or reducing the dependence over time.
Your own commitments, rest and plans are routinely moved aside for their emergencies.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They ask clearly for specific help and accept a 'no' without fuss.
They are working on the skill or have a plan to need you less.
The struggle is real, visible to others and consistent in every setting.
They offer help back, in ways that matter to you, when you need it.
They thank you without implying you owe them more.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Genuine skill gaps and situational struggles are common and do not require strategic intent.
Depression, anxiety, neurodivergence or illness can make everyday tasks truly hard, and visible struggle may be the best the person can manage.
Some people were taught never to ask directly, so they hint instead.
People naturally divide labor based on real differences in ability or interest.
common_false_positives: A partner who is bad with paperwork and who gladly takes on the cooking in return.
A friend recovering from surgery who really does need rides and groceries for a few weeks.
A new arrival in the country who needs help with forms and language and is clear about it.
A parent who is not good with technology and asks you to set up a phone.
discernment_questions: Would they ask me plainly for this, or do I step in because the need is shown to me?
Does the difficulty look the same when I am not there, or when someone else is?
What happens if I say I can't help today?
Is there any sign of effort to learn the skill or build another source of help?
Do I feel like a partner, or like a manager of their life?
less_concerning_if: The need is stated plainly and they accept refusals without distress.
There is visible progress or a plan to rely on you less over time.
They give back, in practical or emotional ways, when you are the one struggling.
more_concerning_if: Any step back on your part is met with guilt, tears, anger or sudden crises.
Your work, health, money or other relationships are suffering from the help you give.
You are told, or come to feel, that the relationship would end if you stopped.
pattern_over_time_signs: The list of things you do for them keeps growing and rarely shrinks.
New difficulties appear when old ones are solved, so your involvement never ends.
You find yourself pre-empting problems so they do not distress them, and giving up plans to do so.
Others have noticed you are tired, or that you do more than your share, and you have defended it.
codex_completed.repair_check: Look for needs that start arriving as plain requests you can answer yes or no to. Repair also includes tackling tasks themselves, even clumsily. A warm thank-you, then the same sighing helplessness a week later, means the setup is still running.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Decline one thing, kindly, and see what happens next. Do they ask someone else, work it out, or accept the delay? Or does the day turn into a crisis that makes your refusal look cruel? The reaction to one small 'not today' tells you more than any speech.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Seeing someone who seems unable to cope pulls many of us toward helping, and stepping in unprompted feels like a free choice. Since help was never requested, refusing later looks like abandoning someone instead of declining a favor. Responsibility drifts to the helper and comfort to the other person, without either of them deciding it.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe tiredness, resentment they feel guilty about, and the sense of being needed more than known. Some say they lost track of their own plans and friendships, and found it hard to explain what was wrong because they had volunteered every time. Others describe relief when they realized that they could offer help without being the only source of it.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for requests, not hints: 'When something's hard, can you tell me what you'd like from me? I'm happy to say yes or no.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Set a limit on a specific task: 'I won't take over your bills any more, but I'll sit with you while you sort them out this once.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop anticipating. Let a smaller problem sit for a day before responding, and notice what they do in the gap.
response_options.support_seeking: List what you currently do for them on paper and show it to a friend or counselor, asking whether it looks like a fair share.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, redirect repeated requests to the proper channel, such as a manager or a help desk, and keep a record of what you covered.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I care about you, and I can see this is hard. I can't be the one who fixes everything. Tell me what you'd like from me and I'll tell you honestly whether I can do it. I'll also help you find someone else who can."
codex_completed.safety_note: This pattern is mostly about workload and guilt, not danger. Take more care if stepping back leads to threats, self-harm statements, anger or the loss of housing or income you rely on. If someone says they might hurt themselves, contact local emergency services or a crisis line for them and for yourself, rather than carrying that alone.
misuse_warning: Labeling everyone who needs help as a hook can leave truly struggling people without support. Illness, disability and hard seasons are not tactics.
Using the label to justify walking away from someone with real needs, without any attempt to talk, treats a pattern as a verdict.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Conditional Love ties affection to obedience, whereas the rescue hook ties it to your continuing to give. Adoration at the start is the territory of Love Bombing, but here the pull is need, not worship. Hoovering draws you back after distance with promises of change; the rescue hook works as a daily rhythm rather than a comeback.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Emotional Parasitism
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A steady, one-way arrangement in which one person's feelings take most of the attention and care while the other is left drained, with little given back.
codex_completed.short_definition: A steady, one-way arrangement in which one person's feelings take most of the attention and care while the other is left drained, with little given back.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Emotional parasitism describes a relationship in which one person reliably receives comfort, attention and emotional work, and the other reliably provides it, over a long period. Every friendship has uneven weeks, and a friend in crisis may take much more than they give. The pattern is the imbalance that does not even out: conversations circle back to one person's difficulties, your concerns get little follow-up, and you leave feeling emptied while they seem lifted.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You give most of the listening, comfort and energy, they give little back, and over months or years you are tired in a way that rest does not fix.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Depletion accumulates so gradually that it registers as a personal failing, such as tiredness or low tolerance, rather than as the arithmetic of a relationship that never balances. You may blame yourself for running out of patience.
what_it_is: A lasting imbalance where one person is nearly always the giver and the other nearly always the receiver of emotional support.
Conversations that return to the same person's crises, with your news getting a sentence or two.
A pattern that holds across years rather than weeks, whatever else is happening in either life.
A cost to the giver that builds slowly: tiredness, dread before calls, a sense of being used up.
Found in friendships, families, partnerships, workplaces and online communities.
what_it_sounds_like: Anyway, enough about you. Let me tell you what happened with my sister.
You're so good at this. Nobody listens like you do.
I know you've got a lot on, but I really need you tonight.
That sounds hard. Anyway, mine was worse.
You always know what to say. I don't know how you cope.
I can't talk about your thing right now. I'm too stressed.
You're the only one I can tell all of this to.
what_it_is_not: A friend going through a genuinely hard stretch needs more for a while, and reciprocity resuming once things stabilize is ordinary.
Someone with their own significant unmet needs may be unable rather than unwilling to give back.
What distinguishes the pattern is an imbalance that is stable across years rather than weeks.
A caring role you chose, such as supporting a sick relative or a person in recovery, where the imbalance is understood and agreed.
A therapist, counselor or helper who is paid for a one-sided relationship.
Different needs for talk: a more expressive friend who talks more, yet shows up for you in other ways.
this_may_be_it_when: When you share your own troubles, they are quickly steered back to theirs.
You feel more drained than uplifted after most of your contact with them.
Over a year or more, you cannot recall a time they showed up for you in a comparable way.
Naming the imbalance is met with hurt, defensiveness or a new crisis.
You find yourself avoiding their calls, or saving energy for them in advance.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They checked in with you after a hard stretch of their own had passed.
They remember what you told them and ask about it later.
The current imbalance has a clear cause, such as a bereavement or illness, and is changing.
They thank you and look for other supports as well.
You get things from the friendship that matter to you, such as laughter, history or shared work.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People going through genuinely hard times often need more support without intending any lasting imbalance.
Different people have different baseline needs for emotional connection.
Someone may simply not realize how much they have been taking, especially if you rarely say what you need.
Mental illness or exhaustion can reduce a person's ability to notice or give anything back.
common_false_positives: A friend who has just lost a job and talks about it constantly for a month.
A sibling who is in recovery and is leaning heavily on the family for support.
A talkative friend who loves to share, and who also shows up for you with practical help.
A one-sided stretch caused by your own reluctance to ask for anything.
discernment_questions: Has the imbalance lasted for months or years, or is it linked to a crisis that is passing?
When I need something, can I recall the last time they gave it to me?
Do I feel drained after most contact, and is that different from how I feel with other people?
Have I told them directly what I need, and what happened?
Would they notice if I stopped reaching out?
less_concerning_if: The imbalance has a clear cause that is easing, and they have begun to give back.
When you name it, they listen and change something.
You have other relationships where the giving and receiving feel fair.
more_concerning_if: Your attempts to name the imbalance lead to blame, guilt or accusations that you are selfish.
The drain has begun to affect your health, work, sleep or other relationships.
You feel unable to end or reduce contact without a scene or a crisis.
pattern_over_time_signs: The balance is the same year after year, regardless of what is happening in either life.
You find that you prepare for each contact by bracing yourself.
Your other friends have commented on how much time and energy you give.
Your own news, worries and achievements have stopped being shared with this person because they do not land.
codex_completed.repair_check: Over the next several weeks, check whether questions about you start being remembered and whether other people share the load. A tearful thank-you that slides back to the old balance within days does not count. Real change shows up as space for your worries.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Consider how you would feel cutting one conversation short. Is it met with a gracious goodbye, or with hurt that you are made to repair? Also notice whether, a week later, anything is different in how they ask about you. One kind reaction is nice, but the longer pattern is the answer.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Giving support is rewarding, and the person receiving it may come to depend on one source without noticing what it costs. If the giver also finds it hard to ask for anything, the arrangement settles into place with nobody choosing it. Because tiredness builds slowly, it reads as a personal flaw rather than the result of a lopsided deal.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe dread before calls, a feeling of being used up, and guilt about the dread. Some say they started to believe they were bad at friendship, or that their own problems were too small to mention. Others describe relief and anger on seeing the long-run balance written down, and difficulty knowing how to change a relationship of many years.

response_options.soft_clarification: Say what you would like once, kindly: 'I'd love to hear about you, and I also need some time for what's going on with me. Can we share the time?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Put a limit on the format: 'I can talk for twenty minutes tonight. After that I need to rest.'
response_options.disengagement: Reduce how often you reach out first, and let contact settle at a level that doesn't cost you. Notice what they do with the space.
response_options.support_seeking: Spend time with people who ask about you, and consider a counselor to help you practice asking for what you need without apology.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, redirect repeated emotional venting to an appropriate channel, such as a mentor or employee assistance program, and keep your own workload visible.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I care about you, and I've noticed that most of our time goes to your side of things. I need a bit of space for mine as well. Could we try taking turns, so I'm not worn out by the end?"
codex_completed.safety_note: A lopsided friendship is draining but not usually dangerous. That changes if stepping back brings threats, self-harm statements, harassment or demands for money or housing. Then pause contact where you can, keep a record of what was said, and speak to a counselor, advice service or crisis line for a plan that keeps you both safe.
misuse_warning: Calling a friend in a hard season a parasite can abandon someone who truly needs you. The pattern requires a stable imbalance over a long period.
Using the term as a character label for someone with greater needs, such as an unwell relative, turns a description of a relationship into a verdict on a person.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Premature Vulnerability is an early burst of heavy disclosure that creates a duty, while parasitism is a long-run imbalance that can exist in a relationship of many years. The Rescue Hook draws you into practical tasks through visible helplessness, whereas parasitism is about emotional attention. Warmth poured on at the start is the opposite of this slow drain, and belongs to Love Bombing.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Information Control
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Narrowing what someone reads, hears and learns, and who they talk to, so that one person's account becomes the main version of events available to them.
codex_completed.short_definition: Narrowing what someone reads, hears and learns, and who they talk to, so that one person's account becomes the main version of events available to them.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Information Control is the filtering of what reaches someone: which news, advice, people and records they see, and whose account of events counts. It can look like advising against sources, holding the post or the accounts, answering for the person, or reacting sharply whenever outside information appears. It is close to Isolation, but the focus is the flow of facts and the story, not who you may see. Warning about a bad source is ordinary. What marks it is outside views being shut off again and again, leaving the person little way to check anything for themselves.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: One person decides what you get to read, hear and know, so their version of events is the only one you have to think with.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A second opinion never reaches you, so a single account of events is all you have to reason with, and your doubts about it have nothing to be checked against.
what_it_is: Steering away from particular sources, such as a doctor, a relative, a news site or a support group, and offering a replacement that comes from the same person.
Handling the flow: opening the post, holding the passwords, speaking for you on calls, or sitting in on appointments.
Labeling outsiders as unreliable or hostile in advance, so what they say is discounted before you hear it.
Reacting with anger, hurt or mockery whenever you bring in something from elsewhere.
Occurring in couples, families, workplaces and groups where a leader decides what members may read.
what_it_sounds_like: You don't need to read that, it's all lies.
Your sister doesn't understand our situation. Don't tell her about this.
I'll call the bank for you. You'll only get confused.
Where did you hear that? Who's been filling your head?
That doctor doesn't know us. Just ask me.
Don't bother with the group chat, they only stir things up.
Everything you need to know, I'll tell you.
what_it_is_not: Warning someone about a source that really is unreliable, while leaving them free to look at it for themselves.
Someone who is simply uninformed and has no outside views to pass on, so is filtering nothing.
Limits on what young children watch or read, which loosen as the child grows.
A confidentiality rule at work that is disclosed to everyone, such as not discussing client files.
Taking over paperwork at your request, like a partner who handles the post while you recover from surgery and hands it back when you ask.
A friend who disagrees with an article you shared and says why.
this_may_be_it_when: Nearly everything you know about money, health or family reaches you through one person.
Outside sources are dismissed as a whole category instead of being judged one at a time.
Mail, accounts or appointments are handled for you without you asking.
Bringing in something from elsewhere gets anger or ridicule, not discussion.
Checking a fact for yourself brings a reaction about your trust.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They have told you why they doubt a source, and you remain free to read it.
You can open your own post, accounts and appointments whenever you wish.
Their doubt is limited to named sources and shifts when shown a better one.
You asked them to manage something for you, and you can take it back.
They pass on outside views as readily as their own.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Some people simply don't pass on news or opinions from elsewhere, because it doesn't occur to them.
A busy or anxious person may take over phone calls or forms because it is faster, and be glad to hand them back.
Households often split reading and paperwork without anyone meaning it as a ruling.
common_false_positives: A friend who tells you a health site gave them bad advice, and leaves the decision to you.
A carer who screens scam calls for an older relative who asked them to.
A team lead who keeps an announcement quiet until the company has cleared it.
discernment_questions: If I wanted to find something out on my own, could I do it without anyone minding?
Do I hear important things first from this person, or from several places?
When I bring up something from outside, do we talk about what it says or about the fact that I looked?
Is their doubt about outsiders specific, or does it cover everyone I know?
Have I stopped mentioning what I read or hear from other people?
less_concerning_if: You can read, call and visit freely, and nobody remarks on it.
Their opinion of a source comes with reasons you are invited to weigh.
You learn about the world from more than one person.
more_concerning_if: Mail, devices or accounts are held by them and access is refused when you ask.
The people you are told to avoid are the ones most likely to question the account you have been given.
You are told what you said or agreed to, and have no way to check.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find out from someone else that something you were told never happened, or happened differently.
You have dropped sources, friends or groups one at a time, each for a reason that seemed fair then.
You hesitate before sharing anything you find with this person.
Your picture of your own finances, health or family comes mostly from one voice.
codex_completed.repair_check: What comes back to you is the measure: passwords handed over, post opened by you, calls you make alone, outside sources discussed without a sneer. An apology while the same person still answers the phone for you leaves the channel as it was.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself a plain question after you request something: was it simply handed to you, and could you talk about it afterwards? If the conversation turns to why you needed to look, the request is being treated as the problem.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A person's sense of what is true leans heavily on cross-checking with others. When one source supplies most of the facts and discounts the rest in advance, the cross-check weakens, and the person may come to treat that source as the only reliable one. The more they depend on it for housing, money or belonging, the harder it can be to test its version.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Many are oddly unsure what is happening in their own finances, health or family, lean on one voice for facts, and feel guilty for wanting to look something up. Some find later that what they were told was incomplete, and grieve the lost time. Others feel foggy or isolated even when surrounded by people.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the information itself, calmly: 'Can you forward me that letter so I can read it too?' Their answer shows whether sharing is possible.
response_options.firm_boundary: State a plain need once: 'I want to see my own statements and open my own mail.' You can repeat the same sentence without justifying it each time.
response_options.disengagement: Stop explaining where you got a piece of information. You can read, call or ask someone in your own time and keep what you learn to yourself until you know what to do with it.
response_options.support_seeking: Check one or two facts you were given with an outside source you trust, like your own doctor, a bank, a library or a friend who knew you before, and compare.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In an organization, ask for the policy or notice in writing, and ask who else has seen it. Written records give you something to check against if information is withheld.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Could you send me a copy so I can read it myself? After that, I want to hear what you think of it."
codex_completed.safety_note: Control over information turns serious when it covers your phone, mail, identity documents, medical care or money, or when asking for them brings anger or threats. Keep a list of key numbers and copies of key documents somewhere only you can reach, such as a trusted friend's home, and ask a domestic abuse advocate about safe ways to rebuild your own access.
misuse_warning: Labeling a person who recommends one source over another as 'controlling' mistakes an opinion for a block. The question is whether you can go and look.
Applying it to a clinic, school or company that keeps things confidential assumes control where there is only a duty of privacy.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Isolation works on your relationships and who you may see, while Information Control works on what you may know, and can operate with you in a room full of people. Monitoring & Surveillance watches what you do; here the focus is what reaches you. "I Know Best" Paternalism overrides your choices openly, whereas this one narrows what you have to choose from.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Device Access Demands
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Insisting on passwords, an unlocked phone or account logins as proof of trust, so that having a private space is read as a sign of hiding something.
codex_completed.short_definition: Insisting on passwords, an unlocked phone or account logins as proof of trust, so that having a private space is read as a sign of hiding something.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Device Access Demands means requiring someone to hand over passwords, unlock their phone on request, or share logins to email, messages and social accounts. The demand is usually offered as reassurance, safety or the price of trust, or backed by an institution's authority. Sharing that both people chose, and can end, is a different thing; couples, families and workplaces do share some access. What marks it is access that is required rather than offered, a scope that keeps growing, and a refusal read as proof of concealment.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You are expected to hand over your phone or passwords whenever asked, and saying no is treated as if it proves you have something to hide.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Once saying no looks like guilt, privacy has to be defended instead of assumed. People can lose the ordinary sense that their messages, searches and private thoughts belong to them.
what_it_is: A request to see, unlock or log in to a phone, email, social accounts or cloud storage, often on demand and at any time.
Passwords or fingerprint unlock handed over as proof of loyalty or honesty.
Made by partners, parents of adults, employers asking about personal phones, or institutions that cite their authority.
Often worded as reassurance, such as 'so I know you're safe', which makes objecting feel like confessing.
Different from shared access that both people chose, because the key question is whether it can be taken back.
what_it_sounds_like: If you have nothing to hide, you won't mind me looking.
Unlock it. Now.
Give me your password, or I'll assume the worst.
Why did you change your passcode?
Couples shouldn't have secrets from each other.
Hand over the phone while we talk.
I just need to check that you're being safe online.
what_it_is_not: A mutually agreed, revocable arrangement, such as managing a young child's tablet or sharing a family account that either person can leave.
A disclosed institutional requirement applied to everyone, such as monitored work accounts with the policy in writing.
A streaming login, shared calendar or photo library that you both set up and either of you can end.
A one-off, like handing over a phone to show a specific message, with permission asked and the scope limited to that message.
Sharing a phone code with a trusted person while traveling, which you choose and undo.
this_may_be_it_when: Access is treated as a condition of the relationship or the job, not something offered.
Hesitation or refusal is read as an admission.
The demand covers more over time, from one account to all, from occasional to continuous.
A changed password or a deleted message is met with suspicion or anger.
What was read is used to question you about conversations with friends, family or colleagues.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You offered the access yourself and can decline it later without a penalty.
The openness is two-way, and they accept the same checks.
The scope is narrow and written down, such as a work email only.
A no was met with, at most, a question about why, and then accepted.
The device is a child's and the access matches the child's age.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Someone who has been cheated on, or who worries a great deal about safety, may ask for reassurance clumsily, and may let it go once the fear has been talked through.
Couples who grew up sharing everything may treat a shared phone as natural.
Some workplaces, schools and clubs require monitored accounts and say so up front.
common_false_positives: A partner who asks to look at your phone map while you're lost.
A parent who checks the settings on an eight-year-old's tablet.
An IT team that audits a company laptop, as the contract states.
discernment_questions: Did I offer this access, or was it asked for in a way that made refusing hard?
Could I take it back tomorrow without a fight?
Do they offer the same openness in return?
Has what I'm asked to share grown since the first time?
Is anything I've shared used to question me about friends, plans or whereabouts?
Would I feel safe changing my password today?
less_concerning_if: Both people share by choice and either can stop without a penalty.
The scope is stated and limited, such as a work account only.
A refusal was met with a question and then accepted.
more_concerning_if: Access is demanded in the middle of an argument, or used to check on your friends and where you have been.
Changing a password or setting a lock brings anger or accusations.
Apps or settings you did not install or agree to are on your device.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your passwords or unlock rights extend to more places, one request after another.
You delete messages or avoid friends to get ahead of the next inspection.
You check your phone before they do, in case something sets off a row.
They know about conversations you only had privately, or arrive already knowing where you were.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair means the access ends because you asked, and the phone stays yours afterwards. Pay attention to whether they let you change passcodes, stop asking, and cope with their own unease without a check. A promise to 'only look sometimes' keeps the demand alive.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself what happens when you simply keep the phone locked. Is there a conversation about the worry underneath, or a growing case that you are hiding something? Respect for privacy can sit beside the other person feeling uneasy; it does not require you to prove innocence.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Refusal gets recast as evidence, so a person who keeps privacy can look guilty just by keeping it. Over time, people may start to get ahead of the checks by deleting, avoiding or editing what they say, which shrinks their private life to what would survive being seen. Being observed can also make it harder to think, speak or confide freely.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Self-censorship creeps in: rewording texts, avoiding friends, feeling watched even when the phone is out of sight. Some feel ashamed for objecting and wonder whether they really do have something to hide. Others describe exhaustion from managing what might be read, and drifting away from people who were once easy to talk to.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask about the worry underneath rather than defending the phone: 'You sound frightened of something. Can you tell me what, and we can see what would help?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Offer what you will share, in terms of one item: 'I'll show you the photo you asked about. I'm not going to unlock the whole phone.' If you expect anger, choose a calm moment or talk to an advocate first.
response_options.disengagement: If a demand starts mid-argument, say you'll talk about it later and move on to another task. Keep your phone with you and use a code only you know.
response_options.support_seeking: Use someone else's phone or a library computer to talk to a friend, helpline or advocate about the demands, in case your own device is being read.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If an employer asks about a personal phone, ask which written policy requires it, and check with HR or a union before handing over anything beyond work accounts.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I can tell you're worried, and I want to talk about that. I'd rather tell you things than have my phone checked. What would help you feel more settled right now?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Access demands can sit alongside stalking, or threats about what will be done with whatever is found. Warning signs: the other person knows things you never told them, apps you did not install, or fear of what happens if you change a passcode. Contact a domestic abuse advocate from a device they cannot reach, and ask how to check your phone safely for tracking software.
misuse_warning: Treating a parent's age-appropriate checks on a child's device, or a partner's one-off 'show me that text', as this pattern overlooks consent and scope.
The label can be used to avoid accountability after someone has actually broken a trust, when a mutual conversation about rebuilding it would be fairer.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Monitoring & Surveillance covers any constant accounting of your day, whereas Device Access Demands is the specific act of getting into your phone and accounts. Location Tracking follows where you are; a device demand reveals what you say and to whom. Behavior Control sets rules about what you do; a device demand is one way those rules get checked.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Enforcing Trivial Demands
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Insisting on exact compliance with small, pointless-seeming rules, with a seriousness out of proportion to the stakes, until going along becomes routine.
codex_completed.short_definition: Insisting on exact compliance with small, pointless-seeming rules, with a seriousness out of proportion to the stakes, until going along becomes routine.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Enforcing Trivial Demands means holding people to small rules with no clear purpose, such as which way the towels hang, the order of a morning routine or the exact words of a greeting, and reacting strongly when they are missed. One fussy preference means little, and many rules have a reason not everyone knows. What marks it is rules that multiply, a reaction far bigger than the stakes, and no reason given, or a reason that keeps changing. Over time, complying becomes the default.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Petty rules with no point are enforced as if they mattered enormously, and you learn to follow them to keep the peace.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: When going along with petty rules becomes automatic, going along with big ones can feel like the same small step. The person also loses the ability to tell what truly matters to the other and what is just upkeep.
what_it_is: Rules about details with no visible purpose: how the dishwasher is stacked, how a bed is made, where the keys hang, the order of a morning routine.
Enforced with weight, such as sighs, a lecture, silence or a redo, that doesn't fit the thing that was missed.
Rules that tend to multiply or move, so a person who gets one right finds another waiting.
Reasons that are absent, or that shift when questioned.
Seen in homes, workplaces, sports teams and groups where a leader sets the rituals.
what_it_sounds_like: No, the cups go handle-out. I've told you.
Do it again. Properly.
It's not about the towel, it's about listening.
Why can't you just do it the way I asked?
We do it my way in this house.
You walked in with your shoes on. Is that how little you care?
I said the lid faces left.
what_it_is_not: A personal preference about how things are done, explained and flexible, which is ordinary fussiness and nothing more.
A rule with a function the person hasn't been told, like the food-safety order in a kitchen or a lab's labeling system.
High standards in a craft or role the person cares about, applied to themselves as much as to you.
A routine that helps someone with sensory needs or anxiety, which they explain and which is open to adjustment.
House rules agreed jointly, like a chore chart everybody wrote.
A family or cultural custom with a meaning everyone understands, like taking shoes off at the door.
this_may_be_it_when: You can't find the purpose of the rule, and asking for one produces irritation.
The reaction to a slip is large, such as an hour's lecture or a day's silence, for something that took a second.
New rules appear as soon as you've got the old ones right.
Others in the household or team aren't held to them.
The rule shifts: fine last week, wrong this week.
this_may_not_be_it_when: There is a simple reason, and once you hear it the rule makes sense.
The same rule applies to the person who made it.
A slip brings a reminder, and then the matter ends.
You can suggest a different way and it's considered.
The rule came from a shared decision.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people have strong habits about order that matter far more to them than they sensibly should, and are easily satisfied.
Stress makes some people tighten their grip on small things when bigger things feel out of control.
A rule may come from childhood or an earlier job, and not occur to them as needing explanation.
common_false_positives: A flatmate who cares intensely about how knives are washed, and listens when you explain you can't always manage.
A coach whose warm-up order seems arbitrary but ties to injury prevention.
A partner with an exacting way of folding laundry who happily lets you do it your way when asked.
discernment_questions: Can anyone, including me, explain what the rule is for?
Is the reaction in proportion to what happened?
Does the person who set the rule follow it too?
Are the rules growing or changing as I get them right?
What happens if I do it differently once, and how do I feel about the answer?
Is there anywhere in this relationship where my way is simply accepted?
less_concerning_if: Rules come with reasons, or with a shrug and a willingness to drop them.
Slips are met in proportion and then forgotten.
The person following the rules has a say in making or changing them.
more_concerning_if: Tiny breaches bring raised voices, threats about the relationship or things taken away.
The list grows until most of your day is spent keeping to it.
The rules touch on food, sleep, money, clothes or contact with other people.
pattern_over_time_signs: You check each step of a task for the 'right' way before you start.
You are worn out by evening from vigilance, though little has happened.
You apologize for things you can't name afterwards.
Bigger requests, about money, time or friends, now get a quicker yes than they would have before.
codex_completed.repair_check: Something has shifted when a rule is dropped or explained and the strong reaction does not simply move on to the next small thing. Watch what happens to the list: does it shrink, and can you do things your own way without a penalty? A single apology while the rules stay does not change the day-to-day.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Compare two responses. One person lets you load the dishwasher your way and may say it isn't how they would do it. Another has you redo it, or finds a new rule once the old one lapses. The first leaves your way of doing things alone; the second keeps the structure.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Small repeated compliance can build a habit that no longer needs thought. When pushing back on something petty brings a big reaction and giving in brings calm, people may learn to choose calm, and the habit can carry over to larger requests. Missing reasons can also leave a person anxious, trying to guess what the rules are.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe tiredness from constant vigilance, feeling like a child or a new employee in their own home, and doubting their own sense of what is reasonable. Some feel shame at having obeyed rules they could not defend. Others notice that they now defer on bigger things as well, and cannot say when that began.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask what the rule is for in a curious tone: 'Help me understand why the cups go that way, so I can get it right.' A reason or a shrug will both tell you something.
response_options.firm_boundary: Say plainly that you will do this task your way: 'I'll load the dishwasher, and I'll do it how I do it.' Keep your tone level and your reasons short. If you expect anger, pick a calmer moment or skip this one.
response_options.disengagement: Pick one or two rules that cost you nothing and let others pass without comment, so your energy goes to the ones that matter. Choosing what to follow is different from giving in to all of it.
response_options.support_seeking: List the rules you follow in a typical week and show the list to someone outside the home or team. Their reaction to the length of it can help you see what has become normal.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: For petty procedures from a manager, ask for them in the written process and note who else has to follow them. If you are singled out, keep dated examples for HR or a union representative.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Getting this right matters to me. Can you tell me what the rule is for? If there's no particular reason, let me try it this other way and see how that goes."
codex_completed.safety_note: Petty rules become a safety issue when missing one brings shouting, threats, damage to your things, or the loss of food, sleep, money or a place to live. Rules about who you contact or what you wear deserve attention too. If the reaction to a small slip frightens you, tell someone outside the home and ask a domestic abuse advocate how to think through next steps.
misuse_warning: Calling a strong preference 'trivial demands' can dismiss someone with real sensory or safety reasons they find hard to explain. Ask for the reason before judging.
A single fussy request, or a house rule you simply dislike, is not the pattern; the label needs rules that multiply and reactions out of proportion.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Behavior Control sets rules about big areas, such as clothing, movement and friends, while this one is about small, purposeless details and the weight put on them. Infantilization treats you as unable to manage your affairs, which can include picky rules but is about capacity. "I Know Best" Paternalism has a stated reason, 'for your own good'; trivial demands often have none.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Boundary Testing
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Crossing a stated or implied limit in small steps, where each step that goes unchallenged is followed by a slightly bigger one.
codex_completed.short_definition: Crossing a stated or implied limit in small steps, where each step that goes unchallenged is followed by a slightly bigger one.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Boundary Testing is a run of small crossings of a limit someone has stated or clearly implied: arriving an hour early, a touch on the arm, borrowing without asking, repeating a personal question after a no. Each step is minor enough that objecting feels petty, which lets the line shift without any moment where it was held. A single mistake, or someone unsure where the line is, is not this. What marks it is crossings that repeat after the limit has been made clear, each a little bigger than the last.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone keeps nudging past a line you have drawn, a little further each time, so that it never seems big enough to make a fuss about.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Since no single step seems worth a row, the line can move a long way without one clear moment to hold it. The person on the receiving end often feels the shift only afterwards, and wonders why they didn't say something sooner.
what_it_is: A series of crossings, each slightly past the last: a late-night text, then a call, then turning up uninvited.
Landing on limits that were stated, or that the situation makes obvious, such as privacy, touch, time, money or the scope of a job.
Often followed by a gap, after which a bigger crossing may appear if the first went unremarked.
Met, when objected to, with 'it's nothing' or 'you're overreacting'.
Seen in friendships, dating, parenting, workplaces and between clients and professionals.
what_it_sounds_like: It's just a hug, relax.
I only borrowed it. You never mind.
Oh come on, one more drink won't hurt.
I know you said no calls after nine, but this was important.
You're making a big deal out of nothing.
I wasn't going to ask, but I'm already outside.
You didn't say anything last time.
what_it_is_not: A one-off misjudgement with nothing following it, which is a mistake.
Someone unclear where the line sits who adjusts once told, and so has done exactly the right thing.
Good-faith negotiation about where a reasonable limit should sit, such as asking whether a rule can bend for a special occasion.
A toddler or teenager pressing on edges as part of growing up, who needs a steady reply rather than suspicion.
A new colleague who doesn't yet know the office habits and stops when told.
Different customs about closeness or timing, such as dropping in unannounced being normal in someone's family.
this_may_be_it_when: The same limit is crossed again after you have stated it plainly.
Each crossing is a little larger than the one before.
When you object, the answer is that it's small, or that you didn't mind before.
The crossings come at moments when objecting would be awkward, such as in company.
A nearby version of the same crossing turns up after you hold one line, like a text where a call used to be.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Once you have said where the line is, it stays put.
They apologize when told and don't repeat it.
The crossing happened somewhere the limit couldn't have been known.
It is one event, and nothing bigger followed.
They ask permission first and take no for an answer.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Norms differ between families, cultures and workplaces, and people can honestly misjudge what is welcome.
People sometimes check mildly whether a limit still stands after circumstances change, like a new job or an illness.
Young children and teenagers learn by pressing on edges, and a steady reply is ordinary parenting.
common_false_positives: A friend who asks again, a month later, whether you'd like to come, after you said no once.
A neighbor who forgets your parking request until reminded.
A coworker who messages at 7 pm and was never told your hours.
discernment_questions: Did I state this limit clearly, and did it hold afterwards?
Is each crossing a bit bigger than the one before?
When I object, do they adjust, or move to a nearby crossing?
Do the crossings come when it would be awkward for me to object?
Would I be comfortable with where the line is now, if it had been there from the start?
less_concerning_if: The person stops when told and doesn't try the same thing again.
The crossings come from honest uncertainty, and they ask where the line is.
The size of the crossings stays the same or shrinks.
more_concerning_if: Crossings move from objects and time toward your body, your privacy or your safety.
Objecting makes things worse, through sulking, retaliation or being told you are difficult.
They seem to choose moments when no one else is present.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your limits now sit somewhere different from where you started, and you can't point to when they moved.
You catch yourself saying 'it's not that bad' more often.
You weigh up whether each new thing is worth raising.
You have started arranging your days to avoid certain moments with them.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair looks like the limit holding after you have named it: the early arrivals stop, the midnight text doesn't come, and a nearby version doesn't appear in its place. Lasting change is seen over months, not in an apology made while the next small step is already under way.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: State the limit in one clear sentence and then watch what comes in its place. Is the same step repeated, a neighboring one tried, or does the limit simply hold? One neighboring step is information; a string of them is a pattern.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Small steps can make resistance feel out of proportion. After a person has let several pass, objecting to the next may feel inconsistent, as if permission had been given earlier, and it takes more effort to hold a line they have already let slide. Being told it is nothing can add doubt about whether their own sense of a line is reasonable.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A nagging unease that is hard to justify is common, along with replaying moments to see whether they overreacted and feeling foolish for not objecting earlier. Some become wary of the person without being able to explain why to others. Many say they felt relief when they saw the steps laid out in order.

response_options.soft_clarification: Describe the sequence in neutral terms and ask whether they knew: 'This is the third call after nine. I'd said I'd rather not take calls then, so I wasn't sure you remembered.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Restate the limit in one short sentence and add no reasons: 'No calls after nine.' If a neighboring version appears, point to the same limit in the same calm tone.
response_options.disengagement: Let late messages wait until morning and answer in the form you prefer. Not replying at once is a limit in itself, and needs no announcement.
response_options.support_seeking: Write down dates and what happened, then tell someone you trust the whole list at once. Seen together, the small steps often look different from how they felt one at a time.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work or with clients, restate the limit in writing, such as 'Please contact me during office hours only', and keep dated copies of the crossings for your manager or HR.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I said no calls after nine, and this one came at ten. I'd like us to keep to that, and I'm happy to talk about what was so urgent."
codex_completed.safety_note: Testing becomes a safety matter when the steps move toward your body, your home, your location or your belongings, or when saying no to a small step brings anger. Trust the discomfort you notice early. If the crossings include touch you did not agree to, following you, or turning up uninvited at home, keep a dated record and contact an advocate or the police non-emergency line.
misuse_warning: Reading every awkward misstep as testing can punish people who simply didn't know the limit. The label needs a limit that was clear and a crossing that repeated.
Telling someone they are 'testing' you in the middle of a disagreement can end the chance for them to just say sorry and adjust.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Behavior Control issues rules about your clothes, movement or friends, while boundary testing pushes at rules you have set yourself. Monitoring & Surveillance asks for standing access and accounting; testing can be a single extra question or visit, repeated and growing. Location Tracking is a fixed condition, whereas a testing step may be arriving unannounced where you are, once, and then again.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Velvet Glove Control
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Narrowing someone's choices through warmth, concern and gentle persistence instead of force, so that the loss of their say is hard to see.
codex_completed.short_definition: Narrowing someone's choices through warmth, concern and gentle persistence instead of force, so that the loss of their say is hard to see.
