this_may_be_it_when: Forgiveness is requested before anyone has said out loud what happened.
The person asking has a stake: they caused the harm, or they want to avoid conflict at an event.
You are given a date by which you are expected to feel better.
Refusing is described as bitterness, holding a grudge, or ruining the day.
Talking about the harm is treated as more disruptive than the harm.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They acknowledged what happened before asking, and have asked what you need.
You are told you can take as long as you need.
Forgiveness is offered as a hope, as in 'I hope someday', not as a demand.
The person asking has nothing to gain and is open to hearing no.
You wanted to move on and started the conversation yourself.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Relatives who hate conflict may press for peace because they love both people and fear a rift, not to excuse the harm.
Some cultures and faiths treat forgiveness as a duty of community and urge it as a kindness.
People who have forgiven something themselves may wish the same relief for you.
common_false_positives: A couple agreeing to drop an argument after each has said their part.
A grandparent saying 'I don't want to see you two apart' as a wish for reunion, with no demand attached.
A therapist who explores forgiveness as one of several options at your pace.
discernment_questions: Has what happened been said out loud and acknowledged by the person responsible?
Who benefits if I forgive today?
Is the deadline mine, or someone else's?
Is 'no' an acceptable answer, or does it cost me something?
Am I allowed to forgive and still keep my distance?
less_concerning_if: Forgiveness is asked as a gift, and a 'not yet' is accepted.
The people urging it have also heard your account.
You feel free to say no without a penalty.
more_concerning_if: Others are brought in to urge you, such as family, clergy or mutual friends who have not heard your side.
Your refusal costs you something: invitations, support, belonging.
The harm is described as past, while the conduct behind it continues.
pattern_over_time_signs: You become more careful about mentioning what happened, because the mention is seen as the problem.
You act more forgiving in public than you feel.
You are invited to events on the understanding that you will behave as though nothing happened.
The list of subjects you cannot bring up gets longer.
codex_completed.repair_check: Where forgiveness follows real repair, the order is visible: acknowledgment first, then change, then room for you to decide in your own time. If the request to forgive arrives first, or 'moving on' is the only repair on offer, the sequence has been turned round.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: What happens when you say 'not yet' or 'no'? Respect looks like patience and perhaps a question about what you need. Disrespect looks like a cooler tone, a reminder of how much time has passed, or other people being sent to persuade you.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Forgiveness is widely praised, so being asked for it can make hesitation feel like a personal failing. When the request comes from family or a community, the cost of refusing can include losing belonging. Hurrying toward peace can also spare everyone the discomfort of the facts, letting the group relax while the hurt person absorbs the cost.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe swallowing anger to keep the peace, feeling guilty for still being hurt, and being shut out of the conversation they needed. Some say they pretended to forgive and felt more alone afterwards. Others describe losing trust in the people who urged them to move on.

response_options.soft_clarification: Separate the two things: 'I do want us to be okay, and I need to talk about what happened before I can get there.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline the deadline: 'Forgiveness isn't something I can schedule. I'll tell you if and when I get there, and until then, please don't ask.'
response_options.disengagement: You can skip events or conversations where you will be expected to act as if nothing happened, without explaining yourself to everyone.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk to someone outside the family or group who will not be asked to take sides, such as a counselor, a faith leader you trust, or a friend, and ask what they would want from you.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager asks you to bury the hatchet before a complaint has been looked at, ask in writing how the complaint is being handled, and make clear that forgiving is not a condition of the process.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'd like things to be better between us. Before I can forgive, I need what happened to be acknowledged, and I can't rush that. Please don't ask me again for now. I'll tell you when I'm ready."
codex_completed.safety_note: Pressure to forgive can keep a person in contact with someone who hurt them, which matters most when the harm was violence, abuse or threats. Forgiving in your heart does not oblige you to see anyone or be alone with them. If you are being pushed to go back to a person you fear, a domestic violence or sexual assault advocate can help you plan how to say no and stay safe. In immediate danger, call emergency services.
misuse_warning: Telling anyone who urges peace that they are 'forcing forgiveness' can silence people who sincerely want to help, or who are themselves hurt by the rift.
The label can harden into a rule that forgiveness must never be asked of anyone. A gentle invitation is not coercion.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Minimization says the harm was small, so your reaction looks too big; forced forgiveness may accept the harm was real and still demand that you stop feeling it. Denial disputes the events, where this skips past them. A Non-Apology Apology offers a hollow sorry to close things; here the sorry may be missing entirely, and the pressure falls on your forgiveness instead.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Plausible Deniability
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Acting in ways that can always be explained as concern, policy or accident, so no single incident can be called harmful without the accuser sounding unfair.
codex_completed.short_definition: Acting in ways that can always be explained as concern, policy or accident, so no single incident can be called harmful without the accuser sounding unfair.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Plausible deniability is a structure in which each action arrives with a reasonable explanation attached: 'I was worried about you', 'it's company policy', 'I didn't mean it like that', 'that must have been a mistake'. Often the explanation is simply true. What makes it a pattern, rather than a run of ordinary events, is that the effects add up in one direction while every single example can be defended. In politics and law the term has a formal sense of leaders arranging to claim ignorance. This entry covers the everyday version, and it does not show what anyone intended.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Every time something harmful happens, there is a decent-sounding reason, so you can never point to one thing without feeling unfair. Only the whole pile shows the shape.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Every incident comes with a fair-sounding explanation, so raising any one of them can make the person raising it look unreasonable. The pattern can only be described by pointing at things that, taken separately, look like nothing.
what_it_is: A reasonable explanation attached to each act: concern, rules, humor, accident or misunderstanding.
Visible across many incidents more than in any one, as the same direction of effect repeats over time.
Works through ambiguity: things left unsaid, a 'suggestion' standing in for an order, or responsibility spread thin through a process.
Found in homes, workplaces, institutions and friend groups.
Can be a feature of a system as well as a person, when nobody is clearly responsible for outcomes.
what_it_sounds_like: I was only worried about you. That's why I read your messages.
It's just policy. My hands are tied.
I didn't mean it that way. You're reading into it.
It was a joke. Where's your sense of humor?
I was just being honest.
I never told you not to go. I just said I'd be upset.
I must have forgotten to tell you about the change to your shifts.
Nobody said you couldn't. We just thought it would look bad.
what_it_is_not: People do follow policy and do worry about others. Often the innocent explanation is simply the true one.
Someone careful and honest can sound identical to someone producing cover. One ambiguous incident cannot separate the two, which is why this belongs at the level of a pattern.
Honest mistakes that happen to cluster, such as a disorganized manager whose errors hit everyone.
Tact and indirectness. Hinting to avoid conflict is the polite norm in many families and cultures.
An understaffed office where problems come from chaos and not from any design.
this_may_be_it_when: Effects line up in one direction across months, such as your access to money, friends or time narrowing, while each reason differs.
The explanations arrive quickly, before you have said what troubled you.
Asking about one incident prompts a response about how suspicious you are.
The reasons change with the circumstance but the outcome does not.
Policy or concern is applied to you in ways it is not applied to others in the same position.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The outcomes vary: sometimes they help you, sometimes they do not.
The same rule affects others in your position equally.
When you object, the action stops or is adjusted.
They invite checking: 'Ask HR', 'read the policy yourself'.
Laid out over time, there is no consistent direction of harm.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People often explain themselves because they expect to be misread.
Genuine care can be clumsy and intrusive without being a strategy.
Organizations often apply rules rigidly through staff who cannot change them.
Indirect speech is the polite norm in many families and cultures.
common_false_positives: A manager enforcing a policy that applies to everyone, who says 'it's policy' because it is.
A worried parent or partner who checks in, and stops when asked.
A joke that landed badly, followed by a sincere 'sorry, that was off'.
discernment_questions: If I set the explanations aside and look only at what happened, is there a direction?
Are the same reasons used for different incidents, or does a new one appear each time?
Does the same rule apply to others in my position?
What happens when I describe the effect on me and leave the reasons alone?
If I wrote down five incidents with dates, would they point the same way?
less_concerning_if: Laid out on paper, the incidents show no consistent harmful effect.
When you tell them the effect on you, they change what they do.
Others in the same position are treated in the same way.
more_concerning_if: Each reason is plausible, and the combined effect cuts you off from money, people or options.
Naming the effect, rather than the reason, is met with annoyance or the suggestion that you are paranoid.
When the first explanation is checked, a different one appears and the action continues.
pattern_over_time_signs: You collect incidents, each too small to bring up.
Your list of things you cannot do or cannot see keeps growing, with a reason beside each.
You rehearse how to raise something so that it will not sound unreasonable.
You wonder whether you are being unfair, even when the effects are plain.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair here means the effect changes, not only the explanation. If you tell them what the pattern is doing to you and the behavior adjusts, so that you get your information or access back, that is repair. A fresh, equally reasonable reason for the same outcome is not.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: State the effect you need to stop, without arguing over their reasons, and watch the next few weeks. Respect shows as the effect ending, whatever their explanation. If a new justification appears for the same outcome, the boundary has been routed around, not honored.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When every action comes with a reasonable explanation, the listener tends to judge each incident alone, and each looks too small to object to. Objecting then carries a social cost, since it can make the objector seem suspicious or ungrateful. Doubt can turn inward, with the person wondering whether their reaction is the problem rather than the pattern.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe a creeping doubt about whether they are being unreasonable, a habit of saving up incidents that each feel too small, and difficulty explaining to others why they are troubled. Some feel isolated by how reasonable everything sounds. Others describe relief when they put the incidents on paper and see the shape for the first time.

response_options.soft_clarification: Describe the effect and leave the reason alone: 'I know you were worried. What happens is that I no longer see my own messages. Can we find another way?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Stop arguing over intent: 'Whatever the reason, this is what it is doing to me, and I need it to stop.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop accepting each explanation as a final answer. You can say 'I hear the reason' and still keep your own copies of documents, accounts and contacts.
response_options.support_seeking: Write the incidents down with dates and take the list to someone outside the situation. Ask whether the direction looks as clear to them as it does on paper.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask for the policy in writing and ask whether it is applied the same way to others. If the answers do not hold, take your dated list to HR or an ombuds.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I believe you may have good reasons each time, and I'm not asking you to prove them. What I'm telling you is that, taken together, these things leave me with less say over my own days. I need that to change."
codex_completed.safety_note: Concern and rules are a common explanation for controlling behavior such as reading your messages, tracking your location, holding your documents, or limiting your contact with friends and money. If the explanations lead to you losing access to those things, or you fear the response to questions, take your dated list to a domestic abuse advocate or, at work, an employment lawyer. Keep copies of key documents somewhere safe outside the situation.
misuse_warning: Not every explanation is a cover story. Treating all reasons as cover makes honest explanation impossible and makes the label impossible to disprove.
Because the term describes a pattern, using it on a single incident turns an ambiguous event into an accusation it cannot support.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Denial says the act did not happen; here the act is admitted and given a good reason. Minimization plays down harm after it has been named, while here the explanation arrives before anyone has named any harm. Blame-Shifting places the fault on you; here nobody is at fault, because the explanation says nothing went wrong.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Feigned Ignorance
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Acting as if you do not know or cannot follow something, so that a responsibility is dropped or a hard conversation is put off.
codex_completed.short_definition: Acting as if you do not know or cannot follow something, so that a responsibility is dropped or a hard conversation is put off.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Feigned ignorance is a show of not knowing: blank looks, requests to have things explained again, or a sudden fog over an agreement made last week. What stands out is where the fog lands. The same person follows plans, schedules and jokes without trouble, but cannot seem to grasp the one thing that would cost them something. One lapse means little, since people forget and misunderstand. The telling feature is the not-knowing arriving, again and again, on the same inconvenient subjects.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone acts clueless about exactly the thing they would have to answer for, while understanding everything else just fine, so the matter stays unsettled.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: When a person seems not to understand, nothing can be settled, because the shared basis for settling it is missing. Whoever raised the issue ends up explaining it again and again instead of getting an answer.
what_it_is: A selective fog: normal understanding on most subjects, and puzzlement mainly on the one that carries a cost.
Often shows up as a request to be told again, which restarts the conversation from the beginning each time.
Seen in households (chores, bills, promises), at work (instructions, deadlines, policies) and among friends (plans, borrowed things).
Different from refusing outright: the person may seem willing and even apologetic, yet nothing changes because the point was never taken in.
what_it_sounds_like: "Wait, what promise? I honestly don't remember us agreeing to that."
"Can you explain the due date again? I'm not sure I ever saw it."
"I had no idea that was a rule here." (said about a rule they signed off on)
"I didn't realize that was a problem." (said after the third conversation about it)
"You'll have to walk me through what you mean. I'm lost."
A blank look and "huh?" when the topic turns to their share of the work, followed by easy chat about something else.
what_it_is_not: Ordinary forgetting, which is strongest in busy or sleepless stretches and hits many subjects, including ones that matter to the person.
A real gap in knowledge on a hard topic, such as taxes, a legal form or a medical term, where confusion matches difficulty and not convenience.
Someone who was truly not in the room, never saw the message, or got a different version of the plan.
A person who asks for a second explanation, listens, and then acts on it. Asking twice is not evasion.
Cultural or language differences that make an instruction land differently than it was meant.
this_may_be_it_when: The confusion appears only on topics that would ask something of the person, and clears up on topics that benefit them.
There is a record, such as a text, a signed form or a witness, showing they understood at the time.
Each explanation is followed by a new round of not-knowing rather than by action.
The person reads, calculates and remembers well in other parts of life, such as work, hobbies or money they care about.
The questions they ask are never the ones that would move things forward, only ones that restart the explanation.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The confusion shows up on many topics, including ones they care about, and eases after a clear reminder.
After one more explanation they do the thing, and keep doing it.
They tell you what they are missing, such as 'I never got that email', and it checks out.
The subject really is technical or new to them, and they ask the kind of questions someone learning would ask.
They say 'I don't remember, but I believe you' and then act on it.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A week of poor sleep, grief or illness can blur memory of everyday agreements.
People often hear a request while distracted, and later honestly have no memory of agreeing.
Some people freeze or go blank under criticism and truly cannot recall details in that moment, then remember them later.
An unclear instruction can fail to register even with the best will.
common_false_positives: A relative who really does not follow how a bank app or benefits form works.
A coworker who never received the policy update because it went to a different mailing list.
A partner who says 'I don't remember that' about something said while they were on a work call.
discernment_questions: Does the not-knowing land on certain subjects only, while the person is sharp about others?
Is there anything in writing, or a witness, showing what they understood at the time?
After a clear explanation, does anything actually change, or does the same question return?
If the topic were one they cared about winning, would they still be confused?
Have I been assuming they should know, when I never actually told them in a way they could have received?
less_concerning_if: The confusion spreads across many subjects and fades once you give a short written reminder.
They act on the explanation the first or second time it is given.
They are open about what they do not know and ask for what would fill the gap.
more_concerning_if: There is clear evidence they understood, and the confusion still appears each time the topic returns.
The topic is a safety, money or care matter, so each round of 'I didn't know' leaves you carrying the cost.
You are now writing everything down and sending reminders because verbal agreements keep vanishing.
pattern_over_time_signs: You stop raising the issue verbally because you know you will be asked to explain it from scratch.
A growing list of things you now do yourself, because waiting for them to 'get it' took too long.
The same topic has been 'explained' several times over months with no change in what happens.
You start saving messages and writing agreements down, not out of distrust of everyone, but of this one subject.
codex_completed.repair_check: Look for them to repeat back, in their own words, what was agreed and then do it without being asked a second time. Something that only looks like repair is a warm apology for the misunderstanding, followed by the same blank look next month.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: After you say you will explain it once, in writing, does the writing get read and used? A respectful answer is a reply like 'got it, I will do that by Friday'. A telling answer is a request to go through it all again out loud.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Appearing not to know can shift the work of the conversation onto the person who raised the issue. They tend to start explaining, defending the reasonableness of the request, or wondering whether they were clear enough, and the original concern slides out of view. Each repeat explanation can also wear down the energy people have to keep raising it.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Common accounts include a particular tiredness from explaining the same thing over and over, a growing habit of doing the task alone, and a nagging question of whether the request was ever clear. Some end up feeling that nagging has become their job, with trust wearing away in small steps long before any single incident stood out.

response_options.soft_clarification: Put the point in one clear sentence and ask them to restate it: 'So we're on the same page, can you tell me what you heard me ask for?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say you will explain once and then expect action: 'I've gone over this twice. I'm not going to explain it a third time, but I'll send it in writing.'
response_options.disengagement: When the explanation loop restarts, end it for now: 'I can tell we're going round again. Let's stop and pick it up after you've read what I sent.'
response_options.support_seeking: Ask someone who knows you both whether the agreement as you describe it sounds clear, to check whether the problem is in how it was said.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Confirm instructions and deadlines by email straight after the conversation, and ask for a reply that restates the task, so the record shows what was understood.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I've explained this twice, and I think it was clear. I'm going to send you the plan in writing today. I'd like you to read it and tell me by Friday what you will take on."
codex_completed.safety_note: This is rarely a danger on its own. It deserves more care if the 'I didn't know' covers money, medication, children's needs or a legal deadline, where the cost of a missed duty falls on you or someone dependent. Then put the specific duty in writing, and if a deadline or a child's welfare is involved, contact the relevant office or a legal aid service.
misuse_warning: Deciding that someone is 'faking it' because they didn't remember is a quick way to be unfair to people with real memory, attention or language difficulties.
Using the label to dismiss every honest question can punish people who just need a clearer explanation.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Denial says the thing did not happen or was not wrong, while feigned ignorance claims not to have known or understood it. Minimization admits it happened but shrinks the harm. Blame-Shifting assigns the fault to you instead of to a gap in knowledge. Here the claim is 'I did not know', and the test is whether that fits what else you have seen them understand.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Victim Role Reversal
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Presenting oneself as the injured party when asked to answer for harm, so that sympathy and comforting move away from the person who was actually hurt.
codex_completed.short_definition: Presenting oneself as the injured party when asked to answer for harm, so that sympathy and comforting move away from the person who was actually hurt.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Victim role reversal happens when someone asked to account for a harm answers by describing their own suffering, and the person harmed ends up comforting them or apologizing. It is also called role reversal traps, and the two are the same tactic under different names. The hurt they describe may be real. The pattern is in the effect: a talk about what was done to you becomes a talk about how awful this is for them. One tearful reaction proves little. Repetition is what matters.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: After hurting you, they become the one who is hurt, and you, and maybe everyone around you, end up looking after them while what happened to you drops out of the room.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Sympathy that should have gone to the person harmed goes elsewhere, and the person harmed ends up soothing and apologizing. Onlookers form an impression that is very hard to correct later, and the person harmed may start doubting whether they have the right to be upset.
what_it_is: A swap in who is treated as wounded, usually after someone is told how their behavior landed.
Often delivered to an audience such as family, a friend group, a team or a congregation, not just to the person harmed.
The distress may be sincere. What defines the pattern is that it takes over the space where the other person's injury should be heard.
Ends in a trade: the person harmed reassures, defends themselves, or goes quiet to avoid causing more pain.
Can be built from several smaller moves, such as tears, a speech about how hard things are, or a plea for patience.
what_it_sounds_like: "After everything I've done, this is how I'm treated? I'm the one who's been hurt here."
"Do you have any idea how hard this has been for me?" (after you raised what they did)
"I'm the one everyone piles onto. Nobody ever asks how I'm doing."
A mutual friend saying, "I just don't think you realize how much you've hurt them." (about the person who raised the complaint)
"I guess I'm just a terrible person, then. Is that what you want me to say?"
"I can't handle this right now. I need you to be supportive."
You, a few minutes after you were the one wronged: "I'm sorry I brought it up."
Tearful silence and withdrawal as soon as the complaint is named, followed by you finding yourself offering a hug.
what_it_is_not: Two people who were both hurt in the same conflict, each with a fair claim to be heard.
Someone overcome by guilt who cries or goes quiet but still hears you out and acknowledges what they did.
A person who is also going through something painful and separate, such as a loss, an illness or a job crisis, and says so without using it to close the topic.
Mutual reassurance after a conflict, which is a normal part of making up when the harm has been named first.
A person who is overwhelmed, steps away briefly and returns to deal with what happened.
this_may_be_it_when: The claim of being hurt appears right when responsibility is raised and not at other times.
Others start comforting them and your account gets less airtime each time it is told.
You end up reassuring them about the very thing you came to talk about.
The harm done to you is never restated by them, even in summary.
Over several incidents, the conversation ends with them as the most wronged person present.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They stay with your account first and talk about their own pain afterward.
Their distress existed before the conversation and has an independent source you can see.
Both of you leave feeling heard, even if neither fully won.
They can say, in their own words, what happened to you, and the sympathy for you is plain.
The tears or withdrawal were brief and the discussion then went on.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people feel real shame on hearing they hurt someone, and it can look like self-focus.
A conflict can have two injured parties, and some of what sounds like reversal is each person naming their own hurt.
A person who is already struggling may have little left to cope with criticism and may respond with visible despair.
Some people were raised in homes where upset meant someone had to be soothed, and repeat that without thinking.
common_false_positives: A friend who says 'I feel awful about this' and then asks what they can do to make it right.
A partner who is also hurt by a shared argument, and says so after hearing you.
A relative in grief who snaps at you and later apologizes.
discernment_questions: After the conversation, whose pain was discussed the most, and whose was dropped?
Does the hurt they describe appear only when I raise something that asks them to answer?
Have other people started taking their side based on how they tell it, without hearing mine?
Can they, at any point, say back what happened to me?
Do I now apologize or comfort first, before I have said what I came to say?
less_concerning_if: Their feelings were voiced after yours were acknowledged.
You still came away with your original concern on the table and a plan for it.
This happened once during a very hard week and has not repeated.
more_concerning_if: Other people now treat the person harmed as the aggressor, based on what they were told.
The pattern repeats on every topic where accountability could be asked for.
The person harmed has stopped raising concerns at all because it always costs them the relationship.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your complaints now come with a mental note: how will this make them cry, and what will it cost me?
People close to you have formed a picture of you as the harsh one, though you rarely raise things.
Over months, a long list of things you stopped mentioning to avoid hurting them.
You find yourself explaining to others that you were not attacking, before they have said anything.
codex_completed.repair_check: Genuine repair starts with the original harm being named by them, in specific terms, before their own distress is brought in, and with the person harmed no longer asked to carry their feelings. Warm words about how sorry they are that you are upset do not do this.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself whether, once you said you needed to finish your point, you were allowed to. Notice if their sadness deepens until you stop, or if they can sit with discomfort while you speak. The first leaves your point unheard; the second does not.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Most people are quick to comfort someone who is visibly distressed, and slow to keep pressing a point while they do. When a person shows suffering at the moment of accountability, that habit can pull attention away from the harm. Onlookers who only hear the distressed version tend to settle on it, and a person who was harmed may feel guilty for causing visible pain.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Accounts often mention guilt at having 'made them cry', hesitation to bring anything up again, and anger or confusion at being cast as the aggressor. Some recall ending up the soother, others the one whose version nobody asked for. Over time a few pull back from friends or family who only heard one side.

response_options.soft_clarification: Acknowledge the pain and keep your point: 'I can see this is really hard for you. I still need to finish telling you what happened to me.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline the comforting role for now: 'I care that you're hurting, but I can't look after you in this conversation. I need us to talk about what happened.'
response_options.disengagement: If the tears or accusations take over, ask for a pause: 'Let's stop for today and come back to this tomorrow, when we've both slept.'
response_options.support_seeking: Tell your account to someone before the other version spreads, and ask them to hear the whole thing before saying anything about the other person.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, write down what happened with dates before meeting a manager or HR, and ask for a process that lets both accounts be recorded separately.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'm sorry you're hurting, and I want to hear about it later. Right now I need you to hear what happened from my side first. After that, I will listen as long as you need."
codex_completed.safety_note: This pattern alone is not a physical-safety concern. It changes when the person who is 'hurt' also says they will harm themselves if you pull back, spreads the story to cut you off from friends, or uses it to shape custody or workplace decisions. Keep a dated record of what was said and who heard it, and contact a crisis line about any self-harm statement, or a legal aid service about custody or work.
misuse_warning: Calling every upset reaction 'victim reversal' can make you deaf to someone who really is hurt, including in a conflict where both of you hurt each other.
Saying it to a person in tears, in the middle of the argument, tends to turn a description into an accusation.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: DARVO runs a whole sequence: deny, attack, then claim to be the victim. Victim role reversal is only the last move, or only its outcome, with no denial or attack needed. Blame-Shifting points at you as the cause and does not need any claim of being hurt. The Non-Apology Apology regrets your reaction without owning the act, and may carry no claim of suffering. Minimization shrinks what happened to you, while this one swaps whose pain is the subject.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Preemptive Accusation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Accusing someone of a fault before they have spoken, often the same fault that is about to be raised about the accuser, so their later account sounds like a copy.
codex_completed.short_definition: Accusing someone of a fault before they have spoken, often the same fault that is about to be raised about the accuser, so their later account sounds like a copy.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Preemptive accusation puts a charge on the record first. The accuser may name the other person's supposed fault before any concern has been voiced, sometimes the very thing they expect to be told about themselves. When the other person later speaks, the account already sounds familiar or like payback. One early complaint can be a coincidence, since two people often notice the same problem. Look at the timing: the early charge keeps landing just before a conversation that could have gone the other way.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: They accuse you of something first, often what they are doing, so that when you finally raise it, it sounds like you are just copying them or getting even.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: By the time the other person speaks, the ground has been prepared. An accurate account arrives sounding like retaliation for one already made, and the person raising it spends their effort defending their motives.
what_it_is: An accusation placed ahead of time, usually before the target has said or done anything to prompt it.
Often a mirror image: the charge is the one the accuser expects to face.
Seen in friend groups, workplaces, families and online communities, wherever others will later judge between two accounts.
The earlier charge works as a kind of cover story, so the later true account has to push past it.
what_it_sounds_like: "I just want you to know I've noticed how you talk about people behind their backs." (said before you have said a word about them)
"I'm sure you're going to say I'm the difficult one, but it's you who always makes things hard."
"Funny, she's going to tell you I ignored her. She's the one who never replies to anything."
"That's what they said I would say, so I'm telling you first: she lies about this stuff." (to a mutual friend)
When you do raise it: "See, this is exactly what I said you'd do."
"Don't be surprised if she twists this. She did it to me last year."
what_it_is_not: A real concern someone raises early because they noticed first. Being first to speak does not make a claim false or strategic.
A person who braces for a hard talk by saying 'I know this may sound defensive, but...' while still engaging with your point.
Two people with true complaints about each other that happen to land in the same week.
A manager or friend giving advance feedback about a pattern they have actually seen.
An honest guess about what someone will say, based on a long history of a fight, followed by real listening.
this_may_be_it_when: The charge appears before you have said or done anything to set it off.
It mirrors, almost word for word, the account you were about to give.
It is told to third parties who will later hear your side, and not to you.
When you do raise your concern, it is met with 'I said you'd do this' and not with an answer.
The first accusation has no specific example behind it, only a general label.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The early complaint comes with a specific, checkable example.
They respond to your account on its merits even though they spoke first.
Both of you are in a long-running dispute and each has been voicing grievances for weeks.
They told you directly, not behind your back, and invited a reply.
The overlap in your complaints can be explained by a shared, visible event.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: When two people are in conflict, both often raise it with others around the same time.
Someone who senses tension may speak up early from nerves, not strategy.
A person can honestly expect to be blamed and say so, to ease their own anxiety.
A concern that has been building can come out on whichever day a person feels able to say it.
common_false_positives: A coworker who flags a process problem before you do, and happens to name yours.
A friend who vents to others about a fight and so is first to tell the story.
A relative who brings up an old argument early because it is weighing on them.
discernment_questions: Did their accusation come before I said anything, or in reply to something I did?
Does it match what I was about to raise, or just resemble it in general?
Who heard it first, and did they tell me or only others?
Is there a specific example behind it that I can check, or only a label?
When I speak, do they answer the content, or only point to having said it first?
less_concerning_if: The early accusation names something specific and can be checked, and I can tell they are open to the answer.
They hear my account without referring back to what they said earlier.
Others heard it as one person's view and are still willing to hear mine.
more_concerning_if: The accusation is repeated to many people before I have a chance to speak.
My account is dismissed as 'exactly what they predicted' by the people who heard the first one.
It happens again on each new subject I might raise.
pattern_over_time_signs: You hear secondhand that a story about you was told before you ever had the chance to raise your concern.
Whenever a conflict seems to be coming, an accusation about you appears.
People you rarely speak to seem to have decided in advance what kind of person you are.
You hesitate to speak up at all, because anything you say sounds like a rerun of what they said about you.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair would mean they retract the early charge to the people who heard it, and then answer your original concern on its merits. A statement like 'I was only worried' that leaves the first claim in circulation and your account still in the shadow is not that.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask whether your concern gets a reply in its own right, or only a reference to the fact they said it first. After you ask them to deal with your point separately, watch whether the earlier accusation stays in their answer.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People tend to give more weight to the first account of a dispute they hear, and to treat a later one as a reaction. An early accusation can use that habit, so a later true account is compared to the first and sounds like an echo. It also tends to put the second speaker on the defensive, spending time on proving they are not retaliating.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: There can be anger at learning an accusation was already circulating, and anxiety about how to raise anything without sounding like payback. Some stay silent, feeling the chance to tell their story has passed. Standing with people who never heard the other side may slip.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name what you are seeing without attacking: 'You raised this about me before I'd said anything. Can I tell you what I was going to bring up?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask to take the topics one at a time: 'I'll answer your point, and then I'd like mine heard on its own, not as a reaction.'
response_options.disengagement: If every attempt to raise your concern gets 'I said you would', stop that line and put your account in writing for later.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone neutral your account, with dates, before the first accusation hardens, and ask them to note when you raised it.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Keep dated notes of when you first noticed the problem, and say in any report when your concern began and why it was not voiced sooner.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I heard you raised this about me before we talked. I'd like to answer that, and I'd also like my own concern heard separately, on what happened, not as a response to your complaint."
codex_completed.safety_note: This is usually a reputation problem, not a physical one. It moves toward danger when the early accusation is made to an employer, a court, a landlord or the police, where the first account can affect your job, housing or legal position. In that case save your own dated records now, and take them to an employment or legal aid advisor before any formal process starts.
misuse_warning: Saying 'you're preempting me' can silence a person who really did notice a problem first and is entitled to report it.
Treating every early complaint as strategy ignores the fact that sometimes the person who speaks first is simply right.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Whataboutism answers an accusation you have made by pointing at some other fault of yours. Preemptive accusation comes before yours exists. DARVO needs you to have accused them first, so that they can deny and reverse it. Blame-Shifting also follows an act or a complaint. This one is defined by its timing: the charge is placed ahead of the account it is meant to cover.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Complaint Weaponization
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Using a formal or informal complaint, often filed first, to shape how a later and truthful report from the other person will be received.
codex_completed.short_definition: Using a formal or informal complaint, often filed first, to shape how a later and truthful report from the other person will be received.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Complaint weaponization is using the machinery of reporting, such as HR, a manager, a school, a landlord, a congregation or a family elder, to get a favorable account in place before the other person speaks. The first report can be exaggerated, selective or simply early. Once it is on file, a second report about the same events looks like a counter-move. Prompt reporting is normal and often right. It becomes this pattern when timing and content seem aimed at blocking a coming account.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone files a complaint about you first, so that when you report what really happened, it looks like revenge instead of a first account.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Whichever account reaches the record first tends to set the frame, so a truthful second report is read as a response rather than as information. The person harmed may lose time, credibility, a job or standing before being heard.
what_it_is: A complaint made through an official or semi-official channel, often within hours or days of an incident.
Frequently made by someone who suspects a complaint is coming, in the hope their version will be the one on file.
Can occur at work, in schools, housing, clubs, custody disputes and religious or family groups.
The effect depends on sequence: a second complaint on the same events is compared to the first, and may be seen as retaliation.
what_it_sounds_like: "I've already spoken to HR about the way you treated me." (said before you have contacted anyone)
A manager telling you, "There's already a complaint about you on file. Anything you raise now will be looked at in that light."
"Funny that you're only bringing this up now, after I reported you."
A mutual friend saying, "She told the group leader first, so I'm not sure it's wise to push this."
A formal letter listing your faults, sent a day after a heated argument with no earlier warning.
"I had to protect myself. Someone had to go to them first."
what_it_is_not: Reporting a real problem quickly through the right channel, which is exactly what people are told to do.
Someone who files first because they are frightened and have never faced a process like this before.
Both people filing independently around the same time, each unaware of the other's report.
A complaint that is accurate, even if it is unwelcome and was filed before yours.
A person asking a supervisor for advice about a conflict without making any formal charge.
this_may_be_it_when: The complaint was filed shortly after you said you would raise a concern, or after you were seen to be preparing one.
The content is heavy on character claims and light on specific events you can check.
The filing is mentioned to you or to others as a reason your later report should be discounted.
It describes events differently from how you and witnesses recall them.
Your own report, once made, is described as a response to theirs.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The complaint describes events that others confirm, even if it is uncomfortable for you.
The timing is explained by something unrelated, such as a policy deadline.
They have said openly that they want both accounts heard fairly.
They did not mention the report to anyone else or use it against your account.
Both of you had concerns about the same incident and each reported separately.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many workplaces and schools tell people to report quickly, so early filing is often compliance.
Someone who feels unsafe or wronged may go to an authority first because they do not know what else to do.
A person may report without knowing the other party is also upset.
People sometimes file in a rush after an emotional day, and add detail later.
common_false_positives: A coworker who reports a safety issue on Monday, just before you report an unrelated one on Tuesday.
Two roommates who each complain to the landlord about the other after the same fight.
A person who files first because they were advised to by a union rep or lawyer.
discernment_questions: Was the complaint filed before I had said anything formal, and what had happened right before?
Does it describe what other people saw, or mostly judgments about my character?
Is it being used to dismiss what I report, or only to give context?
Would they have filed if they did not expect me to raise something?
Is there a process that lets both accounts be investigated, and is it being followed?
less_concerning_if: The first complaint is accurate and the process hears both accounts on equal terms.
No one is using its existence to wave off your report.
Each side's account is being investigated by someone neutral.
more_concerning_if: The first report contains claims that are plainly false, and it is acted on before anyone checks.
You are warned, formally or informally, about the consequences of filing your own.
The complaint threatens your job, home, access to your children or immigration status.
pattern_over_time_signs: Each time a conflict nears a head, a complaint about you reaches an authority first.
A file about you grows while no matching file about the other party is opened.
Your later reports are met with 'you also have a complaint against you' by more than one person.
You begin to feel that you cannot raise anything without it being read as payback.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair would mean the complaint being corrected or withdrawn where it was false, and both accounts being heard by the same process. Someone telling you they 'only wanted to be heard' while leaving the original file in place and your report still tied to it is not repair.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask for the two reports to be handled separately and on their merits. Watch whether the process, and the other person, agree. If your report is still described as 'a response', the request has not been respected.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Institutions and groups often treat the first record of a conflict as the baseline, and anything that follows is compared to it. A person who files early can benefit from that habit, because a second account then has to overcome both the content of the first and the suspicion of retaliation. Listeners also tend to assume that someone who reports quickly is more worried and thus more credible.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Learning a complaint exists can bring a drop in the stomach, fear that nothing said will be taken at face value, and weeks of strain while a process runs. Some stop reporting because it feels futile. Worry about a job or family arrangement while waiting to be heard is common.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask neutrally what was filed and when: 'Can you tell me what the complaint says and when it was made? I'd like to respond to it properly.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask that both accounts be handled on their own merits: 'I'd like my report treated as its own matter and not as a reaction to theirs.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop discussing the incident with the other person directly, and route all further contact through the official process.
response_options.support_seeking: Speak with a union representative, employment or tenant advisor, or legal aid service before you reply, and bring your dated notes.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Put your own account in writing as soon as you can, with dates, witnesses and documents, and ask the process in writing to record when your concern first arose.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I understand a report was made. I'd like it investigated fairly, and I'd also like my own account looked at as a separate matter, with the dates of what happened set out in writing."
codex_completed.safety_note: A complaint can put your income, housing, custody of children or immigration status at risk, so treat a surprise filing as more serious than an ordinary dispute. Watch for threats to report you if you speak, or a deadline to respond. Get your own dated records together at once and contact an employment lawyer, tenant advocate, legal aid clinic or union representative before replying.
misuse_warning: Using this label against someone who reported first, in good faith, can discourage people from reporting real problems.
Saying 'you filed first so you must be doing this' treats timing as proof, and timing alone does not show it.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: DARVO answers an accusation by denying it, attacking you and claiming to be the victim, and it happens in the argument itself. Complaint weaponization happens in a formal channel and depends on who gets on the record first. Blame-Shifting is an answer given in conversation, while this one lives in a file. Whataboutism answers a charge with another charge. This one does its work through the file.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Counterfeit Calm
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Putting on an unbothered, composed manner so that someone's honest upset looks irrational or excessive by comparison.
codex_completed.short_definition: Putting on an unbothered, composed manner so that someone's honest upset looks irrational or excessive by comparison.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Counterfeit calm is composure used as a contrast. The person stays level, soft-voiced or faintly amused while the other person, who has a real reason to be upset, rises. The calm is not the issue. The issue is that it replaces the answer, and the other person's feelings become the topic. One steady response proves nothing, since many people stay calm when they care. The giveaway is composure that deepens as upset deepens while the concern never gets a reply.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: They stay cool and gentle while you are upset, and somehow your being upset becomes the problem, while what you said never gets answered.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A proportionate emotional response gets read as instability by contrast. A person is left choosing between being upset and being believed, and may start suppressing real feelings to be taken seriously.
what_it_is: Composure that works as a comparison: the calmer they appear, the more upset you look.
Often accompanied by a soft tone, slow speech, a small smile or a sigh.
Shows up in arguments between partners, parent and adult child, coworkers, and in customer or official settings.
Defined by what the calm replaces. It stands in for an answer to your point.
what_it_sounds_like: "I'm not upset at all. I just think you're getting a bit worked up."
"Let's take a breath. I'm happy to talk when you're ready to be reasonable."
"I'm just trying to keep things peaceful. Why are you so angry?"
A slow, quiet "Okay." in answer to a long, painful explanation.
"I'm not going to argue. I'll wait until you've calmed down."
A gentle smile and a glance at others in the room as your voice rises.
what_it_is_not: A naturally even-tempered person who is just as steady in every situation, including ones that concern them.
A person who keeps their voice low to cool a heated moment and says they want to return to the issue, which they then do.
A cultural or family style where raised voices are seen as disrespectful and calm is the norm.
A person who is calm because they are not very affected, and who says so plainly without implying you should feel the same.
A trained professional such as a nurse or mediator keeping a steady voice because the job calls for it.
this_may_be_it_when: Their calm grows more noticeable the more upset you become.
Your tone is named more often than your point.
They say they will talk 'when you calm down' and then do not return to the topic.
They appear calm only in this kind of conversation, and are animated about other things.
Others in the room begin treating you as the one who needs managing.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They stay steady and then actually address what you raised.
They are equally even in good and bad moments, including when something affects them.
They ask for a short pause and set a time to return, then keep it.
They say they are upset too, but are choosing to speak slowly.
You are asking them to stay calm and they are doing exactly that to help.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Some people go quiet and still under stress as a way of coping, not as a message to anyone.
Many families and workplaces prize composure, and people raised there find raised voices hard.
A person who knows they tend to say hurtful things when angry may stay calm to avoid that.
A steady tone may be a deliberate attempt to lower the temperature.
common_false_positives: A friend who talks softly and slowly when you are upset, and then asks what you need.
A coworker who stays level in a tense meeting and goes through each of your points.
A partner who takes a walk to cool off and returns to the discussion on time.
discernment_questions: After the calm response, was my actual concern answered?
Does their composure change with mine, or is it the same everywhere?
Do I feel looked at as the problem after every difficult conversation?
Would I be less upset if the question had been answered, whatever the tone?
Have I started toning down real feelings to avoid being called overreactive?
less_concerning_if: The calm comes with real answers to what you raised.
They show strong feeling in other contexts, so steadiness is not a mask.
They are open to hearing that their manner felt dismissive.
more_concerning_if: The calm is used in front of others to make you look unreasonable.
The same pattern appears every time you raise something important, however gently you start.
You have begun to doubt whether your reactions are normal.
pattern_over_time_signs: You rehearse a flat, careful tone before raising things, because any rise in voice ends the conversation.
You get a reputation among shared friends as the volatile one, though you seldom raise your voice elsewhere.
Important topics stay unresolved, while the 'you were too emotional' line gets repeated.
You notice you cry or shake afterward more than during the talk.
codex_completed.repair_check: They go back to the topic you raised and answer it, then say their calm had come across as dismissal. If they only apologize for how you 'took' their tone, and the question is still unanswered, nothing has been repaired.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice whether, once you ask them to answer the question first and set tone aside, they do. If they do, the calm was just a manner. If they keep naming how you sound, your request has not been heard.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People often read the calmest person in a room as the most reasonable, and the most visibly upset as the least. A composed manner can tap into that shortcut, so the content of a complaint gets judged by who sounds steadier. The upset person may also start to monitor themselves, which uses up the attention they need to make their case.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Feeling foolish for having cried or raised a voice is common, as is replaying how you sounded instead of what was said, with a creeping worry that your reactions are out of scale. Some hide feelings and raise problems only when they can stay perfectly even, which is hardest when the stakes feel high.

response_options.soft_clarification: Separate tone from topic: 'I know I'm upset, and I still need an answer to the question I asked about Thursday.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline the tone review: 'My voice is not the subject. I'm happy to talk more quietly if you'll answer what I asked.'
response_options.disengagement: Step away on your own terms, with a time to return: 'I'm going to take twenty minutes, and when I come back I'd like us to start with my question.'
response_options.support_seeking: Describe what was said, not the tone, to someone you trust, and ask whether your concern sounds reasonable on its own.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Write your concern in an email, with the specific question, so the response is judged on content, not on how either of you sounded.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I may be upset, and that is allowed. Please don't judge my point by my volume. I'll slow down, and I'd like you to answer what I asked about Thursday, in words."
codex_completed.safety_note: A composed voice is not a danger signal by itself. It becomes one if the calm sits next to quiet threats, a pattern of cold withdrawal after you disagree, or fear that your upset will be used against you in custody, work or legal matters. If so, write down what was said without describing tone, and discuss it with a counselor or legal advisor.
misuse_warning: Calling any composed person 'fake calm' can punish people who stay steady because that is who they are.
Using the label to justify shouting, on the grounds that the other person is hiding something, can turn a description into permission.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Tone Policing criticizes how you said something and treats that as the reason not to answer; counterfeit calm does not need to say anything about your tone, since the contrast does the work. Minimization shrinks what happened. Denial refuses the facts. An apology aimed at your reaction is a different move. Here the thing that stays unmatched is the person's own steady manner placed next to your visible upset.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Double Binds
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Giving someone demands that contradict each other, so that whatever they choose, they are told they chose wrong.
codex_completed.short_definition: Giving someone demands that contradict each other, so that whatever they choose, they are told they chose wrong.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A double bind sets up two demands, or a demand and its opposite, so that meeting one means failing the other. A person is told to speak up and then punished for speaking, or to be more affectionate and then accused of faking it. Everyone gets conflicting messages now and then. The concern is when no response is ever the right one and the person stays at fault in every version. The idea comes from communication research in the 1950s.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Whatever you do is wrong. If you do one thing you are criticized for it, and if you do the opposite you are criticized for that too.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Every available response is wrong, so effort produces fault whatever is chosen. A person begins to conclude that the problem must be themselves, and may stop trying or become hypervigilant.
what_it_is: Two messages that cannot both be obeyed, delivered with the expectation that you will obey them.
Often one message is spoken and the other is implied through tone or consequence.
Appears in parenting, partnerships, workplaces and caregiving, anywhere one person's approval matters a lot to another.
The key feature is that no exit exists inside the rules as stated, and pointing that out is itself treated as another fault.
what_it_sounds_like: "Be more independent." Then, when you decide something alone: "You never include me."
"Just tell me what's wrong." Then, when you do: "I can't believe you'd say that to me."
"You never take initiative." Then: "Now you're just doing it because I complained."
"Take your time with it." Followed by irritation that it is not finished.
"I want your honest opinion." Followed by silence or anger if the opinion differs.
"Don't be so sensitive." And then: "Why don't you care how this affects me?"
what_it_is_not: Feedback on two different matters that happen to pull in opposite directions, such as 'be more concise' on emails and 'be thorough' on reports.
A person whose preferences honestly change over time and who has not noticed the shift.
A hard job with competing real demands, such as a manager asked by their own boss for speed and perfection.
General dissatisfaction from someone stressed, without any trap in the structure.
A mixed message that is acknowledged and fixed once pointed out.
this_may_be_it_when: The two demands apply to the same moment, and obeying one directly breaks the other.
You have tried both options and been faulted for each.
When you name the contradiction, the answer is that you are being difficult.
The standard seems to move to whatever you did not just do.
The consequences of 'failure' are real, such as cold treatment, anger or loss of something you need.
this_may_not_be_it_when: One of the options is sometimes accepted as the right one.
The two instructions concern different settings, such as home and work, or different tasks.
They say 'you're right, I was asking for two things' and adjust.
The conflict is in the circumstances, such as a tight deadline, not in what they ask of you.
A third person looking at the demands would see room to meet both.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Stressed people send mixed signals without noticing, such as saying 'it's fine' and meaning 'ask me again'.
Needs can truly conflict, such as wanting closeness and wanting space on the same day.
Organizations often give staff clashing priorities, and no single person means to trap anyone.
Preferences can drift, leaving an older instruction in conflict with a newer one.
common_false_positives: A boss who asks for fast and perfect work in the same email, and when you raise it, clarifies which matters more.
A parent who says 'be careful' and 'don't be so timid' about the same activity.
A friend who wants both reassurance and honesty, and is hurt when you cannot do both at once.
discernment_questions: Is there any response, even a partial one, that has ever been accepted as right?
Do both demands apply to the same situation, or to different ones?
When I point out the conflict, is it acknowledged, or is it treated as another failing?
Does the criticism follow what I did, or whatever I did not just do?
Would a neutral person see the two demands as genuinely impossible to satisfy together?
less_concerning_if: The conflicting asks can be talked through, and one of them gives way.
You are able to satisfy at least one of them at least some of the time.
They accept being told the messages clash.
more_concerning_if: Nothing you do is ever accepted, and the goal posts move after each attempt.
Calling out the contradiction brings anger, silence or punishment.
Your life depends on their approval, such as your housing, income or your place in the family.
pattern_over_time_signs: You freeze before acting, because you can see ahead how each choice will be criticized.
You find yourself guessing at the response most likely to avoid blame and rarely finding it.
You apologize in advance, whichever way you turn.
You start to describe yourself in the other person's words: 'I'm just never good enough.'
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair would sound like them admitting that two things were being asked at once, picking which one matters, and keeping that choice for weeks. Warm words that slide back into the same crossed demands your next attempt are not repair.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Name the clash once, calmly, and see whether it can be discussed. A sign of respect is them choosing one standard and sticking to it. A sign of the opposite is a new complaint about your raising it, or a third demand that contradicts the first two.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When every option leads to disapproval, a person can lose the sense that their actions affect anything. They may try harder, monitor themselves constantly, or give up. Because pointing out the contradiction is often also penalized, the person may conclude that the confusion is their own failing and not a feature of the demands.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Walking on eggshells, dread before any choice and worn-down confidence in one's own judgment are typical accounts. Some lie awake over what might have counted as 'right'. Others freeze, avoid decisions or over-explain, and report that it took distance before the demands could be seen as contradictory.

response_options.soft_clarification: Point at the clash without blame: 'I heard two different things there. Which one matters more to you right now?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to guess: 'I can't meet both of those at once. Tell me which you want, and I'll do that one.'
response_options.disengagement: If the demands keep shifting, step out: 'I can't win this conversation as it stands, so I'm going to stop for now.'
response_options.support_seeking: Write down two or three of the contradictory instructions word for word and show them to someone outside, to check whether they seem as impossible as they feel.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask your manager to rank competing demands in an email, so there is a written priority to work from and to cite.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "You asked me to do two things that can't both happen. I'm not going to guess which is the right one. Tell me which you want, and I'll do it. I won't be criticized for the other."
codex_completed.safety_note: Double binds alone are not a safety signal. The risk grows if the person setting them holds power over your home, income, children or immigration status, or if breaking one demand brings threats or physical intimidation. Then keep a record of the exact instructions and what followed, and speak to an advocate or legal aid service who can look at the whole picture.
misuse_warning: Calling every mixed message a 'double bind' can hide that many are just muddled, rushed or the result of real competing needs.
Using the term to refuse any feedback ('you're putting me in a bind') can be a way of avoiding all correction.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Minimization makes your reaction seem too big for what happened. Whataboutism turns the conversation to a different past fault. DARVO flips who is accused. A double bind is not about one dispute; it is a rule set where two instructions block each other. The mark is that you cannot comply with one without breaking the other, and no exit is offered.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Sarcasm as Weapon
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Using a mocking tone to deliver real criticism or contempt, so that any objection can be answered with "it was a joke."
codex_completed.short_definition: Using a mocking tone to deliver real criticism or contempt, so that any objection can be answered with "it was a joke."
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Sarcasm says the opposite of what is meant, usually with a tone that signals it. Used as a weapon, the real message is a criticism, and the tone gives the speaker a way out if challenged. Plenty of sarcasm is harmless, and many friendships run on it. The difference is who it lands on, how often, and what happens when someone says it stung. Strip off the tone, and the sentence is a plain insult.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: It sounds like a joke, but the message is a put-down. When you say it hurt, you are told you cannot take a joke.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Criticism lands in full while objecting to it means arguing about a joke, so the hurt has nowhere to go.
what_it_is: A comment whose literal meaning is praise, and whose real meaning is a criticism of you.
Delivered with a smile, eye-roll or drawn-out tone that lets it be denied afterward.
Most often aimed at the same sore spots, such as your job, body, cooking or intelligence.
Often said in front of others, where objecting would look petty.
what_it_sounds_like: "Wow, great parking. Was that a goal of yours?"
"Oh, sure, because you're the expert on everything."
"Nice of you to finally join us."
"No, please, tell me more about your amazing career."
"I'm kidding! God, you take everything so seriously."
"Thanks for the help. Really, I could not have done it without you ruining it."
what_it_is_not: Mutual, affectionate teasing that both people enjoy is not this, and a generally sarcastic style applied evenly to everyone has no particular target.
One sharp remark in a bad moment, acknowledged and not repeated, is friction rather than a pattern.
Dry humor in a team that roasts everyone, including the boss, and where anyone can say it is too much and be heard.
Sarcasm directed at an idea or a situation, such as a broken printer, rather than at a person.
A habit the speaker is honestly unaware of, who stops when told and thanks you for saying so.
this_may_be_it_when: The jokes keep landing on the same subject, such as your weight, job or family.
When you say it hurt, the answer is that you are too sensitive.
The remarks come mostly when there is an audience, or when you have just done something well.
Without the tone, the sentence reads as a clear insult.
You are the one doing the laughing along, while feeling something else.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You joke back in the same way and enjoy it.
The remark ended when you said it stung, and they apologized.
The sarcasm is aimed at everyone, in the same measure, and nobody is left out as the target.
It was about a task or situation, not about you.
You were already in a bad mood and read the tone as sharper than it was meant.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: In some families and friendships, sarcasm is the usual way to show affection, and it is read that way by all.
Some people use irony as a nervous habit, and say it without noticing how it sounds.
Text and tone are easy to misread, so a dry joke by message may carry a sharper edge than meant.
common_false_positives: Siblings who trade barbs and laugh together.
A colleague who mocks the company's new policy, and not any person.
A friend's ironic remark about their own cooking.
discernment_questions: If the same sentence were said straight, would it be an insult?
Do I ever get to say it back, or only absorb it?
Does it land on the same sore spot every time?
When I say it bothered me, is there any change, or only a new joke about my reaction?
Do I feel smaller around this person, or only occasionally stung?
less_concerning_if: Both people give and take in the same way, and both can say when it has gone too far.
The target of the joke is a shared situation, not the other person.
It stops, with a real apology, when someone says it hurt.
more_concerning_if: Telling them it hurts leads to more jokes, or to a charge that you have no sense of humor.
The jokes mostly arrive in front of other people, or in moments when you are vulnerable.
You have begun to avoid mentioning your plans or achievements in case they become material.
pattern_over_time_signs: You have stopped sharing good news with this person to avoid the comeback.
You catch yourself pre-empting the joke by mocking yourself first.
Others have begun to join in the remarks about you, taking their cue from the tone.
You go quiet in groups where this person is present.
codex_completed.repair_check: Raise one kind of remark and see whether it is still made. If that subject is simply left alone, and they can accept that something that felt like a joke to them did not feel like one to you, that is change. A promise to be more careful, followed by the same jokes with a wink, is not.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Say once, calmly, that a certain joke does not work for you, then watch the weeks that follow. Is the topic dropped without a comment? Or does it turn into a running joke about how you cannot take a joke?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Because the words are literally positive, a person has to decode the insult before reacting, and then pay the extra price of looking humorless if they object. That small gap can make people laugh along and swallow the sting. Repeated over time, the jabs can start to sound like an accurate view of oneself, particularly when others laugh too.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe laughing along while feeling a small drop in the stomach, rehearsing comebacks afterward, and wondering whether they really are too sensitive. Some say they went quiet in groups to avoid being the target. A long-delayed realization that they had not enjoyed the joking for years is common.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the plain version: "If you mean that I did that badly, can you just tell me directly?"
response_options.firm_boundary: Mark the topic as closed without joining the joke: "I'm not laughing at that one. Please leave it."
