response_options.disengagement: Do not play along or counter with your own jab. A flat "hm" and a change of subject takes the audience out of it.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask a friend who sees you with this person whether the jokes sound affectionate to them, and listen to what they say about the tone.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, note down the remark, the date and who heard it. If it continues, ask your manager to address the tone of the team, naming the behavior and not the person.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "That joke is about something that actually bothers me, so it doesn't land as funny. Please drop it."
codex_completed.safety_note: Sarcasm is not a safety signal in itself. It deserves more attention if it is paired with threats, with monitoring, or with a fear of how the person will react if you object. In that case, a counselor or domestic abuse advocate can help you assess it, and a workplace ombuds can help if it is a boss or colleague.
misuse_warning: Calling every dry remark a weapon can shut down humor in friendships where teasing is a loved way of connecting.
Quoting a sarcastic line out of context to prove someone is cruel may drop the tone and history that made it a joke between the two of them.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Contempt is an open expression of disgust and needs no joke as cover. Shame Installation goes after your basic adequacy, where sarcasm can sting over something small. Emotional Invalidation rules your feelings out of bounds. Sarcasm instead says the opposite of what is meant, often as mock praise, and the tone is the whole vehicle.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Public Humiliation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Embarrassing or belittling a person in front of others, or putting their private matters on show, so the audience adds to the sting.
codex_completed.short_definition: Embarrassing or belittling a person in front of others, or putting their private matters on show, so the audience adds to the sting.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Public humiliation is a correction, joke, revealed secret, story or post aimed at one person where others can see or hear it. Public exposure is this tactic under another name, so this entry covers both. Feedback given in company is sometimes unavoidable, so context matters. It raises concern when the audience seems to be part of the point, when the same words would be gentler in private, and when it keeps landing on one person.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You are put down, corrected, laughed at or have something private shown to others, in a way that would have been handled differently one on one. The audience is what makes it hurt.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: An audience makes the injury durable in a way private criticism is not: everyone present carries a version of it afterwards, including the person it was about. It cannot be taken back privately later, and it can change how the group treats you.
what_it_is: Criticism, ridicule or private information put on show where other people can see or hear it.
Forms include a correction in a meeting, a story told against you at dinner, a group message quoting your private words, or a post that names you.
More lasting than a private remark, because witnesses remember it and the target remembers them remembering.
Seen in workplaces, classrooms, families, friend groups and online.
Sometimes the venue is the one with the largest audience, such as an all-staff call or a holiday table, when a quiet word was available.
what_it_sounds_like: "Let me show everyone how it should have been done."
"Tell them what you did last weekend. Go on, it's hilarious."
A manager reading out your error on a team call, with your name attached.
"Oh, don't mind her, she never gets the details right."
A group chat message that quotes something private you said, followed by laughing faces.
"Do you want to tell them, or shall I?"
"Since we're all here, we might as well go through your review."
what_it_is_not: Necessary, time-sensitive feedback that has to be given where others happen to be, such as a safety problem in a room full of people.
Settings where feedback is normal and applied evenly to everybody, such as a design critique, which humiliate nobody.
An awkward moment that was only poor timing, or carelessness with something private, such as an offhand mention at a party.
A public award or roast that the person agreed to and enjoys.
Information that is public for a real, disclosed reason, such as a published result or a minuted decision.
A story told with affection that the person is happy to have told, and might tell themselves.
this_may_be_it_when: The criticism is harsher with people around than when you are alone together.
Private things, such as a mistake, a diagnosis or a secret, are brought out in front of others.
The same person is picked out in group settings more than anyone else is.
A quiet word would have been easy to arrange and was never tried.
Others glance at you or look away afterwards, and the room seems to settle on you as the joke.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The feedback is the same for everyone and given in a way that is meant to be useful.
It was an emergency or a safety issue that needed fixing straight away.
You agreed to the format, such as a review session where all work is critiqued.
The speaker followed up privately to check how you felt and repaired it.
The comment was clumsy but kind in tone, and the person was visibly sorry.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A busy meeting or live session leaves no time for private notes, and a quick correction may be the only option.
Some cultures and teams treat open correction as normal and respectful.
A person telling a funny story may not realize you find it embarrassing.
common_false_positives: A choir director correcting a section's timing.
A friend sharing an old photo that you also find funny now.
A manager reading out a company-wide error without naming anyone.
discernment_questions: Would the same words have been said in private, in the same way?
Did the audience seem to matter to the person speaking?
Is the same person the target again and again?
Was anything I had told in confidence used?
After it happened, did the person check in or acknowledge it?
less_concerning_if: Everyone is treated the same, and the setting makes public correction expected.
The person speaks to you in private afterward and makes it right.
The topic was a work task, and no personal detail was used.
more_concerning_if: Private information, like health, money or family trouble, is brought out in front of others.
The audience is the one that matters most to you, such as your family, your team or your online followers.
Mentioning it leads to more of it, or to being told you embarrassed yourself.
pattern_over_time_signs: You begin to dread gatherings, meetings or group chats where this person will be present.
You prepare your answers in advance, to avoid being caught out in front of others.
Other people start to treat you as the butt of the joke, taking their cue from the way you are treated.
You speak less in groups, and your contributions are noticed less.
codex_completed.repair_check: Meaningful change would show in public as well as in private: the person corrects you, if they must, in a way that does not expose you, and speaks up for you when others laugh. Apologizing in a private message while repeating the behavior in front of others leaves the audience part unchanged.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask for correction to happen one on one, then see what the next group setting brings. Is your request kept when other people are present, which is the moment it matters most? Or does the next public remark show it was put aside?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People are highly attuned to how their group sees them, and being lowered in front of others is a hit to standing, not only to feelings. Witnesses add to it by laughing, going quiet or looking away. A person may begin to expect it, and the dread alone can change how they speak and act around others.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe heat in the face, loss of words, replaying the moment for days, and avoiding the people who saw it. Some say the worst part was a bystander's silence. Many talk about shrinking in later meetings, and about checking whether anyone still remembers.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for privacy next time, in a matter-of-fact tone: "If there's a problem with my work, I'd find it easier to hear it one on one."
response_options.firm_boundary: Name it lightly, in the moment if you can: "That was hard to hear in front of everyone. Could we pick it up later, just the two of us?"
response_options.disengagement: Leave the room, the chat or the table for a few minutes without explanation, and return only when the subject has moved on.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk to someone who was there, and ask what they saw and heard. Knowing that a witness found it unfair can lift the doubt you carry.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Write down the date, the setting, the words used and who was present, then take the record to HR, a union rep, or a manager one level up.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'm glad to hear your feedback on my work. I'd just like to have it in private, not in front of the team."
codex_completed.safety_note: Humiliation is mostly about standing and dignity, but it can sit alongside danger when it involves intimate images or private details shared without consent, hints that something will be revealed unless you comply, or exposure that follows you from the household into work or online spaces. Save dated screenshots, and ask a legal aid service or an advocate who handles image-based or domestic abuse about next steps before replying.
misuse_warning: Calling a fair, public correction humiliation can let real problems with performance go unaddressed. The label fits when the audience is the point, not when the venue is.
Telling a group that someone humiliated you, as a way to turn people against them, can become a humiliation of its own.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Shame Installation works on your sense of being fundamentally inadequate and can happen in private, whereas this relies on witnesses. A Smear Campaign spreads distorted claims about you to build a reputation over time; public humiliation is a moment played to the people in the room or the group chat. Humiliation Rituals dress the degradation as initiation or discipline and say the pain proves it is working.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Labeling as Identity Warfare
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Pinning a fixed defect label on a person, such as 'the difficult one', until others read everything they do through it.
codex_completed.short_definition: Pinning a fixed defect label on a person, such as 'the difficult one', until others read everything they do through it.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: This is what happens when one description, such as 'the difficult one', 'the unstable one' or 'the troublemaker', gets attached to a person and then travels. It turns up in team meetings, family group chats, school files and case notes. After that the label does the interpreting: a calm question reads as hostility, and a good week reads as a mask. One unkind nickname is not this. The pattern appears when the description spreads past whoever coined it and nothing you do can count against it.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone gets a one-line description like 'the difficult one', and from then on everything they do, good or bad, is taken as proof of it.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Once a label sticks, ordinary behavior is read as confirming it, so nothing you do can count as evidence against it. You may start managing how you appear instead of simply acting, and people who never met you can arrive already holding the verdict.
what_it_is: A single phrase, such as 'the sensitive one' or 'the flaky one', standing in for a whole person.
Passed along: repeated to new coworkers, relatives, teachers or officials until it arrives before you do.
Self-sealing: calm behavior is called putting on an act, and upset is called proof.
Sometimes written down in an email, a performance file, a school note or a case record, which gives it weight it never earned.
Different from feedback on one behavior, which names what happened and leaves you room to act differently next time.
what_it_sounds_like: Oh, that's just Dana being Dana.
Careful with him, he's the difficult one.
She seems fine today, but you know how unstable she can be.
A new hire is introduced to you as 'our resident troublemaker', with a laugh.
Your polite email is called passive-aggressive and your direct one is called aggressive.
Of course you'd say that. That's exactly what someone like you would say.
A meeting note files your three questions under the heading 'attitude'.
what_it_is_not: An unflattering description that is accurate, such as calling a colleague who has missed every deadline for a year unreliable.
A reputation that formed because many people independently had similar experiences with you.
Specific feedback about one act, such as 'you interrupted three times today', that leaves the rest of you alone.
A nickname you chose, or gladly accept, because it is affectionate.
A role word like 'the newest member', which describes a position and not a defect.
this_may_be_it_when: The same one-line description comes back from people who never saw you in the situation it describes.
Good behavior gets a footnote ('she's being nice today') instead of counting.
Your explanation is answered with the label rather than with a reply to what you said.
The label has been put in writing, in a file, an email thread or a group chat.
You have become over-careful to avoid fitting it, and the carefulness is read as more evidence.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The description names a specific behavior and a date, and would fall away if the behavior did.
The person using it can also tell you about times you went against it.
Several people who never talk to each other describe the same behavior in similar terms.
The label began as your own joke about yourself and you still like it.
When you disagree with the description, they listen and adjust the way they talk about you.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Busy people compress others into a word or two to remember who is who, without any plan to pin anyone down.
One rough first meeting can set an impression through ordinary memory habits, with nobody working to keep it there.
Someone repeating a colleague's word without checking it may not know it is unfair.
common_false_positives: A manager's review noting that you missed all four deadlines this quarter.
Friends calling you 'the planner' because you do run every trip.
A teacher's note that a pupil 'struggles with transitions', written to get support in place and not to settle a verdict.
discernment_questions: Can the person using the label name two or three specific things I did, with dates?
Is there anything I could do that they would accept as evidence against it?
Where did the label start, and has it spread to people who never saw me in that situation?
Is the same behavior read differently when someone else does it?
Did I choose this description, or was it handed to me?
less_concerning_if: The label is tied to named behaviors and is dropped when the behavior changes.
You know who coined it and they will talk with you about it.
It exists only in conversation, not in files or introductions.
more_concerning_if: It has been written into records that decide your pay, grades, care or access to your children.
People you have never met repeat it.
Others who pushed back on the label soon found labels of their own attached.
pattern_over_time_signs: New people treat you warily within days of arriving, as if briefed.
You rehearse looking relaxed so as not to prove the label right.
Your successes are credited to luck or circumstance while your mistakes are credited to you.
You begin to use the label about yourself in jokes.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair here shows in how you are introduced and recorded. Someone who takes it seriously retracts the label to the people who heard it, corrects the file or note, and starts describing specific events. A private 'I didn't mean it like that' while the nickname keeps circulating leaves the label standing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: After you object, listen for whether the word drops out of what people say about you, or whether you are now also described as touchy about labels. The next description of you is the answer: is it about something you did?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: A label hands people a ready-made lens, and once they hold it they tend to notice what fits and pass over what does not. People can also treat someone according to the expectation, which may draw out the very behavior expected. The person labeled can begin to watch themselves through the same lens, so the label comes to feel like their own judgment.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe a tiring watchfulness: choosing words so as not to fit the description, then finding that the caution is read against them. Some start to wonder whether the label is true. Others describe anger at being introduced as a summary, and a pull to withdraw from groups where the word circulates.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the evidence in plain words: 'You called me difficult. Which thing I did do you mean? I'd like to hear it.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline the shorthand: 'Please describe what I did, not what I am. I'm glad to talk about the behavior.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop auditioning against the label. Do the work or join the event without adjusting your manner to disprove a word.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask someone who has seen you in several settings to describe you in their own words, then set that beside the label.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask in writing that feedback name specific events, request to see anything filed about you, and add your own dated account beside it.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'd like feedback about specific things I did, with examples. One word for me as a person gives me nothing I can change, so I'm asking that we leave it out of how I'm described."
codex_completed.safety_note: This pattern is not usually a danger in itself. It changes when the label reaches records that decide custody, housing, employment or care, or travels with threats or isolation. Then keep copies of whatever is written about you and take them to a legal aid office, union representative or advocate before replying in writing.
misuse_warning: Calling an accurate, earned description a 'label' can become a way to dodge feedback you need. Check whether it names real events.
Reading every nickname as warfare turns teasing and shorthand into accusation. The concern is the fixed, spreading kind that nothing can disprove.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Contempt is scorn shown in the moment through face and voice, while a label can be delivered flatly, even in a file, and outlasts the moment. Name-Calling Disguised as Humor needs a joke and a laugh; a label is often said gravely. Shame Installation works inward, on how you judge yourself. Labeling works outward, on how other people see and treat you.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Rage as Control
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Explosive anger that, whatever lies behind it, reliably ends a disagreement because the people around it learn to give way.
codex_completed.short_definition: Explosive anger that, whatever lies behind it, reliably ends a disagreement because the people around it learn to give way.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: This entry describes what an outburst does, not what is inside the person. Shouting, slamming a door, hitting a table, or going rigid and cold with fury can all close a conversation. The people nearby learn to calm things down first, and whatever raised the issue gets dropped. One blow-up under strain is common. The pattern shows when outbursts arrive as you push back, the topic does not return afterwards, and your world shrinks around avoiding the next one.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: After enough blow-ups, you stop raising things that might set one off, so the anger ends up deciding what can be talked about.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: People around an outburst learn to put calming things down ahead of whatever started it, so topics stop being raised long before anyone decides to stop raising them. Over time one person's temper quietly sets the limits of a household or workplace.
what_it_is: An outburst whose effect is to close the topic: raised voices, objects hit or thrown, a face gone hard, a sudden cold fury.
Judged by its effect, not its sincerity. It can be fully felt and still work as a stop sign.
Followed by an aftermath that takes over: you comfort, apologize or tidy up, and the original issue never comes back.
Sometimes aimed at objects or the room rather than at you, yet it still teaches everyone to step carefully.
Different from ordinary anger in what comes after. Ordinary anger gets heard, and then the conversation resumes.
what_it_sounds_like: Don't you dare bring that up again! shouted, followed by a slammed door.
Look what you made me do, said over a broken plate.
A fist on the table and 'We're done talking about this.'
Jaw tight, voice low: 'Go ahead. Keep pushing.'
You know how I get. Why do you do this?
Others in the home whispering 'not tonight, they're in a mood'.
Everyone going quiet at the sound of keys in the door.
what_it_is_not: Proportionate anger at something truly upsetting that is voiced, heard, and followed by a conversation that can still change the outcome.
Someone working on regulating anger who slips, owns it the same day, and uses an agreed break afterwards.
One blow-up during a crisis such as a bereavement, acknowledged afterwards.
A family or friend group where everyone raises their voice and everyone carries on with the topic.
Panic or overwhelm that looks like rage, where the person needs to leave the room and comes back to resume the subject.
this_may_be_it_when: The anger rises right when you disagree, ask a hard question or state a limit, and is rare otherwise.
By the end the disputed subject is gone and you are the one smoothing things over.
You choose times, wording and moods in advance to avoid setting it off.
Doors, tables or objects near you take the force, and you go quiet.
Other people in the home or office also adjust their behavior around it.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The anger fades quickly and the issue is picked up again, with you getting your say.
You can disagree on most subjects without it, and 'no' gets a reasonable response.
They step away on their own and come back ready to talk.
The anger follows a real injury or loss rather than pushback.
You are not changing how you act around them.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Poor sleep, pain, hunger, grief or a medication change can make anyone short-fused.
Some people were raised where loud argument is ordinary and carries no threat.
Emotional flooding can produce shouting the person regrets and does not link to getting their way.
common_false_positives: Two siblings who yell at each other and then laugh about it.
A stage manager shouting during a live-show emergency, where the tone belongs to the moment and nobody gives way to it afterwards.
A tired parent who snaps once over a spilled drink, apologizes, and cleans up with the child.
discernment_questions: Which subjects have I stopped raising, and what did they have in common?
After an outburst, does the original problem ever get talked about?
Do I plan how they will react before deciding what to say?
Does the anger show up with strangers or bosses, or only with people who live with them or depend on them?
Do I feel relief when the subject is dropped, even though nothing is settled?
Has anyone else in the home or team changed how they behave around it?
less_concerning_if: Nothing is struck or broken, and a break is taken by agreement.
They return later and talk about what set it off.
You can say you are unhappy and the conversation continues.
more_concerning_if: Objects are thrown or hit, your way out of a room is blocked, or there is any touching in anger.
Anger comes with threats, taking your phone, keys or money, or remarks about what could happen to you.
You have started to be afraid, not just uncomfortable.
pattern_over_time_signs: A list of unsayable subjects grows quietly.
You apologize for things you did not do wrong to bring things back to calm.
You read the early signs, a change of tone, footsteps, breathing, and act before a word is said.
Friends or family notice you go quiet or change the subject when the person is near.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair for this tactic means the original issue gets its turn. After the outburst, the person comes back when calm, names what they did in plain words, and then discusses what you had raised. Gifts, a quiet week or sudden tenderness that leave the topic untouched have only restored calm.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Watch what happens to a request to continue later. If the pause is allowed and the topic returns on schedule, the anger is not setting the agenda. If the pause is shouted down, or the later talk never happens, the subject has been closed in practice.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Fear responses are fast and bodily: a raised voice or a slammed object can trigger vigilance before thought. If giving way ends the noise and the tension, the relief rewards giving way, and the habit can be learned without anyone discussing it. Over time a person may predict reactions and edit themselves in advance, which can feel like simply choosing to keep the peace.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe walking on eggshells, rehearsing sentences, and feeling a drop in the stomach at a tone or a key in the door. Some stop raising money, parenting or health topics altogether. Others feel responsible for the other person's moods, or ashamed of how often they backed down. Children in a home may learn to leave the room or go silent.

response_options.soft_clarification: Pick a calm moment, away from the last blow-up: 'I've noticed I stop mentioning things when your voice goes up. Can we find a way to talk about hard things that works for both of us?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Only if it feels safe, name what you need in a few words: 'I can't think while I'm being shouted at. Can we pick this up in an hour?'
response_options.disengagement: Lower the stakes without announcing anything: go to another room for a glass of water or a phone call, and let the topic wait. Keep your phone and keys within reach.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell one person outside the home exactly what happens, in order, and agree a code word that means you want them to call or come over. A domestic violence advocate can talk through options in confidence.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, write down dates, words and who was present, and take it to HR or a manager above them, describing the effect on the work rather than the person's character.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Once voices are raised I can't do this well, though I do want to talk about it. Could we take twenty minutes and then pick it up again?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Anger that makes you afraid is a safety question, not only a communication one. Warning signs include thrown or broken objects, blocked doorways, grabbing, threats, being followed from room to room, and damage to your belongings. If you see them, keep a phone charged and papers where you can reach them, and call a domestic violence hotline or advocate to plan privately. If a rage turns physical, or you fear it will within minutes, leave if you can and call emergency services from wherever you are safe.
misuse_warning: Calling any anger 'control' can silence honest frustration, including your own. The words fit anger whose result is a closed topic and a wary household, not every raised voice.
Describing someone as 'raging' to others to win support in a dispute turns the label into a weapon. Describe what happened, with dates.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Intimidation carries a spoken or implied consequence for not complying; rage can carry none, and its force comes from fear of the next outburst. Contempt is cold and aimed at your worth, while rage is hot and aimed at the exchange. Emotional Invalidation tells you your feelings are wrong; rage often makes them impossible to voice at all, because the topic itself disappears.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Credit Theft
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Presenting another person's work, idea or effort as one's own, or letting the credit drift away from the person who produced it.
codex_completed.short_definition: Presenting another person's work, idea or effort as one's own, or letting the credit drift away from the person who produced it.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Credit theft covers a range. At one end, a finished piece of work is shown to an audience under another name. At the other, credit leaks slowly: an idea you raised is repeated in a later meeting by someone else, thanks are given in private, and by the time it reaches decision-makers its source is forgotten. One slip is common and often fixed once pointed out. The pattern is the same person's contributions repeatedly ending up under someone else's name.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Your work or idea is shown as someone else's, once or over and over, until the people who matter no longer know it was yours.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Work continues while recognition accrues elsewhere, and by the time the pattern is visible the original attribution is hard to prove. Pay, promotion, references and your own sense of competence can all follow the credit rather than the work.
what_it_is: A slide deck, piece of code, draft, research finding or idea shown to a bigger audience under another name.
A slower form, where a suggestion is restated later with no name attached and the credit is absorbed by whoever is speaking.
Aimed at the people who decide things: senior meetings, funding panels, clients, byline lists.
Helped by informality. Ideas shared in hallways, chats and calls leave no record to point to.
Includes leaving a name off an author list, a patent, a credits page or a release note.
what_it_sounds_like: As I was saying, opening a point you made in the last meeting.
I put together a draft, about a draft you wrote.
The team came up with this, and your name is missing from every slide.
A thank-you sent to you privately while the all-staff message names someone else.
The byline order changes after you have sent the final file.
On a client call, your report is called 'my analysis'.
You don't mind, do you? It's all one team anyway, said after the fact.
what_it_is_not: Two people reaching the same idea independently, which happens often in shared fields.
A team product where credit is spread by agreement without erasing anyone.
An honest oversight in a list of names, corrected once it is pointed out.
Work done on behalf of an organization or client by agreement, such as ghostwriting or staff writing under a department name.
A manager saying 'my team shipped this', which claims the group and not your piece.
Someone building openly on your idea and naming you as its start.
this_may_be_it_when: You have a timestamp, draft, email or file showing the idea was yours first.
Your name drops off material as it moves up toward people with authority.
When you raise it, you are told it was a team effort or that credit does not matter.
The same person's contributions are the ones that keep getting reattributed, and in one direction.
Your suggestions are acknowledged more readily when someone else repeats them.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The idea came out of a shared brainstorm and nobody can say who said what first.
The person names you when asked and corrects the slide or email.
Credit follows a rule everyone knows, such as the lead author being whoever ran the analysis.
It happened once and the next project credits you.
Your only evidence is a version of events from rooms you were not in.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: After a long discussion memory merges, and people can honestly recall an idea as their own.
Time pressure produces short credit lines that omit names without anyone noticing.
Some workplaces and cultures credit the team or department by default.
common_false_positives: A senior colleague polishing your draft and then listing both of you.
A client report issued under the company brand with every contributor listed internally.
Two people presenting similar findings to different audiences, each having worked independently.
discernment_questions: Can I show when and where the idea or work first appeared, in writing?
When I mention a missing name, is it fixed, or explained away?
Does credit move in one direction, toward the same person, across projects?
On this kind of project, is credit shared by a rule or only withheld from me?
Who sees the version without my name, and does it matter to my job or study?
less_concerning_if: Your name is added as soon as it is mentioned, and the next document has it.
Credit practices are written down and apply to everyone on the team.
You are thanked publicly at other times for work of the same size.
more_concerning_if: The missing credit affects a promotion, a contract renewal, a grade or a publication.
You have been told to stop sending your work directly to senior people.
Raising it has been followed by lost projects, a colder tone or being left out of meetings.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your ideas turn up in later meetings under a different name, after a delay.
You start emailing wider lists and copying people just to make a record.
Opportunities that follow visible work, like being asked to present, go to someone else.
You stop sharing early ideas in rooms where they may be picked up.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair for credit can be measured: a correction sent to the same people who saw the wrong version, your name restored on the file or list, and the next project crediting you without being asked. A warm private thank-you with the public record unchanged repairs nothing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: After asking for your name on the work, watch the very next piece. Is the name there before you have to ask again? Or have you become the person who is difficult about credit?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Credit tends to go to whoever stands visibly behind the work in front of decision-makers. When an idea travels by informal routes, memory of its source is thin, and listeners often attach it to the person presenting. Each repetition makes the new attribution feel more settled, and challenging it later can feel petty even when it is accurate.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe a specific kind of anger: the work was real and the reward went elsewhere. Some stop sharing ideas early or start documenting everything. Others doubt whether the idea was that good, or whether they are petty for caring. Careers can stall because the evidence of contribution sits on someone else's record.

response_options.soft_clarification: Assume a slip and ask: 'I noticed my name isn't on the slide for the analysis I wrote. Can we add it before it goes out?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Name the fact and the fix: 'This section is my work, drafted on the third. I'd like it credited to me in the circulated version.'
response_options.disengagement: Share early ideas in writing, by email with a date and to the group, instead of in hallway talk or live calls where nothing is recorded.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask a colleague who saw the original work to confirm in writing when it was first shown, and talk to a mentor outside your reporting line about how to raise it.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Keep dated drafts and sent messages. Raise it with your manager first. If the reporting line is the problem, an HR, union or ombuds route can look at the record.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "The record needs to be right. I wrote this proposal and sent the first draft on the twelfth, so please credit it to me when it goes to the director's list."
codex_completed.safety_note: Credit theft rarely endangers you physically. It becomes more serious when it is tied to job security, a visa or sponsorship that depends on your employer, a degree, or retaliation after you speak. Gather dated proof of your own authorship, without copying confidential material before checking policy, and speak to an employment lawyer, union representative or student ombuds before escalating inside the organization.
misuse_warning: Claiming theft whenever a project's credit is less than you hoped can hurt a colleague who gave you a fair share. Check the record first.
Posting a screenshot of a missing name as a public accusation can turn a fixable oversight into a feud. Ask for the correction first.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Comparative Devaluation measures you unfavourably against other people; credit theft needs no comparison, because it moves the work itself. Emotional Invalidation is what you may hear when you raise it ('you're being petty'), but it is a separate act from the taking. Shame Installation attacks your adequacy as a person. Credit theft leaves your adequacy alone and takes the evidence of it.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Sabotaging Success
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A run of setbacks, such as a canceled lift, a lost message or a sudden crisis, that keeps landing just as someone is about to advance.
codex_completed.short_definition: A run of setbacks, such as a canceled lift, a lost message or a sudden crisis, that keeps landing just as someone is about to advance.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Here, delays and obstacles keep arriving just before something important to you: an exam, an interview, a launch, a course, a move. Each event looks ordinary alone, like a forgotten lift, a message that was not passed on, or a crisis that needs you tonight. What makes it a pattern is the timing and the repetition, and that the same person is near the trouble. Looking back across months can reveal a link no single event showed. It cannot tell you why anyone did it.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Things keep going wrong just before your big moments, and when you look back, the same person is close to the problem each time.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Progress keeps stalling for reasons that each look like bad luck, so you start doubting your own competence rather than the timing. Over months, chances to earn, learn or move out can quietly pass, which matters most where you depend on one person for money or a home.
what_it_is: Setbacks that cluster near a milestone: the night before an exam, the morning of an interview, a week before a deadline.
Events that are each deniable alone, such as an empty fuel tank, a vanished charger, a forgotten message or a family crisis.
Help that was reliable at other times, like childcare, rides or a quiet house, withdrawn exactly when it counts.
Emotional versions: a fight started the evening before a presentation, or bad news delivered late at night.
Sometimes discouragement in place of obstacles, such as 'Are you sure you want to?' repeated each time you apply or enroll.
what_it_sounds_like: I know your exam's tomorrow, but I really need to talk about us tonight.
Oh, I forgot to tell you the recruiter rang.
I can't do pickup after all, so you'll just have to miss the interview.
Do you really think you're ready for that course? It'll only end in tears.
Keys, charger or paperwork go missing on the morning of the interview, and nobody knows where.
We can't afford the fee this year, maybe next, said each time you sign up.
A crisis in their life on the eve of your milestone, for the third time this year.
what_it_is_not: Plain coincidence. Unrelated trouble does cluster around big days, partly because those are the days you are watching.
A person who is unreliable about everything, not only around your milestones.
Genuinely competing demands, such as shift work or a sick relative, that clash with your timeline.
A worried 'Are you sure?' from someone who says it once, names the cost to you, and helps anyway.
Your own nerves or avoidance before big moments producing mishaps that are then blamed on someone else.
Self-sabotage, which has a different cause and a different remedy.
this_may_be_it_when: Setbacks fall within days of milestones far more often than on random days once you check a calendar.
The same person is close to the problem each time, with a different reason each time.
Help available at other times is unavailable at exactly the key moment.
Your progress is met with sulking or unease, not interest.
When you succeed anyway, the response is cool or dismissive.
this_may_not_be_it_when: A calendar check shows setbacks spread evenly through the year.
They put in effort at the key moment, with rides, cover for childcare, or a quiet house.
Their own plans suffer from the same mishaps at the same rate.
The reason for each event holds up when you check it. A bus strike is a bus strike.
When you say a date is crucial, they rearrange things.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Families and workplaces run at a steady rate of mishaps, and important days are simply the ones you notice.
Anxiety about your milestone can make a partner or parent say 'Are you sure?' out of fear for you.
Overloaded people drop balls. They forget the message for the same reason they forget the groceries.
common_false_positives: Missing the train on interview day because a signal fault delayed everyone.
A friend who is poor at logistics and forgets all arrangements, not just the important ones.
A partner who cannot cover childcare because their shift changed, and who tries to find a replacement.
discernment_questions: If I mark every milestone on a calendar for a year, how do the setbacks line up with them?
Is the same person near the problem each time, or do the sources vary?
Does this person have the same trouble with their own plans, or only with mine?
When I explained that something mattered, did anything change in what they did?
What happened the last time I did well, and how did they react?
less_concerning_if: The setbacks come from many different sources, and some are clearly outside anyone's control.
The person celebrates when you advance.
They answer 'this date matters' by changing their plans.
more_concerning_if: The obstacles target things that would make you more independent: a job, a qualification, savings, a license, a move.
Money, transport, identity documents or your phone are involved.
Doubts about you are voiced to others, so that help dries up before you ask for it.
pattern_over_time_signs: You stop announcing plans in advance because trouble seems to follow.
A list of abandoned courses, applications and offers grows, each with its own good reason.
You rate your own ability lower, though results in other areas have been fine.
You feel a flicker of dread, not just excitement, when something good is about to happen.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair shows in what happens before the next milestone. Someone engaging with this asks which dates matter, protects them, and checks in afterwards. A heartfelt apology after you missed the chance, followed by the same last-minute trouble next time, addresses only the last event.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Tell them in advance that a particular date matters, then see what that week looks like. Do they ask what you need? Or does a fresh emergency appear, and does the talk turn to why you are making a fuss about the date?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Repeated disruption near goals can teach a person to link ambition with trouble and anxiety. Because each event has an ordinary explanation, the cost tends to be absorbed as a personal failing: not ready enough, not organized enough. Where someone also depends on the other person for money, a ride or a home, they may scale plans down in advance to protect the peace.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe the tiredness of preparing twice, once for the milestone and once for the interference. Some stop telling anyone their plans. Others came to believe they were bad at finishing things, and only saw the timing when they lined events up on a calendar. Hope can start to feel risky, and good news can arrive with dread.

response_options.soft_clarification: Say what the date means, early and plainly: 'The fourteenth is my exam. What would help me protect that evening? I'm asking for practical backup.'
response_options.firm_boundary: State the need, not the pattern: 'I need Wednesday evening free so I can prepare. Please don't plan anything for it.'
response_options.disengagement: Keep key plans and papers out of the line of disruption: tell fewer people the date, keep copies of documents elsewhere, and line up backup transport with a friend.
response_options.support_seeking: Show a trusted friend your calendar of milestones and setbacks side by side and ask what they see. A counselor or advocate can help you judge whether the timing is more than chance.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work or school, tell a supervisor or advisor about key dates early and ask in writing for flexibility, such as a later start or a deadline extension, so outside trouble can be absorbed.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "This course matters a lot to me, and my first assessment is next Tuesday. I'd like to talk about how we can keep that evening free, and what you can take on so I can study."
codex_completed.safety_note: Sabotage becomes a safety matter when it targets your independence: your job, qualification, savings, ID documents, phone or transport, or when it comes with threats or checking on where you go. Keep copies of key papers and a little money with someone you trust, and call a domestic abuse or financial-abuse service to talk it through confidentially before changing anything visibly.
misuse_warning: Reading every canceled plan as sabotage turns real bad luck and honest busyness into an accusation. A timeline kept over months is the evidence, not one bad week.
Telling someone they are sabotaging you before you have checked the pattern can end a conversation they would have joined. Start by describing the dates.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Setting Up to Fail hands you a task built to be lost; here the task is sound and the road to it keeps getting blocked from outside. Impossible Metrics keeps the bar out of reach, while this leaves the bar fine and the timing bad. Intimidation puts a threat on the table; sabotaging success arrives as ordinary bad timing, with nothing threatened.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Setting Up to Fail
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Giving someone a task or a standard they are unlikely to meet under the conditions provided, then treating the shortfall as proof of their inadequacy.
codex_completed.short_definition: Giving someone a task or a standard they are unlikely to meet under the conditions provided, then treating the shortfall as proof of their inadequacy.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: This covers two shapes: one assignment with the odds stacked, such as a deadline too short, a budget too small or information held back, and a standing bar kept out of reach by vague, shifting or contradictory criteria. Impossible metrics is just this tactic seen in its standing-bar form, so this entry covers both. Hard tasks are normal. The pattern shows when requests for what is needed are brushed aside, the finish line moves, and the miss is later cited as a fact about you.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You get a job or a target that few people could meet with what you were given, and when you fall short, the blame lands on you and not on the set-up.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Conditions disappear from the account and only the outcome remains, so a predictable failure becomes durable evidence about the person who was handed it. Effort rises while the record of misses grows, and that record can be quoted in reviews and decisions about you long after the conditions are forgotten.
what_it_is: A single task whose conditions make success unlikely: an impossible timeline, a thin budget, no access to people or data.
A standing target whose criteria, such as 'be more strategic', are vague enough to be reread after the fact.
A number that rises just as you approach it, or a new condition added when you meet the old one.
Contradictory demands, like cutting costs and doubling quality with the same team and hours.
A retelling that drops the conditions: 'the launch failed' instead of 'the launch had two weeks and no designer'.
Found in jobs, schools, households and caregiving, wherever one person sets the terms and another is judged on them.
what_it_sounds_like: "I know it's due Friday and the data isn't in yet, but I have faith in you."
"There's no budget for that, just make it work."
"You don't need to see the client brief. Just draft it."
"Hit ninety-five percent and we'll talk." Then, once you do: "Now we need ninety-eight."
"It just needs to be more polished," with no description of what polished means.
"I want it fast, perfect and cheap, and I'm not discussing which one gives."
"Why did you let it fail? I gave you everything you needed."
"Remember the Henderson project? That's why I can't trust you with this."
what_it_is_not: Hard tasks with real constraints, which are ordinary work, and resources that are unavailable to everyone rather than withheld from you.
Something that turned out harder than anyone anticipated, with nobody having arranged it.
A stretch goal or pilot framed openly as aspirational, with a fallback in place, so a miss is understood to be fine.
A demanding bar that others in your role have met under the same conditions, or that you have cleared before.
Clumsy delegation by someone who underestimated the task and revises the plan when told.
Hard but specific performance management, with written criteria and support.
this_may_be_it_when: Asked for what you need, you get a refusal without a reason.
Others got more time or support on comparable tasks.
Nobody under similar conditions has met the bar, and the goal changes shape just as you near it.
Asked what success looks like, you get adjectives instead of numbers or examples.
The record afterwards leaves out the constraints you flagged, and lists your misses more carefully than your hits.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You and the person assigning it both knew the odds and agreed to go ahead for a stated reason.
Your requests for support were met, even partly.
A post-mortem examined the conditions as well as your work.
Others in your role have hit the target and can describe how, and the criteria are in writing.
The missing information turned out to be unavailable to everybody.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Planners often underestimate how long things take, so the deadline may reflect a poor estimate.
Budgets get cut mid-quarter, and the person who assigned the task may have no say.
A busy person delegates with a thin brief because they do not have time to write a fuller one.
A manager can be unclear because the company is unclear, and vague goals often start with vague strategy.
common_false_positives: A start-up where everyone is stretched and the founder's own tasks are just as tight.
A coach's tough preparation set where the difficulty is the point and the athlete knows it.
A sales quota that is hard but hit by half the team.
discernment_questions: Could a competent person with these resources and this time have succeeded, and can I name someone who did?
Did I flag the constraints in writing before I began?
How were my requests for help handled, and how were other people's?
Can I write down what a pass looks like, and would the other person sign it?
Did the target move after I got near it?
When it failed, was the set-up discussed at all, or only me?
less_concerning_if: The shortfall in resources is shared by comparable tasks and acknowledged openly.
Requests for help get a real answer, even if the answer is no.
When you meet the target it is recognized, with no new condition appearing.
more_concerning_if: The same person hands you doomed tasks repeatedly while others get workable ones.
Your written flags of risk are ignored and the failure is then recorded as yours alone.
The record of misses is used to justify removing responsibility, pay, hours or a role.
pattern_over_time_signs: You begin sending a note in writing before each task listing what you would need.
Review meetings are mostly lists of what is missing.
You work longer hours each quarter for results that are no better received.
Colleagues or family members remember the failure but not its conditions.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair starts with the retelling and the bar. A person who has noticed this goes back to the people who heard you failed, corrects the account to include the deadline and missing staff, and gives the next assignment the resources it needs or a pass line written down. Praise for effort that leaves the record unchanged is a different thing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Watch the next request you send. Ask in writing for what the task needs, or for the definition of done. A yes, a partial yes with a reason, or a clear no that is noted in the plan means you were taken seriously. A cheerful 'you'll manage' with no reply is another answer.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Failure tends to be read as information about the person, and the conditions that produced it fade from memory faster than the outcome. If whoever set the task also describes the result, that account can become the accepted one. When a standard cannot be reached, effort stops translating into success, and people often turn the blame inward because the standard was presented as reasonable.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe replaying the project to find what they should have done, working longer for less sense of achievement, and dreading review days and the next hand-off. Some start to believe they are bad at jobs they once did well, or stop volunteering ideas. Others say that writing down the original conditions brought a grim relief, because the failure looked different on paper.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask about the gap before starting: "This needs three people and I have one, with two weeks. What would you like me to put first?"
response_options.firm_boundary: Put your concerns on record: "I'll start, and I want it noted that without the client data this deadline is not realistic."
response_options.disengagement: Offer the version of the task that can be done and be plain about what is left out, rather than quietly absorbing the shortfall with unpaid overtime.
response_options.support_seeking: Walk a mentor or friend outside the project through the brief, deadline and resources, and ask whether they would have seen it as doable. Compare targets with peers in the same role.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Send a short written summary after the assignment conversation: scope, deadline, resources, what you asked for. Keep it for any review, and ask HR or a union representative how your targets compare with your peers'.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I want this to go well, so I'm saying now that I can't finish it by Friday without the sales figures. Could we agree what counts as done, in writing, and when I can have the figures?"
codex_completed.safety_note: This is rarely a physical danger, but the record of misses can feed probation, dismissal, or job decisions that affect an immigration status or housing tied to the post. Keep the written brief, your flags and the outcome together, and ask a union representative, employment lawyer or legal aid service for advice before attending a disciplinary meeting alone.
misuse_warning: Calling every hard assignment a set-up can stop you learning from a failure that was partly yours. Ask whether the conditions were the same for others.
Treating a manager's vague wording as proof of a plan against you ignores that vagueness is often just an unfinished idea. Ask for specifics in writing first.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Comparative Devaluation holds you up against other people; here the comparison is to a target nobody has met, or to unnamed peers who 'manage'. Shame Installation turns a failure into a judgment about who you are, whereas this tactic supplies the failures that judgment can feed on. Intimidation threatens consequences; here nothing is threatened, and the record carries the consequence.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Scapegoating
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Placing blame for a shared, systemic or leadership failure on one individual, who then absorbs the consequences while the cause stays in place.
codex_completed.short_definition: Placing blame for a shared, systemic or leadership failure on one individual, who then absorbs the consequences while the cause stays in place.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Blame for a collective failure lands on one person, in a family, team, school, congregation or organization. That person may have played a small part, or none, yet they carry the consequences: a reprimand, dismissal, shunning, the shame. The conditions that caused the failure usually stay unchanged because the matter is now called solved. Real individual mistakes exist. The pattern lies in the mismatch between the blame and the person's actual authority and role.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: When something goes wrong for a whole group, one person is named as the cause and punished, and the real problem stays untouched.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: One person absorbs consequences out of proportion to a collective failure, and the conditions that produced it stay exactly as they were, because the matter has been declared solved. The person blamed can lose standing, income or belonging, while the same problem waits for the next name.
what_it_is: One person made to carry blame for an outcome shaped by many: a leadership decision, a team culture, a family tension.
A blamed person who typically has less power or standing than those who made the decisions.
A way of closing the matter: once someone is blamed or removed, the group can say the problem is dealt with.
Formal at times, as in a dismissal or a report naming one person, and informal at others, such as the relative blamed for every holiday argument or a member shunned by the group.
Often fast, with blame arriving before evidence has been gathered.
what_it_sounds_like: We found the problem. It's Priya.
If it weren't for him, we'd all be fine.
A report names one junior employee as sole cause and leaves out the sign-off chain.
She's always the one who stirs things up, said in a family after a group row.
Let's not look backward. The person responsible has been dealt with.
The group chat turns on one member after a mistake everyone shared.
The organization says one individual acted outside procedures, while the procedures stay unchanged.
what_it_is_not: A case where one person did make the consequential mistake.
A situation where shared responsibility really does concentrate in one person's decisions.
Accountability that matches the person's real authority, which can feel harsh and still be proportionate.
A fair investigation that names an individual among several findings and also addresses the system.
Group frustration that fades once the cause is discussed, without anyone being punished.
A leader who owns a group's failure publicly instead of pushing it down.
this_may_be_it_when: The person blamed had little authority over the decision that failed.
The group's own role, or its leaders' decisions, are missing from the account.
Blame is assigned before facts are gathered, or the facts change to fit it.
The problem comes back after the person is gone.
The same person tends to be blamed for failures of different kinds.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The review looked at decisions at every level and still found this person's error the main cause.
The person had the authority and the information to make the call.
The process was fixed as well as the person dealt with.
Others who were involved also face consequences.
The person agrees with the account of what they did.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Groups under pressure grab simple explanations, and one name is easier to repeat than a complicated cause, without any plan behind it.
People often misjudge how much control a person had. A manager may believe an employee had more authority than they did.
A person's own error can be the trigger, with the deeper problems found only later.
common_false_positives: A safety review that finds one person's error was the trigger and also lists changes to the system.
A team member who missed every deadline and is named in a fair review.
A friend group deciding that one member's repeated lateness really did cost them their reservation.
discernment_questions: How much authority and information did this person really have over what went wrong?
Have the people above or alongside them been asked the same questions?
What changed after the blame was assigned, apart from the person?
Was the person heard before the blame was fixed?
Has this person been blamed before for things beyond their role?
less_concerning_if: The investigation reviewed several levels and the person had a chance to respond.
Consequences match the person's role and the degree of fault.
The conditions that let the failure happen were fixed as well, not only the person.
more_concerning_if: The blame is attached to firing, expulsion, shunning or public naming.
The blamed person has little power or protection, such as a junior, an outsider, or someone who depends on the group for housing or income.
Those who question the story become targets in turn.
pattern_over_time_signs: Each new failure produces a new name, often someone with little standing.
The same underlying problem keeps coming back under different people.
The group's story settles quickly into 'it was them' and stops being examined.
People who might speak up in the person's defense grow quiet.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair means the cause gets examined after the blame. In practice that looks like a revised account naming what leaders or the group decided, a restored reputation or role for the person, and a changed process. An apology to the one person with the rest of the structure left alone has not reached the source.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: If you ask for the same questions to be put to others involved, does the group agree, or does the questioning itself get treated as defending the culprit? What happens to the next person who asks may tell you more than the answer does.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Groups under pressure tend to want a quick, simple cause, and a single person is easier to hold responsible than a system. Blame can also relieve the group's discomfort: if one person caused it, nobody else needs to change. People with less power are easier targets, and once a story is repeated it tends to feel settled. The person blamed may start to accept it.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe being cut off from colleagues or relatives who used to be friendly, replaying whether they really were the cause, and being unable to correct a story everyone has already heard. Some lose a job or standing. Others describe lasting wariness of groups and a sense of being watched for the next error.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the full picture in a calm voice: 'Can we look at who signed off on this and what the process was? I'd like the account to be complete.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Correct the record on what you did: 'I carried out the instruction I was given on the third. I'm happy to go through the emails.'
response_options.disengagement: Don't try to win the group over in the moment. Write down your account while it is fresh, and hold off replying in group chats while feelings are high.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk to someone outside the group, such as a friend, a union representative or an ombuds, who can hear your account without a stake in it and say whether the blame matches your role.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask in writing for the findings and a chance to respond. Gather the instructions, approvals and emails showing who decided what, and bring them to HR, a union or an employment lawyer.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'm willing to answer for the part that was mine. I'd like the decisions made above and alongside me to be looked at in the same review, and I'd like to see the findings before they are shared."
codex_completed.safety_note: Scapegoating becomes a safety matter when blame is attached to dismissal, loss of housing, exile from a group, harassment or threats, or when the group is one you cannot easily step away from, such as a family or a faith community. Keep copies of your own account and any messages, and see an employment lawyer, tenants' service or advocate before agreeing to any statement or exit terms.
misuse_warning: Calling every disciplinary outcome scapegoating can turn away fair accountability for a mistake that was truly yours. Check whether the consequences match your authority.
Naming someone else as the group's scapegoat in a dispute can itself pin a role on them. Describe what happened to the person instead.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Setting Up to Fail arranges conditions so that one assignment goes wrong, whereas scapegoating happens after a failure that was already shared. Comparative Devaluation lowers you against other people. Scapegoating makes you the single carrier of something that belonged to everyone. Shame Installation says you are inadequate as a person; scapegoating concerns who pays for one specific failure.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Flying Monkeys
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Friends, relatives or colleagues drawn in to carry pressure or criticism to someone, or to report back on them, for another person who stays out of the room.
codex_completed.short_definition: Friends, relatives or colleagues drawn in to carry pressure or criticism to someone, or to report back on them, for another person who stays out of the room.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Flying monkeys are third parties who carry another person's pressure, messages or watching to someone, often believing they are simply helping. Proxy Recruitment is the same tactic under another name: one name stresses the go-between acting in good faith, the other stresses the asking itself. A single relative checking in is ordinary. It starts to look like this tactic when the same message arrives from several people, shaped by one person's account, while the original person never has to answer for it.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: People close to you start passing on someone else's demands or questions, usually thinking they are helping, while the person behind it stays out of sight.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Pressure arrives from several directions at once, from people who believe they are acting on their own concern, which makes it nearly impossible to answer without appearing to attack them. The person whose concern it is never has to stand behind what is being demanded.
what_it_is: A person asked or persuaded to carry a message, a demand or an apology to you, so that they, and not the original person, face you.
A messenger who usually holds only one side's account, often believes it, and may be sincerely worried.
Contact that can run the other way too: messengers gathering news about where you are, who you see and how you are, and passing it back.
The same request arriving from several people within a short span, in similar words.
Found in families, friend groups, congregations and workplaces, and after separations.
what_it_sounds_like: I'm not taking sides, but they're really hurting. Can't you just call them?
They asked me to talk to you. I don't want to be the bad guy, but somebody has to say it.
I only know what they've told me, but you need to hear this.
I promised I'd pass this on, so please don't shoot the messenger.
How are you doing? Where are you staying these days?
Three different people have rung me about you this week, and they're all saying the same things.
They said you wouldn't pick up their calls, so I thought I'd try.
A cousin you rarely hear from repeats a phrase you first heard from the other person.
what_it_is_not: Friends noticing things on their own and reaching out unprompted, and family members who discuss shared worries and reach similar views.
Asking a mutual friend how to approach a hard conversation, which is different from asking them to have it for you.
A go-between set up openly where direct contact is not safe or possible, such as a mediator or a lawyer.
Someone who hears about a conflict and decides by themselves to raise it, speaking for themselves.
A relative who relays a message because both people asked them to, and who is clear about whose message it is.
Someone checking in out of their own long relationship with you.
this_may_be_it_when: The messenger quotes details that only one person could have supplied, or uses that person's phrases.
They tell you they were asked to get in touch, or let it slip.
Several people with little recent contact raise the same issue within days.
Their questions concern where you are, who you are with or what you plan to do, more than how you feel.
What you say in reply reaches the original person, who then responds to your exact words.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The person has a record of reaching out on their own, with no sign of contact with the other side.
They are as willing to hear your account as the other person's, and are clear they will not carry it back.
Their concerns include things the other person never raised.
Their worry looks the same whether or not you answer.
They tell you plainly whose message it is and accept a no without pressing.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People who love both sides often try to patch a rift without anyone asking them to.
A relative with a one-sided account may honestly be passing on what they heard.
News travels fast among relatives, so concern can seem to arrive all at once.
People ask for news of you simply because they miss you.
common_false_positives: A sister who calls after hearing you have been unwell because she is worried.
A coworker who delivers a team's feedback because the manager asked them to, in an openly stated process.
Several friends who each separately notice you have gone quiet and say so.
A mutual friend who, with both people's knowledge, hands back borrowed belongings.
discernment_questions: Does this person's account match what I know, or do they hold only one version?
Did they say they were asked? If I ask, will they tell me?
Would they have contacted me if the other person had not been upset?
Does what I tell them stay with them?
Are the questions about me, or about where I am and what I am doing?
Do they hear my side as well, or only carry theirs?
less_concerning_if: The messenger is open about who asked them and accepts your answer without pressing.
They also listen to your account and say they will keep it to themselves.
The contact happens once and ends when you reply.
more_concerning_if: Messengers ask for your address, your plans or the names of people you are staying with.
The people relaying are those you used to lean on for support, so it feels as though support is being withdrawn.
You have already created distance for your own safety and contact keeps arriving through new people.
pattern_over_time_signs: New people start contacting you with the same talking points after earlier ones have been turned down.
Private news you shared with one person turns up in the original person's replies.
Relatives or friends who were warm begin to hedge or hold back.
You start to hesitate before telling anyone anything, wondering who it will reach.
codex_completed.repair_check: Changed behavior looks like the original person speaking for themselves, or going quiet, and the messengers stopping and saying so. If a go-between keeps sending the same message under a softer name, or an apology only reaches you through other people, nothing has changed.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice whether a no given to the messenger stays with the messenger. If the requests stop and nothing you said comes back to you secondhand, it was respected. If a different person turns up within days on the same topic, the boundary is being routed around.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Trust in relatives and friends is usually higher than in strangers, so a request from someone close is harder to refuse than the original demand. The go-between often believes the account they were given, and their sincerity lends it weight. Several voices can leave a person feeling outnumbered, and answering one may seem like attacking someone who means well.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A common account is feeling cornered by loved ones, not knowing whom to trust with news, and tiptoeing around relatives in case what they say is passed back. Some describe losing contact with people caught in the middle, and carrying guilt about refusing someone who was only trying to help.

response_options.soft_clarification: Thank the messenger for caring and answer only about how you are doing, nothing about plans or whereabouts. You can reply on your own schedule.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline the topic, not the person, and keep it brief: 'I'd rather not get into that through you, but I'm glad you're thinking of me.'
response_options.disengagement: Say nothing about plans, location or new contacts to anyone who might relay it, and let a call go unanswered when you feel pressed. You do not owe a reply on the spot.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell an advocate or a trusted person outside the circle who is contacting you and what they ask. They can help judge whether it is concern or tracking, and what to keep private.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If colleagues are being sent to press you, keep dated notes of who said what and bring them to HR or a manager you trust as a pattern, not as accusations.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Caring about this is good of you. I'm not going to talk about it through someone else, so I'd rather keep our conversation to how you're doing. Can we talk about something else?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Most messengers mean well, so this is not usually dangerous in itself. It becomes a safety matter when the questions concern where you live, who you are with or when you are alone, or when contact keeps arriving after you have gone quiet for protection. Share nothing about your location or routine with anyone who might pass it on, and ask a domestic abuse advocate to help plan who can know what.
misuse_warning: Calling a worried relative a flying monkey can end a friendship that was only concern. Ask first whether they were asked to get in touch; many will say.
The label describes a role in an exchange, not a verdict on the person carrying the message.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Triangulation pulls a third party into the conflict as ammunition, by comparing you to them or quoting them against you, while here the third party is sent to you or sent to look at you. Concern Trolling wraps a control directive in worry, whether or not anyone else is involved. Forced Teaming builds a 'we' that erases your choice. Flying monkeys is the one defined by someone else standing in for the original person.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Smear Campaign
