codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Spreading distorted or false accounts of a person to those who matter to them, so they are doubted, shunned or not believed before they have spoken.
codex_completed.short_definition: Spreading distorted or false accounts of a person to those who matter to them, so they are doubted, shunned or not believed before they have spoken.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A smear campaign is a sustained effort to shape what others believe about someone, through exaggeration, selective framing or invention. It is also called Reputation Poisoning, when the doubt is placed quietly with a few key people before any dispute, and Reputation Warfare (Post-Separation), when it follows a break-up or exit into work and friendships. These are the same tactic at different moments and scales. One angry vent to a friend is not it. The pattern is a consistent story, repeated to people whose opinion matters, that outlasts correction.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone spreads a distorted story about you to the people whose view of you matters, so you are doubted or dropped and your own account is heard as a reaction.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The account travels faster than any correction, and it often reaches people before you know there is anything to correct. When you finally speak, you may be heard as proof of what they were warned about, and you can lose work, friends or standing without a single conversation to point to.
what_it_is: A damaging story built from distortion: true details stripped of context, small matters inflated, or claims with no basis.
Told to people whose belief matters most, such as colleagues, a new partner's family, a congregation, a club or a future employer.
Sometimes planted early as reluctant concern ('I worry about them'), so that a later complaint is already discounted.
After a break-up or departure, able to reach references, shared friends and professional networks.
Usually discovered second-hand, if at all, because the target is not in the room.
what_it_sounds_like: I probably shouldn't say this, but I've always worried about how stable they are.
I'm only telling you because I care what happens to you.
I'm not saying they're lying, but I'd check everything they tell you.
I heard you were the reason the last team fell apart.
Oh, I was warned about you.
A reference you expected to be glowing is lukewarm, and the person says they 'heard some things'.
Friends who were warm go quiet, and one lets slip a phrase you have never said yourself.
You wouldn't believe what they put me through. I don't like to talk about it.
what_it_is_not: Venting honestly to a close friend after a painful break-up, with no follow-up and no spread.
Independent, accurate criticism from several people who each have their own basis for it.
A specific, warranted concern passed to someone who genuinely needs it, such as an employer checking a documented problem.
Ordinary gossip that nobody started and nobody steers.
Social circles thinning out after a separation, with no account being pushed.
A public dispute in which both sides sincerely believe their own version.
this_may_be_it_when: The same unusual detail or phrase shows up in different people's mouths, each saying they heard it from someone.
The claims can be checked and are false or twisted, and correction changes nothing.
Doubt about you was placed in someone's mind well before any conflict between you.
The story follows you into new settings, such as a new job, club or relationship, soon after you join.
Everyone has heard it and no one will say from whom.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Different people raise different concerns, each from their own contact with you.
The people who doubt you can describe something they saw first-hand, and it is accurate.
The claims are true, even if unflattering.
Only one friend ever heard it, and it went no further.
The cooling off matches ordinary distance after a split, and nobody repeats a story.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Hurt people sometimes talk a great deal, to many friends, in the first raw weeks, without wanting to shape anyone's reputation.
Mutual friends can form concerns of their own from what they saw.
People retell stories with their own slant, so a rumor drifts from the facts with nobody steering it.
A person anxious about being judged may explain their side in advance to everyone.
common_false_positives: A former colleague who gives an honest, mixed reference.
Friends who side with an ex after a split because they have known them longer.
A group chat where a complaint about you snowballed in a single evening.
One negative post by a single person that others then repeated.
discernment_questions: Can I trace the story to one source, or does it vary from person to person?
Is it false or distorted, or accurate but unflattering?
Was doubt placed with these people before there was any dispute?
Has the story changed when I supplied corrections?
Is it following me specifically into places that matter for my work or standing?
Have I heard this from the people themselves, or only through one second-hand report?
less_concerning_if: What circulates is limited, accurate and fades as the dispute cools.
The people who heard it are willing to hear your side, and some tell you what they were told.
The talk ends within weeks and does not travel to new settings.
more_concerning_if: The story reaches your employer, licensing body, landlord or anyone who decides about money, housing or contact with children.
It continues for months after a separation, in new places, and a new version appears each time an old one is corrected.
It comes alongside other pressure after separation, such as tracking, repeated legal filings or contact you have asked to stop.
pattern_over_time_signs: People you hardly know treat you coolly and cannot say why.
You learn of each new version of the story second-hand.
Opportunities, references or invitations cool off in the same circles.
You begin to second-guess everyone's warmth and to explain yourself before anyone has asked.
codex_completed.repair_check: Change would look like the account being corrected to the same people who heard it, and then stopping, not a private apology to you. A promise to stop that leaves the story standing in every other room has not reached where the harm is.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Watch the story, not the promise. A month after you raised it, are new people still hearing it? If the account goes quiet and stops following you into new places, your request was heard. If a fresh version appears, it was not.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: First impressions tend to come from whoever speaks first, especially someone who sounds reluctant or worried, and an early impression colours how later information is read. A warning placed in advance can turn a later complaint into confirmation. Hearing a story from several people can make it feel independently confirmed, even when all of them heard it from one place.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe discovering that others have been treating them differently for months, feeling they must defend themselves to people who have not asked, and fearing that every explanation sounds defensive. Some describe lost jobs, references or friendships, and a wariness about trusting any group again.

response_options.soft_clarification: If someone you trust mentions what they heard, ask what exactly was said and thank them. You do not need to refute it on the spot, only learn what is circulating.
response_options.firm_boundary: When asked directly about the story, answer briefly with facts and no counter-accusations: 'That isn't accurate, and I'm happy to show you what happened.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop trying to correct everyone. Concentrate on the few people whose view affects your work or safety, and let the rest of the circle go.
response_options.support_seeking: Write down dates, names and the exact claims, and share them with a lawyer, advocate or counselor who can say whether any of it is actionable or bears on a court case.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If the story reaches your workplace, give HR or your manager a short factual note, ask that any complaint be put in writing, and keep copies.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I've heard that some things are being said about me that aren't accurate. Whenever you're ready, I can tell you what happened in my own words. You don't have to take my word for it."
codex_completed.safety_note: A smear alone is not physical danger, but it becomes a safety matter when it travels with tracking, repeated filings, threats, or a push to turn a court, employer or school against you. Do not answer the story in public or by contacting the person directly. Keep dated copies of what you can and take them to legal aid or a domestic violence advocate who can advise on safe responses.
misuse_warning: Not every unflattering account is a smear. People are entitled to honest bad opinions, and calling accurate criticism a campaign can silence legitimate complaints.
Telling people your own story about someone who hurt you is not in itself a smear. The label fits distortion that spreads, not an honest account of what happened.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Flying Monkeys sends people to you with a message, while a smear tells people about you behind your back. Public Humiliation embarrasses someone in front of others, face to face, where a smear works out of the target's sight. Legal Abuse (Post-Separation) works through courts and filings, and a smear works through opinion and trust. The smear is the one carried entirely by what others have been led to believe.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Silent Coalitions
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: A group quietly agreeing, without any open discussion, to keep one person on the margins so that no clear incident ever exists.
codex_completed.short_definition: A group quietly agreeing, without any open discussion, to keep one person on the margins so that no clear incident ever exists.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A silent coalition is a group that sidelines one member through many small, deniable acts: plans made elsewhere, replies that arrive late, jokes that nobody explains. There is no announcement and often no explicit agreement, so the person has nothing concrete to name and may conclude the fault lies with them. Any one slight is ordinary. It starts to look like a coalition when the same person is left out consistently, across settings, while others in the group are not.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A group keeps one person on the edge through lots of small, hard-to-prove moments, so the person starts to think the problem must be them.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: There is no incident to point at, only a consistent absence, which turns the search for an explanation inward. The person ends up blaming themselves for something nobody will admit to.
what_it_is: Consistent small exclusions from invitations, group chats, inside jokes and decisions, with no single moment that could be called unfair.
Exclusion that looks coordinated, though the coordination itself can never be seen.
Shared reactions across several people, such as the same polite silence when the person speaks.
Denial when the person raises it, often with real surprise, because each individual feels they did nothing.
what_it_sounds_like: A group chat that quietly moves to a new thread without you, and no one mentions it.
Plans mentioned on Monday that you learn about only after they happened.
Replies to your messages that are polite but shorter and later than the replies others get.
When you ask whether something is going on, several people say 'no, of course not' in similar words.
Your suggestions in meetings get a pause, then the same idea is picked up when someone else says it.
People who are friendly one-on-one are distant in a group.
what_it_is_not: Social anxiety can produce the same feeling with nothing at all behind it, and some groups are simply less inclusive as a general dynamic rather than towards one individual.
A low period colors ordinary social gaps and makes a pattern out of them.
A tight friend group that has history together and is not hostile to new people, only slow to open up.
A busy season in which everyone is slow to reply, including to each other.
Drifting apart because interests, schedules or life stages have changed.
this_may_be_it_when: Others who joined at the same time are included, and you are consistently not.
The distance shows up across different settings, such as work, chat and social events.
One-on-one, people are warm, but in the group the warmth disappears.
A trusted outside person has seen the pattern on their own.
When you name it, the group responds with matching denials and no curiosity about how it feels to you.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The feeling comes and goes with your mood and fades when you are rested or in better spirits.
You can find examples of the group including you in the last month.
Another person in the group feels equally left out, which suggests a loose group and not a target.
When you ask directly, someone explains a reason and the exclusion stops.
Your own contact has dropped, so replies simply mirror yours.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Groups drift into habits, such as a chat that formed before you arrived, with no intention behind it.
People with their own problems may be slow to reply to everyone.
A low mood or anxiety can make neutral silence feel personal.
common_false_positives: A team lunch that happened on a day you were away and was never planned to leave you out.
A friend group that has an established chat and forgot to add a newcomer.
A period after a loss or illness when you feel on the outside, though people are in fact reaching out.
discernment_questions: How are other members treated in the same situations, and is the difference consistent?
Does the feeling hold across weeks, or does it shift with your own state?
Has someone outside the group, who has no stake, noticed the same thing?
When you ask a calm, direct question, is there curiosity or a matching denial?
Is there one person in the group who still treats you the same way, and what do they say?
less_concerning_if: Comparing notes shows that others feel the same way and the group is simply loose.
Asking directly leads to an explanation and a change.
The feeling lifts when your mood improves.
more_concerning_if: An outside observer independently describes the same consistent pattern.
Your work, housing or status is being affected by the exclusion.
The sidelining began right after you disagreed with someone or raised a concern.
pattern_over_time_signs: You keep a mental list of events you were not told about, and the list grows.
You begin to question your own tone, clothes or habits as the cause.
Where you once spoke freely in the group, you now rehearse everything.
Friends outside the group notice that you seem smaller whenever it is mentioned.
codex_completed.repair_check: Something real has shifted when someone in the group notices the gap and says so aloud, includes you in the next plan and keeps doing it. A rush of warmth for a week followed by the old silence is not that. What counts is the next month of ordinary invitations.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: After you say 'I've felt left out', consider whether anyone asks what that has been like. Curiosity suggests that people take it seriously. If you hear 'you're overthinking' in several voices at once, that shared script is worth noticing, though it does not prove a plan.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People rely on a group's reactions to know where they stand. When exclusion arrives in small, deniable pieces, there is no single event to evaluate, so the mind may supply an explanation and tends to pick one about the self. Humans are also sensitive to being left out, and ambiguity can feel worse than a clear rejection.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe replaying conversations to look for the mistake, withdrawing from the group, and feeling embarrassed to say they feel left out. Some begin to avoid places where the group meets. Some feel a mix of relief and anger when they learn that others noticed too.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask one person you trust in the group: 'I've felt a bit on the outside lately. Have you noticed anything, or am I reading too much into it?'
response_options.firm_boundary: State the experience without accusing anyone: 'I've noticed I'm often not included. I'd like to be told about plans, and I'll take it from there.'
response_options.disengagement: Spend your time where you are welcomed, and let the group's access to you reflect how it treats you, without announcing it.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe a few specific examples to someone outside the group and ask whether they see what you see, and whether the story rings true to them.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, keep a dated list of meetings and decisions you were left out of, and ask your manager for clear communication about how projects are shared.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I've noticed I'm often out of the loop on plans, and it's been weighing on me. I'm not blaming anyone. I'd just like to be included, and I'd welcome hearing if there is something I'm missing."
codex_completed.safety_note: Group exclusion hurts, but it rarely creates physical danger. It changes if the group's silence follows you into your home, your job or online spaces through threats, rumors that could cost you work or housing, or sharing of private images. At that point, save evidence and speak to a trusted person, an employer's process or a local support service.
misuse_warning: Treating every unreturned message as a coalition can turn ordinary social drift into a story of persecution and push away people who are not hostile.
Telling others that a group is conspiring against you, without evidence, can itself damage relationships that might have recovered.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Triangulation is active and spoken, with third parties quoted against you, while a silent coalition is made of absences that nobody ever voices. Flying Monkeys act, pressing or checking on you for someone else, and the coalition simply withholds. A polite hostile environment punishes people for speaking up, whereas a silent coalition can sideline someone who has said nothing at all.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Group Consolidation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Publicly punishing one person harshly enough that everyone watching learns what disagreement will cost them.
codex_completed.short_definition: Publicly punishing one person harshly enough that everyone watching learns what disagreement will cost them.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Group consolidation uses one person as a lesson. Someone who pushed back, questioned a decision or broke an unwritten rule is reprimanded, mocked or removed in front of others, and the severity fits the warning better than the offense. The real audience is everyone else. Ordinary accountability can also be visible, and a serious breach may deserve a visible response. What gives it away is a penalty out of proportion, staged for onlookers and followed by a quieter group.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: One person is punished in front of everyone, and the punishment is bigger than what they did, so the rest of the group learns to keep their heads down.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Everyone watching learns the price of dissent without being told, and the lesson outlasts the person it was demonstrated on.
what_it_is: A reprimand, demotion, removal or ridicule delivered where others can see it, in a way that is bigger than the matter calls for.
A penalty whose timing and setting seem chosen for the onlookers, such as at a meeting, in a group chat or at a family dinner.
An example made after someone questioned a leader or broke an unspoken norm, and not after a clear rule violation.
A change in the group's behavior afterward: fewer questions, more careful words, more agreement.
what_it_sounds_like: A person who questioned a plan is called out by name at the all-hands, with a long list of past mistakes.
A leader says 'let this be a lesson to everyone' after a minor error.
A group chat member who disagreed is removed, and the rest are told it was 'for the good of the group'.
A dismissal is announced to the whole department the same day, with no private conversation first.
After a public dressing-down, the room goes quiet and the next meeting has no questions.
A relative who disagreed at a family dinner is mocked in front of the table, and others laugh nervously.
what_it_is_not: Proportionate accountability can be visible simply because of the setting, such as an open-plan office, a meeting or a family gathering.
A genuinely serious matter can warrant a visible response on its own merits.
Consequences applied consistently and announced as policy are not calibrated to an audience.
A leader explaining why a rule was enforced so that others understand the standard, without humiliating the person.
A group removing someone who harassed other members, where the removal protects people and is in proportion.
this_may_be_it_when: The size of the penalty is clearly larger than the act that led to it.
It was staged where others would see it, when a private conversation was available.
The person punished had challenged a leader or a norm, and not broken a clear rule.
Others in the group became visibly quieter and more cautious after it happened.
People who made similar mistakes without challenging anyone were not treated the same way.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The same consequence has been applied in the same way to others, regardless of who watched.
The person broke a clear, known rule, and the consequence matches what was written down.
A private attempt to resolve it came first, and the visible step followed only after it failed.
The response was about safety or the protection of others and not about dissent.
Group members still raise concerns freely afterward and nothing changes in the room.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Small organizations and families have little privacy, so even gentle accountability may be seen by others.
A leader under pressure may overreact in the moment without any intention to teach a lesson.
Some workplaces and teams publish consequences openly as a matter of fairness.
common_false_positives: A coach who benches a player for missing practice in front of the team, as the team rules state.
A manager who ends a contract with a person who broke a safety rule and tells the team why, to prevent a repeat.
A family that holds a visible talk with a relative who did something serious, as part of a plan to help.
discernment_questions: Is the consequence in proportion to what the person actually did?
Could this have been handled privately, and if so, why was it not?
Has the same consequence been applied to others who did the same thing but never challenged anyone?
Did the mood of the group change afterward, and in which direction?
Would you feel free to raise the same concern the person punished had raised?
less_concerning_if: The consequence is proportionate and follows a written or well-understood rule.
The same response would have been given to anyone, whoever was watching.
People feel free to ask about it afterward and receive honest answers.
more_concerning_if: The punishment targets someone who raised a safety, ethics or fairness concern.
People are warned not to speak to or support the person punished.
Livelihood, housing or standing in a community is put at stake to make the example stick.
pattern_over_time_signs: Meetings gradually go quiet, and questions are sent privately or not at all.
People begin to refer to the punished person in the past tense, as a warning story.
New members are told quietly about the one who 'didn't last'.
Each time someone is made an example of, the next dissent appears later and softer.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair looks like the group's leader acknowledging in public that the response went beyond what the matter warranted, and then allowing questions to be raised without penalty. A private apology to the person alone, while the audience continues to carry the lesson, leaves the main effect in place.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: The next time someone raises a similar concern is the test. If it is heard and answered, the example has lost its force. If the room goes silent or looks to the leader first, the lesson is still active, whatever has been said about openness.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People often learn the rules of a group by watching what happens to others, and seeing someone punished can teach more than a written policy. Fear of being next can lead to self-censoring before any threat is made. Observers may also distance themselves from the person punished, which can deepen that person's isolation.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People who were made an example of describe humiliation and isolation, and sometimes shame that lasts after the group has moved on. Onlookers describe guilt about staying silent, tension in meetings, and a habit of checking the leader's face before speaking. Some leave quietly, and some say they stopped believing they could raise problems.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the leader privately what rule or standard applied: 'Can you help me understand what the expectation is, so I know how to handle it next time?'
response_options.firm_boundary: State your own limit without confronting anyone in public: 'I will keep raising concerns through the proper channel, and I'd like a clear response when I do.'
response_options.disengagement: Reduce your visibility in the room if you feel at risk, while you decide privately what to do, and avoid joining in the mockery of the person punished.
response_options.support_seeking: Reach out quietly to the person who was singled out, and to someone outside the group, so that no one carries the lesson alone.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Write down what happened, when and who saw it, and bring it to HR, an ombuds office, a union representative or an employment lawyer if the response affected someone's job.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I think the issue deserved a conversation, but I don't think it needed to be handled in front of everyone. I'd like us to agree on how concerns are raised, so that people feel able to speak up."
codex_completed.safety_note: Public punishment is a status and fairness issue in most cases. It becomes more serious if it is used to threaten livelihood, housing or standing in a close community, if people are told to shun the person, or if it is combined with intimidation. Keep notes with dates and witnesses, and speak with an employment lawyer, a union or a trusted outside advisor early.
misuse_warning: Reading every public reprimand as an example being made can overlook cases where visible accountability was fair and proportionate.
Calling a leader's decision 'consolidation' without evidence about timing, proportion and audience can turn a disagreement into an accusation of motive.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: A polite hostile environment punishes quietly and deniably, while group consolidation depends on being seen. Silent Coalitions exclude without any announcement, and here the announcement is the point. Triangulation sets two people against each other with borrowed voices, but consolidation addresses the whole group through one person's example.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Pile-Ons
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Many people pile criticism onto one person in a short span, so the sheer volume becomes the problem.
codex_completed.short_definition: Many people pile criticism onto one person in a short span, so the sheer volume becomes the problem.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A pile-on happens when a large number of people pour criticism onto one person in a short window, usually online but also in group chats, staff channels and school hallways. Each message may be mild, and some may even be fair. The weight comes from the count and the speed, because nobody can answer fifty people at once. It needs no organizer; people often join because others already have. One angry reply means little. What defines a pile-on is scale and pace.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Lots of people criticize you at the same moment, so even small comments add up to something you cannot answer or escape.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Fifty versions of the same criticism land as something different from one, and there is no way to answer them at the scale they arrive. The person may lose sleep, leave a platform or stop speaking up, even when a few of the points were fair.
what_it_is: A sudden surge of replies, comments or messages aimed at one person after a post, a mistake or a rumor.
Often fueled by a screenshot or quote shared outside its original context, so newcomers react to the clip instead of the whole story.
Joiners frequently add one more line without reading what came before, so the tone hardens as the thread grows.
Possible in a comment section, a group chat, a classroom or a staff channel, not only on big platforms.
Different from a one-on-one argument because the target faces a crowd and cannot reply to each person.
what_it_sounds_like: Did you really say that? Everyone is talking about you.
A reply thread where the first twenty responses are the same sentence in different words.
I haven't read the whole thread but wow.
A group chat where people who had been quiet each type 'same' under a complaint about you.
Ratio'd. Just delete your account.
Notifications arriving faster than you can open them.
what_it_is_not: A serious concern genuinely shared by many people. When many people independently say a statement was harmful, that is feedback, not a pile-on.
Proportionate public criticism of a public figure for a public statement.
Varied, independent responses that disagree with each other and include some support.
Several friends each raising the same worry with you privately, at different times.
Customers all complaining about the same real defect in a product.
Critics who quote you accurately and answer what you actually said, even if there are many of them.
this_may_be_it_when: Replies arrive in a burst over minutes or hours rather than trickling in over days.
Many responders react to a quoted piece or screenshot, not the full original.
The wording of the criticism converges, with the same phrase or insult repeated.
Responses are about you as a person more than about the specific statement.
Accounts with no earlier contact with you join, often right after a larger account shares the post.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The responses disagree with one another and include people who defend you.
Most people quote what you actually said and respond to its content.
The criticism comes from people you know, raised in separate, calm conversations.
The volume is small and spread over weeks.
Someone from the group offers to talk it through, and then does.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A post can simply reach many people quickly, and a large audience produces a large reaction without anyone coordinating.
People who join late often assume the earlier replies were reasoned, so they add their own without any ill will.
Some commenters were upset about a real harm in the post and said so in a line.
common_false_positives: A widely shared demand for an apology after a genuinely harmful statement.
A product page filling with the same complaint about a real defect.
Fans of a team all groaning at one referee call in the same match thread.
discernment_questions: Do the responses engage with what I actually said, or with a clipped version of it?
If I set the number aside, would any single comment be a fair point?
Are the replies varied, or do they converge on one line?
Did the volume jump after a larger account shared my post?
Is it fading within a day or two, or being renewed by new posts?
less_concerning_if: The replies disagree with each other and some defend you.
It fades within a day or two without new fuel.
At least one criticism is accurate and you can answer it directly.
more_concerning_if: Replies move from criticism of what you said to your workplace, address or family.
The same accounts keep returning with new posts after the first wave has faded.
The pile-on spills into your real-life groups, such as your team, school or neighborhood.
pattern_over_time_signs: You check notifications compulsively and reread the same cutting lines.
You edit or hold back what you post, even in places the crowd never visited.
Old screenshots resurface whenever you say something new.
People you barely know mention the episode as though it defined you.
codex_completed.repair_check: After a pile-on, repair shows in the crowd's behavior: people who joined correct a mistaken claim, drop the clipped screenshot and stop circulating it. A general call to move on, with no correction, leaves the target carrying the original story.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: What happens after you state your position once, calmly, and then stop replying? If the thread slows and the replies thin out, the crowd was reacting to a moment. If new replies keep arriving to bait you, the silence is not being respected.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Seeing many others react tends to signal that the reaction must be deserved, so each joiner needs less evidence than the one before. Adding one line feels low-cost, which makes joining easy. For the target, a large count of strangers can be read as a verdict on their whole character, even when most replies were quick and shallow.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Every notification can set off a racing heart, and people describe rereading each line to find the fair point, then distrusting their own judgment. Some delete posts or accounts, stop speaking up in groups or dread opening the app. Others say a few supportive messages from people who knew them mattered more than any rebuttal.

response_options.soft_clarification: If a few replies raise a genuine point, answer one of them with a short, specific reply and leave the rest. Replying to everyone gives the thread more fuel.
response_options.firm_boundary: State once what you stand by and what you got wrong, then stop responding. One clear statement is easier to defend than a long thread of replies.
response_options.disengagement: Mute the thread, turn off notifications for a day, and ask a friend to watch for anything that crosses into threats. You do not need to read every reply to know what is in them.
response_options.support_seeking: Show a trusted friend the thread and ask which points, if any, are fair. Someone outside the surge can tell you what is signal and what is volume.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If it spreads into a work or school channel, save dated screenshots and ask the moderator, manager or HR to step in on the channel as a group-behavior problem.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I've read the criticism, and I'll answer the points that were about what I actually said. I won't reply to every message, and I'd ask people to stop passing around the clipped screenshot and link to the full post instead."
codex_completed.safety_note: A pile-on becomes a safety matter when replies move from criticism to your address, workplace, children or school, or when threats arrive. Screenshot everything with dates, tighten account privacy, report to the platform, and contact local police or a legal aid service if you or your family are threatened.
misuse_warning: Calling any heavy criticism a pile-on can dismiss people who are right and numerous. Volume alone proves nothing; ask whether the points are fair.
Someone with real power can use the label to cast the people they harmed as a mob.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Triangulation recruits third parties, real or invented, to carry one side against another, so a specific person is behind the recruiting. Flying Monkeys are people enlisted, often unknowingly, to pressure a target for someone else. A pile-on needs neither a recruiter nor a plan; the crowd forms because people see others already reacting. What defines it is many separate voices stacked on one person in a short window.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Ostracism
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Leaving a person out of invitations, conversations, decisions or information until they end up on the outside of their own group.
codex_completed.short_definition: Leaving a person out of invitations, conversations, decisions or information until they end up on the outside of their own group.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Ostracism is being left out in practice: off the invite list, out of the group chat, missing from the meeting where the decision was made. Any single omission can be explained as an oversight, which is part of why it is hard to name. What makes it a pattern is that it runs one way, lasts, and often begins after the person disagreed, set a limit or said something unwelcome. The pattern does not show what anyone meant.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You keep being left out of plans, messages and decisions that the rest of the group gets, and you cannot point to one moment you could complain about.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Exclusion from information and decisions has practical consequences well beyond the social ones, and each omission is small enough to be explained away. A person can miss deadlines, a promotion or a friend's news, and then be blamed for being out of touch.
what_it_is: Being left off a group invitation, thread or chat that the rest of the circle receives.
Being skipped in a meeting, email chain or decision that affects your own work.
A conversation that stops or shifts when you enter, or replies to you that shrink to one word.
Being the only one not told about a changed time or place.
Possible in a family, friend group, congregation, team or class.
what_it_sounds_like: Oh, we figured you were busy. (said after plans you were never told about)
It was just a small get-together, we didn't think to invite everyone.
Didn't you see the group chat? (when you were never added)
Nothing's wrong, we just didn't think of you.
A team calendar where every colleague on your project is invited to the planning meeting except you.
A room that goes quiet when you walk in and picks up again when you leave.
what_it_is_not: One forgotten invitation with nothing following it is an oversight.
A group drifting apart because jobs, moves and children changed everyone's schedules.
Someone who has quietly opted out of events themselves and now seems excluded when they chose it.
A private gathering of a few close friends that was never meant to be group-wide.
A manager limiting a meeting to the people with a role in the decision, and telling you why.
Space that you or others asked for, such as a friend needing time alone after a loss.
this_may_be_it_when: You are the only person missing from messages that everyone else in the circle received.
The exclusion began or deepened soon after you disagreed, set a limit or raised something awkward.
When you ask about it, you get vague answers or are told you are overreacting.
Others are invited while you are out of the room, then mention the event in front of you.
Information you need to do your role reaches you late or secondhand.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You were told kindly why one event was small, and you were included in the next.
Several people are out of the loop, not only you.
When you asked to be added, you were added.
The gap tracks a clear change such as a new job, a move or different hours.
The omissions stopped after you reminded people once.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Organizers of loose groups often forget people, especially when the list lives in someone's head.
People under strain pull back from everyone, including those close to them.
Group chats split by topic, and some people simply end up in a different one.
common_false_positives: A friend who keeps a small dinner small.
A coworker not copied on a thread because the subject is outside their role.
Your own withdrawal during a hard season, later read as others pushing you out.
discernment_questions: Is it only me, or are other people also missing from these messages?
When I have asked to be included, what happened?
Did this start after something specific I said or did, and is there another explanation for the timing?
Could I have opted out of things earlier and forgotten?
Does missing this information cost me something practical, like a deadline or a decision?
less_concerning_if: The group tells you plainly why you were left out of a particular event and includes you in the next one.
Other members are left out at times too.
You have stepped back from some things and the invitations have thinned to match.
more_concerning_if: Schedules or decisions reach you late or not at all, and then you are blamed for the gap.
Other people seem to be told, or to sense, that they should keep their distance from you.
The exclusion spreads to new groups, or carries on after you raised it plainly.
pattern_over_time_signs: You start scanning social media or other people's mentions to learn what you were not told.
You change what you say in the group to avoid being left out next time.
Invitations that used to come regularly stop, and nobody mentions the change.
People you used to talk to easily now answer briefly and move on.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair would show on the invite list: you appear on it again without having to ask, and information reaches you at the same time as everyone else. An apology for any misunderstanding, followed by the same gaps next month, has not changed what happens to you.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask to be included in one specific thing, such as the next planning meeting, and watch whether it happens or you hear 'we'll see.' Being added once and dropped again points one way; staying on the list through several weeks points the other.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: The sting of being left out registers quickly and tends to pull a person toward whatever brings them back in. Because each omission can be explained away, the person may blame their own sensitivity instead. The silence around it can also discourage them from asking directly, which lets the pattern continue unchecked.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Checking messages for what they missed and rehearsing how to ask without sounding needy is how many describe it. Some pull away first to avoid the sting, lose track of work details, or doubt whether the exclusion was real because nobody ever said anything.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask one person you trust in the group a low-key question: 'I noticed I wasn't on the thread about Saturday. Is there a reason I wasn't included?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask to be included going forward: 'Please add me to the thread and the invite list from now on. I'm asking for that directly.'
response_options.disengagement: Put your time into people and groups where you are included without asking, and give the group that keeps leaving you out less of it.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone outside the group which specific things you missed, and when. They can help you tell a pattern from a rough patch and remind you who does want you around.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask your manager in writing which meetings and threads your role needs and request to be added. Keep dated notes of what you missed and how it affected your work.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I've noticed I was left off several invitations and messages lately. Please add me to the next one, and tell me directly if there is a reason I'm not on the list."
codex_completed.safety_note: Being left out is not a physical-safety signal on its own. It changes character when it sits alongside control of your money or housing, being kept from anyone else, or fear of what happens if you speak up. If so, a domestic abuse advocate, a counselor, or a labor or tenant legal aid office can help you plan.
misuse_warning: Reading every unanswered text or missed invite as ostracism can turn ordinary social drift into a grievance. Ask whether the gaps run one way and follow a specific event.
Using the label to demand a place at a private gathering treats a host's ordinary choices as punishment.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Triangulation brings a third party into a dispute to carry one side's message, so words travel. Ostracism removes you from the circle without anyone saying anything. Flying Monkeys are recruited to pressure or monitor you, which means contact; ostracism shows up as the absence of contact. The difference is silence: you are left out of what everyone else is told.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Mobbing
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Sustained harassment of one person by a group over weeks or months, most often at work or in a community, wearing down their standing.
codex_completed.short_definition: Sustained harassment of one person by a group over weeks or months, most often at work or in a community, wearing down their standing.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Mobbing is a term from workplace research for a group repeatedly turning on one person through gossip, exclusion, belittling remarks, withheld information, hostile jokes and unusual scrutiny. One cold shoulder or tense meeting is not mobbing. The pattern is duration and breadth: several people take part over months, often without ever agreeing to, and the person's efforts to address it tend to be read as proof there was a problem. The cost can be a job, a role or standing in a community.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: A group keeps picking on one person over weeks or months, and every attempt to raise it gets treated as more proof that the person is the problem.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Attempts to address it get absorbed as further evidence, so the ordinary responses open to someone under sustained group pressure tend to make the position worse. Over months the person can lose work, references or standing, and their account is doubted because so many people seem to disagree.
what_it_is: Repeated hostile behavior from several people toward one person, across many separate occasions.
A mix of small acts: eye-rolls, being talked over, rumors, jokes at the person's expense, being left off messages, unusual scrutiny of their work.
Common in workplaces, schools, teams, congregations and volunteer groups, where people depend on one another.
Frequently escalates when the person objects, because the objection becomes the next thing to criticize.
Can include people who joined in only because others already had, and some who privately feel uneasy.
what_it_sounds_like: Everyone has noticed it, not just me.
You're being very sensitive. No one is out to get you.
We've had several people raise concerns about you. (with no names and no examples)
Did you see what she did in the meeting? Again.
If you were easier to work with, this wouldn't be happening.
A manager's file with half a dozen vague complaints from different people, none dated or specific.
Colleagues who go silent when you walk by, then are friendly when alone with you.
what_it_is_not: Separate conflicts with different people that happen to land in the same month.
One serious dispute with a colleague that others have taken sides on, which is contentious rather than orchestrated.
A documented instance where the person really was responsible and others responded to it.
Several people giving direct, specific feedback because each saw the same lapse.
A tense stretch around a deadline or reorganization when everyone is short with everyone.
One meeting where several people disagreed with your proposal.
this_may_be_it_when: The same small group appears across many different incidents over months.
Complaints about you are vague and secondhand, with no dates, examples or names.
When you raise one concern, it is answered with a new complaint.
Colleagues are friendly one-on-one but cold in groups, or say privately that they cannot be seen backing you.
Your work is checked or measured more closely than that of others in the same role.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Each complaint is specific, dated and describes something you recognize doing.
The people involved do not know one another or have no contact.
Feedback is offered to your face with a chance to respond and improve.
It was a few weeks around a crisis and has eased.
Others in the same role get similar scrutiny.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Teams under strain turn on whoever is closest to the problem without anyone planning it.
Reorganizations change who attends what, and people lose access for reasons unrelated to them.
Several people may independently find the same real problem with someone's work and say so.
common_false_positives: A review process with several reviewers who all note the same missed deadlines.
Friction after a change of manager, where norms shifted for everyone.
A neighborhood committee disagreeing sharply with a member's proposal across several meetings.
discernment_questions: Can I name specific incidents, with dates and who was involved each time?
Are the same people showing up across them, or different people each time?
When I raised a concern, did anything change, or did a new complaint appear?
Would a neutral colleague, shown my notes, see a pattern or separate disagreements?
Is any of the criticism accurate, and have I been given a fair chance to address it?
less_concerning_if: Concerns are put to you directly, with specifics and a chance to answer.
The people involved change over time and the tension fades.
A neutral party who reviewed the situation found separate causes for each incident.
more_concerning_if: Your job, pay, schedule or reputation has been affected, or you have been told your position may change.
Colleagues who were supportive have gone quiet after someone senior sided against you.
Sleeplessness or dread before work is growing, and it is affecting your health.
pattern_over_time_signs: Incidents arrive in clusters after you object or succeed at something, not at random.
The list of people who are cold to you grows month by month.
Your attempts to clarify are cited later as examples of being difficult.
You rehearse every conversation and dread ordinary interactions that used to be fine.
codex_completed.repair_check: Whether anything has been mended shows in what the group does: complaints are written down, put to you specifically, and closed once answered. If the group only softens its tone for a week while the unwritten grievances stay open, nothing underneath has moved.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask for one concern to be put in writing with an example and a date. Notice whether the request is met, or heard as one more sign you are hard to work with. A group acting in good faith can produce a specific example.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When several people appear to hold the same view, a target can start to think the problem must be them. Each participant may feel their own part is minor, and later joiners take earlier ones as a signal. Because objecting becomes the next complaint, the target can end up doubting their own account and withdrawing, which the group may then read as confirmation.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe dread before shifts or meetings, sleeplessness, losing confidence in work they were good at, and feeling invisible among people who used to be warm. Some describe a drop in performance that then seemed to prove the complaints, and anger at being asked to prove what they could not safely say.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask one colleague you trust to describe what they see: 'Have you noticed a change in how people deal with me? I'd like an honest read.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask that concerns be given to you in writing, with an example and a date, so you can answer each one directly.
response_options.disengagement: Reduce one-on-one time with the people most involved and keep communication in writing. Work out any change of team or role privately with an advocate first, and keep it quiet until it is settled.
response_options.support_seeking: Keep a dated log of incidents, with who was present, and share it with an employment advocate, union representative or counselor who can read it with fresh eyes.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask HR or a neutral manager for a meeting with a note-taker, bring your log, and request that the process be documented. A third party in the room changes what can be said.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Could we put each concern about me in writing, with an example and a date, and have someone neutral sit in on our next conversation? I can respond to specifics, but I can't respond to a feeling that everyone shares."
codex_completed.safety_note: Mobbing can put your income, housing or professional standing at risk, and months of it can wear down health. Watch for threats, being followed or photographed, sudden changes to your position, or retaliation after you raise it. An employment lawyer, union representative or legal aid office can explain your protections before you do anything formal. If anyone makes you fear for your physical safety, call emergency services.
misuse_warning: Calling one hard season of friction mobbing can turn ordinary disagreement or fair feedback into a campaign story, making it harder to hear what is accurate.
Using the word against a group of people who each raised a real concern treats honest feedback as persecution.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Flying Monkeys are people enlisted by one person to pressure or monitor you; mobbing can happen with no organizer at all, only many people pushing the same way. Triangulation routes messages through a third party, but a mob acts directly. A Polite Hostile Environment penalizes truth-telling from everyone, and mobbing singles out one person for months of accumulating pressure.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Splitting
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Seeing a person or group as all good or all bad, with no middle ground, and flipping that view suddenly after a minor event.
codex_completed.short_definition: Seeing a person or group as all good or all bad, with no middle ground, and flipping that view suddenly after a minor event.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Splitting is black-and-white thinking about people. Someone is a hero, the best friend, the only one who understands, and then, after a small disagreement or a late reply, becomes the enemy or a disappointment. There is little room for 'good person, bad day.' The flip can be about you, about other people, or about oneself. One harsh judgment after a real wrong is not splitting. The pattern is swings that outrun what actually happened, repeated across people and months.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone puts you on a pedestal, then drops you to the bottom after something small, and the swing seems to have little to do with what you did.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Standing shifts without reference to anything actually done, so there is no behavior available that reliably keeps a person in favor. You can end up walking on eggshells, and watching others around them be built up and torn down in turn.
what_it_is: Describing someone in absolute terms, such as perfect, the best, evil or worthless, with nothing in between.
A sudden reversal in how the same person is described, sometimes within a day, after a small trigger.
Applied to individuals, to groups such as a team or one side of a family, and sometimes to oneself.
Earlier praise often disappears from memory when the flip comes, so past good times are recast as fake.
Frequently produces camps, where others are pressed to join the all-good or all-bad view.
what_it_sounds_like: You're the only person who truly gets me.
I thought you were different. You're just like all the rest.
She's perfect, I can't believe how lucky we are. (weeks later) I can't believe I ever trusted her.
After all that, you did one thing wrong, so I'm done.
Everyone in that department is useless.
You were never my friend. You were pretending the whole time.
I'm a complete failure, there's nothing good in me.
what_it_is_not: A serious breach of trust that permanently changes how someone is seen is a proportionate reassessment, not a swing.
Gradual disillusionment as you get to know a person better is ordinary.
Someone more reactive during a hard period who still sees nuance when calmer.
Strong enthusiasm for a new friend or hero that mellows over months into a balanced view.
A person describing a bad experience with one organization without generalizing to everyone in it.
A firm opinion about someone's conduct that stays tied to specific events.
this_may_be_it_when: The same person has been called wonderful and worthless within the same year.
What triggers the flip is trivial, such as a delay or a differing opinion.
Past good events are redescribed as fake or forgotten once the view turns.
Several people in their life describe the same swings.
Reassurance and evidence do not move the new view until it flips back by itself.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The change followed something serious that you can name.
They can still say good things about the person they are upset with.
Their view of others changes slowly and for stated reasons.
After a cooling-off period they can describe both the problem and what they value.
Other reasonable people who saw the same events hold the same view.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People in the first weeks of a friendship or job often overpraise and then correct to a more realistic view.
Grief, illness or stress can make anyone speak in extremes for a while.
Some families and teams talk in exaggerations as a style, with no real change in how they feel.
common_false_positives: A friend who is furious after a betrayal and sees you differently afterward.
A manager who rated you highly and then gave honest critical feedback after a real mistake.
Fans who adore a performer and turn away after a scandal that was real.
discernment_questions: Did the change follow something specific that happened, or come out of the blue?
Can they still name things they valued in me or in the other person?
Is this the first such swing, or have I seen it with others in their life?
Do I feel pressure to stay perfect to keep my standing?
Has the view shifted back on its own, with nothing changing?
less_concerning_if: The flip followed an actual breach and is proportionate to it.
They can hold both the good and the problem in view once the first heat passes.
The swings are rare, and you have been able to talk about them afterward.
more_concerning_if: You are being asked to join one side, and people who disagree are being cut off.
You try harder and harder to avoid the drop, rearranging your life around not triggering it.
The all-bad view brings real consequences for you, such as being shut out of work, a family event or a friend group.
pattern_over_time_signs: You notice who is currently in favor in their stories, and the list keeps changing.
Warm periods are followed by cold ones without a clear cause.
You adjust what you say and do to stay on the right side of the line.
People once praised are later mentioned only in negative terms.
codex_completed.repair_check: When the view swings back, check whether the reversal comes with any account of what changed. Being welcomed warmly again without a word about the cold stretch repeats the cycle. A step toward repair would be naming the swing and agreeing together on what to do when the next one starts.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: State once that you do not want to be described to others in all-or-nothing terms. The useful measure comes later: are you still spoken of in specifics in their stories, or does the old extreme return as soon as there is friction?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Black-and-white views can ease the discomfort of holding mixed feelings about someone, because sorting a person into good or bad makes them simple. For the person on the receiving end, unpredictable praise and withdrawal tend to keep attention fixed on avoiding the next drop, much as unpredictable rewards hold attention. This can erode a sense of steady footing.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Wondering which version of the person will show up becomes a daily habit. People describe being flattered and then stunned by the drop, doubting their own value after being cast as the villain, feeling pressure to take sides in a group, or grieving a friendship that was rewritten as fake.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name what you noticed once, without labels: 'Last week I was the best thing in your life and today I can't do anything right. What changed?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to be ranked: 'I'm not perfect and I'm not the villain. I'll talk about what happened, but not about who I am in total.'
response_options.disengagement: When the conversation is running on all-or-nothing language, pause it and come back when both of you can describe the problem in specifics.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask someone who knows you both for a reality check on one recent flip. Seeing the swing from outside helps you remember you did not earn it.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If the swings come from a manager or teammate, keep a dated log of feedback, ask for criteria in writing, and take it to HR or a mentor if your standing affects your role.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I care about this friendship, and I can't be all good one week and all bad the next. If I did something that hurt you, tell me what it was and I'll listen. I won't agree that I was never a friend."
codex_completed.safety_note: Swinging views of a person are not a safety signal on their own. Watch for shifts that bring threats, cutting off your contact with others, control of money or a place to live, or humiliation in front of others. If those appear, an advocate or counselor can help you plan, and a friend outside the relationship can help you keep perspective.
misuse_warning: Calling a friend's anger at you 'splitting' turns a descriptive idea into a verdict about someone's mind, which this entry cannot support.
The word describes a pattern in how someone talks about people. It should not be used to explain away a real wrong done to you, or to excuse it.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Triangulation brings a third party in as ammunition; splitting needs no third party at all, only a swing in how one person is seen. Forced Teaming builds a 'we' to override your separate choices, so closeness is imposed from the start, while the closeness in splitting collapses without warning. Flying Monkeys carry the verdict to others; splitting is the verdict itself.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Golden Child Elevation
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Holding up one family member as the model of excellence, and using that standard to measure everyone else and find them short.
codex_completed.short_definition: Holding up one family member as the model of excellence, and using that standard to measure everyone else and find them short.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: In Golden Child Elevation, one person in a family or group is treated as the standard: praised constantly, excused more easily, and named whenever anyone else falls short. The favored person may not ask for any of it and can be hurt by it too, since their worth is tied to staying on top. One proud remark about a sibling's award means little. The pattern is comparison used again and again, so the others never feel they measure up.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: One person is held up as the example, and everyone else is regularly measured against them and found lacking.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Achievement by one family member becomes the measure applied to the rest, so nothing they accomplish arrives without a comparison attached. Over years, people can grow up believing they are the disappointing one, while the favored one fears losing their place.
what_it_is: One child, relative or team member is praised far more than the others, whatever the others do.
The favored person's wins are raised in conversations about other people's lives, as a yardstick.
Their mistakes are explained away as stress or a phase, while the same mistakes in others count against character.
Often seen at holidays, in family chats, at school and in family businesses, where everyone can see the ranking.
The favored person carries pressure too, because the praise can be withdrawn if they slip.
what_it_sounds_like: Why can't you be more like your brother?
Your sister never needed reminding.
Look what Daniel did this year. Now that's someone who takes things seriously.
She's just going through a phase. You, on the other hand, should know better.
We never had to worry about him.
A parent toasts one child's promotion at a family dinner and skips another's.
what_it_is_not: Pride in a specific achievement, expressed without reference to anyone else, is just pride.
Different family members having different strengths celebrated differently is not a ranking.
A parent venting their own stress may land comparatively without the comparison being the point.
A parent giving extra help to a child with greater needs, such as an illness or a disability.
A sibling who really is thriving, noticed with warmth rather than used as a yardstick.
A coach pointing to a teammate's technique as an example of one specific skill.
this_may_be_it_when: The comparison turns up in unrelated conversations, not only when the favored person's work is relevant.
Excuses made for one person are not made for the others for the same behavior.
Your wins get a brief nod, then a mention of what the favored person did.
Other relatives repeat the same comparisons, as if it were family policy.
You have been measured against the same person for years, not only at one age or phase.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Comparisons are rare and tied to one concrete skill.
Everyone's accomplishments get noticed in a way that feels balanced.
The comparisons stopped after you mentioned them.
Differences in treatment follow real differences in need, and have been explained to you.
The favored person pushes back on the comparisons too.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Parents often brag about a recent win without noticing how it sounds to the others.
A child with greater needs, or in a crisis, takes more of a family's attention for a time.
Some families praise a particular milestone, such as graduating or marrying, for everyone who reaches it.
common_false_positives: A grandparent proudly telling the story of the first grandchild's graduation.
A family spending more on one child's medical treatment.
A teacher holding up one student's essay as a model of structure.
discernment_questions: Is the comparison tied to a specific skill or event, or is it a general ranking?
Are the same standards applied to everyone for the same behavior?
Has it gone on for years, or only during one period?
Has the favored person said it is uncomfortable for them too?
What happens when I raise it plainly?
less_concerning_if: Comparisons are occasional and attached to specific accomplishments.
The family can laugh about it and adjust once someone says it hurts.
Everyone gets attention for their own strengths over time.
more_concerning_if: Money, inheritance, housing or support are handed out according to who is the favorite.
You are cast as the problem if you object, or told you are jealous.
It follows you into adulthood, shaping who is invited, believed or helped.
pattern_over_time_signs: You catch yourself preparing evidence of your achievements before family visits.
The comparison person changes at times, but the ranking never does.
You hesitate to share good news because you expect it to be measured against someone else's.
The favored person grows anxious or withdraws, afraid of slipping.
codex_completed.repair_check: A shift would show in small, repeated ways: your accomplishments get their own mention without anyone else attached, the same lapses draw the same response from everybody, and the favored person is allowed a bad year. A single heartfelt apology with no change in who gets toasted does not move anything.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask a family member to leave siblings out of conversations about you, then watch the next holiday. If your news is received on its own terms, the request was heard. If you are told you are too sensitive about being compared, it was not.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Comparison to a fixed standard tends to turn ordinary effort into a verdict. A person measured against a favorite can learn to work for approval that never arrives, and the favorite can learn that love depends on performance. Over years the roles can harden into identities such as the achiever and the disappointment, and each person may start to act them out.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Nothing feeling like enough is the common thread. People describe dreading family gatherings and carrying the comparison into adult jobs and friendships. Some describe resentment toward the favored sibling that sits uneasily with love for them, while the favored person often describes pressure, loneliness and fear of letting anyone down.

response_options.soft_clarification: Say what you notice once, without blame: 'When you mention my brother's job right after I tell you about mine, it feels like mine doesn't count.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask for the comparison to stop: 'Please stop measuring me against my sister. I'm glad to hear about her, but not as a yardstick.'
response_options.disengagement: When a conversation turns into a ranking, change the subject or end the call, and favor family settings where comparisons are less likely.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk with the favored person if the bond allows it, or with a cousin or friend who saw it happen. Learning it affected them too can ease the rivalry.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a boss holds up one colleague as the model, ask for written criteria for your own role and request feedback tied to your goals instead of to a person.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'm glad my sister is doing well. When I'm compared to her, I stop hearing the news and hear only that I fall short. Please talk about my work on its own, without her name in the sentence."
codex_completed.safety_note: Favoritism is a painful pattern, not a physical-safety one in itself. It becomes more serious when it reaches money or housing, such as threats of being cut off, or when a child is treated very differently from siblings in ways that affect food, care or protection. A family therapist, a school counselor or, where a child's care is at stake, a child protection service can help.
misuse_warning: Labeling a proud parent with this term can turn warm praise for a real achievement into an accusation. Ask whether the praise is being used to measure others.
The favored person is often a bystander, and blaming them for the family's pattern repeats the same unfairness.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Triangulation sets two people against each other through a third, such as repeating what one said about the other. Golden Child Elevation uses one person's real achievements as the measure for others. 'We're Family' Erasure invokes loyalty to override your limits, while this pattern works through ranking, not loyalty. Forced Teaming builds a 'we' that erases your separate choices; here the point is a difference in standing.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Social Proof Pressure
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Using the claim that everyone else already agrees to push one person into going along, whether or not the agreement is real.
codex_completed.short_definition: Using the claim that everyone else already agrees to push one person into going along, whether or not the agreement is real.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Social proof pressure presents group agreement as a reason you should give in, at the moment you are being asked to decide. False Consensus is the same tactic under another name, and the two are one pattern: sometimes the group's agreement is stretched, and sometimes it is only implied by 'everyone' or 'people' with nobody named. One mention of what others think is ordinary. The pattern is a crowd that cannot be checked, appearing just as you hesitate, with holding out treated as the problem.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You are told everyone else already agrees, so your hesitation looks odd, and it turns out nobody can say who 'everyone' is, or they agree less than claimed.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A judgment that felt sound a minute earlier starts to feel eccentric. Disagreeing seems to mean disagreeing with everyone, and the claim is vague enough that there is no one to check it with, so the decision gets made against an apparent majority and not on its merits.
what_it_is: A claim about what a group thinks or has already done, offered right when you hesitate.
Often unnamed: 'everyone', 'the team', 'people', 'all the parents', with no names to ask.
Sometimes partly true, with two friendly voices stretched into a consensus, or silence counted as agreement.
Pressure on the wish to belong, so that holding out starts to cost standing and not only a difference of opinion.
Seen in meetings, family decisions, group chats, committees, sales conversations and online groups.
what_it_sounds_like: Everyone else has already signed off. You're the only one holding things up.
People have noticed you've been difficult lately.
All the other parents agreed. I don't see why you need to be different.
Nobody else has a problem with this.
We talked about it as a group and it was unanimous.
Everyone thinks you've been unfair about this.
Most people in your position just do it.
A screenshot of a group chat is shown with only the agreeing messages in view.
what_it_is_not: A genuinely unanimous decision, accurately described, that you happen to disagree with.
Social proof offered openly as one input among several, such as 'most people book early, but it's up to you'.
Groups reaching quick, real consensus on something straightforward.
A friend telling you, with names, that several people raised the same worry, so you can ask them yourself.
Summarizing a truly shared concern without naming each person, which people do in good faith.
Workplace or cultural habits of speaking in 'we' language as a courtesy.
this_may_be_it_when: The group is cited just before you are asked to agree, and not otherwise.
When you ask 'who?', the answer is vague or turns into annoyance.
The people named, when you ask them, hold milder or different views.
The consensus happens to match exactly what the speaker wanted.
Your disagreement is treated as the issue, with comments about your attitude and not your reasons.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Named people confirm the position when you ask them.
The speaker invites you to talk to the others and say what you think.
The decision rests on stated reasons, with the head-count as a side point.
You are free to hold out, and the group carries on without hostility.
The count is shown openly, such as a vote or signed list, and you can read it.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People summarize group moods loosely, as in 'everyone's tired of this', without checking every head.
Someone who feels outnumbered may reach for 'everybody' out of nervousness.
Real majorities exist, and a person in the minority can feel pressed by them with no one pressing.
A chatty person may assume that what their few friends think is what all think.
