common_false_positives: A club vote you lost, with a count anyone may see.
A friend who says 'everyone loves that restaurant' and shrugs when you disagree.
Reviews and ratings that show what people actually thought.
A family truly of one mind about a plan, who say so warmly and still welcome your view.
discernment_questions: Can I name any of the people said to agree, and would they say the same if I asked them?
Why is the group's view being raised now, at the point I hesitate?
Would the request still make sense on its merits if nobody else's opinion counted?
Does anyone say it is fine if I disagree?
Does the claimed unanimity match what I have seen myself?
What would I lose, concretely, if I were the only one to say no?
less_concerning_if: The people mentioned can be asked, and they confirm.
Disagreement is welcomed, and you can say no without a change in how you are treated.
The group's view is one point among reasons, not the whole argument.
more_concerning_if: The claim is used to push you into something hard to undo, such as signing, paying or moving.
You are told that others who disagreed were 'difficult' or were left out.
You ask to speak to the others and are told there is no need, or no time.
pattern_over_time_signs: 'Everyone' shows up each time you hesitate, and never with names.
You begin to give way before the group has even been mentioned.
You learn that the group was less united than described, but only after you agreed.
Being the one who disagrees becomes a role people comment on.
codex_completed.repair_check: The test is whether the claim becomes checkable afterwards: names, a count, or a plain 'I don't know what the others think'. An apology for 'overstating it' followed by 'everyone' again at the next decision has shifted nothing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask to speak with one of the people said to agree, then watch what follows. If they put you in touch or let that person answer for themselves, the request was taken seriously. If it would be awkward, or you are called distrustful, the crowd was doing the persuading.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People often use what others seem to think as a guide to what is safe and reasonable, particularly when unsure or when the group matters to them. An unnamed majority cannot be questioned, so doubt tends to turn inward. The fear of being the odd one out can feel more pressing than the original disagreement.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe giving in and feeling uneasy afterwards, suspecting they were mistaken about their own judgment, and finding out later that the support was weaker than described. Some describe pulling back from the group, or saying yes to avoid being the one who stands out.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for names: 'Who specifically has said that? I would like to hear it from them.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Separate your answer from the head-count: 'Even if everyone agrees, I need to decide this for myself, and my answer is no.'
response_options.disengagement: Pause the conversation when the crowd is cited and decide later, alone, once you have spoken to a couple of the people involved.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk privately with one or two group members and ask what they think. Their own words show how wide the agreement really is.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In a meeting, ask for the decision and its reasons to be recorded in the minutes, with who agreed, so the claim can be checked later.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Others being on board is good to know. Before I decide, I want to hear what each of them thinks. If you can tell me the reasons, I'm happy to weigh those."
codex_completed.safety_note: This is rarely a danger on its own. It deserves more care when the 'everyone' is a household, congregation or community you depend on for housing, income or belonging, and refusing brings threats or being cut off. Then, before deciding, talk privately with someone outside that group, such as a caseworker, adviser or friend with no stake.
misuse_warning: Mentioning what others think is not automatically pressure. Calling every appeal to a majority manipulation can make honest group decisions impossible to discuss.
A vague 'people say' is a reason to ask who, not proof that the speaker invented it.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Forced Teaming builds a 'we' that includes you whether you agreed or not, while social proof pressure describes a 'they' you are expected to join. Triangulation quotes or compares real or invented third parties against you in a conflict, and here the third parties form a crowd behind a request. Flying Monkeys sends actual people to you, where in this tactic the people usually never appear.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Divide and Conquer
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Distance or distrust between people who might otherwise support one another, so that they do not compare notes or act together.
codex_completed.short_definition: Distance or distrust between people who might otherwise support one another, so that they do not compare notes or act together.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Divide and Conquer is a pattern where people who could back each other up are kept apart. It often runs on selective retelling: one person hears a sharpened version of what the other said, and the other hears the reverse. It can also look like private favors or secrets that make each person feel they alone hold a special place. One garbled message means little. The pattern is that gaps keep opening between the same people who might compare notes. This does not show what anyone meant.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: People who would normally compare notes and back each other up end up distrustful or distant, each holding a different version of what the other said.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Two people who might have compared notes stop speaking, and each carries a version of the other that neither gets the chance to correct. Meanwhile no one is in a position to say that something is wrong, because each person is dealing with it alone.
what_it_is: Relaying what each person said to the other in trimmed, sharpened or invented form.
Privately telling several people that each is the one trusted or the one who really understands.
Handling people one at a time so no one sees how everyone else is treated.
Discouraging joint conversations with lines such as 'no need to bring everyone in.'
Seen in families, teams, friend groups, congregations and between co-parents and their children.
what_it_sounds_like: I probably shouldn't tell you this, but here's what Priya really said about you.
You know what they really think of you, right?
Let's keep this between us. The others wouldn't understand.
You're the only one I can trust with this.
I wouldn't bring it up with her. It will only make things worse.
A group chat goes quiet after one person has spoken privately to each member.
Two coworkers are each told they were the one picked for a project, and each is asked not to mention it.
what_it_is_not: Miscommunication between two people that has nothing to do with anyone else.
Relationships drifting apart for unrelated reasons such as distance, new jobs or new children.
Someone relaying a conversation inaccurately because they remembered it badly.
A person sharing a confidence with one friend because that friend is the one they trust.
A manager meeting employees one at a time for routine reviews.
Two people who simply do not get along and would be at odds with or without a go-between.
this_may_be_it_when: Each person has heard something about the other that the other swears they never said.
Several people are told they are the only ones trusted with certain information.
Attempts to talk to each other are discouraged, or one person stays the only channel.
The conflict eases or vanishes once the people involved compare notes directly.
Alliances between two people tend to cool soon after they form.
this_may_not_be_it_when: When you compare accounts, the stories match.
Information about everyone is shared freely, in groups.
The person relaying information stops once corrected.
The two people have had a conflict of their own for some time.
The distance followed life changes, such as a move or a new job.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people are poor go-betweens; they paraphrase, forget, and soften or sharpen without noticing.
Friends confide in different people because they are close in different ways.
Managers hold one-on-ones for privacy and fairness, not to keep anyone apart.
common_false_positives: A friend who repeats something you said to another person in a clumsy way.
A parent who confides in one adult child about a health matter.
Two coworkers who drift apart after being assigned to different teams.
discernment_questions: Have the two of us ever checked directly with each other about what was said?
Is one person the only source of what each of us supposedly said?
Are we each being told we are special or trusted, in a way the others do not know?
Does the tension fall when we talk directly?
Would the story change if the third person were not part of it?
less_concerning_if: When people compare notes, the accounts line up.
The go-between welcomes a three-way conversation when asked.
The distance between the people predates the go-between's involvement.
more_concerning_if: People who compared notes are then criticized, or told they are plotting.
Everyone is kept uncertain about who is trusted, so no one can ask for help.
A group about to raise a concern together falls apart just before it can.
pattern_over_time_signs: You stop trusting a friend over a story you cannot verify, and later learn it was altered.
Plans for people to meet fall through, and the reason always runs through the same person.
Each person stops checking with the others.
A new friendship or alliance cools within weeks.
codex_completed.repair_check: A real shift would show in the open: the person at the center agrees to a joint conversation, repeats things in the same words to everyone, and does not object when others compare notes. Apologizing separately to each person, in private, keeps the same shape as before.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask whether a three-way conversation can happen, and pay attention to the answer. Is it agreement, or an excuse for why it would be unkind, risky or unnecessary? What matters is whether you are allowed to hear it directly from the person concerned.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Hearing something unflattering about yourself from a trusted person is hard to ignore, and checking it can feel disloyal or risky. Being told you are specially trusted can feel good and make you guard that place. Both can keep people from the simple step of comparing notes, which is usually how a distorted account comes apart.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A creeping sense that something is off with a friend or colleague is how many describe the start, followed by sharp embarrassment on learning a story was distorted. Some say they lost months of a friendship over a sentence nobody could source. Others feel alone at the center of a group linked only through one person.

response_options.soft_clarification: Check directly with the other person, in neutral words: 'I heard you said this about me, and I'd rather ask you than assume. Did you?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to carry or accept messages: 'I'd rather hear that from her directly. Can the three of us talk?'
response_options.disengagement: Stop trading secondhand reports about other people, and take a report at face value only after you have checked it with the person it concerns.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell two or three people the same account in the same words and ask what they have heard. Consistency across several mouths is a better check than one retelling.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask for decisions and feedback to be shared in writing or in a group, and compare the instructions you each received before acting.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "If something about me needs saying, please let me hear it from the person who said it. Can the three of us sit down together, or agree that anything about each other gets checked with each other first?"
codex_completed.safety_note: This pattern is mainly about trust, not physical danger. It matters more when someone keeping you from comparing notes also controls your time, money, housing or contact with family. Signs include being told whom you may speak to, or being cut off from anyone who might offer another view. A counselor, domestic abuse advocate or relative outside the situation can help you check.
misuse_warning: Calling every misunderstanding between friends 'divide and conquer' can turn clumsy relaying into a conspiracy story and cost you a friendship that could be repaired.
The label can also be used to cast a person's honest report of what they heard as a campaign.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Triangulation puts a third person in the position of ammunition, with the focus on winning a dispute between two people. Divide and Conquer is about the gap: its effect is that people who might have compared notes do not. Flying Monkeys are third parties who carry pressure to you, often unknowingly, while here the thing carried is distorted talk about each other. Forced Teaming builds closeness to override your choices; this pattern builds distance between people.

codex_completed.name: Foot-in-the-Door
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Winning a small yes first, then using it to secure a larger one, so each agreement makes the next harder to refuse.
codex_completed.short_definition: Winning a small yes first, then using it to secure a larger one, so each agreement makes the next harder to refuse.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Foot-in-the-door begins with something easy to agree to, then follows with something bigger that leans on the first yes. It can be one jump or a ladder of many small steps. Graduated Compliance and Commitment Traps are other names for exactly this: one stresses the small steps, the other the obligation piled up by the end. One favor followed by a bigger one means little, since requests grow in ordinary friendships. The pattern is that the earlier yes is cited as the reason for the next.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You agree to something small. Then a bigger ask arrives, and your first yes is used as a reason you should not say no to this one.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: The larger request is judged against what you already agreed to, not on its own terms. You can end up carrying an obligation you never chose at any single moment, and refusing starts to feel like going back on your word.
what_it_is: A small, easy request that gets a yes, followed by a larger request on the same theme.
Either a single jump (a quick favor, then a big one) or a ladder of many steps, each barely bigger than the last.
Draws on the common habit of staying consistent with what we have already said and done.
Appears in sales, fundraising, volunteering, workplaces and close relationships, for example a free sample followed by a plea to buy.
Leaves a final obligation that nobody named at the start and that you never agreed to as a whole.
what_it_sounds_like: Could you just look over this one page? It'll take two minutes.
You already helped with the first part, so it makes sense for you to finish it.
You said yes to the trial, so signing the full contract is really just the next step.
It's only a small change from what we did last time.
Since you covered one shift, could you take the whole weekend?
We've come this far together. You wouldn't back out now.
A free gift is handed over, and the request for a donation that follows mentions the gift.
what_it_is_not: Small favors that grow into larger ones naturally and mutually, with real consent at each stage, are how most relationships work.
Someone who asks for something small, gets it, and only later finds they need something bigger, with no sequence in mind.
A large request that stands on its own merits whatever came before it.
A trial whose price and cancellation terms were shown clearly before you began.
A role that grows as trust is earned, with each increase named out loud and agreed.
Volunteering for more because you enjoy the work.
this_may_be_it_when: The bigger request cites your earlier yes as its main reason.
The first request was unusually small or easy compared with what followed.
Looking back, you could not have named the full scope at the beginning, because it was never said.
Trying to scale back is described as going back on your word.
Each step is called basically the same as the last, though the total is far larger.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The bigger ask would sound reasonable if it came cold, and you could say no to it easily.
Both of you would describe the current arrangement in the same terms.
Saying no to a stage leaves your earlier help appreciated, not canceled.
The person told you early what the whole task might involve.
The increases were discussed and agreed at each stage.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many tasks show their real size only once begun, and a person may honestly ask for more after seeing it.
People naturally ask those who have helped before, because they know them to be willing.
Trust grows in steps, and a bigger request can be a sign of closeness.
common_false_positives: A neighbor who borrows a ladder, then asks to borrow the car later in the month, and accepts a no.
A volunteer coordinator who asks someone who enjoyed one event to help with the next.
A clearly priced trial whose terms were on screen before you started.
discernment_questions: If the bigger request had come first, with no earlier yes, would I agree to it?
Can I name what was said about the full scope at the start?
Is my earlier agreement being used as the reason, in place of a reason about the request itself?
Can I scale back without hearing that I am going back on my word?
Are the steps growing faster than the relationship, or the pay, can carry?
less_concerning_if: The bigger ask is made openly with its full size stated, and a no is received calmly.
The earlier yes is mentioned as history, not used as a lever.
You feel free to return to an earlier level of involvement.
more_concerning_if: Your past yeses are tallied up whenever you hesitate.
The steps keep growing and there is never a point at which the total is stated.
Stepping back costs something concrete, such as your standing in the group or at work.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find yourself doing things you would have refused if asked outright, with no single moment you can point to.
Requests tend to arrive right after you say yes to something.
You start refusing small things early, to avoid where they might lead.
Reminders of what you already did come up whenever you hesitate.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair means the whole size of the ask is said out loud, and you get a real chance to start again from where you want to stand. Being thanked for earlier help while the extra load stays exactly where it was is appreciation, not repair.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice whether your earlier yes is thanked or tallied. When a boundary is respected, the first favor stays a gift. When it is not, the favor turns into a debt that gets raised each time you hesitate.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Most of us like to act in line with what we have said and done before, and a first yes can make a later request seem a continuation of who we are. Small steps keep the cost of each yes low, so no single step prompts a pause. The total shows itself only when you compare the start with where you stand now.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A creeping sense of being stuck in something never signed up for is common, along with a hard time saying when it began. Some feel embarrassed at having said yes so often. Others begin refusing small, harmless requests early to avoid where they might lead, which can strain ordinary generosity.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the whole picture: 'Before I say yes to this part, what else would come next? I'd like to know the full size of it.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Separate the steps: 'I agreed to the first part. This is a new request, and I'm deciding it on its own.'
response_options.disengagement: Finish the part you agreed to, and decline to start the next stage until it is written down.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend the whole sequence in order and ask whether they would have agreed to the last step if it had come first.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask for new duties to be added to your role description or confirmed by email, with any change in pay or hours, before you take them on.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I was glad to do the first part, and I'm treating this as a new request. Can you tell me what the whole thing involves? I'll decide about this part once I can see that."
codex_completed.safety_note: By itself this is a pressure pattern, not a danger sign. It changes when the steps start to involve money, signing legal papers, sexual activity or secrecy, or when stopping brings threats. Before agreeing to anything with legal or financial weight, show the papers to someone outside the situation, such as a legal aid service or a trusted adviser.
misuse_warning: A follow-up request after a favor is not automatically a trap. Applying the label to ordinary friends can make it hard to ask for or give help at all.
Naming a sequence tells you what happened, not what anyone planned. Treating it as proof of a plan turns a description into an accusation.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Sunk Cost Exploitation points at what you have already invested to stop you from leaving; foot-in-the-door points at a past yes to win a new yes. Ultimatums force an either-or under threat of loss, while here nothing is threatened and the first agreement carries the weight. Urgency Manufacturing squeezes the clock, whereas the lever in this tactic is your own earlier consent, however unhurried the asking.

codex_completed.name: Door-in-the-Face
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Making a big request that is likely to be refused so that the smaller request that follows seems modest and hard to turn down.
codex_completed.short_definition: Making a big request that is likely to be refused so that the smaller request that follows seems modest and hard to turn down.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: The name comes from a salesman slamming a door: the first ask is expected to get a no. The second, smaller ask is the one that was wanted all along. Agreeing to it can feel like returning a favor, because the other person seems to have backed down. Plenty of honest bargaining works this way, so one round proves nothing. It is a pattern when the big ask is never really meant and the same two-step shows up again and again.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone asks for far too much, you say no, and then they ask for less. The smaller request feels like a favor to them, so it is hard to refuse.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Relief at the smaller ask stands in for judging it. The second request gets measured against the first, not against what is fair, and a yes given to feel gracious can leave you carrying more than you chose.
what_it_is: A two-step request: an oversized ask, then a reduced one soon after your refusal.
The reduction is framed as a concession, as though a favor were being granted to you.
Common with fundraising, sales, favors between relatives and workplace volunteering.
Powered by the urge to match a concession with one of your own, which is what makes the smaller ask hard to decline.
what_it_sounds_like: "Could you take the whole month of shifts? No? Okay, then how about just next weekend?"
"Would you lend me ten thousand? That's too much, I get it. Could you do two?"
"I met you halfway, so now it's your turn to meet me."
"Fine, forget the donation. Surely you can sign up for the monthly plan?"
"I was going to ask you to move in for a year, but a few weeks would be okay."
"I came down a lot. The least you can do is say yes to this."
what_it_is_not: Ordinary negotiation, where both sides know the opening position is high and expect to settle in the middle.
Someone who truly wanted the larger thing, asked for it, and then settled for less in good faith.
A person who learns your limits from your first answer and then asks for something that fits them.
Two separate requests that happen to arrive close together.
A reasonable request that you find uncomfortable only because it follows a stressful one.
this_may_be_it_when: The first request was so extreme that no one could have expected a yes.
The smaller request comes within minutes or days, and is presented as a concession you now owe something for.
You notice the same big-then-small order in several separate dealings with this person.
The smaller ask would have seemed too much if it had been the first thing said.
They draw attention to how much they came down, instead of explaining why they need the thing.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The first ask matched a real need, and they scaled it back after hearing your constraints.
They accept no to the smaller ask as easily as to the larger one.
They tell you plainly what they are really after and what the minimum would be.
There is no talk of what you owe in return for their flexibility.
The sequence happened once and has not repeated.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People often ask for the ideal and then adjust once they hear what is realistic.
A person unsure what you can give may start high just to find out.
A team asking for a big budget may expect to receive part of it.
common_false_positives: A haggle at a market, where both sides expect it.
A charity that offers a lower-cost option to people who cannot afford the main program.
A relative who asks for a whole weekend of help, hears you are busy, and then happily takes an hour.
discernment_questions: Would I consider the smaller request fair if it had been the first thing they asked?
Do I feel I owe them because they came down?
Has the same big-then-small order happened before?
Did they ask what I could do, or go straight to a lower number of their own?
What is the actual size of this request without the first one beside it?
less_concerning_if: The smaller request is something you would have been glad to do if asked first.
They are as content with a no on either request.
They explain why the first ask was so large, in terms that make sense.
more_concerning_if: The small ask involves your money, housing, legal paperwork or access to your accounts.
A refusal of the big ask is followed by hurt or anger, and the small ask then arrives as the way back to their good graces.
The big ask always seems designed to fail.
pattern_over_time_signs: You catch yourself saying yes to the second ask without any thought, because the first one made it feel light.
You begin bracing for the huge ask as the opening of a routine.
The 'small' asks add up to far more than you would ever have agreed to in one go.
You feel more indebted to this person than the facts support.
codex_completed.repair_check: Ask what happens when you go back and say you will reconsider the smaller request. Honest acknowledgment sounds like 'you're right, I made it harder to say no.' A repeat of the sequence next month, with the same pair of asks, shows nothing has changed.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Try declining both requests and see how the conversation goes. If a clean no to the second ask is received calmly, the first ask was probably just an opening position. If the second no brings guilt about their concession, that is informative.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People tend to feel they should answer a concession with a concession. A smaller request after a refusal can read as a step toward you, so saying yes feels like fairness. The first, extreme ask also changes the reference point, which can make a moderate request feel light even if it is not.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe agreeing and then feeling oddly cornered, as if a yes had been taken out of them. Some say they could not work out what had bothered them until they separated the second request from the first. Others mention resentment toward a favor that felt requested and also owed.

response_options.soft_clarification: Pull the smaller request apart from the first: 'Forget the first ask for a second. On its own, this one is bigger than I can do.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline without trading: 'I did not say no to the first one to get a better deal on the second. My answer to both is no.'
response_options.disengagement: Do not answer straight away. Say you will get back to them tomorrow, and use the gap to look at the second ask alone.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone you trust both requests in order and ask what they would say to the second if it had come first.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask for the request in writing with the actual scope and deadline, so the small version is judged on its own terms and not against the big one.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I see you have scaled it down, and I appreciate that. Taken on its own, it is still more than I can take on, so my answer is no. I would be glad to help with something smaller than this."
codex_completed.safety_note: On its own this is a pressure tactic about requests, not a danger signal. It would raise concern if the asks involve money, signing papers, access to your accounts or your home, or if a refusal brings threats. In those cases, take time before agreeing and talk to someone independent, such as a legal aid clinic or a financial counselor.
misuse_warning: Calling normal bargaining 'door-in-the-face' can make you suspicious of every negotiation, including honest ones.
Using the label to dismiss a real, reduced request can leave a person without help they genuinely needed.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: A False Dilemma shrinks your choices to two and treats both as costly; the door-in-the-face first ask is simply meant to be refused, so the second feels light. Urgency Manufacturing works through a clock, while this works through your sense that a concession deserves one in return. Sunk Cost Exploitation leans on what you have already put in, and here you have put in nothing until the second yes.

codex_completed.name: Anchoring
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Putting forward a first number, price or claim that then shapes how every later figure and offer is judged.
codex_completed.short_definition: Putting forward a first number, price or claim that then shapes how every later figure and offer is judged.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: People tend to judge a value by comparing it to the first one they hear, even when the first one is arbitrary. A seller names a high price, a manager names a salary band, a relative says how much you 'usually' give. Everything after is measured against that figure. Stating an opening number is normal in any negotiation. It becomes a tactic when the number has no basis and is used to make a worse offer look generous.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: The first number you hear sticks in your mind and makes later numbers look big or small by comparison, even when that first number was made up.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Everything that follows gets measured against a figure or framing that was never justified, so an offer that would look unreasonable on its own can seem fair, and you may feel you won something when you did not.
what_it_is: An opening price, salary, deadline or amount that sets the range for the whole discussion.
Often a crossed-out 'original' price beside a sale price, or a 'suggested' tip or donation amount.
Works even when people know the first number is arbitrary, which is why it is used in sales, pay talks and settlements.
Different from a real constraint: an anchor is chosen for its effect, not because it reflects cost, rules or facts.
what_it_sounds_like: "The listing price is four hundred, but for you, three-fifty."
"People with your experience usually ask for much more than that." (said before any figure is mentioned)
"We're thinking about forty thousand for this role." (when the going rate is well above)
"Everyone else in the family gave a hundred, but give what you can."
A 'was $199, now $89' tag on an item that was never sold for $199.
"The other side wants a million. I think we can get them down to six hundred thousand."
what_it_is_not: An honest opening position in a bargain, where both sides know the first number is a starting point.
A real price list, rate card or pay scale that states what something costs.
Someone with little experience of pricing blurting out a high number without any strategy behind it.
A reference you picked yourself, such as the price you saw last week at another shop.
Natural comparison: noticing one thing is cheaper than another is just using information.
this_may_be_it_when: A number is said first, with nothing explaining where it comes from.
The figure falls well outside the real range, and later 'concessions' still land above fair.
Questions about where the number came from get a vague answer or a change of subject.
You notice you are bargaining down from their figure and not up from your own.
The same sort of high first figure turns up in a pattern across their dealings with you.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They can show how the number was built, such as costs, comparable sales or a published scale.
They will happily hear your figure first, or ask for it.
The opening figure is close to what the market supports.
It is a standard fixed price and no movement is offered or implied.
They explain the number is a starting point and invite you to counter.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Sellers and employers often start a little high because they expect to move.
A person may genuinely not know what is typical and quote the first figure that comes to mind.
A stated price may reflect costs you cannot see.
common_false_positives: A shop's sticker price in a store that does not haggle.
A friend quoting what they paid for a similar item last year.
A mediator's opening suggestion that both parties are free to reject.
discernment_questions: Where did this first number come from, and can they show me?
If I had heard a different first number, would my view of this offer be different?
Do I know what the typical range is from a source other than them?
Am I judging the deal on its own merits or only against their opening figure?
Would I think the later offer was fair if I had not heard the first one?
less_concerning_if: You can check the figure against independent sources, and it holds up.
They are open to a counteroffer, including one well below theirs.
The first number is labeled plainly as an opening position.
more_concerning_if: The anchored figure involves a settlement, a debt, rent, a wage or legal fees, where a bad outcome is hard to undo.
You are pressed to answer before you can look up the range.
They treat any counter below the anchor as an insult or a sign of bad faith.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your own sense of what something is worth drifts toward their numbers.
You find yourself pleased with deals that, on later checking, were ordinary or poor.
Their first figure keeps being the highest or lowest one in the room.
You start asking for less than you wanted, to stay near the range they set.
codex_completed.repair_check: If you point out that the first number had no basis, a straight answer would be to explain how it was set and to restate the offer from a fair starting point. Quietly lowering it a bit while insisting the first figure was reasonable moves the number without changing the habit.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Try putting your own number on the table before they answer, or ask where theirs came from. Do they engage with the question, or press on as if you had not spoken? Their ease with being challenged tells you most.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People tend to adjust from the first figure they hear, and usually stop adjusting too soon. Even a number known to be random can pull judgments toward it. The pull can be stronger when you are short of information or time, and a later 'discount' can feel like a gain that you earned.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe agreeing to a price or a pay level and later working out that they had accepted the other side's frame. Some feel foolish when they compare notes with others. Some describe a lingering sense of having been handled, even though nothing false was said.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the source: 'How did you get to that number? I'd like to understand it before I answer.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Reset the frame yourself: 'I'm going to work from my own research on this, not from your opening figure. Here is what I have found.'
response_options.disengagement: Do not respond to the figure straight away. Take a day, look up typical ranges, and return with your own range.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask someone who has bought, sold or been paid in this field what a normal figure is, before you reply.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In pay or contract talks, research the range from published scales or peers first, and state your number before they state theirs if you can.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Thanks for the opening figure. I would like to see how it was worked out, and I've done my own research on the range. Can we start from what comparable cases show?"
codex_completed.safety_note: A high opening number is a financial pressure, and rarely a danger by itself. It matters more where the stakes are heavy and hard to undo: a legal settlement, a debt payment plan, a lease, or a pay offer tied to your immigration status. For those, get independent advice from legal aid or a financial counselor before you answer.
misuse_warning: Calling every opening price 'anchoring' can make normal negotiation look like manipulation and leave you unable to bargain at all.
Accusing someone of anchoring when they simply quoted a figure they believe in shuts down a fair talk.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Urgency Manufacturing shortens your time, while anchoring distorts your sense of the figure, however long you take. A False Dilemma limits your choices to two; an anchor leaves your choices open but tilts where you land. Sunk Cost Exploitation uses what you have already spent to keep you in, whereas an anchor works on the very first figure you hear, before you have spent anything.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Choice Restriction
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Closing off or hiding realistic alternatives one by one, so that a single outcome ends up looking like the only sensible choice.
codex_completed.short_definition: Closing off or hiding realistic alternatives one by one, so that a single outcome ends up looking like the only sensible choice.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Choice restriction narrows what you can realistically do, through money, access, information or the way options are described, until one outcome is left standing. Choice Architecture Manipulation is simply another name for this: some readers notice the closed doors, others notice how the menu was laid out. No demand is ever made, so there is nothing to refuse. One short list of options means little. The pattern is that the list keeps shrinking in the same direction.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Your options get closed off or made to look unworkable one at a time, until the choice someone else would prefer is the only one that seems left.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: No demand is made, so there is nothing to push back on. By the time you notice, you may have agreed to something you never really picked, with no single moment to point to when you ask how you got here.
what_it_is: Alternatives removed in practice: an account closed, a ride not offered, a form never handed over, a deadline you were not told about.
Alternatives made to sound unworkable by the way they are described, so one choice sounds sensible and the rest sound foolish or costly.
The preferred option made easiest, as the default, the one already filled in, scheduled or paid for.
Information held back or sorted so you cannot compare, such as quotes you never see.
Found in households, workplaces, sales settings, families and care arrangements, wherever one person handles the money, paperwork, schedule or information.
what_it_sounds_like: You don't really have a choice here.
You could do the second one, but you'd lose your whole routine and it never works out. The first is simple.
I already booked the one that works. You just need to sign.
There's no point looking at other places. I called around and they're all full.
The third option? Honestly, nobody sensible picks that.
I have the forms for this one ready. The others take weeks of paperwork.
Only one form is on the table, already filled in, and the other routes are never mentioned.
Looking back, every path I was offered ended in the same place.
what_it_is_not: Options are often truly limited by outside constraints nobody arranged, such as a tight budget, a small town or a full calendar.
Honest advice about which of several real options is best, with the others left available to you.
A sensible default set for practical reasons, like a standard meeting time you can change.
A person who only knows a few options, shares them, and welcomes the others when you find them.
A menu of fixed packages shown openly with prices side by side.
Circumstances narrowing over time, as a lease ends or a workplace closes, with nobody steering.
this_may_be_it_when: Each time you name another possibility there is a reason it will not work, and the reasons all point the same way.
The person describing the options also controls the money, paperwork, schedule or information you would need to check them.
Options you would normally consider have disappeared without any conversation about removing them.
Looking into an alternative on your own is met with irritation, or you find it was more open than you were told.
The outcome that is left happens to suit the person doing the narrowing.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You can look up alternatives yourself and the other person is happy for you to do it.
The options that are gone were closed by a landlord, bank, rule or deadline that neither of you controls.
When you pick the option they like less, they help you carry it out.
They set out the trade-offs for every option, including the ones they like least.
Checking shows the other options really are unworkable for reasons you can verify.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People with a strong view often describe the options they dislike less kindly, without noticing they are doing it.
Someone short of time may offer one workable plan instead of a full menu, to save effort.
Real costs such as price, distance or waiting lists make some options unattractive for anyone.
common_false_positives: A tutor or gym that offers three fixed packages and shows the prices openly.
A friend helping with a move who says the only day they can come is Saturday.
A doctor who recommends one treatment strongly while telling you the others exist and what they involve.
discernment_questions: If I looked for another option on my own, what would I find, and who told me it was not possible?
Who gains from the option that is left?
Do the reasons for ruling out each alternative come from the person, or from something I can check?
Can I get my own quotes, copies of paperwork or advice from someone else without trouble?
Would a neutral person who saw all the same facts name the same single option?
less_concerning_if: The limits come from a source you can check, such as a published rule or price list.
You can freely ask others for advice and the answer is not met with displeasure.
When you do pick differently, nothing about your life gets harder.
more_concerning_if: The person narrowing your options also controls your money, housing, documents or contact with other people.
Looking for alternatives is discouraged, or you are told the people who might offer them cannot be trusted.
Choosing a different option brings a loss, such as support being withdrawn or a long punishing silence.
pattern_over_time_signs: The things you feel free to do on your own shrink, one exception at a time.
You stop looking for alternatives because past searches always came to nothing.
Decisions that used to be yours, such as where to live, work or spend, are now described as obvious.
You struggle to name one thing you chose that went against what the other person wanted.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair here is practical: the closed doors reopen. The missing options get named, information you were not given is shared openly, and a choice that goes against their preference is accepted without a penalty. A warm apology while the same short menu stays in place changes little.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Watch what happens to the second option once you ask about it. Does it get a fair description with its real costs, or one more reason it will not work? And if you choose it, does your ordinary day stay as it was?
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: We usually choose from what is in front of us and seldom go looking for what is missing. When alternatives are removed or described as costly, the remaining option may read as your own conclusion, because no one ever asked you for anything. Objecting afterwards is hard, since you can recall agreeing but not choosing.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Many report a puzzled sense of having said yes to something they never wanted, and trouble explaining how it happened. Some feel foolish for not looking harder. Others say they started to distrust their own judgment, or stopped making plans because the plans never seemed to survive the facts they were handed.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the missing options by name: 'Could we write down every way this could go, including the ones you think are unlikely, before we settle on one?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep the decision open: 'I'm not ready to treat that as the only option. I'd like to look into one or two others myself before I answer.'
response_options.disengagement: Without announcing anything, keep a private note of which options disappeared, when, and who said so, somewhere only you can reach. Weigh big decisions about housing or money quietly, with an advocate.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe the situation to someone outside it, or to an advocate, and ask them to list the options they see. If their list is longer than yours, that is useful information.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask in writing which alternatives were considered and who ruled them out. If the answer is vague, ask a union representative, HR or an ombuds office to look at it.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'd like to see all the options laid out side by side, including the ones that look unlikely. Could we list what each one involves, and then I'll take it from there?"
codex_completed.safety_note: The picture changes when the closed options involve money, housing, documents, medical care or contact with other people, and the person closing them is the one who controls those things. Watch for being told you could not manage elsewhere, or being unable to see accounts or papers. Speak with a domestic abuse advocate or legal aid service before changing anything, and plan any change privately.
misuse_warning: Calling it whenever an option you liked becomes unavailable can turn landlords, budgets and bad luck into someone's strategy. Check first whether the limit is real and can be verified.
Telling someone who gave you honest, strongly worded advice that they restricted your choices can turn a plain disagreement into a charge.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: False Dilemma is a statement, usually spoken, that there are only two options when more exist, so it can be challenged on the spot. Choice restriction often has no statement at all; the other options are closed in practice or described out of reach. Ultimatums attach a threatened loss to a forced either-or, while no threat is needed here. Resource Sabotage removes what you need to succeed, then blames you for the result, while this removes the alternatives to one outcome.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Emotional Flooding
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Pouring on emotion so fast and so hard that the other person cannot think, and speed or intensity is mistaken for closeness.
codex_completed.short_definition: Pouring on emotion so fast and so hard that the other person cannot think, and speed or intensity is mistaken for closeness.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Flooding is a state of being so emotionally overwhelmed that thinking narrows, and it can happen to anyone in a heated moment. As a tactic, it means keeping someone there on purpose or by habit: back-to-back declarations, crises and reconciliations, with no ordinary days in between. Strong feelings are not a tactic, and many real relationships are intense. The question is whether the intensity leaves you any quiet time in which to judge what is happening.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Things move through such big highs and lows, so quickly, that you never get a calm moment to think. The intensity can feel like love, but it also keeps you from seeing clearly.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Sustained intensity leaves no quiet stretch in which to assess anything. Speed gets mistaken for depth, and there is no calm vantage point from which to notice what you are agreeing to.
what_it_is: A run of big emotional events: declarations, fights, tearful reconciliations, urgent crises, in quick succession.
A shortage of ordinary time: no flat, boring, restful days when you could step back.
Often runs along with fast commitment, such as talk of forever within weeks.
Different from one overwhelming conversation: it is the sustained pace that matters.
what_it_sounds_like: "I've never felt this way about anyone. I know you're the one." (said in the first week)
"I can't breathe when you're not here. Please don't leave me tonight."
A midnight fight, a dawn apology and a gift by noon, repeated most weeks.
"If you really cared, you would have dropped everything."
"I'm in pieces. I need you to fix this right now."
Dozens of long, intense messages a day, swinging between adoration and despair.
what_it_is_not: The early excitement of a new relationship, which can be intense and then settle into something steadier.
A person in a real crisis, such as a death or job loss, who is overwhelmed because the situation is.
A naturally expressive person whose feelings are big and quickly shown, with nothing engineered behind it.
A single heated argument that left both of you shaken.
Your own flooding in a hard talk. Anyone's thinking narrows when they are overwhelmed.
this_may_be_it_when: You cannot remember the last ordinary, quiet day together.
Big declarations or commitments arrive faster than you have had time to get to know the person.
Every attempt to slow down is met with hurt, panic or a new crisis.
You often make decisions, such as moving in or sending money, in the middle of an emotional peak.
You feel exhausted, as well as swept up.
this_may_not_be_it_when: There are calm stretches, and the relationship is fine in them.
Slowing down, when you ask, is accepted without punishment.
The intensity matches something real going on in their life and eases when it passes.
Decisions are made on ordinary days and not only at emotional peaks.
You feel energized and clear-headed in the relationship, and not drained.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: New love can feel overwhelming to both people at once.
Someone with a history of stormy relationships may know no other pace and not intend any pressure.
Grief, illness or loss can fill a relationship with intense feelings for a while.
common_false_positives: A holiday romance or the first month of dating, where both people are swept up.
A friendship in which one person is going through a divorce and needs a great deal of support.
A family reunion that is emotional from beginning to end.
discernment_questions: When did we last have an ordinary, quiet stretch together?
Do I make big choices when I am calm, or when I am at an emotional peak?
Can I ask to go slower without causing a storm?
Do I feel more like myself or less in the calm moments?
Would my closest friend say this pace looks right for how long we have known each other?
less_concerning_if: There are real calm stretches, and you enjoy them.
You can slow things down without being punished for it.
The intensity belongs to a clear, passing event.
more_concerning_if: Big commitments, money or moving in are pressed through at the peak of an emotional episode.
You are cut off from friends and family during the whirlwind.
Every pause you ask for is answered with a crisis or a threat of self-harm.
pattern_over_time_signs: You cannot recall what you actually like about the person when things are calm.
You are sleeping less, and your friends have seen less of you.
You feel constant relief when a storm passes, and dread when it is quiet.
The highs are what you stay for and the lows are what you apologize for.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair in this case shows up as the pace itself changing: ordinary days appear, and a request to slow down is met with agreement and not a new crisis. A moving apology in the middle of another peak does not change the rhythm.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: A quiet evening alone is a small test. Someone who respects the request lets it be quiet, even if disappointed. If the temperature rises the moment you ask for calm, or a fresh crisis lands at your door, the request itself is being met with more flooding.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: When feelings run very high, thinking tends to narrow and people lean on gut sense and the wish to end the discomfort. Strong highs followed by relief can feel like deep bonding, and a sense of urgency can be read as proof of love. Without calm stretches, there may be few chances to compare what is said with what is done.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Whirlwind relationships are often remembered as exhausting and thrilling in the same breath. Some report poor sleep, lost touch with friends and a fog about what they actually wanted. Some say they only saw the pace once they had a quiet month for the first time.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name the pace without blame: 'I care about you, and I am worn out. I would like to try a few ordinary days.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Defer big decisions: 'I don't make decisions like this in the middle of a hard night. We can talk about it on Saturday.'
response_options.disengagement: When the intensity peaks, say you need to sleep on it and leave the conversation until morning.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend you trust about the last month, day by day, and ask whether the pace looks right from the outside.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager or client sets a constant crisis tone, ask for requests in writing and respond within a set window, not in the moment.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I do care, and I'm too tired to think clearly tonight. I'm going to sleep, and we can talk through this properly tomorrow afternoon."
codex_completed.safety_note: Intensity alone is not an emergency. Pay attention if the whirlwind is paired with threats of self-harm if you step back, pressure to move in or hand over money, cutting off your friends, or any physical fear. Then reach out to a trusted person, and consider a domestic violence advocate or a crisis line, depending on what you are facing.
misuse_warning: Calling a passionate new relationship 'flooding' can make real, mutual excitement look suspicious.
Using the word to describe a person's real distress can dismiss someone who is struggling.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Urgency Manufacturing is about time: a deadline you are given. Flooding is about feeling: a pace of emotion that leaves no space. An Ultimatum is a single hard choice with a penalty attached, while flooding is a sustained atmosphere with no clear demand. Interrogation demands justification from you, and flooding mostly offers you emotion to respond to.

codex_completed.name: Cognitive Overload
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Burying someone in more information, steps or demands than they can take in, so they cannot judge a decision clearly.
codex_completed.short_definition: Burying someone in more information, steps or demands than they can take in, so they cannot judge a decision clearly.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Everyone can only hold so much in mind at once. Past that point, people skim, guess, or agree just to be done. Cognitive overload as a tactic means a decision arrives wrapped in a flood of detail, jargon, paperwork or competing demands, often with a deadline. Complicated things are often truly complicated, so the amount alone proves nothing. What matters is whether the volume is needed, and what happens when you ask for less.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You are handed so much to read, learn or do at once that you cannot think straight, and saying yes becomes the quickest way out.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Agreement becomes the fastest way out of the overwhelm, so the decision that results was never really weighed, and you may find later that you consented to things you did not understand.
what_it_is: A heavy dose of detail, terms or tasks delivered right before a decision is needed.
Pages of small print, a long list of changes, or many people asking for different things at once.
Requests for time met with more material, and not with a pause.
Found in contracts, medical or insurance paperwork, workplace changes, and arguments where ten complaints arrive in one go.
what_it_sounds_like: A forty-page agreement handed over at the signing table with 'it's all standard, just initial here.'
"There are twelve things I need to go through with you, and we are going to do them all tonight."
"I've sent you the whole file, and I need your answer by the morning."
"Do you want me to explain the policy? It will take an hour, and most people just sign."
A long email with seven different questions and a note that all must be answered today.
"If you had read the terms, you would know this."
what_it_is_not: A decision that is truly complex, such as a mortgage or a medical consent, which does need a lot of real information.
An anxious person who explains everything because they want to be thorough, with no wish to hurry you.
A busy period at work when many real tasks pile up, with nobody designing it.
Plain jargon from someone who forgot you are not an expert in their field.
Your own tiredness or stress, which lowers how much you can take in on any day.
this_may_be_it_when: The amount of material is out of proportion to the choice, and a deadline hangs over it.
Asking for a summary or more time produces more material.
Key terms sit deep in the pile where they are easy to miss.
You are made to feel slow or difficult for needing to read it.
The same person has used volume to wear you down on earlier decisions.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They offer a short summary, and also give you the full version if you want it.
You are given real time, and your questions are answered plainly.
The deadline is set by an outside body, such as a court or a benefits office, and not by them.
The extra detail is mostly there to protect you, such as listing risks.
They are willing to slow down when you ask.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A professional who deals with this every day may forget how dense it looks to you.
Legal and medical documents are often long because the law requires it.
A colleague may send everything at once because they are worried about leaving something out.
common_false_positives: A lease or loan agreement that is long because of legal requirements.
A hospital discharge sheet that covers a lot because the situation needs it.
A friend planning a wedding who messages you about ten details in one evening.
discernment_questions: Is the amount of material needed for this choice, or more than it needs?
When I ask for a summary or for more time, do I get it?
Could I explain the key terms back in my own words right now?
Would I agree to this if I had a week and a calm room?
Is the deadline real, and who set it?
less_concerning_if: A plain summary is available on request and matches the full text.
You can take the documents away and answer later without penalty.
Someone qualified, who has no stake in the outcome, can walk you through it.
more_concerning_if: The decision involves your home, income, health or legal rights.
You are told that asking for time will cost you the offer or the job.
The overload arrives alongside a deadline you cannot verify.
pattern_over_time_signs: You sign or agree to things you could not summarize afterwards.
You have begun to avoid opening their messages because of their length.
You feel stupid after most dealings with them, though you are not stupid in other areas.
Mistakes you were warned about in the fine print have cost you money or time.
codex_completed.repair_check: Ask for the one-page version and see what comes back. Repair looks like a real summary, an honest answer about the parts that matter most, and an extension if you need one. A longer document or a sigh does not count as a change.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Say what you can manage: one question at a time, or the key terms on one page. Do they adapt? A person who respects the limit shortens the list. A person who does not will repeat the full load, or tell you everyone else coped.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Working memory is limited, and when it is full people tend to rely on shortcuts such as trusting whoever sounds confident or agreeing to finish. Stress and time pressure can reduce capacity further. Choosing the easiest path out can feel like a free choice in the moment, though it may be a response to overload.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A fog, a sense of shutting down, and a signature given with vague unease are common accounts. Some feel ashamed that they did not understand, and so did not ask. Afterwards, some go through the documents and find terms they did not know they had accepted.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for a narrower version: 'This is a lot. Can you give me the three points that matter most, and I will read the rest tonight?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Refuse to decide in the pile: 'I am not going to sign something I have not read. I will take it home and give you an answer on Thursday.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop the meeting or call when you reach your limit: 'I have taken in all I can for today. Let's pick this up tomorrow.'
response_options.support_seeking: Have someone with no stake in the outcome read the documents with you, such as a legal aid clinic, a patient advocate or a trusted friend who reads closely.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask for a written summary of changes and priorities, and confirm back in writing which items you will do first and which will wait.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I want to understand this properly before I decide. Please send me the key terms on one page, and I will respond by Thursday afternoon."
codex_completed.safety_note: Being overloaded is not itself a danger. It matters more where the decision touches your housing, income, health care or legal position, such as a lease, a benefits form or a settlement. For those, take time and ask a legal aid office, advocate or counselor to read it first. Never sign under pressure of time you cannot verify.
misuse_warning: Calling a genuinely complicated process 'overload' can lead you to distrust the people who are trying to explain it.
Using the label on a nervous over-explainer can punish someone who was trying to be careful.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Urgency Manufacturing shortens the clock; overload fills the time with so much material that the clock hardly matters. Interrogation demands answers from you, while overload pours material onto you. A False Dilemma shrinks your options to two, whereas overload buries them under detail so you cannot see how many options exist.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Bait and Switch
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Advertising or promising an appealing deal, then swapping in a worse one after the person is committed or has given something up.
codex_completed.short_definition: Advertising or promising an appealing deal, then swapping in a worse one after the person is committed or has given something up.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: The bait is the attractive offer: a low price, a job title, a promised role, a shared plan. The switch comes once you have said yes, moved, paid a deposit or turned down alternatives, and the terms turn out to be different. Plans and prices change honestly, and an apology with a real fix is a different matter. It is a pattern when the better terms were never available, or the change always favors the person who made it.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You are drawn in by one offer, and after you commit, you are handed a worse one. By then, walking away costs more than going along.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: By the time the terms change, you have often given something up: a deposit, another offer, a move, a plan. Walking away costs more than accepting, and that cost is what makes a worse deal acceptable.
what_it_is: An offer made to attract you that was never going to be delivered in full.
A change in the terms that arrives after you have paid, moved, quit or declined something else.
Seen in ads and sales, job offers, rentals, services, and in personal promises.
The gap is explained as bad luck or 'things changed', though the change always benefits the one making it.
what_it_sounds_like: "That model just sold out, but I can offer you this one for a bit more."
"The role turned out to be different from what we discussed, but you'll grow into it."
"The price I gave you did not include the fees. Everyone pays them."
"I know I said we would live near your family, but this place makes more sense."
"The flat is gone, but there is another one, slightly further out and pricier."
"That's not what I meant. You must have misunderstood."
what_it_is_not: A real change in circumstances that is explained openly and renegotiated fairly.
An honest error in a quote that the person corrects as soon as they notice, without leaning on you to accept it.
Terms that were clearly described as tentative or subject to approval at the time.
An item that actually sold out, where the seller truly has nothing else and says so.
Your own memory or hope shaping what was said. Writing things down is the only way to know.
this_may_be_it_when: The offer you were drawn in by was not available in the first place, or never would have been.
The change arrives only after you have committed, and not before.
The new terms favor them in every respect.
Your reminders of what was promised are met with 'that's not what I said'.
The same change has happened to other people dealing with them.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The change is explained, with documents, and you are free to walk away at no cost.
They offer a real remedy, such as refunding the deposit.
The terms moved in your favor as often as against.
The first offer was clearly marked as an estimate.
A third party, such as a supplier or an authority, truly changed the situation, and they told you promptly.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Stock, budgets and schedules do change, and honest people are sometimes forced to revise.
Someone may have overpromised out of enthusiasm and later face limits they had not foreseen.
A misunderstanding between two people can produce the same sense of a switch.
common_false_positives: A shop that really did run out of the advertised item and offers a rain check.
A job whose duties shifted when the company reorganized, and which was discussed openly.
A friend who planned a trip, then had to change it because of a family emergency.
discernment_questions: What exactly was promised, and do I have it in writing?
Did the change come before or after I committed?
Does the change benefit only them?
Would I have agreed if the current terms had been the first terms?
Am I being offered a fair way out, such as my money back?
less_concerning_if: They tell you about the change as soon as they know and offer a fair way out.
You can cancel with nothing lost.
The original offer was written down and they honor what they can.
more_concerning_if: You have given up housing, a job, a visa step or large sums before the switch.
They deny the original terms ever existed.
There is pressure to accept immediately or lose everything you have put in.
pattern_over_time_signs: You begin to keep screenshots and emails of what was said, because you expect it to change.
Each promise comes with a quiet exception that shows up later.
You are always the one adjusting to a new version of the deal.
You stop believing the first version of anything they say, and still feel unable to leave.
codex_completed.repair_check: Honest correction means the original terms are acknowledged, and you are offered a remedy that puts you back where you were, such as refund, release or the original deal. A new explanation that leaves you with the worse terms is not a fix, even when it comes with a warm apology.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: State the terms as you remember them and ask for a written confirmation. Does the person confirm, or argue about what was said? One who respects the limit puts it in writing and lets you decide.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Once people have invested money, effort or hope, they tend to feel pulled to stay with the choice and to explain away discrepancies. A good first offer also anchors expectations, so the swapped version can seem like a small loss and not a different deal. Giving up other options makes walking away feel more costly.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Feeling foolish, cornered and unsure whether you misheard is a common account. Some are left out of pocket, or stuck in a job or home that is not what they chose. Some say the hardest part was that nothing could be proven, because the first offer had only been spoken.

response_options.soft_clarification: Restate it plainly: 'What I understood at the start was this price and this role. Has something changed that I should know about?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Insist on the original: 'I agreed to the first terms. I am not able to accept the new ones.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop adding to what you have already put in, such as more deposit, more time or more work, until the terms are confirmed in writing.
response_options.support_seeking: Show the original offer and the new one to someone neutral, such as a consumer advice office, a tenants' group or a friend who reads contracts.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask for the role, pay and duties in a signed letter before you start, and keep the original offer message. If terms shift, raise it in writing with HR.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "That is different from what we agreed at the start. I would like the original terms confirmed in writing today. If that cannot be done, I would like my deposit returned."
codex_completed.safety_note: Most switches cost money or time, but the stakes rise if the bait was housing, a job abroad, a visa-linked position or a loan. If you have moved, handed over documents, or owe money, keep records and talk to a tenants' group, legal aid, a labor rights group or a consumer protection office before you accept new terms.
misuse_warning: Calling an honest change of plans 'bait and switch' can punish someone who told you promptly and offered a fair fix.
Using the term without checking what was actually promised can turn a misunderstanding into an accusation.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Sunk Cost Exploitation uses what you have already invested to keep you in; the switch is the change in terms that triggers that pull. A False Dilemma gives you two options at the time of choosing, while here the choice was made on one set of terms and then changed. An Ultimatum attaches a penalty to a demand, whereas the switch simply alters what you agreed to.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Pre-Punishment
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Shutting yourself down before anyone else can, by not applying, speaking or trying, because past experience taught you that being seen gets punished.
codex_completed.short_definition: Shutting yourself down before anyone else can, by not applying, speaking or trying, because past experience taught you that being seen gets punished.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: This is something a person does to themselves, so there may be no second party in the moment. After being mocked, shamed or hurt for standing out, a person can learn to remove the chance of being seen: skipping the application, staying silent in the meeting, never sending the draft. The punishment is imagined and delivered in advance. Caution is not the same thing. It becomes a pattern when it follows you into places where nothing like that has happened.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You turn yourself down before anyone else gets the chance. You do not apply, speak or try, because it once felt dangerous to be noticed, and not trying feels safer.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Opportunities close before anyone else has the chance to refuse them. The cost, which includes jobs not applied for and things not said, stays invisible because nothing happened, and your life can narrow without anyone noticing.
what_it_is: Declining to try, apply, ask or speak based on a punishment you expect, not one that has happened.
A learned reflex: at some point, visibility was followed by ridicule, anger or loss, so staying small became a way to stay safe.
It can attach to success as well as failure, so that both feel unsafe.
Self-directed: the inner critic does the work that a critical person once did.
what_it_sounds_like: "There's no point applying. They would only laugh."
"If I speak up in the meeting, they will tear it apart."
"I'd rather not send it. Then no one can say it is bad."
"If I do well, they will expect more, and then I will be punished when I cannot keep it up."
Writing an email, rereading it eleven times and deleting it.
"Who do I think I am?" (in your own voice, before you have done anything)
what_it_is_not: A realistic judgment that the odds are poor, such as not applying for a job whose requirements you clearly do not meet.
Ordinary caution or humility, which needs no painful history behind it.
Choosing not to pursue something because of competing priorities, such as family, health or money.
Introversion or a preference for staying out of the spotlight, if it brings you no distress.
A needed rest. Pulling back during a hard season can be healthy.
this_may_be_it_when: You pull back from things you want, before anyone has said no.
The fear is specific: being noticed, laughed at, or held to a higher standard.
You can trace the reflex to an earlier place or person where standing out cost you.
The expected punishment is vivid, though you cannot point to anything like it happening in your present life.
Relief comes when you stay out of it, followed by quiet regret.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You have weighed the odds and honestly decided it is not for you.
You pass on things that do not interest you, and take up the ones that do.
Your caution fits a real risk in your present situation.
You turn down opportunities without distress, and do not later wish you had tried.
The pullback is brief, tied to a hard stretch, and lifts when your circumstances improve.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Nerves before a big step are ordinary, and most people feel them.
Tiredness, grief or illness can make everything look pointless for a while.
Some people simply prefer a quieter life and are content in it.
common_false_positives: Skipping a competition because you honestly do not enjoy competing.
