Deciding not to apply for a role that would mean a long commute you cannot manage.
Shyness in new groups, which eases as you know people.
discernment_questions: What exactly do I expect to happen if I try, and has it ever happened to me?
Do I pull back from things I want, or things I do not care about?
When did I first learn that being seen was not safe?
Is there someone in my present life who would punish me, or only someone from my past?
If I imagined a kind friend in my place, what would I tell them to do?
less_concerning_if: You can name a clear, current reason for holding back that you are comfortable with.
You sometimes take the risk anyway, and it goes fine.
You do not feel regret afterwards.
more_concerning_if: Your life is shrinking: fewer applications, fewer friends, fewer words.
The fear is accompanied by hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm.
You still live or work with someone who does punish you for being visible.
pattern_over_time_signs: You keep a list of things you wanted to do and never did.
You watch others take chances you quietly wanted, and feel a pang.
Your reasons for not trying change, but the outcome never does.
You have begun to think of yourself as someone who is simply not made for opportunities.
codex_completed.repair_check: Healing shows up in small, real tries: sending the application, speaking once in a meeting, and finding that the feared punishment did not come. Telling yourself it is time to be braver, without any actual try, leaves the reflex where it was.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Take one small step into view and notice the room. Does it respond the way you feared, or is the alarm mostly inside you while the room stays unmoved? That gap between expected and actual reaction is the useful fact.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: If being visible was once followed by criticism or loss, the mind can learn to treat visibility as a threat. Avoiding the situation brings immediate relief, which tends to strengthen the avoidance. Because nothing bad happens when you do not try, the expectation is never tested.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A quiet shrinking is the usual account: applications never sent, ideas never spoken, praise deflected. Some describe a tiredness from constant self-monitoring, and grief for what they did not try. Many say that seeing the reflex as old, and not as truth, was what first loosened it.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask yourself plainly: 'Who is the person I am afraid will react, and are they in this room?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Set a very small test: send one email or speak once this week, and write down what actually happened afterwards.
response_options.disengagement: When the inner critic starts its case, step away from the decision for a day and come back with a calmer eye.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a trusted person or a counselor about the old experience. Talking about when it began can loosen its hold.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Pick one low-stakes place to be visible, such as a short comment in a meeting, and ask a trusted colleague for plain feedback afterwards.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I notice I am talking myself out of this before anyone has said a word. That is an old habit, not today's facts. I am going to send the application and see what really happens."
codex_completed.safety_note: Holding yourself back is a painful pattern but not by itself a danger. It deserves more care if it comes with hopelessness, thoughts of self-harm, or if you still live or work where being visible really is punished. In that case, talk to a counselor, a doctor or a crisis line, and think about what makes your present situation safe.
misuse_warning: Naming someone else's hesitation as 'pre-punishment' can dismiss a reasonable decision they made for sound reasons.
Treating all caution as an old wound can push a person to take risks that are not safe for them.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Ultimatums, False Dilemma and Interrogation all come from another person who presses on you. Pre-Punishment has no one pressing in the moment: the pressure is a remembered one, now carried inside. Sunk Cost Exploitation keeps you in something because of what you have already put in; pre-punishment keeps you out of things because of a punishment you expect.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Lying
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Saying something the speaker knows to be untrue so that another person will believe it and act on it.
codex_completed.short_definition: Saying something the speaker knows to be untrue so that another person will believe it and act on it.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A lie is a statement the speaker knows is false, offered so that the listener will believe it. The key is what the speaker knew, which an outsider usually cannot see at the time. A wrong statement is not a lie, and a lie need not be large: it can be an invented reason for being late or a false claim about money. Kind white lies are common and differ from lies that steer someone's decisions. Checkable claims that keep failing, and accounts that change only once evidence appears, point toward lying.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone tells you something they know is not true, and you make choices based on it.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You decide things with false information, and finding out costs more than one belief. It makes you doubt everything else that person has told you, including the parts that were true.
what_it_is: A statement of fact, not an opinion, made by someone who knows it is false.
It can be a flat denial, an invented detail, a false reason, or a claim that something happened when it did not.
Different from omission: a lie asserts something, while silence merely hides it.
It ranges from an invented excuse to a false statement about money, health or whereabouts.
What marks it is the speaker's knowledge, which only the speaker, or later evidence, can show.
what_it_sounds_like: I was at work until nine.
I never got your message.
The payment went through last week.
I haven't spoken to her in years.
It wasn't me who told them.
That's the first I'm hearing of it.
what_it_is_not: An honest mistake stated sincerely. A rounded or simplified figure that is not technically precise may carry no deception at all, and someone who corrects their account because they later remembered better is doing the right thing.
A prediction or opinion that turned out wrong, such as 'it'll be fine'.
A refusal to share, such as 'I can't discuss that', which declines to answer and states nothing false.
A cover story for a surprise party that everyone laughs about afterwards.
A child's imaginative story told as play.
this_may_be_it_when: A checkable record, such as a receipt, a log or a message, contradicts what was said.
The account changes only after evidence appears.
A detail is oddly specific and offered without being asked.
When confronted, the story gets a new version instead of a correction.
Other people, with documents, tell it differently.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They correct themselves quickly and without being pushed.
The error is in a date, a number or a detail that is easy to mix up.
Their account matches the records on every point you can check.
You have only a feeling and no contradicting fact.
They tell you plainly when there is something they can't share.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Memory is reconstructed each time it is used, and stress and tiredness distort it.
Secondhand information is often passed on as believed.
Embarrassment can make a person avoid a fact until they are ready, which is closer to omission than to a lie.
People simplify for children or when in a hurry.
common_false_positives: A colleague gives a delivery date that then slips.
Someone says 'I'm fine' to get through a work day.
A friend remembers a name or place wrongly.
Two witnesses describe an event differently from where they stood.
discernment_questions: What do I actually know, from a record or a witness, as opposed to a feeling?
Could the speaker have believed it when they said it?
When the facts came out, was the account owned or did it change?
Is this one claim, or one of several that haven't held up?
Would I decide differently with the true version, and does it matter here?
less_concerning_if: The correction is offered without prompting when they realize.
The false detail has no bearing on your decisions.
Their other claims check out when you look.
more_concerning_if: The false claim shaped a big decision about money, health, someone's whereabouts or a legal matter.
Further claims keep failing when checked.
Owning it is followed by blaming you for checking.
pattern_over_time_signs: You start verifying small things you would once have accepted.
Corrections arrive only after you find the record yourself.
Explanations of earlier claims keep changing.
True statements from the same person start to be doubted as well, and sorting true from false becomes your job.
codex_completed.repair_check: A plain correction names what was untrue and what it cost you, and information is then volunteered before you ask for it. An apology that spends most of its length on why you shouldn't have checked has repaired nothing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: If you say you need claims you can check, such as the receipt or the message, watch the next few weeks. Respect looks like being handed the document without a fight. Being told you are paranoid for asking suggests the request was not taken in.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People generally assume that what they are told is true, because checking everything is exhausting. A lie uses that default. Once it is discovered, trust tends to break wider than the lie itself, since the listener cannot easily tell which other statements were true. Rebuilding the picture takes effort, and some people stay watchful long afterwards.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A sharp jolt on discovery comes first, then going back through past conversations to sort true from false. Believing is an ordinary default, yet many feel foolish for having done it. Others turn into checkers, and some find the relationship, or the institution, harder to rely on afterwards even when the lie was small.

response_options.soft_clarification: Lead with the fact rather than the accusation: 'The bank record shows the payment on the 14th. Help me understand what happened.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say that on money and safety matters you need claims you can back up: 'On this kind of thing, I need to see the record, not just hear it.'
response_options.disengagement: Where the stakes are high, stop acting on this person's unverified claims. Decide using what you can check yourself, and let the rest wait.
response_options.support_seeking: Check your reading with someone neutral who can look at the documents, so you are not relying on memory alone or on the other person's version.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask for important statements in writing and keep the record. If a false statement affected a decision, take the documents to a supervisor or HR rather than arguing the point out loud.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Being able to rely on what you tell me matters to me. When it's about money or plans, I'll ask to see the confirmation. That isn't an accusation, it's how I'm going to make decisions from now on."
codex_completed.safety_note: Lying becomes safety-relevant when the false claims concern where someone is, what has been done with your money or documents, or when asking about the truth is met with anger or threats. Keep copies of records you can verify, and if questions bring fear, speak to an advocate or lawyer before raising it again.
misuse_warning: Calling someone a liar when they may have been mistaken or remember differently closes the conversation and treats a guess about what they knew as fact.
Treating one inaccurate statement as proof that everything else the person says is false.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Lying by Omission says nothing false but leaves out the piece that would change your decision; a lie puts a false statement on the table. Fabricated Evidence adds a manufactured document or screenshot to back the claim, so there is a physical thing to examine. Exaggeration begins with something true and stretches it. A lie stands alone as a flat statement the speaker knows is untrue.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Lying by Omission
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Leaving out information the other person needs for an accurate understanding, while everything that is said stays technically true.
codex_completed.short_definition: Leaving out information the other person needs for an accurate understanding, while everything that is said stays technically true.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Lying by omission is a true account with the important piece missing. What is said holds up; the gap is where the false picture forms. Gaslighting by omission and selective information sharing are simply other names for this, and nothing separates the three. Sometimes the missing piece is a single fact, sometimes it is a steady filtering of which facts one person gets. One forgotten detail means little. It becomes a pattern when the missing pieces are the ones that would have changed your decision, and they keep being missing.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You are told true things, but not the one fact that would have changed what you decided. You find out later, from someone else or by accident, that it was known all along.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Nothing said was false, so there is no untruth to point at, only a conclusion you reached on grounds you did not know were incomplete. The missing piece usually appears too late to change what you chose, and you may blame yourself for not asking.
what_it_is: An account that is accurate in every sentence, with the one piece that would change its meaning absent.
Can be a single missing fact, such as a debt or a diagnosis, or an ongoing filter on which facts reach you.
Often found by chance, from a letter, a third person or a record, not from the person who knew.
Sometimes the information was mentioned in a way that buried it, such as a passing remark in an unrelated conversation that later counts as 'I told you.'
Matters most where the listener is deciding something, such as signing, buying, moving, lending or trusting.
The line between privacy and concealment is whether the other person is relying on the incomplete picture to decide.
what_it_sounds_like: 'I never said that wasn't true.'
'I told you about it.' (a passing remark, months ago, in a different conversation)
'You never asked.'
'It didn't seem relevant.' (said about the one detail the decision turned on)
A version of a story that includes everything favoring one side and nothing that complicates it.
'Why would I bring that up? It wasn't your business.' (after you had to deal with its effects)
You learn from someone else a fact they had known all along and never mentioned.
what_it_is_not: Not thinking to mention something that did not seem relevant at the time is ordinary.
Plenty of information is legitimately nobody else's business, such as a friend's confidence or a person's private medical history.
A gap held briefly, with a plan to close it once the timing is right, such as waiting for test results before telling the family. That is a delay, not a concealment.
Context can be missing because the speaker never had it, which is a gap and not a filter.
Sharing what you know as you learn it, across several conversations, differs from choosing in advance which facts another person gets.
A short summary that drops detail for length and would readily expand if asked.
this_may_be_it_when: The missing detail is exactly the one that would have changed your decision.
The person knew the fact at the time, and a record or a third party shows it.
Direct questions on the topic get answers that are accurate but still go around it.
Earlier accounts from them have a similar shape: the favorable parts in, the complicating ones out.
When the fact comes out, the first response defends the omission ('you didn't ask') rather than addressing the fact.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They tell you the missing piece as soon as they realize it matters.
They did not know it themselves until recently.
The omitted matter is truly theirs, or a third party's, to keep private, and does not affect your decision.
They volunteered a bigger and uncomfortable fact just before, which does not fit a filter.
When asked directly, they answer directly.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People forget to mention things all the time, especially when busy or anxious.
Some find it hard to share bad news and put it off until they have the words.
Families and workplaces differ in what gets passed on and who is thought to need to know.
A person may believe the information was already known to you.
common_false_positives: A planner of a surprise party who keeps one fact back until the day.
A colleague who did not mention a change because the notice went to everyone.
A clinician, lawyer or counselor bound by confidentiality who cannot tell you.
discernment_questions: Would knowing the missing piece have changed a choice I made?
Did the person have the information when we last spoke about this?
Is the information theirs to withhold, or does it affect me?
Was it shared voluntarily once it mattered, or only after I found it?
Do the things left out tend to be the ones that would change outcomes?
If I ask directly now, what do I get?
less_concerning_if: The missing piece was small and had no bearing on any choice you made.
They fill the gap quickly when asked and say how it was missed.
It happened during a hectic period and has not repeated.
more_concerning_if: The missing information involves money, health, safety, children or legal matters.
You are told the omission was your fault for not asking the right question.
Others in your circle turn out to have known what you were not told.
pattern_over_time_signs: You begin to ask 'is there anything else I should know?' before every decision.
You regularly learn big facts secondhand.
Your picture of events keeps getting corrected by later discoveries.
You cross-check what they say against other sources, and feel uneasy doing it.
codex_completed.repair_check: Mending it means the person hands over the whole picture, including what they knew and when, without being asked twice, and then volunteers things before they are discovered. A version that supplies the missing fact but blames you for not asking leaves the habit in place.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Tell them in plain terms what you need to know in order to decide, then watch the next few weeks. Do the facts that matter reach you first, or do you still hear them from other people? The gap between what is promised and what arrives is your answer.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People build decisions on what they believe is the whole story, and trust that a person would speak up if something important were missing. A gap in the account is invisible from the inside, so the listener fills it with the most ordinary assumption. When the omission is found, being told that nothing false was said can lead a person to doubt their own judgment or their memory of what they were told.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: On finding out, some feel foolish and then betrayed, even though no lie can be quoted. They may go over old conversations looking for what they missed, hesitate to trust good news, or start asking so many questions that they feel like an interrogator. Some doubt their memory of what they were told.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the open question in a neutral voice: 'Is there anything about this that I'd want to know before I decide?' It makes it easy to add the missing piece without anyone feeling accused.
response_options.firm_boundary: Say what you need in order to trust the account: 'If something affects my decision, I need to hear it from you before I find it out myself.'
response_options.disengagement: Do not decide anything large on this person's account alone. Get the key facts from the document, the records or a third person, and hold off until you have them.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe what you were told and what you later found to someone not involved, and ask whether the missing piece would have changed their decision. It helps separate fair upset from self-blame.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask for decisions, terms and changes in writing, and include the line 'Is there anything else that affects this?' in the message. Keep the reply as a record of what you were told and when.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'm not saying anything you told me was false. What I found out later changes how I see it, and I would have decided differently. From here, I need to hear anything that affects me from you, first and plainly."
codex_completed.safety_note: Usually this is a trust problem and not a danger. That changes if the hidden matter is a debt in your name, a health risk such as an infection, a legal case, or where children or money are, or if asking is met with anger. Then get documents and records from the source and talk to a lawyer, doctor or financial counselor before acting on the person's account.
misuse_warning: Treating every unmentioned detail as a lie turns privacy and forgetfulness into charges. The label needs a gap that mattered to a decision and that the other person knew about.
People are entitled to keep some things to themselves. 'You didn't tell me' is not always a complaint the other person owes an answer to.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Lying states something false, while omission states only true things. Strategic Incompleteness gives you just enough to act on and keeps you coming back for the rest, so the gap is ongoing and builds dependence; here the gap is a hidden piece in an otherwise finished account. Countering flatly contradicts your version of events, whereas omission contradicts nothing and leaves your picture incomplete.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Strategic Incompleteness
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Giving someone enough information to take the next step but never enough to see the whole picture, so they keep coming back for more.
codex_completed.short_definition: Giving someone enough information to take the next step but never enough to see the whole picture, so they keep coming back for more.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Information arrives in installments. Each one is enough to act on, and none gives the whole plan, the full cost or the real timeline, so the person has to return to the same source for the next piece. Nothing false need be said, and plenty of honest situations work this way, such as a new job or a medical treatment explained in stages. Concern rises when asking for the full picture is answered with reassurance, and the person never becomes able to act alone.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You get the next instruction but never the whole plan, and every time you ask for the big picture you are told not to worry.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: You can act, but you can't act well, so every step sends you back to the same source, and independence never arrives.
what_it_is: Information released in pieces sized to the next step, never the whole route.
Each answer is true or close to true. It is the total that is missing.
Found in jobs, contracts, projects, family arrangements and advisory or caregiving roles.
A loop: act, hit a gap, return for the next piece.
Unlike silence, you do get answers, which makes the gap harder to notice.
what_it_sounds_like: Just do this part for now, I'll explain the rest later.
You don't need to worry about that yet.
Trust me, I'll handle that side.
I'll send you the next step once you've finished this one.
I'll walk you through that when we get there.
We'll cross that bridge when we come to it.
what_it_is_not: Genuinely complex things are often explained in stages because that is the only comprehensible order. Someone who does not yet have the full picture can only pass on what they have, and need-to-know structures exist for reasons unconnected to any one person.
A mentor who holds back advanced material until the basics are learned, and says so.
A project whose later phases genuinely have not been decided yet.
A surprise being planned, where the holder of the plan is open about keeping it.
A safety or legal rule that limits who may receive which information.
this_may_be_it_when: Asking for the overall plan, cost or timeline gets reassurance and no document.
After months you still cannot describe what the whole arrangement involves.
Each step needs approval from the same person.
Fees, terms or risks you needed to weigh show up only after you have committed.
Other people involved have fuller information and have been asked not to share it.
this_may_not_be_it_when: A written outline with phases is available on request, even if later phases are marked tentative.
The person tells you what they don't know yet.
You can get the information elsewhere easily, and nobody discourages that.
The staging follows a published curriculum or standard process.
You need to ask less as time goes on, because your independence is growing.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Honest uncertainty: plans change, and the full detail may not exist yet.
Overload: people sometimes give small portions to a nervous learner.
A busy person gives the next instruction first and the background later.
Legal and safety rules can limit who receives which information.
common_false_positives: A surgeon explaining recovery stage by stage.
A new employer onboarding someone over several weeks.
A course or game that unlocks later chapters by design and says so.
A parent telling a child only what they need for today's trip.
discernment_questions: Could I describe the whole plan, cost and timeline today? If not, who does know?
When I ask for the full picture, do I get an answer, a document or reassurance?
Do I need to return to this source less over time, or more?
Are there pieces I only discovered after committing?
Is anyone discouraging me from asking elsewhere or comparing notes?
less_concerning_if: A written outline is given when you ask.
You are becoming more independent as time goes on.
Gaps are named openly: 'we don't know that yet'.
more_concerning_if: The hard parts, such as costs, limits or risks, appear only after you have committed.
Requests for the whole picture are met with annoyance, or with being told to just trust.
Your ability to act without this source is shrinking, because they hold the login, the contact or the paperwork.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your bigger questions are answered with smaller and smaller pieces.
You have done the work for months without being able to explain it to an outsider.
Each new step commits you further, or costs more, than the one before.
Alternatives drop out because only the source knows enough to advise.
codex_completed.repair_check: A complete outline handed over without being chased is the sign: what the whole arrangement involves, what remains unknown, and what you can now do without asking. A promise to be more open while the next piece still arrives alone is a repeat.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask for the full outline in writing and see whether you receive something you could take to another person for a second opinion. A document you can show others suggests the request was heard. Talk about how complicated it all is, offered instead of the document, suggests it was not.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Small pieces make each next step look like a modest commitment, and effort already spent makes stopping harder. Without the whole, risk is hard to judge, alternatives are hard to compare, and growth in the total goes unnoticed. Needing to return for the next piece can also make the source feel indispensable.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: The usual report is feeling busy but not oriented: unable to explain to a friend what you are involved in, and discovering late that the total cost or demand was larger than any step suggested. Some feel they should have asked sooner; others notice they asked often and were soothed.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the overall outline in one go: 'Could you give me the whole plan, even roughly, with the costs and the end date? I'd like to see it before I do the next piece.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Make the next step depend on the picture: 'I'll carry on once I have the full terms in writing. Until then I'm holding where I am.'
response_options.disengagement: If the whole picture never comes, treat what you have been told as all there is and decide on that basis. You can stop adding commitments.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe the whole arrangement to someone outside it and notice where they ask questions you can't answer. Those gaps show where the missing information lives.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask for the scope, deadlines and decision-makers for your project in writing, and for who holds the parts you lack. Send a manager your own summary to confirm.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Before I take the next step, I need to see the whole thing laid out: what it involves, what it costs and when it ends. I'm happy to wait while you put it together, and I may ask someone else to look it over with me."
codex_completed.safety_note: Staged information is mostly a risk to your money and time. It becomes more serious when whoever holds the missing pieces also controls your housing, immigration papers, wages or accounts, since then you cannot easily verify or step back. Copy the documents you have and get independent advice, such as legal aid or a workers' rights center, before committing further.
misuse_warning: Calling any staged explanation manipulation can make teachers, doctors and new managers look sinister when they are simply sequencing hard material.
Demanding everything at once from someone who honestly does not have it yet.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Lying by Omission keeps back one fact that would change a single decision; here information keeps coming, always in pieces, and the repeated need to return defines it. Vague Allegations leaves out detail so nothing can be checked, while here each piece is concrete and usable and only the whole is missing. Lying states a falsehood, which this pattern may never involve.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Catfishing
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Building a relationship, usually online, behind a made-up identity such as borrowed photos or an invented life story, so the other person bonds with someone who does not exist.
codex_completed.short_definition: Building a relationship, usually online, behind a made-up identity such as borrowed photos or an invented life story, so the other person bonds with someone who does not exist.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Catfishing is forming a close online connection under a false identity: another person's photos, an invented job, a made-up age or location. Because the person is met through messages and pictures, the missing step is verification, and each new excuse for avoiding live video or a meeting pushes it further away. People use false profiles for many reasons, including loneliness and play, and also for money or images. From the receiving end you usually cannot tell which until you can check. Shifting basic facts and live contact that never happens are what mark it.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: You grow close to someone online who turns out not to be who they said, so the feelings were real but the person was not.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Everything built on the connection rests on ground that was never there, so what is lost on discovery includes the relationship's entire history, not merely its ending.
what_it_is: A profile built from someone else's photos or from a fictional person's details: name, job, location, family.
Usually lives in messaging apps, dating apps, games and social platforms, where a face is not required.
Contact is often warm, attentive and fast-moving, though speed alone proves nothing.
Live checks keep falling through: video calls fail, meetings are postponed, voice notes stand in for calls.
May lead to requests for money, gifts, private images or personal details, though not always.
what_it_sounds_like: Photos that, on a reverse image search, belong to a different name or a model's portfolio.
'My camera is broken' or 'bad signal' every time a video call is planned.
A glamorous remote job, such as offshore work or overseas service, that explains being out of reach.
Life details that clash across chats: a hometown, a sibling or a timeline that changes.
'I've never felt this way about anyone', said within days of meeting.
A sudden emergency that needs money from someone met only online.
No friends or family who ever comment, appear in photos or can be introduced.
what_it_is_not: Reasonable caution about identifying details early in an online relationship is not a fabricated identity.
Outdated photos and flattering presentation fall short of accurate without being wholesale invention.
Reluctance about video calls or meeting in person is frequently social anxiety.
A username or pseudonym used for privacy, with the real name shared as trust grows.
A person with safety or health reasons, such as someone hiding their location from a former partner, who wants control over what they show.
Role-play in a game or fiction community where everyone knows the characters are invented.
this_may_be_it_when: A reverse image search leads to someone else's profile.
Every plan to see or hear them live falls through, with a new reason each time.
Basic facts about age, job or place change between conversations.
Money, gift cards or private images are requested by someone you have never seen live.
Nothing exists beyond the profile: no history, no friends who interact with it.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They agree to a video call, even awkwardly, and roughly look like the photos.
Their profile has history older than your contact, with friends interacting.
The differences are small, like photos a few years old or height rounded up.
They are shy but offer other ways to verify, such as a work email, a phone call or a mutual contact.
Nobody has asked you for money or images, and the pace is gradual.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People avoid giving a real name and workplace to strangers, which is sensible privacy.
Anxiety about appearing on video, or a weak connection, can delay calls.
Shame about appearance can lead someone to use older photos.
Time zones and shift work can make live contact hard to arrange.
common_false_positives: A dating match who is slow to video call because of shyness.
A friend whose profile photos are four years old.
A gaming friend you have always known through an avatar and handle.
Someone on a forum built around anonymity, such as a peer-support group.
discernment_questions: Have I ever seen or heard this person live, in a way I could not mistake?
Do the photos and details match when I search the images, name and job?
Do their reasons for avoiding verification keep changing?
Has anything been asked of me, such as money, images or secrecy, that I would not give a stranger?
If a close friend described this relationship to me, what would I tell them to check?
less_concerning_if: Verification happens without fuss when you ask.
Nobody has asked for money, images or secrecy.
The profile's history and mutual contacts check out.
more_concerning_if: Requests for money, gift cards, crypto or investments come from someone you have never met live.
Private images are asked for, or you are told to keep the relationship secret from friends and family.
Anger, guilt or pleading follows when you ask to verify.
pattern_over_time_signs: Plans to meet or call are set repeatedly and then fall through.
Emotional intensity rises faster than the verifiable facts.
Requests grow from small, a favor or a gift card, to larger.
Details you were told need quiet patching whenever they conflict.
codex_completed.repair_check: If the person is open about the false identity, they volunteer the true name and situation without being questioned, and leave you to decide what to do with it. Further explanations that require you to send money or keep quiet are not that.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Think about what happens when you say you would like a live video call before going further. Someone who is who they say usually finds a way, even if nervous. A new reason, a guilt-laden message or a deadline in reply is information too.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Messaging lets you fill a blank with your hopes. Warm attention, constant contact and early self-disclosure build closeness fast, and shared secrets seem like proof of trust. When the only evidence is a profile, the mind supplies the rest, and each small excuse is easy to accept because the feelings are already real to you.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe grief that other people don't recognize, because the person they were attached to never existed in that form. Many feel embarrassed or foolish, though closeness with someone online is ordinary. Some describe money lost, trust in later dating damaged, and replaying messages to find what they missed.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for a live check as a normal next step: 'I'd love to see you on video this week. What day works?' Notice whether a time is found.
response_options.firm_boundary: State your limit on money and images once, in plain words: 'I don't send money or private photos to anyone I haven't met in person.' Then hold to it, whatever the reply.
response_options.disengagement: Stop replying and send nothing further. Save the messages and profile links first, then report the account to the platform.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend or family member what happened, even if it feels embarrassing, and show them the messages. If money or images were sent, contact your bank and a fraud-reporting or victim-support service promptly.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a profile approached you through a professional network, report it to the platform and to your workplace's security or IT team, with screenshots and links.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I've enjoyed talking. Before we go further, I want us to have a live video call. I also don't send money or private photos to anyone I haven't met properly, so that isn't something I'll be doing."
codex_completed.safety_note: Danger signals are requests for money, gift cards or crypto, requests for intimate images, pressure to keep the relationship secret, and threats to share what you have sent. Send nothing more. Keep screenshots, profile links and payment records, report the account to the platform, and contact your bank. If images were shared or threats made, a victim-support service or the police can advise on takedown options.
misuse_warning: Treating every shy or private online contact as a fake identity can hurt people who are cautious for good reasons.
Publicly accusing a real person of catfishing without checking can expose a private individual to harassment.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Lying is one false statement that can sit inside an otherwise real relationship; catfishing replaces the whole person the relationship is with. Exaggeration inflates real qualities such as height or income, while a fabricated identity can't be fixed by toning it down. Fabricated Evidence manufactures documents or screenshots to prove a claim; a catfish profile may contain staged photos, but what defines it is that the person at the other end is not who they say.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Half-Truth Framing
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Choosing and arranging statements that are each true so that the listener ends up with a false overall picture.
codex_completed.short_definition: Choosing and arranging statements that are each true so that the listener ends up with a false overall picture.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: Half-truth framing is building a false impression out of true statements. Each sentence can be checked and holds up, but the pieces are chosen and ordered so the listener reaches a conclusion the full facts would not support. Paltering is simply another name for this, and nothing separates the two. It often appears as a technically accurate answer to a direct question, followed by 'everything I said was true.' One hurried summary proves little. It becomes a pattern when answers keep steering the same way on the same kind of topic.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Everything said is true, yet you walk away believing something that is not. Each fact checks out, so the problem only shows when you see what was left around it.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: Every fact checks out, so a careful listener who verifies still reaches the wrong conclusion. When you object you are told, correctly, that nothing false was said, which can leave you doubting your own reasonable inference instead of the account.
what_it_is: A set of true statements, chosen and ordered so that they imply something the whole story would not support.
Often a true answer to a slightly different question than the one asked.
Works because most people assume a truthful answer is an honest one, and rarely check what sits around it.
Different from an outright lie, since every sentence can be defended, and from plain omission, since the pieces are fitted together to point somewhere.
Found in sales pitches, job references, relationship disputes, apologies and reports to bosses.
what_it_sounds_like: 'Did the repair pass inspection?' / 'The inspector spent an hour at the house.'
'Were you out with anyone last night?' / 'I was at the pub until eleven.' (the question was who)
'But everything I said was true.' offered after you discover the gap.
'The company has never missed a payroll.' (said of a firm about to close)
'I never told her she was fired. I only said her role was changing.'
'Sales are up 20 percent this month.' (after a 40 percent drop the month before, left unsaid)
Asked a direct question, they answer fully and warmly, about something next to it.
what_it_is_not: An accurate summary necessarily omits detail for length.
People often present facts in whatever order those facts occurred to them, with no steer in mind.
A genuinely different, honestly held interpretation of the same true facts is disagreement rather than arrangement.
Careful, precise people answer exactly what was asked and nothing more. That can sound evasive without steering anyone anywhere.
An honest answer given with an incomplete picture, because that was all the speaker had.
Things people are entitled not to disclose at all, such as medical history, where they say it is private and do not imply something else.
this_may_be_it_when: The answer addresses a neighboring question, not the one you asked.
When the missing context is added, the impression it created falls apart.
Challenging the impression gets 'but everything I said was true' and no acknowledgement of what you were led to believe.
It shows up on topics where the full picture would cost the speaker something.
A plain yes or no was available, and a longer answer was given instead, again and again.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Adding the missing context leaves the picture unchanged.
They accept 'that's not what I understood' and fill in the rest without being pressed.
The same wordy, precise style shows up on every topic, including ones with nothing at stake.
The speaker did not know the full picture themselves.
You were told the limits at the start: 'I can only speak to this part.'
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Nervous speakers often answer a nearby question because they are rushing to say something.
Professional training in saying only what is certain can make answers sound slippery.
Some people fear a plain 'no' will start a fight, and soften it with true but beside-the-point detail.
Asked in a hurry, people give the first true thing that comes to mind.
common_false_positives: A friend telling a story in the order it happened, with the ending last.
A status report that stresses good news because it was asked to be brief.
A witness who answers a narrowly worded question narrowly.
discernment_questions: If I put the full set of facts in front of a neutral person, would they reach the conclusion I was led to?
Was the question I asked answered, or a nearby one?
Was there a plain, still-honest way to answer that was not used?
When I add what was missing, does the person take it on board or resist?
Does this show up only on subjects where the full picture is inconvenient?
less_concerning_if: The person fills in the missing context as soon as you ask.
The slanted account came from a hurried summary and not from a conversation about something that mattered.
The impression was minor, and correcting it costs neither side anything.
more_concerning_if: You made a decision, such as signing, paying or staying, on the strength of the impression.
The same kind of answer keeps coming about money, whereabouts or health.
When you check the facts, you are told you should have asked more precisely.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find yourself asking questions in more and more exact wording to get a straight answer.
You learn what the gaps were later, from other people and not from them.
'Technically true' becomes a phrase you hear from them, or say about them.
You trust their literal words less while still being unable to point to a lie.
codex_completed.repair_check: Mending this starts with the person saying what picture they let you form and what they knew that would have changed it, then volunteering the rest. Watch whether later answers to direct questions get plainer. An apology that defends every sentence as true has repaired nothing.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Ask a question that has only one honest short answer and notice what comes back. A yes or a no, even an unwelcome one, shows the request was heard. Another accurate but roundabout reply shows the old shape returning.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Listeners tend to assume a speaker is being cooperative, so they fill gaps with the most natural meaning of what they hear. True statements pass the checks people normally run, which leaves the false conclusion as the listener's own inference. That can make a complaint harder, because the speaker can truthfully say that every sentence was accurate.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: Some feel foolish for believing something that was never technically said, and are unable to explain the complaint to others. They may begin to cross-examine every answer, or blame themselves for not asking the right question. Some describe losing the sense that plain conversation with this person is possible.

response_options.soft_clarification: Restate the answer you were given and ask the one thing it left open: 'That's true, but it doesn't tell me whether you went. Did you?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say you want direct answers to direct questions on this topic, and that 'technically true' will not do: 'When I ask yes or no, I need yes or no.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop trying to corner the person with sharper wording. Get the facts from the original source, such as the document, the account or a third party, and let the conversation go.
response_options.support_seeking: Lay out the exchange to someone neutral and ask what conclusion they would draw from what was said. It checks whether your inference was reasonable.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In writing, ask for confirmation of the specific facts you need ('Please confirm whether the contract includes overtime') and keep the reply. A written yes or no is harder to blur.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Thank you, I believe what you told me is accurate. I'd still like a plain yes or no to my question: did it happen or not? I make decisions based on the picture I'm left with, so I need the whole picture."
codex_completed.safety_note: A misleading frame with true parts is a communication problem, not a danger signal. That changes if the missing piece concerns safety, money, a health risk or custody, or if asking questions brings anger or retaliation. Then check the facts through documents or an independent source before acting, and take the matter to a lawyer, advisor or doctor rather than relying on the person's own account.
misuse_warning: Calling any careful or incomplete answer a half-truth treats privacy and precision as lies. The label needs a gap between the impression left and the facts, shown with the facts.
'Technically true' can be thrown at someone to win an argument about interpretation. If both readings fit the facts, it is a disagreement.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Lying states something false; half-truth framing states nothing false and works through selection and order. Lying by Omission is a gap, a fact left out of an otherwise complete account, whereas here the stated facts are fitted together to point at a conclusion. Frame Control sets what the conversation is about, while a half-truth can sit inside any frame, as long as the facts told lead somewhere the whole would not.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: False Reports
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Filing complaints or accusations with an employer, school, agency or police that contain claims the filer knows are untrue, so the target must answer for something that never happened.
codex_completed.short_definition: Filing complaints or accusations with an employer, school, agency or police that contain claims the filer knows are untrue, so the target must answer for something that never happened.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A false report is a formal complaint whose central facts did not happen: an invented incident, a made-up date, an act the target could not have done. It goes to a body with power, such as a manager, a school, a licensing board, a child-protection agency or the police, which must respond. Mistaken reports and honestly disputed ones are different, and a report that cannot be proved is not necessarily false. What marks the pattern is a report contradicted by independent records, sometimes repeated to more than one body.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone makes a formal complaint about you to an authority about something that did not happen, and you have to defend yourself before anyone finds out whether it is true.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A fabricated complaint puts a real job, license or family arrangement in jeopardy, and the person has to answer for something that did not happen before anyone establishes whether it did.
what_it_is: A formal complaint, accusation or document sent to an authority whose core facts are untrue.
Recipients include employers, schools, landlords, licensing bodies, child-protection services and police.
Different from a real grievance badly reported: here the event itself is missing.
Its force comes from process. Institutions must respond to reports, and the response can carry consequences before any finding is made.
It can be a single report or a series sent to different bodies.
what_it_sounds_like: A letter from HR describing a meeting you can show you did not attend.
A welfare check or investigation notice triggered by a claim you can disprove.
A complaint that names a date when you were provably elsewhere.
Details in the report that match an argument you had, but nothing that actually happened.
Several agencies receiving similar reports from the same source within weeks.
what_it_is_not: A genuine report that characterises events in a way the subject disputes still reflects the reporter's honest perception. Institutions also make their own errors in processing legitimate reports.
Two people who disagree factually about what happened, where neither is inventing anything.
A report made in good faith and found unsubstantiated. Unproven is not the same as false.
A mandated reporter, such as a teacher or nurse, passing on a concern as their role requires.
A true complaint that is also embarrassing or inconvenient for the person it concerns.
this_may_be_it_when: Independent records, video, logs or witnesses contradict the central event.
The report cites something that could not have happened as described.
The complaint follows a dispute, breakup or refusal and was never mentioned before it.
The same source files similar reports with more than one body.
Details change between the first report and later retellings.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Records show something did happen, though not as the complainant described it.
The complainant's account matches an independent witness.
It is a good-faith concern from someone obliged to report.
The differences come down to interpretation: tone, meaning, what someone intended.
The report was withdrawn with an honest correction such as 'I misunderstood'.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Details misremembered in an otherwise honest complaint.
A misunderstanding of what was seen or heard, such as a child's remark misread.
An institutional error like the wrong name or the wrong file.
Information distorted as it passed from person to person before it was reported.
common_false_positives: A school inquiry that follows a mandated reporter's concern and finds nothing.
A poor performance review you believe unfair but that is based on real events.
A neighbor's noise complaint that overstates a real party.
A report dismissed for lack of evidence.
discernment_questions: What independent records exist, and what do they show?
Is the central event missing, or is it a real event described in a way I dispute?
Has the institution told me exactly what I am accused of, so I can answer it?
Who could confirm where I was and what I did?
Do I actually know who filed it, or am I assuming?
less_concerning_if: The institution is clear and fair, and lets you respond with evidence.
The report mentions real events that were read differently.
The person who filed it corrects or withdraws it.
more_concerning_if: A consequence lands before anyone has told you what the accusation actually says.
Records contradict the report, yet the process continues or repeats.
The consequences reach custody, employment, housing or immigration status.
pattern_over_time_signs: A second and third report follows soon after the first is closed.
You have begun documenting your whereabouts with timestamped photos, just in case.
You avoid ordinary things, like a child handover or a one-to-one meeting, for fear of another report.
Managers, relatives or neighbors are approached and asked about you.
codex_completed.repair_check: A written withdrawal or correction, sent to the same body that received the report, plus a plain acknowledgement to you that the claim was not true, is what repair would involve. Saying 'I only wanted someone to listen' while the file stays open leaves the consequences where they were.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: What matters is whether the reports stop and whether anything is corrected on the record. Words said to you in private, such as 'I'm sorry it went that far', count for little if the institution has not been told. Notice which bodies have heard the correction.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Institutions are built to take reports seriously and to act while the facts are unknown, which is sensible but can cause harm if the report is invented. Being accused by a body with power can produce fear, shame and urgency to defend oneself before anything is checked. People around you may keep a lingering doubt even after a clearing.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe shock at being formally accused, sleeplessness, and a sense of being watched by the process. Some face suspension, interviews or temporary limits on contact with children while a report is looked at. Even after being cleared, many describe lasting caution about being alone with others or doing ordinary things.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the body for specifics: 'Could you tell me what I am accused of, with dates, so I can respond accurately?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Answer in writing and stay with verifiable facts, leaving the complainant's motives out of it: 'Here are the records for those dates.'
response_options.disengagement: Keep contact with whoever filed to a minimum and in writing, through a lawyer or mediator if one is involved. Don't confront them privately about the report.
response_options.support_seeking: Contact a lawyer or legal aid early, before any interview, and bring documents showing where you were. A union representative or a parents' or tenants' rights group can also help.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask HR for the written allegation and the process, bring a representative or colleague to meetings, and supply dated records or witnesses.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I take this seriously and I want to respond properly. Please send me the allegation in writing, with dates, and I'll provide records for each of them. I'd like a representative with me at any meeting."
codex_completed.safety_note: A false report can threaten work, a license, housing or time with your children, and the person who made it may be someone you share a home or children with. Don't confront them about it. Save every notice, get legal advice before any interview, and if you fear for your safety, tell your lawyer or a domestic abuse advocate what else has happened.
misuse_warning: Calling a complaint false because it was not upheld can silence real reporters. Unproven is not untrue, and many genuine reports cannot be proved.
Telling someone who raised a concern that they filed a 'false report' can itself be a way of punishing them for speaking up.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Lying is a false statement made to a person; a false report puts it into a formal file where an institution must act. Fabricated Evidence manufactures proof, such as a forged message, while a false report can rest on words alone, though the two can be combined. Vague Allegations stays unspecific so nothing can be checked, whereas a false report is usually specific enough for records to contradict it.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Paper-Trail Traps
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Creating or shaping written records, such as write-ups, emails and notes, that build a one-sided case against someone who does not know it is being assembled.
codex_completed.short_definition: Creating or shaping written records, such as write-ups, emails and notes, that build a one-sided case against someone who does not know it is being assembled.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: A paper-trail trap is a record that gathers quietly: emails that restate a conversation in a slanted way, notes about 'concerns' never raised with the person, write-ups that leave out context. Each item may look minor. Together they can read like a long history when finally shown, at a review, a hearing or a custody dispute. Ordinary record-keeping is common and fair, so one memo says little. Concern rises when documentation concentrates on one person, is kept from them, and differs from what happened.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Someone quietly collects written 'evidence' against you that you never saw or got to answer, and it all appears at once when it counts.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: A record accumulates that the person has no opportunity to answer as it is built, and by the time they see it, it reads as damning.
what_it_is: Emails, notes or formal write-ups that frame events one way and leave out the other side.
'Confirming' emails sent after a conversation that restate it in a slanted form, so that silence reads as agreement.
Documentation concentrated on one person while others doing the same things go unrecorded.
Built out of sight, so the first time the person hears of the 'history' is when it is used.
Found at work, in schools and care settings, in tenancy disputes, and in family and custody conflicts.
what_it_sounds_like: Just to confirm what we discussed... followed by a version you do not recognize.
A review that cites 'several previous concerns' no one raised with you.
An email thread about problems with your work that copied you in late, or not at all.
It's all documented, in reply to a question about a concern you have never heard.
A file containing small events from months ago, such as a late arrival or a tone of voice.
A folder of screenshots shown at a meeting, picked to show one side of a long exchange.
what_it_is_not: Standard documentation applied to everyone is not targeting. A genuine record of concerns that were actually raised with the person is legitimate even if they wish it did not exist.
Someone keeping notes on their own experience for their own reference.
Meeting minutes circulated to all attendees with a chance to correct them.
Records required by law or policy in regulated settings such as care or finance.
A manager who writes an informal summary to help them remember, and shares it when asked.
this_may_be_it_when: You learn of written concerns for the first time at a formal meeting.
The record names you but not others who did the same thing.
Events in write-ups are described in ways that conflict with emails or timestamps.
You were not given the chance to respond or correct at the time.
Your replies to 'confirming' emails are ignored and the original stays as the version on file.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Each item was shared with you at the time, and your replies are in the file.
Other people have similar records kept on them.
The record matches what you remember, even if you dislike seeing it.
There is an agreed process, such as warning letters that follow a stated policy.
Corrections you asked for were added.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Busy managers write notes late and from memory, so details go wrong honestly.
Organizations often document everything to protect themselves legally, which feels personal but is routine.
People confirm conversations by email to avoid misunderstanding, and nothing more.
Different people hold honestly different memories of the same meeting.
common_false_positives: A performance improvement plan that follows several conversations you really had.
A landlord's inspection records that apply to every tenant.
A teacher's incident log kept for every child in a class.
Your own notes of a difficult month.
discernment_questions: Have I seen what is in the file, and can I ask for a copy?
Was each item raised with me when it happened?
Is anyone else's behavior recorded as carefully as mine?
Does the record match emails, timestamps and other witnesses?
Was I able to add my own account at the time?
less_concerning_if: You were told each time and your answers are attached.
The same practice applies to everyone.
A copy is provided on request without delay.
more_concerning_if: A hearing, review or dismissal is being prepared and you are not told what is in the file.
Records are refused to you, or appear only at the point of a decision.
The file will be used where much is at stake: a job, custody, a tenancy or immigration status.
pattern_over_time_signs: 'Confirming' emails arrive after each conversation, and the version differs from yours.
Small matters get recorded that were never mentioned face to face.
You have begun keeping your own record in self-defense and checking every conversation.
People around you are asked to provide statements about you.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair means the file is opened to you: a copy of everything held, a chance to add your reply to each item, and removal of entries shown to be wrong. A promise to stop writing things down while the existing record stays unchanged leaves its effects in place.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: After you reply in writing to correct a record, check where your correction ended up. If it sits beside the original in the file and gets mentioned, it was respected. If the original is the only version ever quoted, your correction was filed away unread.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: Written records carry authority: a paper account often outweighs a spoken one, and later readers frequently see only the file. Repetition across many items can make a pattern look established even when each is thin. Because the person is not told, they have no moment to dispute the framing, and a late reply can seem defensive.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: First sight of the file often brings a sinking shock, then a feeling of being watched and measured. Some begin writing everything down, rehearsing conversations and avoiding one-to-one meetings. Others find that colleagues or relatives who read the record already hold a view of them.

response_options.soft_clarification: Reply in writing to any 'confirming' email within a day with your own account: 'Thanks for the summary. Here is what I recall being agreed.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask for the record directly: 'I would like a copy of everything in my file, and I would like my response added to it.'
response_options.disengagement: Move conversations about disputed matters into writing or into a room with a witness, and keep each exchange short and factual.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk early to a union representative, employment adviser, tenants' organization or family lawyer, depending on the setting, and bring copies of what you hold.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, request your personnel file in writing where policy or law allows, and keep dated notes of your own, following your employer's rules on company data.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "Please give me a copy of anything written about me, and add my responses to the file. And when there is a concern, tell me when it happens so I can answer it at the time."
codex_completed.safety_note: This tactic matters most when the record may be used in decisions about your job, tenancy, immigration status or time with your children. Signs of high stakes are meetings called without notice, requests to sign things you haven't read, and being told 'it's all documented'. Sign nothing unread. Keep your own dated notes somewhere the other person cannot reach, and see a lawyer or union representative before any formal meeting.
misuse_warning: Keeping your own notes is not a paper-trail trap, and calling honest record-keeping a trap can excuse behavior that really was a problem.
Believing every unwelcome review is a plot can stop a person from seeing feedback that is accurate.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Fabricated Evidence invents a single item, such as a doctored screenshot; a paper-trail trap may include no forged item at all, only slanted wording and omissions that accumulate. Lying by Omission shapes one account by what it leaves out, while here the omissions are spread across many documents. Vague Allegations has nothing on paper to examine; here there is plenty, and the problem is what it adds up to.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Compartmentalization
codex_completed.detectability_note: This tool cannot establish this from pasted text at all. It is included for literacy only, so you can learn to recognize the concept — not as something this tool detects, scores, or flags.
codex_completed.core_meaning: Keeping information in separate pockets, with different people knowing different parts, so that nobody can see enough to notice a problem or ask the right question.
codex_completed.short_definition: Keeping information in separate pockets, with different people knowing different parts, so that nobody can see enough to notice a problem or ask the right question.
codex_completed.expanded_definition: In compartmentalization, each person is told something true, but only their own slice. One relative hears about the money, another about the move, a third about the health scare, and nobody has the three together. Questions that would link the slices are discouraged or redirected. Most families and workplaces have private matters and need-to-know rules, so a gap in who knows what says little. Concern rises when the slicing is consistent, follows what would raise questions if joined, and comparing notes is met with displeasure.
codex_completed.plain_language_summary: Everyone in the family or team is told a different piece, so no one can see the whole story or notice that something doesn't add up.
codex_completed.why_this_matters: No single person can see enough to raise a question, so accountability fails not because anyone refused it but because nobody had the view required to ask for it.
what_it_is: Information sorted into slices by listener: each person gets a true but partial version.
Seen in families (money, health, the past), workplaces (budgets, decisions) and groups (what leaders know).
It can work without a single false statement, because the structure of who knows what does the work.
Linking is what undoes it: the picture appears when two people compare notes.
One person usually holds the whole map, or is the only link between the pockets.
what_it_sounds_like: Don't mention this to your brother, he'd only worry.
That's between you and me.
You don't need to talk to finance about that, I'll sort it.
I've told Mom the dates and Dad the cost, there's no need for them to compare.
Why are you asking her? I said I'd handle it.
Please don't discuss this with the other team.
what_it_is_not: Confidentiality and need-to-know structures exist for good reasons in most organizations, and information silos form naturally in any large family or workplace. Someone who simply did not think to pass something on has partitioned nothing.
A surprise being planned, where the planner is open about keeping it.
Medical or client privacy that is stated and fits the situation.
Keeping your own private matters from some relatives.
Role-based access required by law, such as patient records.
this_may_be_it_when: When two people compare what they were told, the accounts differ in ways that matter.
The same person is the only route between the groups.
Requests for secrecy are steady and sit around the matters that would draw questions.
Asking 'who else knows?' gets evasion.
Someone who asked across groups was told to leave it.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The reason for separation is stated and fits, such as the privacy of a medical matter or a client.
The person encourages you to share and compare what you know.
Information flows when you ask for it.
The separation follows role, like payroll versus marketing, and applies equally to everyone.
Nothing important differs between accounts when you compare them.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People tell the most relevant details to those most affected without thinking of the others.
Privacy norms: not every relative needs every health detail.
Sparing a sick or elderly person upsetting news.
Large organizations split into silos without anyone planning it.
common_false_positives: An estate lawyer speaking separately with each heir for legal reasons.
A manager telling each team only what it needs for its own project.
A parent sparing young children adult worries.
A friend group where news simply travels unevenly.
discernment_questions: If I put what each person has been told side by side, do the accounts agree?
Who is the only one who knows all of it?
What happens when someone asks a question that crosses between groups?
Who is protected by this being kept apart, and has that been said?
Could I check any part of this with someone else without a penalty?
less_concerning_if: A reason is offered and you can check it.
You are openly encouraged to speak to anyone.
The accounts agree when you compare them side by side.
more_concerning_if: Comparing notes brings anger or hurt, or you are told you are stirring things up.
Decisions about money, care or housing rest on pieces that no one else can verify.
The person holding the map controls access to resources or to someone vulnerable.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find out something major through a third person by chance.
The sentence 'don't tell' recurs, with a different person named each time.
Each person describes the situation differently, and each thinks they alone know.
At a crisis the accounts converge and many people say 'I didn't know that'.
codex_completed.repair_check: Repair would show up as a gathering of the separate pieces: everyone affected hears the same account, in the same room or the same message, and questions that cross groups are welcomed. A private apology to each person, one at a time, re-creates the same arrangement.
codex_completed.boundary_respect_check: Notice the response to a simple question: 'Who else has been told this?' A direct answer, even a partial one, honors the question. A change of subject, or irritation that you asked, does not.
codex_completed.psychological_mechanism: People judge what is normal from what they are told, and when each person's slice looks reasonable alone, nothing seems to need explaining. Doubts that would arise on seeing the whole can stay below the threshold of speaking up. Each person may also assume others know more, so they hesitate to ask, which keeps the separation going without anyone being told to stay quiet.
codex_completed.possible_impact_on_receiver: A jolt comes on discovering that others were told something different, then questions about what else was kept apart. Some feel angry at relatives or colleagues drawn into the arrangement; some lose trust in group conversations. The shared sense of everyone knowing can fall away, and with it some relationships.

response_options.soft_clarification: Invite the pieces together without blame: 'I was told about the loan, and I think you were told about the move. Can we put what we know side by side?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to carry secrets between people: 'I'll keep your privacy, but I won't hold back information about shared money or care from the people it affects.'
response_options.disengagement: Decline to be the keeper of the secret. Tell the person asking that you would rather not be told anything you would be asked to hide from someone it concerns.
response_options.support_seeking: Compare notes quietly with the other people affected, such as a sibling, a colleague or a friend, and write down what each was told and when.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask who owns each decision and request one shared summary of budget or status that all affected teams can see. Raise gaps with a manager or a compliance contact.

codex_completed.boundary_script: "I'm glad to keep your private things private. I'm not comfortable keeping something from my brother when it affects his money. Can the three of us talk about it together?"
codex_completed.safety_note: Separate pockets of information are most worrying when the person holding the map also controls money, care or housing for someone who depends on them, such as an older parent or a partner without their own accounts. Then the gaps can hide real harm. Gather the facts from others involved, ask the bank, doctor or care manager what you are entitled to see, and contact an adult-protection or elder-care service if someone's welfare is at risk.
misuse_warning: Treating every confidence as compartmentalization punishes ordinary privacy, such as someone's diagnosis or a surprise being planned.
Using the label to demand that one person reveal another's private matters.
codex_completed.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Lying by Omission is about what one person leaves out of an account for one listener; compartmentalization is about how pieces are divided across many listeners so they cannot be joined. Strategic Incompleteness feeds one person pieces so they keep returning, whereas here no one needs to return and the cost falls on the group's oversight. Vague Allegations hints at the whole with no detail, while each pocket here holds specific, true detail.
codex_completed.detection_notes: Not matched or scored by this tool. Pasted text cannot establish this concept — included in the Field Guide purely as a literacy reference.

codex_completed.name: Thought Control
